# Artificial intelligence

## Page contents

**Artificial intelligence (AI)** is key to leveraging large volumes of regulatory and health data as well as new tools. This will encourage research and innovation. It will also support **regulatory decision-making** for safe, effective and high-quality medicines that reach patients faster.

This approach is in line with the European medicines regulatory network's plans on how to make use of AI.

It is also documented in the [Network Data Steering Group](/en/about-us/how-we-work/data-regulation-big-data-other-sources/network-data-steering-group-ndsg "Network Data Steering Group (NDSG)")'s workplan for 2025-2028.

The workplan identifies actions in four key AI-related areas:

This workplan integrates and expands on the AI workplan set up by the former Big Data Steering Group. This document is available in the 'Related documents' section on this page.

For more information, see:

## AI in medicinal product lifecycle reflection paper

A **reflection paper** on the use of artificial intelligence (AI) in the medicinal product lifecycle is available:

It includes considerations to help medicine developers and marketing authorisation applicants use **AI** and **machine learning** in a safe and effective way at the different stages of a medicine lifecycle.

This paper reflects EMA's current experience in the evolving field of AI.

Medicine developers and applicants should understand the paper's considerations in the context of EU legal requirements and principles on AI, data protection, and medicines regulation.

The [Methodology Working party](/en/committees/working-parties-other-groups/chmp/methodology-working-party "Methodology Working Party") developed the paper with support from the former Big Data Steering Group.

The Committee for Human Medicinal Products (CHMP) and the Committee for Veterinary Medicinal Products (CVMP) both adopted the paper in September 2024.

## Large language model guiding principles

Guiding principles are available for European medicines regulatory network staff on how to use **large language models** in their work.

This document aims to promote the safe, responsible and effective use of this category of **artificial intelligence** (AI) technology.

Large language models focus on **text generation**.

They can help staff at medicine regulators across the EU in areas such as processing extensive documentation, automating data mining and optimising routine administrative tasks.

They also present challenges such as providing irrelevant or inaccurate responses and posing potential data security risks.

The overarching purpose of these guiding principles is to convey both capabilities and limitations of large language models.

### Guiding principles

The document covers the following principles and recommendations on the use of large language models:

EMA and the Heads of Medicines Agency (HMA) published the first version of this document on September 2024. It is regularly updated.

![Multi-annual artificial intelligence workplan](/sites/default/files/styles/oe_bootstrap_theme_medium_no_crop/public/2023-12/2023-12-AI%20workplan_WEB_square.png?itok=XE0ehsEO)
![LLMs factsheet](https://www.ema.europa.eu/sites/default/files/2024-09/2024-09_LLMs%20factsheet-2-_WEB_square_en.png)

### [Factsheet: Four principles for safe and responsible use of large language models](https://www.ema.europa.eu/en/documents/other/factsheet-four-principles-safe-responsible-use-large-language-models_en.pdf)

## AI Observatory reports

**AI observatory reports** support the [Network Data Steering Group (NDSG)](/en/about-us/how-we-work/data-regulation-big-data-other-sources/network-data-steering-group-ndsg "Network Data Steering Group (NDSG)") to monitor AI activities and trends.

They also help the European medicines regulatory network build **knowledge** and prepare for future **regulatory needs**.

EMA and the Heads of Medicines Agencies (HMA) publish AI observatory reports every year.

The 2025 AI observatory report provides an overview of activities and trends focused on four broad areas:

EMA and HMA published the **2025 AI observatory report** in June 2026.

AI observatory reports cover both human and veterinary medicines.

They inform the implementation of the NDSG workplan for 2026-2028 and the [European medicines agencies network strategy (EMANS)](/en/about-us/how-we-work/european-medicines-regulatory-network/european-medicines-agencies-network-strategy "European medicines agencies network strategy (EMANS)") to 2028.

2025 AI Observatory report

Select the expandable panel below for information about the 2024 AI observatory report:

### AI Observatory report and horizon scanning for 2024

The first annual report of the European medicines regulatory network's **AI Observatory** is available, including the results of a horizon scanning.

The report compiles the Network's experience with **artificial intelligence** (AI) during 2024 in:

In addition to the report, two other related documents are also available:

The horizon scanning report was based on the review of scientific literature and EU-funded projects. It helps identifying gaps, challenges and opportunities for integrating AI in medicine regulation.

The observatory captures and shares experiences and trends in AI to inform the work of the Network Data Steering Group. It ultimately supports the implementation of the group's multi-annual AI workplan.

2024 AI Observatory report

## AI tools and technology

EMA extended the functionality of its **AI**-enabled **knowledge mining** tool Scientific Explorer to support EMA and national competent authorities (NCAs) in finding information related to initial marketing authorisation applications of human medicines.

This includes public assessment reports.

The extended search functionality is available as of March 2026.

### Efficient search for regulatory scientific information

The tool enables easy, focused and precise **search** of **regulatory scientific information** from European medicines regulatory network sources.

EMA and NCA assessors are able to use the tool to customise their search for related information based on medicine name, disease or relevant keywords.

This supports decision-making via efficient retrieval of regulatory precedents.

EMA introduced the tool in March 2024, initially focusing on improving searches for EMA **scientific advice procedures** for human and veterinary medicines.

### Who can access Scientific Explorer

The tool is available only to approved and authenticated users representing the European medicines regulatory network.

### Frequently asked questions

For more information, see the document below with answers to frequently asked questions about this tool:

Scientific Explorer - Frequently Asked Questions

English (EN) (178.61 KB - PDF)

## First qualification opinion on AI methodology

EMA’s human medicines committee (CHMP) accepts clinical trial evidence generated by an **artificial intelligence** (AI) tool supervised by a human pathologist.

This is the first time EMA will consider data generated with the assistance of an AI-based tool to be scientifically valid.

This tool helps pathologists analyse liver biopsy scans to determine the severity of metabolic dysfunction associated steatohepatitis (MASH). This was formerly known as non-alcoholic steatohepatitis (NASH). The previous denomination gives the tool its name: AIM-NASH.

It helps researchers obtain clearer evidence on the benefits of **treatments** in **clinical trials** with fewer patients.

EMA reached this milestone after its human medicines committee (CHMP) issued a qualification opinion on this AI-based innovative development methodology, in March 2025.

The qualification opinion was available for public consultation between December 2024 and January 2025.

Qualification opinion for artificial intelligence-based measurement of non-alcoholic steatohepatitis histology in liver biopsies to determine disease activity in NASH/MASH clinical trials

English (EN) (213.84 KB - PDF)

## Principles for AI in medicine development

EMA and the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) have jointly identified ten principles for good **artificial intelligence (AI)** practice in the **medicines** lifecycle.

The principles will guide AI use in evidence generation and monitoring across all phases of a medicine, from early research and clinical trials to manufacturing and safety monitoring.

They apply to both human and veterinary medicines.

Guiding principles of good AI practice in drug development

This is the European Medicines Agency (EMA) webpage on Artificial Intelligence (AI), detailing the agency's strategy and activities for integrating AI into medicine regulation. Key content includes:

**AI Workplan & Strategy:**
- AI is key to leveraging regulatory and health data, supporting regulatory decision-making, and getting medicines to patients faster.
- Documented in the Network Data Steering Group (NDSG) workplan for 2025-2028, which identifies actions in four key AI-related areas and expands on the earlier Big Data Steering Group's AI workplan.

**Reflection Paper on AI in the Medicinal Product Lifecycle:**
- A reflection paper on AI and machine learning use across medicine lifecycles is available, helping medicine developers use AI safely and effectively.
- Developed by the Methodology Working Party, adopted by CHMP and CVMP in September 2024.

**Large Language Model (LLM) Guiding Principles:**
- Published September 2024 by EMA and the Heads of Medicines Agency (HMA), these principles guide European regulatory network staff on safe, responsible use of LLMs for tasks like processing documentation, data mining, and administrative tasks.
- Addresses challenges including inaccurate responses and data security risks.
- A factsheet on "Four principles for safe and responsible use of large language models" is available.

**AI Observatory Reports:**
- EMA and HMA publish annual AI observatory reports to monitor AI trends and prepare for regulatory needs, covering human and veterinary medicines.
- The 2025 AI observatory report was published in June 2026, covering four broad areas and informing the NDSG workplan 2026-2028.
- The 2024 report includes horizon scanning based on scientific literature and EU-funded projects, compiling 2024 AI experience.

**AI Tools & Technology (Scientific Explorer):**
- EMA extended its AI-enabled knowledge mining tool, Scientific Explorer, to help EMA and national competent authorities (NCAs) search initial marketing authorisation applications (including public assessment reports) as of March 2026.
- Originally introduced March 2024 for scientific advice procedures. Available only to approved European medicines regulatory network users.

**First Qualification Opinion on AI Methodology (AIM-NASH):**
- In March 2025, EMA's CHMP issued its first qualification opinion considering clinical trial evidence generated by an AI tool (AIM-NASH) as scientifically valid.
- The tool helps pathologists analyze liver biopsy scans to determine severity of metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis (MASH, formerly NASH), helping obtain clearer evidence with fewer patients.
- Public consultation ran December 2024–January 2025.

**Joint EMA-FDA Principles:**
- EMA and the U.S. FDA jointly identified ten principles for good AI practice in the medicines lifecycle, covering evidence generation and monitoring from research through manufacturing and safety monitoring, applying to human and veterinary medicines.
- Guiding principles document available (567.21 KB PDF).

**Timeline Highlights:**
- Scientific Explorer introduced: March 2024; extended functionality: March 2026.
- LLM guiding principles published: September 2024.
- Reflection paper adopted: September 2024.
- AIM-NASH qualification opinion: March 2025.
- 2025 AI observatory report published: June 2026.

## European position paper on AI in medicinal product lifecycle

###### Home/Guidelines | Posted 20/06/2025 post-comment0 [Post your comment](#postComment)

At the end of 2024, the European Medicine’s agency (EMA) published a reflection paper on ‘The use of Artificial Intelligence (AI) in the medicinal product lifecycle,’ [1]. This was based on the draft guidance issued in 2023 [2].

![AI Project V25B25](/var/gabi/storage/images/media/images/ai-project-v25b25/168663-1-eng-GB/ai-project-v25b25_large.jpg "AI Project V25B25")

In the final guidance, the EMA uses the definition of AI systems developed by the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD), which states that an AI system is “a machine-based system designed to operate with varying levels of autonomy and that may exhibit adaptiveness after deployment and that, for explicit or implicit objectives, infers, from the input it receives, how to generate outputs such as predictions, content, recommendations, or decisions that can influence physical or virtual environments”[1].

In the guidance, the EMA emphasizes a risk-based and human-centered approach to the use of AI across all stages of the medicinal product lifecycle, from drug discovery to post-authorization activities.

**1. Risk-Based and Human-Centered Regulation**

* EMA expects AI regulation to be grounded in continuous risk assessment, with safeguards tailored to the AI’s autonomy level and the specific use case.
* Higher-risk applications (e.g., precision medicine) require more robust controls than lower-risk uses (e.g., early-stage data analysis).
  + This is given in a two-pronged approach, focusing on patient safety and impact on regulatory decisions. For example, the categories *‘high patient risk’* and *‘high regulatory impact’*, are included to prevent confusion with the definition of high-risk AI under the EU AI Act.
* A human-centric approach is essential, especially during data collection and modelling, addressing concerns such as algorithmic bias and the use of non-transparent (black box) models.

**2. Guidance Highlights**

* The guidance provides lifecycle-based risk mitigation strategies, addressing technical elements like data quality, model training/testing, explainability, and governance.
* EMA aligns AI practices with existing frameworks (e.g., GxP, ICH Q8/Q9/Q10) while promoting traceability and compliance.
* While transparency in AI is key, in some low-risk circumstances black-box models may be acceptable if transparent ones underperform.
* Emphasis that the market authorisation applicant, marketing authorisation holder and the (named) clinical trial sponsor and manufacturer are responsible parties. At all stages of development and marketing these stakeholders can make use of AI and their responsibilities are underlined.

In terms of outlook, the EMA currently positions itself as regulatory yet innovation-friendly, differentiating from more conservative data protection regulators. The EMA emphasizes the need for a balanced collaborative approach prioritizing patient safety and regulatory integrity while facilitating the transformative potential of AI. It is key to note that the reflection paper considers the AI Act [3] during finalization to ensure that the EMA’s approach aligns with the broader regulatory framework governing AI.

The US Food and Drug Administration issued draft guidance on the use of AI in pharmaceutical regulation in January 2025 [4].

This webpage from GaBI Online (Generics and Biosimilars Initiative) presents a European position paper on the use of Artificial Intelligence (AI) in the medicinal product lifecycle. At the end of 2024, the European Medicines Agency (EMA) published a final reflection paper on 'The use of Artificial Intelligence (AI) in the medicinal product lifecycle,' based on draft guidance issued in 2023.

Key points of the EMA guidance include:
- The EMA adopts the OECD definition of AI systems: "a machine-based system designed to operate with varying levels of autonomy and that may exhibit adaptiveness after deployment and that, for explicit or implicit objectives, infers, from the input it receives, how to generate outputs such as predictions, content, recommendations, or decisions that can influence physical or virtual environments."
- The EMA emphasizes a risk-based and human-centered approach to AI use across all stages of the medicinal product lifecycle, from drug discovery to post-authorization activities.
- AI regulation should be grounded in continuous risk assessment with safeguards tailored to the AI's autonomy level and specific use case. Higher-risk applications (e.g., precision medicine) require more robust controls than lower-risk uses (e.g., early-stage data analysis). This is given in a two-pronged approach focusing on patient safety and regulatory impact, including categories like 'high patient risk' and 'high regulatory impact' to prevent confusion with the EU AI Act's definition of high-risk AI.
- A human-centric approach is essential, especially during data collection and modelling, addressing concerns such as algorithmic bias and non-transparent (black box) models.
- The guidance provides lifecycle-based risk mitigation strategies covering data quality, model training/testing, explainability, and governance, while aligning with existing frameworks (GxP, ICH Q8/Q9/Q10).
- While transparency in AI is key, in some low-risk circumstances black-box models may be acceptable if transparent ones underperform.
- The market authorisation applicant, marketing authorisation holder, and named clinical trial sponsor and manufacturer are identified as responsible parties.

The EMA positions itself as regulatory yet innovation-friendly, emphasizing a balanced collaborative approach prioritizing patient safety and regulatory integrity. The reflection paper considered the EU AI Act during finalization to align with the broader regulatory framework. The US FDA issued its own draft guidance on AI use in pharmaceutical regulation in January 2025.

11 June 2026

by Nick Paul Taylor

# Euro Roundup: EMA researchers share regulatory research priorities for AI across the lifecycle

![euro-roundup-300x250-2022.png](https://www.raps.org/static/7caaaf4a-914a-4d34-be74a7b97b6d23ff/1e6c05ee-e1bd-43b0-8e1b8a67d9a9488a/440x248_highestperformance__4a7c7e45a350/euro-roundup-300x250-2022.jpg)

Researchers from the European Medicines Agency (EMA) have published a paper on regulatory research priorities for AI across the medicine lifecycle.

Published as a preprint, the paper features the findings of a survey of 273 people, including regulators, pharmaceutical industry professionals, patients, academics, and healthcare professionals. EMA and its collaborators ran the survey to understand priority research areas for AI, from product development to post-authorization monitoring and evaluation.

“Accuracy and reliability of AI tools” was the highest priority across all groups “by a substantial margin,” the researchers said. Respondents were most concerned with how AI-generated outputs can be trusted when they inform evidence generation and regulatory decisions. “Data governance, confidentiality, and consent” and “ethics, fairness, and bias prevention” were the next highest priorities.

Based on the findings, the researchers drafted 10 priority research areas. The top three areas all relate to accuracy and reliability, with the researchers wanting to understand how AI systems can remain robust in the face of changing data and when it is important for models to be explainable.

The researchers published the paper one day after EMA released its 2025 AI Observatory report. EMA used the report to provide an overview of AI guidance and policy, applications, collaborations, and engagement activities. The report includes a list of AI uses EMA has discussed with applicants, such as the use of generative AI to draft regulatory submissions or to generate answers to queries.

EMA shared the preprint paper and AI Observatory report as part of the agenda for a meeting scheduled for next week. The one-hour session will cover topics such as approaches for generating evidence on methodologies that enable safe and reliable AI integration. EMA included the session in a regulatory science research meeting that will also cover topics such as new approach methodologies.

[EMA Paper](https://zenodo.org/records/20554817), [Observatory Report](https://www.ema.europa.eu/system/files/documents/report/2025-ai-observatory-report_en.pdf), [Draft Agenda](https://www.ema.europa.eu/system/files/documents/agenda/2026-06-16-draft-agenda-meeting-european-platform-en.pdf)

##### European Commission posts first joint clinical assessment report under HTAR

The European Commission has published a joint clinical assessment (JCA) report on tovorafenib, marking a key milestone in the implementation of the Health Technology Assessment Regulation (HTAR).

Under HTAR, European Union nations jointly evaluate the clinical benefits of new medicines and certain medical devices. The collaboration is intended to reduce duplication, save time, and give companies a clearer and more predictable process. EU Member States will use JCA reports to inform their decisions on which products to make available to patients.

Having started 18 JCAs since HTAR took effect in January 2025, Member States have now completed the first report. The document covers tovorafenib, Ipsen Pharma’s treatment for the most common type of pediatric brain tumor. The Commission granted a one-year conditional marketing authorization to the kinase inhibitor on 20 April.

The JCA report is a 154-page document that describes the medical condition and drug product, assesses the evidence on the treatment, and includes appendices about the joint clinical assessment process. The Member State Coordination Group on Health Technology Assessment also provided a 20-page summary of the report.

The report focuses on the evidence in three populations, namely the full claimed indication and two subsets of patients with a BRAF mutation. Within each population, the assessors reviewed different interventions, comparators, and health outcomes, referred to by the acronym PICO.

Ipsen provided evidence for two of the eight PICOs and argued that it was unable to address four PICOs because of a lack of data on the specified comparators in the target population. The company tried to create external control arms for the four PICOs without relevant data but was unable to find a suitable source.

The assessors found the information insufficient to support assessment of one of the PICOs for which Ipsen submitted results, limiting the report to one of the eight scenarios. For the one PICO with evidence to inform the analysis, the assessors found “major, general uncertainties” relating to evidence synthesis methods, the small sample size, and the differences between the study populations.

[Press Release](https://health.ec.europa.eu/document/download/b853b3f5-39d1-4aa3-8787-b1125d0d06d1_en?filename=hta_20260609_news-first-jca-report_en.pdf), [JCA Report](https://health.ec.europa.eu/publications/joint-clinical-assessment-report-tovorafenib-ojemda_en)

##### MHRA’s AI sandbox project reveals need for new and updated UK guidance

The UK Medicines and Healthcare products Regulatory Agency (MHRA) has named areas where guidance needs creating or updating to address issues identified in its AI Airlock program.

Having finished the second phase of the program, MHRA noted a need for guidance on predetermined change control plans (PCCPs). The guidance should provide “principles-based clarity on the limits of changes that could be included in a PCCP,” MHRA said. Managing iterative updates to AI systems safely and proportionately across the device lifecycle using PCCPs was a focus in phase two of the program.

Guidance on performance metrics for AI-powered in vitro diagnostics (IVDs) is needed too, MHRA said. The planned guidance will include examples and practical approaches and address “the circumstances in which additional metrics add value, and how analytical performance concepts can be adapted for AI systems,” MHRA said.

The agency also proposed updating its software qualification and intended purpose guidance. MHRA wants the “foundational pieces of guidance to clearly address the changing device landscape, including AI-specific considerations and adaptive systems.”

MHRA published the recommendations alongside new simulation workshop [reports](https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/ai-airlock-simulation-workshops) on IVDs, PCCPs, and the scope of intended purpose. The agency also [shared](https://www.gov.uk/government/news/pioneering-ai-health-innovations-regulatory-sandbox-launched) details of a secure sandbox for testing AI-enabled devices in the London healthcare service.

[MHRA Report](https://assets.publishing.service.gov.uk/media/6a27ece1e371d9d2c0052aca/AI_Airlock_Phase_2_Programme_Report.pdf)

##### EMA finalizes external control paper, staying on course for consultation in Q4

EMA has finalized its concept paper on using external controls for evidence generation in regulatory decisions.

The agency ran a consultation on a draft version of the paper last year to gather views on its plans to create a reflection paper. EMA argued a reflection paper is needed to address the rise in proposals to use external controls to support regulatory decisions. The trend created a need for general principles for assessing when external controls are appropriate, EMA said.

EMA’s final concept paper features tweaks to the draft released for consultation. The agency expanded the problem statement, adding that terms such as synthetic data and digital twins need clarifying, and noting issues with the replication and reproducibility of results.

Maintaining the timeline established in the draft, EMA’s Committee for Medicinal Products for Human Use aims to discuss the draft reflection paper in the fourth quarter and hold a three-month consultation. EMA plans to finalize and adopt the reflection paper by the second quarter of next year.

[Concept Paper](https://www.ema.europa.eu/en/documents/scientific-guideline/concept-paper-development-reflection-paper-use-external-controls-evidence-generation-regulatory-decision-making_en.pdf)

##### EFPIA urges lawmakers to strengthen Biotech Act’s extended protection proposal

EFPIA is pushing EU legislators to strengthen the 12-month supplementary protection certificate (SPC) extension proposed in the Biotech Act.

The trade group welcomed the European Commission’s proposed extension for biotechnology-derived products and advanced therapy medicinal products. However, as the European Parliament starts work on the Biotech Act, EFPIA wants legislators to expand the scope of the extension to all innovative medicines and to establish “clear and predictable award criterias.”

EFPIA backed its request with research showing that the scope and eligibility of the SPC extension will determine its impact. The EFPIA-commissioned research found the extension could attract €45 billion ($52 billion) in inward investment into the EU over 15 years under the broadest scenarios, compared to €4 billion under the narrowest scope. EFPIA predicts the scope will also affect clinical trial enrollment.

[Press Release](https://www.efpia.eu/news-events/the-efpia-view/statements-press-releases/extending-supplementary-protection-certificate-spc-could-increase-european-rd-investment-tenfold/), [EFPIA Feedback](https://www.efpia.eu/media/gu5bvtym/strengthening-europe-s-biotechnology-ecosystem-through-a-competitive-and-coherent-biotech-act.pdf)

args.summary:
This RAPS "Euro Roundup" article (11 June 2026, by Nick Paul Taylor) covers five major European and UK regulatory developments:

1. **EMA AI Research Priorities**: EMA researchers published a preprint paper on regulatory research priorities for AI across the medicine lifecycle, based on a survey of 273 people (regulators, industry, patients, academics, healthcare professionals). "Accuracy and reliability of AI tools" was the highest priority across all groups "by a substantial margin," followed by data governance/confidentiality/consent and ethics/fairness/bias prevention. The paper drafted 10 priority research areas. It was released one day after EMA's 2025 AI Observatory report, ahead of a regulatory science research meeting covering AI integration methodologies.

2. **First JCA Report Under HTAR**: The European Commission published its first joint clinical assessment (JCA) report under the Health Technology Assessment Regulation on tovorafenib, Ipsen Pharma's treatment for the most common pediatric brain tumor. The 154-page report is the first of 18 JCAs started since HTAR took effect in January 2025. Tovorafenib received a one-year conditional marketing authorization on 20 April. The assessment was limited by insufficient evidence—Ipsen could only address one of eight PICOs due to lack of comparator data; assessors found "major, general uncertainties" relating to evidence synthesis methods, small sample size, and population differences.

3. **MHRA AI Airlock Phase 2**: After finishing phase two of its AI Airlock sandbox program, the UK MHRA identified needs for new/updated guidance: guidance on predetermined change control plans (PCCPs), performance metrics for AI-powered in vitro diagnostics (IVDs), and updates to software qualification and intended purpose guidance to address AI-specific considerations. MHRA also launched a secure sandbox for testing AI-enabled devices in London healthcare.

4. **EMA External Controls Paper**: EMA finalized its concept paper on using external controls for evidence generation in regulatory decisions, tweaking the draft to clarify terms like synthetic data and digital twins and noting issues with replication/reproducibility. The CHMP aims to discuss the draft reflection paper in Q4 with a three-month consultation, finalizing by Q2 next year.

5. **EFPIA and the Biotech Act**: EFPIA urged EU legislators to strengthen the proposed 12-month supplementary protection certificate (SPC) extension in the Biotech Act, expanding it to all innovative medicines with "clear and predictable award criterias." EFPIA-commissioned research found the extension could attract €45 billion ($52 billion) in inward investment to the EU over 15 years under the broadest scenarios, versus €4 billion under the narrowest scope.

<webpage_content>
[Blog](/blog)›AI models for Life Sciences in 2026

# AI models for Life Sciences in 2026AI models for Life Sciences in 2026

OpenAI, Anthropic, Google DeepMind, NVIDIA, Microsoft, and Meta all sell life sciences products as of 2026. This guide compares the six on access, pricing, and integration cost.

AI modelsDrug discoveryLife sciences

10min read

![2026 comparison of AI models for life sciences across Google DeepMind, NVIDIA, Anthropic, Microsoft, Meta, and OpenAI](/_next/image?url=%2F_next%2Fstatic%2Fmedia%2Fai-models-for-life-science.d5578266.webp&w=3840&q=75)

![Myroslav Syrko](/_next/image?url=%2F_next%2Fstatic%2Fmedia%2Fcoo.1a2fd7db.jpg&w=128&q=75)[## Myroslav Syrko

COO & Co-Owner at CodePhusion](https://www.linkedin.com/in/myroslav-syrko/)

![calendar](/_next/image?url=%2F_next%2Fstatic%2Fmedia%2FClock.df22d0d3.png&w=32&q=75)

## Google DeepMind and Isomorphic Labs

DeepMind has the longest tenure in production biology of the six labs. [AlphaFold 2 reset target validation in 2021](https://blog.google/innovation-and-ai/products/google-deepmind-isomorphic-alphafold-3-ai-model/), and AlphaFold 3 carried the work into protein-with-ligand and protein-with-nucleic-acid territory in May 2024, with roughly a 50% accuracy gain on protein-molecule interactions. The science is the strongest of the six labs. The hard part is buying it. AlphaFold Server is free for non-commercial use, and the [AlphaFold 3 code plus request-gated model parameters](https://github.com/google-deepmind/alphafold3) went to academia in November 2024 under a non-commercial license. Commercial AF3-class capability flows through [Isomorphic Labs](https://www.isomorphiclabs.com/articles/the-isomorphic-labs-drug-design-engine-unlocks-a-new-frontier), the DeepMind spinout that holds the pharma deal pipeline. Eli Lilly and Novartis signed at up to $3 billion combined in January 2024, Isomorphic raised $600 million in March 2025 led by Thrive Capital, [Johnson & Johnson joined in a January 2026 research collaboration](https://www.isomorphiclabs.com/articles/isomorphic-labs-enters-into-a-research-collaboration-with-johnson-johnson), and a [$2.1 billion Series B closed in May 2026](https://www.isomorphiclabs.com/articles/isomorphic-labs-announces-series-b-investment-round). Isomorphic's stated goal is to advance programs toward clinical development.

Around AlphaFold sits a wider biology stack:

* AlphaProteo (September 2024) designs novel protein binders for cancer and diabetes targets.
* [AlphaGenome (June 2025)](https://deepmind.google/blog/alphagenome-ai-for-better-understanding-the-genome/) reads regulatory effects of mutations across DNA sequences up to a million bases and is free for non-commercial use.
* AlphaMissense scores pathogenicity of missense variants across the human genome.
* [Med-Gemini](https://research.google/blog/advancing-medical-ai-with-med-gemini/) is Gemini fine-tuned for medicine, scoring 91.1% on MedQA. Google presents it as research rather than a productized enterprise offering.

Best for: Teams whose primary bottleneck is structure prediction, target validation, or protein design. Less useful when the work is literature synthesis or regulatory drafting.

## NVIDIA

NVIDIA does not compete on the model layer alone. It sells the infrastructure plus a curated catalog of biology models running on its hardware, which makes it the only one of the six labs whose business depends on every other lab succeeding.

The core stack is the [BioNeMo Platform](https://nvidianews.nvidia.com/news/nvidia-opens-bionemo-to-scale-digital-biology-for-global-biopharma-and-scientific-industry), a generative AI framework for drug discovery built around pre-trained models, NIM microservices for containerized inference, and reference Blueprints. BioNeMo runs on DGX Cloud and on AWS, GCP, and Azure. The [Generative Virtual Screening Blueprint](https://github.com/NVIDIA-BioNeMo-blueprints/generative-virtual-screening) chains MSA-Search, OpenFold2, GenMol, and DiffDock for hit identification.

Around BioNeMo, NVIDIA wraps three other frameworks:

* MONAI handles [medical imaging across CT, MRI, pathology, and endoscopy](https://developer.nvidia.com/blog/breaking-barriers-in-healthcare-with-new-models-for-generative-ai-and-cellular-imaging/). Its components include MAISI for synthetic CT, VISTA-3D with 130 anatomical classes, and VISTA-2D for cellular imaging, with more than one million downloads.
* Parabricks accelerates genomics on GPU (BWA-MEM, GATK, DeepVariant), with HaplotypeCaller dropping from around 36 hours on CPU to around 25 to 35 minutes on GPU depending on the platform.
* Clara is the umbrella spanning BioNeMo for discovery, Holoscan for medical devices, Parabricks for genomics, and MONAI for imaging.

The pharma partnership list is the longest of any of the six labs:

* NVIDIA and Eli Lilly announced a [co-innovation AI lab on January 12, 2026](https://nvidianews.nvidia.com/news/nvidia-and-lilly-announce-co-innovation-lab-to-reinvent-drug-discovery-in-the-age-of-ai), valued at up to $1 billion over five years and built on BioNeMo plus the Vera Rubin architecture.
* [Recursion took a $50 million strategic investment from NVIDIA in 2023](https://blogs.nvidia.com/blog/drug-discovery-recursion-supercomputer/) and now hosts its Phenom foundation model on BioNeMo.
* [Amgen runs a DGX SuperPOD at deCODE Genetics in Iceland](https://www.fiercebiotech.com/medtech/nvidia-expands-drug-discovery-footprint-new-amgen-recursion-alliances) for training on human datasets.
* Genentech integrated BioNeMo into its lab-in-a-loop workflows.
* [Novo Nordisk uses BioNeMo together with NIM and NeMo](https://investor.nvidia.com/news/press-release-details/2025/NVIDIA-Partners-With-Novo-Nordisk-and-DCAI-to-Advance-Drug-Discovery/default.aspx) for agentic drug discovery through DCAI.

Access is multi-cloud (DGX Cloud, AWS, GCP, Azure) and the customer pays for compute, not per seat. This is the only platform among the six where the cost structure scales with workload rather than headcount.

Best for: Biotechs and pharma running high-volume computational workflows where GPU economics dominate the bill. The clearest fits are virtual screening, genomics pipelines, structural and imaging analysis at scale, and agentic discovery workflows.

## Anthropic

Anthropic moved from horizontal LLM to a vertical pharma product on October 20, 2025, when it [launched Claude for Life Sciences](https://www.anthropic.com/news/claude-for-life-sciences) with five named pharma anchor customers and pre-built connectors into the systems pharma already runs.

[Claude for Life Sciences](https://claude.com/solutions/life-sciences) is a bundle of MCP connectors and biomedical skills wrapped around the Claude Enterprise stack. Launch connectors covered Benchling for ELN and LIMS, [10x Genomics for single-cell and spatial analysis](https://www.prnewswire.com/news-releases/10x-genomics-and-anthropic-partner-to-make-single-cell-and-spatial-analysis-more-accessible-through-claude-for-life-sciences-302588055.html), PubMed, BioRender, Synapse.org, and Wiley Scholar Gateway. Medidata and ClinicalTrials.gov were added after launch. Anthropic's launch materials cite improvements in Claude Sonnet 4.5 on figure interpretation, computational biology, and protein understanding benchmarks. The biomedical capability comes from prompting, tools, and connectors layered on a general-purpose Claude rather than from specialized biology weights.

The five anchor customers at launch were Novo Nordisk, Sanofi, AbbVie, AstraZeneca, and Genmab. The headline case study sits with [Novo Nordisk](https://claude.com/customers/novo-nordisk), where clinical study report drafting moved from 10+ weeks to around 10 minutes per report. Novo Nordisk started on Claude 3.5 Sonnet before the Life Sciences bundle existed. In May 2026, [Bristol Myers Squibb signed a strategic agreement to roll Claude Enterprise plus Claude Code to more than 30,000 BMS employees](https://www.fiercepharma.com/pharma/bristol-myers-taps-anthropic-claude-enterprise-wide-ai-adoption-speed-drug-rd-global) across R&D, manufacturing, and commercial. In 2026, Anthropic also [acquired Coefficient Bio for around $400 million](https://www.biospace.com/business/ai-giant-anthropic-leans-into-life-sciences-with-400m-coefficient-bio-catch), around 10 people largely drawn from Genentech computational biology, folded into the life sciences division.

Access is per-seat Claude Enterprise pricing with MCP connectors handling the system integrations. There are no specialized biology weights to license separately.

Best for: Teams whose dominant work is regulatory writing, clinical study reports, literature synthesis, protocol drafting, and translation across legacy lab data formats. Not the right pick when structure prediction or molecule generation is the bottleneck.

## Microsoft

Microsoft has the deepest and longest-running life sciences stack of any cloud provider. Five years of Microsoft Research output sits alongside a healthcare model catalog in Azure AI Foundry, EHR-integrated voice products from the Nuance acquisition, and a 2019 Novartis alliance that has been extended multiple times.

The biomedical model catalog inside [Azure AI Foundry](https://techcommunity.microsoft.com/blog/azure-ai-foundry-blog/announcing-healthcare-ai-models-in-azure-ai-model-catalog/4282460) covers most of Microsoft Research's biology output:

* [BioGPT](https://huggingface.co/microsoft/biogpt) is a generative transformer pre-trained on around 15 million PubMed abstracts, state-of-the-art on biomedical relation extraction and QA at release.
* [BiomedCLIP](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/research/publication/biomedclip-a-multimodal-biomedical-foundation-model-pretrained-from-fifteen-million-scientific-image-text-pairs/) is a vision-language foundation model trained on PMC-15M, 15 million figure-caption pairs from PubMed Central.
* MedImageInsight, MedImageParse, and CXRReportGen are healthcare imaging foundation models covering embedding and classification, segmentation across X-ray, CT, MRI, ultrasound, dermatology, and pathology, and chest X-ray report generation. Mass General Brigham (MedImageInsight) and the University of Wisconsin-Madison (CXRReportGen) are cited customers.
* [TamGen](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/research/blog/accelerating-drug-discovery-with-tamgen-a-generative-ai-approach-to-target-aware-molecule-generation/) is a target-aware molecule generator published in Nature Communications in 2024, demonstrated on TB ClpP protease with 14 candidate compounds and a lead IC50 of 1.9 μM.
* Hist-AI handles pathology and ECG-FM handles electrocardiogram analysis.

The pharma partnerships are older and deeper than at most of the other labs. [Novartis signed an AI Innovation Lab alliance with Microsoft in October 2019](https://blogs.microsoft.com/blog/2019/10/01/bringing-together-deep-bioscience-and-ai-to-help-patients-worldwide-novartis-and-microsoft-work-to-reinvent-treatment-discovery-and-development/) and has extended it multiple times since, covering generative chemistry, image segmentation for cell and gene therapy, and personalized treatment for macular degeneration. [Paige.AI partnered with Microsoft in January 2023](https://www.paige.ai/press-releases/paige-collaborates-with-microsoft-to-transform-cancer-diagnosis-and-treatment-with-the-use-of-pathology-ai), expanded in September 2023, and built Virchow2 and Virchow2G, the latter a 1.8 billion parameter pathology foundation model trained on 3 million slides using Microsoft supercomputing.

The clinical and EHR layer is what no other lab on this list offers:

* [Dragon Copilot launched at HIMSS in March 2025](https://news.microsoft.com/source/2025/03/03/microsoft-dragon-copilot-provides-the-healthcare-industrys-first-unified-voice-ai-assistant-) as a unified voice AI assistant from the Nuance acquisition stack, covering ambient documentation, dictation, and generative summarization. It was extended to nurses in October 2025.
* Healthcare Agent Orchestrator and Copilot Studio provide healthcare-specific templates with EHR connectors.
* Microsoft Fabric Healthcare data solutions, generally available since 2024, handle FHIR ingestion, OMOP transformations, DICOM imaging pipelines, and SDOH datasets.

Foundry deployment is Azure-only. Some underlying models also ship via Hugging Face, GitHub, or partner provider channels, but customers running them through Microsoft commit to Azure spend and pull from the Foundry catalog. The strongest fit is in regulated environments already cleared on Azure's existing compliance posture.

Best for: Pharma and clinical health systems already on Azure. Microsoft is the only lab on this list with a complete clinical voice, EHR, healthcare imaging, data pipeline, and biomedical model stack under one cloud account.

## Meta and EvolutionaryScale

Meta's biology work continues through EvolutionaryScale, founded in 2023 by former members of Meta's FAIR ESM team. The protein language models in this lineage (ESM2, ESM3, ESMFold) are the most-used open biology models in the world, and the open-weight access route is what separates Meta's line from every other lab on this list.

[ESM2 and ESMFold](https://github.com/facebookresearch/esm), released in 2022, gave the field a protein language model and a structure predictor that works from sequence alone, faster than AlphaFold 2 with some accuracy tradeoffs. The ESM Metagenomic Atlas, built using ESMFold, has more than 600 million predicted structures. [ESM3 was released by EvolutionaryScale in June 2024](https://press.aboutamazon.com/aws/2024/6/evolutionaryscale-launches-with-esm3-a-milestone-ai-model-for-biology) as the first generative model jointly reasoning over protein sequence, structure, and function, trained on 2.78 billion proteins. The launch demo generated a novel green fluorescent protein roughly equivalent to 500 million years of evolution. EvolutionaryScale raised over $142 million in seed funding, with Amazon and NVIDIA among the backers.

Access splits across the lineage. ESM2 and ESMFold are fully open weights through the original Meta GitHub repository. [ESM3 is hosted on AWS](https://github.com/evolutionaryscale/esm), with only a smaller variant available on Hugging Face under a non-commercial license. EvolutionaryScale, not Meta, is the active developer.

Best for: Teams that need open-weight protein models for in-house training, fine-tuning, or air-gapped deployment. Particularly attractive to academic groups and biotechs holding proprietary protein data they are unwilling to send to a third-party API.

## OpenAI

OpenAI ships into pharma as a generalist with a recently added biology-specific entry. The strategy combines ChatGPT Enterprise deployments, selective scientific partnerships, a healthcare benchmark, and, as of April 2026, [GPT-Rosalind](https://openai.com/index/introducing-gpt-rosalind/), OpenAI's first dedicated life sciences model.

The public enterprise deployments to date:

* [Moderna started in April 2024](https://openai.com/index/moderna/), with ChatGPT Enterprise rolled across around 3,000 employees and more than 750 custom GPTs built internally, including a Dose ID tool for clinical-trial dose review and analytics.
* In May 2024, [Sanofi, Formation Bio, and OpenAI announced a three-way collaboration](https://www.sanofi.com/en/media-room/press-releases/2024/2024-05-21-05-30-00-2885244) to fine-tune OpenAI models on Sanofi's proprietary data and build purpose-built AI agents for drug development.
* [Color Health released a GPT-4o-based cancer copilot in 2024](https://openai.com/index/color-health/) that builds patient-specific cancer screening and workup plans for clinicians, validated with the UCSF Helen Diller Family Comprehensive Cancer Center. Color reports four times more identified missing labs and imaging compared to status quo, and a shift from weeks to around 5 minutes to surface care gaps.

Before GPT-Rosalind, OpenAI's closest biology-specific work was [GPT-4b micro, released in January 2025 through a Retro Biosciences collaboration](https://openai.com/index/accelerating-life-sciences-research-with-retro-biosciences/). GPT-4b micro is a GPT-4o-derived model specialized for protein engineering, used to redesign the Yamanaka factors (Sox2 and Klf4) with a reported 50 times improvement in pluripotency marker expression and a reduction in iPSC generation time from around 3 weeks to around 1 week. GPT-4b micro is a research collaboration rather than a generally available product.

[HealthBench, released in May 2025](https://openai.com/index/healthbench/), is OpenAI's open-source healthcare benchmark, built from 5,000 multi-turn conversations annotated by 262 physicians across 60 countries with around 48,562 rubric criteria. OpenAI uses HealthBench to position o3 and GPT-4.1 nano as healthcare-grade.

Access is ChatGPT Enterprise per seat and the OpenAI API per token, with GPT-Rosalind as the dedicated life sciences entry on the price sheet.

Best for: Pharma and biotech where the dominant use case is enterprise productivity (literature review, document drafting, internal copilots) and the buyer wants a generalist model with the widest reach across third-party tools.

## Side-by-side comparison of AI tools for life sciences

The six labs differ across flagship offering, specialized biology model, access route, pricing structure, and target buyer. The table below summarizes the comparison in one view.

| Lab | Flagship offering | Specialized biology model | Access | Pricing | Best for |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Google DeepMind | AlphaFold 3, Isomorphic Labs | AlphaFold 3, AlphaProteo, AlphaGenome, Med-Gemini | Server (non-commercial), Isomorphic partnership (commercial), Google Cloud | Free non-commercial; commercial via Isomorphic deal | Structure prediction, target validation, protein design |
| NVIDIA | BioNeMo, MONAI, Parabricks | MolMIM, Phenom (Recursion), DiffDock | DGX Cloud, AWS, GCP, Azure | Compute-based | High-volume computational workflows, GPU-bound work |
| Anthropic | Claude for Life Sciences | None (general-purpose Claude plus connectors) | Claude Enterprise plus MCP connectors | Per seat | Regulatory writing, clinical reports, literature synthesis |
| Microsoft | Azure AI for Health, Dragon Copilot | BioGPT, BiomedCLIP, TamGen, MedImage models, Virchow2G | Azure AI Foundry catalog | Azure consumption | Pharma already on Azure; clinical health systems |
| Meta / EvolutionaryScale | ESM3, ESMFold | ESM2, ESM3, ESMFold | Open weights (ESM2), AWS plus Hugging Face (ESM3) | Free or compute-only | Open-weight protein models, air-gapped deployment |
| OpenAI | GPT-Rosalind, ChatGPT Enterprise | GPT-Rosalind, GPT-4b micro (Retro collaboration) | GPT-Rosalind, ChatGPT Enterprise, OpenAI API | Per seat or per token | Enterprise productivity, broadest third-party tool reach |

## How to integrate a foundation model into a LIMS or ELN

Buyers ask this question after they pick a model, and the answer is the same regardless of which lab they picked. The data layer is the harder problem. Foundation models are useless without clean, structured input, and biotechs consistently underspend on the data substrate and overspend on the model itself. We covered the upstream version of this in our analysis of [lab software data lock-in](/blog/lab-software-data-lock-in), which is the form the problem takes before any AI gets near the stack.

The integration lift varies by lab. Anthropic Claude for Life Sciences offers the lowest lift because the pre-built MCP connectors cover Benchling, 10x Genomics, PubMed, and most of what pharma already runs, but it ties the buyer to Claude. NVIDIA BioNeMo is API-first and runs against the buyer's data, which means higher integration lift but more flexibility on what the model sees. Microsoft Azure AI Foundry has the lowest lift if the buyer is already on Azure and the highest if they are not. Google DeepMind's AlphaFold Server is fine for one-off predictions, but production use needs a wrapper, and Med-Gemini ties the buyer to Google Cloud. Meta and EvolutionaryScale's ESM3 sits at the highest integration lift because the buyer is doing everything in-house, but it also gives full control and runs in the buyer's own VPC. OpenAI is API-first with a growing third-party tool layer, and the integration work falls on the buyer.

Regardless of which lab the buyer picks, four things have to work before any of this lands in production:

1. Instrument and ELN data flow into a structured store the model can read
2. An audit trail captures every input, every model output, and every human review
3. Validation evidence sits beside the output for regulated use cases under 21 CFR Part 11 and EU Annex 11
4. A model-to-human handoff is built in, and no model output goes to a regulator without a sign-off step

Picking the model is the small part. Wiring it into a LIMS, ELN, and the broader data pipeline is where time and budget actually go. Our broader take on adoption patterns sits in the [state of AI in biotech 2026](/blog/ai-in-biotech-2026), which covers the pilot-to-production gap from the data side.

Deploying one of these models in a regulated lab? CodePhusion builds custom LIMS, ELN, and data infrastructure for biotechs running AI in production. if you want to talk through the integration.

## Conclusion

The model layer commoditized faster than anyone predicted. Six labs now ship usable biology offerings, with deals running into the billions and the first AI-designed Isomorphic programs heading toward clinical development. The differentiator has moved from access to a frontier model to whether a biotech can wire that model into a LIMS, ELN, and data pipeline without breaking validation. The next 24 months will reward the biotechs that put integration budget ahead of model budget.

## Frequently Asked Questions

### What does OpenAI offer for life sciences and drug discovery?

![arrow](/_next/static/media/backIcon.ba6caa3b.svg)

OpenAI sells ChatGPT Enterprise and the OpenAI API into pharma and biotech, and in April 2026 introduced GPT-Rosalind, its first dedicated life sciences model. Notable case studies include Moderna (around 3,000 employees on ChatGPT Enterprise), the Sanofi and Formation Bio collaboration, Color Health's cancer copilot, and Retro Biosciences (GPT-4b micro for protein engineering). HealthBench is OpenAI's open-source healthcare benchmark.

### What is Claude for Life Sciences used for?

![arrow](/_next/static/media/backIcon.ba6caa3b.svg)

Claude for Life Sciences is Anthropic's October 2025 vertical product for pharma, built on Claude Enterprise with MCP connectors into Benchling, 10x Genomics, PubMed, BioRender, Synapse.org, Wiley Scholar Gateway, and other systems pharma already runs. Medidata and ClinicalTrials.gov were added after launch. Anchor customers at launch were Novo Nordisk, Sanofi, AbbVie, AstraZeneca, and Genmab. It is best suited to regulatory writing, clinical study reports, and literature synthesis.

### What is NVIDIA BioNeMo and who is it for?

![arrow](/_next/static/media/backIcon.ba6caa3b.svg)

NVIDIA BioNeMo is a generative AI framework for drug discovery, with pre-trained biology models, NIM microservices for containerized inference, and reference Blueprints such as the Generative Virtual Screening Blueprint. BioNeMo runs on DGX Cloud and on AWS, GCP, and Azure. It is best for biotechs and pharma running high-volume computational workflows where GPU economics dominate the bill.

### AlphaFold 3 vs ESMFold vs RoseTTAFold, which should you use?

![arrow](/_next/static/media/backIcon.ba6caa3b.svg)

AlphaFold 3 has the highest accuracy on protein-with-ligand and protein-with-nucleic-acid structures, with academic weights and an Isomorphic Labs commercial path. ESMFold is open weights and faster, which makes it the right pick when fine-tuning on proprietary data or running an in-house pipeline. RoseTTAFold is open-source and competitive on certain protein families. The right pick depends on data residency, throughput, and whether commercial use is in scope.

### How do OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google DeepMind compare for biotech?

![arrow](/_next/static/media/backIcon.ba6caa3b.svg)

OpenAI sells enterprise productivity through ChatGPT Enterprise and added GPT-Rosalind, its first biology-specific model, in April 2026. Anthropic ships Claude for Life Sciences with MCP connectors aimed at regulatory writing and clinical reporting. Google DeepMind ships the deepest specialized portfolio for structure prediction and target validation, with commercial use routed through Isomorphic Labs. The three answer different buyer questions and the picks are not interchangeable.

### Does Microsoft have a life sciences AI model?

![arrow](/_next/static/media/backIcon.ba6caa3b.svg)

Yes. The Azure AI Foundry catalog includes BioGPT (biomedical text), BiomedCLIP (biomedical vision-language), TamGen (target-aware molecule generation), MedImageInsight and MedImageParse for imaging, CXRReportGen for chest X-ray reports, and Virchow2G (1.8 billion parameter pathology model). Microsoft also ships Dragon Copilot for clinical voice and Microsoft Fabric Healthcare for FHIR, OMOP, and DICOM pipelines. Foundry deployment is Azure-only, though some underlying models also ship via Hugging Face, GitHub, or partner provider channels.

### What does Meta offer for biotech?

![arrow](/_next/static/media/backIcon.ba6caa3b.svg)

Meta's biology work continues through EvolutionaryScale, founded in 2023 by former members of Meta's FAIR ESM team. The ESM family of protein models (ESM2, ESM3, ESMFold) is the most-used open biology lineage in the world. ESM2 and ESMFold ship as open weights. ESM3 is a generative model trained on 2.78 billion proteins, hosted on AWS, with only a smaller variant available on Hugging Face under a non-commercial license.

### How do you integrate a foundation model into a LIMS or ELN?

![arrow](/_next/static/media/backIcon.ba6caa3b.svg)

Picking the model is the smaller half of the problem. Production integration requires instrument and ELN data flowing into a structured store the model can read, an audit trail covering every input and output, validation evidence under 21 CFR Part 11 and EU Annex 11, and a model-to-human handoff step before any output reaches a regulator. The data substrate matters more than the model choice.

This guide (published May 28, 2026, by Myroslav Syrko of CodePhusion) compares the AI models for Life Sciences offered by six major labs as of 2026: Google DeepMind, NVIDIA, Anthropic, Microsoft, Meta/EvolutionaryScale, and OpenAI, covering access, pricing, and integration cost.

**Google DeepMind/Isomorphic Labs:** Has the strongest science and longest tenure in production biology. AlphaFold 2 reset target validation in 2021; AlphaFold 3 (May 2024) covers protein-ligand and protein-nucleic acid with ~50% accuracy gain on protein-molecule interactions. AlphaFold Server is free non-commercial; commercial capability flows through Isomorphic Labs (Eli Lilly/Novartis deals up to $3B combined in Jan 2024, $600M raise in March 2025, J&J collaboration Jan 2026, $2.1B Series B in May 2026). Wider stack includes AlphaProteo, AlphaGenome (free non-commercial), AlphaMissense, and Med-Gemini (91.1% on MedQA). Best for structure prediction, target validation, protein design.

**NVIDIA:** Sells infrastructure plus curated biology catalog via BioNeMo Platform (pre-trained models, NIM microservices, Blueprints). Runs on DGX Cloud, AWS, GCP, Azure with compute-based pricing (only lab where cost scales with workload, not headcount). Other frameworks: MONAI (medical imaging, 1M+ downloads), Parabricks (genomics; HaplotypeCaller from ~36h CPU to ~25-35min GPU), Clara umbrella. Longest pharma partnership list: Eli Lilly co-innovation lab (Jan 2026, up to $1B/5 years), Recursion ($50M investment), Amgen/deCODE, Genentech, Novo Nordisk. Best for high-volume GPU-bound computational workflows.

**Anthropic:** Launched Claude for Life Sciences (Oct 20, 2025) built on Claude Enterprise with MCP connectors (Benchling, 10x Genomics, PubMed, BioRender, Synapse.org, Wiley Scholar Gateway; later Medidata, ClinicalTrials.gov). Capabilities come from prompting/tools/connectors, not specialized weights. Five anchor customers: Novo Nordisk, Sanofi, AbbVie, AstraZeneca, Genmab. Novo Nordisk case study: clinical study report drafting from 10+ weeks to ~10 minutes. BMS signed strategic deal in May 2026 for 30,000+ employees. Acquired Coefficient Bio (~$400M, 2026). Per-seat pricing. Best for regulatory writing, clinical reports, literature synthesis.

**Microsoft:** Deepest/longest-running stack. Azure AI Foundry catalog includes BioGPT (15M PubMed abstracts), BiomedCLIP (PMC-15M), MedImageInsight/MedImageParse/CXRReportGen, TamGen (TB ClpP lead IC50 1.9 μM), Hist-AI, ECG-FM, plus Virchow2G (1.8B parameter pathology model via Paige.AI). Deep partnerships: Novartis AI Innovation Lab (since Oct 2019), Paige.AI (2023). Unique clinical/EHR layer: Dragon Copilot voice AI (March 2025, extended to nurses Oct 2025), Healthcare Agent Orchestrator, Microsoft Fabric Healthcare (FHIR, OMOP, DICOM, SDOH). Foundry is Azure-only. Best for pharma/health systems already on Azure.

**Meta/EvolutionaryScale:** Most-used open biology models (ESM2, ESM3, ESMFold). ESM2/ESMFold are fully open weights via Meta GitHub; ESM metagenomic atlas has 600M+ predicted structures. ESM3 (June 2024, by EvolutionaryScale) is first generative model jointly reasoning over sequence/structure/function, trained on 2.78B proteins. EvolutionaryScale raised $142M+ (Amazon, NVIDIA backers). Hosted on AWS; only smaller variant on Hugging Face under non-commercial license. Best for open-weight/air-gapped deployments with proprietary data.

**OpenAI:** Generalist with biology entry. GPT-Rosalind (April 2026) is first dedicated life sciences model. Deployments: Moderna (3,000 employees, 750+ custom GPTs since April 2024), Sanofi/Formation Bio (May 2024), Color Health cancer copilot (4x more identified missing labs/imaging), GPT-4b micro (Jan 2025, Retro Biosciences; 50x improvement in pluripotency, iPSC generation from ~3 weeks to ~1 week). HealthBench benchmark (May 2025; 5,000 conversations, 262 physicians). Per-seat or per-token pricing. Best for enterprise productivity.

**Integration guidance:** The data layer is the harder problem; integration lift varies (Anthropic lowest with pre-built connectors; ESM3 highest). Four prerequisites for production: (1) instrument/ELN data into structured store, (2) audit trail for all inputs/outputs/reviews, (3) validation evidence under 21 CFR Part 11 and EU Annex 11, (4) model-to-human handoff with sign-off before regulator submission. Key conclusion: the model layer commoditized fast; the differentiator is wiring models into LIMS/ELN/data pipelines without breaking validation, so the next 24 months reward integration budget over model budget.

## Abhijit Roy's Post

---

### [**Abhijit Roy**](https://www.facebook.com/abhijit.roy.media?__cft__[0]=AZb6OZYrA85ttJdBeleOm_CAiM7gYvCjLDeWExTm_YYz7y7EpQ8aQ2MpKi-XSvCriQH1cjlovobRRZ_PRTIIQ67EFoWoQoemyPYvGwjLv6jttqMjI0jujxoD98PYRW6XOLPllBq8VY-MerdFaIuaQRrR-QJeRiiuA9jZqkodMe5lbA&__tn__=-UC%2CP-R)

[July 12](https://www.facebook.com/abhijit.roy.media/posts/pfbid0EVSPSRNo6ADi6FkQQbnjA1A9sCsk1NNhycVwxMKqfsr6g9eJcw1N24VKJ4hmhj3Vl?__cft__[0]=AZb6OZYrA85ttJdBeleOm_CAiM7gYvCjLDeWExTm_YYz7y7EpQ8aQ2MpKi-XSvCriQH1cjlovobRRZ_PRTIIQ67EFoWoQoemyPYvGwjLv6jttqMjI0jujxoD98PYRW6XOLPllBq8VY-MerdFaIuaQRrR-QJeRiiuA9jZqkodMe5lbA&__tn__=%2CO%2CP-R)  ·

Claude Science AI to Shake up Global Pharma Industry

Anthropic launched Claude Science on June 30, 2026. The company did not frame it as an experiment. It positioned the product as a flagship offering alongside Claude Code and Claude Cowork. That framing matters. Anthropic is telling the market that AI for science deserves the same commercial priority as software engineering.

Claude Science is a multi-agent workbench. A generalist agent coordinates sub-agents and specialist agents created by users. A separate reviewer agent checks citations and calculations. The system ships with over 60 pre-configured connectors for genomics, proteomics, structural biology, and cheminformatics. It runs locally on macOS or Linux, or remotely via SSH and HPC login nodes. Every output carries an auditable history.

The architecture is deliberate. Anthropic learned from Claude Code that autonomous agents work best when they can decompose complex objectives into discrete steps, invoke domain-specific tools, and verify results before proceeding. Claude Science applies that same loop to biological datasets, molecular simulations, and pharmacological pipelines. Where Claude Code calls compilers and test runners, Claude Science calls protein folding predictors, docking algorithms, and ADMET property calculators.

The launch event included a live demonstration. Claude Science autonomously identified drug candidates for phenylketonuria, a rare metabolic disorder. Anthropic announced it will use the product to pursue its own research into rare and neglected diseases. This is not philanthropy. It is product validation at industrial scale. If Anthropic can find viable candidates for diseases that pharma traditionally ignores, every biotech and pharma company watching will ask why they are not using the same tool.

Early beta users have already produced measurable results. Stephen Francis, an associate professor at the UCSF Brain Tumour Centre, used Claude Science to analyze the molecular epidemiology of glioma. He reported that analyses now take roughly one-tenth of the time they previously required. Manifold Bio, a company designing tissue-targeting medicines, used the system to nominate targets for its latest experiments. For each tissue and target, Claude Science assessed surface expression, trafficking, and safety, ranking candidates against proprietary criteria. What distinguished it from a general coding assistant, Manifold said, was the end-to-end capability: gathering the right data and applying the right judgment with the context of past programs built in.

The competitive context is sharp. OpenAI released GPT-Rosalind in April 2026, a specialized biology model gated behind enterprise contracts. Google DeepMind has AlphaFold and decades of scientific AI credibility, but it remains a research lab, not a product company. Anthropic's bet is different: broad subscription access over narrow enterprise gating. Claude Science is available to paid subscribers on Pro, Max, Team, and Enterprise plans, with discounted academic pricing. Anthropic is wagering that workflow integration beats a specialized model locked behind sales cycles.

Then there is the personnel story. On June 19, 2026, eleven days before the Claude Science launch, John Jumper announced he was leaving Google DeepMind for Anthropic. Jumper shared the 2024 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for AlphaFold, the system that solved the 50-year protein-folding problem and has since predicted over 200 million protein structures for researchers across 190 countries. He was 39 years old, the youngest chemistry Nobel laureate in over 70 years. His departure came just one day after Noam Shazeer, Gemini co-lead and co-author of the transformer paper that underpins modern AI, announced he was leaving Google for OpenAI. Alphabet stock fell roughly 7 percent on June 22, erasing approximately 250 billion in market value, its worst single session in over a year.

Jumper's role at Anthropic has not been disclosed. Neither he nor the company has named a title, team, or start date. What is on the record is that Anthropic had been building toward this moment for months. In February 2026 it announced partnerships with the Allen Institute and Howard Hughes Medical Institute. In April it reportedly acquired Coefficient Bio, a stealth biotech startup with Genentech-lineage founders, for approximately 400 million in stock. In May it hired Andrej Karpathy for its pre-training team. The sequence reads as deliberate strategy, not opportunism.

For pharma, the implications are structural. Claude Science lowers the barrier to computational drug discovery. Academic labs, mid-tier biotechs, and nonprofits now have access to the same multi-agent environment that Anthropic itself is using for rare disease research. The moat around computational biology is shrinking. Reproducibility is built in, not bolted on. Every figure carries its provenance. In an industry where irreproducible preclinical data costs billions in failed trials, that is not a feature. It is a risk management tool.

Rare disease economics are also shifting. Pharma has historically ignored small markets because the return on investment does not justify the cost. If Anthropic's own program produces viable candidates for phenylketonuria and similar disorders, the business case for neglecting orphan indications collapses. AI makes the math work. Claude Science could be the catalyst that forces every major pharma company to re-examine its rare disease portfolio.

Data sovereignty is another factor. The system runs on local infrastructure or existing HPC clusters. For pharma, where intellectual property and patient data are existential risks, that is table stakes. Anthropic understands that a cloud-only product would never clear compliance at a major pharmaceutical company.

The talent signal is equally important. SignalFire's 2025 State of Talent Report found that engineers at Google DeepMind were nearly 11 times more likely to leave for Anthropic than the reverse. OpenAI engineers were 8 times more likely to move to Anthropic than the other direction. Anthropic's two-year retention rate of 80 percent leads all frontier labs. When a Nobel laureate chooses Anthropic over the lab that built AlphaFold, the message to the scientific community is unmistakable.

Anthropic is also putting money behind the ecosystem. It is supporting up to 50 Claude Science AI for Science projects with up to 30,000 in credits each. Modal is providing up to 2,000 in compute for select projects. Applications are open until July 15, 2026. The company is explicitly looking for work that spans domains and explores the boundaries of science, with an early focus on biology and biomedical research.

For pharmaceutical executives, the calculus is shifting. Discovery timelines are compressing. Rare disease programs are becoming viable. The competitive advantage is moving from who has the biggest lab to who uses AI best. And the window to build internal AI competency before it becomes a commodity is closing. Anthropic did not launch a research tool. It launched a scientific co-worker. The industry now has to decide whether to adopt it or be outpaced by those who do.

It raises a question.

Claude and OpenAI provide increasingly capable reasoning engines and scientific workflows.

But companies like agemica aren't trying to build another Claude.

Their value lies in decades of domain-specific knowledge, proprietary datasets, specialised algorithms, experimental feedback loops and scientific judgement built around a single problem.

Claude can reason about drug discovery.

A dedicated drug discovery platform reasons within drug discovery.

Those are different things.

One is a general intelligence platform.

The other is a scientific instrument.

I suspect the future isn't one replacing the other.

It's general AI becoming the orchestration layer while specialist scientific models, databases and algorithms continue to provide the deep expertise.

That's probably why people like agemica moved into biology years ago. The frontier wasn't software any more. It was applying software and AI to domains where the hardest questions still remain.

I think that's the transferable idea.

PS Agemica is a hypothetical name. There are over fifty such companies though. All engineers from rummelhart days. Funding top bio and pharmacists.

Outsourcing everything bar a core team.

args.summary:
This is a Facebook post by Abhijit Roy (dated July 12, 2026, though it references events in 2026) analyzing the launch of Anthropic's "Claude Science" AI platform and its potential disruption of the global pharmaceutical industry.

**Key facts about Claude Science:**
- Anthropic launched Claude Science on June 30, 2026, positioning it as a flagship offering alongside Claude Code and Claude Cowork, signaling equal commercial priority for AI for science as for software engineering.
- It is a multi-agent workbench with a generalist agent coordinating user-created sub-agents and specialist agents, plus a separate reviewer agent that checks citations and calculations.
- Ships with over 60 pre-configured connectors for genomics, proteomics, structural biology, and cheminformatics.
- Runs locally on macOS or Linux, or remotely via SSH and HPC login nodes, with auditable history for every output.
- Available to paid subscribers on Pro, Max, Team, and Enterprise plans, with discounted academic pricing.

**Launch demonstration and early results:**
- At launch, Claude Science autonomously identified drug candidates for phenylketonuria, a rare metabolic disorder. Anthropic announced it will use the product for its own research into rare and neglected diseases.
- Stephen Francis, associate professor at the UCSF Brain Tumour Centre, reported analyses now take roughly one-tenth of the previous time for glioma molecular epidemiology.
- Manifold Bio used the system to nominate tissue-targeting medicine targets, with end-to-end capability noted as distinguishing it from a general coding assistant.

**Competitive context:**
- OpenAI released GPT-Rosalind (a specialized biology model) in April 2026 behind enterprise contracts; Google DeepMind has AlphaFold but is a research lab, not a product company. Anthropic's bet is broad subscription access over narrow enterprise gating.

**Hiring/news timeline:**
- June 19, 2026: John Jumper (2024 Nobel Chemistry laureate for AlphaFold, youngest chemistry Nobel laureate in over 70 years, age 39) announced he was leaving Google DeepMind for Anthropic, 11 days before the Claude Science launch.
- June 2026: Noam Shazeer (Gemini co-lead, transformer paper co-author) left Google for OpenAI. Alphabet stock fell ~7% on June 22, erasing ~$250 billion in market value.
- February 2026: Anthropic partnerships with Allen Institute and Howard Hughes Medical Institute.
- April 2026: Reported acquisition of Coefficient Bio (stealth biotech, Genentech-lineage founders) for ~$400 million in stock.
- May 2026: Hired Andrej Karpathy for pre-training team.

**Industry implications discussed:**
- Lowers the barrier to computational drug discovery, shrinking the moat around computational biology; built-in reproducibility serves as risk management for irreproducible preclinical data.
- Could shift rare disease economics—if Anthropic's phenylketonuria program produces viable candidates, the business case for ignoring orphan indications collapses.
- Data sovereignty supported via local/HPC deployment, critical for pharma IP and patient data compliance.
- SignalFire's 2025 State of Talent Report: DeepMind engineers ~11x more likely to leave for Anthropic than reverse; OpenAI engineers 8x more likely; Anthropic's 80% two-year retention rate leads frontier labs.
- Ecosystem support: up to 50 Claude Science AI for Science projects with up to $30,000 in credits each; Modal providing up to $2,000 in compute for select projects. Applications open until July 15, 2026.

**Comment section:** Soumitra Roy argues that general AI (like Claude) becomes the orchestration layer while specialist scientific platforms (e.g., hypothetical "agemica") providing domain-specific knowledge, proprietary datasets, and experimental feedback loops remain necessary—the future is a combination, not replacement.

The post concludes that competitive advantage in pharma is shifting from who has the biggest lab to who uses AI best, and that Claude Science represents a "scientific co-worker" rather than just a research tool.
