# A survey of LLMs in drug discovery and precision medicine

Hasi Hays \*

William J. Richardson \*

Department of Chemical Engineering, University of Arkansas, Fayetteville, AR, United States

Article metrics

## Abstract

The convergence of artificial intelligence and biomedical research has catalyzed emerging impact in drug discovery and precision medicine. Large language models (LLMs), originally developed for natural language processing, have emerged as powerful tools capable of processing complex biomedical data, from molecular structures to clinical records. This comprehensive review examines the state-of-the-art applications of LLMs across the drug development pipeline, spanning target identification, molecular generation, property prediction, and drug repurposing in drug discovery, as well as clinical decision support, patient stratification, treatment personalization, and genomic interpretation in precision medicine. We analyze the technical methodologies underlying these applications, including multi-modal architectures, knowledge-guided approaches, and retrieval augmented generation systems. Through examination of recent advances, we highlight key achievements such as end-to-end drug discovery pipelines, multi-agent systems for clinical simulation, and knowledge-enhanced models achieving state-of-the-art performance. We critically assess current challenges, including data privacy, model interpretability, hallucination risks, and ethical considerations. Finally, we discuss future directions, emphasizing the potential for federated learning, explainable artificial intelligence, and integrated multiscale approaches to advance the field toward more reliable, transparent, and clinically applicable systems.

## 1 Introduction

The pharmaceutical industry faces unprecedented challenges in developing safe, effective, and personalized therapeutics. Traditional drug discovery remains a lengthy and expensive endeavor, with average development timelines exceeding 10–15 years and costs surpassing $2.6 billion per approved drug ([DiMasi et al., 2016](#B29); [Wouters et al., 2020](#B142)). The attrition rate in clinical trials remains alarmingly high, with approximately 90% of drug candidates failing to receive regulatory approval, often due to unforeseen toxicity or lack of efficacy that could not be predicted during preclinical development ([Vamathevan et al., 2019](#B132); [Paul et al., 2021](#B99)). Simultaneously, the promise of precision medicine, which aims to tailor treatments to individual patient characteristics including genetic makeup, lifestyle, and environmental factors, remains partially unfulfilled due to the inherent complexity of integrating multiscale biomedical data across molecular, cellular, tissue, and organismal levels ([Esteva et al., 2019](#B33); [Rajkomar et al., 2018](#B106)). The convergence of artificial intelligence and biomedical research offers emerging impact to address these longstanding challenges, with large language models emerging as particularly powerful and versatile tools capable of processing and synthesizing information across diverse data modalities ([Figure 1](#F1)) ([Wang et al., 2023](#B135); [Thirunavukarasu et al., 2023](#B128)).

FIGURE 1

![Infographic outlining the integration of large language models (LLMs) with multimodal biomedical data such as biomarkers, clinical data, and molecular structures, illustrating workflows in AI-driven drug discovery pipelines, precision medicine applications, and future challenges including data privacy, model explainability, hallucination, ethics, multi-agent systems, explainable AI, global integration, and model efficiency.](https://www.frontiersin.org/files/Articles/1854899/xml-images/fddsv-06-1854899-g001.webp)

Overview of large language models in drug discovery and precision medicine. LLMs integrate multi-modal biomedical data (text, molecular structures, proteins, genomics) through knowledge-guided architectures. In drug discovery, these models enable target identification, *de novo* molecule generation, ADMET property prediction, and drug repurposing. In precision medicine, LLMs support patient stratification, genomic interpretation, personalized treatment selection, and clinical decision support by integrating genomics, single-cell data, and clinical records. Key challenges and future directions include addressing data privacy, model explainability, hallucination risks, and regulatory considerations, while advancing multi-agent systems, explainable AI, federated learning approaches, and development of novel and efficient models. Created in BioRender. Hays (2026) <https://BioRender.com/879058c> (Academic Publication License, agreement number LZ29VNAPVN).

Large language models represent a paradigm shift in artificial intelligence, demonstrating remarkable capabilities in understanding and generating human language through deep learning on massive text corpora ([Vaswani et al., 2017](#B133); [Devlin et al., 2019](#B28); [Brown et al., 2020](#B12)). Models such as GPT (Generative Pre-trained Transformer), BERT (Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers), and their derivatives have achieved unprecedented performance across diverse linguistic tasks, from text classification and question answering to creative writing and code generation ([Radford et al., 2019](#B105); [OpenAI, 2023](#B93)). The fundamental insight driving their success is that self-supervised learning on vast amounts of text enables the extraction of rich semantic representations that capture not only syntactic patterns but also complex reasoning capabilities and world knowledge ([Brown et al., 2020](#B12); [Wei et al., 2022](#B139)).

This insight has proven surprisingly transferable to biomedical domains, where diverse data types including molecular SMILES strings, protein amino acid sequences, genomic nucleotide sequences, and clinical narratives can be treated as specialized languages with their own syntax, grammar, and semantic relationships ([Lee et al., 2020](#B64); [Luo et al., 2022](#B78); [Singhal et al., 2023](#B120)). The ability of these models to learn meaningful representations from sequential data, regardless of whether that data represents English text or chemical structures, has opened new avenues for computational approaches to drug discovery and clinical decision making.

Recent years have witnessed explosive growth in applying LLMs to drug discovery and precision medicine, fundamentally reshaping how researchers approach complex biomedical problems ([Schneider et al., 2020](#B114); [Mak and Pichika, 2019](#B81)). These models can process and integrate heterogeneous data types spanning multiple scales of biological organization, from atomic level molecular structures and protein sequences to patient level electronic health records and population level epidemiological data ([Vamathevan et al., 2019](#B132); [Shickel et al., 2018](#B118)). In drug discovery, LLMs enable tasks that previously required extensive domain expertise or costly experimental validation, including target identification from disease biology, *de novo* molecular generation with desired properties, absorption, distribution, metabolism, excretion, and toxicity (ADMET) prediction, and systematic drug repurposing through knowledge synthesis ([Stokes et al., 2020](#B122); [Zhavoronkov et al., 2019](#B163); Bilodeau et al., 2022). In precision medicine, these models are transforming clinical decision support by analyzing unstructured clinical notes, enabling sophisticated patient stratification based on multi-modal data, personalizing treatment recommendations, and interpreting complex genomic variants ([Singhal et al., 2023](#B120); [Nori et al., 2023](#B90)). The ability of LLMs to perform zero-shot and few-shot learning, making accurate predictions on novel tasks with minimal or no task-specific training examples, is particularly valuable in biomedical contexts where labeled data for specific applications may be scarce, expensive to obtain, or simply nonexistent for emerging diseases or novel therapeutic targets ([Brown et al., 2020](#B12); [Kojima et al., 2022](#B62)).

The evolution of biomedical LLMs has followed a distinct trajectory from their general-purpose counterparts, with successive waves of domain-adapted text models (BioBERT, PubMedBERT, ClinicalBERT), generative biomedical models (BioGPT, Med-PaLM 2, MEDITRON-70B), and modality-specific foundation models for molecules, proteins, genomes, and single cells (ChemBERTa, ESM-2, DNABERT-2, scGPT) ([Lee et al., 2020](#B64); [Luo et al., 2022](#B78); [Singhal et al., 2023](#B120); [Gu et al., 2021](#B42); Alsentzer et al., 2019; [Chithrananda et al., 2020](#B20); [Lin et al., 2023](#B73); [Zhou et al., 2023](#B166); [Cui et al., 2024](#B25)). A full technical treatment of these architectures, their pretraining strategies, and their multi-modal extensions is given in [Section 2](#s2); here we highlight only that this diversification has produced an ecosystem of specialised models rather than a single general-purpose biomedical LLM, and that multi-modal architectures linking molecules, sequences, and natural language remain an active and unsettled research frontier ([Cao et al., 2023](#B15); [Liu S. et al., 2023](#B74); [Taylor et al., 2022](#B126)).

The emerging impact of LLMs in biomedicine extends beyond individual predictive tasks to encompass entire workflows and research paradigms. Recent work has demonstrated the feasibility of autonomous AI systems capable of designing, executing, and analyzing chemical experiments with minimal human intervention (Boiko et al., 2023). Multi-agent architectures employing specialized LLM agents for different aspects of drug discovery, from literature review and hypothesis generation to molecular design and virtual screening, are beginning to mirror the collaborative nature of real world research teams ([Bran et al., 2024](#B11); [Park et al., 2023](#B95)). These developments suggest a future in which AI systems serve not merely as tools for specific tasks but as collaborative partners in the scientific discovery process, accelerating the pace of biomedical research while potentially democratizing access to sophisticated computational capabilities ([Wang et al., 2023](#B135)). At the same time, the evidence base for these capabilities remains uneven: most reported gains come from benchmark accuracy on retrospective datasets rather than prospective clinical or wet-lab validation, and statements such as “expert-level performance” or “transformative potential” should therefore be read as conditional on the specific dataset, task, and evaluation protocol. As discussed in [Section 7](#s7), claims of expert-level performance on USMLE-style questions ([Singhal et al., 2023](#B120); [Nori et al., 2023](#B90)) are not equivalent to expert-level performance in real clinical workflows, and current AI-designed drug candidates have begun Phase I/II trials but have not yet produced an approved therapeutic ([Xu et al., 2025](#B149)). However, realizing this potential requires careful attention to the limitations and risks associated with LLM deployment in high stakes biomedical applications, including concerns about hallucination, interpretability, data privacy, and algorithmic bias that could perpetuate or exacerbate health disparities ([Thirunavukarasu et al., 2023](#B128); [Obermeyer et al., 2019](#B92); [Gerke et al., 2020](#B40)).

This review provides a comprehensive examination of LLM applications in drug discovery and precision medicine, synthesizing findings from the rapidly evolving literature published between 2018 and 2025. We analyze the technical foundations underlying these approaches, including transformer architectures, pretraining strategies, multi-modal integration methods, and knowledge enhancement techniques. We survey key applications across the drug development pipeline, from early stage target identification through clinical trial design, as well as precision medicine applications spanning clinical decision support, patient stratification, and genomic interpretation. We critically assess current limitations, including challenges related to data quality and availability, model interpretability, hallucination risks, data privacy concerns, computational resource requirements, and ethical considerations. Finally, we discuss future directions that hold promise for advancing the field toward more reliable, transparent, and clinically applicable systems. Our goal is to provide researchers, clinicians, and industry practitioners with a thorough understanding of how LLMs are reshaping biomedical research and clinical practice, while highlighting both the tremendous opportunities and the substantial challenges that must be addressed to realize their full potential for improving human health. The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. [Section 2](#s2) provides background on the evolution of LLMs and their adaptation to biomedical contexts, covering foundational architectures, pretraining strategies, and key design considerations for biological applications. [Section 3](#s3) examines applications in drug discovery, spanning target identification, molecular generation, property prediction, drug repurposing, and integrated discovery pipelines. [Section 4](#s4) discusses precision medicine applications, including clinical decision support, patient stratification, treatment personalization, and genomic interpretation. [Section 5](#s5) presents technical methodologies and architectural innovations that enable these applications. [Section 6](#s6) surveys current applications and case studies demonstrating real world impact. [Section 7](#s7) addresses challenges, limitations, and risks associated with LLM deployment in biomedicine. [Section 8](#s8) explores future directions and emerging opportunities. Finally, [Section 9](#s9) concludes with a synthesis of key insights and recommendations for advancing the field.

## 2 Background and theoretical foundations

### 2.1 Evolution of large language models

Large language models represent the culmination of decades of progress in natural language processing and deep learning, building upon foundational advances in neural network architectures, optimization algorithms, and distributed computing infrastructure ([Vaswani et al., 2017](#B133)). The transformer architecture, introduced by Vaswani and colleagues in 2017, provided the critical innovation enabling modern LLMs through its self-attention mechanism, which allows models to capture long-range dependencies in sequential data without the vanishing gradient problems that plagued earlier recurrent architectures ([Vaswani et al., 2017](#B133)). The self-attention mechanism computes a weighted sum of all positions in a sequence, where the weights are determined by the relevance of each position to the current position being processed, enabling the model to directly attend to any part of the input regardless of distance ([Hays, 2026a](#B46)). This architectural innovation, combined with positional encodings to preserve sequence order information, has proven remarkably effective for modeling both natural language and biological sequences, establishing the foundation for essentially all modern large language models ([Devlin et al., 2019](#B28); [Brown et al., 2020](#B12)).

The evolution of LLMs can be characterized by two complementary paradigms that have shaped the field: bidirectional encoder models exemplified by BERT and autoregressive decoder models exemplified by GPT ([Devlin et al., 2019](#B28); [Radford et al., 2019](#B105)). BERT, introduced by Devlin and colleagues in 2018, employs masked language modeling as its pretraining objective, where the model learns to predict randomly masked tokens in a sequence by attending to context on both sides ([Devlin et al., 2019](#B28)). This bidirectional approach produces rich contextual representations that have proven particularly effective for understanding and classification tasks, where the full context is available at inference time. In contrast, the GPT family of models employs autoregressive language modeling, predicting the next token given all previous tokens, which naturally supports open-ended generation tasks but processes context in only one direction ([Brown et al., 2020](#B12); [Radford et al., 2019](#B105)).

GPT-3, with its 175 billion parameters, demonstrated the remarkable emergent capabilities that arise from scaling model size and training data, including the ability to perform novel tasks through in-context learning without parameter updates ([Brown et al., 2020](#B12)). GPT-4 further extended these capabilities with improved reasoning, reduced hallucination, and multi-modal understanding incorporating both text and images ([OpenAI, 2023](#B93)). The PaLM family from Google demonstrated that further scaling to 540 billion parameters yields additional improvements in reasoning and multilingual capabilities ([Chowdhery et al., 2023](#B22)), while open-source models such as LLaMA and LLaMA-2 have democratized access to capable foundation models that can be fine-tuned for specific applications ([Touvron et al., 2023a](#B129); [Touvron et al., 2023b](#B130)).

A particularly important development in recent years has been the emergence of instruction tuning and reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF) as techniques for aligning LLM behavior with human intentions and values. Rather than simply predicting the next token in training text, instruction-tuned models are trained to follow natural language instructions describing desired tasks, substantially improving their ability to generalize to novel tasks at inference time ([Wei et al., 2022](#B139)). RLHF further refines model outputs by training a reward model on human preferences and then optimizing the language model to produce outputs that maximize predicted reward. These alignment techniques have proven essential for creating models that are helpful, harmless, and honest in their interactions with users, considerations that are particularly important for high-stakes biomedical applications where misleading or harmful outputs could have serious consequences. The combination of massive pretraining, instruction tuning, and human feedback alignment has produced models with unprecedented capabilities for understanding complex queries, following multi-step instructions, and engaging in nuanced reasoning across diverse domains including medicine and biology.

### 2.2 Biomedical language models

Biomedical language models represent specialized LLMs trained on domain-specific data to capture the unique vocabulary, syntactic patterns, and semantic relationships that characterize biomedical domains ([Figure 3](#F3)) ([Lee et al., 2020](#B64); [Gu et al., 2021](#B42)). The biomedical literature contains highly specialized terminology, acronyms, and naming conventions that differ substantially from general English text, and biomedical reasoning often requires understanding complex causal and mechanistic relationships between biological entities ([Peng et al., 2019](#B100)). Early work demonstrated that general-purpose language models pretrained on web text and books underperformed specialized models on biomedical natural language processing tasks, motivating the development of domain-adapted alternatives ([Lee et al., 2020](#B64); Alsentzer et al., 2019). BioBERT, introduced by Lee and colleagues in 2020, pioneered the approach of continued pretraining of BERT on biomedical literature, using PubMed abstracts and PubMed Central full-text articles to adapt the model’s representations to biomedical language ([Lee et al., 2020](#B64)). This relatively simple approach of domain-adaptive pretraining yielded substantial improvements on biomedical benchmarks including named entity recognition, relation extraction, and question answering. PubMedBERT, developed by Gu and colleagues, demonstrated that pretraining from scratch on an in-domain corpus, rather than continued pretraining from a general-domain checkpoint, could yield additional improvements by avoiding the domain shift between general and biomedical vocabularies ([Gu et al., 2021](#B42)). ClinicalBERT adapted the approach specifically for clinical text, pretraining on clinical notes from the MIMIC-III database to capture the distinctive characteristics of clinical documentation including abbreviations, templated language, and references to specific clinical workflows (Alsentzer et al., 2019). These foundational models established biomedical NLP as a distinct subfield with its own benchmarks, datasets, and evaluation protocols.

More recent developments have extended biomedical language models to generative tasks and larger scales. BioGPT, developed by Luo and colleagues, applied the GPT architecture and autoregressive pretraining to biomedical literature, demonstrating state-of-the-art performance on biomedical text generation and question answering tasks ([Luo et al., 2022](#B78)). Med-PaLM and Med-PaLM 2 from Google demonstrated that appropriately prompted and aligned large language models can achieve benchmark-level performance on medical licensing examinations and clinical reasoning benchmarks ([Singhal et al., 2023](#B120)). MEDITRON-70B represents an open-source effort to create a large medical language model by continued pretraining of LLaMA-2 on carefully curated medical literature and guidelines ([Chen et al., 2023](#B19)). These generative models offer capabilities beyond the classification and extraction tasks that characterized earlier work, enabling interactive question answering, clinical decision support, and synthesis of complex medical information.

Biomedical language models are typically pretrained on diverse data sources that provide complementary perspectives on biomedical knowledge:

Scientific literature: PubMed contains over 35 million citations to biomedical literature, with abstracts providing concise summaries of research findings, while PubMed Central provides full-text access to millions of articles enabling richer contextual learning

Clinical documentation: Electronic health records capture the longitudinal medical history of patients, including clinical notes, laboratory results, imaging reports, and medication records that reflect real-world clinical practice

Biomedical databases: Structured resources such as DrugBank, ChEMBL, UniProt, and the Gene Ontology provide curated information about drugs, proteins, genes, and their relationships ([Wishart et al., 2018](#B141); [Mendez et al., 2019](#B85))

Clinical guidelines: Evidence-based practice guidelines from organizations such as the National Comprehensive Cancer Network and the American College of Cardiology codify expert consensus on clinical decision making

Regulatory documents: FDA drug labels, clinical trial protocols, and adverse event reports provide authoritative information on drug safety and efficacy

The choice of pretraining data significantly impacts model capabilities and biases. Models trained primarily on research literature may excel at answering scientific questions but struggle with practical clinical scenarios, while models trained on clinical notes may capture the nuances of clinical practice but lack access to cutting-edge research findings. Increasingly, developers are exploring strategies that combine multiple data sources to create models with broad biomedical competence.

### 2.3 Molecular and protein language models

A particularly exciting development in biomedical AI has been the recognition that molecular structures and biological sequences can be treated as specialized languages, enabling the application of transformer architectures and language modeling techniques to chemical and biological data ([Ross et al., 2022](#B111); [Rives et al., 2021](#B109)). This insight has given rise to a family of molecular and protein language models that learn meaningful representations from sequence data without requiring labeled examples, analogous to how text language models learn from unlabeled corpora. For small molecules, the simplified molecular input line entry system (SMILES) notation provides a text-based representation of molecular structures that can be processed by language models ([Segler et al., 2018](#B117)). ChemBERTa and its successor ChemBERTa-2 apply BERT-style masked language modeling to SMILES strings, learning representations that capture chemical substructure patterns and molecular properties ([Chithrananda et al., 2020](#B20); Ahmad et al., 2022). MolGPT applies autoregressive language modeling to molecular generation, learning to produce valid SMILES strings with desired properties (Bagal et al., 2022). Chemformer uses a sequence-to-sequence transformer architecture for tasks including reaction prediction and retrosynthesis ([Irwin et al., 2022](#B55)). More recent work has explored larger-scale pretraining, demonstrating that neural scaling laws observed in natural language also apply to chemical language models, with larger models exhibiting improved performance on property prediction and generation tasks ([Ross et al., 2022](#B111); [Frey et al., 2023](#B38)).

Protein language models have achieved remarkable success by treating amino acid sequences as natural language and applying similar pretraining strategies. ESM-1b and ESM-2, developed by Meta AI, demonstrated that transformer models pretrained on millions of protein sequences through masked language modeling learn representations that capture evolutionary relationships, protein structure, and functional properties without any explicit structural supervision ([Lin et al., 2023](#B73); [Rives et al., 2021](#B109)). The attention patterns learned by these models correlate with protein contact maps, suggesting that the models implicitly learn three-dimensional structural information from sequence data alone ([Rives et al., 2021](#B109)). ESMFold leverages these learned representations to predict protein structures with accuracy approaching AlphaFold2 for many proteins, while requiring orders of magnitude less computation at inference time ([Lin et al., 2023](#B73)). ProtTrans applied multiple transformer architectures to protein sequences, demonstrating that different architectures capture complementary aspects of protein biology ([Elnaggar et al., 2021](#B32)). ProtGPT2 uses autoregressive language modeling to generate novel protein sequences that fold into stable structures and exhibit desired functional properties ([Ferruz et al., 2022](#B36)). ProGen demonstrated that protein language models can generate functional enzymes across diverse protein families, with some generated sequences experimentally validated to have catalytic activity ([Madani et al., 2023](#B80)). Genomic language models extend similar approaches to DNA and RNA sequences, capturing regulatory patterns and sequence-function relationships. DNABERT applies BERT-style pretraining to DNA sequences, learning representations that improve performance on tasks including promoter prediction, splice site identification, and transcription factor binding site recognition ([Ji et al., 2021](#B57)). DNABERT-2 improves upon this approach with more efficient tokenization and larger-scale pretraining ([Zhou et al., 2023](#B166)). The Nucleotide Transformer represents a particularly large-scale effort, pretraining on genomes from thousands of species to learn representations that capture cross-species evolutionary patterns ([Dalla-Torre et al., 2023](#B26)). HyenaDNA introduces efficient long-range sequence modeling through the Hyena architecture, enabling modeling of sequences up to 1 million nucleotides at single-nucleotide resolution ([Nguyen et al., 2024](#B89)). These genomic language models are enabling new approaches to variant effect prediction, gene expression modeling, and regulatory sequence design.

### 2.4 Multi-modal integration

A critical advancement in biomedical LLMs is the integration of multiple data modalities within unified architectures ([Cao et al., 2023](#B15); [Liu S. et al., 2023](#B74)). Drug discovery and precision medicine inherently involve diverse data types including molecular structures, protein sequences, genomic variants, clinical phenotypes, medical images, and natural language descriptions that must be jointly analyzed for comprehensive understanding. Multi-modal LLMs address this challenge by learning aligned representations across modalities, enabling reasoning that spans different data types. Multi-modal architectures typically employ separate encoders for different data types, with alignment mechanisms that map representations into a shared semantic space where meaningful cross-modal operations become possible ([Liu S. et al., 2023](#B74)). For example, a model might use a graph neural network to encode molecular structures, a transformer to encode protein sequences, and another transformer to encode natural language, with contrastive learning or cross-attention mechanisms to align these representations. The aligned representation space enables capabilities such as text-based molecular retrieval (finding molecules matching a natural language description), molecule captioning (generating natural language descriptions of molecular properties), and cross-modal prediction (predicting molecular properties from text descriptions). InstructMol represents a pioneering approach to multi-modal molecular understanding, aligning molecular structures with natural language through a two-stage instruction-tuning approach ([Cao et al., 2023](#B15)). In the first stage, separate encoders for molecules and text are pretrained on their respective data types. In the second stage, the combined system is fine-tuned on instruction-following tasks that require reasoning across both modalities, such as answering questions about molecules or generating molecules matching text descriptions. This approach enables the model to leverage both the structural information encoded in molecular representations and the semantic knowledge captured in language model representations, bridging the gap between chemical and natural language understanding.

Text-molecule translation represents another approach to multi-modal integration, treating the problem of connecting molecules and language as a machine translation task ([Edwards et al., 2022a](#B30)). Models trained for this task can translate between SMILES representations and natural language descriptions of molecular properties, mechanism of action, or therapeutic indications. MolT5 and related approaches use sequence-to-sequence transformer architectures to perform bidirectional translation between molecules and text, enabling both molecule captioning and text-conditioned molecule generation ([Edwards et al., 2022a](#B30)). More recent work has explored multi-modal molecule-text models that learn to jointly embed molecules and text in a shared space, enabling text-based retrieval and editing of molecules ([Liu S. et al., 2023](#B74)). ChatMol and similar systems provide interactive interfaces for molecular discovery, allowing users to explore chemical space through natural language conversation ([Zeng et al., 2024](#B159)). Beyond molecules, multi-modal integration in biomedicine increasingly encompasses images, structured data, and complex biological entities. Galactica represents an ambitious effort to create a language model capable of scientific reasoning across modalities including text, mathematical equations, chemical formulas, and protein sequences ([Taylor et al., 2022](#B126)). BiomedGPT aims for a unified generalist model capable of handling vision, language, and multi-modal biomedical tasks ([Zhang et al., 2024](#B160)). These efforts toward general-purpose biomedical AI systems suggest a future where a single model can seamlessly integrate information from literature, molecular databases, clinical records, and medical images to support complex biomedical reasoning.

### 2.5 Knowledge-guided approaches

Pure data-driven approaches, while powerful, may struggle with the inherent complexity and sparsity of biomedical data, particularly for rare diseases, novel therapeutic targets, or patient populations underrepresented in training data ([Mohamed et al., 2021](#B87); [Bonner et al., 2022](#B8)). Knowledge-guided LLMs address these limitations by explicitly incorporating structured domain knowledge, including biomedical ontologies, knowledge graphs, and curated databases, to constrain and enhance model reasoning. Biomedical knowledge graphs provide structured representations of entities such as drugs, diseases, genes, proteins, and pathways along with their relationships ([Mohamed et al., 2021](#B87); [Bonner et al., 2022](#B8)). Resources such as DrugBank catalog drug-target interactions and pharmacological properties ([Wishart et al., 2018](#B141)), ChEMBL aggregates bioactivity data from medicinal chemistry literature ([Mendez et al., 2019](#B85)), and disease ontologies like the Disease Ontology and Human Phenotype Ontology provide standardized terminologies for describing diseases and phenotypes. These knowledge resources encode decades of biomedical research in machine-readable form, providing a foundation of reliable information that can ground and constrain LLM reasoning. Integration of knowledge graphs with language models can take several forms. Graph neural networks can be used to encode knowledge graph structure, with the resulting representations incorporated into language model architectures through cross-attention or concatenation ([Mohamed et al., 2021](#B87)). Alternatively, knowledge graph information can be serialized into text and provided as context to the language model, leveraging the model’s text understanding capabilities to reason about structured relationships. Retrieval-augmented approaches retrieve relevant knowledge graph triples based on the input query and include them in the model context, combining the flexibility of language models with the reliability of curated knowledge sources.

Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) represents a particularly promising approach for knowledge enhancement of LLMs ([Lewis et al., 2020](#B68); [Zakka et al., 2024](#B157)). Rather than relying solely on knowledge encoded in model parameters during pretraining, RAG systems retrieve relevant documents or knowledge base entries at inference time and include them in the model’s context. This approach offers several advantages for biomedical applications: it enables access to current information beyond the model’s training cutoff, reduces hallucination by grounding outputs in retrieved evidence, provides transparency through citation of sources, and can be updated simply by changing the retrieval corpus without model retraining ([Hays and Richardson, 2026a](#B48)). Almanac demonstrated the effectiveness of RAG for clinical medicine, using retrieval over medical guidelines and literature to ground clinical recommendations in authoritative sources ([Zakka et al., 2024](#B157)). Benchmarking studies have confirmed that RAG substantially improves accuracy on biomedical question answering tasks while reducing factual errors ([Xiong et al., 2024](#B146)).

### 2.6 Zero-shot and few-shot learning

A distinguishing capability of modern LLMs is their ability to perform zero-shot and few-shot learning, making accurate predictions on novel tasks with minimal or no task-specific training examples ([Brown et al., 2020](#B12); [Kojima et al., 2022](#B62)). This capability emerges from large-scale pretraining, which equips models with broad world knowledge and general-purpose reasoning abilities that can be applied to new situations through appropriate prompting. For biomedical applications, this capability is particularly valuable given the many scenarios where labeled data is scarce or expensive to obtain. Zero-shot learning enables LLMs to perform tasks they have never explicitly been trained on, guided only by natural language descriptions of the task ([Kojima et al., 2022](#B62)). For example, a model might be prompted to classify whether a clinical note indicates a diagnosis of diabetes, without ever having been trained on diabetes classification specifically. The model draws on its general understanding of medical terminology and the relationship between symptoms, tests, and diagnoses to perform the task. Studies have demonstrated that large language models can achieve impressive zero-shot performance on medical licensing examinations, clinical reasoning benchmarks, and biomedical question answering tasks ([Singhal et al., 2023](#B120); [Nori et al., 2023](#B90); [Kung et al., 2023](#B63)). Few-shot learning extends this capability by providing a small number of examples in the prompt that demonstrate the desired input-output mapping ([Brown et al., 2020](#B12)). These examples guide the model toward producing outputs in the desired format and help disambiguate task requirements. Few-shot prompting has proven particularly effective for structured prediction tasks where the output format might be ambiguous from the task description alone. In biomedical contexts, few-shot learning enables rapid adaptation to new prediction tasks without the need for large labeled datasets or model fine-tuning. Chain-of-thought prompting represents an important advancement that improves LLM reasoning on complex tasks by encouraging the model to produce intermediate reasoning steps before reaching a final answer ([Wei et al., 2022](#B139)). Rather than producing an answer directly, the model is prompted (through instructions or examples) to show its work, breaking down complex problems into smaller steps that can be verified. This approach has been shown to substantially improve performance on tasks requiring multi-step reasoning, mathematical calculation, or logical inference. For biomedical applications, chain-of-thought prompting can improve performance on clinical reasoning tasks and provide transparency into the model’s decision-making process, though the generated reasoning chains do not always faithfully reflect the model’s internal computations.

## 3 Large language models in drug discovery

Drug discovery is a complex, multistage process encompassing target identification, hit discovery, lead optimization, preclinical testing, and clinical trials, typically requiring over a decade of effort and billions of dollars in investment before a new therapeutic reaches patients ([DiMasi et al., 2016](#B29); [Wouters et al., 2020](#B142)). The high attrition rate at each stage, with approximately 90% of candidates failing in clinical trials, underscores the need for improved computational methods that can more accurately predict drug efficacy, safety, and pharmacokinetic properties early in the discovery process ([Vamathevan et al., 2019](#B132); [Paul et al., 2021](#B99)). Large language models are being applied across this entire pipeline, offering the potential to accelerate timelines, reduce costs, and improve success rates by leveraging patterns learned from vast amounts of biomedical data (see [Figures 4](#F4)–[8](#F8) for a quantitative overview of architectures, application domains, benchmarks, openness, and reported performance across the 102-model corpus considered in this review). This section examines key applications of LLMs in drug discovery, from early-stage target identification through lead optimization and beyond.

This is a comprehensive review article published in Frontiers in Drug Discovery (August 20, 2026, Volume 6) titled "A survey of LLMs in drug discovery and precision medicine" by Hasi Hays and William J. Richardson from the Department of Chemical Engineering, University of Arkansas. The article surveys state-of-the-art applications of large language models (LLMs) across the drug development pipeline and precision medicine.

**Key Context/Background:**
- Traditional drug discovery takes 10–15 years with costs exceeding $2.6 billion per approved drug
- Approximately 90% of drug candidates fail in clinical trials
- The review synthesizes literature published between 2018 and 2025

**LLM Foundations:**
- Traces evolution from the 2017 transformer architecture (Vaswani et al.) through BERT (bidirectional encoder) and GPT (autoregressive decoder) paradigms
- Covers scaling developments including GPT-3 (175B parameters), GPT-4, PaLM (540B parameters), and open-source models LLaMA/LLaMA-2
- Discusses instruction tuning and reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF) for alignment in high-stakes biomedical applications

**Biomedical Language Models:**
- Domain-adapted text models: BioBERT, PubMedBERT (pretraining from scratch on in-domain corpus), ClinicalBERT (trained on MIMIC-III clinical notes)
- Generative models: BioGPT, Med-PaLM/Med-PaLM 2, MEDITRON-70B
- Pretraining data sources include PubMed (35+ million citations), electronic health records, biomedical databases (DrugBank, ChEMBL, UniProt), clinical guidelines, and regulatory documents

**Molecular and Protein Language Models:**
- Molecule-focused: ChemBERTa (masked language modeling on SMILES), MolGPT, Chemformer (reaction prediction/retrosynthesis)
- Protein models: ESM-1b/ESM-2 (masked language modeling on protein sequences, implicit structural learning), ESMFold (structure prediction approaching AlphaFold2 accuracy with much less computation), ProtGPT2 (novel protein generation), ProGen (functional enzyme generation with experimental validation)
- Genomic models: DNABERT, DNABERT-2, Nucleotide Transformer (cross-species training), HyenaDNA (sequences up to 1 million nucleotides at single-nucleotide resolution)

**Multi-modal Integration:**
- Across modalities: molecules, protein sequences, genomic variants, clinical phenotypes, images, and natural language
- Notable systems: InstructMol (two-stage instruction tuning for molecular understanding), MolT5 (bidirectional text-molecule translation), ChatMol (interactive molecular discovery), Galactica, BiomedGPT

**Knowledge-Guided Approaches:**
- Incorporation of biomedical knowledge graphs (DrugBank, ChEMBL, Disease Ontology, Human Phenotype Ontology)
- Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) as particularly promising: grounds outputs in retrieved evidence, reduces hallucination, enables access to current information, provides citation transparency. Almanac demonstrated effectiveness for clinical medicine.

**Zero-Shot and Few-Shot Learning:**
- Valuable for biomedical contexts where labeled data is scarce
- Chain-of-thought prompting improves multi-step reasoning but generated reasoning chains don't always faithfully reflect internal computations

**Applications in Drug Discovery:**
- Target identification, de novo molecular generation, ADMET property prediction, drug repurposing, and end-to-end discovery pipelines

**Applications in Precision Medicine:**
- Clinical decision support, patient stratification, treatment personalization, genomic interpretation

**Key Caveats/Challenges:**
- Most reported gains come from benchmark accuracy on retrospective datasets rather than prospective clinical or wet-lab validation
- "Expert-level performance" on USMLE-style questions is not equivalent to expert-level performance in real clinical workflows
- Current AI-designed drug candidates have begun Phase I/II trials but no approved therapeutic yet
- Challenges include data privacy, model interpretability, hallucination risks, computational resource requirements, and ethical considerations (algorithmic bias, health disparities)

**Future Directions:**
- Federated learning, explainable artificial intelligence (XAI), integrated multiscale approaches, multi-agent systems, and development of more efficient models

**Includes data visualizations:** evolutionary tree of biomedical LLMs (2018–2025) across encoder-only, encoder-decoder, and decoder-only branches; timeline of 93-102 representative models; domain-coverage heatmaps; benchmark usage charts; and comparative tables of LLM frameworks used in drug discovery and precision medicine.

# FDA AI Guidance 2026: Drug Manufacturing & Digital Health

April 10, 2026  
35 min read

Analyze the FDA CDER 2026 guidance pipeline for artificial intelligence in drug manufacturing and digital health technologies in pharmaceutical development.

IntuitionLabs Report

01

## Executive Summary

The U.S. Food and Drug Administration’s Center for Drug Evaluation and Research (CDER) is actively preparing new guidance documents for 2026 to address emerging technologies in [drug development](https://intuitionlabs.ai/articles/fda-ema-good-ai-practice-drug-development), specifically **[artificial intelligence (AI) in pharmaceutical manufacturing](https://intuitionlabs.ai/articles/ai-pharma-smart-factory-gmp-manufacturing)** and **digital health technologies (DHTs) in drug development**. In late 2025, FDA announced a draft guidance framework for AI models supporting regulatory decisions in drug approvals ([[1]](https://www.fda.gov/news-events/press-announcements/fda-proposes-framework-advance-credibility-ai-models-used-drug-and-biological-product-submissions#:~:text=The%20FDA%20has%20substantial%20experience,data%20from%20digital%20health%20technologies)). Similarly, the agency has begun issuing and planning guidances on [digital health in clinical trials](https://intuitionlabs.ai/articles/decentralized-clinical-trials-platforms-software-guide) (e.g., a December 2023 guidance on remote data acquisition ([[2]](https://www.fda.gov/regulatory-information/search-fda-guidance-documents/digital-health-technologies-remote-data-acquisition-clinical-investigations#:~:text=This%20guidance%20provides%20recommendations%20on,and%20make%20participation%20more%20convenient))) and is soliciting feedback on broader DHT uses via a March 2026 Request-for-Information ([[3]](https://regulations.justia.com/regulations/fedreg/2026/03/31/2026-06184.html#:~:text=DHTs%20are%20systems%20that%20use,describes%20plans%20for)) ([[4]](https://www.raps.org/resource/fda-s-cder-agenda-includes-new-guidance-on-digital.html#:~:text=This%20year%27s%20agenda%20also%20includes,with%20payors%2C%20formulary%20committees%2C%20and)). CDER’s 2026 guidance agenda (released February 2026) explicitly includes new items on digital health in clinical investigations and AI/ML in manufacturing ([[5]](https://www.raps.org/resource/fda-s-cder-agenda-includes-new-guidance-on-digital.html#:~:text=Since%20last%20year%2C%20the%20agenda,Regulatory%20Focus%2023%20January%202025)) ([[6]](https://www.raps.org/resource/fda-s-cder-agenda-includes-new-guidance-on-digital.html#:~:text=New%20guidance%20has%20been%20added,on%20distributed%20manufacturing%20application%20content)).

This comprehensive report examines the background, current status, and future directions of these initiatives. We review historical FDA activities and regulations (including 21st Century Cures Act and FDA’s FRAME initiative) that shape today’s framework, survey both industry and regulatory perspectives, and analyze data on technology adoption. Key guidance documents, workshops, and publications are detailed, alongside [case studies](/resources/case-studies) illustrating AI and digital health in pharmaceuticals. We examine stakeholder feedback (e.g., a May 2025 report on AI in manufacturing ([[7]](https://aapsopen.springeropen.com/articles/10.1186/s41120-025-00110-w#:~:text=FDA%E2%80%99s%20Center%20for%20Drug%20Evaluation,Manufacturing%3A%20An%20Opportunity%20for%20Stakeholder)) ([[8]](https://aapsopen.springeropen.com/articles/10.1186/s41120-025-00110-w#:~:text=parties%20expressed%20a%20desire%20to,AI%20in%20the%20PQS%20framework))), and compare international efforts (such as ICH Q13 for continuous manufacturing and the [EU’s AI Act](https://intuitionlabs.ai/articles/eu-digital-omnibus-pharma-ai-medical-device-compliance)). The report also discusses challenges (data integrity, validation, equity) and forward-looking topics (e.g., FDA’s TemPro pilot for digital devices ([[9]](https://www.fda.gov/news-events/press-announcements/fda-launches-tempo-first-its-kind-digital-health-pilot-expand-access-chronic-disease-technologies#:~:text=The%20U,devices%20while%20safeguarding%20patient%20safety))). We conclude with implications for sponsors, suggestions for regulatory engagement, and prospects for 2026 and beyond.

02

## Introduction and Background

### AI and Digital Health in Pharma: Definitions and Scope

Artificial intelligence (AI) refers to computer-based models that “make predictions, recommendations, or decisions influencing real or virtual environments” ([[10]](https://www.fda.gov/about-fda/center-drug-evaluation-and-research-cder/artificial-intelligence-drug-development#:~:text=Artificial%20Intelligence%20,a%20task%20based%20on%20data)). [Machine learning](/solutions/digital-transformation/process-automation) (ML), a subset of AI, uses data-driven algorithms to improve performance over time ([[11]](https://www.fda.gov/about-fda/center-drug-evaluation-and-research-cder/artificial-intelligence-drug-development#:~:text=such%20perceptions%20into%20models%20through,a%20task%20based%20on%20data)). In drug development, AI/ML can be embedded at multiple stages: identifying drug candidates, optimizing clinical trial designs, analyzing safety data, and automating manufacturing quality control. **Digital health technologies (DHTs)**, a related but distinct category, include mobile apps, wearables (heart-rate monitors, insulin pumps, etc.), and remote sensors that collect health data. When connected to drug development, DHTs can provide remote participant monitoring, novel clinical endpoints, or digital therapeutics that complement drugs. Both AI and DHTs offer opportunities to make drug development more efficient and patient-centered, but also pose unique regulatory challenges around data validity, bias, and integration with existing frameworks ([[12]](https://jamanetwork.com/journals/jama-health-forum/fullarticle/2832434#:~:text=Digital%20health%20technologies%20,room%20sensors%20that%20monitor%20sleep)) ([[1]](https://www.fda.gov/news-events/press-announcements/fda-proposes-framework-advance-credibility-ai-models-used-drug-and-biological-product-submissions#:~:text=The%20FDA%20has%20substantial%20experience,data%20from%20digital%20health%20technologies)).

Over the last decade, innovation in these areas has accelerated. Global spending on digital health is projected to reach tens of billions of dollars by the mid-2020s, and the market for standalone medical software ([[13]](https://intuitionlabs.ai/articles/fda-ai-ml-samd-guidance-compliance)) was roughly $18.5 billion in 2019, growing ~22% annually ([[14]](https://intuitionlabs.ai/articles/fda-digital-health-technology-guidance-requirements#:~:text=Since%20early%202010s%2C%20DHT%20innovation,these%20SaMD%20products%20are%20advanced)). FDA device clearances for software-based products have skyrocketed (581 cumulative SaMD cleared by 2021) ([[15]](https://intuitionlabs.ai/articles/fda-digital-health-technology-guidance-requirements#:~:text=activity%3A%20the%20first%20FDA,and%20monitoring%20systems)). Likewise, AI/ML components are increasingly reported in [FDA submissions](https://intuitionlabs.ai/articles/fda-ai-510k-submission-guidelines-best-practices): by 2021, more than 100 drug and biologic applications contained AI/ML elements ([[16]](https://www.fda.gov/news-events/fda-voices/fda-releases-two-discussion-papers-spur-conversation-about-artificial-intelligence-and-machine#:~:text=The%20regulatory%20uses%20are%20real%3A,technologies%20in%20different%20developmental%20stages)), and CDER has seen “an exponential” rise in submissions using AI since 2016 ([[1]](https://www.fda.gov/news-events/press-announcements/fda-proposes-framework-advance-credibility-ai-models-used-drug-and-biological-product-submissions#:~:text=The%20FDA%20has%20substantial%20experience,data%20from%20digital%20health%20technologies)). These trends underscore the need for regulatory policies that ensure patient safety while accommodating innovation.

### Regulatory Framework: FDA Centers and Legislation

Under the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act (FD&C Act), FDA’s **Center for Drug Evaluation and Research (CDER)** oversees drugs and biological products, while the **Center for Devices and Radiological Health (CDRH)** regulates most digital health devices (including many software-based medical devices). The two centers often collaborate on AI and DHT issues, reflecting their convergence. For example, CDER and CDRH jointly contributed to the January 2025 draft guidance on AI for drug submissions ([[1]](https://www.fda.gov/news-events/press-announcements/fda-proposes-framework-advance-credibility-ai-models-used-drug-and-biological-product-submissions#:~:text=The%20FDA%20has%20substantial%20experience,data%20from%20digital%20health%20technologies)). FDA’s **Digital Health Center of Excellence (DHCoE)**, established in 2017, leads cross-agency efforts on digital health policy.

Key legislative milestones have shaped this space. The 21st Century Cures Act (2016) amended the FD&C Act to **exclude certain software** from the device definition. In particular, “general wellness” apps and many clinical decision support (CDS) functions are exempt from regulation ([[17]](https://intuitionlabs.ai/articles/fda-digital-health-technology-guidance-requirements#:~:text=The%20FDA%20regulates%20DHT%20under,CDS%29%20functions)) ([[18]](https://www.nixonpeabody.com/insights/alerts/2026/01/27/for-2026-fda-signals-shifts-in-digital-health-framework#:~:text=marked%20shift%20in%20the%20agency%E2%80%99s,definition%20of%20a%20medical%20device)). This carve-out has enabled consumer health apps (e.g., fitness trackers) to be sold without FDA clearance, so long as no disease-specific claims are made ([[19]](https://intuitionlabs.ai/articles/fda-digital-health-technology-guidance-requirements#:~:text=Cures%20Act%20,CDS%29%20functions)) ([[18]](https://www.nixonpeabody.com/insights/alerts/2026/01/27/for-2026-fda-signals-shifts-in-digital-health-framework#:~:text=marked%20shift%20in%20the%20agency%E2%80%99s,definition%20of%20a%20medical%20device)). However, higher-risk digital health (like diagnostic software or apps driving treatment) remains in FDA’s remit.

Similarly, government initiatives like the 2022 Food and Drug Omnibus Reform Act (FDORA) and Prescription Drug User Fee Act (PDUFA) VII include mandates for digital/trial modernizations.For instance, PDUFA VII requires FDA to publish a **framework for using DHTs in drug development**, establish a Digital Health Steering Committee, hold public meetings, and fund demonstration projects ([[20]](https://www.fda.gov/science-research/science-and-research-special-topics/digital-health-technologies-dhts-drug-development#:~:text=The%20Prescription%20Drug%20User%20Fee,These%20activities%20include)). The FDORA and infrastructure bills also encourage advanced manufacturing (including continuous and distributed manufacturing and AI-based methods) by launching centers of excellence and pilot programs ([[21]](https://www.agencyiq.com/blog/fda-publishes-discussion-paper-on-ai-in-drug-manufacturing/#:~:text=The%20FDA%20has%20now%20published,AI%29%20AI%20in%20drug)) ([[22]](https://www.fda.gov/about-fda/center-drug-evaluation-and-research-cder/cders-framework-regulatory-advanced-manufacturing-evaluation-frame-initiative#:~:text=,public%20comment%20in%20Fall%202022)).

On digital health, FDA has so far issued multiple guidances: for example, the 2019 “Cures Act Software” guidance explained which apps are excluded ([[23]](https://intuitionlabs.ai/articles/fda-digital-health-technology-guidance-requirements#:~:text=%28,9)). In January 2026, FDA overhauled its General Wellness and CDS guidances ([[24]](https://www.nixonpeabody.com/insights/alerts/2026/01/27/for-2026-fda-signals-shifts-in-digital-health-framework#:~:text=On%20January%206%2C%202026%2C%20the,by%20the%2021st%20Century%20Cures)) ([[25]](https://www.nixonpeabody.com/insights/alerts/2026/01/27/for-2026-fda-signals-shifts-in-digital-health-framework#:~:text=In%20January%206%2C%202026%2C%20remarks%2C,will%20foster%20a%20healthier%20America)), clarifying that many low-risk apps (including wearables that passively measure vital signs) need no pre-market review under certain conditions. FDA also maintains a “List of AI-Enabled Medical Devices” and numerous guidances on software validating, cybersecurity, interoperability, and AI/ML-specific issues ([[26]](https://intuitionlabs.ai/articles/fda-digital-health-technology-guidance-requirements#:~:text=cover%20topics%20such%20as%20mobile,12)) ([[27]](https://jamanetwork.com/journals/jama-health-forum/fullarticle/2832434#:~:text=research,guidance%20emphasizes%20the%20importance%20of)).

On the manufacturing side, CDER’s **FRAME (Framework for Regulatory Advanced Manufacturing Evaluation)** initiative, begun in 2021, is explicitly focused on modern manufacturing technologies (continuous, distributed, point-of-care manufacturing) and AI/ML integration ([[28]](https://www.fda.gov/about-fda/center-drug-evaluation-and-research-cder/cders-framework-regulatory-advanced-manufacturing-evaluation-frame-initiative#:~:text=Advanced%20manufacturing%20technologies%20have%20the,could%20bring%20benefits%20to%20patients)) ([[29]](https://www.fda.gov/about-fda/center-drug-evaluation-and-research-cder/cders-framework-regulatory-advanced-manufacturing-evaluation-frame-initiative#:~:text=at%20healthcare%20facilities.%20,interpret%20data%2C%20and%20decide%20actions)). FRAME has engaged stakeholders through discussion papers and workshops (e.g., on distributed manufacturing in 2022 and AI in 2023) and signals future guidance development ([[30]](https://www.fda.gov/about-fda/center-drug-evaluation-and-research-cder/cders-framework-regulatory-advanced-manufacturing-evaluation-frame-initiative#:~:text=CFR%20211,public%20comment%20in%20Fall%202022)) ([[31]](https://www.fda.gov/about-fda/center-drug-evaluation-and-research-cder/cders-framework-regulatory-advanced-manufacturing-evaluation-frame-initiative#:~:text=1,to%20enable%20timely%20adoption%20of)).

Together, these legislative and policy actions show FDA’s intent to modernize oversight for software, devices, and data-driven methods in line with technological advances, while still upholding safety and efficacy standards.

03

## AI in Pharmaceutical Manufacturing

### Current Landscape and Opportunities

**AI/ML in manufacturing** refers to using data-driven models to optimize production processes. Use cases include **process design/scale-up**, **advanced process control (APC)**, **fault detection**, and **trend analysis** ([[32]](https://www.agencyiq.com/blog/fda-publishes-discussion-paper-on-ai-in-drug-manufacturing/#:~:text=introduction%2C%20FDA%20offers%20a%20%28non,algorithms%20or%20models%20that%20exhibit)) ([[29]](https://www.fda.gov/about-fda/center-drug-evaluation-and-research-cder/cders-framework-regulatory-advanced-manufacturing-evaluation-frame-initiative#:~:text=at%20healthcare%20facilities.%20,interpret%20data%2C%20and%20decide%20actions)). In practice, AI can analyze large volumes of real-time sensor and process data to predict equipment failures (predictive maintenance), detect product quality deviations early, and adjust control parameters automatically. For example, *soft sensors* powered by ML can infer difficult-to-measure attributes (e.g., blend uniformity) from correlated signals ([[33]](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0022354926000894#:~:text=Artificial%20intelligence%20,for%20successful%20implementation%20within%20regulated)). A 2026 review notes that combining AI with Process Analytical Technology (PAT) and Quality-by-Design (QbD) enables anomaly detection and advanced control systems in both small-molecule and biologic plants ([[33]](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0022354926000894#:~:text=Artificial%20intelligence%20,for%20successful%20implementation%20within%20regulated)).

Major pharmaceutical manufacturers and CMOs are piloting such technologies. For instance, **Perrigo** (a generics/OTC producer) reported deploying AI-driven predictive maintenance systems on facility equipment to reduce downtime, and real-time image analysis to flag manufacturing defects ([[34]](https://www.cash-platform.com/leveraging-artificial-intelligence-in-pharmaceutical-manufacturing-a-case-study-of-perrigo-company-plc/#:~:text=AI,Perrigo%20employs%20AI%20for)) (predictive maintenance and quality control). Digital “twins” – virtual replicas of production lines – are another example: they allow simulation of process changes without risking real batches. Industry conferences and trade publications frequently highlight AI applications in equipment monitoring, robotics, and supply chain logistics ([[35]](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0022354926000894#:~:text=Studies%2C%20and%20GxP%20Implementation%20Considerations,AI)) ([[34]](https://www.cash-platform.com/leveraging-artificial-intelligence-in-pharmaceutical-manufacturing-a-case-study-of-perrigo-company-plc/#:~:text=AI,Perrigo%20employs%20AI%20for)). These case studies (while often proprietary) illustrate the potential for AI to enhance yield, consistency, and efficiency.

From a quantitative perspective, investments in AI for pharma manufacturing are rapidly growing. A November 2021 National Academies report identified AI-based advanced process controls as a key innovation likely in the next 5–10 years ([[36]](https://www.agencyiq.com/blog/fda-publishes-discussion-paper-on-ai-in-drug-manufacturing/#:~:text=,the%20utility%20of%20the%20high)). That report recommended FDA build expertise to oversee such technologies. Likewise, supply chain disruptions during COVID-19 underscored the need for agility (e.g., via distributed manufacturing and AI-driven forecasting) ([[37]](https://www.agencyiq.com/blog/fda-publishes-discussion-paper-on-ai-in-drug-manufacturing/#:~:text=,these%20new%20technologies%20may%20run)). While exact numbers on industry adoption are scarce (as many projects are internal), the rapid increase in AI-related regulatory engagements suggests momentum: CDER’s Emerging Technology Program (ETP) has fielded hundreds of inquiries on AI-enabled manufacturing, and FDA reports over 500 drug/biologic submissions with AI components from 2016–2023 ([[1]](https://www.fda.gov/news-events/press-announcements/fda-proposes-framework-advance-credibility-ai-models-used-drug-and-biological-product-submissions#:~:text=The%20FDA%20has%20substantial%20experience,data%20from%20digital%20health%20technologies)). In short, AI in manufacturing offers improved quality and reduced costs, but has been slow to deploy due to technical and regulatory hurdles.

### Regulatory Initiatives and Guidance

FDA’s **FRAME Initiative** provides the primary regulatory context for AI in manufacturing. As of 2023, FRAME has prioritized AI alongside continuous and distributed manufacturing ([[29]](https://www.fda.gov/about-fda/center-drug-evaluation-and-research-cder/cders-framework-regulatory-advanced-manufacturing-evaluation-frame-initiative#:~:text=at%20healthcare%20facilities.%20,interpret%20data%2C%20and%20decide%20actions)). In March 2023, CDER published a **discussion paper** “Artificial Intelligence in Drug Manufacturing” for public comment ([[38]](https://aapsopen.springeropen.com/articles/10.1186/s41120-025-00110-w#:~:text=technologies%20that%20could%20benefit%20patients,This%20paper%20summarizes%20public%20feedback)) ([[22]](https://www.fda.gov/about-fda/center-drug-evaluation-and-research-cder/cders-framework-regulatory-advanced-manufacturing-evaluation-frame-initiative#:~:text=,public%20comment%20in%20Fall%202022)). This paper (linked from FRAME’s website) defines Industry 4.0 concepts and proposes areas where AI could apply (process scale-up, process control, monitoring, etc.) ([[32]](https://www.agencyiq.com/blog/fda-publishes-discussion-paper-on-ai-in-drug-manufacturing/#:~:text=introduction%2C%20FDA%20offers%20a%20%28non,algorithms%20or%20models%20that%20exhibit)). It identifies five “areas of consideration” for regulatory policy, including cloud computing, IoT data management, oversight scopes, validation standards, and data integrity ([[39]](https://www.agencyiq.com/blog/fda-publishes-discussion-paper-on-ai-in-drug-manufacturing/#:~:text=touched%20upon%20by%20the%20introduction,The%20paper%20further%20acknowledges)) ([[40]](https://www.agencyiq.com/blog/fda-publishes-discussion-paper-on-ai-in-drug-manufacturing/#:~:text=reorganization,policy%20approaches%20may%20be%20needed)). The goal was to gather feedback on regulatory bottlenecks.

Following that, FDA held a **public workshop** on Sept 26–27, 2023 (joint with PQRI) to engage stakeholders on the regulatory framework for AI in pharmaceutical manufacturing ([[41]](https://aapsopen.springeropen.com/articles/10.1186/s41120-025-00110-w#:~:text=pharmaceutical%20manufacturing%20capabilities,This%20paper%20summarizes%20public%20feedback)) ([[42]](https://www.fda.gov/about-fda/center-drug-evaluation-and-research-cder/cders-framework-regulatory-advanced-manufacturing-evaluation-frame-initiative#:~:text=Action%20Plan%20,2023%2C%20as%20a%20virtual%20event)). CDER leadership (Dr. Patrizia Cavazzoni) emphasized in remarks that AI/ML can bring “safe, effective, and high-quality treatments to patients faster” ([[43]](https://www.fda.gov/news-events/fda-voices/fda-releases-two-discussion-papers-spur-conversation-about-artificial-intelligence-and-machine#:~:text=AI%2FML%E2%80%99s%20growth%20in%20data%20volume,quality%20treatments%20to%20patients%20faster)), but also flagged ethical and data bias concerns ([[44]](https://www.fda.gov/news-events/fda-voices/fda-releases-two-discussion-papers-spur-conversation-about-artificial-intelligence-and-machine#:~:text=As%20with%20other%20evolving%20fields,has%20released%20a%20discussion%20paper)). The workshop addressed topics like risk-based validation of AI/ML models, data governance, and integration into the pharma quality system (PQS).

In the wake of these activities, FDA collected stakeholder feedback. An open-access summary (AAPS Open, May 2025) synthesized public comments from the AI manufacturing discussion paper and workshop ([[38]](https://aapsopen.springeropen.com/articles/10.1186/s41120-025-00110-w#:~:text=technologies%20that%20could%20benefit%20patients,This%20paper%20summarizes%20public%20feedback)) ([[8]](https://aapsopen.springeropen.com/articles/10.1186/s41120-025-00110-w#:~:text=parties%20expressed%20a%20desire%20to,AI%20in%20the%20PQS%20framework)). Key findings included industry desire for clear guidance and global harmonization: respondents emphasized good data management, model validation best practices, and uncertainty about integrating AI into existing Quality Systems ([[8]](https://aapsopen.springeropen.com/articles/10.1186/s41120-025-00110-w#:~:text=parties%20expressed%20a%20desire%20to,AI%20in%20the%20PQS%20framework)). They expressed concerns about explainability of complex models, use of third-party data, and meeting CGMP requirements with novel technologies. The consensus was that AI models need robust lifecycle plans and should align with current strategies for drug quality. This feedback is being used by FDA to shape further policy.

Building on stakeholder input, CDER’s **2026 Guidance Agenda** (issued Feb 2026) lists draft guidances related to advanced manufacturing. Notably, it includes *“AI/ML Quality Considerations in Pharmaceutical Manufacturing”* under the Pharmaceutical Quality/CMC category ([[6]](https://www.raps.org/resource/fda-s-cder-agenda-includes-new-guidance-on-digital.html#:~:text=New%20guidance%20has%20been%20added,on%20distributed%20manufacturing%20application%20content)). This upcoming guidance will likely address how to ensure product quality when AI models are part of manufacturing controls. Also on the agenda is guidance on *“Distributed Manufacturing Application Content,”* reflecting interest in decentralized production ([[6]](https://www.raps.org/resource/fda-s-cder-agenda-includes-new-guidance-on-digital.html#:~:text=New%20guidance%20has%20been%20added,on%20distributed%20manufacturing%20application%20content)). While FDA cautioned that the agenda is not binding, these inclusions confirm that guidance on AI in manufacturing is imminent.

To date, FDA has not yet issued binding regulation on AI in manufacturing, but it has several related activities. For example, in January 2025, FDA issued a draft guidance on **“Advanced Approaches to Pharmaceutical Manufacturing and Distribution”** (21 CFR 211.110 compliance) ([[45]](https://www.fda.gov/about-fda/center-drug-evaluation-and-research-cder/cders-framework-regulatory-advanced-manufacturing-evaluation-frame-initiative#:~:text=,of%20Drugs%3A%20Stakeholder%20Feedback%20and)). FRAME’s website also links to final documents like a Stakeholder Feedback report (Nov 2023) and a forthcoming ICH Q13 guideline adoption. FDA’s collaboration with International groups (e.g., ICH’s continuous manufacturing guideline) and acknowledgment of Industry 4.0 concepts suggest it is moving toward explicit policies. The planned 2026 AI manufacturing guidance will likely clarify verification of AI models, data integrity in cloud/IoT systems, and how CGMP inspections adapt to advanced data flows ([[46]](https://www.agencyiq.com/blog/fda-publishes-discussion-paper-on-ai-in-drug-manufacturing/#:~:text=,occur%20in%20the)) ([[40]](https://www.agencyiq.com/blog/fda-publishes-discussion-paper-on-ai-in-drug-manufacturing/#:~:text=reorganization,policy%20approaches%20may%20be%20needed)).

**International and Industry Perspectives:** Globally, pharma regulators similarly recognize AI’s role. The ICH has begun updating guidelines (e.g., Q13 on continuous manufacturing) that are AI-enabled. Other regulators (EMA’s advanced manufacturing working groups) are exploring analogous frameworks. Industry usually supports harmonized guidance; for instance, a global consortium (industry & academies) advocates for AI models consistent with QbD principles and risk-based validation. Many companies note that without clear FDA expectations, investment in AI is risky. Congress has also encouraged FDA technical capacity for overseeing these technologies ([[47]](https://www.agencyiq.com/blog/fda-publishes-discussion-paper-on-ai-in-drug-manufacturing/#:~:text=a%20manufacturing%20or%20production%20system,to%20be%20aligned%20toward%20innovation)). Thus, as guidance emerges in the U.S., it likely will align with international standards to facilitate global drug production.

### Case Studies and Examples

While FDA’s pipeline is primarily policy-focused, real-world examples illustrate AI’s impact. In one case, a company implemented ML-driven process control in continuous manufacturing: by analyzing real-time spectra data, AI adjusted process parameters to maintain critical quality attributes within tighter limits ([[33]](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0022354926000894#:~:text=Artificial%20intelligence%20,for%20successful%20implementation%20within%20regulated)). In another, a biologics manufacturer uses image-recognition AI to inspect cell culture bags for contamination, reducing manual inspection time. A published case study of Perrigo (a generics maker) describes using AI for predictive maintenance (forecasting equipment failures from sensor data) and for in-line imaging to detect defective pills ([[34]](https://www.cash-platform.com/leveraging-artificial-intelligence-in-pharmaceutical-manufacturing-a-case-study-of-perrigo-company-plc/#:~:text=AI,Perrigo%20employs%20AI%20for)). In R&D, firms use AI for **digital twins** that simulate scale-up from lab to plant, though implementation is still emerging.

In regulatory submissions, manufacturers have started including AI data: for instance, some have proposed using AI to analyze near-infrared spectroscopy for blend uniformity, replacing time-consuming lab assays. FDA has reviewed such submissions using its emerging credibility framework ([[48]](https://www.fda.gov/regulatory-information/search-fda-guidance-documents/considerations-use-artificial-intelligence-support-regulatory-decision-making-drug-and-biological#:~:text=This%20guidance%20provides%20recommendations%20to,COU)) and has worked with sponsors via its Emerging Technology Program. These pilot programs demonstrate feasibility but also continuous monitoring needs: AI models may “drift” as processes change, so maintaining trust is an open concern. The forthcoming FDA guidance on credibility will directly address expectations for model validation, adaptation, and documentation ([[48]](https://www.fda.gov/regulatory-information/search-fda-guidance-documents/considerations-use-artificial-intelligence-support-regulatory-decision-making-drug-and-biological#:~:text=This%20guidance%20provides%20recommendations%20to,COU)) ([[1]](https://www.fda.gov/news-events/press-announcements/fda-proposes-framework-advance-credibility-ai-models-used-drug-and-biological-product-submissions#:~:text=The%20FDA%20has%20substantial%20experience,data%20from%20digital%20health%20technologies)).
