args.summary:
The European Commission has published draft guidelines to help companies determine whether their products, including AI-incorporated medical devices, are classified as high-risk under the EU's Artificial Intelligence Act (AI Act). For devices subject to the AI Act, these requirements will layer on top of (rather than replace) existing obligations under the Medical Device Regulation (MDR) and In Vitro Diagnostic Regulation (IVDR).

Key dates: The AI Act takes effect on 2 December 2027 for stand-alone high-risk AI systems and 2 August 2028 for high-risk AI systems embedded in products. The deadline for submitting comments on the draft guidelines is 23 June.

The Commission published three separate guidelines: (1) general principles on determining whether an AI system is high-risk, (2) guidance on Annex I of the Act, and (3) guidance on Annex III (148 pages). Under Article 6, an AI system is high-risk if intended as a safety component of a product (or is itself a product) covered by Annex I harmonisation legislation requiring third-party conformity assessment. The guidelines clarify the classification process but do not specify device types, which is why they appear broad.

The Annex I guidance defines "safety function" as including preventive/mitigative functionalities such as monitoring and detection of situations that may lead to physical harm. Products covered include safety components of machinery, toys, lifts, medical devices, IVDs, and products in automotive and aviation sectors. The Annex III guidance notes that emergency healthcare patient triage systems may qualify as medical devices and be classified as high-risk.

Expert commentary: Nils Lölfing, an AI attorney at Bird & Bird in Germany, explained that AI medical devices are high-risk when they are either a device in their own right (e.g., software analyzing scans to flag/diagnose diseases) or a safety component of one (e.g., AI regulating dosing in an infusion pump), where the device needs notified body sign-off (roughly Class IIa and above under MDR, and most IVDs). Simple, self-certified Class I devices fall outside the high-risk category.

Two reforms aim to prevent dual regulation:
1. The Digital Omnibus on AI keeps medical devices under the AI Act but postpones high-risk obligations until August 2028 and allows delegated acts to exempt AI Act requirements where MDR/IVDR already mandate the same standards (agreement reached but not yet formally adopted).
2. A planned MDR/IVDR revision (issued December 2025) would make device rules the main rulebook, handling AI requirements within normal device approval rather than a separate AI Act process.

Lölfing recommended evidencing AI-specific points (data governance, robustness, human oversight) through MDR/IVDR documentation instead of a separate AI Act exercise. According to a 2024 IQVIA blog post, a large segment of AI's use in healthcare would be classified as high-risk under the Act.

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage is a Mayo Clinic research publication describing DRPLLM (Drug Response Prediction using Large Language Model), a novel framework for predicting cancer drug responses using multi-omics data. DRPLLM integrates the Llama-8b large language model (LLM) with a deep neural network (DNN) regression head, using embeddings from cell line gene expression, mutations, and drug properties formatted into natural language prompts. It was trained on the Genomics of Drug Sensitivity in Cancer v2 and Cancer Cell Line Encyclopedia datasets. The framework achieved a Spearman rank correlation coefficient (SCC) of 0.71, improving to 0.74 after hyperparameter optimization. Validation on a patient-derived xenograft (PDX) cohort showed the embedding-based approach significantly outperformed traditional prompt-engineering (SCC = 0.45, p < 1e-16 versus SCC = 0.06, p > 0.05), demonstrating its potential for accurate, generalizable drug response predictions in precision oncology.

The work is a conference contribution presented at the 17th International Conference on Bioinformatics and Computational Biology (BICOB 2025), held March 17, 2025 in San Francisco, United States. It was published in 2025 in the proceedings "Bioinformatics and Computational Biology" (Communications in Computer and Information Science, Volume 2535 CCIS) by Springer Science and Business Media Deutschland GmbH, pages 189-203. Authors include Rohan Gnanaolivu, Priyanka Vasanthakumari, Brenna C. Novotny, Jamie C. Overbeek, Yuanhang Liu, Alexander Partin, Nicholas D. Chia, Yitan Zhu, and Chen Wang. The paper proposes GraphTCDR, a model based on heterogeneous graph neural networks and multi-omics data for predicting cancer drug responses. The methodology involves: (1) constructing a cell line-drug heterogeneous network using multi-omics data and drug features as node attributes, (2) conducting node feature learning on the heterogeneous network, and (3) feeding learned features into fully connected layers to predict IC50 values.

Key technical details: The model integrates cell line genomic, epigenomic, and transcriptomic profiles (gene expression, CNV, and miRNA data) along with drug molecular fingerprints. High-dimensional omics data undergo dimensionality reduction via an autoencoder, while molecular fingerprints are processed using one-dimensional convolutional networks as drug node features. A heterogeneous graph Transformer architecture encodes the constructed network. Cell line and drug similarity networks are built through correlation analysis of DNA methylation profiles and molecular fingerprint data.

Results: Extensive experiments on the PRISM database (distinct from GDSC or CCLE) demonstrate GraphTCDR outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods across all evaluation metrics. Compared to the current best-performing model, GraphTCDR achieves improvements of 3.60% in PCC, 4.30% in SCC, 6.50% in R², and a 1.60% reduction in RMSE. It was compared against traditional deep learning methods (MLP, CNN), an advanced deep learning method (DeepTTA), and graph neural network methods (DeepCDR, NerD, GraphDRP). GraphTCDR maintains stable performance even with reduced training data, demonstrating superior robustness.

The paper highlights three key contributions: constructing a heterogeneous cell-drug graph network with heterogeneous graph Transformer for cancer drug response prediction; integrating multi-omics data for more biologically relevant and robust cell line feature learning; and utilizing the PRISM database, which is distinct from GDSC/CCLE and holds promise for discovering new anticancer medications.

## scDrugMap: Benchmarking Large Foundation Models for Drug Response Prediction

This is a scientific research article (arXiv preprint, May 8, 2025, PMCID: PMC12083700, PMID: 40386575) from the University of Florida, Houston Methodist Research Institute, and Weill Cornell Medicine, authored by Qing Wang, Yining Pan, Minghao Zhou (equal contribution), Zijia Tang, Yanfei Wang, Guangyu Wang, and Qianqian Song (corresponding author: qsong1@ufl.edu). The work is licensed under Creative Commons Attribution-NonCommercial-NoDerivatives 4.0.

### Purpose
The study addresses drug resistance as a major barrier to effective cancer therapy, noting that of 85 FDA-approved cancer drugs, the median response rate is 41%, with nearly half below 40% and two-thirds showing complete response rates below 10%. The authors developed **scDrugMap**, the first comprehensive benchmarking framework evaluating ten large foundation models (eight single-cell-specific and two general-purpose language models) for drug response prediction from single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) data.

### Data Resources
- **Primary collection**: 326,751 cells from 36 single-cell datasets across 23 studies
- **Validation collection**: 18,856 cells from 17 datasets across 6 studies
- Total: 345,607 single cells spanning 14 cancer types, 3 therapy types, 5 tissue types, and 21 treatment regimens
- Models evaluated: eight single-cell foundation models (tGPT, scBERT, Geneformer, cellLM, scFoundation, scGPT, cellPLM, UCE) and two LLMs (LLaMa3-8B and GPT4o-mini)

### Methods
Two evaluation scenarios were used:
1. **Pooled-data evaluation**: Models trained and tested on aggregated data from multiple studies
2. **Cross-data evaluation**: Models trained on certain studies and tested on independent, unseen datasets

Two training strategies were applied: **layer-freezing** (averaged token embeddings passed to MLP classifier) and **fine-tuning** using **Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA)** (rank 8, alpha 8, dropout 0.05). GPT4o-mini was assessed via zero-shot prompt engineering.

### Key Results
- **Pooled-data evaluation**: scFoundation outperformed all others, achieving highest mean F1 scores of 0.971 (layer-freezing) and 0.947 (fine-tuning), outperforming the lowest-performing model by 54% and 57% respectively. scBERT performed worst.
- **Fine-tuning generally outperformed layer-freezing** across models.
- **Cross-data evaluation**: UCE achieved the highest performance (mean F1: 0.774) after fine-tuning on tumor tissue; scGPT showed superior performance (mean F1: 0.858) in zero-shot learning on tumor tissue. scFoundation showed reduced generalizability in cross-data settings.
- **GPT4o-mini** showed limited performance (near or below baseline in most settings), with its best performance in liver cancer (mean F1: 0.690) and notably poor results in pancreatic cancer (0.190) and melanoma (0.320).
- **Validation data**: scFoundation demonstrated the best performance across all categories (cell line: 0.901, tumor tissue: 0.965, organoid: 0.951 F1).
- UMAP visualizations revealed scFoundation, UCE, and scGPT effectively distinguished drug-resistant and drug-sensitive cells.

### Computational Scalability
scFoundation (encoder-decoder, 121.2 million parameters, output dimension 3,072) demonstrated the most efficient training (23.26 it/s) and inference (69.98 it/s) speeds. scGPT had 52.5M parameters and was less efficient (1.43 it/s training, 1.44 it/s inference).

### Availability
scDrugMap is available as a Python command-line tool and an interactive web server at https://scdrugmap.com/.

### Study Contributions
1. Model selection guidance based on dataset characteristics and evaluation scenarios
2. An integrated, interactive tool for drug response prediction, biomarker discovery, and resistance mechanism analysis
3. A benchmark framework to inform future drug discovery research

### Future Directions
The authors identify needs for: incorporating domain-specific knowledge into model training, integrating multi-modal data (transcriptomic, proteomic, genomic), exploring hybrid models combining single-cell and natural language foundation models, and incorporating explainable AI techniques for better model interpretability.

URL: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12499773

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a scientific review article published in Briefings in Bioinformatics (2025 Oct 06;26(5):bbaf533, doi: 10.1093/bib/bbaf533, PMCID: PMC12499773, PMID: 41052279) titled "Computational toxicology in drug discovery: applications of artificial intelligence in ADMET and toxicity prediction." Authors: Jiangyan Zhang, Haolin Li, Yuncong Zhang (contributed equally), Junyang Huang, Liping Ren, Chuantao Zhang, Quan Zou, and Yang Zhang. Corresponding authors are from the Hospital of Chengdu University of Traditional Chinese Medicine and the University of Electronic Science and Technology of China. The article is Open Access under a Creative Commons Attribution Non-Commercial License.

Key content and findings:
- Toxicity risk assessment is crucial for clinical success and market potential of drug candidates; ~30% of preclinical candidate compounds (PCCs) fail due to toxicity, and ~40% of preclinical candidate drugs fail due to insufficient ADMET profiles, while nearly 30% of marketed drugs are withdrawn due to unforeseen toxic reactions.
- Traditional animal testing is costly, time-consuming (6–24 months per test), expensive (often exceeding millions of dollars per compound), and ethically controversial (3Rs principle: replacement, reduction, refinement), driving the shift to computational toxicology.
- The review surveys over 20 ADMET prediction platforms, categorized into three types: rule/statistical-based methods, machine learning (ML) methods, and graph-based methods.
- Broad-spectrum platforms mentioned: admetSAR 3.0, ADMETlab 3.0, vNN-ADMET, ADMETboost, Deep-PK; pharmacokinetic-focused platforms: Swiss ADME, FAF-Drugs4.0, ADMET-AI; toxicity-focused platforms: ProTox 3.0, VenomPred 2.0; CYP450-related tools: CypRules, BioTransformer 3.0, XenoSite, SOMP, SMARTCyp 3.0.
- The ADMET prediction platform framework consists of: input component (chemical structural data, experimental data, literature-derived data), tools/methods component (physicochemical property calculation via RDKit/Scopy, and ML/AI prediction module using SVMs, RFs, neural networks, gradient boosting trees), and output component (endpoints; comprehensive platforms can evaluate over 100 endpoints).
- ML methods (e.g., vNN-ADMET, ADMETboost with XGBoost, ProTox 3.0 with RF/DNN) handle complex patterns but depend on high-quality training data. Graph-based methods (GNNs: ADMET-AI, Interpretable-ADMET, HelixADMET, ADMETlab 3.0 with DMPNN, admetSAR 3.0, pkCSM) analyze molecular graph structures but require substantial computational resources and large training datasets.
- Toxicological databases are classified into four categories: chemical toxicity databases, environmental toxicology databases, alternative toxicology databases, and biological toxin databases.
- Chemical toxicity databases include PubChem (>119 million compounds, NIH-maintained), ChEMBL (>2.1 million, EMBL-EBI), HSDB (~5600 chemicals), CCRIS (>9000, carcinogenicity/mutagenicity), CompTox Chemicals Dashboard (EPA), TOXRIC (113,372 compounds, ML-ready), SuperToxic (~60,000), DrugBank, and specialized databases DILIrank, DILIst, LTKB (hepatotoxicity), hERGCentral (cardiotoxicity), and LCDB (carcinogenicity data from 1726 chemicals and 7745 experimental records).
- The field is transitioning from single-endpoint predictions to multi-endpoint joint modeling with multimodal features, incorporating generative modeling and interpretability frameworks.
- Network toxicology is applied to evaluate safety of traditional Chinese medicines (TCMs), and large language models (LLMs) show potential in literature mining, knowledge integration, and molecular toxicity prediction.
- Current challenges include data quality, model interpretability, and causal inference; future directions include multi-omics integration, interpretable AI models, and domain-specific LLMs for more efficient and precise preclinical toxicity assessments.
</summary>

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a review article published in Frontiers in Chemistry (July 8, 2025) titled "Recent advances in AI-based toxicity prediction for drug discovery" by Hyundo Lee, Jisan Kim, Ji-Woon Kim, and Yoonji Lee. The article provides an in-depth examination of AI-driven toxicity prediction in drug discovery and its impact on improving safety assessments.

KEY TOPICS COVERED:

**Background/Context:** Toxicity failures in late-stage drug development lead to substantial financial losses, driving the need for reliable early toxicity prediction. AI models can predict various toxicity endpoints (hepatotoxicity, cardiotoxicity, nephrotoxicity, neurotoxicity, genotoxicity) using diverse molecular representations from traditional descriptors to graph-based methods. The workflow includes four stages: data collection, preprocessing, model development, and evaluation. A virtuous cycle is created by integrating AI predictions into virtual screening and feeding experimental outcomes back to improve models.

**Benchmark Datasets:** Key public datasets include:
- Tox21 (8,249 compounds across 12 biological targets)
- ToxCast (~4,746 chemicals across hundreds of endpoints)
- ClinTox (approved vs. failed drugs)
- hERG datasets (over 13,000 compounds; hERG Central has 300,000+ records)
- DILIrank (475 compounds for liver toxicity)
- SIDER (1,400+ marketed drugs with side effect annotations)
- AMES (7,255 compounds for mutagenicity)
- Carcinogens (278 compounds)
- LD50_Zhu (7,385 compounds, regression modeling)
- Challenges include data scarcity, protocol heterogeneity, class imbalance, and annotation noise.

**General ADMET Tools:** ADMETLab 3.0 (119 endpoints, DMPNNs, AUROC ~0.94 for hERG), Deep-PK (73 endpoints, 35 toxicity-related), ProTox 3.0 (61 predictive models, integrates AOPs), Helix-ADMET (self-supervised and multi-task learning), FP-ADMET (50+ endpoints, random forest with 20 fingerprint types), and admetSAR 2.0 (47 endpoints, traditional ML algorithms).

**Endpoint-Specific Models:**
- *Hepatotoxicity:* InterDILI (2024, AUROC 0.97 hold-out), DILI Predictor (2024, two-stage approach with proxy-DILI labels), GeoDILI (2023, GeoGNN+ResNet, AUROC 0.908), OvA-QSTR (2023, one-vs-all strategy), Rao et al. (2023, physicochemical + off-target profiles), ResNet18DNN (2022, converts SMILES to molecular images, AUROC 0.958).
- *Cardiotoxicity:* hERGBoost (2025, XGBoost regression, R²=0.622), hERGAT (2025, GAT+GRU, AUROC 0.907), AttenhERG (2024, GNN with uncertainty estimation, AUROC 0.835), DMFGAM (2023, multimodal fingerprints+graph, AUROC 0.894), CardioToxNet (2021, meta-ensemble of GCN/FCNN/1D-CNN), DeepHIT (2020, minimizes false negatives, includes safer analog generation).
- *Nephrotoxicity:* Gong et al. (2022, fingerprints of chemical drugs and herbal medicines, AUROC 0.915), Shi et al. (2022, consensus model, AUROC 0.93), Zhang et al. (2019, Naïve Bayes classifier, accuracy 0.84). Traditional ML models perform better than deep learning when data are limited.
- *Neurotoxicity:* Studies develop multiple models for distinct tasks including BBB permeability, neuronal cytotoxicity, and general neurotoxicity, using DMPNN, MFBERT, MLP, and tree-based methods.

**Key Facts on Toxicity Incidence:** Drug-induced nephrotoxicity affects 14-26% of adults; drug-induced renal failure accounts for ~25% of acute kidney injury cases in hospitalized patients. Liver toxicity agreement between animals and humans averages ~55%. The FDA issued boxed warnings in 2021 for JAK inhibitors (tofacitinib, baricitinib, upadacitinib) due to cardiovascular risks. hERG evaluation is required per ICH S7B guidelines.

**Methodological Observations:** GNNs align well with graph-based molecular structures and enable substructure identification. Transformer-based models show promise in cheminformatics. --- SOURCE 4: The future of large language models in toxicological risk assessment: Opportunities and challenges ---
URL: https://www.publichealthtoxicology.com/The-future-of-large-language-models-in-toxicological-risk-assessment-Opportunities,202241,0,2.html

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a Letter to the Editor published in Public Health Toxicology (2025;5(1):3, DOI: 10.18332/pht/202241) authored by Ananth R. Kattamreddy (University of Eastern Finland, Kuopio) and Harisrujan Chinnam (Tampere University), published on February 28, 2025. The letter discusses the opportunities and challenges of large language models (LLMs) in toxicological risk assessment (RA).

**Key Points:**

- **Context:** Traditional risk assessment has used single-stressor models evaluating chemicals in isolation, but the field is evolving with real-life risk simulation (RLRS), multi-stressor approaches, and dynamic exposure modeling. The post-COVID AI era has created unprecedented pressure to shorten turnaround times for market authorization of new substances.

- **Current AI Applications:** Quantitative Structure-Activity Relationship (QSAR) modeling using regression, random forests, and support vector machines is already an accepted AI approach. Predictive toxicology models like DeepTox have shown promise in risk characterization. LLMs can be trained/fine-tuned on public repositories including PubChem, ChEMBL, ACToR, and Tox21/ToxCast.

- **EFSA AI4NAMS Project:** The European Food Safety Authority investigated LLM potential in toxicology by benchmarking LLM performance on Bisphenol A (BPA) data. A fine-tuned Curie (GPT-3) outperformed out-of-the-box models (text-davinci-002 and text-davinci-003) due to its domain knowledge and structured response features. Recent models like GPT-4 and GPT-4o have improved contextual understanding, but performance degrades on extremely long documents.

- **Practical Applications:** LLMs could streamline dossier preparation under REACH regulations, reducing the manpower needed. Regulatory agencies like ECHA could use LLMs to automate back-end review and integration of submitted dossiers. The authors propose fine-tuning separate LLM models tailored to specific regulatory frameworks (EFSA-EU, REACH-EU, EPA-US) and different compound classes (pesticides, pharmaceuticals, industrial chemicals).

- **Human Role:** The authors emphasize that LLMs should not replace human decision-making. "The LLM role is to collate, compile, extract, and present data in the required format... Human decision making remains crucial at every juncture."

- **Challenges:** LLMs risk leaking sensitive information through privacy attacks (membership inference, data extraction); centralized training raises GDPR data breach issues. Other challenges include data bias, lack of standardization, need for multidisciplinary collaboration, model interpretability, and regulatory acceptability. Federated Learning (FL), combined with differential privacy, homomorphic encryption, and blockchain-based auditing, can strengthen data security.

- **Cost Advantage:** Fine-tuning LLMs is cheaper than traditional toxicological assessments. Traditional methods require large teams and millions of dollars per chemical. LLM training costs range from $0.0004 to $0.03 per 1000 tokens, with usage costs of $0.0016 to $0.12 per 1000 tokens.

- **Conclusion:** The authors advocate for hybrid AI-human workflows as the future gold standard, where AI handles data aggregation and pattern recognition while experts validate conclusions and provide nuanced risk evaluations. LLMs can democratize access to toxicological data and enable low-income countries and smaller organizations to conduct risk assessments with limited resources.

The letter declares no conflicts of interest, no funding, and was not commissioned (internally peer-reviewed). It contains 11 references.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"The goal of integrating AI, particularly large language models (LLMs), in toxicology is not to replace or supplement human decision-making, but to focus on their practical utility in tasks such as preparing dossiers, regulatory compliance documents, and analysis reports."

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a review article published in the journal Toxics (2025 Jun 23;13(7):525, DOI: 10.3390/toxics13070525) titled "Artificial Intelligence-Driven Drug Toxicity Prediction: Advances, Challenges, and Future Directions." The article, authored by Ruiqiu Zhang, Hairuo Wen, Zhi Lin, Bo Li, and Xiaobing Zhou (corresponding author, zhxb@nifdc.org.cn) from the National Institutes for Food and Drug Control, Chinese Academy of Medical-Sciences and Peking Union Medical College, and the State Key Laboratory of Drug Regulatory Science, is an open-access article (CC BY 4.0 license). PMID: 40710970, PMCID: PMC12299075.

The review focuses on the application of AI in drug toxicity prediction and addresses the fact that safety factors (toxicity and side effects) account for 30% of drug development failures. Traditional toxicity prediction methods (in vitro and animal experiments) are limited by high cost, low throughput, and uncertainty in cross-species extrapolation.

Key content areas:
1. **Toxicity Databases**: The article details seven primary databases - TOXRIC (comprehensive toxicity database), ICE (Integrated Chemical Environment, includes LD50/IC50 data), DSSTox (with Toxval component), DrugBank, ChEMBL, OCHEM (contains 4,064,457 records with 695 attributes from 20,932 references), and PubChem. Table 1 additionally lists 18 databases including Tox21 (10,000+ chemicals, 150+ million data points), Comp Tox Dashboard (1.2+ million chemicals), ToxRefDB, T3DB, TTD, SIDER, The Marker, CTD, GEO, DrugMatrix, KEGG, UniProt, TDC, Toxbank, LiverTox, GEN, TCGA, and GeneCards.

2. **Data Types**: Includes in vitro cytotoxicity test data (MTT test, CCK-8 test), animal experiment data, and clinical data from FDA's FAERS system and electronic medical records (EMR). EMR data faces challenges including inconsistent formats, missing key fields (approximately 30% dose omissions, 41% unrecorded concomitant drugs, and 25-60% missing organ toxicity biomarkers), and non-standardized terms, requiring integrated preprocessing pipelines.

3. **Machine Learning Methods**: Traditional ML algorithms covered include Logistic Regression (simple, interpretable, but limited in nonlinear relationships), Random Forest (used for chemotherapy side effects, liver toxicity, drug toxicity risk assessment), Support Vector Machine (good classification ability for small sample toxicity data, used for liver/kidney injury, cardiotoxicity, immunotoxicity, bone marrow toxicity), and Extreme Gradient Boosting (XGB, fast computing, strong scalability, but complex to tune). Deep learning approaches include multi-label classification methods where the classifier chain algorithm performed best, and an integrated model for multi-organ toxicity prediction where the average AUC improved from 0.68 (single pathological prediction models) to 0.88 (integrated model).

4. **Molecular Representations**: Morgan fingerprint (circular substructure-based), MACCS fingerprint (166 fixed substructure features), Rdkit fingerprint, molecular descriptors, and molecular graphs (used with graph neural networks/GNN).

5. **Acute Toxicity Prediction**: Defined using LD50 (dose killing 50% of test animals within 24h); WHO classifies drugs with LD50 below 5 mg/kg as highly toxic. Notable studies include: Lou et al.'s cross-species model (1,735 rabbit and 1,679 rat cases) where Random Forest performed best, proposing two-stage optimization (data screening via outlier detection and data enhancement via SMILES enumeration); Li et al.'s super learner integrated model predicting rat acute toxicity (9843 compounds, 16 meta models) achieving R² values of 0.61 (cross-validation) and 0.64 (test set), RMSEs of 0.55 and 0.64; and Feitosa et al.'s cyto-safe tool using Light GBM with ECFP4 fingerprints achieving 83% sensitivity.

6. **Organ-Specific Toxicity**: Covers hepatotoxicity, cardiotoxicity, nephrotoxicity, respiratory toxicity, and neurotoxicity, with hepatotoxicity (including DILI) being one of the most common and serious drug toxicities.

Keywords: Artificial Intelligence, machine learning, deep learning, toxicity endpoints, transfer learning.
</summary>

--- SOURCE 10: Applications of Federated Large Language Model for Adverse Drug Reactions Prediction: Scoping Review ---
URL: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12516295

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a scoping review published in the Journal of Medical Internet Research (2025 Sep 8; Vol 27, e68291; PMCID: PMC12516295; PMID: 40921101) by David Guo and Kim-Kwang Raymond Choo from the University of Texas at San Antonio, exploring the application of Federated Learning with Large Language Models (FedLLM) for Adverse Drug Reactions (ADR) prediction.

Background and Purpose: ADRs pose significant challenges to healthcare, with an estimated 98,000 deaths per year from medical errors in hospitals—more than deaths from motor vehicle accidents, breast cancer, or AIDS. The FDA reported over 1.25 million serious adverse events in 2022 alone, with nearly 175,000 fatalities. Traditional supervised learning struggles with heterogeneous, unstructured healthcare data due to privacy regulations (HIPAA, GDPR). FL enables decentralized training across clients while maintaining privacy, while LLMs effectively process unstructured data.

Methods: Following the PRISMA-ScR framework, a scoping review was conducted using Google Scholar and Semantic Scholar for peer-reviewed publications from 2019-2024. After screening, 145 articles (83 from Google Scholar, 62 from Semantic Scholar) from PubMed, arXiv, IEEE, and ACL Anthology met inclusion criteria; 12 were selected for in-depth review. Inclusion criteria required: unstructured data usage, incorporation of FL, and full text availability.

Key Findings:
- ADRs are categorized into 3 types: Type 1 (augmented/dose-dependent), Type 2 (time-dependent/chronic), and Type 3 (idiosyncratic/unpredictable)
- ADR outcomes can be unstructured (text) or structured (discrete codes like FAERS outcome codes: DE for death, LT for life-threatening, HO for hospitalization)
- ADR data sources include: Cadec, EMA's Union Pharmacovigilance Database, FDA's FAERS, CAERS (Canada), DAEN-medicines (Australia), SMM4H (social media), n2c2, ADE_Corpus_V2, and CTCAE v5.0
- BERT-based models are commonly used as base encoders with additional decoder layers for prediction tasks
- Fine-tuning open-source LLMs (Llama-3, Gemma, Mistral/Mixtral, Falcon, DeepSeek, Qwen on Hugging Face) is a practical approach for domain adaptation

Strategies for FedLLM on ADR include: configuring high dropout rates on client models, quantization (4-bit vs 16-bit precision), segmenting parameter matrices, and transferring only distilled-federated knowledge. Distilled models have shown superior performance—DistilBERT outperformed fine-tuned xlm-RoBERTa and GPT-Neo-125M on 4 metrics, and PubMedBERT (0.1% of GPT-3.5's size) outperformed its parent model by over 6 absolute F1-score points.

Evaluation metrics for unstructured predictions include: G-Eval, BLEU_N, ROUGE_N, BERTScore, SEMScore, and ANLS*, each with documented strengths and limitations.

Conclusions: FedLLM for ADR prediction remains in its early stage with limited documented use cases. Key focus areas for future research include fine-tuning and merging algorithms, fairness and unbiasedness, implementation challenges, and real-world deployment strategies. The review aims to lay groundwork for future privacy-preserving and scalable ADR prediction systems.
</summary>

Traditional supervised learning methods struggle to address heterogeneous health care data due to their unstructured nature, regulatory constraints, and restricted access to sensitive personal identifiable information."

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This paper, published in the 2025 Conference of the Nations of the Americas Chapter of the ACL (Volume 1: Long Papers, pages 11083–11113), investigates whether large language models (LLMs) can effectively detect adverse drug reactions (ADRs) from psychiatric medications and align with expert responses to related queries. Led by researchers from Georgia Tech, Hospital General Universitario Gregorio Marañón, Hofstra University, and Columbia University, the study addresses a critical gap: ADRs from psychiatric medications are a leading cause of hospitalizations (51.9% to 91.8% of cases) among mental health patients, yet nearly 70% of individuals worldwide lack access to mental health professionals, leading many to seek help on social media.

The authors introduce two key resources: the Psych-ADR benchmark (239 Reddit posts from January-December 2019, labeled for ADR detection and multiclass classification across five ADR types—dose-related, non-dose, dose- and time-related, time-related, and withdrawal) and the Adverse Drug Reaction Response Assessment (ADRA) framework, which evaluates LLM responses against expert responses across four axes: text readability, emotion/tone expression, harm-reduction strategy alignment, and actionability.

Key findings for RQ1 (ADR detection and classification): The best models achieved only 75.38 F1 in detection and 76.69 F1 in multiclass classification. All models exhibited "risk-averse" behavior with false-positive rates over 70%, struggling to distinguish nuanced ADR types (GPT-4 Turbo misclassified 51% of non-dose-related and 50% of time-related ADRs). Claude 3 Opus achieved the highest zero-shot detection accuracy at 77.41%, while Llama 3.1-405B performed best in few-shot classification (F1 76.69).

For RQ2 (expert-LLM response alignment): LLM responses were significantly harder to read than expert responses (higher SMOG scores vs. 12.44 for experts). There was no significant difference in emotional/tone alignment, though experts showed higher anticipation, affection, and helping tones while LLMs used more optimistic, polite, and trust-based tones. The best model (OpenBioLLM-70B) achieved only 70.86% alignment with expert harm-reduction strategies, and LLMs provided 12.32% less actionable advice on average. Notably, expert responses scored higher on practicality (0.83) and contextual relevance (0.73) but lower on specificity (0.17) and clarity (0.13), while LLMs showed the opposite pattern.

The authors emphasize the importance of "lived experience"—first-hand knowledge possessed by clinicians—which LLMs lack, and caution against increasing human-like features (anthropomorphism) in LLMs due to risks of over-trust in high-risk healthcare domains. Instead, they advocate for fine-tuning on specialized data. The study was funded by NSF grant #2230692 and grants from AFSP, JPMorgan AI Research, and Microsoft's AFMR program. The benchmark and code are available at https://github.com/mohit3011/Lived-Experience-Not-Found.
</summary>

--- SOURCE 14: JMIR Medical Informatics - Predicting Drug–Side Effect Relationships From Parametric Knowledge Embedded in Biomedical BERT Models: Methodological Study With a Natural Language Processing Approach ---
URL: https://medinform.jmir.org/2025/1/e67513

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This paper, published in JMIR Medical Informatics (Vol 13, 2025; doi:10.2196/67513), presents a methodological study on predicting drug–side effect relationships using parametric knowledge embedded in biomedical BERT language models. 

**Background/Objectiive:** Adverse drug reactions (ADRs) pose serious public health risks, with approximately 2 million serious ADRs and 100,000 deaths reported annually in the US. Traditional context-independent word embedding models like Word2Vec have limitations in capturing biomedical domain specificity. The study proposes using BERT-based models pretrained on biomedical corpora to extract parametric knowledge and predict unknown drug–side effect relationships.

**Methods:** The study used 158,096 known drug–side effect pairs from the SIDER database (version 4.1) to build an adjacency matrix with 1,345 drugs and 6,123 side effects. Cosine similarity was calculated between word embedding vectors of drugs and side effects. Relation scores (combining drug-similarity and side-effect-similarity components using equations) were calculated for 8,235,435 total drug–side effect pairs. For Word2Vec training, 14,289,160 sentences mentioning drugs and 32,107,327 sentences mentioning side effects were extracted from PubMed (42,515,246 total abstracts, updated December 8, 2022).

**Results:** The clagator/biobert_v1.1 model achieved the highest AUC of 0.915 at an optimal threshold of 0.289 (sensitivity 0.870, specificity 0.830), outperforming Word2Vec (AUC 0.848) and vanilla BERT (bert-base-uncased, AUC 0.857). Other models tested included BiomedBERT (0.907), dmis-lab/biobert_v1.1 (0.901), and PharmBERT-uncased (0.882). All BERT models pretrained on biomedical corpora outperformed vanilla BERT. The cosine similarity-based extraction method outperformed Euclidean distance, Manhattan distance, Jaccard similarity, and dot product methods. The dual-similarity approach (relation score, AUC 0.915) significantly outperformed single-similarity methods (drug-only: 0.799, side-effect-only: 0.881).

**Validation:** External validation with FAERS data (October 2012–June 2023; 901,361 known relationships) confirmed high statistical significance (P<.001) with an odds ratio of 4.822 (Fisher exact test repeated 2,000 times). Case studies of top-ranked predictions not in SIDER (lenalidomide-arthropathy, rosuvastatin-sleep disturbance, gadolinium-acute pulmonary edema, cefazolin-hepatic failure) were confirmed as reported in literature published after 2016.

**Conclusions:** BERT-based models pretrained on biomedical corpora significantly outperform Word2Vec in predicting drug–side effect relationships due to contextual information capture. The methodology demonstrates practical applicability for pharmacovigilance and ADR prediction. Limitations include the SIDER database being last updated in 2015, challenges with non-dose-dependent reactions, case report generalizability issues, prediction limitations for novel drug candidates, and lack of patient-specific idiosyncratic reaction modeling. The research was supported by the Korea Health Technology R&D Project (grant RS-2022-KH125153).
</summary>

--- SOURCE 1: AI in drug discovery: predictions for 2026 ---
URL: https://www.drugtargetreview.com/ai-in-drug-discovery-predictions-for-2026/1865962.article

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This article by Dr. Raminderpal Singh (Global Head of AI and GenAI Practice at 20/15 Visioneers, founder of HitchhikersAI.org, published February 16, 2026, in Drug Target Review) offers predictions for AI in drug discovery in 2026, framed with "disciplined scepticism" to distinguish evidence-based forecasts from hype. The year is characterized as a pivotal inflection point between clinical validation and market volatility.

**Eleven key predictions:**

1. **Phase III data as the definitive test**: Multiple clinical readouts expected over 18 months will test whether AI improves clinical success rates beyond the industry's persistent ~90% failure rate. Positive data could validate physics-enabled AI design and enable approvals extending into 2027. Contrary view: AI-discovered compounds may show similar progression rates to traditional molecules, potentially demonstrating accelerated timelines without improved efficacy.

2. **Regulatory guidance becomes operative**: FDA draft AI guidance likely finalized in 2026 requiring credibility assessment plans for high-risk AI. The EU AI Act's high-risk provisions take effect August 2, 2026. However, guidance focuses on AI affecting regulatory decisions, explicitly excluding early discovery tools.

3. **Investment discipline replaces exuberance**: Market projected to grow from $5-7 billion (2025) to $8-10 billion (2026), with McKinsey suggesting generative AI could deliver $60-110 billion annually in pharma value. However, smaller companies face existential pressures with multiple shutdowns, 20%+ workforce reductions, and delistings. Valuations have collapsed since 2021-2022 IPOs. Expect consolidation with stronger players acquiring distressed assets.

4. **Early discovery compression without clinical acceleration**: AI compresses early discovery timelines 30-40% and reduces preclinical candidate development to 13-18 months (vs. 3-4 years traditional). Antibody design reports 16-20% hit rates vs. 0.1% computational benchmarks. However, clinical trial duration, regulatory review, and manufacturing scale-up remain unchanged. Claims of '10x faster drug development' are misleading.

5. **Reinforcement learning agents transform scientific workflows**: RLVR (reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards) trains autonomous scientific agents using computational checks as objective reward signals. Architecture employs three server abstractions (models, resources, agents) enabling parallel execution. Jupyter-notebook data-analysis agents in bioinformatics face context growth challenges. Critical limitation: current systems lack creative problem solving when initial hypotheses fail; human scientists remain essential.

6. **Autonomous laboratories expand but remain experimental**: Closed-loop self-driving labs accelerate design–make–test–learn cycles running 24/7, but have not demonstrated independent discovery of validated drug candidates. Integration of wet lab robotics with dry lab AI remains complex and capital-intensive.

7. **Chinese AI dominance amid geopolitical tension**: Chinese companies' share of global biotech licensing deals rose from 21% (2023-2024) to 32% (Q1 2025). AI drug discovery is a priority in China's Five-Year Plan. Geopolitical tensions, data security concerns, and regulatory scrutiny create uncertainty, including scrutiny of Western investment following detention of executives.

8. **Protein structure prediction matures**: Advanced models predict structures with 50%+ improvement over traditional methods, but accuracy doesn't guarantee druggable targets. Models struggle with conformational changes and show persistent biases. Optimal use requires hybrid pipelines combining AI with physics-based refinement.

9. **Data quality remains the primary barrier**: 68% of tech executives identify poor data quality and governance as main reason AI initiatives fail. Federated learning platforms will emerge for privacy-preserving data pooling, but technical challenges including data standardisation and IP concerns persist.

10. **First AI-discovered drug approval possible but not certain**: Approval could occur late 2026/early 2027 if regulatory submissions proceed with priority review, but a more realistic timeframe is 2027-2028. Attribution is complex due to significant human intervention. Until approval occurs, the field remains in 'proof-of-concept' phase.

11. **The 'prove it' year delivers mixed results**: Validation and disappointment in roughly equal measure. Positive Phase III data possible, but additional clinical failures are statistically inevitable. One CEO's assessment quoted: "AI has really let us all down in the last decade when it comes to drug discovery – we've just seen failure after failure."

**Conclusion - disciplined optimism**: AI compresses early discovery timelines, improves hit rates, and enables complex biological data analysis, but has not solved — and likely cannot solve — clinical validation, regulatory approval, and commercial success challenges. The technology is "a powerful tool, not a panacea." Organisations pursuing hype over evidence will face market correction.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"Positive Phase III data could validate physics-enabled AI design for specific targets, potentially enabling regulatory submissions and approval timelines extending into 2027."; "AI-enabled workflows will demonstrably compress early discovery timelines by 30-40 percent and reduce preclinical candidate development to 13-18 months (versus traditional three to four years)."; "AI has really let us all down in the last decade when it comes to drug discovery – we've just seen failure after failure" (CEO assessment cited); "AI compresses early discovery timelines, improves hit rates in certain applications and enables analysis of complex biological data... The technology is a powerful tool, not a panacea."; "Surveys of tech executives found 68 percent identify poor data quality and governance as the main reason AI initiatives fail."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 2: Transforming Drug Safety Through Artificial Intelligence ... ---
URL: https://www.biopharminternational.com/view/drug-safety-artificial-intelligence-large-language-models

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This article from BioPharm International (published March 4, 2026) explores how artificial intelligence, particularly large language models (LLMs) and natural language processing (NLP), is transforming drug safety surveillance in the pharmaceutical industry. Authors Partha Anbil and Niraj B. Patel discuss how these technologies enable automated adverse event detection, large-scale analysis of regulatory labeling data, and faster, citation-grounded safety assessments while maintaining human oversight and regulatory compliance.

Key points include:

**The Challenge:** The FDA manages a database of over 140,000 drug labeling documents constantly updated with new safety information. With 82% of American adults taking at least one medication, the scale of data requires automated solutions. Traditional methods (manual annotation, keyword matching, traditional machine learning) all have significant drawbacks, creating a "data gap" where critical safety information locked in unstructured text cannot be accessed at scale.

**Domain-Specific Models:**
- PharmBERT: BERT-based model achieving 89% accuracy in identifying adverse events from drug labels, outperforming human review and generic BERT models
- RxBERT: Developed by FDA's National Center for Toxicological Research, trained on 44,990 prescription drug labeling documents, achieving 86.5 F1-score in adverse event classification and 87% accuracy in labeling section classification
- AskFDALabel: Combines retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) with locally hosted LLMs, achieving F1-scores of 0.978 for drug-induced liver injury (DILI) and 0.931 for drug-induced cardiotoxicity (DICT) classification

**Performance Metrics:** 91.1% accuracy in adverse event extraction, 99.4% accuracy in identifying DILI risk, and 99.5% accuracy for cardiotoxicity classification. A manual process that once took two to three weeks can now be completed in hours with improved consistency across all 140,000+ labels.

**Real-World Applications (2025/26):** Automated adverse event detection and classification, rapid packaging and label evaluation (with one study predicting patient attention patterns with 90% accuracy), and drug property prediction and comparative analysis across regulatory jurisdictions.

**Regulatory Implementation:** Data security drives development of locally hosted LLM solutions. AskFDALabel runs on in-house GPU servers using open-source models like Llama 3.1-70B, ensuring data never leaves FDA systems. In one FDA implementation, reviewing 211 drugs for DILI risk took approximately 15 minutes compared to an estimated 40-60 hours for manual review. Training domain-specific models requires significant GPU resources (230+ computing hours for pre-training).

**Future Directions:** Integration of multiple data sources (electronic health records, clinical trial data, published literature, real-time pharmacovigilance data), addressing causality (Columbia University researchers are developing methods to classify adverse reactions as causally associated vs. coincidental), and proactive signal detection.

**Limitations:** Context dependency issues, class imbalance making rare adverse events harder to detect (SMOTE techniques help but don't fully solve this), explainability challenges with "black box" models, and significant cost/computational requirements. All AI systems in regulatory science must undergo rigorous validation including testing against benchmark datasets, cross-validation, error analysis, and continuous monitoring.

**Best Practices:** Start with pilot projects, establish performance baselines, invest in team training, maintain human oversight, document all AI system versions and outputs, use domain-specific training data, implement local hosting for regulatory use, design for interpretability with citations and confidence scores, and build continuous feedback loops.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"AI systems can query drug label databases for reported adverse events, categorize results with citations to specific label sections, identify novel safety signals across multiple drugs, and flag potentially severe reactions for expert review."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 3: AI in Drug Discovery: Clinical Failures, Regulatory Reality ... ---
URL: https://www.mdpi.com/1424-8247/19/6/916

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a peer-reviewed narrative review article published in the MDPI journal Pharmaceuticals (2026, 19(6), 916; DOI: 10.3390/ph19060916) titled "AI in Drug Discovery: Clinical Failures, Regulatory Reality, and the Validation Crisis Behind the Hype." Written by Lisa Khairil, Koay Hean Seng Benny, Jesreena Jerry, Farhat Mussa Khatib, Muhammad Danial Che Ramli, and Suresh Kumar, the paper belongs to the Special Issue "Artificial Intelligence: New Molecules, Therapeutic Targets and Discovery of New Drugs." The study was submitted April 6, 2026, revised June 4, 2026, accepted June 6, 2026, and published June 10, 2026.

**Purpose/Hypothesis:** The review evaluates the economic, technical, clinical, and regulatory dimensions of AI adoption in drug discovery between 2022-2026. It hypothesizes that despite substantial computational advances and investment, current AI-driven drug discovery platforms remain constrained by biological complexity, limited reproducibility, and insufficient clinical validation.

**Methodology:** A structured narrative review was conducted using PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, and Google Scholar databases, complemented by regulatory and industry reports from the FDA, EMA, NIH, and major pharmaceutical companies. The search covered 2017-2026 using keywords such as "artificial intelligence," "drug discovery," "AlphaFold," "clinical validation," "reproducibility crisis," and "AI regulation." Priority was given to studies with quantitative validation, regulatory relevance, multicentre datasets, or clinically translated outcomes.

**Key Findings:**
- Clinical attrition rates remain high—approximately 90% of drug candidates entering clinical development fail to achieve regulatory approval.
- Global AI healthcare investment exceeded USD 100 billion in 2024 (an 80% increase from the prior year); Q1 2025 healthcare AI spending nearly tripled to ~USD 1.4 billion. In H1 2025, 62% of all digital health investments went to AI-focused startups.
- More than 950 FDA-authorised AI-enabled medical devices by 2025.
- AlphaFold achieved high structural prediction accuracy (pLDDT scores exceeding 90 for well-structured proteins, RMSD values comparable to experimental methods), but limitations persist in modelling protein dynamics, post-translational modifications, and protein–ligand interactions.
- Among radiology-specific AI diagnostics, only approximately 29% report prospective clinical testing, highlighting a gap between regulatory clearance and rigorous real-world clinical validation.
- AI-assisted platforms may reduce early-stage target identification and hit discovery timelines by approximately 30-70% (some analysts report 50-80%), with cost reductions of 15-22% and modelled savings of USD 500 million to USD 1 billion per approved therapeutic. However, overall clinical success rates remain broadly comparable to traditional development (approval probability baseline of approximately 8-12%).
- Investment concentration: large funding rounds accounted for ~46% of total investment in digital health during Q1 2025. Xaira Therapeutics raised over USD 1 billion; Lila Sciences secured ~USD 550 million. In 2023, the US received USD 67 billion in AI healthcare funding vs. China's USD 7.8 billion.
- Notable market corrections: BenevolentAI, Exscientia, and Recursion experienced valuation declines and internal changes after clinical milestones were missed; Recursion acquired Exscientia in 2024.
- In 2026, NVIDIA and Eli Lilly announced a landmark $1 billion AI co-innovation lab.

**Conclusions:** AI in drug discovery is currently in a transitional phase characterized by high investment but limited validated clinical impact. Future progress depends on strengthening validation frameworks, improving data sharing practices, and aligning regulatory standards with real-world clinical performance. The economic value of AI currently derives primarily from early-stage productivity gains rather than substantial reductions in overall development risk or clinical attrition.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"Current evidence indicates that clinical attrition rates remain high, with approximately 90% of drug candidates entering clinical development failing to achieve regulatory approval."; "Although AI systems such as AlphaFold have achieved high structural prediction accuracy... limitations persist in modelling protein dynamics, post-translational modifications, and protein–ligand interactions."; "Clinical case studies demonstrate that while AI can accelerate early-stage discovery timelines, these advantages do not consistently translate into improved late-stage success rates."; "These findings suggest that AI in drug discovery is currently in a transitional phase characterised by high investment but limited validated clinical impact."; "Among radiology-specific AI diagnostics, only approximately 29% report prospective clinical testing, highlighting the gap between regulatory clearance and rigorous real-world clinical validation."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 4: Artificial Intelligence for Drug Development ---
URL: https://www.fda.gov/about-fda/center-drug-evaluation-and-research-cder/artificial-intelligence-drug-development

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage from the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) provides an overview of Artificial Intelligence (AI) for Drug Development, explaining what AI is, its role in drug development, and how the FDA's Center for Drug Evaluation and Research (CDER) is approaching AI regulation and use.

**What is AI:** AI is defined as a machine-based system that makes predictions, recommendations, or decisions based on human-defined objectives. AI systems perceive environments, abstract perceptions into models through automated analysis, and use model inference to formulate options for action. A key subset is Machine Learning (ML), which uses data to train AI algorithms to improve performance.

**Role in Drug Development:** CDER has seen a significant increase in drug application submissions using AI components over recent years, spanning nonclinical, clinical, postmarketing, and manufacturing phases. AI is also increasingly integrated into Digital Health Technologies (DHTs) and Real-World Data (RWD) analytics.

**CDER's Perspective and Regulatory Approach:** CDER is committed to ensuring drugs are safe and effective while facilitating innovation, and is developing a risk-based regulatory framework promoting innovation and protecting patient safety. The FDA published a draft guidance in 2025 titled "Considerations for the Use of Artificial Intelligence to Support Regulatory Decision Making for Drug and Biological Products." This guidance was informed by: (1) a December 2022 expert workshop convened by the Duke Margolis Institute for Health Policy; (2) over 800 comments on a May 2023 discussion paper; (3) CDER's experience with over 500 submissions with AI components from 2016 to 2023; and (4) hybrid public workshops held on August 6, 2024 and October 7, 2025.

The FDA also published "Artificial Intelligence and Medical Products: How CBER, CDER, CDRH, and OCP are Working Together" (March 2024, revised February 2025), describing how FDA's medical product Centers align efforts to advance responsible AI use.

**CDER AI Council:** Established in 2024, the CDER AI Council provides oversight, coordination, and consolidation of CDER activities around AI use, consolidating the work of the CDER AI Steering Committee, AI Policy Working Group, and CDER AI Community of Practice. It acts as a decisional body coordinating AI-related activities. Novel AI applications like generative AI and large language models are expanding AI use within CDER, requiring increased education and coordination.

**International Coordination:** CDER and CBER collaborated with the European Medicines Agency to develop 10 guiding principles of good AI practice in drug development for industry and product developers.

Content current as of 05/01/2026.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"Artificial Intelligence (AI) refers to a machine-based system that can, for a given set of human-defined objectives, make predictions, recommendations, or decisions influencing real or virtual environments."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 5: A survey of LLMs in drug discovery and precision medicine ---
URL: https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/drug-discovery/articles/10.3389/fddsv.2026.1854899/full

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a comprehensive review article published in Frontiers in Drug Discovery (August 20, 2026, Volume 6) titled "A survey of LLMs in drug discovery and precision medicine" by Hasi Hays and William J. Richardson from the Department of Chemical Engineering, University of Arkansas. The article surveys state-of-the-art applications of large language models (LLMs) across the drug development pipeline and precision medicine.

**Key Context/Background:**
- Traditional drug discovery takes 10–15 years with costs exceeding $2.6 billion per approved drug
- Approximately 90% of drug candidates fail in clinical trials
- The review synthesizes literature published between 2018 and 2025

**LLM Foundations:**
- Traces evolution from the 2017 transformer architecture (Vaswani et al.) through BERT (bidirectional encoder) and GPT (autoregressive decoder) paradigms
- Covers scaling developments including GPT-3 (175B parameters), GPT-4, PaLM (540B parameters), and open-source models LLaMA/LLaMA-2
- Discusses instruction tuning and reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF) for alignment in high-stakes biomedical applications

**Biomedical Language Models:**
- Domain-adapted text models: BioBERT, PubMedBERT (pretraining from scratch on in-domain corpus), ClinicalBERT (trained on MIMIC-III clinical notes)
- Generative models: BioGPT, Med-PaLM/Med-PaLM 2, MEDITRON-70B
- Pretraining data sources include PubMed (35+ million citations), electronic health records, biomedical databases (DrugBank, ChEMBL, UniProt), clinical guidelines, and regulatory documents

**Molecular and Protein Language Models:**
- Molecule-focused: ChemBERTa (masked language modeling on SMILES), MolGPT, Chemformer (reaction prediction/retrosynthesis)
- Protein models: ESM-1b/ESM-2 (masked language modeling on protein sequences, implicit structural learning), ESMFold (structure prediction approaching AlphaFold2 accuracy with much less computation), ProtGPT2 (novel protein generation), ProGen (functional enzyme generation with experimental validation)
- Genomic models: DNABERT, DNABERT-2, Nucleotide Transformer (cross-species training), HyenaDNA (sequences up to 1 million nucleotides at single-nucleotide resolution)

**Multi-modal Integration:**
- Across modalities: molecules, protein sequences, genomic variants, clinical phenotypes, images, and natural language
- Notable systems: InstructMol (two-stage instruction tuning for molecular understanding), MolT5 (bidirectional text-molecule translation), ChatMol (interactive molecular discovery), Galactica, BiomedGPT

**Knowledge-Guided Approaches:**
- Incorporation of biomedical knowledge graphs (DrugBank, ChEMBL, Disease Ontology, Human Phenotype Ontology)
- Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) as particularly promising: grounds outputs in retrieved evidence, reduces hallucination, enables access to current information, provides citation transparency. Almanac demonstrated effectiveness for clinical medicine.

**Zero-Shot and Few-Shot Learning:**
- Valuable for biomedical contexts where labeled data is scarce
- Chain-of-thought prompting improves multi-step reasoning but generated reasoning chains don't always faithfully reflect internal computations

**Applications in Drug Discovery:**
- Target identification, de novo molecular generation, ADMET property prediction, drug repurposing, and end-to-end discovery pipelines

**Applications in Precision Medicine:**
- Clinical decision support, patient stratification, treatment personalization, genomic interpretation

**Key Caveats/Challenges:**
- Most reported gains come from benchmark accuracy on retrospective datasets rather than prospective clinical or wet-lab validation
- "Expert-level performance" on USMLE-style questions is not equivalent to expert-level performance in real clinical workflows
- Current AI-designed drug candidates have begun Phase I/II trials but no approved therapeutic yet
- Challenges include data privacy, model interpretability, hallucination risks, computational resource requirements, and ethical considerations (algorithmic bias, health disparities)

**Future Directions:**
- Federated learning, explainable artificial intelligence (XAI), integrated multiscale approaches, multi-agent systems, and development of more efficient models

**Includes data visualizations:** evolutionary tree of biomedical LLMs (2018–2025) across encoder-only, encoder-decoder, and decoder-only branches; timeline of 93-102 representative models; domain-coverage heatmaps; benchmark usage charts; and comparative tables of LLM frameworks used in drug discovery and precision medicine.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"The convergence of artificial intelligence and biomedical research has catalyzed emerging impact in drug discovery and precision medicine. Large language models (LLMs), originally developed for natural language processing, have emerged as powerful tools capable of processing complex biomedical data, from molecular structures to clinical records."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 6: FDA AI Guidance 2026: Drug Manufacturing & Digital Health | IntuitionLabs ---
URL: https://intuitionlabs.ai/articles/fda-ai-guidance-2026-drug-manufacturing-digital-health

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This IntuitionLabs report (published April 10, 2026) analyzes the FDA CDER's 2026 guidance pipeline for artificial intelligence (AI) in pharmaceutical manufacturing and Digital Health Technologies (DHTs) in drug development.

**Key Context & Regulatory Framework:** The FDA is actively preparing new guidance documents for these emerging technologies. The 21st Century Cures Act (2016) excluded certain software (general wellness apps and clinical decision support functions) from the medical device definition, though higher-risk digital health remains regulated. PDUFA VII requires FDA to publish a framework for DHT use in drug development and establish a Digital Health Steering Committee. CDER's FRAME (Framework for Regulatory Advanced Manufacturing Evaluation) initiative, begun in 2021, focuses on modern manufacturing technologies including AI/ML integration.

**AI in Pharmaceutical Manufacturing:** AI/ML is used for process design/scale-up, advanced process control, fault detection, and trend analysis in manufacturing. Use cases include predictive maintenance, soft sensors, and digital twins. By 2021, more than 100 drug and biologic applications contained AI/ML elements, and FDA reports over 500 drug/biologic submissions with AI components from 2016–2023. Perrigo serves as a notable case study using AI for predictive maintenance and image analysis defect detection. In March 2023, CDER published a discussion paper on AI in drug manufacturing and held a September 2023 public workshop. A May 2025 AAPS Open report synthesized stakeholder feedback showing industry desire for clear guidance, global harmonization, robust model lifecycle plans, and alignment with quality systems.

**Digital Health Technologies (DHTs):** DHTs include mobile apps, wearables, sensors, and telemedicine platforms used for remote monitoring, novel clinical endpoints, and digital therapeutics. Global SaMD market was ~$18.5 billion in 2019 growing ~22% annually; over 1,000 AI/ML-enabled medical devices authorized total. FDA finalized December 2023 guidance on DHTs for remote data acquisition. On March 31, 2026, FDA issued a Federal Register Request-for-Information soliciting comment on advancing DHT use in clinical investigations. Notable examples include Pear Therapeutics' reSET-O and Proteus Digital Health's Abilify MyCite (combination products). FDA launched the "TEMPO" pilot (Dec 2025) for premature access to digital devices for chronic diseases.

**CDER 2026 Guidance Agenda (Feb 2026):** Among 81 listed items, three directly relate to these topics: (1) "Use of Digital Health Technologies in Clinical Investigations of Drugs and Biologics" (Administrative category, New draft planned 2026), (2) "AI/ML Quality Considerations in Pharmaceutical Manufacturing" (Pharma Quality/CMC category, New draft planned 2026), and (3) "Distributed Manufacturing Application Content" (Pharma Quality/CMC). The agenda is not binding but confirms guidance is imminent. FDA also issued a January 2025 draft guidance on AI credibility for drug submissions and an "Advanced Approaches to Pharmaceutical Manufacturing and Distribution" draft.

**Key Challenges:** Data integrity, AI model validation and explainability, model drift, third-party data use, CGMP compliance with novel technologies, statistical handling of continuous data streams, digital endpoint qualification, data privacy, and digital equity. The report concludes with implications for sponsors, suggesting early FDA engagement and consultation with Digital Health and Biostatistics divisions for novel endpoints.
</summary>

--- SOURCE 7: The future of AI regulation in drug development - PMC - NIH ---
URL: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12598624

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This article (Journal of Law and the Biosciences, 2025, by Gabriela Lenarczyk, Timo Minssen, Nicholson Price, and Arti Rai) provides a comparative analysis of AI regulation in drug development between the US FDA and the European Medicines Agency (EMA).

The paper makes three contributions: (1) a comparative analysis of FDA and EMA oversight of AI in drug development incorporating new US executive orders and the EU's AI Act; (2) a novel analytical framework explaining regulatory divergence—the FDA uses a flexible, dialog-driven, case-by-case model while the EMA uses a structured, risk-tiered approach; and (3) an evaluation of whether AI applications (target identification, generative chemistry, clinical trial 'digital twins') are mature enough for standardized regulation.

Key findings on adoption: AI tools are widely used in early-stage discovery where oversight is limited, but uptake in later clinical phases remains cautious—76% of AI use cases involve molecule discovery versus only 3% in clinical outcomes analysis. By fall 2024, the FDA had received over 500 submissions incorporating AI components, yet stakeholders report insufficient guidance on AI/ML regulatory requirements, particularly in clinical phases. Digital twins in clinical trials illustrate the regulatory challenges, raising questions about model validation and reliability standards.

The EMA's approach (articulated in its 2024 Reflection Paper) establishes a risk-based framework focusing on 'high patient risk' and 'high regulatory impact' applications. Requirements become more stringent in clinical/pivotal trials, including pre-specified data curation pipelines, frozen/documented models, prospective performance testing, and prohibition of incremental learning during trials. Technical requirements mandate traceable documentation, data representativeness assessment, and bias mitigation strategies. The EMA prefers interpretable models but permits black-box models when justified, requiring explainability metrics.

The FDA's approach (embodied in the CDER, with its AI Steering Committee and various pilot programs) emphasizes flexible, context-specific oversight via non-binding guidance documents and iterative engagement. The FDA's 2023 discussion paper introduced a risk-based framework emphasizing human-led governance, data quality/reliability, and robust model development. In June 2025, the FDA deployed an agency-wide LLM assistant ('Elsa') for internal scientific review. The January 2025 transition to the Trump administration brought Executive Order 14148, which rescinds Biden's EO 14110 and mandates review of AI policies that might 'impede US AI leadership,' potentially weakening or delaying the FDA's January 2025 draft guidance on AI-driven drug development.

The article (published 04 Aug 2025, authored by Dr. Nils Rauer and Maud van Imhoff) examines uncertainty about whether the EU AI Act's 'high-risk' AI rules will apply to pharmaceutical companies. Key points:

- The EU AI Act's 'high-risk' AI system rules take effect from 2 August 2026, but whether they govern pharmaceutical AI use is currently unclear.
- Pharmaceutical companies use AI in drug development (processing large datasets, identifying biological targets, digital twins/virtual patient models, 'lab in the loop' strategies as used by Roche, clinical trial design, and personalised medicine).
- The EMA (European Medicines Agency) has acknowledged AI's potential but also warned it introduces "new risks" and expects companies to perform regulatory impact and risk analyses. New EMA guidance is under development.
- The AI Act's staggered implementation: a ban on certain AI uses took effect 2 February 2025; general purpose AI rules entered into force 2 August 2025; high-risk rules take effect 2 August 2026.
- AI systems can be classified as high-risk in three ways: products under Annex I subject to EU conformity assessment, safety components of such products, or as listed Annex III high-risk AI systems (e.g., biometric identification).
- The European Federation of Pharmaceutical Industries and Associations (EFPIA) argues AI systems "used solely for the purpose of medicines R&D" are exempt under Articles 2(6) and 2(8), and that most pharmaceutical R&D AI uses would not qualify as high-risk under Annex I or III.

This is a comprehensive IntuitionLabs report (updated August 10, 2026) on the EU Artificial Intelligence Act (AI Act) and its compliance requirements for pharmaceutical companies. **Key Facts:**
- The EU AI Act, the world's first comprehensive AI law, was enacted in August 2024 (entered into force August 1, 2024) and adopts a risk-based approach categorizing AI into four tiers: unacceptable (banned), high-risk, limited-risk, and minimal-risk.
- Prohibited AI practices became binding on February 2, 2025; GPAI (general-purpose AI) obligations followed on August 2, 2025, alongside the final GPAI Code of Practice.
- The Digital Omnibus proposal (November 2025) defers Annex III high-risk obligations to December 2, 2027, and high-risk AI in regulated products (e.g., medical devices) to August 2, 2028.
- Breaches can trigger fines up to €35 million or 7% of global turnover.
- Only 9% of life-sciences professionals report understanding AI regulations well, despite AI's potential to add $100 billion of value to healthcare.
- The global AI-in-pharma market reached an estimated $4.35 billion in 2025, projected to grow to $6.16 billion in 2026 and $35 billion by 2031 (41.5% CAGR).
- AI tools used purely in research contexts (e.g., early drug discovery models) are generally exempt from AI Act obligations.
- The revised Product Liability Directive applies to products placed on market after December 9, 2026.
- GPAI models placed on market before August 2, 2025, have until August 2, 2027, to achieve compliance.

**Risk Classification for Pharma:**
- **Unacceptable Risk:** AI violating fundamental rights (manipulation, social scoring) - prohibited outright; no routine pharma use is explicitly banned.
- **High Risk:** Software as a medical device (diagnostic algorithms, patient monitoring, therapeutic decision support, AI in MD/IVD requiring third-party conformity assessment) and Annex III uses (biometric categorization, eligibility determination for healthcare/insurance, emergency triage). These require conformity assessment, risk management (Article 9), data governance (Article 10), technical documentation (Article 11 & Annex IV), record-keeping/transparency (Articles 12-13), human oversight (Article 14), and accuracy/robustness/cybersecurity (Article 15).
- **Limited Risk:** Chatbots, content generators requiring transparency under Article 50.
- **Minimal Risk:** Internal document processing, administrative analytics, basic R&D models.

**Implementation Timeline:**
- August 1, 2024: Act entered into force
- February 2, 2025: Prohibited practices ban and AI literacy obligations became binding
- August 2, 2025: GPAI obligations applicable; GPAI Code of Practice published July 10, 2025
- August 2, 2026: General application date; Article 50 transparency obligations apply
- July 27, 2026: Regulation (EU) 2026/1744 entered into force amending high-risk timetable
- December 2, 2027: High-risk rules apply to Annex III systems
- August 2, 2028: High-risk rules apply to Annex I (regulated product) systems
- August 2, 2027: GPAI pre-August 2025 model compliance deadline

**Compliance Guidance:**
The report recommends inventorying all AI uses, classifying each by risk, integrating AI compliance into quality systems (e.g., ICH Q9 risk management), establishing governance/documentation practices, and training staff on AI literacy. It emphasizes that pharmaceutical firms should integrate AI risk management into their Quality Management Systems (QMS), with AI model modifications treated under change-control protocols and AI software defects treated as non-conformances. The report begins a six-step compliance flowchart (identify AI system, check for exclusions, etc.) and references EFPIA's observation that "AI-enabled tools used in pharma R&D are exempt" while digital health and medical AI are covered. The GPAI Code of Practice is organized into three chapters: Transparency, Copyright, and Safety & Security.

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This article from MDx CRO explains the EU AI Act (Regulation (EU) 2024/1689) and its implications for Software as a Medical Device (SaMD) developers. AI-powered medical devices are automatically classified as high-risk AI under Annex III. The compliance timeline is critical: February 2026 saw the Commission publish Article 6 guidelines; 2 August 2026 marked when most high-risk AI obligations apply (primarily for Annex III systems NOT subject to Notified Body assessment); and 2 August 2027 is the key deadline for CE-marked MDR/IVDR devices under Article 6(1). The AI Act and MDR/IVDR apply simultaneously (not as alternatives). MDR governs device safety/clinical performance; the AI Act governs how the AI was built, trained, validated, and governed. A streamlined pathway allows a single technical documentation approach, with Notified Bodies covering AI Act conformity for Class IIb/III medical devices (MDR) and Class C/D IVDs (IVDR). Key obligations for high-risk AI include: AI-specific risk management (integrating ISO 14971), data governance (representative, bias-assessed datasets with documented demographic/geographic coverage), technical documentation, transparency/IFU, human oversight (clinicians must always override/reverse outputs), accuracy/robustness/cybersecurity, and conformity assessment.

The AI Act definition covers machine learning models, deep learning (including CNNs for medical imaging), NLP tools, and Bayesian classifiers, but NOT traditional rule-based software with fixed logic. General Purpose AI (GPAI) models add complexity: providers must document training data and publish transparency summaries (since August 2025), while SaMD developers fine-tuning GPAI models become high-risk AI providers with their own validation and oversight duties. Actionable steps include classifying AI systems, assessing technical documentation gaps, reviewing data governance, updating IFUs, engaging Notified Bodies early, and building AI performance monitoring into post-market surveillance (tracking model drift and distribution shift).

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This article by UL Solutions' Sravya Prabhala addresses how AI-enabled medical product manufacturers should prepare for the European Union's AI Act, which has been adopted and is progressively entering into force. The EU AI Act introduces a risk-based framework where most AI-enabled medical products fall into the high-risk category, requiring comprehensive legal and technical obligations. Importantly, the Act complements rather than replaces existing frameworks including the Medical Devices Regulation (MDR), In Vitro Diagnostic Medical Devices Regulation (IVDR), and GDPR, adding oversight for AI-specific risks like algorithmic drift, data bias, and lack of explainability.

The Act uses phased enforcement timelines: the deadline for standalone high-risk AI systems (Annex III) was extended from August 2, 2026 to December 2, 2027, while high-risk AI systems embedded in regulated products under Annex I (including medical devices and IVDs) have a deadline deferred from August 2, 2027 to August 2, 2028. Regulatory focus is sharpening on three core pillars: (1) AI risk management and technical documentation, (2) conformity assessment preparedness integrated into QMS, and (3) post-market monitoring.

Manufacturers must provide auditable evidence across several areas: predictable and robust AI behavior under real-world clinical conditions (including stress testing, drift monitoring, and hardware interoperability); well-governed data pipelines addressing bias risks (noting Article 10 allows sensitive data collection focused on bias detection and correction); clear human oversight mechanisms under Article 14 (allowing healthcare providers to understand, disregard, override, or reverse AI outputs); and secure, resilient AI components throughout the product life cycle.

Recommended preparation steps include identifying/categorizing all AI systems across the portfolio, benchmarking current practices against expected requirements, integrating data governance into ISO 13485 quality life cycles, and leveraging independent third-party assessments aligned with standards like ISO/IEC 42001 and UL's UL 3115 program. The article argues that acting early provides a competitive advantage, builds trust with regulators and notified bodies, and turns regulatory uncertainty into operational clarity, positioning compliance as a point of differentiation.
