--- SOURCE 19: EU Commission drafts guidelines on classifying high-risk systems under the AI Act | RAPS ---
URL: https://www.raps.org/resource/eu-commission-drafts-guidelines-on-classifying-high-risk-systems-under-the-ai-act.html

SUMMARY:
<summary>
The European Commission has published draft guidelines to help companies determine whether their products, including AI-incorporated medical devices, are classified as high-risk under the EU's Artificial Intelligence Act (AI Act). For devices subject to the AI Act, these requirements will layer on top of (rather than replace) existing obligations under the Medical Device Regulation (MDR) and In Vitro Diagnostic Regulation (IVDR).

Key dates: The AI Act takes effect on 2 December 2027 for stand-alone high-risk AI systems and 2 August 2028 for high-risk AI systems embedded in products. The deadline for submitting comments on the draft guidelines is 23 June.

The Commission published three separate guidelines: (1) general principles on determining whether an AI system is high-risk, (2) guidance on Annex I of the Act, and (3) guidance on Annex III (148 pages). Under Article 6, an AI system is high-risk if intended as a safety component of a product (or is itself a product) covered by Annex I harmonisation legislation requiring third-party conformity assessment. The guidelines clarify the classification process but do not specify device types, which is why they appear broad.

The Annex I guidance defines "safety function" as including preventive/mitigative functionalities such as monitoring and detection of situations that may lead to physical harm. Products covered include safety components of machinery, toys, lifts, medical devices, IVDs, and products in automotive and aviation sectors. The Annex III guidance notes that emergency healthcare patient triage systems may qualify as medical devices and be classified as high-risk.

Expert commentary: Nils Lölfing, an AI attorney at Bird & Bird in Germany, explained that AI medical devices are high-risk when they are either a device in their own right (e.g., software analyzing scans to flag/diagnose diseases) or a safety component of one (e.g., AI regulating dosing in an infusion pump), where the device needs notified body sign-off (roughly Class IIa and above under MDR, and most IVDs). Simple, self-certified Class I devices fall outside the high-risk category.

Two reforms aim to prevent dual regulation:
1. The Digital Omnibus on AI keeps medical devices under the AI Act but postpones high-risk obligations until August 2028 and allows delegated acts to exempt AI Act requirements where MDR/IVDR already mandate the same standards (agreement reached but not yet formally adopted).
2. A planned MDR/IVDR revision (issued December 2025) would make device rules the main rulebook, handling AI requirements within normal device approval rather than a separate AI Act process.

Lölfing recommended evidencing AI-specific points (data governance, robustness, human oversight) through MDR/IVDR documentation instead of a separate AI Act exercise. According to a 2024 IQVIA blog post, a large segment of AI's use in healthcare would be classified as high-risk under the Act.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"the Guidelines set out the Commission's interpretation of certain concepts that are relevant for classification purposes and, in accordance with Article 6(5) AI Act, contain practical examples of AI systems that should or should not be classified as high-risk. The examples listed in these Guidelines strive to cover all areas and use cases, but they are not to be considered as exhaustive and may be updated over time.", "the starting point is that AI in medical devices already falls under the EU's device rules, the MDR and IVDR. The AI Act adds a second layer on top, but only for what it calls high-risk systems. An AI medical device is high-risk where it is either a device in its own right or a safety component of one, and where that device needs a notified body (an independent assessor) to sign it off. In practice that is roughly Class IIa and above under the MDR, and most IVDs.", "This plan would make the device rules the main rulebook, so AI requirements are handled within the normal device approval rather than in a separate AI Act process, with the AI-specific obligations likely written into rules sitting under the MDR itself. This mirrors how the EU already treats AI in cars and in machinery and robotics, where the sector law, not the AI Act directly, carries the AI requirements.", "Emergency healthcare patient triage systems may qualify as medical devices in so far as they fulfil the definition of a medical device in Article 2(1) of the Medical Devices Regulation. If such systems meet the conditions in Article 6(1) AI Act, they will be classified as high-risk pursuant to that provision and Annex I AI Act and require streamlined and consistent compliance with sectoral laws.", "the sensible approach is to evidence the AI-specific points, mainly data governance, robustness and human oversight, through MDR and IVDR documentation rather than as a separate AI Act exercise. The detail will depend on the Commission's follow-up acts and on how the MDR revision lands."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 1: Digital twins for accelerating drug discovery and development: opportunities and challenges ---
URL: https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S135964462600022X

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a review article published in Drug Discovery Today (Volume 31, Issue 2, March 2026, Article 104617) titled "Digital twins for accelerating drug discovery and development: opportunities and challenges." It is an open-access article under a Creative Commons license, authored by Sai Phanindra Venkatapurapu, Lindsay Clegg, Andrzej Nowojewski, Holly Kimko, Damilola Olabode, Aarti Sawant-Basak, and Karthick Vishwanathan. The abstract, DOI, and key highlights are provided.

The article reviews applications of digital twins (DTs) across the pharmaceutical R&D value chain, from target discovery and preclinical research to clinical trials, regulatory review, manufacturing, and post-market clinical practice. Key highlights include:
- DT applications span the entire R&D lifecycle
- DTs can be created using QSP (quantitative systems pharmacology) models and/or machine learning
- DTs integrate data with modeling to reduce uncertainty in decision-making
- In manufacturing, DTs can enhance productivity and optimize operational costs
- True DTs enable personalized care and foster shared decision-making in the clinic

The abstract emphasizes that digital twins can revolutionize drug development and personalized care by accelerating timelines, reducing costs and failure rates, and potentially improving the safety and efficacy of new therapies. Key challenges identified include data integration, model reliability, regulatory acceptance, and data privacy. Overcoming these barriers requires innovation, transparency, and collaborative efforts across the healthcare ecosystem.

The article outline covers: Introduction; DT applications in drug development; Clinical development; Regulatory review; Manufacturing; Real-world clinical practice; Opportunities and challenges; Concluding remarks; Author contributions; Conflicts of interest; Funding; Data availability (no data was used for the research); and References. The article includes 2 figures (Figure 1: Comparison of Virtual Population (VPop)-based and Digital Twin (DT)-based analyses; Figure 2: Digital twin applications for accelerating drug development visual abstract) and 2 tables (Table 1: Glossary of terminology; Table 2: DT applications poised to transform drug development, manufacturing, and real-world clinical practice).

Keywords: Digital twins, drug discovery, drug development, mathematical models, machine learning, precision medicine.

The article has been cited by 6 publications (as of the metrics shown), including works on single-cell multiomics in clinical immunology, Chinese Population Medicines development using population genetics and AI, a narrative review of digital twins in health, causal inference and digital twins for clinical trials, nitrogen heterocycles in anticancer drug discovery, and closed-loop agentic AI in drug discovery. Citation index: 5 citations; Mendeley Readers: 30.
</summary>

In this review, we explore different applications of digital twins across the pharmaceutical value chain, from target discovery and preclinical research to clinical trials, regulatory review, manufacturing and post-market clinical practice. Key challenges, however, remain in data integration, model reliability, regulatory acceptance and data privacy. Overcoming these barriers will require innovation, transparency and collaborative efforts across the healthcare ecosystem. --- SOURCE 2: AI in Clinical Trials 2026: How Digital Twins and Machine Learning Are Cutting Drug Development Time by 50% | AI Magicx Blog | AI Magicx ---
URL: https://www.aimagicx.com/blog/ai-clinical-trials-digital-twins-fda-2026

SUMMARY:
<summary>
## AI in Clinical Trials 2026: Digital Twins and Machine Learning Cutting Drug Development Time by 50%

This article (published by AI Magicx Team, ~18 min read) covers how digital twins and AI are reducing clinical trial timelines from 10-15 years to 5-7 years while improving success rates, including technology details, FDA frameworks, key platforms, and implementation strategies.

### The Core Problem

**Traditional drug development:** 
- Average new drug takes 10-15 years from discovery to market approval
- Costs $1.3-2.6 billion
- ~90% of drugs entering clinical trials fail
- 80% of trials miss enrollment deadlines; average Phase 3 trial needs 10,000+ screened patients to enroll 3,000
- Major bottlenecks: patient recruitment, sequential phases, high failure rates, protocol design flaws, and data silos

**AI solutions' impact:** 40-60% faster enrollment via ML patient matching, 15-25% improvement in Phase 2 success, 20-30% fewer protocol amendments, and 50-70% faster data cleaning.

### Digital Twins

Three levels of clinical digital twins: 
- **Level 1 (Population):** Simulate defined patient population responses; most mature/widely deployed
- **Level 2 (Cohort):** Simulate subpopulations for adaptive trial designs and dose optimization
- **Level 3 (Individual Patient):** Simulate specific patient biology with real-time monitoring; emerging technology

**Key applications:**
1. **Synthetic control arms** (Unlearn.AI's TwinRCT platform is the pioneer; FDA has accepted in multiple submissions): reduces enrollment by 30-50%, shortens trials by 6-18 months, cuts costs 20-35% per trial
2. **In silico trial simulation:** Novartis reduced protocol amendment rate by 35% in 2025 (amendments typically add 3-6 months and $500K-2M each)
3. **Adaptive trial designs:** Roche implemented in 8 programs since 2024 with average timeline reductions of 14 months per program

### AI-Powered Patient Recruitment

- 37% of trial sites fail to enroll a single patient; 85% of trials take longer than expected (avg. 6 months added)
- Cost of recruiting one Phase 3 patient: $6,500-$15,000
- Methods include EHR-based matching (Deep 6 AI reduces patient identification from months to minutes, increases eligible patients 3-5x), claims data (Tempus uses data from 7M+ patients), and digital channels
- Multi-channel AI: 4-7 months to full enrollment vs. 12-18 months traditional; cost reduced to $2,500-5,000 per patient

### Real-World Evidence

- Flatiron Health (Roche subsidiary) built the largest real-world oncology database covering 4M+ cancer patients; referenced in 20+ FDA regulatory submissions
- AI enables data harmonization, causal inference, signal detection, and synthetic data generation

### Safety Monitoring

- AI enables proactive (not just reactive) safety monitoring
- Time to detect serious adverse event signal: 6-12 months → 2-6 weeks (80-90% faster)
- 15-25% of serious AEs predicted before occurrence (new capability)
- False positive rate reduced 50%; post-market signal detection 75% faster

### FDA Regulatory Landscape

**Accepted:** AI imaging analysis, ML patient stratification, digital biomarkers as secondary endpoints, NLP for adverse event coding

**Emerging (case-by-case):** Synthetic control arms, RWE as primary evidence, AI-informed adaptive designs, decentralized trial architectures

**Exploratory:** In silico trials as partial replacements, individual patient digital twins, autonomous dose escalation, generative AI for study reports

**Key guidance documents:** AI/ML in Drug Development (2023), Digital Health Technologies (2024), RWE guidance (2024 updated), Synthetic Control Arms (2025), AI-Enabled Adaptive Designs (2025), Digital Twins in Clinical Development (2026 draft)

Compliance requirements include data integrity (audit trails, 21 CFR Part 11), validation against independent datasets, transparency in statistical analysis plans, and patient consent for AI use.

### Head-to-Head Comparison

| Dimension | Traditional | AI-Augmented | Improvement |
|---|---|---|---|
| Total development | 10-15 years | 5-8 years | 45-55% faster |
| Total cost | $1.3-2.6B | $700M-1.5B | 40-50% reduction |
| Phase 2→3 success | 33% | 42-48% | 30-45% improvement |
| Protocol amendments | 57% of trials | 35-40% | 30-40% reduction |
| Screening to enrollment | 4-8 weeks | 1-3 weeks | 60-75% faster |
| Patient dropout | 20-30% | 12-18% | 35-45% lower |

### Key Platforms
- **Digital twins:** Unlearn.AI (synthetic control arms, FDA-accepted), Dassault Systèmes SIMULIA (organ simulation, FDA-accepted for devices), Siemens Healthineers (cardiovascular), Twin Health (metabolic), PredicSis (oncology)
- **Clinical trial AI:** Medidata, Veeva, Deep 6 AI, Tempus, Saama, TrialSpark, Flatiron Health
- **Emerging:** Federated learning (Google Health, NVIDIA Clara), LLMs for clinical documentation, wearable digital biomarkers

### Implementation Strategy
- **Pharma:** Foundation (0-6 months: audit, select high-impact programs, engage FDA early) → Pilots (6-18 months: AI recruitment, digital twin protocol simulation, RWE integration) → Scale (18-36 months: standardize, synthetic controls, adaptive designs)
- **Biotech startups:** Build AI-native from day one, partner strategically with AI CROs, engage regulators early via pre-IND meetings, leverage focused data advantages
- **Academic centers:** Invest in data infrastructure, develop federated learning, train researchers in AI methods, participate in digital twin validation

### Risks
Technical (model bias, generalizability, validation gaps), regulatory (framework uncertainty, jurisdictional differences between FDA/EMA/PMDA/NMPA, audit exposure), and organizational (talent scarcity, cultural resistance, vendor dependency)

### Conclusion
AI and digital twins are fundamentally restructuring drug development. The 50% timeline reduction is being demonstrated in active programs across oncology, neurology, rare diseases, and metabolic disorders. Organizations investing now will gain compounding advantages; the remaining challenge is organizational execution rather than technology or regulation.
</summary>

--- SOURCE 3: Causal inference and digital twins: a roadmap for the future of clinical trials | npj Digital Medicine ---
URL: https://www.nature.com/articles/s41746-026-02871-4

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This Perspective article, published in npj Digital Medicine (volume 9, article 582, 2026), presents a roadmap for integrating causal inference and digital twins to modernize clinical trials. Authored by a collaborative group of leaders in pharmaceuticals, consulting, clinical research, and AI (including Mihaela van der Schaar), the article argues that clinical trials are facing major inefficiencies: Phase III trials frequently cost over $500 million and take years to complete. Furthermore, more than 75% of patients are typically excluded from trial participation, and up to 30% of enrolled participants discontinue before completion, creating a trade-off between internal validity and real-world applicability.

The article identifies three contexts of use for these AI methods: (1) exploratory/design-stage settings (biomarker discovery, subgroup identification, protocol optimization), (2) trial conduct and monitoring (interpreting emerging evidence, simulating patient trajectories for safety monitoring), and (3) confirmatory/regulatory settings (estimand clarification, covariate adjustment, hybrid-control augmentation) where methods must operate within narrow, pre-specified, rigorously validated roles.

Key applications covered include:
- Digital twins as computational models that predict treatment responses, enabling personalized risk-benefit assessments, enhancing safety and trial diversity (rather than excluding high-risk patients), serving as early warning systems during trials, and retaining data from drop-out participants.
- Digital-twin-based control arms (synthetic/hybrid cohorts) that can reduce sample sizes and recruitment needs. The EMA has issued a qualification opinion for PROCOVA (prognostic covariate adjustment). Methods like SyncTwin successfully emulated the Heart Protection Study using UK electronic health records, recovering LDL cholesterol treatment effects that closely matched the original RCT.
- Causal inference for identifying predictive biomarkers (e.g., the OncoBird framework in phase III oncology trials), estimating conditional average treatment effects (CATE) for subgroup analysis and tailored treatment (e.g., causal survival forests in an aldosterone antagonist heart failure trial), and transportability analyses to align trial findings with broader populations.

The article emphasizes a framework for robust validation: defining context of use, ensuring data fitness, evaluating predictive accuracy/calibration/robustness, examining causal assumptions (exchangeability, positivity, consistency), ensuring interpretability, benchmarking against standard methods, and aligning with regulatory pathways (FDA's MIDD Pilot Programme, EMA's Qualification of Novel Methodologies). Practical constraints include the availability of high-quality patient-level data, governance, interoperability, linkage, and consent issues—particularly acute in rare disease settings.

Author recommendations are organized by phase: in the pre-trial phase, co-developing models with retrospective benchmarking and early regulator engagement; in-trial, using pre-specified digital twin outputs for adaptive decision rules, response-adaptive randomisation, arm dropping, and sample size re-estimation. The article stresses that while immediate opportunities lie in design-stage optimization and early-phase exploration, uses in confirmatory settings must be pre-specified, justified, and aligned with statistical and regulatory guidance.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"Causal inference and digital twins offer complementary tools to define estimands, characterise treatment-effect heterogeneity, assess transportability, and simulate patient trajectories under alternative interventions. Integrated responsibly into trial design, recruitment, monitoring, and post-trial translation, they could support faster, fairer, and more informative clinical trials."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 4: Digital Twins in Clinical Trials: Virtual Controls & FDA | IntuitionLabs ---
URL: https://intuitionlabs.ai/articles/digital-twins-clinical-trials-virtual-control-arms

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is an IntuitionLabs report (published March 4, 2026, 40-min read) examining digital twins in clinical trials, focusing on virtual control arms and FDA regulatory guidance.

**Executive Summary / Key Concepts:**
- Digital twins are high-fidelity computational models of individual patients that simulate responses to standard-of-care or placebo, serving as "virtual control arms" that could reduce or replace traditional control groups.
- Key examples: (1) Phesi built a digital twin model of first-line prednisone therapy for chronic graft-versus-host disease (cGvHD) using the Trial Accelerator™ platform, with a predicted 6-month objective response rate (ORR) of 52.7% matching historical data—the authors concluded the digital twin SOC arm "can potentially replace a control arm." (2) A Johns Hopkins cardiology trial used digital twins of individual hearts to guide ventricular tachycardia ablation therapy (FDA-approved pilot for 10 patients), yielding 80% success vs. ~60% typical.
- Regulatory landscape: FDA and EMA collaborated on "Guiding Principles of Good AI Practice" (Jan 2026, 10 principles); FDA released a 7-step risk-based AI credibility framework (Jan 2025); ICH Guideline E10 (2001) allows externally controlled trials; FDA draft guidance (Feb 2023) on externally controlled trials discusses synthetic controls.
- Clinical outcomes figure: VT Ablation Success Rate 80%; cGvHD Objective Response Rate 52.7%.

**Regulatory Details:**
- ICH E10 allows externally controlled trials for serious/rare diseases where randomization is impractical. FDA accepts externally controlled evidence "for serious diseases with high unmet need" when endpoints are objective. **Control Arm Comparison (Table 1):**
- Randomized Control Arm: gold standard, minimizes bias, but requires many participants, ethical concerns with placebo, recruitment challenges.
- External Historical Control: real patient data from prior trials/registries, but potential bias and data heterogeneity.
- Synthetic Control (Aggregate): algorithmically-generated cohort, can incorporate diverse sources, but relies on past data quality and may lack individual matching precision.
- Digital Twin/Virtual Control: high granularity patient-level simulations, potentially smaller/no control group, but requires extensive high-quality data, model risk, "black-box" concerns, regulatory uncertainty (no FDA label yet).

**Case Studies:**
1. **CGvHD (Phesi/Li et al.):** Built digital twin using RWD from 108 million patients, selecting 2,042 virtual patients across 32 cohorts, narrowed to 438 virtual patients (8 real-world cohorts) as twin SOC arm. Predicted 6-month ORR of 52.7% matched historical data. Phesi's CEO: "our hope is this approach will gain regulatory approval in the future."
2. **Cardiac Arrhythmia (Johns Hopkins, 2026):** Dr. Natalia Trayanova's team created electromechanical heart models to identify optimal ablation targets; in actual procedures, 8 of 10 patients had no recurrence over a year, two had only a single mild episode (vs. ~60% typical success).

**Challenges:**
- Digital twins "will always have a level of discrepancy" from real patients and cannot fully replace reality; randomized trials still needed to calibrate and validate predictions.
- Data quality and representativeness are critical; historical/real-world data bring biases and uncertainties.
- Regulatory bodies stress digital controls must meet the "same evidentiary standard" as real controls.
- Strategy: use digital twins to augment (not completely replace) real controls—running a smaller actual control arm alongside the twin allows calibration and preserves blinding.
- Advocates argue that if synthetic control arms provide statistically equivalent evidence to live placebo, "continuing to expose patients to placebo is not methodological rigor – it requires positive justification."

**Terminology:** Digital twins incorporate real-time or historical patient data (genome, imaging, EHR, biomarkers, environmental exposures) into dynamic predictive models, distinct from digital patients, virtual patients, and synthetic control arms.

--- SOURCE 6: FDA, EMA, and ICH Expectations for AI Regulatory Systems ---
URL: https://kitsa.ai/blog/fda-ema-ich-expectations-ai-regulatory-systems

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This article from Kitsa's editorial team provides a practical guide to FDA, EMA, and ICH expectations for AI in clinical regulatory systems, covering credibility, validation, lifecycle governance, and data integrity. The regulatory landscape has converged significantly through several key milestones: EMA finalized its Reflection Paper on AI in September 2024; FDA published its first draft AI drug-development guidance in January 2025 with a 7-step credibility assessment framework; ICH E6(R3) GCP was finalized January 2025 (adopted by FDA September 2025); and FDA and EMA jointly published ten Guiding Principles of Good AI Practice on January 14, 2026 — the first formally converged FDA-EMA statement on AI. ICH M11 CeSHarP protocol standard was finalized November 2025 and adopted by FDA May 2026.

**FDA Credibility Framework (Draft Guidance FDA-2024-D-4689):** Applies to AI models whose outputs inform regulatory decisions on safety, effectiveness, or quality (excluding drug discovery/internal efficiency). Centers on defining the "context of use" (COU), then a seven-step credibility assessment: define the question of interest, define COU, assess AI model risk, develop a credibility assessment plan proportionate to risk, execute the plan, document results and deviations, and determine adequacy for the COU. Risk is a function of the model's influence on the regulatory decision and the consequence of a decision error. Requires lifecycle monitoring for model drift and adherence to ALCOA+ data integrity principles and 21 CFR Part 11 obligations where applicable. FDA encourages early engagement with sponsors.

**EMA Reflection Paper (EMA/CHMP/CVMP/83833/2023):** Places full accountability on sponsors/MAHs to demonstrate AI systems are fit for purpose. Distinguishes "explainability" (understanding why a model predicts) from "interpretability" (whether human oversight can identify and act on problems). Accepts that full explainability isn't always possible but requires interpretability with human oversight. For scientific advice requests, EMA expects full model architecture, development logs, training/validation dataset documentation, and evidence of generalizability.

**Joint FDA-EMA Ten Guiding Principles (Jan 14, 2026):** Non-prescriptive and voluntary: human-centric by design, risk-based approach, adherence to standards, clear context of use, multidisciplinary expertise, data governance and documentation, model design practices, risk-based performance assessment, lifecycle management, and clear essential information. These are expected to shape future binding guidance in both jurisdictions.

**ICH E6(R3):** Adds a dedicated chapter on computerized systems with requirements for validation, access controls, user accountability, and audit trails that apply to AI systems in GCP-regulated trials. Sponsor oversight extends to CROs and technology vendors — responsibility doesn't transfer when tasks are outsourced. **ICH M11 CeSHarP** provides a structured protocol standard that AI-generated protocols should target for alignment to enable electronic regulatory review.

**EMA GMP Annex 22:** Under development for AI in pharmaceutical manufacturing. A July 2025 draft initially restricted dynamic/adaptive/probabilistic AI (including genAI/LLMs) from critical GMP applications; a June-July 2026 multistakeholder workshop is reassessing this following industry pushback.

**EU AI Act (Regulation 2024/1689):** Binding law (entered into force August 2024). High-risk classification requires an Article 6 analysis: Article 6(1) covers AI as a safety component of Annex I-regulated products (notably MDR medical devices); Article 6(2) covers AI in narrow Annex III categories (biometric categorization, public healthcare benefit eligibility, life/health insurance risk assessment, patient triage). General pharma R&D, regulatory document generation, protocol development, and pharmacovigilance analytics aren't automatically high-risk; Article 6(3) provides exemptions for systems not materially influencing decisions or posing significant risk. High-risk obligations include risk management, data governance, technical documentation, record-keeping, transparency, human oversight, and cybersecurity controls. Under the May 7, 2026 Digital Omnibus provisional agreement (pending formal adoption), Annex III standalone deadline would move to December 2, 2027 and Annex I product-integrated deadline to August 2, 2028. Estimated compliance costs: ~EUR 29,277 per AI unit annually, with certification costs of EUR 16,800–23,000 per unit.

**Documentation requirements** consistent across all frameworks: credibility/validation plans developed prospectively, training/validation data provenance, model architecture documentation, and lifecycle monitoring records with audit trails (computer-generated, timestamped, attributed under Part 11/E6(R3)).

This webpage is an article (published May 11, 2026 on Brunslab, a Chinese pharmaceutical packaging materials E&L research blog) providing a deep analysis of the joint FDA-EMA release of "Guiding Principles of Good AI Practice in Drug Development," published January 14, 2026. The document resulted from the April 2024 FDA-EMA bilateral meeting and aligns with EMA's EMANS 2028 strategy and the EU Biotechnology Act proposal. It represents the first systematic collaboration between the two most rigorous regulatory agencies, covering AI systems used to generate or analyze nonclinical, clinical, post-market, and manufacturing evidence for drugs and biologics.

The 10 principles are: 1) Human-centric by design, 2) Risk-based approach, 3) Adherence to standards, 4) Clear context of use, 5) Multidisciplinary expertise, 6) Data governance and documentation, 7) Model design and development practices, 8) Risk-based performance assessment, 9) Life cycle management, and 10) Clear, essential information.

Key official position: EMA explicitly states that existing regulations are sufficient and no new legislation is needed—industry can proceed with AI applications within current GxP frameworks. FDA notes AI use in drug development has grown exponentially since 2016.

Industry background data (third-party, not official): over 70% of large pharma companies have AI projects by 2025; global AI drug development market exceeds $1.5 billion in 2025 (up from ~$1.2 billion in 2024); in 2025 Eli Lilly partnered with NVIDIA on an AI supercomputer.

According to law firm McGuirewoods, the principles serve as a "governance checklist" rather than an "operational manual" with concrete instructions, leaving developers to interpret application. Recommended actions include establishing formal cross-departmental AI governance, implementing risk-tiered classification and validation, ensuring robust documentation (data provenance, model selection, validation reports), and early engagement with regulators via pre-submission meetings.

The principles represent "Good AI Practice" that runs parallel to (not replacing) GCP, GLP, GMP, and GDP frameworks. All data entering regulatory decisions must be traceable to traditional GxP audit paths.

For Chinese pharmaceutical companies, impacts apply mainly to those filing in both FDA and EMA markets. Key requirements are transparency and traceability. NMPA's future alignment is uncertain, so the main driver for implementing FDA/EMA-standard AI data governance documentation is international business rather than domestic regulatory needs.

Practical recommendations: 1) Build an AI tool inventory (aligned with Principle 2 risk-tiering); 2) Prepare AI system documentation templates (Principle 6); 3) Audit existing AI tool documentation completeness (Principle 7); 4) Establish cross-departmental AI governance mechanisms (Principle 5); 5) Add AI documentation and explainability as new evaluation criteria for pharmaceutical packaging material suppliers (Principle 10), a trend expected to propagate to packaging material companies.

args.summary:
This is a GitHub repository (Benchmarking-Single-Cell-Perturbation, also called PerTogether) by Xiang Lin at Harvard Medical School, serving as a curated library and benchmark for single-cell perturbation models. The repository organizes models developed for genetic/chemical perturbation data into a comprehensive table with links, name, year, journal, and title.

The models span from 2018 to 2026 and include: Rachel (2018, Pacific Symposium on Biocomputing), scGEN (2019, Nature Methods), DTD (2019, WWW), CPA (2021, Molecular Systems Biology), CellBox (2021, Cell Systems), CellDrift (2022, BIB), MultiCPA, PerturbNet (2022), scINSIGHT (2022, Genome Biology), scPreGAN (2022, Bioinformatics), GEARS (2023, Nature Biotechnology), cycleCDR (2023), scVIDR (2023, Patterns), Unagi (2023), CINEMA-OT (2023, Nature Methods), ChemCPA (2023, NeurIPS), DREEP (2023, BMC Medicine), ontoVAE (2023, Bioinformatics), scDiff (2023), ContrastiveVI (2023, Nature Methods), sVAE (2023, PMLR), CellOT (2023, Nature Methods), MOASL (2023), samsVAE (2024, NeurIPS), Biolord (2024, Nature Biotech), PDGrapher (2024, Nature Biomedical Engineering), TAT (2024), scVAE (2024), Cell PaintingCNN (2024), scDisInFact (2024), CellCap (2024), CODEX (2024, Bioinformatics), scFM (2024, PertEval-scFM), STAMP (2024), PrePR-CT (2024), PRnet (2024, NC), TranSiGen (2024, NC), BioDiscoveryAgent (2024), DRSPRING (2024), PertKGE (2024), scRank (2024, Cell Reports Medicine), CellFlow (2025), IMPA (2025), PS (2025, Nature Cell Biology), TRADE (2025, Nature Genetics), UNAGI (2025, Nature Biomedical Engineering), STATE (2025), scAgent (2025), CONCERT (2025), Cradle-VAE (2025, AAAI), Pertpy (2025, NM), Scouter (2025), PertAdapt (2025), CausalGRN (2025), Systema (2025, Nature Biotechnology), Stack (2026), AlphaCell (2026), XPert (2026, NMI), PrePR-CT (2026, NMI), SequenTx (2026, NMI), TxPert (2026, NBT), scPert (2026), X-Cell (2026), RegVelo (2026, Cell), and UniPert-G2CP (2026, Cell).

The repository also lists reviews (including a 2026 Nature Reviews Genetics article on "Interpretation, extrapolation and perturbation of single cells"), benchmarks and challenges (including a 2025 Nature Methods finding that deep-learning gene perturbation prediction does not yet outperform simple linear baselines, a 2025 Communications Biology large-scale benchmark for network inference, and PerturBench 2026 at NeurIPS), and perturbation datasets (including SC-perturb, C-MAP, PerturbBase, PerturDB, Tahoe-100M, plus spatial perturbation methods like Perturb-Fish, PerturbView, Perturb-map, Perturb-DBiT, Spatial-perturb-seq, NIS-seq, PERTURB-CAST, and SPAC-seq).

The repository includes FastPert, a tool for quickly checking DEGs and enriched pathways of perturbations. The project has 125 stars, 7 watches, and 7 forks, is licensed under Apache-2.0, and plans to build APIs for the models on TDC (Therapeutics Data Commons) for benchmarking. Contact: Xiang Lin (xiang_lin@hms.harvard.edu). Citation: PerTogether: A tool for perturbation research and modeling (Xiang Lin, Zhenxing Li, Chenyi Li, Hengyu Zhang, 2025, Version 1.0).

## Abstract

Single cell genetic perturbation modeling involves predicting the effects of unobserved genetic manipulations, enabling scalable _in silico_ screens for target discovery. Recent reports have claimed that deep learning-based perturbation models fail to outperform uninformative baselines, raising doubts about their utility. Here, we show that these conclusions largely stem from limitations of benchmarking _metrics_, not from the models themselves. We introduce a framework for evaluating bench-mark metric calibration using positive and negative controls, including a new positive control baseline (the _interpolated duplicate_) and a quantitative calibration measure (the _dynamic range fraction_). Across 14 perturbation datasets and 13 evaluation metrics, we find that conventional metrics such as mean squared error (MSE) and control-referenced delta correlation (Pearson(Δ ctrl)) are often poorly calibrated, whereas weighted and rank-based alternatives exhibit consistent calibration. Under well-calibrated metrics, deep learning models outperform mean, control, and linear baselines, and in some cases even surpass the additive baseline in combination-prediction tasks. Calibrated evaluation thus explains prior reports of model underperformance, revealing that deep learning models _do_ outperform uninformative baselines.

*   Virtual Cells
*   Perturb-seq
*   Benchmarking
*   Foundation Models

## Introduction

Single-cell genetic perturbation modeling aims to predict transcriptomic responses to gene perturbations (typically inhibition or activation) in one or more biological contexts (e.g., cell types). If successful, perturbation response models (sometimes termed “virtual cells”[1](https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2025.10.20.683304v1.full-text#fn-2)) could enable scalable _in silico_ screens to uncover genes which reverse disease or restore youthful cellular states. Recent studies, however, have questioned whether transcriptome-level perturbation modeling is viable. In their recent work, Ahlmann-Eltze et al. ([2](https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2025.10.20.683304v1.full-text#ref-2)) reported that deep learning models do not outperform uninformative baselines across multiple datasets. Likewise, several independent benchmarks have found that a simple “mean baseline,” the average perturbation response in the training set, often matches or surpasses state-of-the-art models on metrics such as mean absolute error (MAE), mean squared error (MSE), or the correlation of control-referenced deltas (Pearson(Δ ctrl)) ([3](https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2025.10.20.683304v1.full-text#ref-3)–[8](https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2025.10.20.683304v1.full-text#ref-8)). Together, these findings invite skepticism about the utility of deep learning-based perturbation response models.

In earlier work, we identified two artifacts that explain why the mean baseline can appear competitive despite lacking perturbation-specific signal ([9](https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2025.10.20.683304v1.full-text#ref-9)). The first, _control bias_, arises when systematic differences between control and perturbed cells inflate control-referenced correlation metrics, a phenomenon also described by Viñas Torné et al. ([3](https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2025.10.20.683304v1.full-text#ref-3)). The second, _signal dilution_, occurs when error metrics dilute meaningful biological signals arising from perturbations with a small but significant number of differentially expressed genes (DEGs), causing mean predictions to appear accurate. Together, these effects allow uninformative predictors to achieve deceptively high scores even when they fail to capture underlying biology, highlighting the need to evaluate whether common benchmarking metrics can distinguish null from meaningful predictions in the first place.

Here, we address this challenge by introducing a framework for evaluating the calibration of perturbation model benchmarking metrics ([Fig. 1](https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2025.10.20.683304v1.full-text#F1)). In this context, “calibration” refers to the degree to which a metric improves in response to a meaningful biological signal and correctly ranks informative predictions above null ones. We formalize the use of positive (informative predictor) and negative (null predictor) controls, introduce a new “interpolated duplicate” baseline that provides a stable positive control, and define a quantitative measure of calibration, the _Dynamic Range Fraction_ (DRF). From an analysis of 14 Perturb-seq datasets and 13 metrics, we find that common metrics such as MSE and control-referenced Pearson correlations are often poorly calibrated, whereas weighted and rank-based alternatives such as weighted MSE (WMSE) ([9](https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2025.10.20.683304v1.full-text#ref-9)), weighted ![Image 3: Embedded Image](https://www.biorxiv.org/sites/default/files/highwire/biorxiv/early/2025/10/21/2025.10.20.683304/embed/inline-graphic-1.gif) ([9](https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2025.10.20.683304v1.full-text#ref-9)), and Normalized Inverse Rank (NIR) ([10](https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2025.10.20.683304v1.full-text#ref-10)) exhibit consistent calibration. We then evaluated eight deep learning models across four datasets and two prediction tasks. Under well-calibrated conditions, deep learning models generally outperform uninformative baselines, indicating that the limitations reported in prior studies largely reflect shortcomings of evaluation rather than of modeling.

## Results

### Negative and positive controls

In biological experiments, positive and negative controls verify that an assay can detect true effects. A negative control is a condition expected to yield a null result, while a positive control is one expected to produce a consistent, strong signal. In perturbation modeling, an uninformative baseline that always predicts the mean of all perturbations (the “mean baseline”, see Sup. Note 1) serves as an effective negative control. However, benchmarks typically lack an equivalent positive control, leaving ambiguity when models perform poorly: low scores may indicate either genuine model failure or insufficient metric sensitivity to detect positive model performance.

In our previous work, we introduced the _technical duplicate_ baseline as a positive control for perturbation modeling ([9](https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2025.10.20.683304v1.full-text#ref-9)). This baseline splits the population of cells receiving each perturbation into two halves, using one subset to predict the other ([Fig. 2A](https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2025.10.20.683304v1.full-text#F2)). Because both halves share the same perturbation-specific signal, the technical duplicate should, in principle, outperform null predictors. We evaluated its performance on two benchmarking datasets, Norman19 and Replogle22 K562 genome-wide Perturb-seq (GWPS), using two common metrics: mean squared error (MSE) and control-referenced delta correlation (Pearson(Δ ctrl)) ([Fig. S1](https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2025.10.20.683304v1.full-text#F4)). As expected, the technical duplicate exceeded the mean baseline on both metrics in Norman19 ([Fig. S1A,C](https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2025.10.20.683304v1.full-text#F4)). In contrast, in Replogle22 K562 GWPS it performed comparably to the mean baseline under Pearson(Δ ctrl) ([Fig. S1D](https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2025.10.20.683304v1.full-text#F4)) and, unexpectedly, _underperformed_ it with MSE ([Fig. S1B](https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2025.10.20.683304v1.full-text#F4)).

To better understand this result, we compared MSE(technical duplicate) and MSE(mean baseline) for each perturbation in Replogle22 K562 GWPS. The technical duplicate underperformed the mean baseline for approximately 95% of perturbations ([Fig. S1E](https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2025.10.20.683304v1.full-text#F4)). Examining representative cases of high (SUPT6H, 435 DEGs), moderate (OGFOD1, 31 DEGs), and low (COX5A, 5 DEGs) perturbation strength showed that genes strongly-affected by a perturbation (adjusted _p_ DEG _<_ 0.05) were predicted more accurately by the technical duplicate, whereas unaffected genes (_p_ DEG _>_ 0.95) favored the mean baseline ([Fig. S2](https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2025.10.20.683304v1.full-text#F5)). Across all perturbations, technical duplicate performance improved with increasing perturbation strength ([Fig. S1E](https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2025.10.20.683304v1.full-text#F4)). A downsampling titration experiment further revealed strong dependence on sampling power: increasing the number of cells used to compute the technical duplicate markedly improved its performance relative to the mean baseline ([Fig. S3](https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2025.10.20.683304v1.full-text#F6)). Together, these findings suggest a straightforward explanation for poor technical duplicate performance: for strongly affected genes, the technical duplicate captures the true signal despite limited sampling, whereas for unaffected genes, the mean baseline provides a more stable estimate because it averages over thousands of cells to calculate unaffected gene expression ([Fig. S4](https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2025.10.20.683304v1.full-text#F7)).

Motivated by these observations, we developed a novel _interpolated duplicate_ baseline that combines the strengths of both approaches (see Sup. Note 1; [Fig. 2B](https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2025.10.20.683304v1.full-text#F2), [Fig. S5](https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2025.10.20.683304v1.full-text#F8)) to create a more stable positive control. This predictor linearly interpolates between the mean baseline and the technical duplicate, weighting each gene by its DEG _p_-value (adjusted): genes with strong evidence of differential expression are shifted to-ward the technical duplicate, while genes with weak or null effects are shifted toward the mean baseline. This design yields a robust positive control that retains stability in weakly perturbed genes while preserving the ability to detect true perturbation effects in strongly perturbed genes ([Fig. S5A,B](https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2025.10.20.683304v1.full-text#F8), [Fig. S6](https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2025.10.20.683304v1.full-text#F9)).

### Measuring the calibration of benchmark metrics

With our positive control (interpolated duplicate) and negative control (mean baseline) in hand, we next defined a _meta_-metric to quantify the calibration of benchmarking metrics. We term this quantity the “Dynamic Range Fraction” (DRF), which measures, for each perturbation, how effectively a metric distinguishes positive from negative controls. For any metric _m_(_·_), DRF is defined as ![Image 9: Embedded Image](https://www.biorxiv.org/sites/default/files/highwire/biorxiv/early/2025/10/21/2025.10.20.683304/embed/graphic-3.gif) where _ŷ_ _n_ is the mean baseline (or any other negative control), _ŷ_ _p_ is the interpolated duplicate (or any other positive control), _y_ represents the ground truth and hence yields perfect performance on the metric (for example, _MSE_ = 0 or _P earson_(Δ ctrl) = 1), and _ϵ_ is a small constant added for numerical stability. As illustrated ([Fig. 2C](https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2025.10.20.683304v1.full-text#F2)), DRF captures the fraction of the theoretical dynamic range [_m_(_y_) _− m_(_ŷ_ _n_)] (“ideal response”) that is realized by the empirical range [_m_(_ŷ_ _p_) _− m_(_ŷ_ _n_)] (“real response”). When the positive control outperforms the negative control (and hence the metric is better calibrated), DRF values increase in proportion. In a miscalibrated scenario, DRF values approach zero, reflecting limited metric sensitivity to detect improvements over the negative control. While in this study, we generally use the interpolated duplicate as the positive control and the mean baseline as the negative control, one could substitute any experimentally-appropriate controls and still utilize the DRF to measure calibration.

We applied the DRF to assess the calibration of MSE and Pearson(Δ ctrl) in Replogle22 K562 GWPS and the Replogle22 K562 essential-gene dataset (termed “Replogle22 K562” here). The latter targets 2,045 genes required for cell proliferation or survival and thus exhibits stronger perturbation effects ([11](https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2025.10.20.683304v1.full-text#ref-11)). In both datasets, most perturbations show low DRF values, indicating poor calibration overall; Pearson(Δ ctrl) performs slightly better than MSE, and calibration improves with stronger perturbations ([Fig. S7A](https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2025.10.20.683304v1.full-text#F10)).

We hypothesized that low DRF may reflect dilution of weak yet biologically meaningful signals rather than the absence of learnable structure. Indeed, for the SP2 transcription factor (TF) in Replogle22 K562 GWPS, DRF(MSE) is near zero ([Fig. S7B](https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2025.10.20.683304v1.full-text#F10)), but gene set enrichment analysis (GSEA) of SP2 differential expression ranks recovers SP2 binding targets among the top ENCODE/ChEA gene sets ([Fig. S7C](https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2025.10.20.683304v1.full-text#F10)). Similar trends across other transcription factors ([Fig. S7D](https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2025.10.20.683304v1.full-text#F10), Supplementary File 1) suggest that MSE underweights sparse but meaningful effects, a bias captured by its low DRF(MSE).

We previously proposed weighted metrics such as weighted MSE (WMSE) ([9](https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2025.10.20.683304v1.full-text#ref-9)) to address the dilution of small but significant biological signals by MSE. Applying this approach largely rescues miscalibration in the Replogle22 K562 GWPS dataset, including for SP2 and the other TF perturbations we tested ([Fig. S7B](https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2025.10.20.683304v1.full-text#F10)). Across datasets, WMSE also shows substantially better calibration than MSE, even for datasets with few DEGs ([Fig. 2D](https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2025.10.20.683304v1.full-text#F2), [Fig. S7E](https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2025.10.20.683304v1.full-text#F10)).

Extending this analysis, we evaluated the calibration of 13 benchmarking metrics across 14 Perturb-seq datasets ([Fig. 2E](https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2025.10.20.683304v1.full-text#F2)). Weighted ![Image 11: Embedded Image](https://www.biorxiv.org/sites/default/files/highwire/biorxiv/early/2025/10/21/2025.10.20.683304/embed/inline-graphic-2.gif), NIR, and WMSE consistently showed strong calibration across most datasets, whereas commonly used metrics such as MSE and Pearson(Δ ctrl) performed well only in datasets with strong perturbation signals (e.g., Norman19). When recalculating DRF using the technical duplicate as the positive control ([Fig. S8](https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2025.10.20.683304v1.full-text#F11)), weighted ![Image 13: Embedded Image](https://www.biorxiv.org/sites/default/files/highwire/biorxiv/early/2025/10/21/2025.10.20.683304/embed/inline-graphic-3.gif), NIR, and WMSE again display consistent calibration, confirming that their apparent calibration is not an artifact of the interpolated duplicate. However, this analysis also high-lights the reduced stability of the technical duplicate across metrics, further supporting the use of the interpolated duplicate as a more robust positive control.

### Benchmarking the unseen gene prediction task

Having evaluated metric calibration across our benchmarking datasets, we next assessed model performance on the un-seen single gene prediction task. In this task, models are trained to predict gene expression responses for single gene perturbations that are held out during training ([Fig. 3A](https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2025.10.20.683304v1.full-text#F3), left). Eight models were evaluated: scGPT ([12](https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2025.10.20.683304v1.full-text#ref-12)), GEARS ([13](https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2025.10.20.683304v1.full-text#ref-13)), PRESAGE ([14](https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2025.10.20.683304v1.full-text#ref-14)), scLambda ([15](https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2025.10.20.683304v1.full-text#ref-15)), and four models that predict gene expression from foundation-model gene embeddings using a multilayer perceptron (foundation MLP or “fMLP” models), including embeddings from Geneformer ([16](https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2025.10.20.683304v1.full-text#ref-16)), ESM2 ([17](https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2025.10.20.683304v1.full-text#ref-17)), scGPT ([12](https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2025.10.20.683304v1.full-text#ref-12)), and GenePT ([18](https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2025.10.20.683304v1.full-text#ref-18)). We also included the linear baseline introduced by Ahlmann-Eltze et al. ([2](https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2025.10.20.683304v1.full-text#ref-2)), which performs PCA on the training-set gene expression matrix and fits a linear model to predict unseen gene perturbation responses using these features.

### Benchmarking the unseen combos prediction task

The unseen combos prediction task evaluates whether a model can predict the effect of an unseen pair of perturbed genes after seeing both genes individually along with other gene pair examples during training ([Fig. 3A](https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2025.10.20.683304v1.full-text#F3), right).

We first benchmarked model performance on Norman19 ([20](https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2025.10.20.683304v1.full-text#ref-20)), the most widely used dataset for this task setting ([2](https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2025.10.20.683304v1.full-text#ref-2)– [6](https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2025.10.20.683304v1.full-text#ref-6), [8](https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2025.10.20.683304v1.full-text#ref-8)). Norman19 comprises 100 single-gene and 124 doublegene perturbations. Ahlmann-Eltze et al. ([2](https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2025.10.20.683304v1.full-text#ref-2)) previously compared models to a control-cell baseline and to an _additive baseline_ that predicts combination effects by summing single-gene effects. The additive baseline performs strongly, which is unsurprising given that 96% of gene-pair perturbation effects are additive ([2](https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2025.10.20.683304v1.full-text#ref-2)). Moreover, the combinatorial space is sparsely sampled: in the present study, the training set includes 31 of 4,950 possible pairs[2](https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2025.10.20.683304v1.full-text#fn-3), or 0.63%, leaving little opportunity for models to learn non-additive interactions.

Consistent with this, we found that most models exceeded the mean and control baselines across metrics, but the additive baseline remained difficult to surpass (although PRESAGE outperformed it on 5 of 13 metrics; [table S3](https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2025.10.20.683304v1.full-text#T4)). Further analysis showed that the additive baseline captured roughly 88% of the _ideal performance gap_ (see Sup. Note 1, metric calibration section) in the best-calibrated metrics, comparable to the interpolated duplicate baseline which accesses held-out combination data ([Fig. S11](https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2025.10.20.683304v1.full-text#F14)). This evidence of additive base-line saturation, together with limited combinatorial coverage, limits Norman19’s value for benchmarking models that aim to learn non-additive genetic interactions.

To test whether models can surpass additivity when exposed to a broader range of gene combinations during training, we evaluated Wessels23 ([21](https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2025.10.20.683304v1.full-text#ref-21)), which includes 28 genes and 157 unique gene pairs (train set includes 39 of 378 possible combinations, or 10.3%). In this setting, multiple models display higher average performance compared to the additive base-line under WMSE ([Fig. 3D](https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2025.10.20.683304v1.full-text#F3); [table 1](https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2025.10.20.683304v1.full-text#T1)) and weighted ![Image 21: Embedded Image](https://www.biorxiv.org/sites/default/files/highwire/biorxiv/early/2025/10/21/2025.10.20.683304/embed/inline-graphic-6.gif) ([Fig. 3E](https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2025.10.20.683304v1.full-text#F3); [table 1](https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2025.10.20.683304v1.full-text#T1)). Across all metrics, at least one model, PRESAGE, exceeded the additive baseline in 12 of 13 metrics ([table 1](https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2025.10.20.683304v1.full-text#T1), [table S4](https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2025.10.20.683304v1.full-text#T5)), and consistently surpassed the mean and control baselines in well-calibrated metrics.

Similar to the unseen gene task, calibrated evaluation shows that several models consistently outperform mean and control baselines in the unseen combos task. When presented with a more robust sampling of the combinatorial search space during training (as in the Wessels23 dataset), at least one deep learning-based model (i.e., PRESAGE) beats the additive baseline in 12/13 metrics. Taken together, these findings suggest that deep learning-based perturbation models can outperform uninformative baselines on the unseen combos task, and that they may be capable of modeling non-additive gene interactions as well.

## Discussion

Our results help resolve a central tension in recent perturbation-response studies: although prior work reported that deep learning models fail to outperform uninformative baselines ([2](https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2025.10.20.683304v1.full-text#ref-2)–[8](https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2025.10.20.683304v1.full-text#ref-8)), we find that these reports largely reflect _metric miscalibration_, not intrinsic limits of model capacity. Common metrics such as MSE and control-referenced Pearson correlations often fail to distinguish true biological signal from noise, particularly in weakly-perturbed datasets. Using the DRF, we show that such metrics are poorly calibrated, frequently ranking null predictors above biologically meaningful positive controls. In contrast, DEG-aware and rank-based metrics (WMSE, weighted ![Image 23: Embedded Image](https://www.biorxiv.org/sites/default/files/highwire/biorxiv/early/2025/10/21/2025.10.20.683304/embed/inline-graphic-7.gif), and NIR) display robust calibration across datasets, correctly rewarding models that capture perturbation-specific signals.

Under calibrated evaluation, a consistent pattern emerges across tasks: In the unseen-gene prediction setting, most deep learning-based models outperformed the mean, control, and linear baselines. This finding challenges prior reports of model failure and establishes that current architectures learn generalizable perturbation-response representations. In the combination-gene task, some models likewise exceeded null baselines and (especially for PRESAGE) even surpassed the additive baseline in the Wessels23 dataset. While models also surpassed this predictor in some metrics in the Norman19 dataset, our findings reveal the degree to which the additive baseline in Norman19 embodies saturated performance on well-calibrated metrics, and thus we recommend that future studies refrain from using this dataset as the sole benchmark of combinatorial perturbation modeling.

Additionally, PRESAGE and scLambda are notable models in our analysis, as both are newer architectures and provide novel approaches to leveraging prior knowledge for predicting perturbation effects. Based on their robust performance, it may be valuable to include these models (and potentially other newer architectures) in future benchmarking studies alongside the typically-benchmarked models like scGPT and GEARS.

Beyond our empirical findings, our study introduces further conceptual contributions. We introduce an interpolated duplicate positive control and we formalize _metric calibration_ as a prerequisite for benchmarking perturbation models, analogous to assay validation in experimental biology. Without positive controls, apparent negative results may reflect low metric sensitivity rather than true model failure.

Taken together, these findings reframe the debate on the feasibility of genetic perturbation modeling. The main limitation is not model capability but the use of uncalibrated bench-marks that obscure true performance. With calibrated metrics, we show that deep learning models can exceed trivial baselines, establishing a more optimistic foundation for _in silico_ perturbation modeling and its application to virtual cells for therapeutic target discovery.

### Limitations and Future Directions

Despite these advances, several limitations remain that motivate directions for future work. First, we explored only a subset of available benchmarking metrics described in prior studies. Additionally, while calibration is essential, a well-calibrated metric is not necessarily biologically meaningful, and future studies should examine which calibrated metrics best reflect interpretable and experimentally relevant perturbation responses. Second, our analysis was limited to a subset of available perturbation datasets. The comparison of performance between Norman19 (provides 0.63% of combo search space in training) and Wessels23 (provides 10.3% of search space) indicated that training set characteristics may influence the performance of both baselines and models on certain tasks. In future studies, it will be interesting to evaluate additional combinatorial datasets and more thoroughly characterize the relationship between factors like training set coverage of the combinatorial landscape and model performance. Finally, we focused on the unseen-gene and combination-gene prediction tasks, leaving the unseen-context task (predicting responses in unobserved cell types, donors, or conditions) unaddressed. Because this task directly tests the generalizability of virtual cell models, extending calibration analysis to context transfer will be a valuable extension of this work in the future.

The datasets used in this preprint were gathered from Zenodo and Figshare as described in the methods (see Sup. Note 1), and no new datasets were contributed. Code to reproduce this work is provided on Github at shiftbioscience/Perturbation-Models-Outperform-Baselines.

This is a bioRxiv preprint (DOI: 10.1101/2025.10.20.683304) titled "Deep Learning-Based Genetic Perturbation Models Do Outperform Uninformative Baselines on Well-Calibrated Metrics." The study addresses prior reports (e.g., Ahlmann-Eltze et al.) claiming deep learning perturbation models fail to beat uninformative baselines, arguing these conclusions stem from limitations of benchmarking metrics rather than the models themselves.

**Key contributions and methods:**
- Introduces a framework for evaluating benchmark metric calibration using positive and negative controls, including a new positive control baseline called the "interpolated duplicate" and a quantitative calibration measure called the "Dynamic Range Fraction" (DRF).
- The interpolated duplicate combines the technical duplicate and mean baseline, weighting each gene by DEG p-values. Strongly perturbed genes are weighted toward the technical duplicate, weak/null genes toward the mean baseline.
- Explains prior artifacts: "control bias" (systematic control/perturbed differences inflating correlation metrics) and "signal dilution" (error metrics diluting meaningful biological signals).
- Analyzed 14 Perturb-seq datasets (~2.5 million cells across 9 cell types) and 13 evaluation metrics.

**Key findings:**
- Conventional metrics (MSE, control-referenced Pearson(Δ ctrl)) are often poorly calibrated, whereas weighted and rank-based alternatives (weighted MSE/WMSE, weighted Δ, Normalized Inverse Rank/NIR) exhibit consistent calibration.
- Under well-calibrated metrics, deep learning models outperform mean, control, and linear baselines on the unseen gene prediction task (validated in Replogle22 K562 and Nadig25 HepG2 datasets).
- Eight models evaluated: scGPT, GEARS, PRESAGE, scLambda, and four foundation MLP models (Geneformer, ESM2, scGPT, GenePT embeddings), plus a linear baseline.
- In the unseen combos task, PRESAGE exceeded the additive baseline in 12 of 13 metrics on the Wessels23 dataset; the additive baseline captures ~88% of the ideal performance gap in Norman19, limiting its value for benchmarking non-additive interactions (training sets cover only 0.63% of combo space in Norman19 vs 10.3% in Wessels23).

**Conclusions:** The apparent weakness of perturbation models arises primarily from metric miscalibration rather than model performance. The study recommends using calibrated metrics and cautions against using Norman19 as the sole benchmark for combinatorial perturbation modeling. PRESAGE and scLambda are highlighted as newer architectures worth including in future benchmarks. Code is available on GitHub at shiftbioscience/Perturbation-Models-Outperform-Baselines. Authors: Henry E. Miller, Gabriel M. Mejia, Francis J. A. Leblanc, Bo Wang, Brendan Swain, Lucas Paulo de Lima Camillo (Shift Bioscience Ltd., Cambridge UK; University of Toronto; University of Cambridge).

* [Constantin Ahlmann-Eltze](#auth-Constantin-Ahlmann_Eltze-Aff1-Aff2-Aff3)

## Abstract

Recent research in deep-learning-based foundation models promises to learn representations of single-cell data that enable prediction of the effects of genetic perturbations. Here we compared five foundation models and two other deep learning models against deliberately simple baselines for predicting transcriptome changes after single or double perturbations. None outperformed the baselines, which highlights the importance of critical benchmarking in directing and evaluating method development.
