--- SOURCE 2: Deep Learning-Based Genetic Perturbation Models Do Outperform Uninformative Baselines on Well-Calibrated Metrics ---
URL: https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2025.10.20.683304v1.full-text

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a bioRxiv preprint (DOI: 10.1101/2025.10.20.683304) titled "Deep Learning-Based Genetic Perturbation Models Do Outperform Uninformative Baselines on Well-Calibrated Metrics." The study addresses prior reports (e.g., Ahlmann-Eltze et al.) claiming deep learning perturbation models fail to beat uninformative baselines, arguing these conclusions stem from limitations of benchmarking metrics rather than the models themselves.

**Key contributions and methods:**
- Introduces a framework for evaluating benchmark metric calibration using positive and negative controls, including a new positive control baseline called the "interpolated duplicate" and a quantitative calibration measure called the "Dynamic Range Fraction" (DRF).
- The interpolated duplicate combines the technical duplicate and mean baseline, weighting each gene by DEG p-values. Strongly perturbed genes are weighted toward the technical duplicate, weak/null genes toward the mean baseline.
- Explains prior artifacts: "control bias" (systematic control/perturbed differences inflating correlation metrics) and "signal dilution" (error metrics diluting meaningful biological signals).
- Analyzed 14 Perturb-seq datasets (~2.5 million cells across 9 cell types) and 13 evaluation metrics.

**Key findings:**
- Conventional metrics (MSE, control-referenced Pearson(Δ ctrl)) are often poorly calibrated, whereas weighted and rank-based alternatives (weighted MSE/WMSE, weighted Δ, Normalized Inverse Rank/NIR) exhibit consistent calibration.
- Under well-calibrated metrics, deep learning models outperform mean, control, and linear baselines on the unseen gene prediction task (validated in Replogle22 K562 and Nadig25 HepG2 datasets).
- Eight models evaluated: scGPT, GEARS, PRESAGE, scLambda, and four foundation MLP models (Geneformer, ESM2, scGPT, GenePT embeddings), plus a linear baseline.
- In the unseen combos task, PRESAGE exceeded the additive baseline in 12 of 13 metrics on the Wessels23 dataset; the additive baseline captures ~88% of the ideal performance gap in Norman19, limiting its value for benchmarking non-additive interactions (training sets cover only 0.63% of combo space in Norman19 vs 10.3% in Wessels23).

**Conclusions:** The apparent weakness of perturbation models arises primarily from metric miscalibration rather than model performance. The study recommends using calibrated metrics and cautions against using Norman19 as the sole benchmark for combinatorial perturbation modeling. PRESAGE and scLambda are highlighted as newer architectures worth including in future benchmarks. Code is available on GitHub at shiftbioscience/Perturbation-Models-Outperform-Baselines. Authors: Henry E. Miller, Gabriel M. Mejia, Francis J. A. Leblanc, Bo Wang, Brendan Swain, Lucas Paulo de Lima Camillo (Shift Bioscience Ltd., Cambridge UK; University of Toronto; University of Cambridge).
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"Calibrated evaluation thus explains prior reports of model underperformance, revealing that deep learning models do outperform uninformative baselines." (Abstract)

"In this context, 'calibration' refers to the degree to which a metric improves in response to a meaningful biological signal and correctly ranks informative predictions above null ones." (Introduction)

"Across datasets, WMSE also shows substantially better calibration than MSE, even for datasets with few DEGs." (Results, Measuring calibration)

"the additive baseline captured roughly 88% of the ideal performance gap in the best-calibrated metrics, comparable to the interpolated duplicate baseline which accesses held-out combination data... This evidence of additive baseline saturation, together with limited combinatorial coverage, limits Norman19's value for benchmarking models that aim to learn non-additive genetic interactions." (Results, Unseen combos prediction)

"The main limitation is not model capability but the use of uncalibrated benchmarks that obscure true performance." (Discussion)

--- SOURCE 3: Deep-learning-based gene perturbation effect prediction does ... ---
URL: https://www.nature.com/articles/s41592-025-02772-6

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a Brief Communication published in Nature Methods (volume 22, pages 1657-1661, 2025) by Constantin Ahlmann-Eltze, Wolfgang Huber, and Simon Anders, with 111,000 accesses and 212 citations. The study benchmarks five foundation models (scGPT, scFoundation, scBERT, Geneformer, UCE) and two other deep learning models (GEARS, CPA) against deliberately simple baselines for predicting transcriptome changes after single or double genetic perturbations. The key finding is that NONE of the deep learning models outperformed the simple baselines.

Key benchmarks and results:
1. DOUBLE PERTURBATION prediction: Used Norman et al. data (100 single and 124 double gene perturbations in K562 cells via CRISPR activation; 19,264 genes; 1,000 read-out genes). Models were fine-tuned on all single perturbations and 62 double perturbations, then tested on the remaining 62 (repeated 5 times with different random partitions). Baselines: 'no change' model and 'additive' model. All models had substantially higher prediction error than the additive baseline (measured by L2 distance). For predicting genetic interactions (5,035 identified at 5% FDR out of 124,000 potential), none of the models was better than the 'no change' baseline.

2. SINGLE PERTURBATION prediction: Used CRISPR interference datasets from Replogle et al. (K562 and RPE1 cells) and Adamson et al. (K562 cells). Baselines: 'mean' model and a simple linear model (equation 1: Y = GWP^T + b). None of the deep learning models consistently outperformed the mean prediction or the linear model.

3. Representation utility: When gene embeddings from scFoundation/scGPT and perturbation embeddings from GEARS were plugged into the simple linear model, performance matched or exceeded the original models. The linear model with pretrained perturbation embeddings (pretrained on Replogle data) consistently outperformed all other models, suggesting pretraining on perturbation data provided benefit but pretraining on single-cell atlas data provided only small benefit over random embeddings.

Conclusions: The authors conclude that the foundation models' goal of providing generalizable representations for predicting outcomes of not-yet-performed experiments "is still elusive." The results align with other benchmarks (Kedzierska et al., Boiarsky et al., Liu et al., and several 2024 preprints) showing deep learning models struggle to outperform simple baselines. They note limitations: only four datasets used, all from cancer cell lines with high mutational burden. They suggest some original comparisons in GEARS/scGPT/scFoundation papers were particularly 'easy' (e.g., CPA was never designed for unseen perturbations; scGPT's linear model reverted to no-change predictions).

Methods details: Software versions used (GEARS 0.1.2, scGPT 0.2.1, scFoundation, CPA 0.8.8, Geneformer 0.1.0, scBERT, UCE). Authors contacted original model developers to review their code. Genetic interactions classified as buffering (2.3%), synergistic (0.6%), or opposite (0%) based on deviation from additive expectation. Code available at github.com/const-ae/linear_perturbation_prediction-Paper and archived on Zenodo.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"None outperformed the baselines, which highlights the importance of critical benchmarking in directing and evaluating method development." (Abstract)

URL: https://www.mdpi.com/2673-9879/5/4/58

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a scientific research article published in *Future Pharmacology* (2025, Vol. 5, Issue 4, Article 58; DOI: 10.3390/futurepharmacol5040058) titled "Decoding Anticancer Drug Response: Comparison of Data-Driven and Pathway-Guided Prediction Models."

**Authors & Affiliations:** Efstathios Pateras (Aristotle University of Thessaloniki), Ioannis S. Vizirianakis (Aristotle University of Thessaloniki & University of Nicosia), Mingrui Zhang (University of Leeds), Georgios Aivaliotis (University of Leeds), Georgios Tzimagiorgis (Aristotle University of Thessaloniki), Andigoni Malousi (Aristotle University of Thessaloniki - corresponding author). The paper was submitted 4 August 2025, revised 11 September 2025, accepted 29 September 2025, and published 2 October 2025.

**Objective:** To compare data-driven vs. biologically informed gene selection strategies for predicting drug response in cancer cell lines and propose an optimized feature selection strategy for precision oncology.

**Methods:**
- Seven targeted anticancer drugs were studied: Afatinib (EGFR/ERBB2, 866 cell lines), Capivasertib (AKT, 838), Dabrafenib (BRAF, 856), Gefitinib (EGFR, 858), Nutlin-3a (MDM2, 868), Osimertinib (EGFR, 857), and Palbociclib (CDK4/6, 868).
- IC50 and AUC values were retrieved from the Genomics of Drug Sensitivity in Cancer (GDSC) database; gene expression data from 1,084 cancer cell lines and 17,611 genes via the PharmacoGX R package (RMA log-transformed).
- ML algorithms tested included SVR, CatBoost, Random Forest, XGBoost, Lasso, KNN, and others; Linear Regression was ultimately selected.
- Feature selection methods compared included Recursive Feature Elimination (RFE) with SVR estimator (which outperformed SelectKBest and RFE with Linear Regression) versus pathway-derived gene sets from KEGG and Comparative Toxicogenomics Database (CTD).
- An integrative approach called BEACON (Biological EnhAncement of COmputation methods for feature selection) was developed, combining data-driven feature selection with drug-target pathway genes.
- Cross-omics transferability was tested using proteomic data (via TMT/LC-MS/MS) from 60 breast cancer cell lines (10,454 unique genes after filtering).

**Key Results:**
- IC50 outperformed AUC as the response variable for all drugs except Afatinib.
- Data-driven feature selection consistently outperformed pathway-based (KEGG or CTD) gene sets. Biologically derived models yielded R² values around 0.2 for Afatinib, Capivasertib, Gefitinib, Osimertinib, and Dabrafenib, while data-driven models reached R² values of 0.6–0.96.
- Capivasertib showed the largest gap (R² 0.15–0.96 for Cancer pathway), while Nutlin-3a showed the smallest gap (R² 0.52 vs. 0.69 for p53 pathway).
- Palbociclib achieved the highest biologically derived performance (R² 0.47–0.55), but data-driven models still outperformed (R² 0.82–0.95).
- Venn diagram analysis showed partial but limited overlap between computationally and biologically selected genes, supporting a hybrid strategy.
- The BEACON integrative approach consistently outperformed solely data-driven methods. For Gefitinib, RMSE was reduced by 12%; reductions of 4.7–8.4% were achieved for Capivasertib, Dabrafenib, Nutlin-3a, and Osimertinib. Palbociclib achieved a 10% RMSE reduction and slightly improved R² while using 107 fewer genes (~20% reduction).
- Cross-omics transferability was poor: models trained on gene expression and applied to proteomic data yielded R² values below zero. RMSE rose substantially (e.g., Afatinib from 1.596 to 11.368; Gefitinib from 0.847 to 8.756), indicating poor transferability across transcriptomic to proteomic levels.

**Conclusions:** Integrating biological knowledge into feature selection enhances both accuracy and interpretability of drug response prediction models. The BEACON integrative approach offers a more robust and generalizable framework with potential applications in biomarker discovery, drug repurposing, and personalized treatment strategies. Key limitations highlighted include low predictive value of proteomic features compared to mRNA profiles.

**Keywords:** pharmacogenomics, drug response prediction, feature selection, precision medicine, machine learning, biologically informed modeling, cancer cell lines.

--- SOURCE 17: Foundation Models Improve Perturbation Response Prediction ---
URL: https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.64898/2026.02.18.706454v1.full-text

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This bioRxiv preprint (DOI: 10.64898/2026.02.18.706454), titled "Foundation Models Improve Perturbation Response Prediction," presents a comprehensive study from GenBio AI researchers (including Elijah Cole, Emma Lundberg, Le Song, Ziv Bar-Joseph, and Eric P. Xing) evaluating the use of biological foundation models (FMs) for predicting cellular responses to genetic and chemical perturbations. 

**Purpose/Context:** The field has seen contradictory results about whether FMs outperform simple baselines for perturbation prediction. This study aims to resolve the controversy through extensive benchmarking.

**Key Methods:** The authors tested over 600 different models across various prediction tasks and evaluation metrics. They took an "embedding-centric view," generating perturbation embeddings from FMs trained on DNA sequences, protein sequences, protein structures, and small molecules, comparing them against simple baselines, classical ML methods, and recent state-of-the-art AI methods. They used datasets including Essential (4 cell lines, ~2000 perturbations each), Tahoe-100M, Sciplex-3, and Norman et al. Predictions were evaluated primarily via log fold-change (LFC) regression and differentially expressed gene (DEG) prediction, using kNN and lasso regression approaches with 5-fold cross-validation.

**Key Results:**
1. **Embeddings vary dramatically in utility:** While on small datasets (Norman) FMs showed no clear benefit, on larger datasets (Essential) some embeddings significantly outperform baselines. Performance is driven primarily by data modality. The strongest embeddings were derived from prior knowledge—interactome data (WaveGC), functional annotations (GenotypeVAE), and textual descriptions (GenePT). On K562, the best embedding closed 77% of the gap between train mean and the estimated experimental error limit.
2. **Fine-tuning is inconsistent:** An InSilico KO fine-tuning method improved AIDO.Cell (3M) performance, but an Indexing method and STRING GNN fine-tuning degraded performance, highlighting overfitting risks with small perturbation datasets.
3. **Complex embedding translation methods (Latent Diffusion, Flow Matching, Schrödinger Bridge) did not outperform simple kNN** with the strongest embedding.
4. **Small molecule perturbations are harder:** In LFC regression on Tahoe, no embedding convincingly outperformed negative controls, though target-based embeddings performed best in DEG formulations. SMILES-based FMs generally underperformed.
5. **Embedding integration/fusion improves genetic perturbation prediction:** An attention-based multimodal fusion model always improved over the best unimodal embedding, and for two cell lines (Jurkat, K-562) matched the estimated experimental error bound. Fusion bridged 86% (Hep-G2) and 53% (hTERT-RPE1) of the gap between random and experimental error.

**Conclusions:** Interactome-based FMs are the best single source of embeddings for perturbation prediction. Genetic perturbation prediction is easier than chemical perturbation prediction (due to higher specificity and much smaller search space ~2×10^4 genes vs ~10^60 small molecules). The authors suggest prioritizing context-specific interactome data over single-cell expression data for virtual cell model development, and note the field lacks a standard small-molecule FM reflecting biological function. Code and data are available at https://github.com/genbio-ai/foundation-models-perturbation.
</summary>

"We conducted an extensive analysis of over 600 different models across various prediction tasks and evaluation metrics, demonstrating that while some foundation models fail to outperform simple baselines, others significantly improve predictions for both genetic and chemical perturbations."

URL: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12499773

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a scientific review article published in Briefings in Bioinformatics (2025 Oct 06;26(5):bbaf533, doi: 10.1093/bib/bbaf533, PMCID: PMC12499773, PMID: 41052279) titled "Computational toxicology in drug discovery: applications of artificial intelligence in ADMET and toxicity prediction." Authors: Jiangyan Zhang, Haolin Li, Yuncong Zhang (contributed equally), Junyang Huang, Liping Ren, Chuantao Zhang, Quan Zou, and Yang Zhang. Corresponding authors are from the Hospital of Chengdu University of Traditional Chinese Medicine and the University of Electronic Science and Technology of China. The article is Open Access under a Creative Commons Attribution Non-Commercial License.

Key content and findings:
- Toxicity risk assessment is crucial for clinical success and market potential of drug candidates; ~30% of preclinical candidate compounds (PCCs) fail due to toxicity, and ~40% of preclinical candidate drugs fail due to insufficient ADMET profiles, while nearly 30% of marketed drugs are withdrawn due to unforeseen toxic reactions.
- Traditional animal testing is costly, time-consuming (6–24 months per test), expensive (often exceeding millions of dollars per compound), and ethically controversial (3Rs principle: replacement, reduction, refinement), driving the shift to computational toxicology.
- The review surveys over 20 ADMET prediction platforms, categorized into three types: rule/statistical-based methods, machine learning (ML) methods, and graph-based methods.
- Broad-spectrum platforms mentioned: admetSAR 3.0, ADMETlab 3.0, vNN-ADMET, ADMETboost, Deep-PK; pharmacokinetic-focused platforms: Swiss ADME, FAF-Drugs4.0, ADMET-AI; toxicity-focused platforms: ProTox 3.0, VenomPred 2.0; CYP450-related tools: CypRules, BioTransformer 3.0, XenoSite, SOMP, SMARTCyp 3.0.
- The ADMET prediction platform framework consists of: input component (chemical structural data, experimental data, literature-derived data), tools/methods component (physicochemical property calculation via RDKit/Scopy, and ML/AI prediction module using SVMs, RFs, neural networks, gradient boosting trees), and output component (endpoints; comprehensive platforms can evaluate over 100 endpoints).
- ML methods (e.g., vNN-ADMET, ADMETboost with XGBoost, ProTox 3.0 with RF/DNN) handle complex patterns but depend on high-quality training data. Graph-based methods (GNNs: ADMET-AI, Interpretable-ADMET, HelixADMET, ADMETlab 3.0 with DMPNN, admetSAR 3.0, pkCSM) analyze molecular graph structures but require substantial computational resources and large training datasets.
- Toxicological databases are classified into four categories: chemical toxicity databases, environmental toxicology databases, alternative toxicology databases, and biological toxin databases.
- Chemical toxicity databases include PubChem (>119 million compounds, NIH-maintained), ChEMBL (>2.1 million, EMBL-EBI), HSDB (~5600 chemicals), CCRIS (>9000, carcinogenicity/mutagenicity), CompTox Chemicals Dashboard (EPA), TOXRIC (113,372 compounds, ML-ready), SuperToxic (~60,000), DrugBank, and specialized databases DILIrank, DILIst, LTKB (hepatotoxicity), hERGCentral (cardiotoxicity), and LCDB (carcinogenicity data from 1726 chemicals and 7745 experimental records).
- The field is transitioning from single-endpoint predictions to multi-endpoint joint modeling with multimodal features, incorporating generative modeling and interpretability frameworks.

Methods: Following the PRISMA-ScR framework, a scoping review was conducted using Google Scholar and Semantic Scholar for peer-reviewed publications from 2019-2024. After screening, 145 articles (83 from Google Scholar, 62 from Semantic Scholar) from PubMed, arXiv, IEEE, and ACL Anthology met inclusion criteria; 12 were selected for in-depth review. Inclusion criteria required: unstructured data usage, incorporation of FL, and full text availability.

Key Findings:
- ADRs are categorized into 3 types: Type 1 (augmented/dose-dependent), Type 2 (time-dependent/chronic), and Type 3 (idiosyncratic/unpredictable)
- ADR outcomes can be unstructured (text) or structured (discrete codes like FAERS outcome codes: DE for death, LT for life-threatening, HO for hospitalization)
- ADR data sources include: Cadec, EMA's Union Pharmacovigilance Database, FDA's FAERS, CAERS (Canada), DAEN-medicines (Australia), SMM4H (social media), n2c2, ADE_Corpus_V2, and CTCAE v5.0
- BERT-based models are commonly used as base encoders with additional decoder layers for prediction tasks
- Fine-tuning open-source LLMs (Llama-3, Gemma, Mistral/Mixtral, Falcon, DeepSeek, Qwen on Hugging Face) is a practical approach for domain adaptation

Strategies for FedLLM on ADR include: configuring high dropout rates on client models, quantization (4-bit vs 16-bit precision), segmenting parameter matrices, and transferring only distilled-federated knowledge. Distilled models have shown superior performance—DistilBERT outperformed fine-tuned xlm-RoBERTa and GPT-Neo-125M on 4 metrics, and PubMedBERT (0.1% of GPT-3.5's size) outperformed its parent model by over 6 absolute F1-score points.

Evaluation metrics for unstructured predictions include: G-Eval, BLEU_N, ROUGE_N, BERTScore, SEMScore, and ANLS*, each with documented strengths and limitations.

Conclusions: FedLLM for ADR prediction remains in its early stage with limited documented use cases. Key focus areas for future research include fine-tuning and merging algorithms, fairness and unbiasedness, implementation challenges, and real-world deployment strategies. The review aims to lay groundwork for future privacy-preserving and scalable ADR prediction systems.
</summary>

"Adverse drug reactions (ADR) present significant challenges in health care, where early prevention is vital for effective treatment and patient safety. Traditional supervised learning methods struggle to address heterogeneous health care data due to their unstructured nature, regulatory constraints, and restricted access to sensitive personal identifiable information."

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This paper, published in the 2025 Conference of the Nations of the Americas Chapter of the ACL (Volume 1: Long Papers, pages 11083–11113), investigates whether large language models (LLMs) can effectively detect adverse drug reactions (ADRs) from psychiatric medications and align with expert responses to related queries. Led by researchers from Georgia Tech, Hospital General Universitario Gregorio Marañón, Hofstra University, and Columbia University, the study addresses a critical gap: ADRs from psychiatric medications are a leading cause of hospitalizations (51.9% to 91.8% of cases) among mental health patients, yet nearly 70% of individuals worldwide lack access to mental health professionals, leading many to seek help on social media.

The authors introduce two key resources: the Psych-ADR benchmark (239 Reddit posts from January-December 2019, labeled for ADR detection and multiclass classification across five ADR types—dose-related, non-dose, dose- and time-related, time-related, and withdrawal) and the Adverse Drug Reaction Response Assessment (ADRA) framework, which evaluates LLM responses against expert responses across four axes: text readability, emotion/tone expression, harm-reduction strategy alignment, and actionability.

Key findings for RQ1 (ADR detection and classification): The best models achieved only 75.38 F1 in detection and 76.69 F1 in multiclass classification. All models exhibited "risk-averse" behavior with false-positive rates over 70%, struggling to distinguish nuanced ADR types (GPT-4 Turbo misclassified 51% of non-dose-related and 50% of time-related ADRs). Claude 3 Opus achieved the highest zero-shot detection accuracy at 77.41%, while Llama 3.1-405B performed best in few-shot classification (F1 76.69).

For RQ2 (expert-LLM response alignment): LLM responses were significantly harder to read than expert responses (higher SMOG scores vs. 12.44 for experts). There was no significant difference in emotional/tone alignment, though experts showed higher anticipation, affection, and helping tones while LLMs used more optimistic, polite, and trust-based tones. The best model (OpenBioLLM-70B) achieved only 70.86% alignment with expert harm-reduction strategies, and LLMs provided 12.32% less actionable advice on average. Notably, expert responses scored higher on practicality (0.83) and contextual relevance (0.73) but lower on specificity (0.17) and clarity (0.13), while LLMs showed the opposite pattern.

The authors emphasize the importance of "lived experience"—first-hand knowledge possessed by clinicians—which LLMs lack, and caution against increasing human-like features (anthropomorphism) in LLMs due to risks of over-trust in high-risk healthcare domains. Instead, they advocate for fine-tuning on specialized data. The study was funded by NSF grant #2230692 and grants from AFSP, JPMorgan AI Research, and Microsoft's AFMR program. This article from BioPharm International (published March 4, 2026) by Partha Anbil and Niraj B. Patel examines how artificial intelligence (AI), particularly large language models (LLMs) and natural language processing (NLP), is transforming drug safety surveillance. The FDA manages a database of over 140,000 drug labeling documents, and with 82% of American adults taking at least one medication, the scale of data necessitates automated solutions.

Best practices include starting with pilot projects, establishing baselines, maintaining human oversight, and using domain-specific training data since generic LLMs significantly underperform.

--- SOURCE 14: JMIR Medical Informatics - Predicting Drug–Side Effect Relationships From Parametric Knowledge Embedded in Biomedical BERT Models: Methodological Study With a Natural Language Processing Approach ---
URL: https://medinform.jmir.org/2025/1/e67513

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This paper, published in JMIR Medical Informatics (Vol 13, 2025; doi:10.2196/67513), presents a methodological study on predicting drug–side effect relationships using parametric knowledge embedded in biomedical BERT language models. 

**Background/Objectiive:** Adverse drug reactions (ADRs) pose serious public health risks, with approximately 2 million serious ADRs and 100,000 deaths reported annually in the US. Traditional context-independent word embedding models like Word2Vec have limitations in capturing biomedical domain specificity. The study proposes using BERT-based models pretrained on biomedical corpora to extract parametric knowledge and predict unknown drug–side effect relationships.

**Methods:** The study used 158,096 known drug–side effect pairs from the SIDER database (version 4.1) to build an adjacency matrix with 1,345 drugs and 6,123 side effects. Cosine similarity was calculated between word embedding vectors of drugs and side effects. Relation scores (combining drug-similarity and side-effect-similarity components using equations) were calculated for 8,235,435 total drug–side effect pairs. For Word2Vec training, 14,289,160 sentences mentioning drugs and 32,107,327 sentences mentioning side effects were extracted from PubMed (42,515,246 total abstracts, updated December 8, 2022).

**Results:** The clagator/biobert_v1.1 model achieved the highest AUC of 0.915 at an optimal threshold of 0.289 (sensitivity 0.870, specificity 0.830), outperforming Word2Vec (AUC 0.848) and vanilla BERT (bert-base-uncased, AUC 0.857). Other models tested included BiomedBERT (0.907), dmis-lab/biobert_v1.1 (0.901), and PharmBERT-uncased (0.882). All BERT models pretrained on biomedical corpora outperformed vanilla BERT. The cosine similarity-based extraction method outperformed Euclidean distance, Manhattan distance, Jaccard similarity, and dot product methods. The dual-similarity approach (relation score, AUC 0.915) significantly outperformed single-similarity methods (drug-only: 0.799, side-effect-only: 0.881).

**Validation:** External validation with FAERS data (October 2012–June 2023; 901,361 known relationships) confirmed high statistical significance (P<.001) with an odds ratio of 4.822 (Fisher exact test repeated 2,000 times). Case studies of top-ranked predictions not in SIDER (lenalidomide-arthropathy, rosuvastatin-sleep disturbance, gadolinium-acute pulmonary edema, cefazolin-hepatic failure) were confirmed as reported in literature published after 2016.

**Conclusions:** BERT-based models pretrained on biomedical corpora significantly outperform Word2Vec in predicting drug–side effect relationships due to contextual information capture. The methodology demonstrates practical applicability for pharmacovigilance and ADR prediction. Limitations include the SIDER database being last updated in 2015, challenges with non-dose-dependent reactions, case report generalizability issues, prediction limitations for novel drug candidates, and lack of patient-specific idiosyncratic reaction modeling. The research was supported by the Korea Health Technology R&D Project (grant RS-2022-KH125153).
</summary>

SUMMARY:

The study was conducted by researchers at University of Colorado (approved by COMIRB #25-1631) and funded by AHRQ and NIH grants.

METHODS: The researchers evaluated three LLMs—GPT-4o-mini, MedGemma-27B, and LLaMA3-70B—using a clinician-annotated benchmark dataset of 750 unique DDI scenarios spanning three levels of diagnostic complexity. Interactions were labeled using LexiDrug categories (A=no known interaction, B=no action needed, C=monitor therapy, D=consider therapy modification, X=avoid combination). Three task formats were used: (1) pointwise two-drug classification, (2) pairwise three-drug discrimination, and (3) listwise 4–6 drug selection. All cases were independently reviewed by three board-certified clinical pharmacists. Standardized zero-shot prompting with nine repeated runs (temperature=0.7) and label shuffling was used. Metrics included precision, recall, F1, accuracy, and self-consistency. Datasets are available at github.com/sikora07/AIChemist.

RESULTS: Performance varied by task structure. In the pointwise two-drug task, LLaMA3-70B had the highest recall (61.7) and F1 (59.7), while GPT-4o-mini had the highest precision (65.7). In the pairwise three-drug task, GPT-4o-mini achieved the highest accuracy (86.6), followed by MedGemma-27B (84.9) and LLaMA3-70B (81.5). In the listwise 4-6 drug task, MedGemma-27B performed best (80.0), followed by GPT-4o-mini (71.3) and LLaMA3-70B (68.6). All models performed worst on Category C (moderate-risk) interactions. Self-consistency decreased as task complexity increased, and no model showed uniformly high reliability. Notably, models failed to identify Category X (avoid combination) DDIs in 24-30% of cases. Undetected high-risk interactions included enoxaparin/alteplase (bleeding risk), sulfamethoxazole-trimethoprim/spironolactone (hyperkalemia), and dronedarone/azithromycin (QTc prolongation).

CONCLUSIONS: The study represents the first clinically validated DDI benchmark dataset. LLMs showed moderate but uneven performance, degrading with increased complexity (more medications and requiring severity specification). The authors note rules-based software (e.g., LexiDrug) performs perfectly, and emphasize that LLMs are not yet safe for routine DDI identification without clinician backup. Limitations include small dataset size by LLM standards and lack of prompt engineering or knowledge-graph augmentation. The authors call for further model improvement and multi-format, reliability-aware evaluation frameworks before clinical deployment.

--- SOURCE 12: Benchmarking Computational Methods for Emerging Drug-Drug Interaction Prediction ---
URL: https://arxiv.org/html/2410.18583v4

SUMMARY:
<summary>
## DDI-Ben: A Benchmarking Framework for Emerging Drug-Drug Interaction Prediction Under Distribution Changes

### Overview
This paper by Zhenqian Shen et al. (Tsinghua University) introduces **DDI-Ben**, a benchmarking framework for emerging drug-drug interaction (DDI) prediction that explicitly addresses distribution changes between known and new drugs—a factor neglected by current evaluation methods. The code and data are available at https://github.com/LARS-research/DDI-Bench.

### Motivation
- Emerging DDI prediction is critical for new drugs with unknown pharmacological risks, as clinical experiments are time-consuming and expensive.
- Existing DDI datasets (DrugBank, TWOSIDES) lack drug approval timeline information, making it hard to simulate realistic drug distribution changes over time.
- Current evaluation methods assume known and new drugs follow the same distribution, using unrealistic i.i.d. drug splits, which makes evaluation results questionable.

### Distribution Change Simulation Framework
The framework uses **distribution changes between drug sets as a surrogate** for real-world DDI distribution changes:
1. **Drug distribution change modeling**: Introduces a cluster-based difference measurement γ(Dk,Dn) = max{S(u,v)} based on drug similarity (Tanimoto coefficient between fingerprints). Smaller γ indicates larger distribution changes.
2. **Drug data split**: Splits drugs into known and new drug sets.

The framework defines two emerging DDI tasks:
- **S1**: Determine DDI type between a known drug and a new drug.
- **S2**: Determine DDI type between two new drugs.

### Data Split Strategies Comparison
Eight split strategies were compared (random, drug frequency, drug usage, scaffold, LoHi, SPECTRA, DataSAIL, and the proposed cluster-based split). Key findings:
- LoHi and SPECTRA discard data points (undesirable given data collection costs).
- Only SPECTRA and the **cluster-based split** enable controllable distribution changes.
- The proposed cluster-based split achieved the **highest consistency index** with realistic drug approval-time-based splits.
- Real-world drug clusters emerge from new drug safety issues (1980s NSAIDs), technological breakthroughs (1990s ACE inhibitors), and new epidemics (2010s HCV NS5A inhibitors).

### Datasets
- **DrugBank**: Multiclass dataset, 1,710 drugs, 86 interaction types, 188,509 DDI triplets.
- **TWOSIDES**: Multilabel dataset, 645 drugs, 209 DDI types (frequency 3000–6000), 116,650 DDI triplets.

### Methods Benchmarked (10 representative methods)
- **Feature-based**: MLP
- **Embedding-based**: MSTE
- **GNN-based**: Decagon, SSI-DDI, MRCGNN, EmerGNN, SAGAN
- **Graph-transformer**: TIGER
- **LLM-based**: TextDDI, DDI-GPT

### Key Results
1. **Most existing methods suffer substantial performance degradation** when distribution changes are introduced, with a more severe decline on DrugBank (harder multiclass prediction) than TWOSIDES.
2. **LLM-based methods (TextDDI, DDI-GPT) are the most robust** against distribution changes. EmerGNN performed best without distribution changes but TextDDI and DDI-GPT outperformed others under distribution changes.
3. **Textual information and LLM processing are key**: TextDDI's LLM extracts key pharmacological knowledge from raw textual data, filters irrelevant information, and enables more accurate predictions. Transferable pharmacological knowledge (e.g., Aclidinium's bronchodilatory activities, Butylscopolamine's muscarinic receptor binding) is not available in fingerprints or biomedical networks.
4. **DDI-type analysis**: MLP and MSTE rely on sufficient labeled data (good on major DDI types, poor on long-tail types). DDI-GPT significantly outperformed others on medium and long-tail DDI types under distribution changes.
5. **Controlling γ**: As distribution change increases (γ decreases), most methods' performance drops significantly; DDI-GPT remains relatively best, suggesting LLM prior knowledge and textual side information help mitigate the negative impact.

### Evaluation Metrics
- **DrugBank**: Macro F1 (primary), accuracy, Cohen's Kappa.
- **TWOSIDES**: Average ROC-AUC (primary), PR-AUC, and accuracy across DDI types.

### Conclusions & Future Work
DDI-Ben highlights the importance of explicitly addressing distribution changes in emerging DDI prediction. Future directions include designing LLM-based methods to alleviate distribution change impact and domain adaptation methods for real-world robustness.
</summary>

This is a systematic review article published in the MDPI journal *Pharmaceuticals* (2026, 19(8), 1225, DOI: 10.3390/ph19081225), titled "Graph-Based Machine Learning for Predicting Drug–Drug Interactions: A Systematic Review." It was authored by Md. Tuhin Reza, Md. Abdul Kader, Wissem Inoubli, Md. Biddut Hossain, and Md. Kamrul Islam (corresponding author), from institutions in Bangladesh (Jashore University of Science & Technology, Daffodil International University, BANBEIS) and France (University of Artois). The article was submitted June 21, 2026, revised and accepted July 31, 2026, and published August 4, 2026, and belongs to the Special Issue "Drug Safety and Real-World Evidence: From Databases to Artificial Intelligence."

**Purpose & Background:** The review evaluates graph-based machine-learning methods for predicting drug–drug interactions (DDIs), which are major medication-safety concerns. Since experimental testing cannot cover the rapidly expanding number of drug pairs, computational DDI prediction is a critical complementary strategy for prioritizing risky combinations and supporting medication-safety workflows. The review focuses on graph neural networks (GNNs) and their architectures, data integration, interpretability, reproducibility, and clinical relevance.

**Methodology:** Conducted following the PRISMA 2020 framework. Searches covered IEEE Xplore (n=74), ScienceDirect (n=96), PubMed (n=67), and Google Scholar (n=53), totaling 290 records for studies published January 2021 through March 2026. After removing duplicates and ineligible records, 60 primary studies were included. Because studies used heterogeneous datasets and methods, findings were synthesized narratively rather than statistically (no meta-analysis). Risk of bias was assessed across seven domains: data leakage, negative sampling, generalization design, baseline/ablation adequacy, reproducibility, interpretability, and clinical applicability.

**Key Results:** Sixty studies met eligibility criteria. Methods progressed from graph convolutional networks and graph attention networks to graph transformers, contrastive learning, multimodal fusion, and LLM-enhanced representations. Representative reported results include 94.47% transductive accuracy for SSI-DDI, 99.74% warm-start accuracy for DrugDAGT, and 95.43% AUROC for KnowDDI on TWOSIDES — but these are study-specific and not directly comparable. Only three studies explicitly addressed data leakage; leakage-aware drug-disjoint, temporal, and external evaluations were uncommon. Uncertainty calibration, computational-resource reporting, complete reproducibility materials, and independently validated explanations were also limited.

The review identified five principal threats to validity: (1) leakage-prone random pairwise splits; (2) incomplete or noisy labels (unobserved interactions treated as confirmed negatives); (3) limited cold-start evaluation on unseen drugs; (4) scarce temporal evaluation; and (5) limited interpretability validation. The review covers three analytical questions: (RQ1) how graph construction, data modality, and validation design influence reported performance; (RQ2) when attention and multimodal fusion add demonstrable value; (RQ3) what evidence supports translation beyond benchmark performance.

Three core modeling concepts were defined: GNN architectures, multimodal fusion (combining molecular structure, SMILES, DDI networks, knowledge graphs, side effects, targets, pathways, or text), and attention mechanisms. Attention categories identified include graph attention, cross-/co-attention, hierarchical attention, knowledge-graph attention, transformer self-attention, feature/modality weighting, and contrastive attention.

**Conclusions:** Graph-based machine learning is promising for DDI prioritization and hypothesis generation but remains insufficient for independent clinical decision-making. The review recommends future studies use standardized benchmarks, leakage-aware validation, calibrated uncertainty, reproducible pipelines, validated explanations, and external or prospective evaluation. Keywords: drug–drug interaction; graph neural network; computational pharmacology; multimodal learning; attention mechanism.

SUMMARY:

On September 20, 2024, Insilico Medicine announced Phase 2a results for its lead drug ISM001-055, a small molecule targeting TNIK (Traf2- and Nck-interacting kinase), for the treatment of idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (IPF). The study of 71 patients achieved its primary goal of demonstrating safety and tolerability, but efficacy details were limited. The drug showed a dose-dependent improvement in forced vital capacity (a measure of breathing) compared to placebo after 12 weeks, though Insilico did not disclose absolute scores for trial groups or whether differences were statistically significant.

CEO Alex Zhavoronkov declined to comment on statistical significance, citing legal restrictions, but pointed to a trend observed across dosing groups as evidence of effectiveness. He acknowledged that current patient numbers were insufficient to claim statistical significance for approval, though the data indicated a clear trend. He suggested a longer efficacy-focused trial would likely show continued dose response. Immediate priorities are publishing results in a medical journal and consulting with regulators.

The announcement follows a similar situation with Recursion, another AI-focused biotech firm, which revealed its first Phase 2 data for REC-994 in cerebral cavernous malformations (CCM). Recursion's data also lacked specifics, causing a 16% stock drop, and met safety/tolerability endpoints but had mixed efficacy results. Recursion plans to advance the program, though it's unclear whether it will proceed with Phase 3 or another Phase 2 trial. Zhavoronkov avoided direct comparisons, noting IPF is more heterogeneous than CCM, but expressed respect for Recursion and CEO Chris Gibson while noting some industry insiders were surprised Recursion did not discontinue REC-994.

# An agentic AI system for automated pharmacogenomic recommendation generation

* [Mike Zack](#auth-Mike-Zack-Aff1)[1](#Aff1),
* [Anton Savinkov](#auth-Anton-Savinkov-Aff1)[1](#Aff1),
* [Danil Stupichev](#auth-Danil-Stupichev-Aff1)[1](#Aff1),

* [Kirill Reshetnikov](#auth-Kirill-Reshetnikov-Aff1)[1](#Aff1),
* [Nurkyz Ydyrysova](#auth-Nurkyz-Ydyrysova-Aff1)[1](#Aff1) &
* …
* [Allan Gobbs](#auth-Allan-Gobbs-Aff1)[1](#Aff1)

[*npj Digital Medicine*](/npjdigitalmed)
**volume 9**, Article number: 541 (2026) [Cite this article](#citeas)

[Save article](/articles/s41746-026-02590-w/save-research?_csrf=xTD31081vK0plqL7jNDuc4KJcJsPzZn0)

* 5129 Accesses
* 1 Citations
* 6 Altmetric
* [Metrics details](/articles/s41746-026-02590-w/metrics)

## Abstract

Pharmacogenomic guidelines are essential for tailoring drug therapy to individual genetic profiles, but current curation workflows are manual, resource‑intensive, time‑bound, and limited in coverage. We introduce an agentic AI system for automated, scalable generation of CPIC-style recommendations using large language models (LLMs) guided by structured evidence. Our modular pipeline retrieves and processes full-text biomedical literature and FDA drug labels, extracts clinically relevant entities with high accuracy (91.9% across 22 articles), aggregates findings across studies, and generates phenotype-specific dosing recommendations for gene–drug pairs. In expert evaluations of 24 random recommendations, our system significantly outperformed leading LLM baselines (GPT-5, Claude, Grok) in clinical clarity and guideline concordance. These results demonstrate the feasibility of using evidence-grounded, agentic AI for end-to-end pharmacogenomic evidence synthesis, offering a path toward broader population coverage, faster updates, and more consistent and explainable decision support.

## Introduction

Pharmacogenomics (PGx) aims to tailor drug therapy based on individual genetic variation, improving both efficacy and safety. To support clinical adoption, expert consortia such as CPIC[1](/articles/s41746-026-02590-w#ref-CR1 "Clinical Pharmacogenetics Implementation Consortium (CPIC). CPIC database. 
                  https://cpicpgx.org
                  
                . accessed 3 June 2025.") (Clinical Pharmacogenetics Implementation Consortium, now part of ClinPGx) and DPWG have developed evidence-based guidelines that map genetic variants to dosing adjustments or drug selection rules. These guidelines are widely used in translational research and precision medicine but suffer from two major limitations[1](/articles/s41746-026-02590-w#ref-CR1 "Clinical Pharmacogenetics Implementation Consortium (CPIC). CPIC database. 
                  https://cpicpgx.org
                  
                . accessed 3 June 2025."): the high cost and slow pace of manual curation, and[2](/articles/s41746-026-02590-w#ref-CR2 "Thorn, C. F., Klein, T. E. & Altman, R. B. PharmGKB: the Pharmacogenomics Knowledge Base. Methods Mol. Biol. 1015, 311–320 (2013).") limited coverage of gene–drug pairs and population contexts. As a result, many actionable variants remain unaddressed, and important guideline updates are often delayed by years.

In this work, we focus not on patient-level treatment recommendations but on the automation of guideline-level evidence synthesis, generating structured drafts that can support expert panels, hospital systems, and clinical laboratories in updating and maintaining pharmacogenomic guidance at scale.

A major bottleneck is that current workflows rely on extensive expert involvement for every stage of guideline creation from identifying relevant literature to extracting evidence and formulating recommendations. Even large curated databases such as PharmGKB (now part of ClinPGx) fall short of full coverage: their annotations are manually created and primarily designed for human readability rather than machine interpretation. As a result, integration into automated reasoning pipelines remains challenging, and updates may lag behind the primary literature[2](/articles/s41746-026-02590-w#ref-CR2 "Thorn, C. F., Klein, T. E. & Altman, R. B. PharmGKB: the Pharmacogenomics Knowledge Base. Methods Mol. Biol. 1015, 311–320 (2013)."). Prior efforts such as PGxMine attempted to automate annotation pipelines for PharmGKB, but these remained focused on entity-level extraction without translation into dosing guidance[3](/articles/s41746-026-02590-w#ref-CR3 "Lever, J. et al. PGxMine: text mining for curation of PharmGKB. Pac. Symp. Biocomput. 25, 611–622 (2020).").

At the same time, large language models (LLMs) have shown increasing promise in biomedical applications, including question answering, summarization, and knowledge extraction. Recent studies have explored the use of LLMs to support or even generate pharmacogenomic recommendations by leveraging structured knowledge bases[4](/articles/s41746-026-02590-w#ref-CR4 "Murugan, M. et al. Empowering personalized pharmacogenomics with generative AI solutions. J. Am. Med. Inf. Assoc. 31, 1356–1366 (2024)."),[5](/articles/s41746-026-02590-w#ref-CR5 "Li, D. et al. Enhancing pharmacogenomic data accessibility and drug safety with large language models: a case study with Llama3.1. Exp. Biol. Med. 249, 10393 (2024).") or free-text literature[6](/articles/s41746-026-02590-w#ref-CR6 "Zack, M. et al. Benchmarking large language models for replication of guideline-based PGx recommendations. Pharmacogenomics J. 25, 23 (2025)."). In parallel, tools such as PubTator3[7](/articles/s41746-026-02590-w#ref-CR7 "Wei, C.-H. et al. PubTator 3.0: an AI-powered literature resource for unlocking biomedical knowledge. Nucleic Acids Res. 52, W540–W546 (2024).") have improved normalization of biomedical entities, enabling more reliable downstream reasoning across heterogeneous corpora. These approaches suggest that LLMs, when properly guided and grounded in context, may be capable of capturing complex gene–drug–phenotype relationships, identifying dosing implications, and mimicking the structure and tone of CPIC-like guidelines.

Recent advances in artificial intelligence have introduced a new class of systems known as “agentic AI”—models that go beyond passive information retrieval to actively perceive, reason, and act within dynamic clinical contexts[8](/articles/s41746-026-02590-w#ref-CR8 "Lee, Y. C. Rethinking artificial intelligence in medicine: from tools to agents. Clin. Exp. Emerg. Med. 12, 101–103 (2025)."),[9](/articles/s41746-026-02590-w#ref-CR9 "Hinostroza Fuentes, V. G., Karim, H. A., Tan, M. J. T. & AlDahoul, N. AI with agency: a vision for adaptive, efficient, and ethical healthcare. Front Digit Health 7, 1600216 (2025)."). Similar frameworks have also been applied in drug development and due diligence, for example, LLM-based agent systems for competitive landscape mapping of drug assets[10](/articles/s41746-026-02590-w#ref-CR10 "Vinogradova, A. et al. LLM-based agents for competitive landscape mapping in drug asset due diligence. Preprint at 
                  https://doi.org/10.48550/ARXIV.2508.16571
                  
                 (2025)."), underscoring the broader utility of agentic workflows in biomedicine. These agentic systems operate through a perceive–reason–act loop, enabling them to analyze unstructured data, formulate task plans, and autonomously execute actions such as generating clinical summaries or initiating decision support[8](/articles/s41746-026-02590-w#ref-CR8 "Lee, Y. C. Rethinking artificial intelligence in medicine: from tools to agents. Clin. Exp. Emerg. Med. 12, 101–103 (2025)."). In healthcare settings, agentic AI has been shown to reduce administrative burdens, enhance diagnostic workflows, and dynamically adapt to changing clinical states—reducing hospital readmissions and improving triage accuracy[9](/articles/s41746-026-02590-w#ref-CR9 "Hinostroza Fuentes, V. G., Karim, H. A., Tan, M. J. T. & AlDahoul, N. AI with agency: a vision for adaptive, efficient, and ethical healthcare. Front Digit Health 7, 1600216 (2025).").

Agentic frameworks are also gaining traction in quantitative clinical pharmacology and translational sciences, where autonomous agents orchestrate multi-step tasks including PK/PD modeling, study simulation, and regulatory document generation[11](/articles/s41746-026-02590-w#ref-CR11 "Shahin, M. H., Goswami, S., Lobentanzer, S. & Corrigan, B. W. Agents for change: Artificial Intelligent workflows for quantitative clinical pharmacology and translational sciences. Clin. Transl. Sci. 18, e70188 (2025)."). This multi-agent paradigm, often described as “agentic workflows,” enables distributed automation across drug development pipelines, providing both scalability and traceability. In this context, pharmacogenomics stands out as a natural candidate for agentic automation, due to the repetitive, evidence-driven nature of guideline development. By deploying structured agentic reasoning, it becomes possible to automatically identify gene–drug relationships, assess supporting literature, and draft CPIC-style recommendations that are explainable, reproducible, and continuously updatable while also maintaining identifiable distinction from manually curated recommendations.

Our initial attempts followed a traditional path: training supervised models to extract structured annotations from literature, mimicking the format of PharmGKB. However, we found that this approach faced serious challenges: inconsistent formatting in PDFs, limited data coverage, normalization issues for genetic variants, and the high cost of gold-standard labels. Importantly, even if perfect entity extraction were achieved, translating raw evidence into coherent, guideline-style recommendations remained a non-trivial task.

Our system is designed to complement existing expert consortia such as CPIC and DPWG, not replace them. By accelerating evidence synthesis and providing transparent, traceable drafts, it aims to support expert reviewers and enable faster, reproducible updates to clinical guidelines.

We therefore propose a generation-first approach, in which LLMs are used directly to synthesize guideline-like recommendations from raw biomedical literature. Instead of replicating existing curation schemas, we build a hybrid pipeline that retrieves relevant documents, identifies supporting evidence using semantic search, and prompts an LLM to generate CPIC-style recommendations, including dosage adjustments and rationale. This system can operate both in de novo mode—proposing guidelines for previously uncurated gene–drug pairs—and in updater mode, suggesting revisions for outdated guidelines, for example when new variants are identified in an underrepresented population.

In this paper, we describe the architecture and evaluation of our system. We benchmark our method using expert-validated recommendations, compare several prompting and retrieval strategies, and analyze limitations. We also position our work within recent efforts to benchmark and specialize LLMs for pharmacogenomics[6](/articles/s41746-026-02590-w#ref-CR6 "Zack, M. et al. Benchmarking large language models for replication of guideline-based PGx recommendations. Pharmacogenomics J. 25, 23 (2025)."),[12](/articles/s41746-026-02590-w#ref-CR12 "Keat, K. et al. PGxQA: a resource for evaluating LLM performance for pharmacogenomic QA tasks. Pac. Symp. Biocomput. 30, 229–246 (2025).") and discuss its implications for scalable guideline development in precision medicine.

## Results

### System overview

To enable automated generation of pharmacogenomic recommendations, we developed a modular system that processes literature and drug label evidence into structured, guideline-style outputs. The PGxAI-Recommender architecture comprises three stages: acquisition of relevant texts, LLM-based extraction of evidence, and recommendation generation based on structured input (Fig. [1](/articles/s41746-026-02590-w#Fig1), Supplementary Fig. [1](/articles/s41746-026-02590-w#MOESM1)).

**Fig. 1: Architecture of the PGxAI-recommender.**

[Full size image](/articles/s41746-026-02590-w/figures/1)

This design reflects the culmination of iterative experimentation with multiple prompting strategies, knowledge injection methods, and evaluation setups. Early trials showed that even state-of-the-art LLMs, when prompted solely with a gene–drug pair, frequently returned vague or generic outputs, often omitting critical dosing adjustments. Simply adding all relevant publications to a single prompt is not feasible, as the complete body of evidence for a given gene–drug pair exceeds the available context window of current LLMs. Moreover, an LLM with internet or web-search access cannot reproduce the systematic, curated evidence aggregation performed by guideline authors: ad hoc retrieval returns a limited and opportunistic subset of publications rather than a comprehensive and structured synthesis. These limitations motivated a more structured, evidence-aware pipeline tailored to the complexities of pharmacogenomic decision-making.

### Evaluation of extraction accuracy

We manually validated the outputs of the LLM-based evidence extraction module on 22 pharmacogenomic articles. Three independent human annotators evaluated the correctness of the extracted answers across 35 predefined binary fields per article. In total, 2310 binary judgments were collected across annotators and articles.

The model achieved an overall accuracy of 91.9%, defined as the proportion of fields marked as correct by the annotators. Errors primarily reflected incorrect or imprecise extractions, including occasional over-specification.

Structured factual fields such as Study design, Genotyping method, and Sample size achieved near-perfect performance, while interpretive or composite fields, including Statistical significance and strength and Phenotypes reported, showed relatively lower accuracy, with the minimum observed for Genotype distribution (56%) (Fig. [2A](/articles/s41746-026-02590-w#Fig2)).

For the model, 94.7% of extracted fields were judged correct by the majority of expert annotators, indicating that model outputs are generally consistent with prevailing expert assessments.

### Evaluation of recommendation accuracy

To assess the clinical quality of generated pharmacogenomic recommendations, we conducted a blinded expert review of outputs from five models. Each recommendation was rated on a 0–10 scale based on alignment with known CPIC guidelines, clinical clarity, and dosing appropriateness. PGxAI-Recommender achieved the highest average expert score (mean 9.0), compared to baseline models with mean scores ranging from 6.2 to 7.8, and outperformed all baseline LLMs in pairwise statistical comparisons (*p* < 0.01; Fig. [3B](/articles/s41746-026-02590-w#Fig3)).

To further contextualize the score-based evaluation, we conducted a pairwise guideline-conformance assessment against CPIC reference recommendations. In this analysis, we derived a relative ranking of models based on expert preferences. PGxAI-Recommender achieved the highest observed pairwise win rate (0.83), whereas baseline LLMs exhibited lower win rates ranging from 0.17 to 0.78, indicating stronger alignment of PGxAI-Recommender outputs with CPIC guidance (Supplementary Fig. [2](/articles/s41746-026-02590-w#MOESM1)).

A notable observation from the baseline comparison was that GPT-5, despite being a more advanced model, did not improve recommendation quality and in several cases produced less guideline-concordant outputs. GPT-5 occasionally generated detailed dosing instructions that contradicted CPIC guidance. In scenarios where all other models correctly returned “No recommendation,” GPT-5 produced full therapeutic regimens with specific milligram dosing and administration schedules, even though such information was neither present in the evidence corpus nor requested by the task. In other instances, GPT-5 returned overly narrow dose values (for example, a single fixed efavirenz dose) where CPIC requires expressing a dose range. These deviations represent over-generation rather than guideline-aligned reasoning and likely contributed to its lower expert scores relative to earlier GPT models.

Three representative cases highlight the model’s strengths.

### Efavirenz – *CYP2B6* (Multiple Phenotypes)

CPIC provides nuanced, phenotype-specific guidance for efavirenz, recommending dose reductions for intermediate and poor metabolizers and careful monitoring or escalation for ultrarapid metabolizers. The PGxAI-Recommender consistently produced accurate and differentiated outputs across all phenotypes. For intermediate and poor metabolizers, it suggested the correct reduced dose range (200–400 mg), while most baseline models either defaulted to the standard 600 mg or gave only partial adjustments. For ultrarapid metabolizers, our system appropriately suggested standard dosing with optional escalation (up to 800 mg) under monitoring, striking a balance between clinical flexibility and evidence caution. Other models frequently omitted dose adjustments or proposed incorrect increases (e.g., 900 mg), diverging from established recommendations. This case illustrates the system’s ability to align with guideline logic even in edge phenotypes requiring therapeutic nuance.

### Fluorouracil – *DPYD* (normal and poor metabolizers)

For normal metabolizers, CPIC advises standard dosing without modification. Most baseline models, however, added unnecessary regimen details (e.g., “400–600 mg/m²/day” or complex bolus + infusion schedules), which could mislead clinicians and complicate justification during adverse events. In contrast, the PGxAI-Recommender returned the concise and guideline-aligned statement, standard dosing with no changes, avoiding extraneous detail. For poor metabolizers, CPIC guidance is clear: avoid fluorouracil or related prodrugs due to the risk of severe, potentially life-threatening toxicity. If no alternatives exist, only a highly reduced dose with intensive therapeutic drug monitoring may be considered. The PGxAI-Recommender precisely captured this “no safe use” stance, stating that fluorouracil should be avoided and offering no ambiguous fallback. Other models tended to hedge, some suggested 25–50% of the standard dose or added vague regimen-specific caveats, which could expose patients to undue risk. Our system’s categorical rejection aligns most closely with clinical best practice, reducing the chance of misinterpretation in critical care settings.

### Atorvastatin – *SLCO1B1* (poor function)

CPIC suggests avoiding high-dose atorvastatin and considering alternatives such as pravastatin. The PGxAI-Recommender explicitly recommended ≤20 mg/day or switching to a safer statin, whereas other models proposed standard dose ranges (e.g., 10–80 mg/day) or omitted alternatives altogether. Our system framed dose reduction in the context of broader therapeutic strategy, yielding a more actionable and complete recommendation.

These findings highlight the value of evidence-aware prompting and structured input design in generating high-quality, guideline-concordant pharmacogenomic recommendations.

## Discussion

Our evaluation demonstrates that LLMs can reliably extract structured evidence when provided with curated, task-specific context. The extraction module achieved an overall field-level correctness rate of 91.9% across 22 pharmacogenomic studies, as assessed by independent expert annotators. Agreement with the majority expert consensus was 94.7%, indicating that the majority of extracted fields were judged acceptable by domain experts. At the same time, inter-rater reliability metrics (Cohen’s and Fleiss’ κ) revealed variability among expert judgments. This variability reflects both the imbalance between correct and incorrect labels and differences in expert interpretation for a subset of fields, rather than systematic extraction errors. Together, these results indicate that while expert consensus provides a useful operational reference, some degree of disagreement is intrinsic to the task and should be taken into account when interpreting extraction performance.

In our expert evaluation, the PGxAI-Recommender consistently outperformed all baseline models in generating pharmacogenomic recommendations aligned with CPIC guidelines. The system achieved significantly higher expert scores across a diverse set of gene–drug–phenotype cases, particularly excelling in scenarios that required non-standard clinical actions. In phenotypes such as *CYP2B6* poor and ultrarapid metabolizers for efavirenz, or *SLCO1B1* poor function for atorvastatin, our model uniquely captured the need for dose reduction, therapeutic monitoring, or alternative agents—clinical subtleties that baseline LLMs frequently missed or expressed imprecisely. In addition to score-based expert evaluation, we performed a pairwise CPIC-guideline conformance assessment to explicitly examine relative model preference. This analysis consistently ranked PGxAI-Recommender above baseline LLMs, reinforcing its stronger alignment with established pharmacogenomic guidelines. These results underscore the importance of grounding generative models in structured, context-specific evidence to enable guideline-concordant outputs that are both actionable and safe for clinical decision support.

A key difference between the PGxAI-Recommender and baseline models such as GPT-4.1 lies in how each system uses evidence. GPT-4.1 relies solely on a single prompt applied to an isolated gene–drug–phenotype description, without access to aggregated multi-study evidence or FDA label information. In contrast, our system integrates structured inputs assembled across several upstream stages, including study-level annotations, multi-document evidence summaries, FDA excerpts, and a qualitative evidence level. This consolidated evidence block provides explicit grounding signals, numeric results, consistency across studies, phenotype definitions, and regulatory context, that the generator is required to use when formulating the final recommendation. This architecture reduces unsupported assertions, improves dose-range fidelity, and enables the system to capture guideline-specific subtleties (such as recommending alternative agents or monitoring strategies) that GPT-4.1 frequently omitted or expressed incompletely. We believe this deeper evidence integration explains the observed performance gap in expert ratings.

Importantly, the observed performance gains reflect the use of structured, guideline-relevant context and prompt design rather than any change to the underlying language models. PGxAI-Recommender does not involve model training or fine-tuning. All models were evaluated in an inference-only setting without internet access.

Together, these findings highlight the utility of evidence-aware prompting for achieving guideline-concordant outputs, and support the use of structured knowledge to enhance reliability in clinical NLP applications.

Beyond accuracy, our system demonstrates the potential for broader coverage and more up-to-date evidence compared to existing expert-curated resources. As summarized in Table [1](/articles/s41746-026-02590-w#Tab1), the CPIC corpus currently includes 316 gene–drug pairs and roughly 8000 cited articles, reflecting guidelines published between 2014 and 2025. In contrast, the proposed automated framework can identify up to 573 gene–drug pairs and retrieve nearly 20,000 relevant pharmacogenomic publications indexed in PubMed (1966–2025), supporting the generation of continuously updated, literature-grounded recommendations that align with the evolving evidence base.

Although the extraction and recommendation evaluations relied on a relatively small set of manually reviewed articles22 and recommendations,24 these analyses were intended as a feasibility assessment rather than a full validation study. The system itself is built to operate at much larger scale, and future work will include validation on substantially expanded and more heterogeneous evaluation sets as additional expert-curated data become available.

Access to full-text articles represents an additional practical limitation. Many pharmacogenomic studies are distributed across heterogeneous publisher platforms with inconsistent open-access availability. To maximize coverage, the retrieval module attempts multiple pathways, including PMC, DOI-redirected publisher pages, and applies PDF parsing and OCR-based extraction when needed. Nevertheless, studies available only behind paywalls remain inaccessible to the current pipeline, which may introduce coverage gaps or bias toward open-access literature. Future iterations could incorporate licensed full-text sources or publisher partnerships where permitted.

Although several domain-specific fine-tuned models exist, including BioMedLM[16](/articles/s41746-026-02590-w#ref-CR16 "Bolton, E. et al. BioMedLM: A 2.7B Parameter Language Model Trained On Biomedical Text. Preprint at
