This webpage is an ARCHIVED clinical guideline from Carelon Medical Benefits Management titled "Pharmacogenetic Testing" (Doc ID: GEN09-1125.2-UC0126). It was archived on 06/14/2026 because it contains outdated information and should not be consulted for clinical use. The document was effective 11/15/2025 with codes updated 01/01/2026, and its last review date was 07/17/2025. It is not effective for Anthem BCBS OH Medicaid.

The guideline establishes clinical appropriateness criteria (medical necessity) for pharmacogenetic testing. According to the framework, genotyping is considered **medically necessary** when ALL of the following conditions are met: (1) the medication is the most appropriate treatment for the individual's underlying condition; (2) the test has demonstrated analytical and clinical validity and utility for the individual; (3) the biomarker testing is focused on specific genetic polymorphisms relevant to treatment; and (4) the testing is referenced in the corresponding FDA package insert or NCCN guidelines. Genetic tests not specifically mentioned in the guidelines are considered not medically necessary.

**Table 1 lists the therapies and biomarkers considered medically necessary for genotyping:** ApoE ε4 (lecanemab, donanemab-azbt – Neurology), CFTR (ivacaftor – Pediatrics), CYP2C19 (clopidogrel – Cardiology), CYP2C9 (siponimod – Neurology; deuruxolitinib – Dermatology), CYP2D6 (eliglustat – Hematology; tetrabenazine – Neurology), DPYD (capecitabine, fluorouracil – Oncology), G6PD (rasburicase – Hematology; tafenoquine, primaquine – Infectious Diseases), HLA-B*1502 (carbamazepine, oxcarbazepine – Neurology), HLA-B*5701 (abacavir – Infectious Diseases), HLA-B*58:01 (allopurinol – Rheumatology), NAGS (carglumic acid – Gastroenterology), POLG (divalproex sodium, valproic acid – Neurology), and TPMT/NUDT15 (mercaptopurine, thioguanine – Hematology).

**Key evidence discussed in the rationale:**
- About 15% of US prescriptions have potential pharmacogenetic influence, but evidence supports genotype-guided prescribing for only a limited number of drugs.
- The INGENIOUS trial (26 drug-gene pairs) was negative for reducing adverse drug events within 1 year.
- **Psychiatric pharmacogenetic testing:** The GUIDED trial (GeneSight, 1167 outpatients with depression) found no statistically significant difference in response/remission rates; the PRIME study (1944 subjects across 22 VA medical centers) found only clinically insignificant gains (less than 2% improvement in remission at 24 weeks). Meta-analyses show risks of bias and lack of clinical utility evidence.
- **DPYD testing for fluoropyrimidines:** Approximately 3%-5% of White populations have partial DPD deficiency and 0.2% have complete deficiency. Four main DPYD variants are associated with impaired DPD activity: c.1905+1G>A (DPYD *2A), c.1679T>G (DPYD *13), c.2846A>T, and c.1129-5923C>G (Haplotype B3). DPYD variant carriers receiving standard fluoropyrimidine doses have ~70% risk of severe toxicity and ~3% risk of fatal toxicity. The NCCN updated guidance in 2025, moving from "not recommended" to stating DPYD testing "should be considered prior to fluoropyrimidine therapy." The EMA has required pretherapeutic DPYD screening since April 2020. A PREPARE trial secondary analysis showed carriers of actionable genotypes receiving dose adjustments had a 90% lower risk of clinically relevant toxic effects.
- **APOE ε4 testing in Alzheimer's disease:** APOE ε4 has worldwide prevalence of 14% and is the strongest genetic susceptibility factor for sporadic Alzheimer's (OR 8-12 for ε4/ε4 vs ε3/ε3), but testing is not recommended in routine clinical evaluation of cognitive impairment. In the Clarity AD trial for lecanemab, 15.8% of patients were homozygous APOE ε4 carriers with higher risk of symptomatic amyloid-related imaging abnormalities (9.2% vs 1.4% for non-carriers), leading to the FDA label recommendation to consider APOE ε4 testing when deciding to initiate lecanemab.

The document also includes comprehensive CPT codes delegated as "May Be Medically Necessary When Criteria are Met" (including codes for CYP2C19, CYP2D6, CYP2C9, DPYD, G6PD, NUDT15, TPMT, HLA typing, and APOE testing) and codes listed as "Not Medically Necessary" (including CYP3A4, CYP3A5, F2, F5, MTHFR, SLCO1B1, TYMS, UGT1A1, VKORC1, psychiatric genomic panels, and warfarin metabolism panels).

## Highlights

*   •AI tailors’ treatment plans by analyzing patient-specific data, improving drug selection and outcomes. 
*   •AI predicts drug interactions, toxicity risks, and accelerates drug development process. 
*   •AI enhances medication safety by identifying drug-drug interactions and recommending cost-effective alternatives. 
*   •AI improves diagnostic accuracy and treatment selection through data-driven insights, enhancing patient care. 

## Abstract

Artificial Intelligence (AI) analyzes complex medical data records using Machine learning (ML), Natural Language Processing (NLP), and Deep Learning (DL) algorithms. These algorithms assist physicians in the optimization of therapeutic decisions that allow for the integration and interpretation of individual biological data, including genomics, [proteomics](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/medicine-and-dentistry/proteomics), and [transcriptomics](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/medicine-and-dentistry/transcriptomics). By identifying complex patterns in these data records, AI-driven systems facilitate the development of personalized treatment strategies that align with individual patient profiles. Furthermore, AI enhances [pharmacovigilance](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/pharmacology-toxicology-and-pharmaceutical-science/pharmacovigilance) by predicting potential drug interactions and conducting in-silico toxicity risk assessments through advanced molecular composition analysis. Moreover, AI accelerates the [drug discovery](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/pharmacology-toxicology-and-pharmaceutical-science/drug-discovery) process by screening and identifying novel drugs, thereby facilitating the development of [targeted treatment](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/medicine-and-dentistry/targeted-therapy). AI empowers physicians to prescribe medications, perform real-time formulary checks, and recommend therapeutic equivalent, economically viable alternatives to patient-specific factors. AI-driven [clinical decision support systems](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/medicine-and-dentistry/clinical-decision-support-system) (CDSS) further assist physicians in improving drug compliance and optimizing population health strategies by identifying pharmacologically cost-effective therapies. Additionally, AI enhances real-time clinical decision-making by improving diagnostic precision, refining therapeutic choices, and patient outcomes. The evolution of AI technologies offers immense potential for seamless integration into healthcare systems despite challenges such as data bias, limited model interpretability, and regulatory complexities. This integration revolutionizes personalized medicines, accelerates the [drug discovery](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/pharmacology-toxicology-and-pharmaceutical-science/drug-discovery) process, and improves the safety, efficacy, and cost-effectiveness of [drug therapy](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/pharmacology-toxicology-and-pharmaceutical-science/pharmacotherapy). In summary, AI plays a significant role in modern medicine, promoting data-based clinical decisions and enhancing the overall quality and efficiency of healthcare delivery.

## Introduction

Artificial Intelligence (AI) encompasses a computerized system capable of executing physical tasks and cognitive functions, addressing distinctive problems, and arriving at decisions without explicit human instructions [1]. The implementation of AI into healthcare carries significant potential for advancing medical knowledge and delivering value-based healthcare solutions like patient-centric care, improved diagnostics, predictive analysis, personalized treatment plans, and streamlined healthcare operations [2]. The evolving interest and accelerated adoption of AI in medication selection are driven by convergence of several key factors such as complexity of drug-drug interactions, proliferation of large-scale clinical and biological datasets encompassing genomics, proteomics, and metabolomics have collectively established a paradigm where AI demonstrates significant transformative potential. Advanced computational model enables the analysis of intricate relationships between patient-specific genetic variations such as single-nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs), gene expression profiles, and clinical data. This integrative approach is fundamental to precision medicine as it allows for optimization of therapeutic strategies, prediction of drug efficacy, and minimization of adverse effects based on an individual’s unique molecular and clinical profile. AI is revolutionizing medication selection through a diverse array of advanced computational methodologies [3]. Machine learning algorithms such as support vector machines (SVMs), random forests, and artificial neural networks (ANNs) are employed to predict drug responses, stratify patients into subpopulations likely to benefit from specific therapies, and identify predictive biomarkers for personalized treatment [4]. Moreover, natural language processing (NLP) plays a crucial role in the extraction and interpretation of key information from unstructured data sources like electronic health records (EHRs), medical literature, and patient-reported outcomes. Convolutional neural networks (CNNs) are extensively used in image-based diagnostics that facilitate the identification of disease biomarkers within medical imaging modalities such as radiographs, MRIs, and histopathological studies. On the other hand, recurrent neural networks (RNNs) variants like long short-term memory (LSTM) networks are highly effective in processing sequential data such as time-series information derived from wearable biosensors or longitudinal EHR data [5].

The potential of AI to aid physicians during health crises, especially in handling and analyzing vast amounts of data is immense due to its ability to quickly process information, identify patterns, and provide real-time insights, ultimately enhancing decision-making and improving patient care. This technology empowers physicians to actively participate in and guide the development of ethical framework pathways that prioritize the future well-being and rights of humans. The integration of artificial intelligence (AI) in healthcare is progressively transforming diagnostic workflows, therapeutic decision-making, and patient monitoring systems [6]. Beyond physician-centric benefits, AI-enabled tools facilitate patient-centered care by promoting individualized therapeutic regimens tailored to genetic, physiological, and lifestyle factors. Patients benefit from improved diagnostic accuracy, reduced trial-and-error in medication selection, shorter time-to-treatment initiation, and more predictable clinical outcomes. Furthermore, AI systems integrated with wearable devices and remote monitoring platforms empower patients through real-time feedback, fostering engagement, adherence, and proactive health management [7]. Despite its transformative potential, the application of AI in medication selection is constrained by several critical challenges such as data privacy, algorithmic bias, informed consent, and trust in AI mediated interventions. Data privacy constitutes a critical ethical and regulatory concern in the deployment of AI-driven healthcare systems as such models typically require access to high-dimensional datasets, including electronic health records (EHRs), diagnostic imaging, and continuous physiological monitoring data. In the absence of robust data governance frameworks and de-identification protocols, a heightened risk of data re-identification, unauthorized access, and secondary exploitation exists. A prominent example is the Royal Free London NHS Foundation Trust’s data-sharing collaboration with Google DeepMind for the "Streams" clinical app, wherein approximately 1.6 million patient records were processed without obtaining explicit informed consent [8]. Furthermore, AI algorithms in healthcare perpetuate and amplify existing biases present in historical data. Outcome prediction models (OPMs) trained on biased datasets reinforce health disparities, particularly for marginalized groups. For example, algorithms that allocate healthcare resources based on flawed proxies systematically disadvantage Black patients compared to white patients, as documented in several large-scale studies. These models create self-fulfilling prophecies, where patients from underserved demographics receive suboptimal care due to biased predictions. For instance, a widely used AI algorithm for breast cancer risk prediction assigned black patients to a “low risk” category at a higher rate than white patients, despite equivalent clinical profiles. The consequence was fewer follow-up scans and more undiagnosed cancers among Black women, exacerbating existing health disparities [9]. Informed consent within AI-integrated healthcare systems presents significant complexities due to the opacity and technical intricacies of algorithmic decision-making. Patients often lack sufficient understanding of how their personal health data are collected, processed, and utilized by AI-driven diagnostic and prognostic tools. As such technologies increasingly enter clinical workflows, healthcare providers face challenges in articulating the scope, function, and limitations of these systems. Empirical studies have shown that patients frequently remain unaware of AI involvement in their care, the nature of the data inputs used, and the safeguards in place for data protection. The inherent "black box" nature of deep learning and other complex AI architectures poses significant concerns regarding interpretability and clinical trust, as they lack transparent model decision-making processes. To address this, recent studies illustrate the integration of explainable AI (XAI) techniques that enhance model transparency and help physicians to understand the algorithmic predictions [10]. Model-agnostic approaches such as Shapley Additive Explanations (SHAP) and Local Interpretable Model Agnostic Explanations (LIME) are commonly used to provide feature attribution and localized explanations for individual predictions. Moreover, SHAP uses game-theoretic principles to assign a quantified importance to each feature by evaluating its contribution to the model’s output across all possible feature combinations [11]. Similarly, LIME uses input data to generate locally linear approximations of the black-box model, enabling clinicians to visualize and comprehend model behavior within clinical applications [12]. Beyond enhancing clinical trust, these interpretability strategies are viewed as prerequisites for ethical and regulatory compliance. International regulatory bodies, such as the United States Food and Drug Administration (U.S. FDA) and the European Medicines Agency (EMA), have mandated explainability as a core requirement for the clinical validation and approval of AI-based medical technologies. Stringent regulatory frameworks necessitate rigorous validation studies to ensure model reliability, clinical efficacy, and patient safety before deployment in real-world healthcare settings. Ethical concerns surrounding data privacy, security, and informed consent further necessitate robust governance mechanisms to prevent unauthorized access and mitigate risks associated with algorithmic biases, potential data breaches, and inequitable healthcare outcomes [13]. This study explores the potential of AI algorithms to improve diagnostic precision and efficiency facilitate the development of treatment regimens based on individual patient profiles and enhance overall health outcomes. The Fig. 1. illustrates the multifaceted role of AI in healthcare highlighting its applications in personalized medicine, drug interaction assessment, clinical decision support, and cost-effective prescribing. It also highlights AI's applications in predicting adverse drug reactions, continuous monitoring, integrating telemedicine, and analyzing medical literature. AI has emerged significantly in decision-making within the clinical sector and disease treatment by assimilating, analyzing, and providing reports on extensive data from diverse modalities. This enables doctors to determine the best medicines, drugs, and other patient needs by offering immediate access to highly relevant information [14]. This review article describes the significant role of AI in assisting physicians in the selection of medicines for patients.

A comprehensive literature review was conducted to identify relevant studies evaluating the applications of artificial intelligence (AI) in medication selection, personalized therapy, and clinical decision support systems. Electronic databases including PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, IEEE Xplore, and Google Scholar were systematically searched for peer-reviewed articles published between January 2017 and March 2024. The search strategy employed Boolean operators combining keywords such as “artificial intelligence,” “machine learning,” “deep learning,” “clinical decision support systems,” “personalized medicine,” “drug-drug interactions,” and “adverse drug reactions.” The inclusion criteria encompassed original research articles, systematic reviews, and meta-analyses published in English that focused on AI applications in clinical pharmacology, therapeutic optimization, or pharmacovigilance. Exclusion criteria included non-English publications, editorials, commentaries, conference proceedings, and studies unrelated to therapeutic or clinical applications of AI. From an initial retrieval of 189 records, 42 duplicates were excluded, and 147 unique articles underwent title and abstract screening. Subsequently, 81 full-text articles were evaluated for eligibility, of which 45 articles met the predefined criteria and were included in this review. The crucial information was extracted regarding AI methodologies, clinical domains, therapeutic endpoints, and implementation outcomes. The selected literature was synthesized narratively to elucidate the current and emerging roles of AI in enhancing precision medicine, improving pharmacological safety, and informing data-driven clinical decisions.

This review critically evaluates the current and emerging applications of artificial intelligence (AI) in drug therapy and clinical pharmacology, with a focus on the enhancement of therapeutic precision, safety, and cost-effectiveness. The scope encompasses AI methodologies such as machine learning (ML), deep learning (DL), and natural language processing (NLP) as they are applied to ten core domains: i. personalized medicine and precision drug therapy, wherein AI is used to individualize pharmacological regimens based on genomic, phenotypic, and clinical data; ii. Risk assessment of drug-drug interactions (DDIs) through predictive modeling and knowledge-based inference; iii. Evaluation of drug effectiveness via AI-driven analysis of real-world evidence (RWE) and clinical datasets; iv. Optimization of cost-effective prescribing strategies incorporating pharmacoeconomic and formulary data; v. Prediction and prevention of adverse drug reactions (ADRs) using AI models trained on pharmacovigilance and clinical data; vi. Development and implementation of AI-augmented clinical decision support systems (CDSS); vii. Continuous therapeutic monitoring and dose adjustment using real-time patient-generated health data; viii. AI-enabled alerts and medication adherence reminders; ix. Integration of AI in telemedicine platforms to support remote pharmacological care; and x. Automated extraction, synthesis, and interpretation of medical literature for evidence-based pharmacotherapy.

Personalized medicine is a rapidly evolving paradigm that aims to tailor therapeutic interventions to an individual's unique genetic, proteomic, and clinical profile. AI plays a pivotal role in advancing the medical field by integrating biological data with electronic health records (EHRs) to optimize drug selection, dosing, and therapeutic efficacy. A key application of AI in precision medicine is genomic data integration, wherein AI-driven algorithms analyze single-nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) and gene expression profiles to predict drug responses and metabolism [15]. Pharmacogenomic insights derived from AI models enable clinicians to customize treatment regimens, reducing the reliance on empirical dose adjustments and trial-and-error approaches. Similarly, AI-driven proteomic analysis facilitates precision therapy by identifying protein biomarkers associated with drug efficacy and toxicity. Advanced proteomic techniques such as mass spectrometry-based quantification generate high-resolution protein expression data that AI models utilize to refine personalized treatment strategies. Moreover, the integration of AI with EHRs enhances data-driven clinical decision-making by using vast repositories of longitudinal patient information, including medical history, laboratory results, and prior pharmacological interventions. However, challenges such as data heterogeneity, standardization issues, and privacy concern necessitate robust frameworks for harmonized data utilization. Initiatives like the Observational Health Data Sciences and Informatics (OHDSI) program advocate for the adoption of standardized data models to facilitate AI-driven insights from observational health data, thereby accelerating the implementation of precision medicine in clinical practice. Several AI-driven platforms have been developed to facilitate personalized drug selection by integrating genomic, proteomic, and clinical data to optimize therapeutic strategies [16]. In oncology, AI-powered clinical decision support systems, such as IBM Watson for Oncology, have been developed to assist oncologists in formulating personalized cancer treatment strategies by integrating vast volumes of clinical and molecular data. IBM Watson for Oncology was designed to analyze patient-specific information, including tumor histopathology, staging, biomarkers, comorbidities, and genomic alterations alongside curated literature, clinical guidelines, and treatment protocols. The system leverages natural language processing (NLP) and machine learning algorithms to interpret unstructured clinical data and provide ranked, evidence-based treatment recommendations tailored to the patient's cancer subtype and clinical context. Similarly, in the domain of cardiovascular medicine, AI-integrated platforms such as those developed by CardioDx have explored the use of machine learning to enhance diagnostic precision and risk stratification that focused on development genomic diagnostics based on peripheral blood gene expression profiling to assess the likelihood of obstructive coronary artery disease (CAD) in patients [17]. One of the company’s most prominent products, Corus® CAD, employed a proprietary algorithm that analyzed the expression levels of a panel of 23 genes in conjunction with clinical variables to generate a score reflecting the probability of obstructive CAD. The algorithm was trained and validated using large clinical datasets and aimed to serve as a non-invasive alternative to more expensive or invasive diagnostic modalities such as coronary angiography or stress testing. These predictive models enable clinicians to tailor medication regimens, optimize preventative strategies, and improve patient outcomes by identifying individuals at higher risk for adverse cardiac events. For instance, Verily Life Sciences, a subsidiary of Alphabet Inc., has positioned itself at the intersection of biomedical research and data science by using artificial intelligence and large-scale data integration to facilitate precision medicine. Through the development of advanced predictive models and machine learning algorithms, Verily aims to extract actionable insights from multi-modal health data, including electronic health records (EHRs), genomic profiles, wearable sensor outputs, and longitudinal clinical datasets. These tools are designed to support early detection, stratification, and individualized management of complex chronic conditions such as diabetes, cardiovascular disease, and sepsis. These efforts have led to a 29 % reduction in sepsis-related mortality and a 14 % decrease in hospital readmission rates. While AI enhances precision in drug selection, challenges persist in data heterogeneity, standardization, and integration across clinical systems. Future research should focus on scalable interoperability frameworks and ethically governed data sharing to ensure robust implementation of AI in diverse healthcare environments.

AI-driven methods can analyze vast datasets of known drug interactions to predict potential drug-drug interactions. AI's role in drug interaction assessment is as follows:
*   •**Identification of drug-drug interactions:** AI plays a pivotal role in identifying potential drug interactions that result in altered therapeutic outcomes or adverse reactions. This identification plays a pivotal role as it facilitates the development of tailored treatment strategies and minimizes the risk of adverse reactions [18]. A key application of this approach is the implementation of advanced AI-driven drug interaction screening systems that analyze patient's medication regimens to detect potential harmful interactions. These systems provide real-time alerts to healthcare professionals that facilitate timely modifications to treatment plans and improve patient safety. Furthermore, AI utilizes vast and continuously updated databases of drug interactions and adverse effects, ensuring precise delivery and evidence-based insights to support clinical decision-making. Platforms such as Lexicomp and Micromedex employ advanced AI algorithms to systematically evaluate pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic interactions, assess clinical risks, and provide evidence-based recommendations for healthcare professionals. These tools integrate extensive drug interaction data, using machine learning and natural language processing (NLP) techniques to continuously update and refine their predictive capabilities. Studies have demonstrated that AI-powered drug interaction detection systems can achieve accuracy rates of up to 90 % in identifying known DDIs. While these AI-driven platforms significantly enhance medication safety and clinical decision-making, ongoing improvements in data standardization, algorithm transparency, and real-world validation are essential for optimizing their clinical utility [19]. For instance, a study was conducted to assess the efficacy of various AI chatbots (Bard, ChatGPT-3.5, ChatGPT-4, Bing AI, and Micromedex) in identifying drug-drug interactions [20]. The study analyzed 255 cases of drug interactions, and clinical DDI datasets were used as reference standards to evaluate the performance of each AI tool. Table 1. summarizes the comparative performance metrics of ML algorithms in various clinical domains. Despite high accuracy in identifying interactions, current AI models lack interpretability and real-time adaptability to novel combinations. Further studies are required to enhance algorithm transparency and validate AI models in heterogeneous patient populations through real-world clinical trials. 
*   •**Toxicity prediction:** AI predicts the toxicity of drugs by analyzing their chemical and physical properties. Machine learning AI models based on extensive toxicity databases, can predict adverse drug reactions (ADRs) and adverse drug events (ADEs) in patients, enabling researchers to develop safer drugs and prioritize compounds with a reduced potential for ADRs [21]. Recently, LD 50 predictors- LDFP-ADMET and Interpretable-ADMET are accessible [22]. The model was developed using a selection of AI models, specifically Naive Bayes (NB), Nearest Neighbors, Binned-Nearest Neighbors, and Extended Connectivity binary fingerprints that comprised a test set of 8992 compounds and evidenced 84 % and 81 % of the highest accuracy and sensitivity, respectively [23]. 
*   •**Drug discovery acceleration:** AI is widely explored in the field of drug discovery hypothesizing extensive drug metabolism and excretion data to predict the drug behavior in the body. In 2016, this was adapted by Pfizer Inc. in collaboration with IBM Watson AI to fast-track the development of immuno-oncology drugs. The partnership leveraged Pfizer to harness AI’s capabilities in processing large datasets and identifying potential drug candidates more efficiently, significantly shortening the timeline for drug development. The IBM Watson machine learning platform for drug discovery processed over 25 million licensed and unlicensed immuno-oncology data points, thereby expediting Pfizer's research efforts. As a result, the integration of AI tools into drug discovery shortened developmental timelines by 20 % thus validating improvement in efficiency [24]. 

The application of artificial intelligence transforms drug effectiveness analysis by extracting meaningful insights from extensive diverse patient datasets. AI algorithms identify subtle correlations and undiscoverable patterns that evade recognition by human medical analysts within vast patient datasets [25]. Furthermore, the AI system provides recommendations through patient profile analysis while continuously learning from new data and tracking treatment outcomes. AI has been used to analyze real-world data from electronic health records (EHRs) and claim data to identify unexpected drug effects and optimize dosing regimens. In a study, AI was used to analyze claims data to identify patterns of inappropriate antibiotic use, leading to targeted interventions to improve prescribing practices [26]. AI analytics elucidate hidden correlations in treatment responses, however the external validity of these models is often compromised by sampling bias and insufficient longitudinal data representation. Future research should emphasize multicenter validation studies and dynamic model updating to ensure sustained clinical relevance.

AI plays a significant role in cost-effective prescribing by leveraging advanced algorithms to guide prescribing decisions, reducing the frequency of adverse drug events, and improving medication management. AI assists medical practitioners in reducing healthcare expenditure by guiding them to prescribe lower-cost medications with similar outcomes. It recommends generic alternatives, considers insurance formularies, and suggests therapeutically equivalent medications, all aimed at reducing healthcare expenses while maintaining high-quality patient care. AI tracks medication adherence together with real-time insurance formulary checks and assists population health management through large-scale identification of cost-effective medications [27], [28]. Platforms such as MedKeeper and DoseSpot utilizes advanced AI algorithms to assess formulary coverage, compare drug pricing across different insurance plans, and recommend less-expensive therapeutic equivalents. By integrating real-time prescription benefit data and pharmacy pricing structures, these systems enable clinicians to make informed prescribing decisions without compromising patient care. The effects of cost-based system recommendations on prescription choice decisions were studied by researchers that involved 160 practicing medical professionals in a clinical environment and measured performance according to time limits and practitioner skill levels. In this experiment, two controlled experiments and a survey using interviews formed the methods used. Medical practitioners received six designed patient cases along with thorough medical background details in each experimental scenario. A real-time recommendation system from the system showed three alternative medications while displaying their prices to healthcare providers during prescription decisions. The study results indicated that varying drug prices led practitioners to choose cheaper medications in 42 % of situations demonstrating that cost-aware recommender systems can influence prescription-choice behavior among medical practitioners with a tendency to prescribe lower-cost medications when provided with price information. Although AI tools can suggest economical therapeutic alternatives, limited integration with real-time insurance databases and variability in drug pricing restrict their effectiveness. Future work should explore standardized data pipelines and health economic models embedded in AI systems to enhance cost-sensitive prescribing.

AI is transforming the healthcare industry by predicting adverse reactions while selecting medication for patients. AI frameworks examine large amounts of patient data to determine potential drug-drug interactions, forecast adverse reactions, and optimize therapy selection based on the analysis of patient data. AI provides timely and accurate predictions of patients that are likely to show adverse drug events before medications are prescribed and enables physicians to make more informed decisions about treatment plans and medication selections [29]. Fig. 2. presents a range of advanced AI tools contributing to modern healthcare systems such as machine learning, natural language processing, and ChatGPT facilitate data-driven clinical decision-making and personalized therapy. Clinical Decision Support Systems (CDSS) enhance diagnostic accuracy and medication selection, while emerging platforms like the metaverse and Distributed Ledger Technology (DLT) offer innovative solutions for patient engagement and secure health data management. A machine-learning model was developed by Liu et al. that predicts adverse drug reactions by utilizing the chemical, biological, and physiological characteristics of drugs. The study used 1385 side effects for 832 drugs from the SIDER database and compared them with five machine-learning algorithms using fivefold cross-validation. Support vector machines (SVM) outperformed the others, with an AUC score of 0.9524 when all three types of properties of the drug were implemented, compared to 0.9054 when only chemical structures were used [30]. The precision improved from 43.37 % to 66.17 %, while recall improved from 49.25 % to 63.06 % and as a result, the implementation of AI in predicting adverse drug reactions holds promise for improving patient safety, supporting drug discovery, and enhancing pharmacovigilance efforts.

CDSS are computerized systems that leverage data analytics within electronic health records to offer prompts and reminders, aiding healthcare providers in delivering enhanced patient care. CDSS serves as an application to analyze data to assist healthcare providers in decision-making and improving patient care. Its primary aim is to assist healthcare providers in analyzing patient’s data and using information to support the diagnostic process, ultimately improving patients’ healthcare.

The advantages of CDSS are as follows:
*   •Supports physicians and primary care with integrated workflows. 
*   •Serves as an alarm system on preventative healthcare, prevents drug interaction, or duplicate testing order making for doctors. 
*   •It enhances efficiency by decreasing unnecessary testing to improve patient safety and prevent dangerous or expensive complications [31]. 

AI-powered CDSS enables clinicians to receive real-time assistance based on patient data, allowing them to make informed decisions about drug selection, dosage, and treatment strategies. CDSS is a pivotal tool in advancing medical decision-making as it synthesizes diverse data types to provide valuable insights to healthcare professionals. In a study, 45 volunteers were selected for the experiment based on the inclusion criteria demonstrating CDSS’s role in aiding physicians to prescribe medications to address a wide range of disorders such as high blood pressure and cardiovascular and respiratory disease. Statistical analysis exhibited a standard deviation in means of 0.084 with a 95 % confidence interval ranging from 0.067 to 0.102 [32]. Another study in 2022 examined oncologist’s perspectives on adopting CURATE.AI, an AI-powered CDSS system for personalized drug dosing. Interviews with 12 oncologists suggested a general willingness for CURATE.AI to optimize doses and enhance therapeutic outcomes. Moreover, an advanced CDSS was developed to provide automated follow-up recommendations for cervical cancer screening, including abnormal results based on the updated American Society for Colposcopy and Cervical Pathology (ASCCP) guidelines. Following system enhancements, a validation study was conducted on a stratified sample of 393 patients drawn from a cohort of 3704 individuals. Manual chart reviews conducted by an expert clinician and a resident revealed a significant improvement in recommendation accuracy from 84 % to 93 % post-enhancement[33], [34]. Implementing CDSS in clinical practice necessitates compliance with regulatory frameworks such as the FDA’s Software as a Medical Device (SaMD) classification. CDSS intended to inform clinical management or drive clinical decisions must undergo rigorous premarket evaluation, including analytical validation, clinical validation, and demonstration of real-world performance. Regulatory pathways such as the FDA’s De Novo or 510(k) clearance require comprehensive documentation of algorithm transparency, training data representativeness, and bias mitigation strategies [35]. However, concerns were raised regarding its "black box" nature and the need for greater transparency. Physicians emphasized maintaining final authority on overdosing decisions, viewing AI as a supportive tool rather than a replacement for clinical judgment. A pilot study validated the potential of AI-optimized dosing led to improved efficacy in 80 patients receiving combination chemotherapy. Although CDSS possess numerous advantages, their implementation is constrained by technological and interoperability barriers, including non-standardized EHR architectures, limited cross-platform integration, and insufficient real-time data exchange mechanisms. The lack of uniform data ontologies and terminologies such as SNOMED CT and LOINC, further impedes semantic interoperability. These challenges necessitate the adoption of standardized frameworks like HL7 FHIR and enhanced API infrastructures to support scalable and interoperable CDSS deployment within clinical environments [36].

AI streamlines drug safety surveillance through electronic health records data from social media networks and additional sources to support immediate monitoring processes. This enables healthcare providers to update treatment strategies through real-time monitoring that involves analyzing both patient drug responses and clinical observations [37]. The continuous analysis of up-to-date information by AI enables fast and well-informed healthcare decisions which lead to enhanced patient outcomes and decrease adverse drug events. This continuous monitoring ensures the patient receives the best possible care while also reducing the risk of adverse responses [38]. In Chile, approximately 5 million individuals are affected by chronic diseases. To address this burden, AccuHealth, a healthcare management company, implemented AI-driven remote monitoring to improve patient care. These systems employ advanced algorithms to support the care of the patients and provide real-time monitoring by utilizing its AI to categorize patients, guaranteeing that healthcare providers concentrate on patients those at high risk and require immediate intervention [39].

AI systems are crucial for sending communications to doctors to inform them of possible changes to medications, updates, or alternatives. These alerts respond to changing patient conditions and recent research breakthroughs, ensuring that physicians stay informed and able to make timely, informed judgments about patient care. In addition, these AI systems send medication reminders to patients to ensure they take their medications as prescribed. They are precisely timed and sent via various communication channels, including text messages, emails, and even voice-activated smart speakers, to improve patient compliance with medication regimens [40]. AI applications like AiCure, MediSafe, and Dosecast use computer vision and machine learning to confirm that patients are taking their medications as prescribed and provide reminders, track remaining quantities of medicines, and offer patient-specific information and support, improving adherence to treatment plans [41].

In the field of telemedicine, AI assists clinicians by providing quick, data-driven prescription recommendations, especially when in-person examinations are not possible. During remote consultations, this functionality guarantees that healthcare providers receive timely and informative advice to help their decision-making process. AI-powered virtual assistants provide patients with a range of services, including answering questions about common medical conditions, tracking symptoms, and connecting patients with healthcare providers [42]. For example, clinicians at the Los Angeles County Department of Health Services introduced diabetic retinopathy telemedicine tests at its safety-net locations, leading to a significant reduction in specialty care provider visits. Over 18 months, the initiative reduced visits by more than 14,000. This telemedicine program resulted in a cost savings of approximately $1.5 million annually, while also increasing access to care for over 12,000 diabetic patients who otherwise faced long wait times for specialist consultations [43].

AI algorithms automatically review and analyze a vast amount of medical literature, including research articles, clinical trials, and case studies. AI assists healthcare professionals in staying informed about the latest research and clinical developments by processing large volumes of scientific literature and clinical trial data. This allows providers to make more informed decisions regarding treatment options and medication choices, leading to better patient outcomes [44]. One notable case study involves the integration of AI into the clinical workflow at Lahey Hospital & Medical Center. These AI tools implemented in the radiology practice provided insights to radiologists, prompting a double-check before finalizing reports. Over 12 months, AI-assisted reviews led to the identification of 15 % more incidental findings that could have been missed. The overall report accuracy increased by 20 % and the turnaround time for radiology reports decreased by 18 %, demonstrating the significant value AI brought to the workflow of radiologists [45].

This is a review article published in Advances in Integrative Medicine (Volume 12, Issue 4, December 2025, Article 100529) by Hrishikesh Khude and Pravin Shende, titled "AI-driven clinical decision support systems: Revolutionizing medication selection and personalized drug therapy."

**Purpose:** The review explores how Artificial Intelligence (AI) is transforming medication selection, personalized drug therapy, and clinical decision-support systems. It evaluates AI methodologies (machine learning, deep learning, and natural language processing) across ten core domains of clinical pharmacology.

**Key AI Applications Discussed:**
1. **Personalized medicine and precision drug therapy** – AI integrates genomic, proteomic, and clinical data with EHRs to predict drug responses and customize treatment regimens. Examples include IBM Watson for Oncology, CardioDx's Corus® CAD (a 23-gene panel diagnostic for coronary artery disease), and Verily Life Sciences (reported 29% reduction in sepsis-related mortality and 14% decrease in hospital readmissions).
2. **Drug-drug interaction (DDI) detection** – Platforms like Lexicomp and Micromedex use AI to evaluate interactions, with AI-powered systems achieving up to 90% accuracy in identifying known DDIs. A study assessed AI chatbots (Bard, ChatGPT-3.5/4, Bing AI) against 255 clinical DDI cases.
3. **Toxicity prediction** – ML models analyze chemical/physical properties to predict adverse reactions; LD50 predictors (LDFP-ADMET, Interpretable-ADMET) achieved 84% accuracy using Naive Bayes and Nearest Neighbors on 8,992 compounds.
4. **Drug discovery acceleration** – Pfizer partnered with IBM Watson (processing over 25 million immuno-oncology data points), shortening drug development timelines by 20%.
5. **Cost-effective prescribing** – AI recommends generic alternatives and therapeutically equivalent lower-cost medications; a study of 160 practitioners found drug price information led to cheaper medication choices in 42% of situations.
6. **Adverse drug reaction (ADR) prediction** – A machine-learning model using drug chemical, biological, and physiological data (SIDER database, 832 drugs, 1,385 side effects) achieved an AUC of 0.9524 with SVM, improving precision from 43.37% to 66.17%.
7. **Clinical Decision Support Systems (CDSS)** – A cervical cancer screening CDSS improved recommendation accuracy from 84% to 93% post-enhancement. CURATE.AI was positively received by oncologists for personalized dosing.
8. **Continuous monitoring** – AccuHealth in Chile uses AI remote monitoring for ~5 million chronic disease patients.
9. **Medication adherence alerts** – Tools like AiCure, MediSafe, and Dosecast use computer vision to track adherence.
10. **Telemedicine integration** – Los Angeles County diabetic retinopathy telemedicine reduced specialist visits by over 14,000, saving ~$1.5 million annually for over 12,000 patients.
11. **Medical literature analysis** – At Lahey Hospital, AI-assisted radiology reviews identified 15% more incidental findings, improved report accuracy by 20%, and reduced turnaround time by 18%.

**Challenges Addressed:** Data privacy (citing the Royal Free London NHS-Google DeepMind case involving ~1.6 million patient records without consent), algorithmic bias (e.g., breast cancer risk algorithms assigning Black patients to "low risk" more often), black-box interpretability (addressed via explainable AI techniques like SHAP and LIME), and regulatory compliance (FDA and EMA requiring explainability; FDA SaMD classifications).

**Methodology:** A systematic literature review searched PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, IEEE Xplore, and Google Scholar (January 2017–March 2024), retrieving 189 records; after excluding 42 duplicates and screening, 45 articles met inclusion criteria.

**Conclusion:** AI-driven systems show significant potential in optimizing personalized medicine, assessing drug interactions, predicting adverse drug reactions, and facilitating cost-effective prescribing, though successful integration requires addressing data heterogeneity, model interpretability, and regulatory complexities. The authors declare no competing interests.

## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12629785)Abstract

Large language models (LLMs) have emerged as tools to support healthcare delivery, from automating tasks to aiding clinical decision-making. This study evaluated LLMs as alternative to rule-based alert systems, focusing on their ability to identify prescribing errors. This was designed as a prospective, cross-over, open-label study involving 91 error scenarios based on 40 clinical vignettes across 16 medical and surgical specialties. We developed and validated five LLM models using a retrieval-augmented generation framework. The best-performing model evaluated three different implementation strategies: LLM-based clinical decision support system (CDSS) alone, pharmacist plus LLM-based CDSS (co-pilot), and pharmacist alone. The co-pilot arm demonstrated the best performance with an accuracy of 61% (precision 0.57, recall 0.61, and F1 0.59). In detecting errors posing serious harm, the co-pilot mode increased accuracy by 1.5-fold over the pharmacist alone. Effective LLM integration for complex tasks like medication chart reviews can enhance healthcare professional performance, improving patient safety.

## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12629785)Abstract

## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12629785)Abstract

•Evaluated LLMs in identifying drug-related problems across complex cases•Developed and validated RAG-LLM to enhance reasoning in clinical decision support tasks•Demonstrated varying LLM accuracy in medication safety-related reasoning•LLM use in real-world clinical practice

## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12629785)Abstract

Ong et al. explored how large language models (LLMs) support safe prescribing by detecting drug-related problems across clinical scenarios. The study demonstrated that LLMs augmented performance of pharmacists and improved overall accuracy of medication chart review. However, limitations in clinical generalizability, bias, and prompt design must be addressed before routine use.

**Keywords:**large language models, medication safety, pharmacy, clinical-AI collaboration, co-pilot

## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12629785)Introduction

Medical errors remain a formidable challenge for healthcare institutions all around the world and are the third leading cause of mortality in the United States. Medication-related errors account for an average of 21% of hospital readmissions, with 69% of these admissions considered preventable.[1](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12629785#bib1),[2](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12629785#bib2) Medication errors can potentially result in prolonged hospitalization stay and elevated risk for morbidity and mortality as well as an increase in healthcare spending.[3](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12629785#bib3) This translates to high economic burden of medication errors, amounting up to USD$40 billion in the United States and £750 million in England per year.[3](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12629785#bib3),[4](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12629785#bib4) In an acute care setting, medication errors can occur at any stage of the medication use process: medication prescribing, dispensing, and administration and patient monitoring. A vast majority of errors occur at the prescribing stage, accounting for 70% of errors that result in adverse patient events.[5](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12629785#bib5) Halting errors at this stage is critical in preventing perpetuation of the error downstream and eventually reaching the patient.

Clinical decision support systems (CDSSs) have become a cornerstone of modern healthcare systems as a direct aid to clinical decision-making. A CDSS is intended to improve healthcare delivery by enhancing medical decisions with targeted clinical knowledge, patient information, and other health information.[6](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12629785#bib6) CDSSs have demonstrated utility in reducing prescribing errors or adverse events when integrated with electronic health records and computerized provider order entry systems.[7](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12629785#bib7) In particular categories of prescribing errors such as drug-drug interactions, the real-world implementation of CDSS was effective in reducing the incidence of errors.[8](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12629785#bib8) However, a vast majority of current systems are rule based, resulting in the generation of voluminous and clinically irrelevant alerts to users.[9](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12629785#bib9) Over time, safety alerts are ignored and overwritten by physicians in as high as 95%. “Alert fatigue,” coupled with heavy patient load and high cognitive burden from the need to process a massive amount of patient health information, poses barrier to effective adoption and utilization of CDSS systems.[10](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12629785#bib10),[11](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12629785#bib11),[12](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12629785#bib12) Greater personalization of alerts, more intuitive interfaces, and lesser emphasis on disruptive alerts show promise in improving current state of CDSS.

The growing capabilities of large language models (LLMs) in medical tasks are becoming more apparent. LLMs are advancing in handling such tasks, particularly those that do not require extensive specialized expertise.[13](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12629785#bib13),[14](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12629785#bib14) This includes simplifying administrative duties like composing medical letters, creating summaries upon patient discharge using information from electronic health records (EHRs) to semi-autonomous decision-making support for managing operating theaters.[15](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12629785#bib15),[16](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12629785#bib16) Finally, LLM-powered healthcare chatbots are capable of providing patients and health professionals with highly professional-sounding, accurate, and personalized responses to medical queries.[17](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12629785#bib17),[18](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12629785#bib18) Healthcare systems are facing critical shortage of healthcare professionals compounded by a mounting issue of healthcare professional burnout.[19](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12629785#bib19),[20](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12629785#bib20),[21](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12629785#bib21) LLM-powered solutions are well poised to improve operational efficiency and standards of patient care when trained with the right data, robustly evaluated in the clinical setting with a deployment strategy armed with appropriate safety measures.

Prior published studies have developed LLM-based tools to support various clinical applications and domains.[22](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12629785#bib22),[23](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12629785#bib23),[24](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12629785#bib24) Generative AI tools, such as LLMs, demonstrate potential to reduce medication-related harm when integrated into the medication use process as clinical decision support tools. LLMs were designed to perform specific tasks such as identifying inappropriate benzodiazepine prescriptions, classifying adverse drug reactions to chemotherapy, and predicting potential drug-drug interactions. The use of LLMs as an innovative substitute to current rules-based CDSS for medication review, however, has not been described. In this study, we propose a modified clinical model of care, leveraging upon LLMs as a tool to improve safety of medication use in acute care settings. The objective of this study was to evaluate the performance of LLM-based tools in correctly identifying prescribing errors and provision of clinically aligned recommendations to rectify identified errors across different medical disciplines. This has implications for the potential integration of such tools in healthcare and attendant improvements in patient safety and quality of care.

## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12629785)Results

Six pharmacists of varying levels of work experience participated in this study. Four participants were junior pharmacists with post-licensure practice experience of between 2 and 5 years, while 2 participants were senor pharmacists with >10 years of post-licensure practice experience. The case vignettes are representative of complex clinical case scenarios with multiple co-morbidities and problem lists ([Table 1](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12629785#tbl1)). The expert panel determined that 31.9% (29 out of 91) error scenarios were capable of causing serious harm and 52.7% (48 out of 91) capable of inflicting moderate harm while the remaining 15.4% (14 out of 91) were rated as capable of causing minor or no harm. Of the native models, Gemini Flash scored the lowest while Claude 3.5 Sonnet performed the best on measures of recall (0.16 vs. 0.51), precision (0.15 vs. 0.35), F1 (0.16 vs. 0.42), and overall accuracy (16% vs. 51%). ### Comparative performance of different modes of delivery

The Claude 3.5 Sonnet (native) model was the adopted model in LLM-CDSS due to the best overall performance during validation. There was no statistically significant differences in mean accuracy between different modes of care: co-pilot (pharmacist with LLM-CDSS), human only (pharmacist without LLM-CDSS), and LLM only (_p = 0.38_) ([Figure 2](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12629785#fig3)A). The mean accuracy in identifying DRPs increased by 32.6% in co-pilot mode when compared against human alone (61%, SD 17.7 vs. 46%, SD 21.1). Precision, recall, and F1 score were all higher in co-pilot mode when compared against human alone (0.57 vs. 0.52, 0.61 vs. 0.46, and 0.49 vs. 0.45) ([Figure 2](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12629785#fig3)B). ## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12629785)Discussion

Previous work evaluating the utility of LLMs in medicine focuses heavily on reporting model performance while few prospective studies have evaluated the practical performance of healthcare professionals when LLMs are incorporated as part of a clinical workflow.[25](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12629785#bib25),[26](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12629785#bib26),[27](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12629785#bib27) In this study, we provide a proof of concept of an application of LLM-based CDSS, designed to improve safety of medication use and prescribing in an acute care practice setting. Our findings are based on 90 different errors and DRPs, embedded within 40 clinical vignettes. Different modes of delivery were tested in a cross-over, open-label study design. We report greater accuracy in DRP identification by 32% when used in a co-pilot mode by pharmacists as compared to pharmacists alone without the tool. Similarly, the accuracy of co-pilot mode in identifying DRPs surpassed that of LLM alone. In co-pilot mode, two-thirds of DRPs with potential for causing serious harm were detected. This study evaluates LLM in assessing prescription appropriateness using patient-specific textual information, which is the most common format encountered by pharmacists during medication reviews. In contrast to prior work that focused on narrow tasks using limited input data,[26](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12629785#bib26) our study used a combination of patient information and medication details to leverage the general reasoning capabilities of LLMs for evaluating clinical appropriateness. We compared three modes of implementation: LLM alone, human alone, and a collaborative setting where the LLM assisted the user. This approach provides a more comprehensive and realistic understanding of how LLMs can be integrated into clinical practice, addressing limitations of previous studies that lacked direct comparisons or real-world application scenarios.[28](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12629785#bib28),[29](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12629785#bib29) In addition, previous studies that included a comparator often evaluated LLMs against human experts under the assumption that LLMs will be deployed autonomously in clinical settings.[30](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12629785#bib30) In contrast, our study examined three configurations: human expert-only, LLM-only, and a co-pilot approach. This provides a more complete and practical understanding of how these models perform when used alongside clinicians in real-world settings.

Our results suggests that, for complex reasoning clinical tasks such as medication chart review, LLMs can potentially augment human performance. However, we observed that, in the co-pilot mode, performance declined in 1 key category of DRP: inappropriate dosage regimen. Variability in medication dosing regimen across different geographical regions and academic institutions has been well described.[31](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12629785#bib31),[32](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12629785#bib32) In our study, we evaluated the performance of Claude Sonnet 3.5, a commercially available LLM, that was pre-trained on a broad dataset not restricted to carefully curated medication content or the most up-to-date drug dosing guidelines.[33](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12629785#bib33) These results are consistent with those reported by Yu et al., who found that inaccurate AI predictions negatively impacted the performance of radiologists.[34](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12629785#bib34) The impact of AI-based decision support tools on user performance has been shown to be heterogeneous, suggesting a need for personalized approaches in the design of clinician-AI interfaces.[35](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12629785#bib35) The differences between clinician and medical AI decisions are due to a basic mismatch in how each defines the clinical problem. AI systems developed for healthcare applications often lack a clear explanation of how decisions are derived. Although explainable AI tools aim to reveal the reasoning behind an AI’s output, they often use technical explanations that remain confusing or are misleading to users.[35](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12629785#bib35) This lack of clarity can make it hard for clinicians to trust or effectively use these systems. In contrast, LLMs with conversational interfaces allow clinicians to ask questions and receive context-specific explanations in plain language. We believe that this interactive and adaptive communication can strengthen the partnership between clinicians and AI, making the technology more useful and trustworthy in clinical decision-making.

CDSSs can be broadly classified into two distinct categories: knowledge-based (KB) and AI-driven systems. KB CDSSs rely on a set of rules and associations derived from clinical guidelines or expert opinions. They function by matching patient-specific data with a knowledge base and providing recommendations or alerts.[36](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12629785#bib36) AI-driven systems, on the other hand, are capable of analyzing large datasets, identify patterns, and make predictions or recommendations based on new data without predefined rules.[7](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12629785#bib7) Our LLM-based CDSS is an interesting approach to an AI-driven system. Widespread adoption of AI-driven CDSS systems is met with barriers, including lack of transparency, uncertainty relating to the evidence, lack of trust in the system, and disruptions to clinical workflow that add time to routine clinical practice.[37](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12629785#bib37),[38](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12629785#bib38) To date, ML-based CDSSs are fairly narrow in application, most being domain specific. LLMs grounded with contextual knowledge present various advantages over ML-based models, including the ability to integrate and process vast amounts of varied data types, including unstructured clinical texts;easily update the clinical knowledge corpus without the need for explicit retraining; and offer explanations in natural language that are more comprehensible to human practitioners. In our study, we leveraged upon the generalist capability of LLMs and tested the model in a wide variety of clinical scenarios from different disciplines and included a wide range of medication classes.

However, despite the strengths of LLM-based CDSS, the potential pitfalls of LLM-CDSS tools must be recognized. Although contextually grounded models show promise in reducing hallucinations and improve clinical accuracy of LLMs, our findings suggest that even supplementing an LLM with a knowledge base through the use of RAG did not yield comparatively better results ([Figure 2](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12629785#fig2)). This might be explained by various reasons. First, our study tested RAG-LLMs on a small number of vignettes and explored a limited range of scenarios. A bigger sample size of scenarios is required to validate this observation. Second, LLMs may demonstrate reluctance to fully accept newly retrieved knowledge, especially when it conflicts with the model’s pretraining data. When conflicting knowledge is integrated, the LLM often produces ambiguous or inconsistent recommendations. Moreover, with regards to LLM-RAG-based CDSSs, RAG systems face challenges due to the lack of a state-of-the-art pipeline or retrieval techniques that have been universally established. This necessitates the creation of highly tailored RAG pipelines for each specific use case, which can be resource intensive and technically demanding. Finally, suboptimal performance of the RAG pipeline in our study can be attributed to the complexity of clinical reasoning required for medication-related tasks, which often exceeds the capabilities of general-purpose retrieval and generation mechanisms. Conflicts between retrieved and pre-trained knowledge and retrieval noise may have compromised the integration of relevant clinical context. Barriers to adopting AI-driven CDSSs, including LLM-based systems, also remain substantial. These systems are met with concerns about their lack of transparency, uncertainty surrounding the evidence base, and disruptions they may cause to clinical workflow, which can add time to routine clinical practice. As such, further refinements and reliable methodologies are required before AI-driven CDSSs can achieve widespread adoption in healthcare.

KB CDSSs are implemented for various purposes and often tailored to the peculiar needs of the healthcare facility. Regarding their efficacy in reinforcing prescribing safety, various studies have shown that KB CDSSs can significantly contribute to the reduction of prescription errors and improve prescribing practices. In a meta-analysis of 68 trials evaluating CDSSs on physician prescribing, positive behavior improved by 4.4% (95% confidence interval [CI] 2.6%–6.2%) with the deployment of KB CDSSs.[36](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12629785#bib36) AI-based CDSSs have similarly demonstrated positive outcomes on prescribing safety and potential cost savings from DRP avoidance.[37](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12629785#bib37),[38](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12629785#bib38) These trials underscore the vital role of CDSSs in enhancing prescribing safety, whether through rule-based systems or through advanced AI-driven analytics. However, the successful implementation and effectiveness of these systems depend on several factors, including system design, user interface, integration into clinical workflows, and training of healthcare professionals. LLM-based CDSSs present with unique advantages such as the ability to process and interpret large volumes of unstructured clinical data, adapt to evolving medical knowledge, and provide personalized treatment recommendations.[39](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12629785#bib39),[40](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12629785#bib40) We foresee that LLM-based CDSSs can be integrated into clinical workflow in co-pilot mode to augment the performance of pharmacists ([Figure 4](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12629785#fig5)). In addition, we envisage that, in low resource settings with manpower constraints, an autonomous/hybrid mode of AI delivery may plug current gaps in clinical services. In our study, we were unable to perform a direct comparison of our LLM-based CDSS against traditional KB CDSS. This is due to high variability of CDSS design across different healthcare institutions, making standardization of KB CDSSs unfeasible. Another reason was that the inclusion of traditional KB CDSS tools could have introduced confounding factors, such as differences in pharmacists’ familiarity with the tools and the potential influence of automation bias.[41](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12629785#bib41)Figure 5An overview of the cross-over study flow

The limitations of our study are as follows. (1) DRPs identified from clinical scenarios were limited to 5 categories, and this might limit generalizability in clinical cases with other DRP categories. Test scenarios were adapted from errors captured by pharmacists and may represent bias toward scenarios that reach intervention and reporting thresholds. (2) The number of fictional clinical scenarios was limited, notwithstanding that each fictional scenario was designed to be highly complex in order to allow for initial exploration of LLM-based CDSS capabilities. (3) Only 5 LLMs in complex clinical decision-making tasks were evaluated. (4) Bias and fairness of output were not evaluated. Studies have shown that LLM outputs may encode gender and racial biases. (5) In this study, we only tested LLM performance based on one prompt. As different prompt strategies may influence model outputs, future research should focus on designing more precise prompts. (6) Rapid development of new LLM models and versions limits conclusions from study results. (7) Knowledge base data were limited, such as the use of only local institutional monographs and drug use guidelines due to copyright constraints, which may affect generalizability.

Future research should consider several key directions to enhance the accuracy and reliability of LLM-based CDSSs. First, improvements to current tested pipeline are needed, particularly through iterative refinement of information retrieval strategies. This includes chunking and indexing methods, as well as exploration of alternative knowledge sources like real-time online browsing or integration with AI agents. Second, research should focus on optimizing human-computer interaction and clinician-AI collaboration. Although our findings indicate better performance when the model is used collaboratively with clinical pharmacists, critical issues such as model bias, automation bias, and the erosion of trust in AI systems require further evaluation, particularly when deployed at scale in real-world settings. Finally, investigating newly released models with advanced reasoning capabilities, such as OpenAI’s o3-mini and DeepSeek’s R1, offers promising potential. These models support chain-of-thought reasoning, which can enhance transparency by revealing the steps behind an output, thereby addressing concerns around the “black box” nature of many AI systems and improving user trust.

The integration of LLM-based CDSSs presents as a potential tool in improving prescription safety. Our study reveals that, when used in tandem with pharmacists, identification of DRPs is enhanced, surpassing the accuracy of humans alone. The combined pharmacist and LLM model (co-pilot mode) demonstrates superior performance in detecting severe DRPs and offers a promising hybrid solution for improving patient safety in medication management. This co-pilot model could represent the next step in CDSS development, merging human expertise with the analytical prowess of AI to improve healthcare outcomes.

### Limitations of the study

This study’s limitations constrain its immediate clinical applicability. It addressed only five DRP categories using a small set of complex, fictional scenarios that may not reflect the diversity of real-world cases. Test cases were drawn from known pharmacist-reported errors, introducing potential bias. The evaluation of five LLMs with a single prompt, without assessing output bias or fairness, further limits generalizability. Additionally, rapid LLM evolution and reliance on local drug references restrict applicability across broader clinical settings. These factors underscore the need for further validation before integrating such tools into routine clinical practice.

### Experimental model and study participant details

This was a prospective, cross-over, open-label study. The institutional ethics review board exempted this study from review as no identifiable patient data was used. An overview of the evaluation workflow is shown in [Figure 5](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12629785#fig1). Participants were registered pharmacists, practicing in 2 different tertiary acute care institutions. Participants were randomized using a random number generator into one of 2 arms. In the first arm, participants reviewed a set of patient case vignettes without LLM-CDS assistance in round 1. Participants waited at least one day before they are asked to review another set of patient case vignettes with appended LLM-CDS output in round 2. In the second arm, participants reviewed a set of case vignettes with LLM-CDS assistance in round 1, followed a set of vignettes without LLM-CDS assistance after the washout period. During each round, participants were asked to complete the reviews of 7–8 case within a time frame of 1.5 h. Rounds consisted of a fresh set of 7–8 vignettes (not used in the previous round). We provide details of response generation in subsection on “Generation of LLM and Pharmacist Responses”.Figure 1Comparative performance of respective native and RAG-LLMsPerformance of different LLMs in terms of (A) precision, (B) recall, (C) F-measure, and (D) accuracy.

#### Development of prescribing error scenarios

A total of 91 different simulated prescribing error scenarios based on 40 case vignettes modeled after complex clinical cases were curated. Prescribing error scenarios were adapted from our institution’s pharmacy intervention and error reporting databases to maintain realism. The vignettes covered clinical scenarios from 16 different medical or surgical subspecialties (Cardiology, Colorectal Surgery, Endocrinology, Emergency Medicine, Family Medicine, Gastroenterology, General Surgery, General Medicine, Haematology, Infectious Disease, Neurology, Oncology, Ophthalmology, Respiratory Medicine, Urology, Vascular Surgery) with some cases involving more than one discipline. Each case vignette consisted of a patient clinical note and medication prescription. Prescribing errors in the clinical scenarios were designed to be reflective of drug-related problems (DRP) encountered in an acute care tertiary medical institution in Singapore. We present a sample of one case vignette in [Figure S1](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12629785#mmc1). A detailed description of all case vignettes is found in [Data S1](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12629785#mmc1). The Anatomical Therapeutic Chemical (ATC) category of medications prescribed in each clinical scenario is also presented in [Table S2](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12629785#mmc1).

#### Development of reference standard

The reference standard was developed through manual grading of DRP categories and severity by a multi-disciplinary expert panel. The expert panel consisted of pharmacotherapy board certified pharmacists and physicians with >10 years of clinical practice experience in tertiary hospitals. Every clinical scenario was graded by at least 1 pharmacist and 1 physician member of the panel. Any disagreements were resolved by a 3 rd independent member. DRPs from each clinical scenario were categorized using the Pharmaceutical Care Network Europe (PCNE) classification V9.1 and ASHP statement of pharmaceutical care as a guide.[42](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12629785#bib42),[43](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12629785#bib43) Types of errors in the clinical scenarios included adverse drug reaction, allergy, drug-drug interactions, duplication of therapy, inappropriate choice of therapy, inappropriate dosage regimen, no indication and omission of drug therapy. The potential severity of these errors were graded according to the Harm Associated with Medication Error Classification (HAMEC) classification tool.[44](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12629785#bib44) In addition, we calculated the MCRI (medication regimen complexity index) for each case. This is a scientific article published in Cell Reports Medicine (Cell Rep Med, 2025 Sep 24;6(10):102323, doi:10.1016/j.xcrm.2025.102323, PMCID: PMC12629785, PMID: 40997804) describing a study evaluating large language models (LLMs) as clinical decision support systems (CDSS) for medication safety.

**Study Design:** The study was a prospective, cross-over, open-label design involving 91 simulated prescribing error scenarios based on 40 complex clinical vignettes across 16 medical and surgical specialties. Six pharmacists (4 junior with 2-5 years experience; 2 senior with >10 years) from two tertiary acute care institutions participated. Participants were randomized into two arms with washout periods between rounds. Expert panel (board-certified pharmacists and physicians with >10 years experience) developed reference standards using PCNE classification V9.1 and HAMEC severity tools.

**Key Findings:**
- Five LLMs were evaluated (Gemini Flash, Gemini 1.5 Pro, GPT-4 Turbo, GPT-4 omni, Claude 3.5 Sonnet) with and without retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) frameworks
- Shown: 31.9% of errors capable of causing serious harm, 52.7% moderate harm, 15.4% minor/no harm
- Claude 3.5 Sonnet was the best native model (accuracy 51%, F1 0.42 vs Gemini Flash's 16%, F1 0.16)
- RAG framework did not improve Claude 3.5 Sonnet's performance (accuracy decreased 2% to 49%)
- Three implementation modes tested: LLM alone, pharmacist alone, and co-pilot (pharmacist + LLM)
- **Co-pilot mode performed best with 61% accuracy** (precision 0.57, recall 0.61, F1 0.59) – a 32.6% improvement over pharmacist alone (46% accuracy)
- Co-pilot mode increased detection of serious-harm errors by 1.5-fold over pharmacist alone (66% vs. 43-52%)
- Performance declined in co-pilot mode for inappropriate dosage regimen detection (52% vs. 43%)
- No significant correlation between case complexity (MCRI score) and accuracy
- Most common drug-related problems: inappropriate dosage regimens, adverse drug reactions, and drug-drug interactions

**Conclusions:** LLMs used in co-pilot mode (in tandem with pharmacists) can augment medication chart review performance and improve patient safety in acute care settings. However, limitations include addressing only 5 DRP categories, small sample of fictional scenarios, lack of bias/fairness evaluation, single prompt testing, rapidly evolving LLM landscape, and dependence on local drug references. The study proposes a clinical workflow where LLM-CDSS acts as a co-pilot to summarize patient information and flag DRPs for pharmacist preview.

**Data availability:** Sample dataset and codes are openly available at https://github.com/Liyuan1Y/CDSS-LLM-Cookbook/tree/main. Lead contact: Dr. Daniel Shu Wei Ting (daniel.ting.s.w@singhealth.com.sg). The study was supported by Singapore National Medical Research Council, Duke-NUS Medical School, and A*STAR grants. This is an open-access article under CC BY license.
