## ESM-3 – Scaling Protein Language Models

**Overview:** ESM-3 is a **protein language foundation model**, focusing on sequence and function rather than direct structure inference. Announced June 2024 by EvolutionaryScale (a startup by ex-Facebook FAIR scientists), it represents a leap in scale and generality for biological sequence models ([[10]](https://www.evolutionaryscale.ai/blog/esm3-release#:~:text=Today%20we%20are%20sharing%20ESM3%2C,structure%2C%20and%20function%20of%20proteins)) ([[11]](https://www.medicalschool.tv/biology-2/meta-alum-launches-ai-biology-model-that-simulates-500-million-years-of-evolution-venturebeat/#:~:text=Described%20as%20a%20frontier%20generative,the%20tracks%2C%20generating%20novel%20proteins)). While not a structure-predictor per se, ESM-3 implicitly “understands” structure and can generate proteins with desired properties. It is *“natively multimodal and generative”* ([[35]](https://www.medicalschool.tv/biology-2/meta-alum-launches-ai-biology-model-that-simulates-500-million-years-of-evolution-venturebeat/#:~:text=The%20task%20sounds%20complicated%2C%20but,of%20years%20to%20evolve%20naturally)) in the sense that its architecture can handle multiple input/output modalities (sequence, structure coordinates, function labels), and it is trained auto-regressively (like GPT) to generate content until no token remains masked ([[10]](https://www.evolutionaryscale.ai/blog/esm3-release#:~:text=Today%20we%20are%20sharing%20ESM3%2C,structure%2C%20and%20function%20of%20proteins)).

**Architecture and Training:** Based on the transformer architecture, ESM-3 is enormous. Official sources state it has on the order of **10^11 parameters** (98B in the largest version) ([[12]](https://www.evolutionaryscale.ai/blog/esm3-release#:~:text=Trained%20on%20one%20of%20the,24%7D%20FLOPS%20and%2098B%20parameters)), making it far bigger than previous ESM-2 models (whose largest was 15B). It was trained on an unprecedentedly large dataset: *billions* of protein sequences from the public metagenomic and UniProt databases (the press notes “2.78 billion sequences and 771 billion tokens” ([[11]](https://www.medicalschool.tv/biology-2/meta-alum-launches-ai-biology-model-that-simulates-500-million-years-of-evolution-venturebeat/#:~:text=Described%20as%20a%20frontier%20generative,the%20tracks%2C%20generating%20novel%20proteins))). The compute was also massive (~10^24 floating operations) ([[12]](https://www.evolutionaryscale.ai/blog/esm3-release#:~:text=Trained%20on%20one%20of%20the,24%7D%20FLOPS%20and%2098B%20parameters)). Despite this scale, EvolutionaryScale reports that ESM3’s training process is a continued unsupervised masked language modeling objective (predict missing amino acids), augmented with structural token prediction. Uniquely, ESM-3’s input vocabulary includes not only amino acids but also discretized structural and functional tokens. That is, the model sees *paired tracks*: one track is the protein sequence, another track contains structural information (e.g. known backbone torsion or Zernike descriptors), and possibly a third track denotes function or enzyme commission (EC) labels. During training it learns to co-attend across these tracks, effectively linking sequence patterns with structural motifs and function annotations.

The model is *generative*: given partial input (e.g. a sequence with some masked positions, or a scaffold of coordinates), it can autoregressively sample the full output. This contrasts with AF3, which is conditional generative (predicting structure given sequence but not vice versa). args.summary:
This IntuitionLabs report (published April 19, 2026) provides an in-depth comparison of AI biology foundation models for molecular biology, focusing on AlphaFold 3 (AF3), ESM-3, Boltz-2, Chai-1, and RoseTTAFold. It analyzes their architectures, training data, capabilities, quantitative benchmarks, and real-world use cases in drug discovery.

**Key Models:**
- **AlphaFold 3 (AF3)**: Released May 2024 by DeepMind/Isomorphic. Uses a generative diffusion architecture predicting full atomic structures of complexes (proteins, nucleic acids, small molecules, modified residues) in one unified model. Achieves ~76% success on PoseBusters ligand benchmark (RMSD <2Å), far surpassing physics-based docking (~30-38%). Dramatically improved protein-ligand, protein-DNA/RNA, and antibody-antigen prediction. Closed-source (free academic use only) and can "hallucinate" structure in disordered regions (mitigated via cross-distillation training).
- **ESM-3**: From EvolutionaryScale (ex-Meta researchers), mid-2024. A 98-billion-parameter multimodal protein language model, generative and autoregressive like GPT. Trained on 2.78 billion sequences (771 billion tokens) using >10^24 FLOPS. Can generate protein sequences from partial cues; demonstrated design of a novel fluorescent protein (58% identity to known GFP, representing ~500M years of natural evolution). Smallest 1.4B version open-source; larger models commercial via AWS/Nvidia.
- **Boltz-2**: Announced June 2025 by MIT Jameel Clinic. Successor to Boltz-1 with equivariant diffusion backbone plus a unique "affinity module" predicting binding strength (IC50-like). Achieves FEP-level accuracy in relative binding energies (Pearson ~0.62) while running >1000× faster than physics-based simulations. Fully open-source (MIT license). Outperformed all submissions on CASP16-style binding challenge; used to identify TYK2 inhibitors in virtual assays.
- **Chai-1**: Released September 2024 by Chai Discovery. Open-source multimodal structure predictor using protein language model embeddings and supporting experimental restraints (crosslinks, epitope maps). ~77% success on PoseBusters ligand benchmark (vs AF3's ~76%). User "steering" with contact constraints doubles antibody-antigen accuracy. Pitched as "AlphaFold 3 power without limitations" - free for non-commercial use.
- **RoseTTAFold**: Released 2021 by Baker Lab using a three-track network (1D sequences, 2D distance maps, 3D coordinates). Achieved CASP14-competitive accuracy comparable to AlphaFold 2. Openly available; "All-Atom" 2024 update weaker on ligand docking (~42% top hits vs ~76-77% for newer models) but remains a standard comparator.

**Headline Benchmark Comparison (PoseBusters protein-ligand):** Physics-based methods 38%, AlphaFold 3 76%, Chai-1 77%, RoseTTAFold All-Atom ~42%.

**Implications:** These foundation models are transforming biology, enabling routine atomistic complex prediction (proteins with drugs, DNA, membranes) in hours rather than years. Drug discovery pipelines are exploiting end-to-end AI for generative compound design and antibody maturation. Concerns include hallucination issues (AF3), dual-use risks, licensing restrictions, and computational demands. The field is evolving rapidly with iterative improvements expected.

## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12806033)Abstract

The evolutionary scale modeling (ESM) series is promising to revolutionize protein science and engineering through large language models (LLMs), providing a robust framework for understanding the relationships among sequences, structures, and functions of proteins. Trained on a large number of unlabeled protein sequences, ESM models are able to capture intricate patterns of mutation and conservation, yielding insights into the structural and functional properties of proteins. Despite a growing body of literature surrounding ESM, existing surveys often fail to comprehensively describe its advancements or applications in a focused manner. This survey covers the latest developments of ESM, categorizing them into techniques of using ESM and downstream applications. Approximately 100 papers are selected and analyzed, highlighting recognized and innovative studies that exemplify the impact of ESM. Furthermore, we critically discuss the strengths and limitations of ESM to envision future applications. This review provides a valuable resource for researchers seeking to explore the power of ESM models and the emerging applications of LLMs in biology and medicine.

**Keywords:**BERT, fine‐tuning, pretraining, prompting, protein design, protein function, protein language model, Transformer

## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12806033)INTRODUCTION

1
The advent of the evolutionary scale modeling (ESM) series of protein language models (PLMs) [[1](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12806033#qub270013-bib-0001), [2](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12806033#qub270013-bib-0002), [3](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12806033#qub270013-bib-0003), [4](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12806033#qub270013-bib-0004), [5](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12806033#qub270013-bib-0005), [6](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12806033#qub270013-bib-0006)] is a significant innovation in the convergence of large language models (LLMs) with protein representation. These models, trained on large amounts of unlabeled protein sequence data, distill the intricate patterns of mutation and conservation that have sculpted protein families through evolutionary history. ESM models are significant primarily because of their ability to model proteins and mirror biological evolution. It provides a foundation upon which many downstream applications can be constructed, offering insights into various aspects of proteins.

Given the rapid development of ESM and its applications in biotechnology and medicine, a survey of the latest advances is both timely and necessary. Although there are already some reviews mentioning ESM [[7](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12806033#qub270013-bib-0007), [8](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12806033#qub270013-bib-0008), [9](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12806033#qub270013-bib-0009), [10](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12806033#qub270013-bib-0010), [11](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12806033#qub270013-bib-0011)], they either focus on specific subdomains of proteins rather than LLMs [[8](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12806033#qub270013-bib-0008), [9](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12806033#qub270013-bib-0009)] or lump together many language models and ignore the specificity of ESM [[7](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12806033#qub270013-bib-0007), [10](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12806033#qub270013-bib-0010), [11](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12806033#qub270013-bib-0011)]. In addition, the ESM series has been expanded and refined over time, but few reviews have a comprehensive account of them. Hence, this review aims to describe the latest technical innovations around ESM with a focus on its downstream applications.

First, we provide a brief overview of the ESM series. Next, we classify the downstream applications of ESM from two perspectives: technical approaches and application domains. Finally, we discuss the strengths and limitations of ESM, as well as its potential future applications. For a comprehensive survey, we selected approximately one hundred representative papers from all papers that have cited at least one of the six original publications of ESM. All of these selected works have been cited at least five times. Given the high volume of citations and the diversity of downstream research associated with ESM, we may not capture all valuable studies in this survey. However, we believe that our review covers most major research directions and the most influential works. Readers are encouraged to explore additional studies following the framework provided here.

## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12806033)OVERVIEW OF ESM SERIES

2
The earliest and foundational work of the ESM series is ESM‐1b [[1](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12806033#qub270013-bib-0001)], a general‐purpose PLM. ESM‐1b adopts a BERT‐style [[12](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12806033#qub270013-bib-0012)] Transformer [[13](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12806033#qub270013-bib-0013)] architecture (see Figure[1](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12806033#qub270013-fig-0001)) and is trained using the masked language modeling (MLM) [[1](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12806033#qub270013-bib-0001)] objective on 250 million protein sequences from UniParc [[14](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12806033#qub270013-bib-0014)]. MLM means that for each sequence _x_, ESM randomly samples a set of positions _M_ to mask, that is, replacing the true token of amino acid at each index _i_ with the mask token. For each masked token, it independently minimizes the negative log‐likelihood of the true amino acid _x_ _i_ given the masked sequence _x/M_ as context, as shown in Equation([1](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12806033#qub270013-disp-0001)). The model not only validated the effectiveness of scaling laws in PLMs but also achieved state‐of‐the‐art (SOTA) performance on several downstream tasks at the time of its release. (1) 

$$
L_{\text{MLM}} = E_{x sim X} E_{M} \underset{i \in M}{\sum} - log p \left(x_{i} \left|\right. x_{M}\right) .
$$

FIGURE 1
[![Image 15: FIGURE 1](https://pmc-oa-opendata.s3.amazonaws.com/PMC12806033.1/QUB2-14-e70013-g003.jpg)](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/core/lw/2.0/html/tileshop_pmc/tileshop_pmc_inline.html?title=Click%20on%20image%20to%20zoom&p=PMC3&id=12806033_QUB2-14-e70013-g003.jpg)

[Open in a new tab](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/figure/qub270013-fig-0001/)

The architecture of evolutionary scale modeling (ESM) models.

Subsequent variants of ESM were built on ESM‐1b by extending it across various protein tasks. Multiple sequence alignment (MSA) Transformer (ESM‐MSA‐1b) [[2](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12806033#qub270013-bib-0002)] replaces common attention with tied row attention and untied column attention to extract and fuse embeddings from MSAs [[15](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12806033#qub270013-bib-0015)], enabling inference of protein structures, including contact and secondary structures. ESM‐1v [[3](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12806033#qub270013-bib-0003)] has the same architecture as ESM‐1b and is specialized for variant effect prediction (VEP) by being trained to score the effect of sequence mutations on protein function. ESM‐IF1 [[4](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12806033#qub270013-bib-0004)] connects Transformer [[13](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12806033#qub270013-bib-0013)] blocks after GVP‐GNN [[16](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12806033#qub270013-bib-0016)], a graph neural network with layers operating on collections of Euclidean vectors, and scales both of them. It can be used for fixed‐backbone sequence design (inverse folding) or predicting functional effects of protein sequence variation for given structures.

ESM‐2 [[5](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12806033#qub270013-bib-0005)] further scales ESM‐1b and is a SOTA general‐purpose PLM. It can be used to predict a wide range of protein properties directly from individual sequences and is one of the most widely used foundation models in the field of protein science nowadays. Released in the same paper is ESMFold [[5](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12806033#qub270013-bib-0005)], an end‐to‐end single‐sequence 3D structure predictor that can achieve comparable performance with AlphaFold2 [[17](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12806033#qub270013-bib-0017)] in some important scenes. ESM3 [[6](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12806033#qub270013-bib-0006)] turns to protein design. It is able to jointly reason across sequence, structure, and function. The timeline and sizes of all the ESM models, as well as other information, are shown in Figure[2](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12806033#qub270013-fig-0002) and Table[1](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12806033#qub270013-tbl-0001), respectively.

FIGURE 2

Note that the paper of ESM‐1 was first released in April 2019, but the release of the final ESM‐1b model was in December 2020. For ESM‐2, we show its largest model.

There are many PLMs [[11](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12806033#qub270013-bib-0011), [23](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12806033#qub270013-bib-0023), [24](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12806033#qub270013-bib-0024), [25](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12806033#qub270013-bib-0025), [26](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12806033#qub270013-bib-0026), [27](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12806033#qub270013-bib-0027)], among which ESM models are outstanding. The advantages of ESM models over other PLMs probably lie in the following: (1) currently, they perform best or close to the best in most scenarios [[28](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12806033#qub270013-bib-0028), [29](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12806033#qub270013-bib-0029), [30](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12806033#qub270013-bib-0030), [31](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12806033#qub270013-bib-0031), [32](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12806033#qub270013-bib-0032), [33](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12806033#qub270013-bib-0033)]; (2) they are well developed and form a complete series, with different models that can be utilized in various fields of protein research; and (3) they are widely used as base models in other works [[34](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12806033#qub270013-bib-0034), [35](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12806033#qub270013-bib-0035), [36](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12806033#qub270013-bib-0036)].

## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12806033)TECHNIQUES OF USING ESM

3
The representation learning capabilities of ESM serve as the basis of various downstream tasks. ESM’s output in the form of protein’s representation acts as the conduit between raw sequence data and high‐level features that machine learning (ML) models can exploit. This is referred to as the “pretraining‐fine‐tuning” paradigm in the field of language models. As shown in Figure[3](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12806033#qub270013-fig-0003), there are different techniques of using ESM, as elaborated in the following subsections.

### Direct use

3.1
“Direct use” means that for models that have already performed specific functions and output in a format suitable for a certain task, they can be directly used for various subtasks in that field. ESM‐IF1 is constantly used for fixed‐backbone protein design. ESMFold, as one of the SOTA protein structure prediction methods, is frequently utilized to predict protein structures in various scenes or compared with other structure prediction methods such as AlphaFold2. Several studies [[37](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12806033#qub270013-bib-0037), [38](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12806033#qub270013-bib-0038), [39](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12806033#qub270013-bib-0039)] have shown that ESMFold is much faster than AlphaFold2 with minor accuracy loss. De novo and orphan proteins are the focal experimental subjects of these studies and are also areas where ESMFold excels in prediction [[39](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12806033#qub270013-bib-0039), [40](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12806033#qub270013-bib-0040)].

### Integration with task‐specific models

3.2
In addition to direct applications, there are integrations of ESM with other models. PLMs such as ESM‐1b and ESM‐2 are followed by task‐specific models, and conducting supervised training on the models solves various downstream prediction tasks. In such works, the output from ESM is treated as a protein representation, encapsulating information about a specific modality of the protein, and is utilized in conjunction with various other models to accomplish a wide range of downstream tasks.

ESM can be followed by an multi‐layer perceptron (MLP) layer (i.e., head/classifier/predictor) for various downstream tasks [[41](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12806033#qub270013-bib-0041), [42](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12806033#qub270013-bib-0042)]. This approach is mainly used in benchmarking studies, where, although ESM models show superior performance, they are not the best models in all cases [[28](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12806033#qub270013-bib-0028), [29](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12806033#qub270013-bib-0029), [30](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12806033#qub270013-bib-0030), [31](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12806033#qub270013-bib-0031), [32](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12806033#qub270013-bib-0032), [33](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12806033#qub270013-bib-0033), [43](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12806033#qub270013-bib-0043), [44](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12806033#qub270013-bib-0044)]. Among several well‐known PLMs, ESM and ProtT5 [[24](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12806033#qub270013-bib-0024)] show the best performance in different scenarios and on different metrics (with ProtT5 slightly better than ESM overall) [[29](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12806033#qub270013-bib-0029), [43](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12806033#qub270013-bib-0043), [44](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12806033#qub270013-bib-0044), [45](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12806033#qub270013-bib-0045)], whereas ProteinBERT [[23](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12806033#qub270013-bib-0023)] tends to perform slightly poorer [[28](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12806033#qub270013-bib-0028), [43](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12806033#qub270013-bib-0043)]. For example, in the “MCC per location” results on the Swiss‐Prot [[14](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12806033#qub270013-bib-0014)] cross‐validation dataset in Ref. [[45](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12806033#qub270013-bib-0045)], ESM‐1b reaches the highest score in “extracellular” and “golgi apparatus” tasks, whereas ProtT5 performs the best in all the other tasks. However, due to the lack of interpretability of current models and the different natures of the tasks, researchers are recommended to first test and compare these models before choosing the most appropriate one when using these PLMs in real‐world scenarios.

The output of ESM can also be combined with ML techniques. Here, various ML models are often employed as classifiers [[46](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12806033#qub270013-bib-0046), [47](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12806033#qub270013-bib-0047), [48](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12806033#qub270013-bib-0048), [49](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12806033#qub270013-bib-0049), [50](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12806033#qub270013-bib-0050), [51](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12806033#qub270013-bib-0051), [52](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12806033#qub270013-bib-0052)], regression models [[53](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12806033#qub270013-bib-0053), [54](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12806033#qub270013-bib-0054), [55](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12806033#qub270013-bib-0055)], or visualization tools [[1](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12806033#qub270013-bib-0001), [41](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12806033#qub270013-bib-0041), [56](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12806033#qub270013-bib-0056)]. In addition, ESM models are integrated with deep learning networks. In this context, the representation from ESM serves as an input, and subsequent neural networks play crucial roles in prediction for downstream tasks. Specifically, long short‐term memory network (LSTM) [[57](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12806033#qub270013-bib-0057), [58](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12806033#qub270013-bib-0058)], convolutional neural network (CNN) [[55](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12806033#qub270013-bib-0055), [57](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12806033#qub270013-bib-0057), [58](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12806033#qub270013-bib-0058), [59](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12806033#qub270013-bib-0059)], attention mechanism [[45](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12806033#qub270013-bib-0045), [56](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12806033#qub270013-bib-0056), [60](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12806033#qub270013-bib-0060)], and gated recurrent unit (GRU) [[61](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12806033#qub270013-bib-0061)] are used as predictors of various downstream tasks. NERE [[62](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12806033#qub270013-bib-0062)] and DSMBind [[63](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12806033#qub270013-bib-0063)] both use an equivariant rotation prediction network derived from Euler’s rotation equations, which receives the embeddings of ESM‐2 as input and outputs the protein’s energy function for binding affinity prediction. Another significant work is ESMFlow [[64](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12806033#qub270013-bib-0064)], which combines ESMFold with flow matching [[65](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12806033#qub270013-bib-0065)], a generative modeling approach to learning and sampling protein conformational landscapes.

In short, ESM contains rich prior knowledge about proteins through pretraining, allowing for convenient extraction of high‐quality protein embeddings.

### Fine‐tuning

3.3
The third major category of methods involves fine‐tuning of ESM models. Compared to works in Section[3.2](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12806033#qub270013-sec-0050), some parameters of the model are not frozen in order to explore a larger parameter space and to achieve better performance in downstream tasks.

In addition to simply adding a naive decoder/predictor (such as a fully connected layer or MLP) [[28](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12806033#qub270013-bib-0028), [66](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12806033#qub270013-bib-0066), [67](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12806033#qub270013-bib-0067), [68](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12806033#qub270013-bib-0068), [69](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12806033#qub270013-bib-0069), [70](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12806033#qub270013-bib-0070)], with the development of LLM technology, parameter‐efficient fine‐tuning (PEFT) has become the mainstream fine‐tuning approach because of its computational efficiency [[71](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12806033#qub270013-bib-0071), [72](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12806033#qub270013-bib-0072)], especially for foundation models such as ESM‐2‐650M, which has a large number of parameters. Among PEFT methods on ESM, adapter tuning [[73](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12806033#qub270013-bib-0073), [74](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12806033#qub270013-bib-0074)], prompt tuning [[75](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12806033#qub270013-bib-0075)], and LoRA [[76](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12806033#qub270013-bib-0076)] are among the most commonly used and effective methods [[68](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12806033#qub270013-bib-0068), [77](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12806033#qub270013-bib-0077)]. Adapter tuning means the incorporation of adapter modules with a bottleneck architecture within the Transformer layer of the ESM‐2 model [[77](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12806033#qub270013-bib-0077), [78](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12806033#qub270013-bib-0078)]. Prompt tuning generally means adding some trainable prompt before input embedding [[75](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12806033#qub270013-bib-0075)]. It is used in ESM‐related works to concatenate new information before a raw protein sequence [[79](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12806033#qub270013-bib-0079), [80](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12806033#qub270013-bib-0080)]. For example, Chen et al. [[80](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12806033#qub270013-bib-0080)] employed a novel masking strategy, integrating the target protein sequence with the masked ligand region as input during the fine‐tuning phase. In the generation phase, the model can accept both the target protein sequence and masking labels to facilitate the creation of peptide segments of specified lengths. Low‐rank adaptation (LoRA)[[76](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12806033#qub270013-bib-0076)], by introducing trainable rank decomposition matrices into the Transformer architecture, can be seen as the most widely used fine‐tuning method [[68](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12806033#qub270013-bib-0068), [77](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12806033#qub270013-bib-0077), [81](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12806033#qub270013-bib-0081)]. PEFT‐SP [[77](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12806033#qub270013-bib-0077)] is a comprehensive work comparing conditional random field, adapter tuning, prompt tuning, and LoRA on ESM‐2 for the classification of signal peptide, and it was shown that LoRA performed the best. Other fine‐tuning strategies include FusOn‐pLM [[82](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12806033#qub270013-bib-0082)], which unfreezes the query weights in the last 11 layers of ESM‐2 and incorporates a novel probabilistic masking strategy. AntiFold [[83](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12806033#qub270013-bib-0083)] employs hierarchical learning rate decay, various masking schemes, and adding Gaussian noise to the predicted structures to fine‐tune ESM‐IF1.

### Multimodality

3.4
The embedding from a single ESM model contains information from only one modality, leading to suboptimal performance in downstream tasks that emphasize other modalities. For example, although PLMs such as ESM‐1b and ESM‐2 exhibit certain emergent capabilities after pretraining on vast amounts of unlabeled sequences, which allows them to learn some information beyond the sequences themselves, they lack explicit consideration of structural information [[34](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12806033#qub270013-bib-0034)], and therefore, their embeddings do not perform well in downstream tasks that focus on structural information [[35](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12806033#qub270013-bib-0035)]. Consequently, researchers have drawn upon the idea of information fusion, combining features from different sources, which complies with the concept of multimodality. This integration enables a more comprehensive representation of proteins by fusing information from various modalities, such as sequence and structure, thereby enhancing performance in a wide range of downstream tasks. There are mainly 3 kinds of modality fusion techniques as stated in ESM‐GearNet [[35](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12806033#qub270013-bib-0035)]: (1)Sequence representations are used as residue features in structure encoders; that is, ESM’s embeddings are used as (one of) the inputs or the node features of GNN, which is the most widely used approach to integrating protein sequence features and structure features [[84](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12806033#qub270013-bib-0084), [85](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12806033#qub270013-bib-0085), [86](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12806033#qub270013-bib-0086), [87](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12806033#qub270013-bib-0087), [88](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12806033#qub270013-bib-0088)]; (2) concatenation of sequence and structure representations [[89](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12806033#qub270013-bib-0089), [90](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12806033#qub270013-bib-0090), [91](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12806033#qub270013-bib-0091), [92](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12806033#qub270013-bib-0092)]; (3) sequence and other representations are combined via attention (mainly cross attention) [[93](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12806033#qub270013-bib-0093), [94](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12806033#qub270013-bib-0094)]. On the other hand, ESMFold can be used to provide structural information, and some works use it as input for GNNs. For example, DeepProSite [[95](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12806033#qub270013-bib-0095)] and GPSFun [[96](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12806033#qub270013-bib-0096)] input protein sequences into ESMFold and another PLM to obtain edge features and node features, respectively, thereby constructing a graph, which is subsequently used for learning through GNNs.

In multimodal information fusion, contrastive learning is an efficient strategy, which learns by maximizing the similarity between related samples while minimizing the similarity between unrelated samples [[97](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12806033#qub270013-bib-0097), [98](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12806033#qub270013-bib-0098)]. For example, ConPLex [[99](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12806033#qub270013-bib-0099)] predicts interaction and performs contrastive learning based on the cosine distance between the projection of PLM’s embedding and the drug’s Morgan fingerprint in the latent space. In their contrastive epoch, they minimize the target‐drug distance while maximizing the target‐decoy distance. One of the popular techniques of contrastive learning is CLIP [[100](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12806033#qub270013-bib-0100)], which jointly trains an image encoder and a text encoder to predict the correct pairings of a batch of (image, text) training examples by computing pairwise cosine similarities between the two modalities. CLIP is a widely used approach in biomedical research [[101](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12806033#qub270013-bib-0101)]. In protein science, PepPrCLIP [[102](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12806033#qub270013-bib-0102)] and Cut&CLIP [[103](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12806033#qub270013-bib-0103)] do CLIP on protein encoders and peptide encoders, which receive ESM embeddings as inputs. CSSP [[104](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12806033#qub270013-bib-0104)] is an approach that updates a sequence encoder using a pretrained structure encoder using CLIP.

Another strategy of modality fusion is based on tasks [[81](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12806033#qub270013-bib-0081), [105](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12806033#qub270013-bib-0105), [106](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12806033#qub270013-bib-0106)]. Training on certain auxiliary tasks before downstream prediction helps models learn other types of information. ESM‐S [[105](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12806033#qub270013-bib-0105)] infuses structural information into the pretrained ESM‐2 by continual training through remote homology detection before fine‐tuning on downstream tasks. FSFP [[81](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12806033#qub270013-bib-0081)] builds auxiliary tasks for meta‐learning, meta‐trains PLMs on the auxiliary tasks, and transfers PLMs to the target task.

Purely using embeddings from pretrained models or fine‐tuning the models is still unsatisfactory sometimes. Researchers have tried retraining ESM for performance improvement and modality compression. This requires much computational resources, though. Here, a well‐known method is SaProt [[34](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12806033#qub270013-bib-0034)], which first uses Foldseek [[107](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12806033#qub270013-bib-0107)] to represent local structures as English letters called 3Di, analogous to using 20 letters to represent amino acids, and then combines the 3Di with amino acid letters to form a “structure‐aware” protein sequence as input to ESM‐2. This is an innovative but straightforward way to fuse structural information into a sequence encoder. Other researchers consider injecting a structure encoder block into the ESM architecture [[108](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12806033#qub270013-bib-0108), [109](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12806033#qub270013-bib-0109)] for retraining, an idea similar to adapter tuning mentioned earlier.

### The use of attention map

3.5
Apart from embeddings, attention maps in the Transformers in ESM are also a popular feature in various downstream works. In essence, attention maps are cosine similarities between residues, capturing the correlation between different positions in a protein sequence.

An attention map can be directly used to predict the contact map because of their similar format [[110](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12806033#qub270013-bib-0110), [111](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12806033#qub270013-bib-0111)]. Additionally, ESM‐MSA’s attention map contains information of MSAs and is often utilized as an extra feature for predicting residue contacts [[112](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12806033#qub270013-bib-0112)]. Furthermore, paired MSAs are used for predicting residue–residue contacts in protein complexes [[113](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12806033#qub270013-bib-0113), [114](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12806033#qub270013-bib-0114)].

### Used for evaluation and validation

3.6
ESM is also used for evaluation or validation within the workflows of various methods. There are two main categories here. Embeddings from models such as ESM‐1b, ESM‐1v, ESM‐MSA‐1b, and ESM‐2 are exploited to assist directed evolution [[115](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12806033#qub270013-bib-0115), [116](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12806033#qub270013-bib-0116)]. For example, Hu et al. [[117](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12806033#qub270013-bib-0117)] combined ESM‐1v’s embedding with their Bayesian optimization‐guided evolutionary algorithms and robotic experiments. ESM’s embeddings can also be used in the recycling of inverse folding as in CarbonDesign [[118](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12806033#qub270013-bib-0118)]. Another group uses ESMFold’s output for evaluation of protein structure, both in structure prediction tasks [[119](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12806033#qub270013-bib-0119)] and validation of mutation [[120](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12806033#qub270013-bib-0120)], where ESMFold generates structures for the proposed protein sequence with mutations in each iteration, which are used to calculate the energy function to guide the optimization process through simulated annealing.

As previously noted, the general language models underlying the ESM family are trained using MLM, making their outputs the probabilities of each amino acid at every position in the sequence. Consequently, leveraging these probability scores is a natural approach and has been extensively applied in downstream tasks, particularly in mutation effect prediction and sequence optimization, where labels can be predicted by position scores under many circumstances [[70](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12806033#qub270013-bib-0070)]. Apart from calculating the log‐likelihood ratio scores for mutation effect prediction [[121](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12806033#qub270013-bib-0121), [122](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12806033#qub270013-bib-0122)], probability distribution is also a source of features in the whole pipeline [[123](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12806033#qub270013-bib-0123), [124](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12806033#qub270013-bib-0124)] or the basis of evaluation [[55](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12806033#qub270013-bib-0055)]. Beyond individual position scores, researchers frequently compute sequence scores, which are functions of position scores in the sequence, mostly for evaluation [[54](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12806033#qub270013-bib-0054), [125](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12806033#qub270013-bib-0125), [126](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12806033#qub270013-bib-0126)]. ESM‐IF1 is frequently utilized for both scoring mutated sequences [[92](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12806033#qub270013-bib-0092), [127](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12806033#qub270013-bib-0127)] and computing self‐consistency perplexity to evaluate the generated protein structures [[128](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12806033#qub270013-bib-0128)]. Similarly, USCF ChimeraX [[38](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12806033#qub270013-bib-0038)], a widely used structure visualization tool, has recently started to employ ESMFold’s predicted local distance difference test score and predicted aligned error [[17](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12806033#qub270013-bib-0017)] to assess the accuracy of predicted structures.

## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12806033)DOWNSTREAM BIOLOGICAL APPLICATIONS

4
The ESM models, through large‐scale pretraining, capture the implicit structural and evolutionary information of protein sequences, thereby playing a role in multiple downstream tasks. These models are capable of implicitly learning how protein sequences determine their structures and functions without relying on explicit homology information. ESM models utilize techniques such as self‐attention mechanisms, contrastive loss functions, and Transformer architectures to identify key features of protein sequences, including secondary structures and long‐range interactions. They learn the characteristics of proteins by predicting masked amino acids and are able to enhance the predictive accuracy of specific tasks. Additionally, ESM models can be used for additional tasks, such as recommending evolutionarily plausible mutations, predicting the impact of mutations, and generating task‐specific molecular fingerprints in conjunction with graph neural networks. Although most papers we surveyed do not explain the specific working mechanisms of ESM models at the algorithmic level, they generally demonstrate the effectiveness and potential of ESM models in protein‐related tasks.

The availability of diverse datasets has further expanded the border of what is achievable with ESM. It can be seen that ESM models can perform many tasks provided a solid dataset exists. By surveying the papers we have collected, we find that ESM models have widespread applications in most popular fields of protein research.

args.summary:
A survey paper published in Quantitative Biology (2025, Vol. 14, e70013) titled "A survey of downstream applications of evolutionary scale modeling protein language models," authored by Qingyu Yang, Jiale Yu, and Jie Zheng from ShanghaiTech University and the Shanghai Engineering Research Center of Intelligent Vision and Imaging. The paper (PMCID: PMC12806033, PMID: 41676321) reviews the ESM (evolutionary scale modeling) series of protein language models (PLMs) and their downstream applications in protein science and engineering.

**ESM Model Series Overview:**
- ESM-1b: First foundational BERT-style Transformer PLM, trained via masked language modeling (MLM) on 250 million protein sequences from UniParc (43M–670M parameters)
- ESM-MSA-1b (MSA Transformer): Uses tied row/united column attention on multiple sequence alignments for structure inference (100M parameters)
- ESM-1v: Specialized for variant effect prediction (650M parameters)
- ESM-IF1 (GVP-Transformer): Combines Transformer with GVP-GNN for inverse folding/fixed-backbone design (124M parameters)
- ESM-2: SOTA general-purpose PLM, one of the most widely used foundation models in protein science (8M–15B parameters)
- ESMFold: End-to-end single-sequence 3D structure predictor, comparable to AlphaFold2 in some key scenarios, significantly faster (3.69B parameters)
- ESM3: Protein design model reasoning across sequence, structure, and function (1.4B–98B parameters)

**Advantages of ESM over other PLMs:** best or near-best performance in most scenarios; well-developed complete series covering various protein research fields; widely used as base models in other works.

**Techniques of Using ESM (5 categories):**
1. **Direct use**: ESM-IF1 for fixed-backbone design, ESMFold for structure prediction (much faster than AlphaFold2 with minor accuracy loss, excels at de novo/orphan proteins)
2. **Integration with task-specific models**: ESM embeddings combined with MLP, ML classifiers, regression models, LSTM, CNN, attention, GRU; e.g., NERE, DSMBind (binding affinity), ESMFlow (flow matching for conformational sampling)
3. **Fine-tuning**: Both full fine-tuning and parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) including adapter tuning, prompt tuning, and LoRA (most widely used; PEFT-SP showed LoRA best for signal peptide classification); also FusOn-pLM and AntiFold
4. **Multimodality**: Fusing sequence and structure information via three main approaches (ESM embeddings as GNN node features; concatenation of representations; cross-attention); contrastive learning (e.g., ConPLex, CLIP-based methods like PepPrCLIP, Cut&CLIP, CSSP); structure-aware retraining (e.g., SaProt using Foldseek's 3Di tokens); continual training (ESM-S)
5. **Attention maps and evaluation**: Attention maps used for contact map prediction; ESM used for directed evolution assistance, mutation validation, structure evaluation (e.g., self-consistency perplexity with ESM-IF1, ESMFold pLDDT/pAE scores in UCSF ChimeraX)

**Key Comparative Findings:** Among well-known PLMs, ESM and ProtT5 show best performance in different scenarios (ProtT5 slightly better overall); ESM-1b highest for "extracellular" and "golgi apparatus" localization tasks; ProteinBERT performs slightly poorer.

**Downstream Biological Applications:** ESM models capture implicit structural/evolutionary information and apply to structure prediction (fold, secondary structure via NetSurfP-3.0, contact maps, 3D structure via OmegaFold, protein complexes via Seq2Symm) and function prediction (EC/GO via SaProt and ESM-GearNet, text-defined function via ProtST, functional annotation via NetGO 3.0, localization via ProtGPS, solubility via NetSolP, homology detection via PLMSearch).

The survey analyzed approximately 100 representative papers (each cited at least five times) from papers citing at least one of the six original ESM publications.

# Simulating 500 million years of evolution with a language model
## ML for protein engineering seminar series
6910 subscribers
192 likes

### Description
7308 views
Posted: 17 Sep 2024
ESM3: Simulating 500 million years of evolution with a language model

Tuesday July 23rd, 4-5pm EST | Roshan Rao, PhD (EvoScale)

Abstract: More than three billion years of evolution have produced an image of biology encoded into the space of natural proteins. Here we show that language models trained on tokens generated by evolution can act as evolutionary simulators to generate functional proteins that are far away from known proteins. We present ESM3, a frontier multimodal generative language model that reasons over the sequence, structure, and function of proteins. ESM3 can follow complex prompts combining its modalities and is highly responsive to biological alignment. We have prompted ESM3 to generate fluorescent proteins with a chain of thought. Among the generations that we synthesized, we found a bright fluorescent protein at far distance (58% identity) from known fluorescent proteins. Similarly distant natural fluorescent proteins are separated by over five hundred million years of evolution.

Preprint: https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2024.07.01.600583v1

args.summary:
This is a seminar presentation by Roshan Rao, PhD, of the company EvoScale, given as part of the "ML for protein engineering seminar series" (posted 17 Sep 2024, ~7308 views). The talk presents ESM3, a frontier multimodal generative language model for proteins that can reason over sequence, structure, and function. The key claims: ESM3 can act as an evolutionary simulator, generating functional proteins far from known proteins. The team prompted ESM3 to design fluorescent proteins and found a bright fluorescent protein at 58% sequence identity from known fluorescent proteins—a distance comparable to over 500 million years of natural evolution.

Key technical details:
- Architecture: A simple Transformer with tokenized input/output tracks for sequence, structure, and function, plus a geometric attention mechanism that encodes 3D coordinates in an SE(3)-invariant and efficient way. Structure is tokenized with a new VQ-VAE (each residue token represents its 16 nearest 3D neighbors) with sub-angstrom RMSD reconstruction.
- Training: Three models trained at 1.4B, 7.7B, and 98.5B parameters. Deeper (rather than wider) architectures were found to be better for proteins. Training used large amounts of metagenomic and synthetic data (found to improve performance once model scale crossed a threshold), FP8 precision, sharding over 1000+ GPUs, and various stability techniques (layer norm on queries/keys, warmup, FP32 for key ops). Optimal masking rate increased with scale (15% at 650M params, 30% at 7B).
- Alignment (DPO fine-tuning): Models are aligned by scoring generated sequences computationally (constraint site RMSD, predicted TM score) and fine-tuning with DPO; larger models respond more strongly to alignment, improving prompt-following fidelity, pTM, and generation diversity.
- Wet lab validation with GFP: ESM3 was prompted with the structure/key chromophore, generating sequences that were synthesized. After one plate experiment and diversification/refinement, a fluorescent protein with high activity and ~58% identity to wild-type GFP was obtained, including mutations in core/alpha-helix positions.

Other points covered: data valuation (PDB is highest value; sequence data scales linearly), use of temporal holdouts and MMS-seq purging to avoid leakage, removal of viruses from the open model for biosafety (internal models retain them for academic partnerships), and future directions (genomic context, protein-ligand interactions, text annotations).

[![](https://cdn.prod.website-files.com/6606dc3fd5f6645318003df4/6678474d9bc697d13fed8127_ES_Logo_White_5.png)![](https://cdn.prod.website-files.com/6606dc3fd5f6645318003df4/6678476dc198b5a75b8c8873_ES_Logo_Black_5.png)](/)[Start working with ESM

June 25, 2024

//

Announcement

# ESM3: Simulating 500 million years of evolution with a language model

[Preview our paper](https://doi.org/10.1101/2024.07.01.600583)

**Update January 2025:**We're thrilled to announce the publication of [ESM3 in Science Magazine](https://www.science.org/doi/10.1126/science.ads0018). We’re opening our API for biological intelligence, now in public beta, allowing scientists in academia and industry a free limited time preview of the capabilities of some of our models through [Forge](https://forge.evolutionaryscale.ai/sign-up).

‍

## EvolutionaryScale

More than 3.5 billion years ago, life on Earth emerged from chemical reactions. Nature invented RNA, proteins, and DNA, the core molecules of life, and created the ribosome, a molecular factory that builds proteins from instructions in the genome.

Proteins are wondrous dynamic molecules with incredible functions—from molecular engines that power motion, to photosynthetic machines that capture light and convert it to energy, scaffolding that builds the internal skeletons of cells, complex sensors that interact with the environment, and information processing systems that run the programs and operating system of life. Proteins underlie disease and health, and many life-saving medicines are proteins.

Biology is the most advanced technology that has ever been created, far beyond anything that people have engineered. The ribosome is programmable—it takes the codes of proteins in the form of RNA and builds them up from scratch—fabrication at the atomic scale. Every cell in every organism on earth has thousands to millions of these molecular factories. But even the most sophisticated computational tools created to date barely scratch the surface: biology is written in a language we don’t yet understand.

If we could learn to read and write in the code of life it would make biology programmable. Trial and error would be replaced by logic, and painstaking experiments by simulation.

As we introduce ourselves as a new company, we’re excited to present ESM3—a frontier language model for the life sciences that advances our ability to program and create with the code of life. ESM3 takes a step towards the future where AI is a tool to engineer biology from first principles in the same way we engineer structures, machines and microchips, and write computer programs.

In a [new preprint,](https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2024.07.01.600583) we describe the generation of a new green fluorescent protein (GFP). Fluorescent proteins are responsible for the glowing colors of jellyfish and corals, and are important tools in modern biotechnology. esmGFP, our new protein, has a sequence that is only 58% similar to the closest known fluorescent protein. From the rate of diversification of GFPs found in nature, we estimate that this generation of a new fluorescent protein is equivalent to simulating over 500 million years of evolution.

The power and potential of these new technologies call for a commitment to principles of responsible development, including transparency and accountability from the start. To that end, drawing on our experience as scientists and researchers, we have crafted a responsible development framework that will guide our progress.

‍

## ESM3: A frontier language model for biology

Today we are sharing ESM3, the first generative model for biology that simultaneously reasons over the sequence, structure, and function of proteins.

ESM3 is trained across the natural diversity of the Earth—billions of proteins, from the Amazon rainforest, to the depths of the oceans, extreme environments like hydrothermal vents, and the microbes in a handful of soil.

Trained on one of the highest throughput GPU clusters in the world today, ESM3 is a frontier generative model for biology created at the leading edge of parameters, computational power, and data. We believe that ESM3 is the most compute ever applied to training a biological model, trained with over 1x1024 FLOPS and 98B parameters.

Across AI we see the power of scaling. As model scale increases in parameters, data, and compute, larger models gain new emergent capabilities that smaller models lack. In many different domains generalist models trained on diverse data are outperforming specialist models. The incredible pace of new AI advances is being driven by increasingly large models, increasingly large datasets, and increasing computational power.

The same patterns hold true in biology. In research over the last five years, the ESM team has explored scaling in biology. We find that as language models scale they develop an understanding of the underlying principles of biology, and discover biological structure and function.

ESM3 represents a milestone model in the ESM family—the first created by our team at EvolutionaryScale, an order of magnitude larger than our previous model ESM2, and natively multimodal and generative.

***Reasoning over the sequence, structure, and function of proteins***. Language models operate over discrete units, or tokens. To create one that can reason over three of the fundamental biological properties of proteins—sequence, structure, and function—we had to transform three dimensional structure and function into discrete alphabets, and construct a way to write every three dimensional structure as a sequence of letters. This allows ESM3 to be trained at scale, unlocking emergent generative capabilities. ESM3’s vocabulary bridges sequence, structure, and function all within the same language model.

ESM3 is trained with a simple objective. For each protein, its sequence, structure, and function are extracted, tokenized, and partially masked. ESM3’s task is to predict the masked positions using the *masked language modeling* objective inspired by natural language processing models. In order to accomplish this task, ESM3 must learn a deep understanding of the connection between sequence, structure, and function across evolutionary-scale data. When scaled across billions of proteins and billions of parameters, ESM3 learns to simulate evolution.

Given the limited volume of experimentally determined structure and function annotations, we augment ESM3’s multimodal training dataset with hundreds of millions of synthetic data points, including predicted structures and functions for diverse sequences.

![](https://cdn.prod.website-files.com/6606dc3fd5f6645318003e20/674f9300d43c2d67f061b281_667a5a5fdb0a455c3ef22520_Figure%25201%2520(5).png)

*ESM3 is a multi-track transformer that jointly reasons over protein sequence, structure, and function.*

***Programming biology.*** ESM3 is a generative model, and makes biology programmable. It can follow prompts to generate new proteins. Scientists can interact with ESM3, guiding it to create for a myriad of applications such as for medicine, biology research, and clean energy.

Proteins can be generated by starting with a fully masked set of tokens and iteratively unmasking until all positions are filled. Because sequence, structure, and function are all masked and predicted during training, ESM3 can generate in all three modalities. This generation process can also be guided by any combination of partial or full specification of sequence, structure, and function.

ESM3’s multimodal reasoning power enables scientists to generate new proteins with an unprecedented degree of control. For example, the model can be prompted to combine structure, sequence, and function to propose a potential scaffold for the active site of PETase, an enzyme that degrades polyethylene terephthalate (PET), a target of interest to protein engineers for breaking down plastic waste.

*ESM3 designs a scaffold for the PETase active site through multimodal prompting with sequence, structure, and function. We prompt ESM3 with the active site structure and amino acids, as well as a function keyword prompt for α/β hydrolase, a fold characteristic of hydrolytic enzymes.*

‍

‍

***Emergence of capabilities with scale***. ESM3’s ability to solve challenging protein design tasks emerges with scale. One such task, atomic coordination, is designing a protein from prompts that specify the atomic positions of amino acids that are distant in the sequence but close in the structure. This measures the ability of the model to achieve atomic level accuracy in structure generation, which is critical for designing functional proteins. ESM3’s ability to solve these tasks improves with scale, i.e., ESM3 solves harder generative problems as a function of scale.

ESM3 further improves with feedback using alignment methods similar to Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF) applied in LLMs. Rather than receiving feedback from humans, ESM3 can self-improve, providing feedback on the quality of its own generations.  Feedback from laboratory experiments or existing experimental data could also be applied to align ESM3’s generations with biological success.

![](https://cdn.prod.website-files.com/6606dc3fd5f6645318003e20/674f9301d43c2d67f061b2ab_667a598828e02ec91e954ef7_DPO_finetuned_figure_for_blog%2520(8).png)

*ESM3 models evaluated on the task of generating proteins that satisfy atomic coordination prompts. ESM3 solves harder generative problems as a function of scale, and the capabilities of larger models become more apparent after alignment.*

‍

## Simulating 500 million years of evolution

Green fluorescent protein, commonly known as GFP, and its family of fluorescent proteins are some of the most beautiful proteins in nature. They occur in just a few branches of the tree of life. The discovery of GFP led to the award of a Nobel Prize and has become one of the most widely used tools in biology, allowing scientists to see proteins within cells.

GFP contains a fluorescent chromophore—a molecular component that absorbs a single photon of one color at a short wavelength, captures some of its energy, and releases the rest as a new photon with a different color and longer wavelength. The natural GFP absorbs blue light and emits green light.

GFP is a protein that transforms itself—its structure is an eleven stranded barrel with a helix that threads through its center—and after GFP folds, a spontaneous reaction occurs. At the center of the protein, the atoms that form the protein chain reform into a new configuration creating a fluorescent chromophore. This mechanism is unique. No other known protein spontaneously forms a fluorescent chromophore out of its own structure, suggesting that producing fluorescence is hard even for nature.

Scientists have discovered many variants of GFP in nature, and created variants of those natural proteins in the lab. The very first artificial variants were found by making a handful of mutations that increased brightness or changed color. With more recent laboratory and machine learning techniques it has been possible to extend this search to find more distant variants that differ by up to even 20% of the sequence. But still the bulk of variation of functional GFPs have come not from protein engineering but by prospecting the natural world.

The process of evolution that gives rise to new fluorescent proteins takes epochs of time—the story of this protein family reaches back into depths of natural history and geologic time where somewhere in the distant past nature invented the first fluorescent protein. Natural fluorescent proteins have diverged over 100s of millions of years from ancestral sequences in deep history to become the proteins they are today.

Prompted with the structure of a few residues in the core of natural GFP, ESM3 reasoned in a chain-of-thought to generate candidates of new GFPs. Generating one by pure chance from among an astronomical number of sequences and structures (20229 x 4096229 to be precise—more possibilities than the number of atoms in the visible universe) would be virtually impossible. We tested 96 generations in a first experiment, and found a number of proteins that fluoresce, including one that was far from any protein in nature. This protein, located in well B8 of our experiment plate, was 50x less bright than natural GFPs and its chromophore matured over the course of a week, instead of in under a day, but it presented a signal of function in an unexplored portion of sequence space. Continuing the chain-of-thought starting from the sequence of B8, we generated another set of 96 proteins. We tested them and found several proteins that have similar brightness to natural GFPs, including the brightest one in well C10 which we call esmGFP. esmGFP differs by 96 mutations (out of 229 amino acids, 58% of the sequence is similar) to the closest fluorescent protein found in nature.

![](https://cdn.prod.website-files.com/6606dc3fd5f6645318003e20/674f9300d43c2d67f061b275_667a5baa7410de72ca5af083_experiments.png)

*In a sequence of two experiments ESM3 generates B8, a dim GFP that is distant from all GFPs known in nature. Starting from B8, ESM3 generates esmGFP, a distant GFP with brightness similar to other natural GFPs.*

Unlike nature, protein language models do not explicitly work within evolutionary constraints. But in order for ESM3 to solve its training task of predicting the next masked token the model must learn how evolution moves through the space of potential proteins. In this sense, ESM3 can be thought of as an evolutionary simulator. A traditional evolutionary analysis of the ancestry of esmGFP is paradoxical as the protein was created outside natural processes, but still we can draw insight from the tools of evolutionary biology on the amount of time it would take for a protein to diverge from its closest sequence neighbor through natural evolution. We find naturally occuring GFPs with similar levels of sequence identity are separated by hundreds of millions of years of evolution. Using an analysis similar to one might perform on a new protein found in the natural world, we estimate that esmGFP represents an equivalent of over 500 million years of natural evolution performed by an evolutionary simulator.

![](https://cdn.prod.website-files.com/6606dc3fd5f6645318003e20/674f9301d43c2d67f061b290_667a5bb780d0ada7dc37d1c0_image%2520(1).png)

*A rendering of esmGFP, a new green fluorescent protein generated by ESM3 that is distant from other fluorescent proteins found in nature.*

‍

## Responsible development

EvolutionaryScale is a public benefit company. Our mission is to develop artificial intelligence to understand biology for the benefit of human health and society, through partnership with the scientific community, and open, safe, and responsible research.

Molecular biology has already undergone one inflection point at the dawn of the recombinant DNA era in the 1970s, when scientists developed the technology of genetic engineering. The outcome of that technological inflection was a revolution in our understanding of genetics, decoding the human genome, and groundbreaking new medicines.

To guide their work during a time of rapid technological development, the scientific community developed a set of principles and recommendations at the Asilomar Conference in 1975. These principles have led to robust frameworks that help to manage risk are in use by nucleotide synthesis companies, molecular biology vendors, and regulators.

As we now enter an era where we can design and program novel biology, we look towards the history of our field as well as [new principles and recommendations](https://responsiblebiodesign.ai) being proposed by the growing community of researchers exploring the frontiers of biological design.

With these inspirations, we have created a Responsible Development Framework to guide our work towards our mission with transparency and clarity.

The core tenets of our framework are

* We will communicate the benefits and risks of our research
* We will proactively and rigorously evaluate the risk of our models before public deployment
* We will adopt risk mitigation strategies and precautionary guardrails
* We will work with stakeholders in government, policy, and civil society to keep them informed

‍

## Open Model

Since inception the ESM project has committed to open science with code and model releases, and our commitment continues. We believe that sharing research and code accelerates progress and contributes to understanding and reducing risk, ultimately maximizing positive impact for the world.

It has been incredible to see the imaginative and impactful applications of ESM models across research and industry. For example, Hie et al. [used ESM-1v and ESM-1b to evolve antibodies](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41587-023-01763-2), improving therapeutically relevant characteristics such as binding affinity, thermostability, and viral neutralization. BioNTech and InstaDeep [fine-tuned an ESM language model on COVID spike proteins to detect variants that would pose a higher risk to public health](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0010482523000835?via%3Dihub#appsec1), successfully flagging all 16 variants of concern before they were designated by the WHO. Brandes et al. [used ESM-1b to predict the clinical effects of mutations](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41588-023-01465-0), and is currently the most powerful method for this important task. Marsiglia et al. [used ESM-1v to engineer novel anti-CRISPR protein](https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2023.12.13.571376v1) variants that maintain on-target editing functionality while reducing off-target side effects. Shanker et al. used [ESM-IF1 to guide evolution of diverse proteins](https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2023.12.19.572475v2.full.pdf), including lab-validated high-potency antibodies against SARS-CoV-2. Yu et al. fine-tuned [ESM-1b to predict function for enzymes](https://www.science.org/doi/10.1126/science.adf2465), including rare and understudied enzymes, and experimentally validated the predictions. Rosen et al. used ESM2 embeddings to [build representations of genes in a single-cell foundation model](https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2023.11.28.568918v1). Høie et al. [fine-tuned ESM-IF1 on antibody structures to achieve state-of-the-art performance in sequence recovery across CDR regions](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2405.03370), to design antibodies with high binding affinity. This is just a small fraction of the amazing work building on the ESM platform!

We will continue to develop and release open models to accelerate research and empower the scientific community. This starts with [releasing the weights and code](https://github.com/evolutionaryscale/esm) for an ESM3 1.4B open model, to allow scientists and developers to build on the ideas and architecture of ESM3. We’re excited to see what you create!

‍

## Where We Are Headed

We believe in a future where AI can help us to understand the complex systems of life at the most basic level, make new scientific discoveries that change our understanding of biology, help us to find cures to disease, and build a more sustainable world.

ESM3 is a tool for scientists. Our API and open model allow scientists to explore the frontiers of protein design and synthetic biology, and invent new solutions for some of the most important problems facing our world.

If you are working on these kinds of problems we would love to hear about how you think ESM3 can help and will be prioritizing beta [access to the API](https://forge.evolutionaryscale.ai) based on potential to expand the frontiers of scientific knowledge and create new tools that can benefit the world.

We are also developing specialized versions of ESM3 to unlock applications at the frontier of drug design. The same capabilities that can be used to design one of the most complex and beautiful proteins in nature will help scientists to create new medicines.

ESM3 is only the first step on our roadmap for programming biology. We think the future will be increasingly multimodal models that learn from biological data and integrate across the scales of life from individual molecules to cells, which will contribute to humanity’s ability to understand and program biology to build a better world.

‍

‍

Table of Contents
