[drug response](/search?q=drug+response); [single-cell RNA sequencing](/search?q=single-cell+RNA+sequencing); [bulk RNA sequencing](/search?q=bulk+RNA+sequencing); [deep learning](/search?q=deep+learning); [interpretability](/search?q=interpretability)

## 1. Introduction

Chemotherapy remains one of the core therapeutic strategies in modern medicine and is widely applied across a range of diseases, from common infections to complex conditions. Among these, cancer is one of the most prominent diseases for which chemotherapy plays a central role in treatment. Although chemotherapy is widely regarded as an effective approach for cancer management and often produces substantial initial responses, therapeutic failure frequently occurs due to tumor cell adaptation to pharmacological agents, ultimately leading to the development of drug resistance [[1](#B1-ijms-26-04365),[2](#B2-ijms-26-04365)]. The mechanisms of chemoresistance are complex, involving tumor cell heterogeneity, interactions within the tumor microenvironment, and dysregulation of signaling pathways [[3](#B3-ijms-26-04365),[4](#B4-ijms-26-04365),[5](#B5-ijms-26-04365),[6](#B6-ijms-26-04365)]. For instance, activation of the NF-κB, STAT3, and PI3K pathways has been widely implicated in causing chemoresistance during cancer therapy [[7](#B7-ijms-26-04365),[8](#B8-ijms-26-04365),[9](#B9-ijms-26-04365)]. Consequently, elucidating the molecular basis of drug resistance holds critical importance for developing novel anticancer therapeutics and optimizing clinical treatment strategies [[10](#B10-ijms-26-04365),[11](#B11-ijms-26-04365)]. However, research on drug response faces challenges. Investigating the biological mechanisms of drug responses at the molecular and cellular levels is inherently difficult. Drug resistance is highly complex and varies significantly across individuals, tissue types, and drugs. Furthermore, the limited availability to obtain samples from clinical trials constrains drug response studies [[12](#B12-ijms-26-04365),[13](#B13-ijms-26-04365),[14](#B14-ijms-26-04365)].

To address these issues, early computational approaches incorporated genomic features, such as somatic mutations and copy number variations, along with pharmacochemical properties like molecular fingerprints, to develop machine learning (ML) models, including random forests (RFs) and shallow neural networks. While these models achieved promising results, they often struggled with high-dimensional omics data and lacked interpretability, limiting their ability to reveal the biological basis of predictions [[15](#B15-ijms-26-04365)].

Recent advances in deep learning (DL) and high-throughput screening technologies have catalyzed developments in drug response prediction [[16](#B16-ijms-26-04365)]. DL models can automatically extract complex features from large-scale biological datasets, enabling more accurate prediction. The increasing availability of data resources has further driven the systematic integration of DL into pharmacogenomic modeling, resulting in a shift from simplistic statistical frameworks to sophisticated deep learning architectures.

MOLI [[17](#B17-ijms-26-04365)] utilized independent encoders to separately extract features from somatic mutations, copy number variations, and gene expression profiles, which were subsequently concatenated and input into a neural network for drug response prediction. DeepDRK [[18](#B18-ijms-26-04365)] employed kernel functions to extract features from cellular omics and drug data, which are fused as inputs. CODE-AE-ADV [[19](#B19-ijms-26-04365)] adopted a deconfounding adversarial autoencoder to learn robust latent representations that align in vitro with in vivo data. In addition to performance improvements, several DL models aim to enhance interpretability. DrugCell [[20](#B20-ijms-26-04365)] integrated a visible neural network (VNN), aligning model architectures with tumor cellular organizations to simulate therapeutic mechanisms. ParsVNN [[21](#B21-ijms-26-04365)] enhanced performance and interpretability through pruning VNN, streamlining biological hierarchies to focus on critical features. Moreover, advanced neural architectures such as convolutional neural networks, graph neural networks, and transformer-based models have also been explored for modeling cellular omics and drug response, yielding promising results [[22](#B22-ijms-26-04365),[23](#B23-ijms-26-04365),[24](#B24-ijms-26-04365)].

Meanwhile, single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) has emerged as a transformative approach for dissecting tumor heterogeneity and elucidating mechanisms of drug response [[25](#B25-ijms-26-04365)]. Compared with bulk RNA sequencing (bulk RNA-seq), scRNA-seq enables the identification of differences among distinct cellular subpopulations and capture subtle molecular changes, making it more sensitive for predicting drug responses [[25](#B25-ijms-26-04365),[26](#B26-ijms-26-04365)]. As a result, it can provide a more precise understanding of the mechanisms driving drug responses. Despite these advantages, the majority of drug response models still rely on bulk RNA-seq data, such as Genomics of Drug Sensitivity in Cancer (GDSC) [[27](#B27-ijms-26-04365)] and L1000 [[28](#B28-ijms-26-04365)]. Although several scRNA-seq datasets, such as MIX-seq [[29](#B29-ijms-26-04365)] and sci-Plex [[30](#B30-ijms-26-04365)], have recently been introduced, systematic collection and analysis of scRNA-seq drug response data remain limited. This is largely due to the relatively high cost of scRNA-seq experiments, as well as the time-consuming and labor-intensive process of manual data annotation [[31](#B31-ijms-26-04365),[32](#B32-ijms-26-04365)]. The limited data hinders accurate prediction and in-depth understanding of mechanisms driving drug response. In contrast, large-scale bulk RNA-seq drug response datasets are already available. Leveraging these abundant datasets to train DL models, which is a data-driven method, and applying transfer learning to adapt the models to single-cell RNA-seq data for accurate prediction and mechanistic investigation, offers a promising strategy to partially overcome the current limitations caused by the scarcity of high-quality scRNA-seq drug response data.

This study systematically processed scRNA-seq drug response data and proposed a transfer learning–based framework to align drug response representations between bulk RNA-seq and scRNA-seq data ([Figure 1](#fig_body_display_ijms-26-04365-f001)). Specifically, we leveraged the GDSC dataset, which is a bulk RNA-seq dataset, to train a predictive model for scRNA-seq drug response. This model employed a shared encoder to project both data into a unified latent space, and the projected embeddings were utilized to predict drug responses. A sparse decoder guided by prior biological knowledge was integrated to align features with predefined biological pathways for enhancing performance and interpretability. The proposed model was evaluated across five curated scRNA-seq drug response datasets and demonstrated superior predictive performance compared to ML models. Meanwhile, we applied integrated gradients (IG) to interpret the relationship between pathways and drug response predictions. Also, we validated interpretability based on the biological information introduced via the sparse decoder. This study contributes to expanding the utility of scRNA-seq in drug response prediction and the application of DL techniques in drug response prediction.

## 2. Results

### 2.1. Data Analysis and Clustering Analysis

Details of data collection and labeling were described in [Figure 1](#fig_body_display_ijms-26-04365-f001)a. The five collected scRNA-seq datasets involved three cancers, including oral squamous cell carcinoma (GSE117872), melanoma (GSE108394), and breast cancer (GSE131984, GSE156246\_BT474, and GSE156246\_HCC1419). These datasets involved four drugs (cisplatin, paclitaxel, PLX-4720, and lapatinib) including two chemotherapeutic agents and two targeted therapies, as shown in [Table 1](#table_body_display_ijms-26-04365-t001). More datasets that do not have corresponding entries in the GDSC database can be found in [Supplementary Material S1](#app1-ijms-26-04365).

**Table 1.**
Summary of scRNA-seq drug response datasets and corresponding data in GDSC.

![](https://pub.mdpi-res.com/img/table.png)

We retrieved corresponding drug response data for these four drugs from the GDSC database (bulk RNA-seq) to construct training sets for predicting drug response. In the drug response dataset of GDSC, the number of cell lines tested for each drug varies, typically ranging from 735 to 903. Datasets include half maximal inhibitory concentration (IC50) (lower values indicate stronger drug efficacy and higher sensitivity) and the area under the dose–response curve (AUC) (lower values indicate higher drug sensitivity). In this study, we used the AUC value as the indicator of drug response. It was employed to define positive and negative samples in the training sets and to train four corresponding binary classifiers of drug response for four drugs, respectively.

We then performed clustering analysis on the collected five collected scRNA-seq drug response datasets with AttentionAE-sc [[33](#B33-ijms-26-04365)], which is our previously proposed method. The clustering results were used to distinguish drug-sensitive and drug-resistant cell subpopulations, serving as a basis for data filtering. To quantitatively evaluate the clustering performance, we computed the average silhouette width (ASW) as an internal validation metric. A higher ASW score indicates better clustering quality, characterized by greater separation between clusters and higher compactness within clusters. Additionally, we visualized the clustering results via Uniform Manifold Approximation and Projection (UMAP).

The results are shown in [Figure 2](#fig_body_display_ijms-26-04365-f002). Across all datasets, the model achieved ASW scores above 0.75. Specifically, four datasets had ASW scores greater than 0.8, reflecting well-separated and internally coherent clusters. These results suggest that the model effectively captures meaningful transcriptional differences between drug-sensitive and drug-resistant subpopulations. This provides a strong foundation for subsequent drug response labeling and downstream prediction tasks. A comparison with other clustering methods is provided in [Supplementary Material S2](#app1-ijms-26-04365).

### 2.2. Performance Evaluation

To evaluate the performance of our model on scRNA-deq test sets, we compared it with several widely used ML algorithms. These included logistic regression (LR), support vector machine (SVM), decision tree (DT), RF, and gradient boosting (GB) and eXtreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost.)

As shown in [Figure 3](#fig_body_display_ijms-26-04365-f003), our model achieved the best performance across the four scRNA-seq drug response prediction tasks. It reached an average accuracy of 0.668 and an average F1 score of 0.676, outperformed LR (0.463 and 0.550), SVM (0.604 and 0.302), DT (0.519 and 0.322), RF (0.448 and 0.335), GB (0.578 and 0.448), and XGBoost (0.491 and 0.236). Although the SVM model slightly outperformed our method in predicting drug response for Cisplatin, the performance gap was marginal (accuracy of 0.730 vs. 0.726, F1 score of 0.844 vs. 0.841) and our model outperformed all other ML models on predicting drug response for Cisplatin. Moreover, our model achieved superior results on the remaining three drugs compared to all ML models. Notably, five ML models yielded an F1 score of 0 in at least one task, particularly on the Lapatinib\_BT474 and Paclitaxel datasets. In contrast, our model maintained consistently high performance across all tasks. This further demonstrates the robustness of our model, especially in handling complex scRNA-seq data and imbalanced datasets.

### 2.3. Impact of Key Hyperparameters on Model Performance

To optimize the predictive performance of our model, we tuned several key hyperparameters that had a significant impact on model performance. Notably, since both the Lapatinib\_BT474 and Lapatinib\_HCC1419 datasets involve the same drug, they were merged to investigate how individual hyperparameters affect the model’s performance in predicting drug responses for Lapatinib.

For a given pathway, only a specific subset of genes is typically expressed. As a result, the corresponding row in the mask matrix of the sparse decoder is dominated by 0. To prevent the decoder from becoming excessively sparse, which may impair its ability to learn meaningful representations and to capture pathway-level prior biological knowledge, we applied a threshold to exclude pathways with an insufficient number of associated genes. [Figure 4](#fig_body_display_ijms-26-04365-f004)a presents the model’s validation performance across multiple datasets using Gene Ontology (GO) [[34](#B34-ijms-26-04365)] pathway data under various pathways thresholds.

![Ijms 26 04365 g004](/ijms/ijms-26-04365/article_deploy/html/images/ijms-26-04365-g004-550.jpg)

**Figure 4.**
The effect of three hyperparameters on model performance. (**a**) The effect of pathways threshold; (**b**) the effect of the number of highly variable genes; (**c**) the effect of dropout ratio.

Given the limited size of each classification training dataset, we only randomly selected 10% of the samples as a validation set for hyperparameter tuning. Each experiment was repeated five times with different random seeds, and the average results were calculated.

The results show that for the Cisplatin and Paclitaxel datasets, the best predictive performance was achieved when the threshold was set to 10. In contrast, the PLX-4720 dataset performed better with a threshold of 2. For the Lapatinib dataset, although thresholds of 2 and 4 both yielded accuracy values above 0.7, the model achieved a higher F1 score when the threshold was set to 4.

Other hyperparameters that influenced model performance included the number of highly variable genes (HVGs), and the dropout ratio used in the neural network. The effects of these two hyperparameters on model performance are shown in [Figure 4](#fig_body_display_ijms-26-04365-f004)a,b.

For the number of HVG, we tested several values and observed that the optimal setting varied slightly across datasets. Specifically, for the Paclitaxel dataset, the model achieved better accuracy and F1 score when HVG was set to 3000. For the other three drugs (Cisplatin, PLX-4720, and Lapatinib), the best validation performance was consistently observed when the number of HVG was set to 2500. This setting provided a favorable trade-off between retaining informative gene expression signals and avoiding overfitting due to noise or redundant features.

As for the dropout rate, we evaluated values ranging from 0.1 to 0.9. The model demonstrated robust performance when the dropout rate was set between 0.1 and 0.4. These results suggest that moderate dropout regularization was beneficial for enhancing the generalization ability of the models.

In addition, we also compared the different pathway information in constructing the sparse decoder. Commonly used biological pathway resources include GO [[34](#B34-ijms-26-04365)], Reactome [[35](#B35-ijms-26-04365)], and Hallmark [[36](#B36-ijms-26-04365)]. GO encompasses all levels of biological systems, from molecular activities to complex cellular and organismal-level networks, offering reliable information of pathways. Reactome is a manually curated database of metabolic and pathways, while Hallmark contains 50 curated, non-redundant gene sets specifically designed for gene set enrichment analysis.

We evaluated the predictive performance of our model with sparse decoders constructed from this three different pathway information on the test set GSE117872. For all pathway information, the minimum gene count threshold was fixed at 10. As shown in [Table 2](#table_body_display_ijms-26-04365-t002), the results indicated that the decoder based on the pathways information from GO achieved the best predictive performance among the three, demonstrating its suitability for modeling scRNA-seq drug response in this context.

### 2.4. Analysis of Modeling Strategies

To evaluate the importance of each module in the proposed model and its contribution to predictive performance, we conducted an ablation study and compared the effects of different strategies for aligning data across sequencing platforms on model performance.

The comparison includes a baseline model consisting of a naive autoencoder without transfer learning (base AE) followed by a multilayer perceptron classifier. To explore the impact of transfer learning, we further examined a previously proposed approach based on autoencoder integrated with generative adversarial networks (adv AE), which was originally proposed to align transcriptomic data between in vitro cell lines and in vivo clinical samples. Beyond these basic components, we further examined the performance of base AE and adv AE when combined with a shared encoder module (share AE). Finally, we assessed the full model (ours), which integrates the shared encoder with a pathway guidance (share AE + pathways).

The experimental results on the test set GSE117872 are summarized in [Table 3](#table_body_display_ijms-26-04365-t003). We observed that the incorporation of generative adversarial networks and a shared encoder significantly improved model performance. Our model, which integrated a sparse decoder to introduce pathway-level prior biological knowledge, outperformed other methods and achieved substantial improvements over the base AE. These results demonstrate that incorporating transfer learning strategies notably enhances performance. Furthermore, the addition of pathway-level guidance not only improves model interpretability but also contributes to improved accuracy.

Performance of different modeling strategies.

![](https://pub.mdpi-res.com/img/table.png)

As shown in [Figure 5](#fig_body_display_ijms-26-04365-f005), we also observed that introducing a generative adversarial strategy into the model made training more difficult and increased the risk of overfitting. This observation contrasts with the findings reported in CODE-AE-ADV, where a generative adversarial strategy is effectively applied to align in vitro and in vivo data.

![Ijms 26 04365 g005](/ijms/ijms-26-04365/article_deploy/html/images/ijms-26-04365-g005-550.jpg)

**Figure 5.**
Comparison of loss between models integrating adversarial strategy and pathway into shared encoder.

### 2.5. Pathways Attribution

Using the test set Lapatinib\_BT474 as an example, we visualized the prediction results and conducted an in-depth interpretability analysis with an external interpretability algorithm to analyze the latent embeddings generated by autoencoder, which is incorporated with pathway information.

Specifically, we employed IG [[37](#B37-ijms-26-04365)] to quantify the contribution of each pathway to the drug response prediction. IG is an interpretability technique that aims to attribute model’s predictions to its input features and is widely used to assess feature importance in DL models [[38](#B38-ijms-26-04365),[39](#B39-ijms-26-04365),[40](#B40-ijms-26-04365)]. In our implementation, we calculated the mean absolute of IG values for each pathway to evaluate the influences of pathways on the prediction. A value close to 0 indicates less influence on the final prediction, while a higher absolute value reflects a stronger contribution. The results of IG were shown in [Figure 6](#fig_body_display_ijms-26-04365-f006)a. Based on this analysis, we identified the top 12 most influential features (i.e., those with the largest absolute IG values), which correspond to the pathways most relevant to the drug-response prediction, as illustrated in [Figure 6](#fig_body_display_ijms-26-04365-f006)b. Among these 12 pathways, 10 were predefined pathways based on prior biological knowledge, while the remaining 2 were additional dimensions specifically introduced in model to capture auxiliary pathway information. Of the 12 selected pathways, 7 exhibited positive contributions, aligning with predictions of sensitive cells, while 5 showed negative contributions across most samples, potentially indicating association with drug resistance mechanisms. Also, as shown in [Figure 6](#fig_body_display_ijms-26-04365-f006)c, UMAP visualization based on the top 12 pathways demonstrated that both of scRNA-seq and bulk RNA-seq were projected into the same low-dimensional space with similar distributions, indicating a high degree of consistency. This further supports the effectiveness of the selected top 12 pathways.

![Ijms 26 04365 g006](/ijms/ijms-26-04365/article_deploy/html/images/ijms-26-04365-g006-550.jpg)

**Figure 6.**
Presents three aspects of the interpretability analysis. (**a**) Results of integrated gradients for pathways; (**b**) heatmap of 12 most contributing pathways; (**c**) UMAP for both of scRNA-seq and bulk RNA-seq.

The contributions of these 12 pathways to individual samples were visualized in [Figure 6](#fig_body_display_ijms-26-04365-f006)b. It can be observed that each pathway exhibits relatively consistent attribution values across all samples. Notably, pathways 96, 75, 329, and 185 showed attribution patterns that aligned with the ground truth drug response labels. These pathways contributed positively to the predictions of sensitive cells, while their contributions to resistant cells remained close to 0. In contrast, pathways 244, 67, 428, and 426 exhibited predominantly negative contributions across nearly all samples, regardless of their actual response labels, suggesting a potential suppressive role in the prediction process.

To further interpret the learned features, we analyzed 10 predefined pathways by examining their associated GO terms. Notably, the 96th dimension (ranked first by IG) and the 185th dimension (ranked eleventh by IG) were associated with GOCC CASPASE COMPLEX and GOCC CULLIN RING UBIQUITIN LIGASE COMPLEX, respectively. These pathways are related to drug sensitivity mechanisms. The former is a protein complex that contains one or more cysteine-type endopeptidases, which may be involved in apoptotic processes. The latter is part of a protein degradation pathway mediated by the Cullin-RING ubiquitin ligase complex [[41](#B41-ijms-26-04365),[42](#B42-ijms-26-04365)]. The high attribution scores of these pathways suggest that the model captured the potential association between drug sensitivity and GO pathways information during training.

We also identified four dimensions associated with pathways involved in drug resistance mechanisms. The 237th dimension (ranked second by IG) and the 55th dimension (ranked tenth) correspond to GOCC CALCIUM CHANNEL COMPLEX and GOCC ENDOPLASMIC RETICULUM LUMEN, respectively, both of which are linked to metabolic stress and cellular stress responses. The former is an ion channel complex through calcium ions pass, while the latter is the volume enclosed by the membranes of the endoplasmic reticulum. In addition, the 75th dimension (ranked third) and the 67th dimension (ranked sixth) are associated with GOCC MICROTUBULE and GOCC MICROTUBULE ORGANIZING CENTER, respectively, which are related to cytoskeletal dynamics and cell cycle arrest. The former is the microtubule, while the latter is the microtubule-organizing center, both of which are part of the cytoskeleton of eukaryotic cells [[41](#B41-ijms-26-04365),[42](#B42-ijms-26-04365)]. These pathway associations further support the model’s ability to learn potential features and knowledge of drug resistance through GO pathways information.

## 3. Discussion

In this study, we collected and curated scRNA-seq drug response datasets. Five datasets were selected for testing, which cover three cancers and four cancer-related drugs. The DL clustering model, AttentionAE-sc, was applied to process the collected data. The clustering results were utilized to exclude normal cells and cells in the control group that exhibit genetic resistance. In addition, high-quality labeling was achieved by incorporating prior biological knowledge derived from published literature. To validate the effectiveness of AttentionAE-sc, we analyzed its clustering results, which yielded ASW scores above 0.75 across all datasets, indicating highly reliable clustering performance.

We utilized these five scRNA-seq datasets as testing data and their corresponding bulk RNA-seq data from the GDSC as training data to construct a drug response predictive model. Compared with ML models, the proposed DL model demonstrated superior performance across five drug response datasets. Our model attained an average accuracy of 0.668 and an average F1 score of 0.676. In comparison, the worst-performing ML model in accuracy was LR, which achieved 0.463 for accuracy and 0.550 for F1 score. Our model outperformed it by 0.205 and 0.126, respectively. The best-performing ML model in accuracy was SVM, which achieved 0.604 and 0.302 in accuracy and F1 score, our model showed improvements of 0.064 and 0.374. Regarding F1 score, the worst-performing ML model was XGBoost, with 0.491 for accuracy and 0.236 for F1 score. Our model surpassed it by 0.177 and 0.440, respectively. Compared to the best-performing model in F1 score, LR (0.463 and 0.550), our model achieved notable gains of 0.205 in accuracy and 0.126 in F1 score. The SVM model slightly outperformed our method in predicting drug response for Cisplatin, which may be attributed to the relative simplicity of this dataset (the feature differences between positive and negative samples are pronounced). As a result, all models achieved strong performance on this dataset. Since SVMs are designed to separate samples using an optimal hyperplane, they tend to excel on binary classification tasks with clear class boundaries and their slight advantage is unsurprising.

Our model exhibited relatively consistent accuracy and F1 scores across all datasets, suggesting improved stability and a stronger ability to capture latent patterns in gene expression related to drug response that are not well detected by ML models. Meanwhile, we observed that several ML models yielded an F1 score of 0 on some datasets. Subsequent analysis revealed that this was caused by a recall value of 0, suggesting that these models classified all samples as negative (resistant). This outcome reflects a failure to learn the underlying associations between transcriptomic features and drug response. The recurrence of such issues across multiple ML models further highlights the advantages of DL in accurately predicting drug response and its ability to interpret latent biological features and relationships.

We developed a shared autoencoder framework incorporating biological pathway information to explore the potential of transfer learning between bulk RNA-seq and scRNA-seq drug response datasets. We found that introducing pathway-level prior biological knowledge and employing a transfer learning strategy significantly enhanced model performance. Notably, Gene Ontology (GO) pathways provided the most reliable source of biological knowledge in our experiments. Moreover, ablation experiments revealed that the inclusion of generative adversarial strategies made the model more challenging to optimize and increase the risk of overfitting. This observation contrasts with previous findings using adversarial strategies on in vitro and in vivo bulk RNA-seq data. We hypothesize that this discrepancy may arise from the larger distributional differences between scRNA-seq and bulk RNA-seq data. Specifically, scRNA-seq data typically exhibit lower total gene expression counts and higher sparsity than bulk RNA-seq data, which may demand larger training sample sizes to ensure effective adversarial optimization.

To assess the interpretability of our model, we employed IG to interpret and visualize the association between the pathway knowledge and the predicted drug response outcomes. The results indicated that integrating biological knowledge improved both the reliability and interpretability of the model. Based on IG values, we identified the top 12 pathways that had a significant impact on the predictions. Among them, we conducted detailed analysis on 10 predefined pathways of these identified pathways. The literature review revealed that two of them were associated with drug sensitivity mechanisms, while four were related to drug resistance mechanisms.

The two pathways associated with drug sensitivity were the caspase complex-mediated apoptotic pathway and the Cullin-RING ubiquitin ligase complex-mediated protein degradation pathway. Lapatinib, as a dual HER2/EGFR tyrosinase inhibitor, may competitively bind the intracellular kinase domain and selectively block HER2 downstream pathways including PI3K/AKT and MAPK, while simultaneously triggering caspase-3/9 cascade activation to induce mitochondrial-dependent apoptosis. Therefore, in HER2-overexpressing BT474 cell lines, Lapatinib may disrupt the balance between proliferation and apoptosis, shifting cells toward a drug-sensitive state. The Cullin-RING complex may also contribute to Lapatinib sensitivity by mediating degradation of prosurvival proteins [[43](#B43-ijms-26-04365),[44](#B44-ijms-26-04365)].

Among the drug resistance-related pathways, two were associated with metabolic stress and cellular stress responses (calcium channel complex and endoplasmic reticulum lumen), while the other two were related to cytoskeletal dynamics and cell cycle arrest (microtubule and microtubule organizing center). Lapatinib may inhibit downstream signaling of HER2, including the PI3K/AKT pathway, resulting in decreased endoplasmic reticulum calcium pump activity. This may trigger endoplasmic reticulum stress and activate the unfolded protein response. Resistant cells may counteract this by upregulating CD36-mediated lipid uptake, which alleviates oxidative stress in endoplasmic reticulum membrane lipid. Additionally, enhanced endoplasmic reticulum associated degradation of misfolded proteins may contribute to the maintenance of proteostasis, enabling cells to withstand drug-induced stress [[45](#B45-ijms-26-04365),[46](#B46-ijms-26-04365)]. Regarding the cytoskeletal-related mechanisms, HER2 signaling regulates microtubule dynamics and cell division. Lapatinib interferes with the interaction between HER2/EGFR and microtubule-associated proteins, disrupting the assembly of γ-tubulin ring complexes and leading to abnormal mitotic spindle formation. In treated cells, metabolic plasticity may enhance ATP production to maintain the activity of microtubule, thereby mitigating cytoskeletal damage induced by Lapatinib. This may potentially contribute to drug resistance [[47](#B47-ijms-26-04365),[48](#B48-ijms-26-04365)].

However, our model was limited to using only gene expression data without integrating drug-specific features or biological context information (such as cancer type). This constraint limits the model’s capacity for pan-drug and pan-cancer generalization. In future work, we plan to incorporate more information, such as drug molecular structures, cancer types, and tissue-specific characteristics, with multimodal learning to enhance prediction performance across diverse drugs and cancer types. Moreover, the continued expansion of available scRNA-seq drug response datasets will support the development of a more generalized and robust predictive framework.

## 4. Materials and Methods

### 4.1. Data Collection and Processing

#### 4.1.1. Collection

The Gene Expression Omnibus (GEO, <https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/geo/>, accessed on 1 November 2024) [[49](#B49-ijms-26-04365)], a public functional genomics data repository maintained by National Center for Biotechnology Information (NCBI), contains high-throughput transcriptomic data submitted by institutions worldwide. In this study, we conducted retrieval and filter based on the following keywords and criteria: based on scRNA-seq platforms; inclusion of control group; exclusion of radiotherapy; exclusion of combination therapy; and drug-treated experimental groups receiving doses and treatment durations sufficient to induce drug resistance.

We retrieved corresponding drug response data for these datasets from the GDSC database (bulk RNA-seq) based on matched drugs and cell lines. Both bulk RNA-seq and scRNA-seq data were used during the pretraining phase to train the autoencoder, aiming to obtain a shared encoder to map both data types into a unified latent space. Subsequently, during the classifier training phase for drug response prediction, bulk RNA-seq data were used as the training and validation sets, while scRNA-seq datasets served as the test set. The classifier trained on bulk RNA-seq was directly transferred to predict on single-cell data to fully leverage the abundance of bulk data and compensate for the current scarcity of scRNA-seq drug response data.

#### 4.1.2. Labeling Strategy for Drug Response

Previous studies on scRNA-seq drug response have typically labeled drug-treated groups as resistant and control group as sensitive. However, due to the presence of genetic resistance to drugs, the control group may contain subpopulations that are intrinsically insensitive to the drug. These cells need to be identified and excluded. Moreover, most in vivo experimental datasets include highly differentiated normal cells, which should also be filtered out.

To address these issues, we proposed an improved labeling strategy. Firstly, we collected individual scRNA-seq drug response datasets. Then, we performed clustering analysis using AttentionAE-sc model to identify cell clusters corresponding to resistant or sensitive states. Based on the clustering results, cells in the control group that were likely to be drug-insensitive were excluded. Subsequently, we incorporated prior biological knowledge from public resources, such as marker gene sets, to filter out highly differentiated normal cells. Furthermore, the literature was used to assign accurate drug response labels to tumor cells.

We applied AttentionAE-sc model for clustering analysis with following parameters: 2500 highly variable genes selected, eight attention heads, cell embedding dimension of 16, Leiden resolution of 0.1, and a Gaussian kernel for graph construction. The number of cells used for the model was limited to 4000. Data preprocessing followed the original pipeline, implemented using the Scanpy toolkit. In our implementation, this parameter set achieved consistently high ASW scores and yielded optimal clustering performance. However, if significantly different parameters were used, especially those resulting in a substantial decrease in clustering quality, the robustness of the exclusion step could be compromised, and downstream predictions might be adversely affected. This is a scientific article from the International Journal of Molecular Sciences (IJMS) titled "A Transfer Learning Framework for Predicting and Interpreting Drug Responses via Single-Cell RNA-Seq Data" by Yujie He, Shenghao Li, Hao Lan, Wulin Long, Shengqiu Zhai, Menglong Li, and Zhining Wen (corresponding author). Published on May 4, 2025, in Volume 26, Issue 9, Article 4365 (DOI: 10.3390/ijms26094365), the work belongs to the Special Issue "Machine Learning in Disease Diagnosis and Treatment."

**Background and Motivation:** Chemotherapy effectiveness is undermined by drug resistance, driven by tumor heterogeneity, complex cellular interactions, and limited clinical sample access. Single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) can reveal resistance mechanisms, but systematic scRNA-seq drug response data are scarce due to high costs. In contrast, large-scale bulk RNA-seq datasets like GDSC (Genomics of Drug Sensitivity in Cancer) are abundant.

**Proposed Framework:** The authors collected scRNA-seq drug response datasets from public sources and built a transfer learning framework aligning bulk and single-cell sequencing data. A shared encoder projects both data types into a unified latent space for drug response prediction, while a sparse decoder guided by prior biological knowledge (pathways) enhances interpretability. The GDSC bulk RNA-seq data were used for training, with scRNA-seq data as test sets.

**Data:** Five scRNA-seq datasets covering three cancers were used: oral squamous cell carcinoma (GSE117872), melanoma (GSE108394), and breast cancer (GSE131984, GSE156246_BT474, GSE156246_HCC1419). Four drugs were tested (cisplatin, paclitaxel, PLX-4720, lapatinib). Drug response was measured using AUC values from GDSC. Clustering was performed with the authors' prior method, AttentionAE-sc, achieving ASW scores above 0.75 across all datasets (four above 0.8).

**Results:**
- The model achieved an average accuracy of 0.668 and average F1 score of 0.676, outperforming logistic regression (LR), support vector machine (SVM), decision tree (DT), random forest (RF), gradient boosting (GB), and XGBoost across all tasks.
- SVM slightly outperformed on cisplatin (0.730 vs 0.726 accuracy), but the gap was marginal.
- Five ML models yielded F1 scores of 0 in at least one task, particularly on Lapatinib_BT474 and Paclitaxel datasets.
- Hyperparameter tuning showed optimal pathway thresholds varied by dataset; GO pathway information provided the best performance compared to Reactome and Hallmark.
- Ablation studies showed the shared encoder and pathway guidance both improved performance over baseline autoencoder; adversarial strategies increased overfitting risk when aligning scRNA-seq and bulk data.

**Interpretability:** Integrated gradients (IG) identified top 12 contributing pathways. Two pathways were linked to drug sensitivity (caspase complex-mediated apoptosis, Cullin-RING ubiquitin ligase complex) and four to drug resistance (calcium channel complex, endoplasmic reticulum lumen, microtubule, microtubule organizing center), consistent with known lapatinib mechanisms in HER2-overexpressing BT474 cells.

**Limitations and Future Work:** The model uses only gene expression data without drug-specific features or cancer type context, limiting pan-drug and pan-cancer generalization. Future work plans multimodal learning incorporating drug molecular structures, cancer types, and tissue-specific characteristics.

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a scientific review article published in Briefings in Bioinformatics (2025 Oct 06;26(5):bbaf533, doi: 10.1093/bib/bbaf533, PMCID: PMC12499773, PMID: 41052279) titled "Computational toxicology in drug discovery: applications of artificial intelligence in ADMET and toxicity prediction." Authors: Jiangyan Zhang, Haolin Li, Yuncong Zhang (contributed equally), Junyang Huang, Liping Ren, Chuantao Zhang, Quan Zou, and Yang Zhang. Corresponding authors are from the Hospital of Chengdu University of Traditional Chinese Medicine and the University of Electronic Science and Technology of China. The article is Open Access under a Creative Commons Attribution Non-Commercial License.

Key content and findings:
- Toxicity risk assessment is crucial for clinical success and market potential of drug candidates; ~30% of preclinical candidate compounds (PCCs) fail due to toxicity, and ~40% of preclinical candidate drugs fail due to insufficient ADMET profiles, while nearly 30% of marketed drugs are withdrawn due to unforeseen toxic reactions.
- Traditional animal testing is costly, time-consuming (6–24 months per test), expensive (often exceeding millions of dollars per compound), and ethically controversial (3Rs principle: replacement, reduction, refinement), driving the shift to computational toxicology.
- The review surveys over 20 ADMET prediction platforms, categorized into three types: rule/statistical-based methods, machine learning (ML) methods, and graph-based methods.
- Broad-spectrum platforms mentioned: admetSAR 3.0, ADMETlab 3.0, vNN-ADMET, ADMETboost, Deep-PK; pharmacokinetic-focused platforms: Swiss ADME, FAF-Drugs4.0, ADMET-AI; toxicity-focused platforms: ProTox 3.0, VenomPred 2.0; CYP450-related tools: CypRules, BioTransformer 3.0, XenoSite, SOMP, SMARTCyp 3.0.
- The ADMET prediction platform framework consists of: input component (chemical structural data, experimental data, literature-derived data), tools/methods component (physicochemical property calculation via RDKit/Scopy, and ML/AI prediction module using SVMs, RFs, neural networks, gradient boosting trees), and output component (endpoints; comprehensive platforms can evaluate over 100 endpoints).
- ML methods (e.g., vNN-ADMET, ADMETboost with XGBoost, ProTox 3.0 with RF/DNN) handle complex patterns but depend on high-quality training data. Graph-based methods (GNNs: ADMET-AI, Interpretable-ADMET, HelixADMET, ADMETlab 3.0 with DMPNN, admetSAR 3.0, pkCSM) analyze molecular graph structures but require substantial computational resources and large training datasets.
- Toxicological databases are classified into four categories: chemical toxicity databases, environmental toxicology databases, alternative toxicology databases, and biological toxin databases.
- Chemical toxicity databases include PubChem (>119 million compounds, NIH-maintained), ChEMBL (>2.1 million, EMBL-EBI), HSDB (~5600 chemicals), CCRIS (>9000, carcinogenicity/mutagenicity), CompTox Chemicals Dashboard (EPA), TOXRIC (113,372 compounds, ML-ready), SuperToxic (~60,000), DrugBank, and specialized databases DILIrank, DILIst, LTKB (hepatotoxicity), hERGCentral (cardiotoxicity), and LCDB (carcinogenicity data from 1726 chemicals and 7745 experimental records).
- The field is transitioning from single-endpoint predictions to multi-endpoint joint modeling with multimodal features, incorporating generative modeling and interpretability frameworks.
- Network toxicology is applied to evaluate safety of traditional Chinese medicines (TCMs), and large language models (LLMs) show potential in literature mining, knowledge integration, and molecular toxicity prediction.
- Current challenges include data quality, model interpretability, and causal inference; future directions include multi-omics integration, interpretable AI models, and domain-specific LLMs for more efficient and precise preclinical toxicity assessments.
</summary>

- ADR data sources include: Cadec, EMA's Union Pharmacovigilance Database, FDA's FAERS, CAERS (Canada), DAEN-medicines (Australia), SMM4H (social media), n2c2, ADE_Corpus_V2, and CTCAE v5.0
- BERT-based models are commonly used as base encoders with additional decoder layers for prediction tasks
- Fine-tuning open-source LLMs (Llama-3, Gemma, Mistral/Mixtral, Falcon, DeepSeek, Qwen on Hugging Face) is a practical approach for domain adaptation

Strategies for FedLLM on ADR include: configuring high dropout rates on client models, quantization (4-bit vs 16-bit precision), segmenting parameter matrices, and transferring only distilled-federated knowledge. Distilled models have shown superior performance—DistilBERT outperformed fine-tuned xlm-RoBERTa and GPT-Neo-125M on 4 metrics, and PubMedBERT (0.1% of GPT-3.5's size) outperformed its parent model by over 6 absolute F1-score points.

Evaluation metrics for unstructured predictions include: G-Eval, BLEU_N, ROUGE_N, BERTScore, SEMScore, and ANLS*, each with documented strengths and limitations.

Conclusions: FedLLM for ADR prediction remains in its early stage with limited documented use cases. Key focus areas for future research include fine-tuning and merging algorithms, fairness and unbiasedness, implementation challenges, and real-world deployment strategies. The review aims to lay groundwork for future privacy-preserving and scalable ADR prediction systems.
</summary>

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This paper, published in the 2025 Conference of the Nations of the Americas Chapter of the ACL (Volume 1: Long Papers, pages 11083–11113), investigates whether large language models (LLMs) can effectively detect adverse drug reactions (ADRs) from psychiatric medications and align with expert responses to related queries. Led by researchers from Georgia Tech, Hospital General Universitario Gregorio Marañón, Hofstra University, and Columbia University, the study addresses a critical gap: ADRs from psychiatric medications are a leading cause of hospitalizations (51.9% to 91.8% of cases) among mental health patients, yet nearly 70% of individuals worldwide lack access to mental health professionals, leading many to seek help on social media.

The authors introduce two key resources: the Psych-ADR benchmark (239 Reddit posts from January-December 2019, labeled for ADR detection and multiclass classification across five ADR types—dose-related, non-dose, dose- and time-related, time-related, and withdrawal) and the Adverse Drug Reaction Response Assessment (ADRA) framework, which evaluates LLM responses against expert responses across four axes: text readability, emotion/tone expression, harm-reduction strategy alignment, and actionability.

Key findings for RQ1 (ADR detection and classification): The best models achieved only 75.38 F1 in detection and 76.69 F1 in multiclass classification. All models exhibited "risk-averse" behavior with false-positive rates over 70%, struggling to distinguish nuanced ADR types (GPT-4 Turbo misclassified 51% of non-dose-related and 50% of time-related ADRs). Claude 3 Opus achieved the highest zero-shot detection accuracy at 77.41%, while Llama 3.1-405B performed best in few-shot classification (F1 76.69).

There was no significant difference in emotional/tone alignment, though experts showed higher anticipation, affection, and helping tones while LLMs used more optimistic, polite, and trust-based tones. The best model (OpenBioLLM-70B) achieved only 70.86% alignment with expert harm-reduction strategies, and LLMs provided 12.32% less actionable advice on average. Notably, expert responses scored higher on practicality (0.83) and contextual relevance (0.73) but lower on specificity (0.17) and clarity (0.13), while LLMs showed the opposite pattern.

The authors emphasize the importance of "lived experience"—first-hand knowledge possessed by clinicians—which LLMs lack, and caution against increasing human-like features (anthropomorphism) in LLMs due to risks of over-trust in high-risk healthcare domains. Instead, they advocate for fine-tuning on specialized data. The study was funded by NSF grant #2230692 and grants from AFSP, JPMorgan AI Research, and Microsoft's AFMR program. This article from BioPharm International (published March 4, 2026) by Partha Anbil and Niraj B. Patel examines how artificial intelligence (AI), particularly large language models (LLMs) and natural language processing (NLP), is transforming drug safety surveillance. The FDA manages a database of over 140,000 drug labeling documents, and with 82% of American adults taking at least one medication, the scale of data necessitates automated solutions.

- AskFDALabel: Combines retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) with locally hosted LLMs, achieving F1-scores of 0.978 for drug-induced liver injury and 0.931 for drug-induced cardiotoxicity classification.

Limitations include context dependency, class imbalance making rare events hard to detect, explainability challenges with "black box" models, cost/computational requirements (230+ computing hours for pre-training), and the need for rigorous validation. Best practices include starting with pilot projects, establishing baselines, maintaining human oversight, and using domain-specific training data since generic LLMs significantly underperform.

--- SOURCE 14: JMIR Medical Informatics - Predicting Drug–Side Effect Relationships From Parametric Knowledge Embedded in Biomedical BERT Models: Methodological Study With a Natural Language Processing Approach ---
URL: https://medinform.jmir.org/2025/1/e67513

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This paper, published in JMIR Medical Informatics (Vol 13, 2025; doi:10.2196/67513), presents a methodological study on predicting drug–side effect relationships using parametric knowledge embedded in biomedical BERT language models. 

**Background/Objectiive:** Adverse drug reactions (ADRs) pose serious public health risks, with approximately 2 million serious ADRs and 100,000 deaths reported annually in the US. Traditional context-independent word embedding models like Word2Vec have limitations in capturing biomedical domain specificity. The study proposes using BERT-based models pretrained on biomedical corpora to extract parametric knowledge and predict unknown drug–side effect relationships.

**Methods:** The study used 158,096 known drug–side effect pairs from the SIDER database (version 4.1) to build an adjacency matrix with 1,345 drugs and 6,123 side effects. Cosine similarity was calculated between word embedding vectors of drugs and side effects. Relation scores (combining drug-similarity and side-effect-similarity components using equations) were calculated for 8,235,435 total drug–side effect pairs. For Word2Vec training, 14,289,160 sentences mentioning drugs and 32,107,327 sentences mentioning side effects were extracted from PubMed (42,515,246 total abstracts, updated December 8, 2022).

**Results:** The clagator/biobert_v1.1 model achieved the highest AUC of 0.915 at an optimal threshold of 0.289 (sensitivity 0.870, specificity 0.830), outperforming Word2Vec (AUC 0.848) and vanilla BERT (bert-base-uncased, AUC 0.857). Other models tested included BiomedBERT (0.907), dmis-lab/biobert_v1.1 (0.901), and PharmBERT-uncased (0.882). All BERT models pretrained on biomedical corpora outperformed vanilla BERT. The cosine similarity-based extraction method outperformed Euclidean distance, Manhattan distance, Jaccard similarity, and dot product methods. The dual-similarity approach (relation score, AUC 0.915) significantly outperformed single-similarity methods (drug-only: 0.799, side-effect-only: 0.881).

**Validation:** External validation with FAERS data (October 2012–June 2023; 901,361 known relationships) confirmed high statistical significance (P<.001) with an odds ratio of 4.822 (Fisher exact test repeated 2,000 times). Case studies of top-ranked predictions not in SIDER (lenalidomide-arthropathy, rosuvastatin-sleep disturbance, gadolinium-acute pulmonary edema, cefazolin-hepatic failure) were confirmed as reported in literature published after 2016.

**Conclusions:** BERT-based models pretrained on biomedical corpora significantly outperform Word2Vec in predicting drug–side effect relationships due to contextual information capture. The methodology demonstrates practical applicability for pharmacovigilance and ADR prediction. Limitations include the SIDER database being last updated in 2015, challenges with non-dose-dependent reactions, case report generalizability issues, prediction limitations for novel drug candidates, and lack of patient-specific idiosyncratic reaction modeling. The research was supported by the Korea Health Technology R&D Project (grant RS-2022-KH125153).
</summary>

**Background & Technology:** Drug discovery traditionally takes over a decade and costs billions, with only ~10% chance of approval for candidates entering trials. The AlphaFold revolution began with AlphaFold 2 (2020) solving the protein folding problem (earning the 2024 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for John Jumper and Demis Hassabis). AlphaFold 3 (released May 2024, a joint DeepMind/Isomorphic effort) extended predictions to molecular interactions with proteins, DNA, RNA, and ligands, achieving "at least a 50% improvement" and in some cases doubling prediction accuracy. **Pipeline:** Isomorphic's internal candidates focus on oncology (cancer) and immunology. Public reports hint at TIM-3 (an immune checkpoint) as a target. The company plans to license its drugs out after early-stage trials.

**Clinical Trials Timeline:** In July 2025, President Colin Murdoch said human trials of AI-designed drugs were "finally in sight" with the company "staffing up" to begin dosing patients. The Indian Express (July 9, 2025) reported the oncology drug created using AlphaFold 3 was set to enter human trials. SUMMARY:
<summary>
On February 10, 2026, Isomorphic Labs announced a significant advancement in AI-powered drug design with the introduction of the Isomorphic Labs Drug Design Engine (IsoDDE), a unified computational drug-design system that moves beyond AlphaFold 3 (AF3), which was released in 2024 in partnership with Google DeepMind. All cases were independently reviewed by three board-certified clinical pharmacists. Standardized zero-shot prompting with nine repeated runs (temperature=0.7) and label shuffling was used. In the listwise 4-6 drug task, MedGemma-27B performed best (80.0), followed by GPT-4o-mini (71.3) and LLaMA3-70B (68.6). All models performed worst on Category C (moderate-risk) interactions. Self-consistency decreased as task complexity increased, and no model showed uniformly high reliability. Notably, models failed to identify Category X (avoid combination) DDIs in 24-30% of cases. Limitations include small dataset size by LLM standards and lack of prompt engineering or knowledge-graph augmentation. The authors call for further model improvement and multi-format, reliability-aware evaluation frameworks before clinical deployment.

--- SOURCE 12: Benchmarking Computational Methods for Emerging Drug-Drug Interaction Prediction ---
URL: https://arxiv.org/html/2410.18583v4

SUMMARY:
<summary>
## DDI-Ben: A Benchmarking Framework for Emerging Drug-Drug Interaction Prediction Under Distribution Changes

### Overview
This paper by Zhenqian Shen et al. (Tsinghua University) introduces **DDI-Ben**, a benchmarking framework for emerging drug-drug interaction (DDI) prediction that explicitly addresses distribution changes between known and new drugs—a factor neglected by current evaluation methods. The code and data are available at https://github.com/LARS-research/DDI-Bench.

### Motivation
- Emerging DDI prediction is critical for new drugs with unknown pharmacological risks, as clinical experiments are time-consuming and expensive.
- Existing DDI datasets (DrugBank, TWOSIDES) lack drug approval timeline information, making it hard to simulate realistic drug distribution changes over time.
- Current evaluation methods assume known and new drugs follow the same distribution, using unrealistic i.i.d. drug splits, which makes evaluation results questionable.

### Distribution Change Simulation Framework
The framework uses **distribution changes between drug sets as a surrogate** for real-world DDI distribution changes:
1. **Drug distribution change modeling**: Introduces a cluster-based difference measurement γ(Dk,Dn) = max{S(u,v)} based on drug similarity (Tanimoto coefficient between fingerprints). Smaller γ indicates larger distribution changes.
2. **Drug data split**: Splits drugs into known and new drug sets.

The framework defines two emerging DDI tasks:
- **S1**: Determine DDI type between a known drug and a new drug.
- **S2**: Determine DDI type between two new drugs.

### Data Split Strategies Comparison
Eight split strategies were compared (random, drug frequency, drug usage, scaffold, LoHi, SPECTRA, DataSAIL, and the proposed cluster-based split). Key findings:
- LoHi and SPECTRA discard data points (undesirable given data collection costs).
- Only SPECTRA and the **cluster-based split** enable controllable distribution changes.
- The proposed cluster-based split achieved the **highest consistency index** with realistic drug approval-time-based splits.
- Real-world drug clusters emerge from new drug safety issues (1980s NSAIDs), technological breakthroughs (1990s ACE inhibitors), and new epidemics (2010s HCV NS5A inhibitors).

### Datasets
- **DrugBank**: Multiclass dataset, 1,710 drugs, 86 interaction types, 188,509 DDI triplets.
- **TWOSIDES**: Multilabel dataset, 645 drugs, 209 DDI types (frequency 3000–6000), 116,650 DDI triplets.

### Methods Benchmarked (10 representative methods)
- **Feature-based**: MLP
- **Embedding-based**: MSTE
- **GNN-based**: Decagon, SSI-DDI, MRCGNN, EmerGNN, SAGAN
- **Graph-transformer**: TIGER
- **LLM-based**: TextDDI, DDI-GPT

### Key Results
1. **Most existing methods suffer substantial performance degradation** when distribution changes are introduced, with a more severe decline on DrugBank (harder multiclass prediction) than TWOSIDES.
2. **LLM-based methods (TextDDI, DDI-GPT) are the most robust** against distribution changes. EmerGNN performed best without distribution changes but TextDDI and DDI-GPT outperformed others under distribution changes.
3. **Textual information and LLM processing are key**: TextDDI's LLM extracts key pharmacological knowledge from raw textual data, filters irrelevant information, and enables more accurate predictions. Transferable pharmacological knowledge (e.g., Aclidinium's bronchodilatory activities, Butylscopolamine's muscarinic receptor binding) is not available in fingerprints or biomedical networks.
4. **DDI-type analysis**: MLP and MSTE rely on sufficient labeled data (good on major DDI types, poor on long-tail types). DDI-GPT significantly outperformed others on medium and long-tail DDI types under distribution changes.
5. **Controlling γ**: As distribution change increases (γ decreases), most methods' performance drops significantly; DDI-GPT remains relatively best, suggesting LLM prior knowledge and textual side information help mitigate the negative impact.

### Evaluation Metrics
- **DrugBank**: Macro F1 (primary), accuracy, Cohen's Kappa.
- **TWOSIDES**: Average ROC-AUC (primary), PR-AUC, and accuracy across DDI types.

### Conclusions & Future Work
DDI-Ben highlights the importance of explicitly addressing distribution changes in emerging DDI prediction. Future directions include designing LLM-based methods to alleviate distribution change impact and domain adaptation methods for real-world robustness.
</summary>

The article was submitted June 21, 2026, revised and accepted July 31, 2026, and published August 4, 2026, and belongs to the Special Issue "Drug Safety and Real-World Evidence: From Databases to Artificial Intelligence."

**Purpose & Background:** The review evaluates graph-based machine-learning methods for predicting drug–drug interactions (DDIs), which are major medication-safety concerns. Since experimental testing cannot cover the rapidly expanding number of drug pairs, computational DDI prediction is a critical complementary strategy for prioritizing risky combinations and supporting medication-safety workflows. The review focuses on graph neural networks (GNNs) and their architectures, data integration, interpretability, reproducibility, and clinical relevance.

**Methodology:** Conducted following the PRISMA 2020 framework. Searches covered IEEE Xplore (n=74), ScienceDirect (n=96), PubMed (n=67), and Google Scholar (n=53), totaling 290 records for studies published January 2021 through March 2026. After removing duplicates and ineligible records, 60 primary studies were included. Because studies used heterogeneous datasets and methods, findings were synthesized narratively rather than statistically (no meta-analysis). Risk of bias was assessed across seven domains: data leakage, negative sampling, generalization design, baseline/ablation adequacy, reproducibility, interpretability, and clinical applicability.

**Key Results:** Sixty studies met eligibility criteria. Methods progressed from graph convolutional networks and graph attention networks to graph transformers, contrastive learning, multimodal fusion, and LLM-enhanced representations. Representative reported results include 94.47% transductive accuracy for SSI-DDI, 99.74% warm-start accuracy for DrugDAGT, and 95.43% AUROC for KnowDDI on TWOSIDES — but these are study-specific and not directly comparable. Only three studies explicitly addressed data leakage; leakage-aware drug-disjoint, temporal, and external evaluations were uncommon. Uncertainty calibration, computational-resource reporting, complete reproducibility materials, and independently validated explanations were also limited.

The review identified five principal threats to validity: (1) leakage-prone random pairwise splits; (2) incomplete or noisy labels (unobserved interactions treated as confirmed negatives); (3) limited cold-start evaluation on unseen drugs; (4) scarce temporal evaluation; and (5) limited interpretability validation. The review covers three analytical questions: (RQ1) how graph construction, data modality, and validation design influence reported performance; (RQ2) when attention and multimodal fusion add demonstrable value; (RQ3) what evidence supports translation beyond benchmark performance.

Three core modeling concepts were defined: GNN architectures, multimodal fusion (combining molecular structure, SMILES, DDI networks, knowledge graphs, side effects, targets, pathways, or text), and attention mechanisms. Attention categories identified include graph attention, cross-/co-attention, hierarchical attention, knowledge-graph attention, transformer self-attention, feature/modality weighting, and contrastive attention.

**Conclusions:** Graph-based machine learning is promising for DDI prioritization and hypothesis generation but remains insufficient for independent clinical decision-making. The review recommends future studies use standardized benchmarks, leakage-aware validation, calibrated uncertainty, reproducible pipelines, validated explanations, and external or prospective evaluation. Keywords: drug–drug interaction; graph neural network; computational pharmacology; multimodal learning; attention mechanism.

Search results: 



--- SOURCE 1: Comparing AI Biology Foundation Models: AlphaFold 3 & ESM3 ---
URL: https://intuitionlabs.ai/articles/biology-foundation-models-comparison

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This IntuitionLabs report (published April 19, 2026) provides an in-depth comparison of AI biology foundation models for molecular biology, focusing on AlphaFold 3 (AF3), ESM-3, Boltz-2, Chai-1, and RoseTTAFold. It analyzes their architectures, training data, capabilities, quantitative benchmarks, and real-world use cases in drug discovery.

**Key Models:**
- **AlphaFold 3 (AF3)**: Released May 2024 by DeepMind/Isomorphic. Uses a generative diffusion architecture predicting full atomic structures of complexes (proteins, nucleic acids, small molecules, modified residues) in one unified model. Achieves ~76% success on PoseBusters ligand benchmark (RMSD <2Å), far surpassing physics-based docking (~30-38%). Dramatically improved protein-ligand, protein-DNA/RNA, and antibody-antigen prediction. Closed-source (free academic use only) and can "hallucinate" structure in disordered regions (mitigated via cross-distillation training).
- **ESM-3**: From EvolutionaryScale (ex-Meta researchers), mid-2024. A 98-billion-parameter multimodal protein language model, generative and autoregressive like GPT. Trained on 2.78 billion sequences (771 billion tokens) using >10^24 FLOPS. Can generate protein sequences from partial cues; demonstrated design of a novel fluorescent protein (58% identity to known GFP, representing ~500M years of natural evolution). Smallest 1.4B version open-source; larger models commercial via AWS/Nvidia.
- **Boltz-2**: Announced June 2025 by MIT Jameel Clinic. Successor to Boltz-1 with equivariant diffusion backbone plus a unique "affinity module" predicting binding strength (IC50-like). Achieves FEP-level accuracy in relative binding energies (Pearson ~0.62) while running >1000× faster than physics-based simulations. Fully open-source (MIT license). Outperformed all submissions on CASP16-style binding challenge; used to identify TYK2 inhibitors in virtual assays.
- **Chai-1**: Released September 2024 by Chai Discovery. Open-source multimodal structure predictor using protein language model embeddings and supporting experimental restraints (crosslinks, epitope maps). ~77% success on PoseBusters ligand benchmark (vs AF3's ~76%). User "steering" with contact constraints doubles antibody-antigen accuracy. Pitched as "AlphaFold 3 power without limitations" - free for non-commercial use.
- **RoseTTAFold**: Released 2021 by Baker Lab using a three-track network (1D sequences, 2D distance maps, 3D coordinates). Achieved CASP14-competitive accuracy comparable to AlphaFold 2. Openly available; "All-Atom" 2024 update weaker on ligand docking (~42% top hits vs ~76-77% for newer models) but remains a standard comparator.

**Headline Benchmark Comparison (PoseBusters protein-ligand):** Physics-based methods 38%, AlphaFold 3 76%, Chai-1 77%, RoseTTAFold All-Atom ~42%.

**Implications:** These foundation models are transforming biology, enabling routine atomistic complex prediction (proteins with drugs, DNA, membranes) in hours rather than years. Drug discovery pipelines are exploiting end-to-end AI for generative compound design and antibody maturation. Concerns include hallucination issues (AF3), dual-use risks, licensing restrictions, and computational demands. The field is evolving rapidly with iterative improvements expected.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"The new AlphaFold model demonstrates substantially improved accuracy over many previous specialized tools: far greater accuracy for protein–ligand interactions compared with state-of-the-art docking tools, much higher accuracy for protein–nucleic acid interactions… and substantially higher antibody–antigen prediction accuracy compared with AlphaFold-Multimer v2.3." (AF3 Nature paper)
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 2: A survey of downstream applications of evolutionary scale modeling protein language models ---
URL: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12806033

SUMMARY:
<summary>
A survey paper published in Quantitative Biology (2025, Vol. 14, e70013) titled "A survey of downstream applications of evolutionary scale modeling protein language models," authored by Qingyu Yang, Jiale Yu, and Jie Zheng from ShanghaiTech University and the Shanghai Engineering Research Center of Intelligent Vision and Imaging. The paper (PMCID: PMC12806033, PMID: 41676321) reviews the ESM (evolutionary scale modeling) series of protein language models (PLMs) and their downstream applications in protein science and engineering.

**ESM Model Series Overview:**
- ESM-1b: First foundational BERT-style Transformer PLM, trained via masked language modeling (MLM) on 250 million protein sequences from UniParc (43M–670M parameters)
- ESM-MSA-1b (MSA Transformer): Uses tied row/united column attention on multiple sequence alignments for structure inference (100M parameters)
- ESM-1v: Specialized for variant effect prediction (650M parameters)
- ESM-IF1 (GVP-Transformer): Combines Transformer with GVP-GNN for inverse folding/fixed-backbone design (124M parameters)
- ESM-2: SOTA general-purpose PLM, one of the most widely used foundation models in protein science (8M–15B parameters)
- ESMFold: End-to-end single-sequence 3D structure predictor, comparable to AlphaFold2 in some key scenarios, significantly faster (3.69B parameters)
- ESM3: Protein design model reasoning across sequence, structure, and function (1.4B–98B parameters)

**Advantages of ESM over other PLMs:** best or near-best performance in most scenarios; well-developed complete series covering various protein research fields; widely used as base models in other works.

**Techniques of Using ESM (5 categories):**
1. **Direct use**: ESM-IF1 for fixed-backbone design, ESMFold for structure prediction (much faster than AlphaFold2 with minor accuracy loss, excels at de novo/orphan proteins)
2. **Integration with task-specific models**: ESM embeddings combined with MLP, ML classifiers, regression models, LSTM, CNN, attention, GRU; e.g., NERE, DSMBind (binding affinity), ESMFlow (flow matching for conformational sampling)
3. **Fine-tuning**: Both full fine-tuning and parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) including adapter tuning, prompt tuning, and LoRA (most widely used; PEFT-SP showed LoRA best for signal peptide classification); also FusOn-pLM and AntiFold
4. **Multimodality**: Fusing sequence and structure information via three main approaches (ESM embeddings as GNN node features; concatenation of representations; cross-attention); contrastive learning (e.g., ConPLex, CLIP-based methods like PepPrCLIP, Cut&CLIP, CSSP); structure-aware retraining (e.g., SaProt using Foldseek's 3Di tokens); continual training (ESM-S)
5. **Attention maps and evaluation**: Attention maps used for contact map prediction; ESM used for directed evolution assistance, mutation validation, structure evaluation (e.g., self-consistency perplexity with ESM-IF1, ESMFold pLDDT/pAE scores in UCSF ChimeraX)

**Key Comparative Findings:** Among well-known PLMs, ESM and ProtT5 show best performance in different scenarios (ProtT5 slightly better overall); ESM-1b highest for "extracellular" and "golgi apparatus" localization tasks; ProteinBERT performs slightly poorer.

**Downstream Biological Applications:** ESM models capture implicit structural/evolutionary information and apply to structure prediction (fold, secondary structure via NetSurfP-3.0, contact maps, 3D structure via OmegaFold, protein complexes via Seq2Symm) and function prediction (EC/GO via SaProt and ESM-GearNet, text-defined function via ProtST, functional annotation via NetGO 3.0, localization via ProtGPS, solubility via NetSolP, homology detection via PLMSearch).

The survey analyzed approximately 100 representative papers (each cited at least five times) from papers citing at least one of the six original ESM publications.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"The evolutionary scale modeling (ESM) series is promising to revolutionize protein science and engineering through large language models (LLMs), providing a robust framework for understanding the relationships among sequences, structures, and functions of proteins."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 3: Simulating 500 million years of evolution with a language model ---
URL: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=qeqbm8a1-ZA

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a seminar presentation by Roshan Rao, PhD, of the company EvoScale, given as part of the "ML for protein engineering seminar series" (posted 17 Sep 2024, ~7308 views). The talk presents ESM3, a frontier multimodal generative language model for proteins that can reason over sequence, structure, and function. The key claims: ESM3 can act as an evolutionary simulator, generating functional proteins far from known proteins. The team prompted ESM3 to design fluorescent proteins and found a bright fluorescent protein at 58% sequence identity from known fluorescent proteins—a distance comparable to over 500 million years of natural evolution.

Key technical details:
- Architecture: A simple Transformer with tokenized input/output tracks for sequence, structure, and function, plus a geometric attention mechanism that encodes 3D coordinates in an SE(3)-invariant and efficient way. Structure is tokenized with a new VQ-VAE (each residue token represents its 16 nearest 3D neighbors) with sub-angstrom RMSD reconstruction.
- Training: Three models trained at 1.4B, 7.7B, and 98.5B parameters. Deeper (rather than wider) architectures were found to be better for proteins. Training used large amounts of metagenomic and synthetic data (found to improve performance once model scale crossed a threshold), FP8 precision, sharding over 1000+ GPUs, and various stability techniques (layer norm on queries/keys, warmup, FP32 for key ops). Optimal masking rate increased with scale (15% at 650M params, 30% at 7B).
- Alignment (DPO fine-tuning): Models are aligned by scoring generated sequences computationally (constraint site RMSD, predicted TM score) and fine-tuning with DPO; larger models respond more strongly to alignment, improving prompt-following fidelity, pTM, and generation diversity.
- Wet lab validation with GFP: ESM3 was prompted with the structure/key chromophore, generating sequences that were synthesized. After one plate experiment and diversification/refinement, a fluorescent protein with high activity and ~58% identity to wild-type GFP was obtained, including mutations in core/alpha-helix positions.

Other points covered: data valuation (PDB is highest value; sequence data scales linearly), use of temporal holdouts and MMS-seq purging to avoid leakage, removal of viruses from the open model for biosafety (internal models retain them for academic partnerships), and future directions (genomic context, protein-ligand interactions, text annotations).
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"Here we show that language models trained on tokens generated by evolution can act as evolutionary simulators to generate functional proteins that are far away from known proteins."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 4: ESM3: Simulating 500 million years of evolution with a ... ---
URL: https://www.evolutionaryscale.ai/blog/esm3-release

SUMMARY:
<summary>
EvolutionaryScale, a public benefit company, announced ESM3, a frontier language model for biology that simultaneously reasons over protein sequence, structure, and function. In a preprint (June 25, 2024) updated with publication in Science Magazine in January 2025, the company described generating a new green fluorescent protein (GFP) called esmGFP. The paper was published in Science (DOI: 10.1126/science.ads0018), and the API is now in public beta through Forge. 

KEY MODEL DETAILS:
- ESM3 is trained on billions of proteins from diverse environments (Amazon rainforest, ocean depths, hydrothermal vents, soil microbes)
- Trained with over 1x10^24 FLOPS and 98B parameters—described as the most compute ever applied to training a biological model
- An order of magnitude larger than the previous model, ESM2 (which itself scaled from ESM-1b/1v and ESM-IF1)
- Uses a masked language modeling objective, tokenizing sequence, structure, and function into discrete alphabets within a single multi-track transformer
- Augmented with hundreds of millions of synthetic data points (predicted structures and functions)
- Uses alignment methods similar to RLHF, but ESM3 can self-improve with feedback on its own generations
- Capabilities emerge with scale (e.g., atomic coordination tasks) and improve with alignment

THE esmGFP RESULT:
- Prompted only with the structure of a few residues in the core of natural GFP, ESM3 reasoned in chain-of-thought to generate candidates
- First experiment: tested 96 generations; found proteins that fluoresce, including B8 (50x less bright, chromophore matured over a week)
- Second experiment from B8: tested 96 more proteins; found esmGFP (well C10), with brightness similar to natural GFPs
- esmGFP differs by 96 mutations out of 229 amino acids (58% sequence similarity to closest known fluorescent protein)
- This corresponds to an estimated equivalent of over 500 million years of natural evolution

RESPONSIBLE DEVELOPMENT:
- Public benefit company focused on AI for human health and society
- Cites the 1975 Asilomar Conference principles as inspiration, plus new responsible biodesign principles
- Four core tenets: communicate benefits and risks, rigorously evaluate risk before public deployment, adopt risk mitigation strategies and guardrails, and work with government/policy/civil society stakeholders

OPEN MODEL:
- Committed to open science; releasing weights and code for an ESM3 1.4B open model on GitHub (github.com/evolutionaryscale/esm)
- Examples of ESM ecosystem applications cited: evolving antibodies (Hie et al. with ESM-1v/1b), COVID variant detection (BioNTech/InstaDeep), clinical mutation effect prediction (Brandes et al.), anti-CRISPR engineering (Marsiglia et al.), protein evolution guidance (Shanker et al.), enzyme function prediction (Yu et al.), single-cell foundation models (Rosen et al.), and antibody design (Høie et al.)

FUTURE DIRECTION:
- API and open model available for scientists to explore protein design and synthetic biology
- Prioritizing beta API access based on potential to expand scientific knowledge
- Developing specialized ESM3 versions for drug design
- Roadmap envisions increasingly multimodal models integrating from molecules to cells
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"ESM3 takes a step towards the future where AI is a tool to engineer biology from first principles in the same way we engineer structures, machines and microchips, and write computer programs."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 5: Evolutionary Scale · ESM Cambrian: Revealing the mysteries of ... ---
URL: https://www.evolutionaryscale.ai/blog/esm-cambrian

SUMMARY:
<summary>
On December 4, 2024, EvolutionaryScale announced ESM Cambrian (ESM C), a next-generation protein language model that defines a new state of the art for protein representation learning. ESM C is a parallel model family to the flagship ESM3 generative models, focusing on creating representations of underlying protein biology rather than controllable generation.

Key details:
- ESM C is trained via masked language modeling at three scales: 300M, 600M, and 6B parameters.
