## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12713570)Abstract

Despite an increasing number of clinical trials, cancer is one of the leading causes of death worldwide in the past decade. Among all complex diseases, clinical trials in oncology have among the lowest success rates, in part due to the high intra- and inter-tumoral heterogeneity. There are more than a thousand cancer drugs and treatment combinations being investigated in ongoing clinical trials for various cancer subtypes, germline mutations, metastasis, etc. Particularly, treatments relying on the (re)activation of the immune system have become increasingly present in the clinical trial pipeline. However, the complexities of the immune response and cancer-immune interactions pose a challenge to the development of these therapies. Quantitative systems pharmacology (QSP), as a computational approach to predict tumor response to treatments of interest, can be used to conduct in silico clinical trials with virtual patients (and emergent use of digital twins) in place of real patients, thus lowering the time and cost of clinical trials. In line with improved mechanistic understanding of the human immune system and promising results from recent cancer immunotherapy, QSP models can play critical roles in model-informed drug development in immuno-oncology. In this chapter, we discuss how QSP models were designed to serve different study objectives, including hypothesis testing, dose optimization, and efficacy prediction, via case studies in immuno-oncology.

**Keywords:**Cancer immunotherapy, Mechanistic modeling, T cell engager, Cytokine release syndrome, Clinical trial simulation

## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12713570)Introduction

1
Cancer is a leading cause of death worldwide with over 19 million estimated new cases and nearly ten million deaths in 2022 ([Bray et al. 2024](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12713570#R10)). Although the number of clinical trials has increased over the past decade, the overall success rate of trials in oncology is among the lowest in the major therapeutic areas ([Wong et al. 2019](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12713570#R80)). Between 2016 and 2021, 207 cancer drugs were approved by the U.S. FDA for a variety of patient subgroups that differ in cancer type, disease stage, germline mutation status, etc., with only 28 drugs displacing standard-of-care treatments ([Benjamin et al. 2022](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12713570#R8)). Further, the median time between drug discovery/patent application and marketing approval is 12 years ([Stewart et al. 2018](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12713570#R65)). From target identification to dose optimization, many factors, such as drug specificity, selectivity, efficacy, and toxicity, have to be investigated, which contributes to the prolonged drug development process and the low success rate of clinical trials ([Sun et al. 2022](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12713570#R67)). More importantly, as immunotherapy and other targeted therapies have become the standard-of-care treatments for multiple patient subgroups, it is increasingly difficult for clinical trials using newly discovered drugs to recruit enough patients from these subgroups to achieve statistical validity ([Thoma et al. 2010](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12713570#R70)).

Since 2013, quantitative systems pharmacology (QSP) models, along with other types of mechanistic models, have begun to play important roles in the drug approval process in the U.S. to accelerate this process. The number of regulatory submissions to the FDA that contain QSP models has continuously increased from 2013 to 2020, with 22% of the submissions for oncology ([Bai et al. 2021](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12713570#R6)). Although QSP models were used for dose optimization in the vast majority of the new drug applications, they have also been developed to waive required clinical studies or address safety concerns in a few cases ([Bai et al. 2021](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12713570#R6)). In addition, QSP models have shown the capability to identify potential drug targets, investigate drug-drug/drug-target interactions, and make prospective efficacy predictions in academic immune-oncology research ([Butner et al. 2022](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12713570#R11)).

Starting from model formulation, QSP model development in oncology faces similar challenges to that in all complex diseases. In most cases, model scope (e.g., mechanisms to be incorporated, time scale, stochasticity, and the necessity of spatial heterogeneity characterization) is first determined based on the study objective, data availability, desired computational efficiency, and accuracy ([Gadkar et al. 2016](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12713570#R22)). For example, whole-body models of the immune system would help investigate interactions among therapeutic agents, immune cells, and cancer cells throughout the body for better prediction of tumor response to treatments; and localized models of signaling pathways involving the targets of drugs of interest would help answer specific questions, such as drug-drug interaction and target identification ([Chelliah and van der Graaf 2022](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12713570#R12); [Zhang et al. 2022](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12713570#R84)). Chelliah et al. analyzed mechanistic models that describe different aspects of the cancer-immunity cycle ([Chen and Mellman 2013](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12713570#R14)) and summarized the cell types and molecular components involved in 141 models ([Chelliah et al. 2021](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12713570#R13)).

Chapter 5, _Data to Inform Models_, provides an overview of the data and data sources used to develop and validate QSP models. Data used to support QSP model development may come directly from in vitro and in vivo experimental data generated by a pharmaceutical company, academic lab, or contract research organization to support either a drug development project or specifically to support model parameterization. Additionally, data found in published in vitro and in vivo experimental studies on different cancer types may be leveraged for QSP model parameterization. Leonov et al. developed a database that stores publicly available in vivo human data on cellular and molecular concentrations measured in different tissues in 280 diseases including various cancers ([Leonov et al. 2023](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12713570#R39)). In addition, Lazarou et al. proposed informing mechanistic models with multi-omics data from public databases, such as the iAtlas and TSNAdb databases ([Lazarou et al. 2020](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12713570#R38)). Notably, data that do not directly correspond to model parameters/species need to be converted into proper units. For example, Zhang et al. analyzed scRNA and whole-exome sequencing data with tools like netMHCpan 4.0 to calculate neoantigen expression in each patient, which is an input parameter in their QSP model ([Zhang et al. 2021](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12713570#R83)). Once a QSP model is parameterized, model applications vary according to study objectives, and methods for model evaluation are similar across all therapeutic areas ([Braakman et al. 2022](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12713570#R9)). In this chapter, we analyze 3 cases of QSP modeling in immuno-oncology with a focus on how models were formulated given different study objectives.

## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12713570)Case Study 1: Inferring Optimal Dosage and Mechanistic Insights of GITR Agonist by QSP Modeling

2
In this case study, we discuss the applicability of immuno-oncology QSP models for generating mechanistic hypotheses and dose optimization for a class of agonist antibodies with multiple mechanisms of action. We consider a representative murine QSP model of anti-GITR antibodies ([Ji et al. 2023](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12713570#R34)) and discuss the motivation, steps involved in model development, and applicability of the corresponding QSP model.

### Study Objective

2.1
Glucocorticoid-induced tumor necrosis factor receptor-related protein (GITR) is a co-stimulatory molecule expressed on regulatory T cells (Treg), effector T cells (Teff), and other immune cells, such as macrophages and natural killer cells. Agonist antibodies are capable of binding to GITR and mimicking the action of GITR ligands. In preclinical studies ([Turk et al. 2004](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12713570#R71); [Ko et al. 2005](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12713570#R36)), GITR agonist antibodies have been shown to promote tumor clearance and induce long-lasting anti-tumor activity. Anti-GITR agonist antibodies display a dual mechanism of action by 1) stimulating Teff proliferation and effector functions and 2) promoting FcγR-mediated depletion of Treg, which together result in a favorable immune microenvironment. Nonetheless, the effectiveness of GITR agonism depends on the interplay among Teff stimulation, Treg depletion, and potential Teff depletion at high doses. Therefore, a quantitative understanding of tumor response is critical to identify the optimal dose of anti-GITR antibodies. To this end, Ji et al. developed the QSP model to recapitulate the action of an anti-GITR antibody DTA-1.mIgG2a on two different murine tumor models derived from: 1) Colon26, a colorectal carcinoma cell line and 2) A20, a murine B lymphoma cell line.

### Model Design

2.2
The model includes ordinary differential equations (ODEs) consisting of about 130 reactions and 135 parameters to consider the pharmacokinetics (PK) of the anti-GITR antibody, dynamics of soluble GITR, a simplified GITR signaling cascade, IL-2, IL-10, and cellular components, including CD8+ Teff, Treg, and macrophage expressing FcγIV receptors. The model was developed in a step-by-step manner using a combination of in vivo and in vitro data. This includes data generated by Ji et al. from experiments specifically designed to support model development, such as measurements of serum antibody/soluble GITR concentrations, Teff/Treg profiles, tumor size from Colon26 and A20 mice models treated with anti-GITR antibody, and cell proliferation estimates from in-vitro T cell stimulation assays, in addition to previously generated data from the literature. A simplified schematic of the model is shown in [Fig. 1](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12713570#F1).

The PK module consists of two compartments, central and peripheral compartments that account for the absorption, distribution, metabolism, and elimination (ADME) of the drug. PK parameters were estimated by fitting the model to serum anti-GITR antibody concentration profiles from Colon26 and A20 tumor models. The antibody is assumed to bind to cells expressing GITR and soluble GITR, which leads to target-mediated drug disposition (TMDD), thus recapitulating a fast drug clearance at low doses.

Cell types explicitly considered include Treg, CD8+ Teff, and macrophage expressing FcγIV receptors. The dynamics of Treg and Teff upon drug administration were substantially different between Colon26 and A20 tumor models. To account for this behavior, the authors considered two subpopulations of Tregs: 1) Treg with high GITR (Treg-hi) and 2) Treg with low GITR expression (Treg-low). They hypothesized that the Colon26 tumor had a higher level of Treg-hi subset than the A20 tumor. In addition, the Treg-hi subset was assumed to produce IL-10, which was a surrogate for all Treg-mediated suppressive effects in the model, and Teff was assumed to be inactive in the tumor due to suppression by Treg. These hypotheses were sufficient to recapitulate the differences in Treg dynamics and anti-tumor responses between the two mouse models, which demonstrates the applicability of QSP models in hypothesis testing to explain observed behavior. Subsequently, subsets of Treg and the prevalence of Treg subsets could be experimentally examined in Colon26 and A20 models to verify these hypotheses.

The PK module was coupled with the cellular module of the tumor microenvironment by considering the drug distribution into the tumor. In the tumor compartment, the antibody binds to GITR receptors on Treg. GITR-bound drugs can also bind to FcγIV receptors on macrophages, which leads to the depletion of Treg-hi cells via antibody-dependent cellular phagocytosis (ADCP) by macrophage through a Michaelis-Menten mathematical function. In contrast, Treg-low cells are assumed to be insensitive to ADCP and rather lead to GITR activation due to the formation of trans-complexes by receptor clustering. Depletion of Treg-hi cells leads to a reduction in IL-10 levels that promotes the transition of Teff to an active state. During this transition, Teff is assumed to upregulate GITR expression. Engagement of GITR on Teff in the activated state is assumed to trigger proliferation and differentiation into cytotoxic T lymphocytes (CTL). A positive feedback loop is considered in the model where the activated Teff and CTL secrete IL-2 that triggers Teff activation, proliferation, and differentiation via a stimulatory rate constant and active cell ratio. In addition, activated Teff and CTL tend to lose their sensitivity to IL-2 over time, which leads to a negative feedback loop. It is also assumed that CTL has a limited lifespan, so the number of CTL declines over time in the model.

Soluble GITR, a potential biomarker of CTL activation, was also incorporated into the QSP model. Experimentally measured soluble GITR levels showed an initial increase after drug administration followed by a steep decline. As the differentiation of CD8+ Teff to CTL was assumed to be associated with the shedding of GITR, the model reproduced the increase in soluble GITR levels. The authors added an empirical mechanism of anti-drug antibody (ADA)-mediated clearance of soluble GITR to recapitulate the decline observed in soluble GITR profiles. In addition to the negative feedback by reduced IL-2 sensitivity and limited lifespan of CTLs, ADA-mediated drug clearance contributes to the decrease in the anti-tumor activity over time. [Figure 2](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12713570#F2) shows the model-generated time profiles of Treg and Teff in the Colon26 mouse model.

### Model Application

2.3
Given the competing mechanisms of anti-GITR agonists, the QSP model developed was then used to predict the optimal dose. Different doses of anti-GITR antibodies were simulated using the QSP model to predict the peak number of CTL that was activated under these conditions. As tumor clearance by CTL was not explicitly considered in the model, the minimum number of CTL required to promote tumor clearance in each of the mouse tumor models was estimated using information, such as the tumor size, density of cells in the tumor, and the number of tumor cells that can be typically killed by a CTL. The lowest dose in the model simulations that was predicted to attain the minimum number of CTL estimated to clear the tumor was considered the optimal dose. The model-predicted doses to promote tumor clearance were compared to the in vivo data for model validation.

A local sensitivity analysis was also performed to identify the most influential individual parameters in both tumor models. Parameters were perturbed around their reference parameter values corresponding to Colon26 and A20 tumor models in this analysis. In both tumor models, the most sensitive parameters were those influencing the formation of GITR-drug-FcγIVR complex, tumor drug disposition, drug clearance, and macrophage-related parameters, such as the number of macrophages, GITR expression, and FcγRIV receptor level. These results also suggested that FcγRIV-expressing macrophages and GITR expression may potentially act as predictive biomarkers for anti-GITR therapy.

Overall, this case study demonstrated how a QSP model was built to analyze mechanistic hypotheses and predict optimal doses without considering the full complexity of the tumor microenvironment. The preclinical model by Ji et al. provides an opportunity to study the translatability of preclinical findings to clinical studies. Using human-specific parameters and mechanisms, the murine QSP model could be modified to develop a corresponding human QSP model and used to predict the efficacy of GITR agonists in combination with other drugs. Moreover, the dual mechanism of action of anti-GITR antibodies highlights the importance of QSP models in predicting the starting dose for first-in-human studies.

## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12713570)Case Study 2: A Parsimonious QSP Model of Cell Therapy to Mitigate Cytokine Release Syndrome

3
### Study Objective and Model Design

3.1
Chimeric antigen receptor (CAR)-T cell therapy is another type of immunotherapy in oncology. Through transduction of the patient’s or a donor’s T cells with genes encoding the CAR molecule, CAR-T therapy aims to redirect the specificity and functions of T cells to cancer ([Sadelain et al. 2013](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12713570#R57)). CARs are recombinant receptors that bind to target molecules on the cancer cell surface and activate CAR-T cells through activation and costimulatory domain(s). One of the most common targets of CAR-T therapies is CD19, which is a protein ubiquitously and exclusively expressed on B lymphocytes and thus an ideal target in B-cell malignancies ([Sermer et al. 2023](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12713570#R59)). In 2017, tisagenlecleucel became the first CAR-T therapy approved by the FDA for relapsed and refractory B-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL) ([O’Leary et al. 2019](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12713570#R53)). When administered with a single weight-based or flat dose of up to 2.5e8 cells, tisagenlecleucel achieved an overall remission rate of 83% among 63 patients with ALL ([O’Leary et al. 2019](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12713570#R53)).

Although CAR-T therapies have achieved high efficacy in many blood cancers, one of the limitations is cytokine release syndrome (CRS) caused by the rapid release of cytokines into the blood from activated CAR-T cells ([Sterner and Sterner 2021](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12713570#R64)). In fact, grade 3 or higher CRS was observed in 49% of the patients in the clinical trial of tisagenlecleucel ([O’Leary et al. 2019](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12713570#R53)). To investigate associations among CRS, disease burden, and CAR-T cell doses, Hardiansyah and Ng designed a QSP model to describe the dynamics of activated and memory CAR-T cells in two compartments (peripheral blood and tissues), malignant B cells, and three cytokines contributing to the severity of CRS (IL-6, IL-10, and IFN _γ_) in peripheral blood ([Hardiansyah and Ng 2019](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12713570#R27)).

The choice of cells and molecules to be incorporated into the model was based not only on the known mechanisms of CAR-T cells and cytokines, but also on the availability of relevant clinical data to reduce model uncertainty. Specifically, kinetic profiles of IL-6, IL-10, IFN _γ_, and total number of CAR-T cells were available from two patients with advanced chemotherapy-resistant chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL) from a pilot clinical study of tisagenlecleucel ([Kalos et al. 2011](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12713570#R35)). Although there are other sources of cytokines related to CRS, such as macrophages that secrete IL-6 and IL-1 in response to CAR-T therapy, they are not incorporated due to the lack of clinical measurements. For the same reason, the kinetics of CAR-T cells and malignant B cells in bone marrow, which are also important components in CLL, are not explicitly described by the model.

[Figure 3](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12713570#F3) demonstrates the incorporated model mechanisms. In addition to cytokine secretion by endogenous immune cells and activated CAR-T cells upon recognition of CD19-expressing tumor B cells, IL-10 inhibits IFN _γ_ production directly by targeting activated CAR-T cells, and also indirectly by reprogramming macrophages and preventing APC maturation, thereby limiting pro-inflammatory cytokine secretion ([Iyer and Cheng 2012](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12713570#R30)). Here, the direct effect of IL-10 was described by a multiplier empirically determined in a model of helper T cell trans-differentiation ([Kogan et al. 2013](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12713570#R37)). Particularly, **1** − **_a_****_G_** is the maximum inhibitory effect of IL-10 on IFN _γ_ production, and **_b_****_G_** is the IL-10 concentration that would result in its half-maximal inhibitory effect. Since macrophages and other immune cells were not explicitly incorporated into the model, the indirect effect of IL-10 on IFN _γ_ production was reflected via parameterization, which will be discussed below.

Kinetics of CAR-T cells in peripheral blood (PB) involves proliferation, death, and two reversible processes: 1) transport between peripheral blood and tissues (T) and 2) differentiation between effector and memory CAR-T cells. Differentiation between effector (CARTE) and memory (CARTM) CAR-T cells was assumed to follow a Michaelis-Menten model of B cells, f(B). Further, the kinetics of B cells (B) in peripheral blood involves proliferation, death, and effector CAR-T cell-mediated killing.

### Model Parameterization

3.2
Among the 23 model parameters, 13 parameters were obtained from the literature. Degradation rates of the cytokines were estimated by experimentally measured half-lives; **_a_****_G_** and **_b_****_G_** were estimated based on the inhibitory effect of IL-10 on IFN _γ_ production by type 1 helper T cells, which can be potentially improved by data from personalized CAR-T cells if available as they contain different proportions of CD8+ and CD4+ cells. The proliferation rate of memory CAR-T cells was assumed to be the same as that of regular CD8+ CD45RO+ T cells whose doubling times were measured by in vivo experiments ([Macallan et al. 2003](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12713570#R45)). With the same assumption, rates of transport between peripheral blood and tissues, **_k_****_in_**_and_**_k_****_out_**, were estimated by clinically measured rates of intravascular and extravascular CD8 T cells ([Storek et al. 2002](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12713570#R66)); and the rate of memory CAR-T cell activation, **_k_****diff**, was assumed to be 1 day−1 ([De Boer and Perelson 2013](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12713570#R17)). The death rate of memory CAR-T cells was estimated by the rate of exponential decline after effector CAR-T cell expansion observed in patients treated with CAR-T therapy, which was much higher than that of regular memory T cells ([Kalos et al. 2011](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12713570#R35)). For malignant B cells, the rate of proliferation and natural death were measured in 15 patients with CLL ([Messmer et al. 2005](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12713570#R49)); and the B-CLL cell level that leads to half-maximal CAR-T cell activation, **_K_****_B_**, was originally fitted to an experiment of macrophage-mediated killing of tumor cells ([De Boer et al. 1985](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12713570#R18)). Notably, saturation parameters in Michaelis-Menten kinetics are often hard to be directly derived from published experimental data and thus could be estimated by indirect experimental results, a dedicated experiment designed for parameter estimation, or an educated guess.

The remaining 10 model parameters were fitted to data from each patient in the pilot clinical study, including cytokine secretion by endogenous immune cells and CAR-T cells, rates of effector CAR-T cell proliferation, death, differentiation to memory CAR-T cells, and CAR-T cell-mediated killing. The clinical data contain measurements of cytokine concentrations (i.e., IL-6, IL-10, and IFN _γ_) and total CAR-T cell level (i.e., _CARTE_ _PB_ + _CARTM_ _PB_) at multiple time points from day 0 to day 176 upon CAR-T cell injection ([Kalos et al. 2011](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12713570#R35)). Importantly, since endogenous immune cells were not explicitly incorporated into this model, the impact of CAR-T therapy on endogenous cytokine secretion was reflected through parameterization. Specifically, the rate of endogenous cytokine secretion before CAR-T cells were administered was fitted to the patient’s baseline cytokine concentration, while after the therapy began, it was fitted to the steady-state cytokine concentration at the end of the therapy.

### Model Applications

3.3
As introduced at the beginning of this case study, the model was designed specifically to investigate the associations between CRS and potential risk factors, including disease burden and CAR-T dose amount. To this end, 8 ODEs were used to describe 5 cellular and 3 molecular species/cytokines ([Fig. 3](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12713570#F3)). The initial condition of all model species, by which model simulation was started, was personalized according to the data from two adult patients UPN1 and UPN3 in the clinical study ([Kalos et al. 2011](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12713570#R35)). Cytokine concentrations were initialized by their measured baseline levels, and the pre-treatment number of B-CLL cells was estimated by the measured number of white blood cells in each patient with the assumption that B cells account for about 40% of the total white blood cells. The initial number of effector CAR-T cells corresponds to the number of cells administered for each patient, while memory CAR-T cells and all CAR-T cells in tissues were initialized with 0 cells. CAR-T cells were administered via 3 doses of intravenous infusion, which was simulated by SimBiology.

For each of the two patients, Hardiansyah and Ng conducted 1,000 model simulations with different CAR-T doses and the initial number of B-CLL cells in the peripheral blood (i.e., disease burden) varied within the clinically observed ranges. For visual validation, the model-predicted pharmacokinetics of CAR-T cells, including maximal CAR-T level in blood and the area under the plasma drug concentration-time curve from day 0 to day 28, were compared with clinical measurements in a later study of tisagenlecleucel ([Hardiansyah and Ng 2019](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12713570#R27)). In addition, the model-predicted relationships between pre-treatment disease burden and maximal CAR-T/IFN _γ_ level in blood were consistent with clinical observation in ALL treated with anti-CD19 CAR-T therapy ([Hardiansyah and Ng 2019](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12713570#R27)).

Once validated, the QSP model was used to investigate the correlation between CAR-T cell dose/disease burden and concentration of cytokines that contribute to CRS in CLL. To this end, the CAR-T cell dose and disease burden were varied by 0.5, 1, 1.5, and two-fold from baseline for each patient. As shown in [Fig. 4](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12713570#F4), the model predicted that the concentration of all cytokines would increase faster and reach a higher maximal concentration as the pre-treatment disease burden increased, while the dose of CAR-T cells had little impact on the cytokine kinetics. Interestingly, in a recent clinical study that analyzed data from 15 pediatric oncology centers, the dose of tisagenlecleucel was not found to be associated with CRS when administered with 1.3–5.1e6 cells/kg ([Stefanski et al. 2023](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12713570#R63)). In summary, this case study demonstrated that a relatively simple QSP model trained by data from early-stage clinical trials can be used to address questions relating to pharmacokinetics and certain toxic effects of the drug(s). By generating random deviations from the two patient models, QSP can inform clinicians about the risk factors for CRS without extensive clinical data collection. Based on the model prediction, future clinical studies can be designed to confirm the correlation between disease burden and CRS and to explore disease burden-based CAR-T dosing to mitigate CRS.

## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12713570)Case Study 3: A Modular Whole-body QSP Platform of the Cancer Immunity Cycle to Identify Biomarkers and Optimal Drug Combinations for Cancer Immunotherapy

4
### Study Objective

4.1
Immune checkpoint blockade is another type of immunotherapy. Immune checkpoints are molecules expressed on the surface of immune cells that maintain self-tolerance and modulate immune response through downstream signaling pathways ([Pardoll 2012](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12713570#R54)). They are also used by cancer cells as an immune evasion mechanism to create an immuno-suppressive tumor microenvironment and inhibit T cell activation in the lymph nodes. Through the blockade of immune checkpoint molecules, immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs) aim to restore the functions of immune cells and facilitate antitumoral response in patients. The common targets of ICIs are cytotoxic T-lymphocyte-associated protein 4 (CTLA-4), programmed cell death protein 1 (PD-1), and its ligand PD-L1. Due to their promising effect observed in clinical trials, ICIs have become the standard-of-care treatment for multiple cancer types, such as melanoma, lung cancer, triple-negative breast cancer, and head and neck carcinoma. Nonetheless, the efficacy of ICIs varies among different cancer types. Although tumor mutational burden and PD-L1 expression are found to be correlated with response to anti-PD-(L)1 therapies in some cancer types ([Yarchoan et al. 2017](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12713570#R82); [Davis and Patel 2019](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12713570#R16)), there is a need to identify predictive biomarkers in the context of specific cancer types, especially those with low overall response rate to ICIs, and to improve the efficacy of ICIs via combination therapy. To address this gap, a modular and expandable QSP platform model has been developed as detailed below.

### Model Design

4.2
Since immune checkpoints have inhibitory effects on both the tumor microenvironment and lymph nodes, it is important to investigate the cancer-immune cell interactions in both compartments. To this end, Milberg et al. ([Wang et al. 2019](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12713570#R73); [Milberg et al. 2019](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12713570#R50)) built a QSP model to describe the cancer-immunity cycle with extensive mechanistic detail, which was later developed into a modular QSP platform, QSP-IO ([Jafarnejad et al. 2019](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12713570#R31); [Sové et al. 2020](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12713570#R62)). The latest version of the platform consists of ten modules, each of which describes the dynamics of a major cellular/molecular species in the model, including cancer cells, T cells (Teff, Treg, and helper T cell), antigen-presenting cells, tumor antigens, immune checkpoints, therapeutic agents (e.g., ICIs, T cell engagers), myeloid-derived suppressor cells (MDSCs), and tumor-associated macrophages (TAMs) ([Wang et al. 2022](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12713570#R76), [2023](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12713570#R77); [Anbari et al. 2023](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12713570#R2); [Arulraj et al. 2023](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12713570#R4); [Ippolito et al. 2023](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12713570#R29)). The modular structure of the model has proven its capability to serve different study objectives. Particularly, some modules can be called more than once to account for different clones of cancer cells, T cells, tumor antigens, etc. In addition, new modules developed for drugs of interest, when incorporated into the QSP model, can be used to simulate combination therapies with ICIs ([Wang et al. 2020](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12713570#R74), [2021](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12713570#R75); [Ma et al. 2020a](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12713570#R43), [b](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12713570#R44)) or novel ICIs with more complex mechanisms of activation, such as a masked antibody ([Ippolito et al. 2023](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12713570#R29)). When integrated with an agent-based model, the spatial QSP model (spQSP) can also investigate spatial heterogeneities in the tumor microenvironment during treatment ([Gong et al. 2021](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12713570#R25); [Zhang et al. 2021](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12713570#R83); [Ruiz-Martinez et al. 2022](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12713570#R56); [Nikfar et al. 2023](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12713570#R52)).

One of the challenges in mechanistic modeling is generating hypotheses for causal mechanisms based on the limited experimental/clinical observations ([Baker et al. 2018](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12713570#R7)). [Figure 5](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12713570#F5) shows all the mechanisms incorporated into the QSP-IO model. Here, we discuss the major mechanisms included in the model. First, the growth of cancer cells can be described by a variety of models, such as exponential, logistic, and Gompertz models. When fitting different models to tumor growth kinetics in 94 animals (including 833 measurements and 3 tumor models), Vaghi et al. concluded that the Gompertz model best predicted the tumor growth and the age of tumors in mice ([Vaghi et al. 2020](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12713570#R72)). Notably, the performance of the Gompertz model depended on the initial tumor size, which corresponded to the volume of the injected tumor and was fixed to 1 mm 3. For clinical translation, Vaghi et al. suggested an initial tumor volume of 10−6 mm 3 (i.e., a single cancer cell), while Garcia-Cremades et al. set the initial tumor volume to the measured tumor size at diagnosis in a translational model of pancreatic and ovarian tumor growth in human ([Garcia-Cremades et al. 2019](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12713570#R23)). Another consideration is the effect of angiogenesis, which can be reflected by a time-dependent tumor-carrying capacity. Hahnfeldt et al. proposed a modified Gompertz model to describe the induction and inhibition of tumor vasculature, which were used in multiple translational models to simulate tumor growth in humans ([Hahnfeldt et al. 1999](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12713570#R26)). More recently, Sayama et al. developed an angiogenesis-driven tumor growth model that explicitly incorporated the effect of mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAPK) signaling ([Sayama et al. 2021](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12713570#R58); [Zhang et al. 2023](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12713570#R85)). Due to the lack of clinical measurements of uncontrolled tumor growth, the performance of various growth models in predicting tumor kinetics in humans and their therapeutic implications require further investigation ([West and Newton 2019](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12713570#R78); [Ghaffari Laleh et al. 2022](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12713570#R24)). In QSP-IO, the cancer module allows switching between the Gompertzian and the logistic tumor growth kinetics to accommodate various study goals and data available ([Wang et al. 2023](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12713570#R77)).

Further, it was found that T cell activation occurs in three stages: transient encounters with APCs, stable contacts with APCs and cytokine production, and rapid proliferation ([Mempel et al. 2004](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12713570#R47)). The first step is modeled as native T cells are activated at a rate estimated by the ratio of mature APCs and native T cells. Once activated, T cells secrete IL-2 and transition to the proliferation stage when they become functional T cells (e.g., Teff, Treg). The number of T cell divisions during rapid proliferation is found to be the linear sum of the effect of three signals: T cell receptor (TCR) upon recognition of peptide-major histocompatibility complex (MHC), co-stimulation, and inflammatory stimuli. The peptide-MHC (pMHC) complex is expressed on APCs upon antigen uptake and processing. In the antigen module of QSP-IO, this process was adapted from a multiscale model of immunogenicity for therapeutic proteins by substituting the antigenic and competing proteins with tumor neoantigens and tumor-associated self-antigens, respectively ([Chen et al. 2014](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12713570#R15)). Assuming that tumor antigens are released from cancer cells at the same rate as the overall cancer cell death, the module describes the internalization, degradation, MHC binding of tumor antigens, and the translocation of the pMHC complex. Then, the total number of TCR bound with pMHC complexes was approximated by the “kinetic proofreading with limited signaling” model, which was found to best describe the experimental data, and used to estimate the number of T cell divisions by TCR via a Michaelis-Menten kinetics ([Lever et al. 2014](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12713570#R40)). Next, the interactions among CD80, CD86, CD28, and CTLA-4 were incorporated by the checkpoint module ([Jansson et al. 2005](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12713570#R32)), where the number of T cell divisions by co-stimulation is estimated by a Hill function of bound CD28 on the surface of APCs in lymph nodes. Alternatively, the ratio between bound CD28 and bound CTLA-4 in the immune synapse can be incorporated into the Hill function to account for the regulatory effects of CTLA-4 signaling. Lastly, the number of T cell divisions by inflammatory stimuli is estimated by a Hill function of IL-2.

When modeling interactions among receptors, ligands, and therapeutic antibodies, binding affinity, avidity, and cross-arm binding efficiency should be considered. Binding affinities are the strength of interactions between receptors and ligands and are equal to the ratio of dissociation and association rates, which depend on the type of interaction and external physical properties and can be measured by in vitro experiments ([Jarmoskaite et al. 2020](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12713570#R33); [Erlendsson and Teilum 2021](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12713570#R20)). Binding avidity, or functional affinity, accounts for cooperativity and multivalency when describing the changes in the rate of association and dissociation between two interacting molecules ([Erlendsson and Teilum 2021](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12713570#R20)). For example, CTLA-4 and CD80 often exist as homodimers on the surface of T cells and APCs, respectively. As a result, the rate of association between CTLA-4 and CD80 with a total of 4 free binding sites should be 4 times higher than that between CTLA-4 and CD80 monomers. It is thus important to note how binding affinity is measured in experimental studies by which model parameters are estimated. Moreover, cross-arm binding efficiency is a property of antibodies that describes the strength of cross-arm binding relative to monovalent binding. Harms et al. defined cross-arm binding as the binding between the free arm of a bivalent antibody and its target when the other arm is already bound, and they showed how mechanistic modeling of cross-arm binding can inform therapeutic antibody designs ([Harms et al. 2014](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12713570#R28)).

### Model Parameterization and Applications

4.3
The QSP-IO platform has 255 parameters with 10 modules, including 1 cancer clone, 1 T cell clone, 1 tumor neoantigen clone, and 1 tumor compartment that represents a primary or a metastatic tumor. Among all the parameters, less than 10% of the parameters are tumor-specific parameters. These are estimated by data on the cancer type of interest. Other parameters are mostly related to the immune system and are estimated by data from experimental studies and healthy individuals. When considering 1 primary and up to 3 metastatic lesions (i.e., 4 tumor compartments), the model was expanded to have 737 parameters with 5 cancer clones, 8 neoantigens, and 8 effector T cell specificities ([Arulraj et al. 2023](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12713570#R4)). Notably, cross-reactivity of effector T cells is not accounted for in this model.

The platform has been applied to multiple cancer types that have received limited survival benefits from currently FDA-approved immunotherapies to predict the efficacy of newly discovered drugs and novel drug combinations via in silico virtual clinical trials. In silico virtual clinical trials aim to simulate tumor response to treatments of interest in virtual patients represented by parameter variations. In most cases, tumor-specific parameters were varied around their baseline values within a physiologically reasonable range to account for inter-patient heterogeneity. Recently, as patient-level data became available, additional algorithms were applied to further select virtual patients that better mimic the actual patient cohort ([Allen et al. 2016](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12713570#R1)). In addition, by integrating transcriptomic data from metastatic breast tumors into the model, Arulraj et al. predicted the clinical response of metastatic lesions to PD-1 inhibition and proposed the responder inclusion score (RIS) to identify patients with the maximized probability of response ([Arulraj et al. 2023](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12713570#R4), [2024](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12713570#R5)).

[Figure 6](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12713570#F6) shows an example of the QSP-IO model predictions from an in silico clinical trial of a PD-1 inhibitor with 1 primary breast tumor compartment and 3 metastatic tumor compartments (i.e., 2 lung metastases and 1 “other” metastatic tumor). Parameters of the metastatic tumor compartments were estimated so that the relative abundance of immune cells with respect to the primary tumor compartment is consistent with immune cell abundances estimated from RNA-seq data ([Siegel et al. 2018](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12713570#R61)) using EPIC ([Racle et al. 2017](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12713570#R55)) and quanTIseq ([Finotello et al. 2019](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12713570#R21)). Waterfall and spider plots are two common visualizations in clinical analyses showing the best tumor size change from baseline in each patient ([Fig. 6a](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12713570#F6)) and the percentage change in tumor size from baseline over time ([Fig. 6b](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12713570#F6)). Here, tumor size is the sum of the diameters of each tumor as defined by RECIST v1.1 ([Eisenhauer et al. 2009](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12713570#R19)). In addition, [Fig. 6c](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12713570#F6) illustrates typical tumor dynamics that fall within each category of clinical response. In this way, the model can make personalized predictions of tumor growth under treatment when parameterized to individual patients’ data, laying the groundwork for future precision medicine applications.

args.summary:
This scientific article (Handb Exp Pharmacol, 2025;289:261, doi:10.1007/164_2024_735, PMID: 39707022) from the Popel lab at Johns Hopkins reviews the role of Quantitative Systems Pharmacology (QSP) modeling in immuno-oncology, covering hypothesis testing, dose optimization, and efficacy prediction through three detailed case studies.

Background: Cancer remains a leading cause of death worldwide, with over 19 million new cases and nearly 10 million deaths in 2022. Oncology trials have among the lowest success rates. From 2016-2021, 207 cancer drugs were FDA-approved but only 28 displaced standard-of-care treatments. The median time from drug discovery to approval is 12 years. Since 2013, QSP models have played increasing roles in regulatory submissions, with 22% of FDA QSP submissions relating to oncology.

Case Study 1 (GITR Agonist): A murine QSP model of anti-GITR antibodies (DTA-1.mIgG2a) was developed for two tumor models (Colon26 colorectal carcinoma and A20 B-lymphoma). The ~130-reaction, 135-parameter ODE model captured PK with target-mediated drug disposition, two Treg subpopulations (GITR-high and GITR-low), ADCP-mediated Treg depletion via FcγIV receptors on macrophages, and Teff activation/proliferation. The model was used for hypothesis testing (explaining differing Treg dynamics between tumor models) and predicting optimal doses based on a minimum CTL threshold for tumor clearance. Sensitivity analysis identified GITR expression and FcγRIV-expressing macrophages as potential predictive biomarkers.

Case Study 2 (CAR-T Cell Therapy): A parsimonious QSP model of tisagenlecleucel (first FDA-approved CAR-T therapy, 2017) was developed to investigate cytokine release syndrome (CRS) risk factors. Of 23 parameters, 13 came from literature and 10 were fitted to data from two CLL patients. The model described effector/memory CAR-T cell kinetics, malignant B cells, and three cytokines (IL-6, IL-10, IFN-γ). Model simulations (1,000 per patient) predicted that disease burden, rather than CAR-T dose, was the primary driver of CRS severity—a finding later confirmed clinically (no dose-CRS association in a 15-center pediatric study).

Case Study 3 (QSP-IO Platform): A modular whole-body QSP platform of the cancer immunity cycle (10 modules covering cancer cells, T cells, APCs, antigens, checkpoints, drugs, MDSCs, TAMs) was described. The 255-parameter base model expands to 737 parameters with metastatic compartments. Key mechanistic features include Gompertzian tumor growth, three-stage T cell activation, TCR/pMHC "kinetic proofreading with limited signaling," and CD28/CTLA-4 checkpoint interactions. Applications include in silico virtual clinical trials, prediction of metastatic breast cancer response to PD-1 inhibition, and the responder inclusion score (RIS) for patient selection.

The article concludes that QSP is a diverse modeling approach without unified development methods, and demonstrates how models can support model-informed drug development through hypothesis testing, dose optimization, and efficacy prediction in immuno-oncology.

# Benefits & Uses of QSP in Drug Development

![Benefits & Uses of QSP in Drug Development](https://www.allucent.com/wp-content/uploads/2020/07/Benefits-and-Uses-of-GSP-in-Drug-Development-e1757437546433.webp)

**Overview**

Quantitative Systems Pharmacology (QSP) uses biological pathways, pharmacology, and computer modeling to make better decisions about drug development by predicting how well drugs will work, improving study design, and lowering the number of failures that happen late in the process. QSP models combine different types of data to help plan clinical trials and find new targets. This makes it easier to make decisions from the preclinical to the clinical stages.

Quantitative systems pharmacology (QSP) is an exciting and powerful convergence of biological pathways, pharmacology, and mathematical models for drug development. QSP has the potential to deliver a significant impact on modern medicine through the discovery and utilization of new molecular pathways and drug targets in the pursuit of novel therapeutics and individualized medicine. Individually, the concepts and components of QSP (studies of biology and drugs) are not new. However, merging these disciplines is generating considerable interest in the pharmaceutical industry to maximize predictions from a pharmacodynamic (PD) perspective, and with the use of advancements in computing power, QSP is now able to improve outcomes in drug development. Many drug candidates fail in Phase 1 due to poor pharmacokinetic (PK) properties or fail in Phase 2 due to less-than-expected efficacy. QSP offers the ability to evaluate critical aspects related to the efficacy of a drug candidate and provide a ‘road map’ to designing Phase 2 clinical studies to potentially improve outcomes. Ideally, QSP would be applied throughout the drug development process, from pre-clinical through [clinical development](https://www.allucent.com/solutions/clinical-development-service), to harness its true power and capacity.

## What is QSP?

QSP is a computational model that examines the interface between discrete experimental data (i.e., studies of the drug/compound) and the “system.” The “system” can be any biological process related to the disease such as the physiological consequences of a disease, a specific disease pathway (e.g., signal transduction or up/down regulation of a pathway, increased heart rate), or any of the “omics” (i.e., genomics, proteomics, metabolomics). Tapping into the “omics” generates substantial opportunities to learn from big data systems by looking for intersecting themes. While “omics” data are not likely to lead to definitive directions during drug development on their own, their coupling with QSP can result in powerful insights that decrease uncertainty at key decision points in the development process. QSP can help guide appropriate study design or suggest what additional experiments might be needed to make more informed choices. Similarly, QSP can greatly reduce missteps that might prolong the drug development process or even result in an unnecessary failure. For example, one way that utilizing big data in QSP can glean powerful insights into drug development is by integrating regulative and metabolic biological pathways with novel drug compound mechanisms to accelerate the pace of innovation with the identification of overlapping moieties. These insights can aid in exploiting possible additive or synergistic effects, planning around potential setbacks, and redesigning experimental direction at critical times during the early stages of the drug development process to help thwart unnecessary failures. As previously unknown and intersecting disease pathways are discovered, QSP can be leveraged to identify new targets, verify current targets, understand potential adverse effects of novel pathways, and repurpose existing drugs to new targets. QSP has built on the insights gained in developing physiologically based pharmacokinetic (PBPK) models (ex: blood flow rates, organ volumes, transporter expression, etc.) and has truly taken the power of understanding drug action to a new level.

## QSP Modeling vs. PBPK Modeling

QSP and PBPK are similar in that both systems are developed with a “bottom-up” approach. However, the difference between QSP and PBPK is that PBPK predicts PK outcomes in patient populations, whereas QSP predicts PD and clinical efficacy outcomes in patient populations. QSP uses biological systems of the therapeutic target for PD outcomes (i.e. predicting heart-rate changes, muscle growth rate, etc.). This is especially important for decision-making based on scaling PD outcomes from animal models to humans and recommending clinical doses in trials.

## When to Use QSP Modeling in Drug Development

QSP can be employed at all stages of drug development (pre-clinical to Phase 3). Given the amount of experimental data generated for diseases, genetics, drug binding, metabolism, polymorphisms, biological pathways, inter-relationships between systems, information from big data, and more, coupled with the availability of necessary computational power, QSP is primed to change the landscape of drug development. Some key factors to consider that can be explored with QSP:

* **Mechanism of Action** – new and old drugs, possible repurposing
* **Simplifying Pathways** – distinguishing between relevant and irrelevant pathways in complex biological systems
* **Important Determinants of Exposure** – pharmacogenomics (rapid/normal or reduced metabolizer of various drug-metabolizing enzymes; transporter expression); drug-drug and drug-gene interactions
* **Efficacy** – define interspecies differences in the expression levels and characteristics of biological targets leading to improved translational understanding of PK/PD responses across species, for better prediction of clinical outcomes from pre-clinical models
* **Comorbidity** – impact and implications on the PD response such as liver disease, kidney disease, heart failure, gastrointestinal variations, etc.
* **Special Populations** – forecasting results of perturbations to the system (such as in pediatrics where receptor expression or endogenous pathways may still be developing relative to adult populations) in a population of *in silico* patients – verifying actions of responses to novel targets and therapeutic agents
* **Dosing Regimen** – choosing doses, rational selection of combination therapies, and dose frequency for different patient populations

### Examples of When to Use QSP

#### 1. Predicting Drug Response

One major use of QSP is to forecast drug responses resulting from perturbations in the system in populations of *in silico* patients before running clinical trials. For example, perturbations might include deteriorating liver function or the biological effects of pregnancy. Responses to these perturbations might include alterations in drug-metabolizing enzyme expression or receptor occupancy needed for therapeutic effect, causing possible alterations in outcomes on clinical trial endpoints. This can be proactively analyzed using computer models to predict PD responses and verify predictions in animal models of disease to predict outcomes in healthy volunteers and other patient populations. Confirmation of clinical responses to biomarkers in healthy volunteers further improves predictions and study design for Phase II trials, in special populations or in selecting appropriate target populations.

#### 2. Integrative Models

QSP has also been shown to be useful in integrative drug-disease models within academia, the pharmaceutical industry, and the FDA for disease areas such as [oncology](https://www.allucent.com/therapeutic-expertise/hematology-oncology-cro), metabolic disorders, neurology, cardiology, pulmonary, and auto-immune diseases, to name a few. The scope and application of QSP, specifically within oncology ranges from combination regimens, immunotherapy and exploring specific pathways such as VEGFR, ERK, PD-(L)1, MEK, AKT, BRAF, and others.

#### 3. Efficacy & Safety

Another capability of QSP is to highlight efficacy and safety concerns through the interactive evolution of a QSP model. This has been used to predict cardiovascular effects using blood pressure and heart rate, identify peripheral resistance, predict hERG mediated Qtc prolongation, linking biomarkers to cell injury and renal dysfunction, or explaining drug-induced liver injury and how to avoid it.

## Benefits of QSP for Drug Development

QSP can save valuable resources during drug development, and importantly, reduce the time to getting therapies to the patients in need. QSP can facilitate the decision-making process in order to get the right drug, to the right patient, for the right disease, at the right time, and in the right dose. In programs where the first clinical study will be in a patient population such as in a [rare disease](https://www.allucent.com/therapeutic-expertise/rare-disease-cro) or in [cell and gene therapies](https://www.allucent.com/therapeutic-expertise/cell-and-gene-therapy), the need to predict a therapeutic dose for the first in human dose is crucial. QSP offers the ability to help make these critical and ethical decisions with more confidence. Having an early understanding of what QSP can provide can guide the design of therapeutics from the very beginning of the drug discovery process.

## Conclusions

QSP can help guide critical choices for valuable resources by providing important and timely pieces of knowledge. With QSP we now have the ability to predict how a patient might respond or provide a further therapeutic understanding that was previously unknown which is extremely valuable throughout the entire drug development process. QSP is becoming an increasingly powerful component of drug development. The power of combining experimental, biological, and physiochemical data for model-informed decision-making is just beginning to be harnessed. Others are surely to follow as our knowledge and understanding of the potential of QSP continues to develop.  [Contact us](https://www.allucent.com/contact) to learn more about Allucent’s QSP experience and services.

## FAQs

Quantitative Systems Pharmacology (QSP) is a way to use computers to model how drugs work in biological systems, how they work in disease pathways, and how they work in experiments. It helps make decisions during drug development and guess what will happen in the clinic.

QSP helps drug development by making it easier to predict how well a drug will work and how safe it will be, helping to plan studies, lowering the number of unexpected failures, and improving treatment plans. It uses data and computing power to help make decisions from the early stages of discovery to the clinical stages.

QSP can be used at any point in the drug development process, from preclinical research to Phase 3 clinical trials. It helps with translational insights and model-informed decisions throughout the entire life cycle of a drug candidate.

Both QSP and physiologically based pharmacokinetics (PBPK) use bottom-up modeling, but PBPK is more interested in predicting pharmacokinetic outcomes like distribution and exposure, while QSP is more interested in predicting pharmacodynamic effects and clinical efficacy by modeling how drugs interact with biological systems.

Yes. QSP can show how different biological and omics data interact, find new targets, understand side effects, and help repurpose existing drugs for new medical uses.

# Digital Twins in Clinical Trials: Synthetic Control Arms and FDA’s Evolving Posture

What an AI-generated digital twin is, how it’s used to shrink a real placebo/control arm via covariate adjustment, the Unlearn.AI/PROCOVA precedent, and FDA’s evolving (not yet settled) regulatory posture.

## Ask about Digital Twins in Clinical Trials: Synthetic Control Arms and FDA’s Evolving Posture

Answers are drawn from this guide and the rest of the CASRAI corpus, with a link to every source.

A **digital twin** in the clinical trial context is an AI-generated, patient-specific prediction of how an individual trial participant would have progressed under a reference condition (typically standard of care or placebo), built from that participant’s own baseline characteristics combined with statistical patterns learned from historical trial data, registries, and other real-world data. The goal is not to replace a control group with pure simulation, but to use these individualized forecasts to make a real, smaller control arm carry more statistical weight — reducing the number of trial participants who need to be randomized to placebo or standard-of-care while preserving the study’s statistical power.

This is an actively developing area of methodology and regulatory policy, not a settled one. This page describes the concept, how it is built, the strongest verifiable regulatory precedent to date, and where the open questions and skepticism sit as of mid-2026. Claims about specific regulatory status are marked as such and should be checked against primary sources before being relied on for a live protocol, since guidance in this area is genuinely still moving.

## What “digital twin” means in this context — and what it doesn’t

The term is used loosely across the industry, so it is worth separating three related but distinct ideas that are often conflated:

## How a digital twin / prognostic covariate adjustment model is built

The general pipeline described across vendors and published methodology work follows a consistent pattern:

Because the prediction is generated from pre-randomization baseline data only, and is used as a covariate rather than as a substitute outcome, this design differs from naively “simulating” trial results — the actual outcome data from real randomized participants still drives the primary treatment-effect estimate.

## The clearest regulatory precedent: Unlearn.AI and PROCOVA

The most frequently cited real-world precedent is Unlearn.AI’s **PROCOVA** (Prognostic Covariate Adjustment) methodology, which is publicly reported to have received a qualification opinion from the **European Medicines Agency (EMA)** in September 2022 — the first time a European regulator formally qualified a machine-learning-based covariate adjustment method for use in reducing sample size in pivotal trials. Unlearn.AI has also reported receiving positive FDA feedback supporting use of the method in covariate-adjusted analyses. This is REPORTED-tier information corroborated across the vendor’s own published materials and independent industry coverage rather than a primary EMA/FDA document reviewed directly for this page — sponsors evaluating the method for a live protocol should confirm current qualification status and scope directly with EMA and FDA rather than relying on secondary summaries, since qualification opinions are typically scoped to a specific methodology and context of use, not a blanket endorsement of “digital twins” as a category.

## FDA’s regulatory posture: engaged, but explicitly cautious and not yet settled

It is important not to overstate where FDA currently stands. The clearest primary-source evidence of FDA’s posture toward AI-generated evidence generally (not digital twins specifically) is a draft guidance, [“Considerations for the Use of Artificial Intelligence to Support Regulatory Decision-Making for Drug and Biological Products,”](https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2025/01/07/2024-31542/considerations-for-the-use-of-artificial-intelligence-to-support-regulatory-decision-making-for-drug) issued January 6, 2025 (comment period closed April 7, 2025; as of this writing it remains draft guidance, not final). The draft guidance proposes a risk-based, seven-step credibility assessment framework for any AI model used to support a regulatory submission: define the question of interest, define the context of use, assess model risk, develop and execute a credibility assessment plan, document results and any deviations, and determine whether the model’s output is adequate for its specific context of use. This framework applies broadly to AI use across nonclinical, clinical, post-marketing, and manufacturing phases — it is not a digital-twin-specific policy, but it is the framework a sponsor proposing a digital-twin-augmented control arm would need to work within.

Separately, FDA’s longer-running **Complex Innovative Trial Design (CID)** pilot meeting program (established under PDUFA VI) gives sponsors a channel to discuss novel statistical and trial-design approaches — including model-informed and simulation-based designs — with the agency before a pivotal trial, and digital-twin-augmented designs are the kind of approach sponsors have used that channel for. A CID pilot meeting is a discussion mechanism, not an approval or a blanket endorsement, and outcomes are specific to the sponsor and protocol involved.

Taken together: FDA has engaged directly with AI-generated covariate adjustment and has given positive feedback in at least the Unlearn.AI/PROCOVA case reported above, and it has published a general framework for assessing AI model credibility. That is meaningfully different from FDA having issued a general endorsement, qualification, or approval of “digital twins” as a category for pivotal trial control arms — each use case is still evaluated on its own methodology, data provenance, and context of use. Sponsors should treat this as an active, evolving regulatory conversation and confirm current agency posture directly (including through FDA’s own guidance page and, where appropriate, a CID or other pre-submission meeting) rather than assuming a settled pathway.

## Open questions and the validation debate

Coverage of digital twins in trial design consistently raises a set of unresolved concerns that sponsors and IRBs are actively working through, rather than issues that have been fully resolved:

## Why sponsors are pursuing this

The underlying motivation is consistent across the reporting on this topic: fewer participants need to be randomized to placebo or standard-of-care, which can reduce enrollment timelines, lower the ethical burden of withholding an investigational treatment from participants (particularly relevant in serious or rare diseases with few effective alternatives), and reduce overall trial cost — all without changing what the trial is powered to detect, if the covariate adjustment is done well. This is the same underlying motivation behind the broader push toward [decentralized clinical trial designs](/guides/decentralized-clinical-trials) and adaptive methodologies more generally: using statistical and operational innovation to make a trial less burdensome to run without weakening its evidentiary value.

## How this relates to other AI use in trials and to data monitoring

Digital twins are one specific, statistically-grounded application within the broader landscape covered in CASRAI’s [AI in Clinical Trials guide](/guides/ai-in-clinical-trials) — which surveys patient recruitment matching, site feasibility, protocol simulation, and safety-signal detection more broadly and situates this same FDA draft guidance in that wider context. For the general regulatory framework FDA is building for AI across drug development and device review, see CASRAI’s [FDA AI Guidance](/guides/fda-ai-guidance) guide.

Because a digital-twin-augmented control arm still relies on a real, monitored control group, the same data-quality and oversight expectations that apply to any trial arm still apply here — see CASRAI’s dictionary entry on [Risk-Based Monitoring (RBM)](/dictionary/term/risk-based-monitoring-rbm) for how sponsors prioritize monitoring resources toward the data points that matter most to a trial’s conclusions, and the [Clinical Trial Monitoring guide](/guides/clinical-trial-monitoring) for how monitoring visit types and source data verification work in practice.

## Frequently asked questions

### Is a digital twin the same as a synthetic control arm?

Not exactly. “Synthetic control arm” and “external control arm” more commonly refer to using an existing dataset (a prior trial’s control arm, a registry, or real-world data) as some or all of a trial’s comparator, a technique FDA has engaged with for longer, often in single-arm oncology or rare-disease trials. “Digital twin” as currently used most often refers specifically to an AI model generating a per-participant predicted outcome used as a statistical covariate to shrink — not replace — a real, concurrently randomized control arm. The terms are sometimes used loosely and interchangeably in industry writing, so it is worth clarifying which specific technique a given source or vendor means.

### Has the FDA approved digital twins for clinical trials?

Not as a blanket policy. FDA has given positive feedback on at least one specific methodology (Unlearn.AI’s PROCOVA, as publicly reported) and has published a general draft framework (January 2025) for assessing the credibility of any AI model used in a regulatory submission, but there is no general FDA approval or qualification of “digital twins” as a category. Each proposed use is evaluated on its own data, model, and context of use, and the January 2025 framework remains in draft form as of this writing.

### Does using a digital twin mean fewer patients get the investigational treatment?

No — the effect runs the other way. Because the technique reduces the number of participants needed in the control/placebo arm while preserving statistical power, a smaller share of total enrolled participants receive placebo or standard-of-care alone, and a larger relative share can be randomized to (or offered access to) the investigational arm, for the same overall trial size.

### What data is a digital twin model trained on?

Historical clinical trial datasets in the same or a related disease area, and in some approaches real-world data such as patient registries or electronic health records, used to train a model that predicts individual disease-progression trajectories from baseline covariates collected before randomization.

# [ASA Biopharmaceutical Report](/)

# Unleashing AI-Generated Digital Twins to Deliver More Efficient Randomized Clinical Trials

### Arman Sabbaghi (Santen Inc.)

[ASA Biopharmaceutical Report](https://substack.com/@asabiopharmaceuticalreport)

##### Disclaimer

Arman Sabbaghi is an employee of Santen Inc. The views and opinions expressed in the following article are those of Arman Sabbaghi only. They do not represent the positions or opinions of Santen Inc.

---

---

**Highlights:**

* The integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into clinical development is rapidly reshaping the landscape of randomized controlled trials (RCTs).
* Recent advances in AI-generated “digital twins”, defined as predictive models that simulate the entire trajectory of control potential outcomes for trial participants, unlock new statistical methods that can improve the power, precision, and efficiency of clinical trials.
* Specifically, summaries of the digital twins constitute “super covariates” for the design and analysis of RCTs, with the corresponding covariate adjustments reliably yielding precise and powerful causal inferences in a regulatory-acceptable manner.
* Ultimately, the integration of AI-generated digital twins with statistical methods can effectively address critical challenges in modern clinical trials.

---

### The Challenge: Eroom’s Law and the Need for Innovation

Modern clinical development faces a daunting challenge. Despite technological progress, the cost and time required to bring new drugs, biologics, devices, and other interventions to market continue to rise. This unfortunate phenomenon is the antithesis of the well-known Moore’s Law, and consequently is known as Eroom’s Law (Lower, 2012; Scannel et al., 2012). Clinical trials, especially RCTs, are a major driver of these costs, often requiring many years and millions of dollars to complete (Sertkaya et al., 2014). There is an urgent need for innovative solutions to counteract Eroom’s Law.

### Covariate Adjustment and the Rise of Super Covariates

Covariate adjustment provides a regulatory-acceptable approach to address Eroom’s Law. Regulatory agencies, including the FDA (2023) and the EMA (2015), have provided guidance on the appropriate use of covariate adjustment for RCTs, emphasizing the careful selection of a small number of covariates for adjustment. By identifying a covariate that is highly correlated with the outcome, one can obtain treatment effect inferences that are more precise and powerful based on the adjustment for the covariate compared to unadjusted analyses, or compared to other analyses that adjust for covariates that are less correlated with the outcome. This helps to reduce the necessary sample size, and consequently shorten the enrollment period, for RCTs.

Enter the “super covariate”: a prognostic score (Hansen, 2008) obtained via AI-generated digital twins that effectively summarizes a multidimensional covariate vector (consisting of baseline data, demographics, and other covariates) into a scalar that is highly correlated with control outcomes. The AI algorithms involved in constructing super covariates should be pretrained on historical control data that are external to a target RCT, and should predict the control potential outcomes for participants in the target RCT as a function of their baseline covariates. The predictive distribution for a trial participant’s control potential outcome obtained from the pretrained AI algorithm is their digital twin distribution (Alam et al., 2024). As a result of the pretraining process, the digital twin generator is prespecified prior to the target RCT. Furthermore, as the digital twin generator has the baseline covariates as its inputs, summaries of the generated digital twins are themselves covariates. In particular, the mean of a participant’s digital twin distribution corresponds to their prognostic score, and serves as a super covariate that enables more powerful and precise treatment effect inferences without inflating bias or Type I error rates (Schuler et al., 2022).

### Regulatory Acceptance and Methodological Advances

Prognostic covariate adjustment (PROCOVATM) is Unlearn.AI’s (EMA, 2022) statistical approach for the design and analysis of RCTs based on the prognostic score obtained from AI-generated digital twins. The essential steps for PROCOVA are:

1. Pretrain an AI model on historical control data.
2. Apply the pretrained AI model to the baseline covariates for treated and control participants in the target RCT to calculate their prognostic scores.
3. Fit a linear regression model for the RCT data in which the response variable is the outcome and the predictor variables are the treatment indicator and the prognostic score.
4. Estimate the treatment effect via the linear regression model.
5. Obtain the standard error of the treatment effect estimate using the sandwich estimator approach.

The EMA qualified PROCOVA as “an acceptable statistical approach for primary analysis” of Phase 2 and 3 trials with continuous endpoints (EMA, 2022). Furthermore, the FDA stated that they concur with the EMA and that PROCOVA does not deviate from their current guidance (Fisher, 2024).

Two extensions of PROCOVA, referred to as Weighted PROCOVA (Vanderbeek et al., 2023) and Bayesian PROCOVA (Vanderbeek et al., 2024), further enhance the power, precision, and efficiency of PROCOVA by incorporating the variances of the digital twin distributions, and dynamically borrowing information from historical controls, respectively. These methods further reduce necessary sample sizes, increase statistical power, and maintain rigorous control of bias and Type I error rates compared to PROCOVA. In particular, Bayesian PROCOVA increases the precision of treatment effect inferences without adding significant bias when historical controls and trial participants are exchangeable, and can discount historical controls when they are discrepant with trial participants so as to control bias and Type I error rates.

AI-generated digital twins are not limited to continuous outcomes. Consequently, statistical methods that incorporate digital twins for RCTs have also been specified for time-to-event (Li et al., 2023), binary (Li et al., 2024), and repeated measures endpoints (Ross et al., 2024).

### Broader Implications for the Future of Clinical Development

The integration of AI with statistics can help to address Eroom’s Law, and usher in a new generation of regulatory-acceptable clinical trials that can be more adaptive, efficient, and informative, thereby accelerating clinical development and improving patient outcomes. Key stakeholders across pharmaceutical companies, biotech, regulatory agencies, and technology companies must work together to realize the full potential of AI in transforming the future of medicine.

For further discussion or collaboration, connect with Arman Sabbaghi (@SabbaghiArman) on LinkedIn or at Santen Inc.

args.key_excerpts: "The integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into clinical development is rapidly reshaping the landscape of randomized controlled trials (RCTs)."
args.summary:
This ASA Biopharmaceutical Report article by Arman Sabbaghi (Santen Inc.) discusses how AI-generated "digital twins" can be used to deliver more efficient randomized controlled trials (RCTs), addressing the challenge of Eroom's Law—the phenomenon where the cost and time to bring new drugs and interventions to market continue to rise despite technological progress.

**Key Concepts:**
- **Digital twins**: Predictive models that simulate the entire trajectory of control potential outcomes for trial participants. Summaries of these digital twins constitute "super covariates" that enable precise and powerful causal inferences in a regulatory-acceptable manner.
- **Super covariates**: Prognostic scores (per Hansen, 2008) obtained via AI-generated digital twins that summarize multidimensional covariate vectors (baseline data, demographics, etc.) into scalars highly correlated with control outcomes. AI algorithms should be pretrained on historical control data external to the target RCT.

**PROCOVA™ Methodology (Unlearn.AI's approach):**
The 5 essential steps are:
1. Pretrain an AI model on historical control data.
2. Apply the pretrained AI model to baseline covariates for treated and control participants to calculate prognostic scores.
3. Fit a linear regression model with the outcome as response and treatment indicator plus prognostic score as predictors.
4. Estimate the treatment effect via the linear regression model.
5. Obtain the standard error using the sandwich estimator approach.

**Regulatory Acceptance:**
- The EMA qualified PROCOVA as "an acceptable statistical approach for primary analysis" of Phase 2 and 3 trials with continuous endpoints (2022).
- The FDA stated they concur with the EMA and that PROCOVA does not deviate from their current guidance (2024).

**Methodological Extensions:**
- **Weighted PROCOVA** (Vanderbeek et al., 2023): Incorporates variances of digital twin distributions to enhance power, precision, and efficiency.
- **Bayesian PROCOVA** (Vanderbeek et al., 2024): Dynamically borrows information from historical controls, increasing precision without adding significant bias when historical controls and trial participants are exchangeable, and can discount discrepant historical controls.
- Methods have also been specified for time-to-event (Li et al., 2023), binary (Li et al., 2024), and repeated measures endpoints (PROCOVA-MMRM by Ross et al., 2024).

**Broader Implications:** The integration of AI with statistics can help address Eroom's Law and usher in a new generation of regulatory-acceptable, adaptive, efficient, and informative clinical trials, accelerating clinical development and improving patient outcomes. Key stakeholders across pharmaceutical companies, biotech, regulatory agencies, and technology companies must collaborate to realize this potential.
