# Population based medicine – Transform medicine with metabolomics – part 4 of 5

by [Anna](https://biocrates.com/author/bc-stuchlika-8du/ "Posts by Anna") | May 12, 2025 | [Blog](https://biocrates.com/category/blog/), [5P medicine](https://biocrates.com/category/5p-medicine/), [Literature](https://biocrates.com/category/literature/), [Metabolomics](https://biocrates.com/category/metabolomics/), [Microbiome](https://biocrates.com/category/microbiome/), [Nutrition](https://biocrates.com/category/nutrition/), [Prebiotics](https://biocrates.com/category/prebiotics/)

This is the fourth in a series of five blogs where I’ll discuss how metabolomics is set to transform medicine as we know it. The applications of omics in biomedical research are vast. To help organize the different ways metabolomics can be used, I’ll discuss this in the context of 5P medicine.

If you are already familiar with the concept of 5P medicine and how omics contribute to the transformation of medicine, click to move forward to the [population-based medicine section](#population) of this blog.

### An introduction to 5P medicine

5P medicine is a concept developed to address the limitations of traditional Western medicine, which typically focuses on reacting to illness or injury. Making use of five components – preventive, predictive, precision, participatory and population-based medicine – 5P medicine aims to shift the focus towards a more proactive and patient-centric practice.

Personally, I first encountered this concept in a book by Leroy Hood and Nathan Price, [The Age of Scientific Wellness](https://www.hup.harvard.edu/books/9780674245945). Hood and Price describe what they call P4 medicine. Rather than the familiar model that treats or manages disease after its occurrence, the authors offer an alternative that leverages the scientific tools at our disposal to understand health and disease. The result is a transition from what they call a “sickcare” system towards a genuine “healthcare” system. The 5P model expands this concept by adding population-based medicine to the original four and incorporating strategies that use the power of large cohort studies to find additional insights.

### Omics and the future of research and health

Omics research has been around for over 30 years, and while genomics is gaining traction and beginning to be used in the clinics, other omics, and [multiomics integration](https://biocrates.com/multiomics-medicine-of-tomorrow/), are still lagging. Each omic addresses a distinct layer of biology, with its own codes, regulatory signals and sensitivity to external influences that offer unique insights.

Genomics is the layer least influenced by environment once a person is born. Of course, mutations can occur and change someone’s DNA, but these happen locally and are most often corrected. In contrast, metabolomics is the layer most sensitive to the environment. It responds to our diet, lifestyle, and exposures. For example, metabolomics profiles can shift in response to year after year of terrible food choices ([Limonciel et al. 2013](https://biocrates.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/07/biocrates-Complex-chronic-diseases-have-a-common-origin.pdf)). Poor diet usually leads to chronic low-grade inflammation, which presents metabolic patterns closely associated with markers of inflammation at the granular level ([Pietzner et al. 2017](http://doi.org/10.1186/s12916-016-0770-8)).

Genomics can tell you about your risk of developing an inflammatory disease, but it cannot track how this risk evolves throughout your life. Similarly, genomics can identify genotypes that will influence response to a specific drug, but it does not respond to influences from the environment that determine our drug response. Metabolomics can. That’s exactly why it’s such a great tool for population-based medicine where the need for measures of disease risk beyond genetic predisposition is high.

Learn more about the power of [multiomics for 5P medicine](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=LFUkrc_Ynh4) in my webinar.

### Population-based medicine with metabolomics

Population-based medicine takes advantage of the statistical power of large epidemiological cohorts to study health and disease at a different scale. At first glance, this seems like the opposite of [precision medicine](https://biocrates.com/precision-medicine-transform-with-metabolomics/), but these large cohort studies can be a great source of biomarkers and complex risk scores to evaluate the health of a single individual.

Applying metabolomics in population-based cohort studies provides a wealth of information that enables:

* Metabolic risk scoring
* Metabotyping
* Multiomics integration

### Metabolic risk scores

Population-based medicine was among the first disciplines to make use of genomics, designing genome-wide association studies (GWAS) that have identified numerous gene variants associated with the risk of developing disease, from type 2 diabetes ([Grant et al. 2006](https://www.nature.com/articles/ng1732)) to coronary artery disease ([Helgadottir et al. 2007](https://doi.org/10.1126/science.1142842)). However, these gene variants rarely explain more than 10% of the risk for developing complex chronic diseases.

In complex diseases such as Alzheimer’s disease, breast cancer or type 2 diabetes, environmental factors play a massive role, reflected in the low percentage of variance explained by genetic variants ([So et al. 2011](https://doi.org/10.1002/gepi.20579)). This means that much of the remaining 90% is likely to be explained by metabolomics, an omic strongly influenced by the environment.

Understanding the external, environmental factors that associate with a disease or trait enables better risk assessment and prevention, more sensitive diagnosis, and ultimately enables precision medicine for the parts of the population exposed to the external factors identified.

For example, ([Hoffman et al. 2024](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.envres.2024.120172)) created a metabolomic risk score that reflects the response of the organism to traffic-related air pollution. To strengthen their model, the authors combined metabolomic data from several cohorts together with simulated data. The power of the associations was relatively low, although the metabolites selected by the models made mechanistic sense, comforting the authors on their relevance to the risk score. The authors emphasized the need for large sample sizes and [standardized metabolomics methods](https://biocrates.com/epidemiology-and-biobanks/) to support this approach.

### Metabotyping

I’ve discussed this approach in previous blogs in this series, but metabotyping is also a great tool for population-based medicine. Metabotyping consists in forming sub-groups of a population based on their metabolomic profile. This type of clustering is a very good way to uncover sub-phenotypes of a disease that may benefit from distinct early diagnostic tools and different treatments.

On [a recent episode](https://themetabolomist.com/epidemiology-and-asthma/) of The Metabolomist podcast, Rachel Kelly explains how she and her group have applied this approach in epidemiological studies focused on asthma ([Kelly et al. 2021](http://doi.org/10.1164/rccm.202105-1268OC)) and autism spectrum disorder ([Prince et al. 2023](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.bbi.2023.03.026)). In both cases, metabolomics was a powerful tool to better understand the condition and begin to think of novel approaches for precision medicine using these cohort-based results.

In 2018, [Lacruz et al.](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-018-27958-1) showed that not only is metabolomics a great tool to stratify a population through metabotyping, but also that monitoring these metabotypes can be very informative. In the Cardiovascular Disease, Living and Ageing in Halle (CARLA) cohort (n=1,409), nearly 60% of the population had a stable metabotype after a four-year interval. Metabotype instability, however, was associated with a higher risk of all-cause mortality. The authors highlighted metabotype variability as a potential early indicator of pre-clinical disease. You can also listen to Gabi Kastenmüller, the senior author on this publication, discussing the use of metabolomics in this and other studies on large cohorts on the [podcast](https://themetabolomist.com/ep1-kastenmueller-metabolomics-bias/).

### Multiomics integration

As mentioned above, the large cohorts used in population-based medicine require robust omics methods to generate meaningful associations. Combining omics is also a way to highlight associations that wouldn’t be visible with a single omics layer.

A well-known example is the integration of metabolomics with GWAS, referred to as mGWAS. I’ve discussed this approach on the podcast with one of the pioneers of mGWAS, Karsten Suhre. In that [episode](https://themetabolomist.com/mgwas-and-metabolite-ratios/), he explains how using metabolomics and ratios of metabolites helps us identify variants that were previously out of scope, and with excellent p values.

Read more about how to perform mGWAS [here](https://biocrates.com/mgwas/).

Large biobanks increasingly include the measurement of multiple omics to enable multiomics analysis for their users. For instance, the Tohoku Medical Megabank Project in Japan created the [jMorp database](https://jmorp.megabank.tohoku.ac.jp/), which compiles multiomics data including genomics, proteomics and metabolomics, as well as related clinical data ([Ogishima et al. 2021](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41439-021-00175-5)). These initiatives help to democratize the use of omics in epidemiology and to the development of FAIR science.

### Outlook

As the most comprehensive measure of phenotype and external influences on human biology, metabolomics is uniquely positioned to provide the missing pieces of the multiomics puzzle so greatly needed in epidemiology.

From the calculation of metabolic risk scores that can complement or even merge with polygenetic risk scores from genomic studies, to the enhanced understanding of disease provided by metabotyping, metabolomics has a lot to offer to population-base medicine.

We explored the application of this omic to cohort studies in our whitepaper on “[FAIR compliant](https://biocrates.com/2021_cohort_whitepaper/)[metabolomics profiling of population-based studies](https://biocrates.com/2021_cohort_whitepaper/).” In particular, we discussed how the level of standardization required for the integration of metabolomics in large cohort studies is a critical point that requires dedicated solutions.

The increasing adoption of metabolomics in large cohort studies and biobanks holds great promise for uncovering the variance related to complex diseases and advancing population-based medicine.

args.summary:
This blog post, published May 12, 2025 by biocrates (a Biognosys group company), is the fourth in a five-part series on how metabolomics is transforming medicine through the framework of "5P medicine" (preventive, predictive, precision, participatory, and population-based medicine). The 5P concept builds on Leroy Hood and Nathan Price's P4 medicine described in "The Age of Scientific Wellness," shifting from a "sickcare" to a true "healthcare" system.

The post argues that while genomics is gaining clinical traction, metabolomics is the omics layer most sensitive to the environment (diet, lifestyle, exposures), making it uniquely suited for population-based medicine. Genomic variants explain less than 10% of the risk for complex chronic diseases (like Alzheimer's, breast cancer, type 2 diabetes), leaving ~90% potentially explained by environmental-influenced factors detectable via metabolomics.

Key applications of metabolomics in population-based medicine include:
1. **Metabolic risk scores**: Reflecting environmental exposures (e.g., Hoffman et al. 2024 created a metabolomic risk score for traffic-related air pollution exposure). These require large sample sizes and standardized metabolomics methods.
2. **Metabotyping**: Sub-grouping populations by metabolomic profile to uncover disease sub-phenotypes. Rachel Kelly applied this to asthma and autism spectrum disorder epidemiological studies. In the CARLA cohort (n=1,409), ~60% had a stable metabotype over four years, but metabotype instability was linked to higher all-cause mortality and may be an early indicator of pre-clinical disease.
3. **Multiomics integration**: Combining metabolomics with GWAS (mGWAS) identifies previously out-of-scope variants. Large biobanks like Japan's Tohoku Medical Megabank (jMorp database) now compile multiomics data to democratize omics use in epidemiology.

The post concludes that metabolomics is uniquely positioned as "the most comprehensive measure of phenotype and external influences on human biology" to complete the multiomics puzzle in epidemiology, with metabolic risk scores potentially complementing or merging with polygenic risk scores.

# Metabolomic Profiling and Population-scale Metabogenomics

![Metabolomic Profiling and Population-scale Metabogenomics](data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB2aWV3Qm94PSIwIDAgMTkyMCAxMDgwIiB3aWR0aD0iMTkyMCIgaGVpZ2h0PSIxMDgwIiB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciPjwvc3ZnPg==)

## There is a Missing Link in the Central Dogma – Metabolomic Profiling

The discovery of DNA’s structure triggered the genomic revolution. Technologies were rapidly developed that could sequence DNA quickly and cost-effectively. The goal was to enhance our understanding of the molecular basis of disease and improve overall human health.1 Parallel advances in RNA and protein profiling fueled the focus on gene, transcript, and protein influence on disease causation, diagnosis, and therapeutic development. It made sense to focus on these influences since the central dogma of molecular biology is the foundation of functional genomics which connects genes to phenotypes. However, a gap in the central dogma is the integral role of small molecules—endogenous, microbiome, and environmental sources exerting significant influence on gene, transcript, and protein expression and functions. Small molecules represent the missing “omic” within the “cause” and “effect” outcomes in functional genomic studies. This information gap attributable to small molecules was first described as an important “missing link” in the central dogma,2 spurring significant investments in profiling and the use of metabolomics in scientific and clinical research.

## Metabolites Fill Critical Information Gaps in Functional Genomics

Small molecules are prerequisites for many fundamental functions in biological systems; they are the building blocks for DNA, RNA, and protein synthesis. They drive energy production and influence the epi-transformation of DNA (epi-genetic), RNA (epi-transcriptomic), and post-translational modifications (PTM) of proteins (epi-proteomic). These transformations have a significant impact on biological response, broadly influencing the phenotype. Metabolites generated within biochemical pathways represent the intermediate phenotype3 and link the gene, transcript, protein, microbiota, and external environmental factors to an observed phenotype and/or clinically relevant endpoint. Put simply, metabolites and lipids have a symbiotic relationship with DNA and RNA on affecting host biology.

Furthermore, evidence suggests the presence and concentration of metabolites impacts the active or dormant state of genes within a sequence.4 The addition of metabolomics to functional genomic studies fills critical information gaps linking observed genomic changes to phenotypic outcomes, i.e., gaps in the “cause” and “effect” information continuum.

## Metabolomics is Ready for Utilization

Over the past decade, technologies supporting large-scale profiling of metabolomics have matured for scalable implementation and utility ranging from discovery research to longitudinal monitoring of health, wellness, disease onset, and outcomes in population health cohorts.5-7 Despite these advances, metabolomic profiling, utility, and adoption within the framework of major scientific investigations are underappreciated and often overlooked. Metabolomics is an important tool that, when incorporated into functional genomic investigations, fills important and insightful information gaps not readily addressed by the other molecular modalities.8-10

**Metabogenomic analysis enables the use of well-curated metabolites and associated biochemical pathways for the functional gene annotation.**

## Gene Annotation is Based on Metabolomics

A compelling rationale for the inclusion of metabolomic profiling within molecular and functional genomic studies for biological and functional insights is found in the construction of KEGG, MetaCyc, and related databases supporting the functional annotation of genes. Some of the earliest gene annotations were the result of linking newly discovered genes to an established framework of biochemical pathways associated with interpretable functional endpoints (phenotype). Pathways for glycolysis and tricarboxylic acid cycle (TCA, Krebs cycle) were some of the earliest characterized biochemical pathways that were part of the metabolic process network created for functional annotation of genes.

The current framework of the biochemical process network is founded on nearly a century of work by biochemists and clinical chemists focused on the metabolism of the parent molecule into its derivatives. Each of the small metabolites within these complex enzymatic networks has a broad spectrum of influences on biological functions. This historical repository of information connecting the enzymatic knowledgebase to protein and eventually to the gene was the basis for the establishment of the Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes (KEGG) in 1995, enabling biological interpretation of sequenced genomes.11 These databases are supported by information from the human metabolomes; the most recent update of the Human Metabolome Database (HMDB) contains comprehensive information on over 200,000 metabolite entries.12

## Metabolomics Advances

The rapid advances in gene sequencing technology enabled the sequencing of the first complete human genome in a span of 13 years (1990 – 2003, HGP), outpacing the discovery and structural elucidation of new metabolites and associated biochemical pathways. This continued divergence of advances over two decades between genetics and biochemistry resulted in a perceptible information gap in associating metabolism-based functional attributes with newly identified genes. Metabolomics technologies have matured significantly in the past decade and now include comprehensive untargeted metabolomic profiling of known metabolites and a significant number of predicted metabolites with unknown structures.5 The remarkable success of metabolomic profiling in the diagnosis of inborn error of metabolism and rare diseases with no known genomic cause provides a convincing argument for the use of untargeted metabolomic profiling in these cases.13-15 Rapid advances in computational capabilities and data analytics, improved statistical modeling, and machine learning have enabled a gradual transition in closing the gap on predictions of linking genes to metabolites within metabolic pathway networks and their potential role in health and disease.6,7,16 These advances are highlighted by the most recent updates in databases such as KEGG, MetaCyc, and others.11,17 Gene ontology (GO) remains the most widely used computational resource for linking genes to phenotypes.18 Despite these advancements, an estimated 30% of genes identified have either unknown functions or are annotated based on predicted function and lack experimental validation.19 Furthermore, the automation of standard annotation processes has major limitations in accurately capturing the biological complexity, multimodality, and redundancies within systems networks.20 Since a significant number of unknown, predicted, or mis-annotated genes encode for potential enzymes, untargeted metabolomic profiling serves as a powerful tool for elucidation of their activity and relationship to physiological function.21

## Population Scale Metabogenomics: Mapping Genetic Determinants of Metabotypes to Understand Mechanism of Action

The value of gene-wide association studies (GWAS) is the ability of well-designed studies to detect genetic variant drivers underlying diseases for potential risk prediction, i.e., identify “cause” factors within large populations.22 GWAS have successfully identified disease-associated variants over the last 15 years, even as samples sizes and study design scope have increased and statistical methods have advanced.22,23 However, the presence of genetic markers associated with disease-specific phenotypic traits, such as those represented by polygenic risk scores, has not been significantly useful in population screening and risk prediction.24,25

Small molecule metabolite panels have served as useful functional markers of good health or a harbinger of impending system dysfunction and disease, e.g., blood creatinine and/or blood urea nitrogen as markers of kidney function. Small molecules serve as good representatives of the cumulative consequence of biological activity, making them excellent candidates to serve as surrogate markers of the “effect” of an observable functional phenotype. Thus, metabolomics provides the opportunity for improved diagnosis, screening, and prediction, specifically when combined with genomics and proteomics.26-28

Population scale metabogenomic analysis successfully identified gene variants associated with metabolic phenotypes and accounted for observed variances within a cohort.6 Furthermore, a functional genomic study that included metabolomics was instrumental in identifying the functionality of “silent” mutations in genes that lacked an obvious overt phenotype.29 Metabolomic-linked GWAS studies have identified genetic determinants influencing metabolites in the blood in distinct ethnic populations.30-32 Furthermore, a metabogenomic study based on genotype-metabotype associations was used for further identification of associated metabolites.33 Most importantly, large metabogenomics studies continue to provide insight into the genetic basis of metabolic individuality and the effects of these associations on diseases ranging from cardiovascular disease, metabolic diseases such as obesity and diabetes, metabolic drivers of cancer, and profiles associated with human health and wellbeing.7,15,34,35 Thus, population-scale metabogenomic studies will continue to add to the existing knowledge base and provide new insights into the genetic underpinnings of biological functions in disease and health.

args.key_excerpts: Small molecules represent the missing 'omic' within the 'cause' and 'effect' outcomes in functional genomic studies. This information gap attributable to small molecules was first described as an important 'missing link' in the central dogma.
args.summary:
This article from Metabolon, titled "Metabolomic Profiling and Population-scale Metabogenomics," argues that small molecules (metabolites) represent a critical "missing link" in the central dogma of molecular biology. While genomics, transcriptomics, and proteomics have advanced, metabolites—from endogenous, microbiome, and environmental sources—exert significant influence on gene, transcript, and protein expression, representing an information gap in the "cause" and "effect" continuum of functional genomics studies. Small molecules are building blocks for DNA, RNA, and protein synthesis, drive energy production, and influence epigenetic, epitranscriptomic, and post-translational modifications, representing the "intermediate phenotype" linking genes, transcripts, proteins, microbiota, and environment to observed phenotypes.

The article notes that metabolomics technologies have matured over the past decade for scalable implementation from discovery research to longitudinal population health monitoring, yet remain underappreciated in major scientific investigations. Gene annotation itself is historically based on metabolomics—early gene annotations linked newly discovered genes to biochemical pathways like glycolysis and the TCA cycle. This framework led to the creation of KEGG in 1995 and MetaCyc, with the Human Metabolome Database (HMDB) now containing over 200,000 metabolite entries.

Key advances highlighted include: the first complete human genome sequencing (1990–2003, Human Genome Project) outpaced metabolite discovery, creating an information gap; untreated metabolomic profiling has proven successful in diagnosing inborn errors of metabolism and rare diseases with no known genomic cause; approximately 30% of identified genes have unknown functions or annotations based on predicted function lacking experimental validation; and since many unknown genes encode potential enzymes, untargeted metabolomics serves as a powerful tool for elucidating activity.

On population-scale metabogenomics, the article notes that GWAS studies have identified disease-associated variants over the last 15 years, but polygenic risk scores have not been significantly useful in population screening and risk prediction. Small molecule metabolite panels (e.g., blood creatinine and blood urea nitrogen as kidney function markers) serve as functional markers representing cumulative biological activity. Population-scale metabogenomic analysis has identified gene variants associated with metabolic phenotypes, helped identify functionality of "silent" mutations, identified genetic determinants of blood metabolites across distinct ethnic populations, and provided insight into diseases ranging from cardiovascular disease, obesity, diabetes, and metabolic drivers of cancer, as well as profiles of human health and wellbeing.

# Machine learning and data-driven inverse modeling of metabolomics unveil key processes of active aging

* [Jiahang Li](#auth-Jiahang-Li-Aff1-Aff2)[1](#Aff1),[2](#Aff2),

## Abstract

Physical inactivity and low fitness have become global health concerns. Metabolomics, as an integrative approach, may link fitness to molecular changes. In this study, we analyzed blood metabolomes from elderly individuals under different treatments. By defining two fitness groups and their corresponding metabolite profiles, we applied several machine learning classifiers to identify key metabolite biomarkers. Aspartate consistently emerged as a dominant fitness marker. We further defined a body activity index (BAI) and analyzed two cohorts with high and low BAI using COVRECON, a novel method for metabolic network interaction analysis. COVRECON identifies causal molecular dynamics in multiomics data. Aspartate-amino-transferase (AST) was among the dominant processes distinguishing the groups. Routine blood tests confirmed significant differences in AST and ALT. Aspartate is also a known biomarker in dementia, related to physical fitness. In summary, we combine machine learning and COVRECON to identify metabolic biomarkers and molecular dynamics supporting active aging.

## Introduction

Physical inactivity is a worldwide health problem, and is ranked as the fourth leading behavioral risk factor for global mortality[1](/articles/s41540-025-00580-4#ref-CR1 "Kohl, H. W. et al. The pandemic of physical inactivity: global action for public health. lancet 380, 294–305 (2012)."). The imperative to maintain body activity, physically and metabolically, is on the rise. The concept of active aging, inspired by Robert Havighurst’s activity theory[2](/articles/s41540-025-00580-4#ref-CR2 "Havighurst, R. J. Successful aging. Process. Aging.: Soc. Psychol. Perspect. 1, 299–320 (1963)."), suggests that maintaining an active lifestyle is crucial for the well-being of older individuals. The thought of active aging emerged and began to develop in the 1990s, placing strong emphasis on the link between activity and health[3](/articles/s41540-025-00580-4#ref-CR3 "WHO, Active ageing: A policy framework. 2002, World Health Organization.").This focus became particularly pertinent due to the worldwide aging population, leading to concerns about inactivity permeating various social domains[4](/articles/s41540-025-00580-4#ref-CR4 "Boudiny, K. & Mortelmans, D. A critical perspective: Towards a broader understanding of’active ageing’. E-journal. Appl. Psychol. 7, 8-14 (2011)."). Within the transition into the 2020 s, there has been an escalating emphasis on harnessing technology to foster healthy aging[5](#ref-CR5 "Offerman, J. et al. Attitudes related to technology for active and healthy aging in a national multigenerational survey. Nat. Aging 3, 617–625 (2023)."),[6](#ref-CR6 "Wongsala, M., Anbäcken, E.-M. & Rosendahl, S. Active ageing–perspectives on health, participation, and security among older adults in northeastern Thailand–a qualitative study. BMC Geriatrics 21, 1–10 (2021)."),[7](/articles/s41540-025-00580-4#ref-CR7 "Malkowski, O. S., Kanabar, R. & Western, M. J. Socio-economic status and trajectories of a novel multidimensional metric of Active and Healthy Ageing: the English Longitudinal Study of Ageing. Sci. Rep. 13, 6107 (2023)."). Beyond longevity, active aging encompasses regular physical activity, better management of chronic diseases, and improved quality of life[8](/articles/s41540-025-00580-4#ref-CR8 "Fernández-Ballesteros, R. et al. Active aging: a global goal. 2013, Hindawi.").

Conventionally, several studies have examined various physical aspects of active aging, such as sleep, sedentary time, muscle strengthening activities, and movement behaviors[9](/articles/s41540-025-00580-4#ref-CR9 "Caprara, M. et al. Active aging promotion: Results from the Vital Aging Program. Curr. Gerontol. Geriatrics Res. 2013. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1155/2013/817813
                  
                 (2013)."),[10](/articles/s41540-025-00580-4#ref-CR10 "Taylor, A. W. Physiology of exercise and healthy aging. 2022: Human Kinetics."). In this study, we focus on a specific aspect of body activity — physical performance (e.g., muscle endurance and strength)- and explore its potential association with individual’s metabolomics profiling. As the new technology to diagnose diseases, metabolomics involves the comprehensive analysis of small-molecule metabolites (<10 kDa) present in a biological sample, including metabolic intermediates, hormones, signaling molecules, and secondary metabolites[11](/articles/s41540-025-00580-4#ref-CR11 "Weckwerth, W. Metabolomics: an integral technique in systems biology. Bioanalysis 2, 829–836 (2010)."),[12](/articles/s41540-025-00580-4#ref-CR12 "Patti, G. J., Yanes, O. & Siuzdak, G. Metabolomics: the apogee of the omics trilogy. Nat. Rev. Mol. cell Biol. 13, 263–269 (2012)."). Functioning as the culmination of all biological processes in the body, metabolites play a pivotal role in energy generation, signal transmission, and carrying essential information about the body’s status and ongoing functions. Consequently, important metabolites possess the potential to serve as aging biomarkers or as integral components of the metabolic signature. This signature mirrors the active state of the organism as it traverses the aging process[13](/articles/s41540-025-00580-4#ref-CR13 "Balashova, E. E. et al. Metabolome profiling in aging studies. Biology 11, 1570 (2022)."). The development of metabolomics empowers us to scrutinize health issues at the molecular level[14](/articles/s41540-025-00580-4#ref-CR14 "Gonzalez-Covarrubias, V., Martínez-Martínez, E. & del Bosque-Plata, L. The potential of metabolomics in biomedical applications. Metabolites 12, 194 (2022)."). Notably, amid the COVID-19 pandemic, metabolomics has demonstrated its potency as a diagnostic, prognostic, and drug intervention tool[15](/articles/s41540-025-00580-4#ref-CR15 "Bruzzone, C. et al. Metabolomics as a powerful tool for diagnostic, pronostic and drug intervention analysis in COVID-19. Front. Mol. Biosci. 10, 1111482 (2023)."). As expected, COVID-19 has been extensively investigated using metabolomics methodologies, contributing to biomarker studies[16](/articles/s41540-025-00580-4#ref-CR16 "Su, Y. et al. Multi-omics resolves a sharp disease-state shift between mild and moderate COVID-19. Cell 183, 1479–1495.e20 (2020)."),[17](/articles/s41540-025-00580-4#ref-CR17 "Sindelar, M. et al. Longitudinal metabolomics of human plasma reveals prognostic markers of COVID-19 disease severity. Cell Rep. Med. 2, 
                  https://doi.org/10.1016/j.xcrm.2021.100369
                  
                 (2021).") and evaluations of drug impacts[18](/articles/s41540-025-00580-4#ref-CR18 "Meoni, G. et al. Metabolomic/lipidomic profiling of COVID-19 and individual response to tocilizumab. PLoS Pathog. 17, e1009243 (2021)."),[19](/articles/s41540-025-00580-4#ref-CR19 "Ghini, V. et al. Serum NMR profiling reveals differential alterations in the lipoproteome induced by pfizer-BioNTech vaccine in COVID-19 recovered subjects and naïve subjects. Front. Mol. Biosci. 9, 839809 (2022)."). Beyond specific disease diagnosis, metabolomics can also illuminate our comprehension of bodily activities (active aging). Recent endeavors have delved into metabolic profiling within aging studies[13](/articles/s41540-025-00580-4#ref-CR13 "Balashova, E. E. et al. Metabolome profiling in aging studies. Biology 11, 1570 (2022)."),[20](/articles/s41540-025-00580-4#ref-CR20 "Panyard, D. J., Yu, B. & Snyder, M. P. The metabolomics of human aging: Advances, challenges, and opportunities. Sci. Adv. 8, eadd6155 (2022)."), providing us with overarching insights into metabolic changes during the aging process. Physical performance (e.g., walking test, muscle strength) is a critical aspect of active aging. In this work, we specifically focus on the metabolomic profiling of older adults and aim to detect key biomarkers and important metabolic interactions linked to physical performance and active aging.

The emerging large scale datasets from OMICS (metabolomics, proteomics, transcriptomic and genomics) measurements empower us to scrutinize any question in biology from a systemic perspective[21](/articles/s41540-025-00580-4#ref-CR21 "Weckwerth, W. Toward a unification of system-theoretical principles in biology and ecology—the stochastic lyapunov matrix equation and its inverse application. Front. Appl. Math. Stat. 5, 29 (2019)."),[22](/articles/s41540-025-00580-4#ref-CR22 "Weckwerth, W. Green systems biology—from single genomes, proteomes and metabolomes to ecosystems research and biotechnology. J. Proteom. 75, 284–305 (2011)."). In the field of systems biology, a central goal is to identify biomarkers and infer biochemical regulations from large-scale metabolomics data[23](/articles/s41540-025-00580-4#ref-CR23 "Weckwerth, W. Unpredictability of metabolism-the key role of metabolomics science in combination with next-generation genome sequencing. Anal. Bioanal. Chem. 400, 1967–1978 (2011)."). Statistical methods, especially when combined with machine learning techniques, have shown power on constructing accurate classifiers capable of distinguishing between diverse sample groups and revealing underlying biomarkers[24](#ref-CR24 "Sidak, D. et al. Interpretable machine learning methods for predictions in systems biology from omics data. Front. Mol. Biosci. 9, 926623 (2022)."),[25](#ref-CR25 "Liebal, U. W. et al. Machine learning applications for mass spectrometry-based metabolomics. Metabolites 10, 243 (2020)."),[26](#ref-CR26 "Pomyen, Y. et al. Deep metabolome: Applications of deep learning in metabolomics. Figure [1](/articles/s41540-025-00580-4#Fig1) illustrates the workflow of this study, which consists of three main steps. In step 1, we aim to cluster the original samples into different groups based on physical and functional measurements, where each group represents different body activity conditions calculated from individual’s physical performance measurements. Step 2 involves building machine learning-based classifiers to identify these different groups using metabolomics data, thus enabling the identification of key metabolites as biomarkers. Finally, in step 3, we employ the inverse Jacobian analysis and the COVRECON workflow to uncover the most important biochemical regulations associated with the identified body activity conditions. By conducting this approach, we intend to contribute to the understanding of active aging from a metabolomics perspective and shed light on the key biochemical regulations underlying different fitness conditions.

## Results

This study was performed in 5 retirement homes in Vienna managed by Curatorship of Viennese Retirement Homes, with the main aim to assess the impact of resistance training and protein-vitamin supplementation or a cognitive training on physical performance[45](/articles/s41540-025-00580-4#ref-CR45 "Oesen, S. et al. Effects of elastic band resistance training and nutritional supplementation on physical performance of institutionalised elderly—A randomized controlled trial. Exp. Gerontol. 72, 99–108 (2015)."). The subjects were randomly assigned to three groups (see Figure [S1](/articles/s41540-025-00580-4#MOESM1) in Supplementary Data [1](/articles/s41540-025-00580-4#MOESM1)): resistance training (RT), resistance training and supplements (RTS) and cognitive training, acting as a control group (CT). Blood samples were collected at the baseline (T1), after three months (T2) and after six months (T3). Oesen et al. have shown resistance training and supplementation can improve the physical performance of the older adults. In this study we analyze all samples from these three groups together, focusing on the relationship between physical performance and the metabolomics profiles of the older adults.

In this secondary analysis, we conducted plasma metabolomics measurement. Plasma plays a crucial role in maintaining body health by transporting nutrients, hormones, and waste products throughout the body. Changes in plasma composition can serve as indicators of various diseases, making it a valuable medium for health monitoring and diagnosis. Numerous studies have demonstrated associations between plasma metabolomic profiles and different health conditions[46](#ref-CR46 "Lv, J. et al. Plasma metabolomics reveals the shared and distinct metabolic disturbances associated with cardiovascular events in coronary artery disease. Nat. Commun. 15, 5729 (2024)."),[47](#ref-CR47 "Tessier, A.-J. et al. Plasma metabolites of a healthy lifestyle in relation to mortality and longevity: Four prospective US cohort studies. Med 5, 224–238.e5 (2024)."),[48](/articles/s41540-025-00580-4#ref-CR48 "Wang, F. et al. Plasma metabolomic profiles associated with mortality and longevity in a prospective analysis of 13,512 individuals. Nat. Commun. 14, 5744 (2023)."). Here we focus on the plasma metabolomics changes and the identification of potential biomarkers and biochemical processes related to physical performance in older adults. Thus, treatment-specific improvements in physical strength are not central to our objective. Instead, we analyze all samples collectively to investigate the relationship between active aging and metabolomics patterns. The cohort of older adults with an average age above life expectancy consisted of 117 participants at baseline and altogether we measured 263 plasma metabolomics samples.

In order to establish the relationship between body physical performance and metabolomics profiles, we initially investigated the physical data measurements, which consisted of two types: body physical performance and body shape. Moreover, the body physical performance measurements can be further divided into resistance exercise and endurance exercise types. Table [1](/articles/s41540-025-00580-4#Tab1) shows the group differences of the physical measurements across the three groups. As expected, compared to the Cognitive Training (CT), the resistance training groups (RT and RTS) exhibit better resistance measurements. Nevertheless, there was no influence on endurance measurements (e.g. walking distance). Notably, endurance exercise has been reported more related to body aging conditions than resistance measurements[49](/articles/s41540-025-00580-4#ref-CR49 "Werner, C. M. et al. Differential effects of endurance, interval, and resistance training on telomerase activity and telomere length in a randomized, controlled study. Eur. heart J. 40, 34–46 (2019)."),[50](/articles/s41540-025-00580-4#ref-CR50 "Cao Dinh, H. et al. Strength endurance training but not intensive strength training reduces senescence-prone T cells in peripheral blood in community-dwelling elderly women. J. Gerontology: Ser. A 74, 1870–1878 (2019)."). This is also consistent with the experimental design, where the old adults were randomly assigned to the three groups regardless of their fitness.

### Canonical Correlation (CCA) based clustering to assess physical fitness in a cohort of older institutionalized adults

Since our aim was to investigate the relationship between metabolomics and body physical performance, we first employed Canonical Correlation Analysis (CCA) to generate a body activity index (BAI) based on the physical performance measurements. Subsequently, we clustered the old adults and samples into two, four, and six groups based on this body activity index.

As demonstrated in Fig. [2a](/articles/s41540-025-00580-4#Fig2), the generated body activity index has a high correlation to the metabolomics index (Pearson Coeff = 0.8471, \(p=1.5\* {10}^{-19}\)), where the CCA loadings of the body activity index is listed aside. Among all physical performance indexes, walking distance showed the most dominant effect within the body activity index. This observation is biologically reasonable since walking distance directly reflects an individual’s endurance condition, which is directly related to the aging process[49](/articles/s41540-025-00580-4#ref-CR49 "Werner, C. The automatic classifier was trained with 50 maximum models, over 30 random datasets separation, the averaged AUCs calculated on the hold-out test sets through a repeated double CV approach were determined to be 91.50%, 82.36%, and 62.17% for the two, four, and six-group clusters, respectively (Fig. [2c](/articles/s41540-025-00580-4#Fig2)). This indicates that the CCA generated body activity index and metabolomics index exhibit a strong correlation. Meanwhile, we group all the old adults into two groups for the inverse Jacobian analysis using the mean body activity index as shown in Fig. [2b](/articles/s41540-025-00580-4#Fig2).

For comparison, we also performed CCA analysis between the metabolomics data and body shape features, such as gender, height, and age. The biplots of the CCA from the metabolomics and body shape analysis are presented in Fig. [S2](/articles/s41540-025-00580-4#MOESM1) in Supplementary Data [1](/articles/s41540-025-00580-4#MOESM1). The highest Pearson’s correlation coefficient obtained was only 0.4963 (\(p=1.5\* {10}^{-19}\)) for the age index. Meanwhile, this correlation can partially originate from the physical performance difference generated in this body shape index (e.g., it is evident that age and BMI may influence individual’s physical performance). Additionally, we conducted a further CCA analysis considering the metabolomics data along with both body functionality and body shape data. However, the Pearson correlation coefficient increased only marginally from 0.8471 to 0.8574. This indicates that the metabolomics data are primarily influenced by the body strength/ functionality aspects. Consequently, this validates both the body activity index and the metabolomics index that we developed.

The results of the CCA-based cluster analysis highlight the strong relationship between our derived body activity index and the metabolomics index. The dominance of walking distance as a key factor indicates its significance as a reflection of an individual’s health condition and metabolic activity. In the following analysis, we will focus on the two old adult groups clustered based on the body activity index, labeled as active group and less-active group.

### Machine learning based classifiers and variables importance reveals strong association of metabolites and fitness

In this following section, we developed several machine learning based classifiers to predict the active/less-active groups from the metabolomics dataset. This approach can provide us valuable insights on the nonlinear influence between the metabolomics index and body activity index. As described in the Methods section, we evaluated the predictive performance of five machine learning algorithms: XGBoosting (XGB), DRF, GLM, GBM, and DeepLearning (DL) algorithms. For each algorithm, the optimal model was selected using an automated machine learning (AutoML) framework.

Classifier construction followed a repeated double cross-validation scheme based on the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC). The dataset was divided into four parts. In each iteration, one part was used as the test set, while the remaining three parts were used for model selection via five-fold cross-validation. The selected model was then evaluated on the held-out test set. The final classifier performance was reported as the average of the evaluation metrics across the four folds. This entire double cross-validation procedure was repeated 30 times with different random splits of the dataset.

As shown in Fig. [3](/articles/s41540-025-00580-4#Fig3), we compared the average performance of the classifiers trained on the full dataset and on three-fourths of the data across the five algorithms. To control potential bias due to random sampling of group labels, we conducted a permutation test with 1500 repeats. All five machine learning models achieved statistically significant results, and all permutation repeats for the five algorithms show negative results, resulting in permutation test *p* values < 1/1500 ~ 0.00067. The details of permutation test are presented in “Methods” section.

### Predictive inverse metabolic interaction modeling using the COVRECON platform

While the machine learning and classifier results provide insights into the variable importance between the measured metabolites and the body activity index, this does not explain the mechanistic change between the two groups. Since for each old adult, metabolomics analysis was done three times, first time point, after 3 months and after 6 months, we plotted the correlation heatmap of the change of all body features and metabolomics measurement changes within two the time intervals in Fig. [6](/articles/s41540-025-00580-4#Fig6). It is evident that the correlation patterns within the metabolomics measurement changes show high similarity. This reflects the internal dynamics of the metabolic networks. Nevertheless, when we check the highly correlated metabolites, we may find no biochemical reactions between the two metabolites from any database. This situation frequently happens, e.g. in Fig. [6](/articles/s41540-025-00580-4#Fig6), Threonine, Tyrosine and Valine show a high correlation, yet no direct biochemical reactions occur among them. This is because the high correlations originate from the network dynamics. Thus, finding the causal interactions among the metabolites is crucial.

Based on this, we have developed the COVRECON toolbox (available at: <https://bitbucket.org/mosys-univie/covrecon/src/main/>)[32](/articles/s41540-025-00580-4#ref-CR32 "Li, J., Waldherr, S. & Weckwerth, W. COVRECON: Automated integration of genome- and metabolome-scale network reconstruction and data-driven inverse modeling of metabolic interaction networks. Bioinformatics 39, btad397 (2023)."). As shown in the method part, we applied the COVRECON workflow to the two group datasets. The COVRECON workflow consists of two steps: building the metabolic interaction network and the inverse Jacobian calculation.

As described in COVRECON[32](/articles/s41540-025-00580-4#ref-CR32 "Li, J., Waldherr, S. & Weckwerth, W. COVRECON: Automated integration of genome- and metabolome-scale network reconstruction and data-driven inverse modeling of metabolic interaction networks. Bioinformatics 39, btad397 (2023)."), we used a default setting in the Sim-Network part to generate a metabolic super-pathway network of the measured metabolites. Each edge in the network represents a feasible pathway between two nodes (metabolites) and reflects a non-zero component in the system Jacobian matrix. The default setting assigns a fixed weight of one to each reaction, and the reverse reaction weight is based on the log value of its delta Gibbs free energy. Additionally, a pathway-step limitation of 4 is set. Detailed information about reactions, enzymes and genes of the resulting metabolic interaction network can be found in the Supplementary Data [3](/articles/s41540-025-00580-4#MOESM3). By integrating the covariance of the metabolomics data from both groups and the Jacobian structure matrix, we can perform the inverse Jacobian analysis in the second part of COVRECON toolbox. The COVRECON workflow and toolbox address the ill-conditioned matrix problem associated with the inverse Jacobian approach through a regression loss-based algorithm, significantly improving its stability and feasibility[32](/articles/s41540-025-00580-4#ref-CR32 "Li, J., Waldherr, S. & Weckwerth, W. COVRECON: Automated integration of genome- and metabolome-scale network reconstruction and data-driven inverse modeling of metabolic interaction networks. Bioinformatics 39, btad397 (2023)."),[33](/articles/s41540-025-00580-4#ref-CR33 "Li, J., Weckwerth W. & Waldherr, S. Network structure and fluctuation data improve inference of metabolic interaction strengths with the inverse Jacobian. npj Syst. Biol. Appl. 137 (2024)."),[42](/articles/s41540-025-00580-4#ref-CR42 "Sun, X., Länger, B. & Weckwerth, W. Challenges of inversely estimating jacobian from metabolomics data. Front. Bioeng. Biotechnol. 3, 188 (2015)."). However, given that the inverse Jacobian approach is based on the Jacobian structure and is more reliable in smaller-sized models, we selected a tailored core part of the whole model containing 10–20 metabolites based on the classifier variable importance results as described in method part. The same network reduction strategy as in Sim-Network was employed, with additional indirect connections added to the reduced model. For example, an additional connection from Proline to Aspartate was added to account for the indirect effects through the connections from Proline to Asparagine and from Asparagine to Aspartate (Fig. [7](/articles/s41540-025-00580-4#Fig7)). In Supplementary Data [1](/articles/s41540-025-00580-4#MOESM1), Figure [S8](/articles/s41540-025-00580-4#MOESM1) presents 12 typical results in the repeated calculation. All the repeated results are available in Supplementary Data [5](/articles/s41540-025-00580-4#MOESM3). It is evident that even though the local results are different due to the influence from the Jacobian structure information, the Inverse Jacobian approach shows stability on several highlighted metabolic interactions. For example, the interactions Proline->Aspartate, Ornithine->Aspartate, Citrate->Aspartate and Glutamate->2-oxo glutaric acid are high valued in the resulted differential metabolic interaction network of many repeats. To present the overall metabolic interaction importance, we integrated all the 200 local results into the full differential Jacobian (DJ) by calculating the average value of each metabolic interaction within the repeats. The final R\* matrix and the differential interaction network are presented in Fig. [7a](/articles/s41540-025-00580-4#Fig7), b, respectively. In Fig. [7b](/articles/s41540-025-00580-4#Fig7), we plot only the highlighted metabolic interactions with calculated value (scaled to 0–1) above 0.5. Here we note, the result showed robustness, with similar overall R\* using 100, 200 and 500 repeats. Further results are using 200 repeats.

args.summary:
This scientific article, published in npj Systems Biology and Applications (volume 11, article 103, 2025), investigates the relationship between metabolomics profiles and physical fitness/active aging in elderly individuals. The researchers analyzed blood plasma metabolomics from 263 samples collected from 117 elderly participants in Vienna (average age above life expectancy) across three treatment groups (resistance training, resistance training with supplements, and cognitive training control), sampled at baseline, 3 months, and 6 months.

METHODOLOGY: The study followed a three-step workflow: (1) Using Canonical Correlation Analysis (CCA) to derive a Body Activity Index (BAI) from physical performance measurements, which showed a high correlation (Pearson = 0.8471, p = 1.5×10^-19) with a metabolomics index. Walking distance was the most dominant factor in the body activity index since it reflects endurance directly related to aging. (2) Building machine learning classifiers (XGBoosting, DRF, GLM, GBM, and DeepLearning) to predict active vs. less-active groups from metabolomics data, using repeated double cross-validation. (3) Using the COVRECON workflow (inverse Jacobian analysis integrated with genome-scale metabolic network reconstruction) to identify causal molecular dynamics and key biochemical regulations.

KEY RESULTS:
- CCA-based clustering achieved classifier AUCs of 91.50%, 82.36%, and 62.17% for 2, 4, and 6-group clusters respectively. Body shape features showed much weaker correlations (max 0.4963 for age).
- Five machine learning models achieved statistically significant results (permutation test p < 1/1500 ≈ 0.00067), with boosting methods (XGB AUC 0.915, GBM AUC 0.913) outperforming others.
- Aspartate consistently emerged as the dominant fitness biomarker, accounting for over 90% of variable importance in the XGB classifier. Proline, Fructose, Pyruvate, and Malic Acid were also consistently identified as top metabolites across classifiers.
- COVRECON inverse Jacobian analysis identified Aspartate-amino-transferase (AST) as among the dominant processes distinguishing the groups, confirmed by routine blood tests showing significant differences in AST and ALT.
- Key metabolic interactions identified included Proline→Aspartate, Ornithine→Aspartate, Citrate→Aspartate, and Glutamate→2-oxo glutaric acid.

CONCLUSIONS: The combination of machine learning and COVRECON successfully identified biomarkers (particularly Aspartate, which is also a known biomarker in dementia related to physical fitness) and molecular dynamics supporting active aging. The study demonstrates that metabolomics data are primarily influenced by body strength/functionality aspects, and highlights the importance of using inverse Jacobian methods (like COVRECON) to uncover causal metabolic interactions that simple correlation analysis cannot reveal, since high correlations between metabolites (e.g., Threonine, Tyrosine, Valine) may occur without direct biochemical reactions, originating from network dynamics.

URL: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12499773

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a scientific review article published in Briefings in Bioinformatics (2025 Oct 06;26(5):bbaf533, doi: 10.1093/bib/bbaf533, PMCID: PMC12499773, PMID: 41052279) titled "Computational toxicology in drug discovery: applications of artificial intelligence in ADMET and toxicity prediction." Authors: Jiangyan Zhang, Haolin Li, Yuncong Zhang (contributed equally), Junyang Huang, Liping Ren, Chuantao Zhang, Quan Zou, and Yang Zhang. Corresponding authors are from the Hospital of Chengdu University of Traditional Chinese Medicine and the University of Electronic Science and Technology of China. The article is Open Access under a Creative Commons Attribution Non-Commercial License.

Key content and findings:
- Toxicity risk assessment is crucial for clinical success and market potential of drug candidates; ~30% of preclinical candidate compounds (PCCs) fail due to toxicity, and ~40% of preclinical candidate drugs fail due to insufficient ADMET profiles, while nearly 30% of marketed drugs are withdrawn due to unforeseen toxic reactions.
- Traditional animal testing is costly, time-consuming (6–24 months per test), expensive (often exceeding millions of dollars per compound), and ethically controversial (3Rs principle: replacement, reduction, refinement), driving the shift to computational toxicology.
- The review surveys over 20 ADMET prediction platforms, categorized into three types: rule/statistical-based methods, machine learning (ML) methods, and graph-based methods.
- Broad-spectrum platforms mentioned: admetSAR 3.0, ADMETlab 3.0, vNN-ADMET, ADMETboost, Deep-PK; pharmacokinetic-focused platforms: Swiss ADME, FAF-Drugs4.0, ADMET-AI; toxicity-focused platforms: ProTox 3.0, VenomPred 2.0; CYP450-related tools: CypRules, BioTransformer 3.0, XenoSite, SOMP, SMARTCyp 3.0.
- The ADMET prediction platform framework consists of: input component (chemical structural data, experimental data, literature-derived data), tools/methods component (physicochemical property calculation via RDKit/Scopy, and ML/AI prediction module using SVMs, RFs, neural networks, gradient boosting trees), and output component (endpoints; comprehensive platforms can evaluate over 100 endpoints).
- ML methods (e.g., vNN-ADMET, ADMETboost with XGBoost, ProTox 3.0 with RF/DNN) handle complex patterns but depend on high-quality training data. Graph-based methods (GNNs: ADMET-AI, Interpretable-ADMET, HelixADMET, ADMETlab 3.0 with DMPNN, admetSAR 3.0, pkCSM) analyze molecular graph structures but require substantial computational resources and large training datasets.
- Toxicological databases are classified into four categories: chemical toxicity databases, environmental toxicology databases, alternative toxicology databases, and biological toxin databases.
- Chemical toxicity databases include PubChem (>119 million compounds, NIH-maintained), ChEMBL (>2.1 million, EMBL-EBI), HSDB (~5600 chemicals), CCRIS (>9000, carcinogenicity/mutagenicity), CompTox Chemicals Dashboard (EPA), TOXRIC (113,372 compounds, ML-ready), SuperToxic (~60,000), DrugBank, and specialized databases DILIrank, DILIst, LTKB (hepatotoxicity), hERGCentral (cardiotoxicity), and LCDB (carcinogenicity data from 1726 chemicals and 7745 experimental records).
- The field is transitioning from single-endpoint predictions to multi-endpoint joint modeling with multimodal features, incorporating generative modeling and interpretability frameworks.
- Network toxicology is applied to evaluate safety of traditional Chinese medicines (TCMs), and large language models (LLMs) show potential in literature mining, knowledge integration, and molecular toxicity prediction.
- Current challenges include data quality, model interpretability, and causal inference; future directions include multi-omics integration, interpretable AI models, and domain-specific LLMs for more efficient and precise preclinical toxicity assessments.
</summary>

This IntuitionLabs report (updated July 21, 2026) provides a comprehensive survey of large language model (LLM) benchmarks in life sciences, covering biomedical NLP, question-answering, drug discovery, and genomics, with industry use cases and state-of-the-art model performance from 2020-2026.

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a review article published in Frontiers in Chemistry (July 8, 2025) titled "Recent advances in AI-based toxicity prediction for drug discovery" by Hyundo Lee, Jisan Kim, Ji-Woon Kim, and Yoonji Lee. The article provides an in-depth examination of AI-driven toxicity prediction in drug discovery and its impact on improving safety assessments.

KEY TOPICS COVERED:

**Background/Context:** Toxicity failures in late-stage drug development lead to substantial financial losses, driving the need for reliable early toxicity prediction. AI models can predict various toxicity endpoints (hepatotoxicity, cardiotoxicity, nephrotoxicity, neurotoxicity, genotoxicity) using diverse molecular representations from traditional descriptors to graph-based methods. The workflow includes four stages: data collection, preprocessing, model development, and evaluation. A virtuous cycle is created by integrating AI predictions into virtual screening and feeding experimental outcomes back to improve models.

**Benchmark Datasets:** Key public datasets include:
- Tox21 (8,249 compounds across 12 biological targets)
- ToxCast (~4,746 chemicals across hundreds of endpoints)
- ClinTox (approved vs. failed drugs)
- hERG datasets (over 13,000 compounds; hERG Central has 300,000+ records)
- DILIrank (475 compounds for liver toxicity)
- SIDER (1,400+ marketed drugs with side effect annotations)
- AMES (7,255 compounds for mutagenicity)
- Carcinogens (278 compounds)
- LD50_Zhu (7,385 compounds, regression modeling)
- Challenges include data scarcity, protocol heterogeneity, class imbalance, and annotation noise.

**General ADMET Tools:** ADMETLab 3.0 (119 endpoints, DMPNNs, AUROC ~0.94 for hERG), Deep-PK (73 endpoints, 35 toxicity-related), ProTox 3.0 (61 predictive models, integrates AOPs), Helix-ADMET (self-supervised and multi-task learning), FP-ADMET (50+ endpoints, random forest with 20 fingerprint types), and admetSAR 2.0 (47 endpoints, traditional ML algorithms).

**Endpoint-Specific Models:**
- *Hepatotoxicity:* InterDILI (2024, AUROC 0.97 hold-out), DILI Predictor (2024, two-stage approach with proxy-DILI labels), GeoDILI (2023, GeoGNN+ResNet, AUROC 0.908), OvA-QSTR (2023, one-vs-all strategy), Rao et al. (2023, physicochemical + off-target profiles), ResNet18DNN (2022, converts SMILES to molecular images, AUROC 0.958).
- *Cardiotoxicity:* hERGBoost (2025, XGBoost regression, R²=0.622), hERGAT (2025, GAT+GRU, AUROC 0.907), AttenhERG (2024, GNN with uncertainty estimation, AUROC 0.835), DMFGAM (2023, multimodal fingerprints+graph, AUROC 0.894), CardioToxNet (2021, meta-ensemble of GCN/FCNN/1D-CNN), DeepHIT (2020, minimizes false negatives, includes safer analog generation).
- *Nephrotoxicity:* Gong et al. (2022, fingerprints of chemical drugs and herbal medicines, AUROC 0.915), Shi et al. (2022, consensus model, AUROC 0.93), Zhang et al. (2019, Naïve Bayes classifier, accuracy 0.84). Traditional ML models perform better than deep learning when data are limited.
- *Neurotoxicity:* Studies develop multiple models for distinct tasks including BBB permeability, neuronal cytotoxicity, and general neurotoxicity, using DMPNN, MFBERT, MLP, and tree-based methods.

**Key Facts on Toxicity Incidence:** Drug-induced nephrotoxicity affects 14-26% of adults; drug-induced renal failure accounts for ~25% of acute kidney injury cases in hospitalized patients. Liver toxicity agreement between animals and humans averages ~55%. The FDA issued boxed warnings in 2021 for JAK inhibitors (tofacitinib, baricitinib, upadacitinib) due to cardiovascular risks. hERG evaluation is required per ICH S7B guidelines.

**Methodological Observations:** GNNs align well with graph-based molecular structures and enable substructure identification. Transformer-based models show promise in cheminformatics. Interpretability techniques include SHAP, attention-based visualizations, permutation feature importance, and gradient-based attribution. Multi-task learning improves genotoxicity prediction by leveraging shared parameters across Ames test strains. Scaffold-based data splitting is used to evaluate generalizability.
</summary>

Security concerns drive locally hosted solutions; AskFDALabel runs on in-house GPU servers using open-source models like Llama 3.1-70B, keeping data within FDA systems. One FDA implementation reviewed 211 drugs for DILI risk in approximately 15 minutes versus 40-60 hours manually.

Limitations include context dependency, class imbalance making rare events hard to detect, explainability challenges with "black box" models, cost/computational requirements (230+ computing hours for pre-training), and the need for rigorous validation. Best practices include starting with pilot projects, establishing baselines, maintaining human oversight, and using domain-specific training data since generic LLMs significantly underperform.

Future directions include integrating multiple data sources (electronic health records, clinical trial data, literature, real-time pharmacovigilance data), addressing causality determination (Columbia University researchers are developing such methods), and proactive signal detection.
</summary>

--- SOURCE 14: JMIR Medical Informatics - Predicting Drug–Side Effect Relationships From Parametric Knowledge Embedded in Biomedical BERT Models: Methodological Study With a Natural Language Processing Approach ---
URL: https://medinform.jmir.org/2025/1/e67513

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This paper, published in JMIR Medical Informatics (Vol 13, 2025; doi:10.2196/67513), presents a methodological study on predicting drug–side effect relationships using parametric knowledge embedded in biomedical BERT language models. 

**Background/Objectiive:** Adverse drug reactions (ADRs) pose serious public health risks, with approximately 2 million serious ADRs and 100,000 deaths reported annually in the US. Traditional context-independent word embedding models like Word2Vec have limitations in capturing biomedical domain specificity. The study proposes using BERT-based models pretrained on biomedical corpora to extract parametric knowledge and predict unknown drug–side effect relationships.

**Methods:** The study used 158,096 known drug–side effect pairs from the SIDER database (version 4.1) to build an adjacency matrix with 1,345 drugs and 6,123 side effects. Cosine similarity was calculated between word embedding vectors of drugs and side effects. Relation scores (combining drug-similarity and side-effect-similarity components using equations) were calculated for 8,235,435 total drug–side effect pairs. For Word2Vec training, 14,289,160 sentences mentioning drugs and 32,107,327 sentences mentioning side effects were extracted from PubMed (42,515,246 total abstracts, updated December 8, 2022).

**Results:** The clagator/biobert_v1.1 model achieved the highest AUC of 0.915 at an optimal threshold of 0.289 (sensitivity 0.870, specificity 0.830), outperforming Word2Vec (AUC 0.848) and vanilla BERT (bert-base-uncased, AUC 0.857). Other models tested included BiomedBERT (0.907), dmis-lab/biobert_v1.1 (0.901), and PharmBERT-uncased (0.882). All BERT models pretrained on biomedical corpora outperformed vanilla BERT. The cosine similarity-based extraction method outperformed Euclidean distance, Manhattan distance, Jaccard similarity, and dot product methods. The dual-similarity approach (relation score, AUC 0.915) significantly outperformed single-similarity methods (drug-only: 0.799, side-effect-only: 0.881).

**Validation:** External validation with FAERS data (October 2012–June 2023; 901,361 known relationships) confirmed high statistical significance (P<.001) with an odds ratio of 4.822 (Fisher exact test repeated 2,000 times). Case studies of top-ranked predictions not in SIDER (lenalidomide-arthropathy, rosuvastatin-sleep disturbance, gadolinium-acute pulmonary edema, cefazolin-hepatic failure) were confirmed as reported in literature published after 2016.

**Conclusions:** BERT-based models pretrained on biomedical corpora significantly outperform Word2Vec in predicting drug–side effect relationships due to contextual information capture. The methodology demonstrates practical applicability for pharmacovigilance and ADR prediction. Limitations include the SIDER database being last updated in 2015, challenges with non-dose-dependent reactions, case report generalizability issues, prediction limitations for novel drug candidates, and lack of patient-specific idiosyncratic reaction modeling. The research was supported by the Korea Health Technology R&D Project (grant RS-2022-KH125153).
</summary>

SUMMARY:

This article from IntuitionLabs (dated April 2026, updated August 2026) examines how Isomorphic Labs – an AI-driven drug discovery spin-off from Google DeepMind – is advancing its first AlphaFold-designed oncology and immunology therapeutics into clinical trials, marking a watershed moment for AI-designed drugs.

**Background & Technology:** Drug discovery traditionally takes over a decade and costs billions, with only ~10% chance of approval for candidates entering trials. The AlphaFold revolution began with AlphaFold 2 (2020) solving the protein folding problem (earning the 2024 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for John Jumper and Demis Hassabis). AlphaFold 3 (released May 2024, a joint DeepMind/Isomorphic effort) extended predictions to molecular interactions with proteins, DNA, RNA, and ligands, achieving "at least a 50% improvement" and in some cases doubling prediction accuracy. Isomorphic Labs was founded in 2021 in London by DeepMind veterans including CEO Sir Demis Hassabis and President Colin Murdoch, with the mission to "solve all disease" using AI.

**Funding & Partnerships:** In March 2025, Isomorphic raised a $600M funding round led by Thrive Capital (with GV and Alphabet). It has forged partnerships with Novartis, Eli Lilly (January 2024 deals valued at up to ~$3B combined), and Johnson & Johnson for AI-driven drug discovery on undisclosed targets.

**Technology - IsoDDE:** Isomorphic built a proprietary AI drug design engine ("IsoDDE") integrating AlphaFold models with generative chemistry models. A February 2026 technical report showcased extremely precise predictions of protein-drug interactions and antibody structures. Columbia computational biologist Mohammed AlQuraishi called it "a major advance, on the scale of an AlphaFold 4."

**Pipeline:** Isomorphic's internal candidates focus on oncology (cancer) and immunology. Public reports hint at TIM-3 (an immune checkpoint) as a target. The company plans to license its drugs out after early-stage trials.

**Clinical Trials Timeline:** In July 2025, President Colin Murdoch said human trials of AI-designed drugs were "finally in sight" with the company "staffing up" to begin dosing patients. The Indian Express (July 9, 2025) reported the oncology drug created using AlphaFold 3 was set to enter human trials. However, at the January 2026 World Economic Forum, Hassabis confirmed first clinical trials are now expected by the end of 2026 (a roughly one-year delay from original projections), still rapid by biotech standards. SUMMARY:
<summary>
On February 10, 2026, Isomorphic Labs announced a significant advancement in AI-powered drug design with the introduction of the Isomorphic Labs Drug Design Engine (IsoDDE), a unified computational drug-design system that moves beyond AlphaFold 3 (AF3), which was released in 2024 in partnership with Google DeepMind. IsoDDE addresses a key limitation of AF3: understanding biomolecular structures alone was insufficient for unlocking real-world in silico drug discovery programs.

Key capabilities and results highlighted include:
- **Structure prediction**: IsoDDE more than doubles the accuracy of AlphaFold 3 on the 'Runs N' Poses' benchmark (Škrinjar et al. 2025), which tests generalisation to novel pockets and ligands. It successfully models out-of-distribution events like induced fits and the opening of cryptic pockets.
- **Complex biologics**: IsoDDE outperforms AlphaFold 3 by 2.3x and Boltz-2 by 19.8x in the high-fidelity regime (DockQ > 0.8) on antibody-antigen structure prediction, with remarkable performance on the CDR-H3 loop (the most variable and difficult part of an antibody to predict), unlocking de novo antibody design possibilities.

The company demonstrated this by recapitulating the discovery of a novel cryptic allosteric site on cereblon (recently found experimentally by Dippon et al. 2026, published in Nature), predicting both the known thalidomide-binding pocket and the novel cryptic site from sequence alone.

IsoDDE is described as a scalable foundation for AI drug design, offering predictive fidelity for navigating novel biological systems. Isomorphic Labs' drug design teams are using these capabilities daily across their programs to understand unseen structures, identify uncharacterised pockets, and create novel chemical matter. The work is detailed in a technical report and cited as: @manual{isodde2026}, doi: 10.5281/zenodo.19699685. The company thanked Google DeepMind for collaboration. SUMMARY:
<summary>
Isomorphic Labs announced AlphaFold 3 (May 8, 2024), a revolutionary AI model developed with Google DeepMind that predicts the structure and interactions of all life's molecules—including proteins, DNA, RNA, ligands, and chemical modifications—with unprecedented accuracy. For protein interactions with other molecule types, it shows at least 50% improvement over existing methods, with doubled prediction accuracy for some important interaction categories. --- SOURCE 6: Multimodal Clinical Trial Outcome Prediction with Large Language Models ---
URL: https://arxiv.org/html/2402.06512v3

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This paper presents LIFTED (muLti-modal mIx-of-experts For ouTcome prEDiction), a novel deep learning approach for clinical trial outcome prediction that addresses limitations of prior methods that rely on manually designed modal-specific encoders. LIFTED unifies multimodal data (disease, drug name, drug description, SMILES string, and eligibility criteria) by transforming them into natural language descriptions using Large Language Models (LLMs), then processes them through unified transformer-based encoders. Key innovations include: (1) a Sparse Mixture-of-Experts (SMoE) framework that dynamically routes representations from different modalities to shared experts, identifying similar information patterns across modalities; (2) representation augmentation with a consistency loss to make encoders noise-resilient; and (3) a Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) integration module that dynamically weighs modality importance for each trial, using only disease information to generate weights. An auxiliary unimodal prediction loss is also introduced to improve representation quality.

The method was evaluated on the HINT benchmark dataset (17,538 clinical trial records across Phases I, II, and III). LIFTED outperformed all baselines including HINT and SPOT across all three trial phases. Key results for PR-AUC were 70.7 (Phase I), 69.8 (Phase II), and 88.3 (Phase III); F1 scores were 71.6, 66.2, and 83.8; and ROC-AUC were 64.9, 65.1, and 73.5 respectively. Ablation studies confirmed the effectiveness of each component (representation augmentation, auxiliary loss, and LLM transformation). Modality analysis showed criteria (patient eligibility) was the most important modality while drug description was least important. The SMoE analysis demonstrated that certain experts (e.g., experts 6 and 7) were consistently selected across modalities, confirming their role in extracting similar patterns. Code is released at https://github.com/shenmishajing/lifted.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"These approaches rely on manually designed modal-specific encoders, which limits both the extensibility to adapt new modalities and the ability to discern similar information patterns across different modalities."

--- SOURCE 7: Predicting Clinical Trial Success: From Machine Learning to Agentic AI and Beyond ---
URL: https://medium.com/keiji-ai/predicting-clinical-trial-success-from-machine-learning-to-agentic-ai-and-beyond-3ab570737f83

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This article by Jimeng Sun (Professor at UIUC and co-founder of Keiji AI), published November 13, 2025 in the Keiji AI publication, explores the evolution of AI methods for predicting clinical trial outcomes. Originally authored November 5, 2025 by Zifeng Wang, PhD of Keiji AI, the article traces the progression from machine learning models to future agentic AI systems.

The piece describes four key models/tools:

1. **HINT (Hierarchical Interaction Network for Clinical Trial Outcome Prediction)**: Defined trial success as regulatory approval of the drug, enabling labeling of over ten thousand trials across phases I-III. Uses a hierarchical model combining drug, disease, and design features.

2. **SPOT (Sequential Predictive Modeling of Clinical Trial Outcome)**: Models trials as evolving sequences grouped into "topics" (e.g., PD-1 inhibitors for lung cancer), using sequential learning and meta-learning to adapt to new patterns even with sparse data. Achieved up to 21.5% better prediction accuracy in early-phase trials and reasons like an experienced clinician-scientist.

3. **CTO (Clinical Trial Outcome labeling)**: Uses LLMs to automatically extract structured outcome labels (positive, negative, terminated, or approved) from hundreds of thousands of trial reports and publications, creating an "ImageNet for trial outcomes."

4. **TrialPanorama**: Aggregates over 1.6 million clinical trials from fifteen global registries, linked with DrugBank, MedDRA, and PubMed, providing a panoramic map of global clinical research and defining benchmark tasks (arm design, eligibility criteria, trial completion prediction).

The article concludes by describing the future shift toward agentic AI systems — multi-agent "AI analyst teams" where one agent scans literature, another monitors live trial databases, and another cross-references biomarkers with patient registries, all feeding evidence to a reasoning core that synthesizes a probability of success. It acknowledges that trial outcome prediction will never be perfectly deterministic due to biological unpredictability, but AI can make surprises "far less costly."

The article includes four academic references (Fu et al. 2022 for HINT in Patterns; Wang et al. 2023 for SPOT in ACM BCB; Gao et al. 2024 for CTO in arXiv; Wang et al. 2025 for TrialPanorama in arXiv), each with DOIs.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"SPOT models trials not as static points, but as evolving stories. It groups similar trials into 'topics', say, all the PD-1 inhibitors for lung cancer, and learns from how those trials have evolved over time."
