--- SOURCE 8: Matching Patients to Clinical Trials with Large Language Models ---
URL: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10418514

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This scientific paper, published on arXiv (Preprint: arXiv:2307.15051v5, November 18, 2024; PMID: 37576126; PMCID: PMC10418514), presents TrialGPT, an end-to-end framework for zero-shot patient-to-trial matching using large language models (LLMs). The study was led by Qiao Jin and colleagues from NCBI/NLM/NIH, University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign, National Cancer Institute, University of Pittsburgh, and other institutions, with Zhiyong Lu as corresponding author.

TrialGPT consists of three modules: (1) TrialGPT-Retrieval, which filters candidate trials from large collections using LLM-generated keywords and hybrid-fusion retrieval (BM25 lexical + MedCPT semantic retrieval with reciprocal rank fusion); (2) TrialGPT-Matching, which predicts criterion-level patient eligibility with natural language explanations, relevant sentence locations, and eligibility classifications; and (3) TrialGPT-Ranking, which aggregates criterion-level predictions into trial-level scores.

KEY RESULTS:
- Evaluated on 183 synthetic patients with over 75,000 trial annotations across three cohorts (SIGIR 2016, TREC 2021 CT, TREC 2022 CT)
- Retrieval: GPT-4-based TrialGPT-Retrieval recalls over 90% of relevant trials using less than 6% (5.5%) of the initial collection; LLM-generated keywords outperformed those produced by four human clinicians
- Matching: TrialGPT-Matching achieved 87.3% criterion-level prediction accuracy on 1,015 patient-criterion pairs, close to expert performance (88.7-90.0%); explanations were 87.8% correct; sentence location F1 score of 88.6%
- Ranking: GPT-4-based TrialGPT-Ranking outperformed best baselines by 43.8% in ranking and excluding trials (NDCG@10 of 0.7275 and AUROC of 0.7979 combined with linear aggregations)
- User study: TrialGPT reduced screening time by 42.6% in patient recruitment, with accuracy of 97.2% vs 91.7% without TrialGPT

Main error types identified in TrialGPT: incorrect reasoning (30.7%), ambiguous label definitions (26.9%), and lack of medical knowledge (15.4%). The study's limitations include reliance on closed-source GPT models, limited scope of user study, and need for future work on EHR integration, longitudinal data, and multi-modal inputs. The authors emphasize that experts should always remain in the loop, with TrialGPT serving as an assistance tool rather than replacing human recruiters.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"Patient recruitment is challenging for clinical trials. We introduce TrialGPT, an end-to-end framework for zero-shot patient-to-trial matching with large language models."

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This medRxiv preprint (2025.12.03.25341549, published December 29, 2025) presents a benchmarking study evaluating large language models (LLMs) for drug-drug interaction (DDI) identification. The study was conducted by researchers at University of Colorado (approved by COMIRB #25-1631) and funded by AHRQ and NIH grants.

METHODS: The researchers evaluated three LLMs—GPT-4o-mini, MedGemma-27B, and LLaMA3-70B—using a clinician-annotated benchmark dataset of 750 unique DDI scenarios spanning three levels of diagnostic complexity. Interactions were labeled using LexiDrug categories (A=no known interaction, B=no action needed, C=monitor therapy, D=consider therapy modification, X=avoid combination). Three task formats were used: (1) pointwise two-drug classification, (2) pairwise three-drug discrimination, and (3) listwise 4–6 drug selection. All cases were independently reviewed by three board-certified clinical pharmacists. Standardized zero-shot prompting with nine repeated runs (temperature=0.7) and label shuffling was used. Metrics included precision, recall, F1, accuracy, and self-consistency. Datasets are available at github.com/sikora07/AIChemist.

RESULTS: Performance varied by task structure. In the pointwise two-drug task, LLaMA3-70B had the highest recall (61.7) and F1 (59.7), while GPT-4o-mini had the highest precision (65.7). In the pairwise three-drug task, GPT-4o-mini achieved the highest accuracy (86.6), followed by MedGemma-27B (84.9) and LLaMA3-70B (81.5). In the listwise 4-6 drug task, MedGemma-27B performed best (80.0), followed by GPT-4o-mini (71.3) and LLaMA3-70B (68.6). All models performed worst on Category C (moderate-risk) interactions. Self-consistency decreased as task complexity increased, and no model showed uniformly high reliability. Notably, models failed to identify Category X (avoid combination) DDIs in 24-30% of cases. Undetected high-risk interactions included enoxaparin/alteplase (bleeding risk), sulfamethoxazole-trimethoprim/spironolactone (hyperkalemia), and dronedarone/azithromycin (QTc prolongation).

CONCLUSIONS: The study represents the first clinically validated DDI benchmark dataset. LLMs showed moderate but uneven performance, degrading with increased complexity (more medications and requiring severity specification). The authors note rules-based software (e.g., LexiDrug) performs perfectly, and emphasize that LLMs are not yet safe for routine DDI identification without clinician backup. Limitations include small dataset size by LLM standards and lack of prompt engineering or knowledge-graph augmentation. The authors call for further model improvement and multi-format, reliability-aware evaluation frameworks before clinical deployment.

--- SOURCE 12: Benchmarking Computational Methods for Emerging Drug-Drug Interaction Prediction ---
URL: https://arxiv.org/html/2410.18583v4

SUMMARY:
<summary>
## DDI-Ben: A Benchmarking Framework for Emerging Drug-Drug Interaction Prediction Under Distribution Changes

### Overview
This paper by Zhenqian Shen et al. (Tsinghua University) introduces **DDI-Ben**, a benchmarking framework for emerging drug-drug interaction (DDI) prediction that explicitly addresses distribution changes between known and new drugs—a factor neglected by current evaluation methods. The code and data are available at https://github.com/LARS-research/DDI-Bench.

### Motivation
- Emerging DDI prediction is critical for new drugs with unknown pharmacological risks, as clinical experiments are time-consuming and expensive.
- Existing DDI datasets (DrugBank, TWOSIDES) lack drug approval timeline information, making it hard to simulate realistic drug distribution changes over time.
- Current evaluation methods assume known and new drugs follow the same distribution, using unrealistic i.i.d. drug splits, which makes evaluation results questionable.

### Distribution Change Simulation Framework
The framework uses **distribution changes between drug sets as a surrogate** for real-world DDI distribution changes:
1. **Drug distribution change modeling**: Introduces a cluster-based difference measurement γ(Dk,Dn) = max{S(u,v)} based on drug similarity (Tanimoto coefficient between fingerprints). Smaller γ indicates larger distribution changes.
2. **Drug data split**: Splits drugs into known and new drug sets.

The framework defines two emerging DDI tasks:
- **S1**: Determine DDI type between a known drug and a new drug.
- **S2**: Determine DDI type between two new drugs.

### Data Split Strategies Comparison
Eight split strategies were compared (random, drug frequency, drug usage, scaffold, LoHi, SPECTRA, DataSAIL, and the proposed cluster-based split). Key findings:
- LoHi and SPECTRA discard data points (undesirable given data collection costs).
- Only SPECTRA and the **cluster-based split** enable controllable distribution changes.
- The proposed cluster-based split achieved the **highest consistency index** with realistic drug approval-time-based splits.
- Real-world drug clusters emerge from new drug safety issues (1980s NSAIDs), technological breakthroughs (1990s ACE inhibitors), and new epidemics (2010s HCV NS5A inhibitors).

### Datasets
- **DrugBank**: Multiclass dataset, 1,710 drugs, 86 interaction types, 188,509 DDI triplets.
- **TWOSIDES**: Multilabel dataset, 645 drugs, 209 DDI types (frequency 3000–6000), 116,650 DDI triplets.

### Methods Benchmarked (10 representative methods)
- **Feature-based**: MLP
- **Embedding-based**: MSTE
- **GNN-based**: Decagon, SSI-DDI, MRCGNN, EmerGNN, SAGAN
- **Graph-transformer**: TIGER
- **LLM-based**: TextDDI, DDI-GPT

### Key Results
1. **Most existing methods suffer substantial performance degradation** when distribution changes are introduced, with a more severe decline on DrugBank (harder multiclass prediction) than TWOSIDES.
2. **LLM-based methods (TextDDI, DDI-GPT) are the most robust** against distribution changes. EmerGNN performed best without distribution changes but TextDDI and DDI-GPT outperformed others under distribution changes.
3. **Textual information and LLM processing are key**: TextDDI's LLM extracts key pharmacological knowledge from raw textual data, filters irrelevant information, and enables more accurate predictions. Transferable pharmacological knowledge (e.g., Aclidinium's bronchodilatory activities, Butylscopolamine's muscarinic receptor binding) is not available in fingerprints or biomedical networks.
4. **DDI-type analysis**: MLP and MSTE rely on sufficient labeled data (good on major DDI types, poor on long-tail types). DDI-GPT significantly outperformed others on medium and long-tail DDI types under distribution changes.
5. **Controlling γ**: As distribution change increases (γ decreases), most methods' performance drops significantly; DDI-GPT remains relatively best, suggesting LLM prior knowledge and textual side information help mitigate the negative impact.

### Evaluation Metrics
- **DrugBank**: Macro F1 (primary), accuracy, Cohen's Kappa.
- **TWOSIDES**: Average ROC-AUC (primary), PR-AUC, and accuracy across DDI types.

### Conclusions & Future Work
DDI-Ben highlights the importance of explicitly addressing distribution changes in emerging DDI prediction. Future directions include designing LLM-based methods to alleviate distribution change impact and domain adaptation methods for real-world robustness.
</summary>

--- SOURCE 13: Graph-Based Machine Learning for Predicting Drug–Drug Interactions: A Systematic Review ---
URL: https://www.mdpi.com/1424-8247/19/8/1225

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a systematic review article published in the MDPI journal *Pharmaceuticals* (2026, 19(8), 1225, DOI: 10.3390/ph19081225), titled "Graph-Based Machine Learning for Predicting Drug–Drug Interactions: A Systematic Review." It was authored by Md. Tuhin Reza, Md. Abdul Kader, Wissem Inoubli, Md. Biddut Hossain, and Md. Kamrul Islam (corresponding author), from institutions in Bangladesh (Jashore University of Science & Technology, Daffodil International University, BANBEIS) and France (University of Artois). The article was submitted June 21, 2026, revised and accepted July 31, 2026, and published August 4, 2026, and belongs to the Special Issue "Drug Safety and Real-World Evidence: From Databases to Artificial Intelligence."

**Purpose & Background:** The review evaluates graph-based machine-learning methods for predicting drug–drug interactions (DDIs), which are major medication-safety concerns. Since experimental testing cannot cover the rapidly expanding number of drug pairs, computational DDI prediction is a critical complementary strategy for prioritizing risky combinations and supporting medication-safety workflows. The review focuses on graph neural networks (GNNs) and their architectures, data integration, interpretability, reproducibility, and clinical relevance.

**Methodology:** Conducted following the PRISMA 2020 framework. Searches covered IEEE Xplore (n=74), ScienceDirect (n=96), PubMed (n=67), and Google Scholar (n=53), totaling 290 records for studies published January 2021 through March 2026. After removing duplicates and ineligible records, 60 primary studies were included. Because studies used heterogeneous datasets and methods, findings were synthesized narratively rather than statistically (no meta-analysis). Risk of bias was assessed across seven domains: data leakage, negative sampling, generalization design, baseline/ablation adequacy, reproducibility, interpretability, and clinical applicability.

**Key Results:** Sixty studies met eligibility criteria. Methods progressed from graph convolutional networks and graph attention networks to graph transformers, contrastive learning, multimodal fusion, and LLM-enhanced representations. Representative reported results include 94.47% transductive accuracy for SSI-DDI, 99.74% warm-start accuracy for DrugDAGT, and 95.43% AUROC for KnowDDI on TWOSIDES — but these are study-specific and not directly comparable. Only three studies explicitly addressed data leakage; leakage-aware drug-disjoint, temporal, and external evaluations were uncommon. Uncertainty calibration, computational-resource reporting, complete reproducibility materials, and independently validated explanations were also limited.

The review identified five principal threats to validity: (1) leakage-prone random pairwise splits; (2) incomplete or noisy labels (unobserved interactions treated as confirmed negatives); (3) limited cold-start evaluation on unseen drugs; (4) scarce temporal evaluation; and (5) limited interpretability validation. The review covers three analytical questions: (RQ1) how graph construction, data modality, and validation design influence reported performance; (RQ2) when attention and multimodal fusion add demonstrable value; (RQ3) what evidence supports translation beyond benchmark performance.

Three core modeling concepts were defined: GNN architectures, multimodal fusion (combining molecular structure, SMILES, DDI networks, knowledge graphs, side effects, targets, pathways, or text), and attention mechanisms. Attention categories identified include graph attention, cross-/co-attention, hierarchical attention, knowledge-graph attention, transformer self-attention, feature/modality weighting, and contrastive attention.

**Conclusions:** Graph-based machine learning is promising for DDI prioritization and hypothesis generation but remains insufficient for independent clinical decision-making. The review recommends future studies use standardized benchmarks, leakage-aware validation, calibrated uncertainty, reproducible pipelines, validated explanations, and external or prospective evaluation. Keywords: drug–drug interaction; graph neural network; computational pharmacology; multimodal learning; attention mechanism.
</summary>

SUMMARY:

This is a peer-reviewed original research article published in Frontiers in Pharmacology (Section: Translational Pharmacology) on June 2, 2025, part of the research topic "Artificial Intelligence in Traditional Medicine Research and Application." The paper introduces DDI-JUDGE, a novel Large Language Model (LLM)-based method for drug-drug interaction (DDI) prediction that integrates in-context learning (ICL) prompts with an ensemble judging mechanism.

**Key Contributions:**
1. A novel ICL prompt paradigm for DDI prediction that uses cosine similarity-based exemplar retrieval to select high-similarity positive and negative samples as prompts.
2. A structured ICL-based prompt template including input requirements (drug names and SMILES), prediction tasks, consideration factors (pharmacodynamics, metabolic pathways, receptor interactions, clinical data), and examples.
3. An ensemble discriminator module using GPT-4 as a judge to score predictions from multiple LLMs based on four criteria (scientific accuracy, clarity/coherence, evidence support, relevance), with results combined via confidence-weighted fusion.

**Methodology:** The method selects optimal prompt samples using drug similarity measures (Tanimoto, Cosine, Dice, graph-based via Weisfeiler-Lehman kernel, and embedding-based via MolBERT), with Morgan fingerprints (2048-bit, radius 2) for molecular scaffold similarity. The model was tested in both zero-shot and few-shot scenarios using Luo's dataset, which integrates DrugBank 3.0, Human Protein Reference Database, CTD, and SIDER data (12,015 nodes including 708 drugs, 1,512 proteins, 5,603 diseases, 4,192 side effects; 10,036 known DDIs).

**Results:**
- DDI-JUDGE achieved best performance in zero-shot settings (AUC 0.642, AUPR 0.629) and few-shot settings (AUC 0.788, AUPR 0.801), outperforming GPT-4, GPT-4o, GPT-3.5, Llama 2, Llama 3, Claude 3.5, DeepSeek V3, and Davinci-003.
- Embedding-based similarity achieved the best overall performance among similarity measures (AUC 0.794, AUPR 0.815).
- Performance improved progressively with more ICL prompt samples (AUC rising from 0.642 at zero-shot to 0.788 with n=8 samples).
- Case studies identified novel DDIs including Rivaroxaban/Dihydroxyaluminum Sodium Carbonate, Romidepsin/Quinidine (QT prolongation risk), and Simvastatin/Fluconazole (myopathy/rhabdomyolysis risk).

**Limitations:** The method lacks domain-specific drug knowledge, and GPT-4 as a discriminator may introduce biases. Future work will incorporate more drug-related data and fine-tuning. Authors: He Qi, Xiaoqiang Li, Chengcheng Zhang (co-corresponding), and Tianyi Zhao (co-corresponding), from Harbin Institute of Technology (Harbin Institute of Technology, Suzhou Institute of Biomedical Engineering and Technology, etc.). Insilico appointed Dr. Carol Satler, MD, PhD, as Vice President of Clinical Development to advance non-oncology programs. The company states it will initiate discussions with regulatory bodies and pursue a pivotal trial, with full Phase IIa data to be presented at an upcoming medical conference and published in medical journals. A Phase IIa trial in the U.S. led by Dr. Toby M. Maher is actively recruiting patients.

The drug's development history: after preclinical candidate nomination, ISM001-055 was tested in multiple animal models of lung, kidney, and skin fibrosis, followed by a Phase 0 microdose trial and two Phase 1 trials in New Zealand and China. This body of work, from target identification to Phase 0/1 completion, was peer-reviewed and published in Nature Biotechnology in March 2024. The medicinal chemistry portion was published in the Journal of Medicinal Chemistry in October 2024, and additional roles of TNIK in age-related diseases were published in Cell Trends in Pharmacological Sciences in June 2024.

IPF is a chronic, scarring lung disease affecting approximately 5 million people worldwide, with a median survival of 3 to 4 years. Current approved antifibrotic treatments slow disease progression but do not stop or reverse it. ISM001-055 is a potentially first-in-class small molecule targeting TNIK, aiming to halt or reverse fibrotic processes. Insilico has nominated 20 preclinical candidates in a portfolio of over 30 assets since 2021 and has received IND approval for 9 molecules. Key quotes from the principal investigator Zuojun Xu, M.D., Dr. Satler, Dr. Maher, and CEO Alex Zhavoronkov highlight the drug's potential to stop or even reverse disease progression.

SUMMARY:

Search results: 



--- SOURCE 1: Comparing AI Biology Foundation Models: AlphaFold 3 & ESM3 ---
URL: https://intuitionlabs.ai/articles/biology-foundation-models-comparison

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This IntuitionLabs report (published April 19, 2026) provides an in-depth comparison of AI biology foundation models for molecular biology, focusing on AlphaFold 3 (AF3), ESM-3, Boltz-2, Chai-1, and RoseTTAFold. It analyzes their architectures, training data, capabilities, quantitative benchmarks, and real-world use cases in drug discovery.

**Key Models:**
- **AlphaFold 3 (AF3)**: Released May 2024 by DeepMind/Isomorphic. Uses a generative diffusion architecture predicting full atomic structures of complexes (proteins, nucleic acids, small molecules, modified residues) in one unified model. Achieves ~76% success on PoseBusters ligand benchmark (RMSD <2Å), far surpassing physics-based docking (~30-38%). Dramatically improved protein-ligand, protein-DNA/RNA, and antibody-antigen prediction. Closed-source (free academic use only) and can "hallucinate" structure in disordered regions (mitigated via cross-distillation training).
- **ESM-3**: From EvolutionaryScale (ex-Meta researchers), mid-2024. A 98-billion-parameter multimodal protein language model, generative and autoregressive like GPT. Trained on 2.78 billion sequences (771 billion tokens) using >10^24 FLOPS. Can generate protein sequences from partial cues; demonstrated design of a novel fluorescent protein (58% identity to known GFP, representing ~500M years of natural evolution). Smallest 1.4B version open-source; larger models commercial via AWS/Nvidia.
- **Boltz-2**: Announced June 2025 by MIT Jameel Clinic. Successor to Boltz-1 with equivariant diffusion backbone plus a unique "affinity module" predicting binding strength (IC50-like). Achieves FEP-level accuracy in relative binding energies (Pearson ~0.62) while running >1000× faster than physics-based simulations. Fully open-source (MIT license). Outperformed all submissions on CASP16-style binding challenge; used to identify TYK2 inhibitors in virtual assays.
- **Chai-1**: Released September 2024 by Chai Discovery. Open-source multimodal structure predictor using protein language model embeddings and supporting experimental restraints (crosslinks, epitope maps). ~77% success on PoseBusters ligand benchmark (vs AF3's ~76%). User "steering" with contact constraints doubles antibody-antigen accuracy. Pitched as "AlphaFold 3 power without limitations" - free for non-commercial use.
- **RoseTTAFold**: Released 2021 by Baker Lab using a three-track network (1D sequences, 2D distance maps, 3D coordinates). Achieved CASP14-competitive accuracy comparable to AlphaFold 2. Openly available; "All-Atom" 2024 update weaker on ligand docking (~42% top hits vs ~76-77% for newer models) but remains a standard comparator.

**Headline Benchmark Comparison (PoseBusters protein-ligand):** Physics-based methods 38%, AlphaFold 3 76%, Chai-1 77%, RoseTTAFold All-Atom ~42%.

**Implications:** These foundation models are transforming biology, enabling routine atomistic complex prediction (proteins with drugs, DNA, membranes) in hours rather than years. Drug discovery pipelines are exploiting end-to-end AI for generative compound design and antibody maturation. Concerns include hallucination issues (AF3), dual-use risks, licensing restrictions, and computational demands. The field is evolving rapidly with iterative improvements expected.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"The new AlphaFold model demonstrates substantially improved accuracy over many previous specialized tools: far greater accuracy for protein–ligand interactions compared with state-of-the-art docking tools, much higher accuracy for protein–nucleic acid interactions… and substantially higher antibody–antigen prediction accuracy compared with AlphaFold-Multimer v2.3." (AF3 Nature paper)
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 2: A survey of downstream applications of evolutionary scale modeling protein language models ---
URL: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12806033

SUMMARY:
<summary>
A survey paper published in Quantitative Biology (2025, Vol. 14, e70013) titled "A survey of downstream applications of evolutionary scale modeling protein language models," authored by Qingyu Yang, Jiale Yu, and Jie Zheng from ShanghaiTech University and the Shanghai Engineering Research Center of Intelligent Vision and Imaging. The paper (PMCID: PMC12806033, PMID: 41676321) reviews the ESM (evolutionary scale modeling) series of protein language models (PLMs) and their downstream applications in protein science and engineering.

**ESM Model Series Overview:**
- ESM-1b: First foundational BERT-style Transformer PLM, trained via masked language modeling (MLM) on 250 million protein sequences from UniParc (43M–670M parameters)
- ESM-MSA-1b (MSA Transformer): Uses tied row/united column attention on multiple sequence alignments for structure inference (100M parameters)
- ESM-1v: Specialized for variant effect prediction (650M parameters)
- ESM-IF1 (GVP-Transformer): Combines Transformer with GVP-GNN for inverse folding/fixed-backbone design (124M parameters)
- ESM-2: SOTA general-purpose PLM, one of the most widely used foundation models in protein science (8M–15B parameters)
- ESMFold: End-to-end single-sequence 3D structure predictor, comparable to AlphaFold2 in some key scenarios, significantly faster (3.69B parameters)
- ESM3: Protein design model reasoning across sequence, structure, and function (1.4B–98B parameters)

**Advantages of ESM over other PLMs:** best or near-best performance in most scenarios; well-developed complete series covering various protein research fields; widely used as base models in other works.

**Techniques of Using ESM (5 categories):**
1. **Direct use**: ESM-IF1 for fixed-backbone design, ESMFold for structure prediction (much faster than AlphaFold2 with minor accuracy loss, excels at de novo/orphan proteins)
2. **Integration with task-specific models**: ESM embeddings combined with MLP, ML classifiers, regression models, LSTM, CNN, attention, GRU; e.g., NERE, DSMBind (binding affinity), ESMFlow (flow matching for conformational sampling)
3. **Fine-tuning**: Both full fine-tuning and parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) including adapter tuning, prompt tuning, and LoRA (most widely used; PEFT-SP showed LoRA best for signal peptide classification); also FusOn-pLM and AntiFold
4. **Multimodality**: Fusing sequence and structure information via three main approaches (ESM embeddings as GNN node features; concatenation of representations; cross-attention); contrastive learning (e.g., ConPLex, CLIP-based methods like PepPrCLIP, Cut&CLIP, CSSP); structure-aware retraining (e.g., SaProt using Foldseek's 3Di tokens); continual training (ESM-S)
5. **Attention maps and evaluation**: Attention maps used for contact map prediction; ESM used for directed evolution assistance, mutation validation, structure evaluation (e.g., self-consistency perplexity with ESM-IF1, ESMFold pLDDT/pAE scores in UCSF ChimeraX)

**Key Comparative Findings:** Among well-known PLMs, ESM and ProtT5 show best performance in different scenarios (ProtT5 slightly better overall); ESM-1b highest for "extracellular" and "golgi apparatus" localization tasks; ProteinBERT performs slightly poorer.

**Downstream Biological Applications:** ESM models capture implicit structural/evolutionary information and apply to structure prediction (fold, secondary structure via NetSurfP-3.0, contact maps, 3D structure via OmegaFold, protein complexes via Seq2Symm) and function prediction (EC/GO via SaProt and ESM-GearNet, text-defined function via ProtST, functional annotation via NetGO 3.0, localization via ProtGPS, solubility via NetSolP, homology detection via PLMSearch).

The survey analyzed approximately 100 representative papers (each cited at least five times) from papers citing at least one of the six original ESM publications.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"The evolutionary scale modeling (ESM) series is promising to revolutionize protein science and engineering through large language models (LLMs), providing a robust framework for understanding the relationships among sequences, structures, and functions of proteins."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 3: Simulating 500 million years of evolution with a language model ---
URL: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=qeqbm8a1-ZA

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a seminar presentation by Roshan Rao, PhD, of the company EvoScale, given as part of the "ML for protein engineering seminar series" (posted 17 Sep 2024, ~7308 views). The talk presents ESM3, a frontier multimodal generative language model for proteins that can reason over sequence, structure, and function. The key claims: ESM3 can act as an evolutionary simulator, generating functional proteins far from known proteins. The team prompted ESM3 to design fluorescent proteins and found a bright fluorescent protein at 58% sequence identity from known fluorescent proteins—a distance comparable to over 500 million years of natural evolution.

Key technical details:
- Architecture: A simple Transformer with tokenized input/output tracks for sequence, structure, and function, plus a geometric attention mechanism that encodes 3D coordinates in an SE(3)-invariant and efficient way. Structure is tokenized with a new VQ-VAE (each residue token represents its 16 nearest 3D neighbors) with sub-angstrom RMSD reconstruction.
- Training: Three models trained at 1.4B, 7.7B, and 98.5B parameters. Deeper (rather than wider) architectures were found to be better for proteins. Training used large amounts of metagenomic and synthetic data (found to improve performance once model scale crossed a threshold), FP8 precision, sharding over 1000+ GPUs, and various stability techniques (layer norm on queries/keys, warmup, FP32 for key ops). Optimal masking rate increased with scale (15% at 650M params, 30% at 7B).
- Alignment (DPO fine-tuning): Models are aligned by scoring generated sequences computationally (constraint site RMSD, predicted TM score) and fine-tuning with DPO; larger models respond more strongly to alignment, improving prompt-following fidelity, pTM, and generation diversity.
- Wet lab validation with GFP: ESM3 was prompted with the structure/key chromophore, generating sequences that were synthesized. After one plate experiment and diversification/refinement, a fluorescent protein with high activity and ~58% identity to wild-type GFP was obtained, including mutations in core/alpha-helix positions.

Other points covered: data valuation (PDB is highest value; sequence data scales linearly), use of temporal holdouts and MMS-seq purging to avoid leakage, removal of viruses from the open model for biosafety (internal models retain them for academic partnerships), and future directions (genomic context, protein-ligand interactions, text annotations).
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"Here we show that language models trained on tokens generated by evolution can act as evolutionary simulators to generate functional proteins that are far away from known proteins."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 4: ESM3: Simulating 500 million years of evolution with a ... ---
URL: https://www.evolutionaryscale.ai/blog/esm3-release

SUMMARY:
<summary>
EvolutionaryScale, a public benefit company, announced ESM3, a frontier language model for biology that simultaneously reasons over protein sequence, structure, and function. In a preprint (June 25, 2024) updated with publication in Science Magazine in January 2025, the company described generating a new green fluorescent protein (GFP) called esmGFP. The paper was published in Science (DOI: 10.1126/science.ads0018), and the API is now in public beta through Forge. 

KEY MODEL DETAILS:
- ESM3 is trained on billions of proteins from diverse environments (Amazon rainforest, ocean depths, hydrothermal vents, soil microbes)
- Trained with over 1x10^24 FLOPS and 98B parameters—described as the most compute ever applied to training a biological model
- An order of magnitude larger than the previous model, ESM2 (which itself scaled from ESM-1b/1v and ESM-IF1)
- Uses a masked language modeling objective, tokenizing sequence, structure, and function into discrete alphabets within a single multi-track transformer
- Augmented with hundreds of millions of synthetic data points (predicted structures and functions)
- Uses alignment methods similar to RLHF, but ESM3 can self-improve with feedback on its own generations
- Capabilities emerge with scale (e.g., atomic coordination tasks) and improve with alignment

THE esmGFP RESULT:
- Prompted only with the structure of a few residues in the core of natural GFP, ESM3 reasoned in chain-of-thought to generate candidates
- First experiment: tested 96 generations; found proteins that fluoresce, including B8 (50x less bright, chromophore matured over a week)
- Second experiment from B8: tested 96 more proteins; found esmGFP (well C10), with brightness similar to natural GFPs
- esmGFP differs by 96 mutations out of 229 amino acids (58% sequence similarity to closest known fluorescent protein)
- This corresponds to an estimated equivalent of over 500 million years of natural evolution

RESPONSIBLE DEVELOPMENT:
- Public benefit company focused on AI for human health and society
- Cites the 1975 Asilomar Conference principles as inspiration, plus new responsible biodesign principles
- Four core tenets: communicate benefits and risks, rigorously evaluate risk before public deployment, adopt risk mitigation strategies and guardrails, and work with government/policy/civil society stakeholders

OPEN MODEL:
- Committed to open science; releasing weights and code for an ESM3 1.4B open model on GitHub (github.com/evolutionaryscale/esm)
- Examples of ESM ecosystem applications cited: evolving antibodies (Hie et al. with ESM-1v/1b), COVID variant detection (BioNTech/InstaDeep), clinical mutation effect prediction (Brandes et al.), anti-CRISPR engineering (Marsiglia et al.), protein evolution guidance (Shanker et al.), enzyme function prediction (Yu et al.), single-cell foundation models (Rosen et al.), and antibody design (Høie et al.)

FUTURE DIRECTION:
- API and open model available for scientists to explore protein design and synthetic biology
- Prioritizing beta API access based on potential to expand scientific knowledge
- Developing specialized ESM3 versions for drug design
- Roadmap envisions increasingly multimodal models integrating from molecules to cells
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"ESM3 takes a step towards the future where AI is a tool to engineer biology from first principles in the same way we engineer structures, machines and microchips, and write computer programs."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 5: Evolutionary Scale · ESM Cambrian: Revealing the mysteries of ... ---
URL: https://www.evolutionaryscale.ai/blog/esm-cambrian

SUMMARY:
<summary>
On December 4, 2024, EvolutionaryScale announced ESM Cambrian (ESM C), a next-generation protein language model that defines a new state of the art for protein representation learning. ESM C is a parallel model family to the flagship ESM3 generative models, focusing on creating representations of underlying protein biology rather than controllable generation.

Key details:
- ESM C is trained via masked language modeling at three scales: 300M, 600M, and 6B parameters.
- The 300M and 600M models are released as open-weight models; the 6B model is available on Forge (academic use) and AWS SageMaker (commercial use), with NVIDIA BioNemo availability coming soon.
- All models are available for academic and commercial use under a new open license structure.
- Performance: The 300M model delivers similar performance to ESM2 650M with reduced memory and faster inference; the 600M model rivals the 3B ESM2 and approaches the 15B model; the 6B model outperforms the best ESM2 models by a wide margin. Contact precision (P@L) computed on CASP15.
- ESM C demonstrates linear scaling across orders of magnitude in parameters with non-diminishing returns up to 6B parameters.
- Training data: protein sequences from UniRef, MGnify, and Joint Genome Institute (JGI), clustered at 70% sequence identity (83M, 372M, and 2B clusters respectively).
- Architecture: transformer with Pre-LN, rotary embeddings, and SwiGLU activations, no biases in linear layers or layer norms.
- Training stages: Stage 1 (first 1M steps) uses 512 context length with 64% metagenomic data; Stage 2 (final 500K steps) increases context to 2048 with metagenomic data reduced to 37.5%.
- Evaluations: Uses Rao et al. methodology measuring unsupervised learning of tertiary structure via contact maps, computing P@L with sequence separation of 6+ residues, averaged on temporally held-out structures (cutoff May 1, 2023) and CASP15.
- A preprint describing the models is forthcoming.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"ESM C establishes a new state of the art. ESM has consistently set the state of the art for protein language models. Now ESM C unlocks a new frontier of performance with scaling up to 6 billion parameters."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 6: AI models for Life Sciences in 2026 ---
URL: https://codephusion.com/blog/ai-models-for-life-sciences

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This guide (published May 28, 2026, by Myroslav Syrko of CodePhusion) compares the AI models for Life Sciences offered by six major labs as of 2026: Google DeepMind, NVIDIA, Anthropic, Microsoft, Meta/EvolutionaryScale, and OpenAI, covering access, pricing, and integration cost.

**Google DeepMind/Isomorphic Labs:** Has the strongest science and longest tenure in production biology. AlphaFold 2 reset target validation in 2021; AlphaFold 3 (May 2024) covers protein-ligand and protein-nucleic acid with ~50% accuracy gain on protein-molecule interactions. AlphaFold Server is free non-commercial; commercial capability flows through Isomorphic Labs (Eli Lilly/Novartis deals up to $3B combined in Jan 2024, $600M raise in March 2025, J&J collaboration Jan 2026, $2.1B Series B in May 2026). Wider stack includes AlphaProteo, AlphaGenome (free non-commercial), AlphaMissense, and Med-Gemini (91.1% on MedQA). Best for structure prediction, target validation, protein design.

**NVIDIA:** Sells infrastructure plus curated biology catalog via BioNeMo Platform (pre-trained models, NIM microservices, Blueprints). Runs on DGX Cloud, AWS, GCP, Azure with compute-based pricing (only lab where cost scales with workload, not headcount). Other frameworks: MONAI (medical imaging, 1M+ downloads), Parabricks (genomics; HaplotypeCaller from ~36h CPU to ~25-35min GPU), Clara umbrella. Longest pharma partnership list: Eli Lilly co-innovation lab (Jan 2026, up to $1B/5 years), Recursion ($50M investment), Amgen/deCODE, Genentech, Novo Nordisk. Best for high-volume GPU-bound computational workflows.

**Anthropic:** Launched Claude for Life Sciences (Oct 20, 2025) built on Claude Enterprise with MCP connectors (Benchling, 10x Genomics, PubMed, BioRender, Synapse.org, Wiley Scholar Gateway; later Medidata, ClinicalTrials.gov). Capabilities come from prompting/tools/connectors, not specialized weights. Five anchor customers: Novo Nordisk, Sanofi, AbbVie, AstraZeneca, Genmab. Novo Nordisk case study: clinical study report drafting from 10+ weeks to ~10 minutes. BMS signed strategic deal in May 2026 for 30,000+ employees. Acquired Coefficient Bio (~$400M, 2026). Per-seat pricing. Best for regulatory writing, clinical reports, literature synthesis.

**Microsoft:** Deepest/longest-running stack. Azure AI Foundry catalog includes BioGPT (15M PubMed abstracts), BiomedCLIP (PMC-15M), MedImageInsight/MedImageParse/CXRReportGen, TamGen (TB ClpP lead IC50 1.9 μM), Hist-AI, ECG-FM, plus Virchow2G (1.8B parameter pathology model via Paige.AI). Deep partnerships: Novartis AI Innovation Lab (since Oct 2019), Paige.AI (2023). Unique clinical/EHR layer: Dragon Copilot voice AI (March 2025, extended to nurses Oct 2025), Healthcare Agent Orchestrator, Microsoft Fabric Healthcare (FHIR, OMOP, DICOM, SDOH). Foundry is Azure-only. Best for pharma/health systems already on Azure.

**Meta/EvolutionaryScale:** Most-used open biology models (ESM2, ESM3, ESMFold). ESM2/ESMFold are fully open weights via Meta GitHub; ESM metagenomic atlas has 600M+ predicted structures. ESM3 (June 2024, by EvolutionaryScale) is first generative model jointly reasoning over sequence/structure/function, trained on 2.78B proteins. EvolutionaryScale raised $142M+ (Amazon, NVIDIA backers). Hosted on AWS; only smaller variant on Hugging Face under non-commercial license. Best for open-weight/air-gapped deployments with proprietary data.

**OpenAI:** Generalist with biology entry. GPT-Rosalind (April 2026) is first dedicated life sciences model. Deployments: Moderna (3,000 employees, 750+ custom GPTs since April 2024), Sanofi/Formation Bio (May 2024), Color Health cancer copilot (4x more identified missing labs/imaging), GPT-4b micro (Jan 2025, Retro Biosciences; 50x improvement in pluripotency, iPSC generation from ~3 weeks to ~1 week). HealthBench benchmark (May 2025; 5,000 conversations, 262 physicians). Per-seat or per-token pricing. Best for enterprise productivity.

**Integration guidance:** The data layer is the harder problem; integration lift varies (Anthropic lowest with pre-built connectors; ESM3 highest). Four prerequisites for production: (1) instrument/ELN data into structured store, (2) audit trail for all inputs/outputs/reviews, (3) validation evidence under 21 CFR Part 11 and EU Annex 11, (4) model-to-human handoff with sign-off before regulator submission. Key conclusion: the model layer commoditized fast; the differentiator is wiring models into LIMS/ELN/data pipelines without breaking validation, so the next 24 months reward integration budget over model budget.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"The model layer commoditized faster than anyone predicted. Six labs now ship usable biology offerings, with deals running into the billions and the first AI-designed Isomorphic programs heading toward clinical development.", "The hard part is buying it. AlphaFold Server is free for non-commercial use, and the AlphaFold 3 code plus request-gated model parameters went to academia in November 2024 under a non-commercial license.", "Anthropic moved from horizontal LLM to a vertical pharma product on October 20, 2025, when it launched Claude for Life Sciences with five named pharma anchor customers.", "Novo Nordisk started on Claude 3.5 Sonnet before the Life Sciences bundle existed. In May 2026, Bristol Myers Squibb signed a strategic agreement to roll Claude Enterprise plus Claude Code to more than 30,000 BMS employees.", "Picking the model is the small part. Wiring it into a LIMS, ELN, and the broader data pipeline is where time and budget actually go."

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a technical review article published in the International Journal of Pharmaceutical Research and Applications (Volume 11, Issue 2, March-April 2026, pp. 1149-1154), authored by Harsh Mahesh Sonavaane of SMES's Mahavir Institute of Pharmacy, Nashik. The article reviews the use of digital twin technology in clinical development during 2025-2026, focusing on three key applications: in silico trials, virtual control arms, and hybrid mechanistic-AI architectures.

Key content sections:

1. **Digital Twins**: Defined as dynamic virtual replicas of physical/physiological systems that update based on real-time data. Core components include the physical object, digital representation, and data exchange infrastructure (using IoT and EHRs). Evolved from Industry 4.0 manufacturing applications into healthcare for personalized medicine, disease prediction, virtual trials, remote monitoring, and surgery planning. Enabling technologies include AI/ML, IoT, big data analytics, and cloud computing. Limitations include data privacy/security concerns, high computational costs, integration difficulties, and lack of standardization.

2. **In Silico Trials**: Multi-layered computer-aided modeling to mimic real-life conditions using virtual patients built from medical reports, genomic data, and proteomics. Key components include disease modeling (understanding biological pathways and disease mechanisms) and PK-PD (pharmacokinetic-pharmacodynamic) modeling for predicting drug efficacy and toxicity. Three types: fully virtual trials, hybrid clinical trials (combining real and virtual patient data), and regulatory-supported simulations. Applications include expediting drug development, dose optimization, and evaluating therapies for rare diseases (proven useful during COVID-19). Limitations include computational expense and inability to fully replace traditional trials.

3. **Virtual Control Arms (VCAs)**: Virtual patient cohorts based on historical clinical data and real-world evidence, used to replace placebo groups. Advantages include avoiding ethical issues with placebo allocation (especially for serious/rare diseases), saving recruitment time, reducing expenses, and faster trial completion. Uses approaches like propensity score matching, Bayesian modeling, and causal inference frameworks. Limitations include data heterogeneity, lack of standardization, potential biases in real-world data, and absence of regulations (though the FDA has begun examining VCA use for rare conditions and cancers).

4. **Hybrid Mechanistic-AI Architectures**: Combine mechanistic models (mathematical equations based on biological laws, providing explainability) with AI (learning from big data, providing adaptability). Three architectures: sequential, parallel, and embedded modeling. Mathematically, these typically combine ODEs with neural networks. Applications include personalized medicine, disease progression modeling, and drug response prediction. Challenges include data integration (structured/unstructured data), computational costs, lack of validation standardization, and absence of regulatory pathways.

**Conclusion**: Digital twin technology offers significant promise for precision healthcare and clinical studies, saving time and money while advancing personalization, but faces obstacles including data collection/integration, verification/validation, regulatory requirements, and ethical considerations. The review references 12 scientific sources on digital twins, in silico trials, hybrid modeling, and related topics.

--- SOURCE 12: TWIN-GPT: Digital Twins for Clinical Trials via Large Language Model ---
URL: https://arxiv.org/html/2404.01273v2

SUMMARY:
<summary>
TWIN-GPT is a novel large language model (LLM)-based approach for creating digital twins of patients to enhance clinical trial outcome prediction. The paper addresses two key challenges in EHR-based clinical trial prediction: (1) Data Gap—the disconnect between data and realistic background knowledge, and (2) Data Inconsistency—discrepancies between data from different sources. TWIN-GPT is the first method to integrate LLMs into digital twin creation, fine-tuning ChatGPT on clinical trial datasets to generate personalized digital twins for individual patients.

**Methodology**: The model operates auto-regressively, predicting the next visit events (focusing on three clinical event types: treatment, medication, and adverse events). It uses a novel prompt-tuning approach that incorporates the patient's EHR history and the five most similar patient EHR records (k-nearest neighbors via cosine similarity) to establish cross-dataset knowledge associations. The model predicts adverse events first, then sequentially deduces medications. During inference, it generates digital twins using previous predictions and similar patient data.

**Applications**: (1) Personalized Generation—replicating patients using EHR data guided by k-nearest neighbors for in-context learning, and (2) Counterfactual Generation—simulating patient trajectories under alternative treatment schedules (e.g., switching from treatment to control arm) to estimate personalized treatment effects and reduce required control-arm sample sizes.

**Experiments**: TWIN-GPT was trained on a Phase III breast cancer trial dataset (NCT00174655) with 2,887 patients, and the multi-modal TOP dataset (with 1,160 Phase I, 4,449 Phase II, and 3,436 Phase III trials). Baselines included EVA, SynTEG, PromptEHR, TWIN-VAE, and k-NN-based methods.

**Key results**: TWIN-GPT achieved higher Pearson correlation coefficients (r) for adverse event distribution properties compared to SynTEG, PromptEHR, and TWIN-VAE (which ranged from -0.07 to 0.99). On the TOP dataset, TWIN-GPT achieved r≥0.96. The counterfactual digital twins achieved an AUROC of 0.821 (close to the 0.838 achieved with real data). For severe outcome prediction, an LSTM achieved nearly identical AUROC scores using TWIN-GPT synthetic data versus real data.

**Privacy evaluation**: Three metrics were assessed—Presence Disclosure (TWIN-GPT sensitivity stable around 20% vs. k-NN's ~50%), Attribute Disclosure (TWIN-GPT mean sensitivity ~0.25 vs. k-NN's ~0.3), and Nearest Neighbor Adversarial Accuracy Risk (NNAA score of 0.271, well below the 0.5 overfitting threshold). TWIN-GPT demonstrated better privacy protection than k-NN while maintaining high data fidelity. However, the authors note TWIN-GPT's slightly higher presence disclosure sensitivity than TWIN-VAE, attributed to the LLM's enhanced capability to capture subtle training data differences.

## In Silico Studies (Digital Models/Digital Twins) - EuroGCT Research Pathway

### Topic & Purpose
This EuroGCT (European Gene and Cell Therapy) webpage provides a comprehensive overview of **in silico studies** (computer modeling and simulation techniques used in health research), covering their definitions, main actors, challenges, advantages, regulatory framework, and opportunities—particularly relevant to the development of gene and cell therapies.

### Introduction & Key Concepts
- The use of digital technology is "significantly changing the methods used in health research," enabling the use of Artificial Intelligence (AI) systems. The French National Consultative Ethics Committee stated in 2018 that pre-clinical and clinical research is "embarking on a digital revolution."
- **In silico trials** are positioned as a "fourth pillar" of health research, complementing in vitro and in vivo research (sometimes called the 3rd pillar by authors who argue it can replace in vivo clinical trials).
- Techniques enable construction of multi-scale models of disease and representation of functional relationships between biological entities.
- **Digital twin technique**: used as a patient-specific virtual representation of real-world systems (from organs to the whole body).
- The IUPS Physiome project (2001) was one of the first to formalize in silico study use in healthcare.
- Over the last 20 years, in silico studies have been used to optimize medical device development and, more recently, human medicines; usage is more dynamic in industry and private research.
- Terminology harmonization is currently lacking (overlapping with Computational Modelling and Simulation / CM&S, Model-Informed Drug Development / MIDD, etc.).

### Main Actors
- **European Medicines Agency (EMA)**: EU agency responsible for scientific assessment of advanced therapy medicinal products; provides support for qualification of in silico methods and acceptance of new evidence for marketing authorization applications.
- **Sponsor**: research organization, pharmaceutical researcher, or industry responsible for initiating, managing, and financing clinical trials.
- **Investigator**: researcher responsible for conducting research and use of in silico methods.
- **Manufacturers of digital tools**: IT start-ups or software publishers developing digital tools in compliance with regulations.

### Definitions
- **In silico**: neologism referring to silicon in computer chips; refers to computer modeling and simulation techniques.
- **In silico studies**: all clinical or preclinical studies conducted using computer modeling and simulation.
- **In silico clinical trials**: virtual clinical trials using computer simulation and/or AI algorithms to support development or regulatory evaluation of medicines, medical devices, or medical interventions.
- **In silico pre-clinical studies**: studies in the pre-clinical phase using computer modeling and simulation.
- Requirements include large amounts of quality data (big data), scientific knowledge, and high-performance digital/computer systems.

### Challenges
- Main challenge: **lack of expertise in Europe** for evaluation and validation of these methods and resulting data.
- Required skills are scarce and expensive; requires pharmaceutical R&D to open up to other scientific practices.
- Requires widespread access to high-quality, standardized data.
- Innovations "break with 'traditional' research methods," requiring new ways of generating scientific evidence, which "may be met with some reluctance in practice."
- Lack of regulatory framework/harmonization of terminology, lack of communication between stakeholders and regulators, and lack of European experts hamper advances.
- Some industries turn to the US FDA for oversight, "thus creating disparities in research at the European level."
- Key concerns: reaffirming principles of transparency and trust, ensuring equitable access, and evolving legal/ethical requirements in line with risks.

### Advantages
- Improves randomized controlled trials by providing new forms of evidence, testing subgroups, anticipating protocol deviations, identifying/refining target populations, and predicting efficacy data (proof of concept).
- Guarantees savings in resources, time, and money; increases trial chances of success through consolidated hypotheses.
- Enables extrapolation of molecular kinetic behavior between species, routes of exposure, doses, and anticipation of molecule interactions; overcomes biases by crossing hypotheses and conditions.
- **For preclinical studies**: analyze toxicity, structure/activity relationships, provide proof of concept, identify most suitable compounds and biomarkers.
- **For clinical trials (Phases I-III)**: optimize dosing and sampling (Phase I), optimize regulatory submissions and "go/no-go" decision-making (Phases II/III); reduce or anticipate risk; enable testing of inter- and intra-individual variability; allow tailoring substances to patient characteristics.
- Particularly useful where parallel groups are impossible due to small participant numbers (paediatrics, geriatrics, rare diseases); better representation of vulnerable/under-represented populations.
- **For other uses (Phase IV/post-marketing)**: population biomonitoring and long-term monitoring of molecule evolution; targeting biomarkers/genes of therapeutic interest; optimizing payloads, designing vectors, assessing genotoxicity; AI tools (machine learning, deep learning, generative AI) help identify therapeutic genes and select donors for allogeneic cell therapies.
- **EU-STANDS4PM consortium** highlights the promise of personalized medicine; key obstacle for gene therapy is access to relevant and controlled data.

### Opportunities & Incentives
- EU encourages in silico (especially pre-clinical) studies as compliant with the **European 3Rs (Refining, Reducing, Replacing animal testing)**.
- EMA provides incentives through qualification of digital technology-based methodologies; EMA's Strategic Action Plan 2025 emphasizes computer modeling and simulation, with hopes to develop a **catalogue of in silico studies by 2030**.
- Consortia supported by the European Commission include the **Avicenna Alliance** and **VHP Institute**.

### Interaction with Regulators
- Interactions are mostly **early interactions** in advance of studies/trials; sponsors can request EMA support.
- CHMP provides scientific advice on innovative protocols/methods, working toward formal qualification of novel methodologies (supported by an operational group of experts on modeling and simulation since 2013).
- EMA may offer a **letter of support** when a methodology is promising but not ready for full qualification, typically including: high-level overview, intended context of use, available data, and details of ongoing/planned investigations.

### European Union Guidance & Timeline
- **2016**: EMA developed guidelines supporting physiological pharmacokinetic (PBPK) modeling and simulation; emphasizes link between verification/validation of methods and qualification.
- **July 2023**: EMA launched public consultation on a discussion paper on AI use in the medicinal product lifecycle (CHMP/CVMP collaboration; part of HMA-EMA Big Data Steering Group).
- **September 2024**: Final reflection paper on AI use in the medicinal product lifecycle adopted (EMA/CHMP/CVMP/83833/2023).
- **November 2024–February 2025**: EMA public consultation on Model-Informed Drug Development (MIDD) guidelines; first ICH M15 draft published 11 February 2026; FDA developing similar project since November 2024 (shared EU-US harmonization commitment). Guidelines set criteria for recognizing digital evidence, emphasizing context of use, model impact on decision-making, risk/error analysis, and requiring analysis plans and structured result reports.
- **July 2026**: Guidelines due to come into force (effectiveness to be confirmed).

- EuroGCT project receives funding from the EU's Horizon 2020 programme (grant agreement No 965241).

TRIAL EFFICACY BENEFITS: DTs generate precise forecasts of individual responses, enable in silico clinical trials (ISCT), support decentralized trials with wearables/mHealth, allow smaller sample sizes, and identify minimum participant numbers needed. In drug development, DTs aid early-stage discovery, preclinical testing (replacing/reducing animal use per the 3Rs principle), clinical trial simulation, regulatory submissions, and post-market surveillance.

SAFETY: DTs predict adverse events before they occur in patients, integrate genetic/physiological/environmental factors, enable continuous monitoring, and optimize dosages.

EXAMPLES/CASE STUDIES: (a) InEurHeart trial (RCT launched 2022, 112 patients) for AI-guided ventricular tachycardia ablation using cardiac DTs - reported 60% shorter procedure times and 15% absolute increase in acute success; (b) 12-week RCT (112 older adults with type 2 diabetes) using smart-speaker virtual assistant lowered HbA1c by 0.48% and improved self-care; (c) Johns Hopkins genotype-specific cardiac-twin program creates 3D heart replicas for informed consent visualization; (d) Twin Health's HIPAA-compliant whole-body DT platform; (e) TWIN-GPT LLM for clinical trial DTs with privacy evaluation (presence disclosure, attribute disclosure, nearest neighbor adversarial).

ETHICS: DTs enhance informed consent (personalized visual narratives instead of abstract risk tables; multimedia consent tools show higher satisfaction and comprehension vs paper forms), privacy/data security (GDPR and HIPAA compliance, encryption, de-identification, BAAs), equity/inclusivity (simulating underrepresented populations), real-time monitoring/ethical oversight (nurse-in-the-loop systems), and transparency/accountability.

CHALLENGES: Re-identification risks, prediction of sensitive future health outcomes (insurability/employment implications), interoperability vulnerabilities, evolving consent needs, algorithmic bias, and regulatory differences in decentralized/cross-border trials. DTs may inherit RCT generalizability limitations when built on trial participant data. Personalization benefits demonstrated in oncology and cardiology (e.g., personalized heart DT detecting substrate abnormalities in scar-dependent ventricular tachycardia).

COMPARISON: DTs offer dynamic adaptability and continuous personalization vs. computationally lighter synthetic control methods (which lack real-time feedback) and agent-based models (which generalize across groups rather than individuals).
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
Digital twins (DTs) can transform randomized clinical trials by improving ethical standards, including safety, informed consent, equity, and data privacy. They also enhance trial efficiency by enabling early detection of adverse events and streamlined design., "A multicenter RCT launched in 2022, the inEurHeart trial, enrolled 112 patients to compare AI-guided ventricular tachycardia ablation planned on a cardiac DT with standard catheter techniques. Early clinical evaluations of this platform report 60% shorter procedure times and a 15% absolute increase in acute success rates.", "industry analyses estimate that each month of slowed enrollment can add roughly USD 500,000 in extra trial expenses and unrealized revenue", "Only one in ten compounds entering clinical trials ultimately gaining regulatory approval... ~80% of trials face delays due to patient enrollment challenges", "Digital twins can transform informed-consent discussions from abstract risk tables to personalized, visual narratives."

--- SOURCE 16: Foundation Models in Chemistry: A 2025 Perspective ---
URL: https://hunterheidenreich.com/notes/chemistry/llm-applications/foundation-models-chemistry-perspective

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a review/summary of a perspective paper by Junyoung Choi, Gunwook Nam, Jaesik Choi (Seoul National University), and Yousung Jung (KAIST), published in JACS Au (2025, 5(4), 1499-1518, DOI: 10.1021/jacsau.4c01160). The paper organizes the rapidly growing landscape of foundation models in chemistry into a coherent taxonomy, distinguishing between "small" foundation models (pretrained for a single domain) and "big" foundation models (adaptable across multiple domains).

The paper motivates the foundation model paradigm for chemistry due to three persistent challenges: (1) data scarcity (chemical datasets are small and expensive to generate), (2) poor generalization to out-of-domain compounds, and (3) limited transferability of traditional ML interatomic potentials (MLIPs). Foundation models address these via learning general representations from large unlabeled datasets that can be finetuned for downstream tasks.

Two primary architecture families are reviewed: Graph Neural Networks (GNNs), including recent equivariant GNNs (NequIP, MACE, EquformerV2) that respect geometric symmetries, and Language Models operating on string representations (SMILES, SELFIES). Pretraining strategies are categorized into contrastive learning (GraphCL, MolCLR, GraphMVP, CrysGNN), predictive learning (GROVER, Hu et al.), generative learning (SMILES-BERT, ChemBERTa-2, MoLFormer), supervised pretraining on DFT data (M3GNet, CHGNet, MACE-MP-0, MatterSim), and multimodal learning (KV-PLM, MoMu, MoleculeSTM, SPMM). A consistent finding is that combining local and global information produces more transferable representations.

The survey maps approximately 40 models across four domains:
- Property Prediction (13 models): MoLFormer, pretrained on 1.1 billion SMILES from PubChem and ZINC, outperformed many baselines on MoleculeNet and QM9. CrysGNN combined contrastive, predictive, and generative learning for crystals.
- MLIPs (10 universal models, all using supervised learning on DFT energies/forces/stresses): GNoME (89M data points) achieved zero-shot performance comparable to trained MLIPs; MatterSim (17M entries, 0-5000K, 0-1000 GPa) achieved SOTA on Matbench Discovery; others include M3GNet (187K), CHGNet (1.58M, predicts magnetic moments), MACE-MP-0 (1.58M), and eqV2 (118M, OMat24).
- Inverse Design (3 models): MatterGen (Microsoft, diffusion on 607K structures, 2x S.U.N. material generation rate), GP-MoLFormer (IBM, pair-tuning for property-guided optimization), and CrystalLLM (finetuned LLaMA-2 70B).
- Multi-Domain Models: Joint multi-domain pretraining (JMP) from Meta FAIR achieved SOTA on 34 of 40 tasks; multimodal models enable text-based inverse design and property prediction.

Future directions include scope expansion (material types, modalities like XRD spectra, downstream tasks), scaling challenges (data quality vs. quantity with noisy DFT labels, GNN scalability rarely explored above one million parameters though scaling to 3B demonstrated, database integration requiring total energy alignment), efficiency (knowledge distillation, quantization/pruning, questioning strict equivariance necessity), and interpretability (addressing hallucination and mode-collapse).

Key limitations acknowledged: the definition of "foundation model" in chemistry is not established, most models focus on molecules with crystalline materials less explored, benchmarks for low-data and out-of-distribution regimes are insufficient, and the paper does not deeply cover retrosynthesis or reaction prediction. This is a review paper introducing no new data, models, or results; it relies on benchmarks from original studies (MoleculeNet, QM9, Matbench, JARVIS-DFT).
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"Foundation models have transformed NLP and computer vision through large-scale pretraining and transfer learning. In chemistry, however, several persistent challenges motivate the adoption of this paradigm: Data scarcity... Poor generalization... Limited transferability."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 17: MoltiTox: a multimodal fusion model for molecular toxicity prediction ---
URL: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12756560

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a scientific research article published in Frontiers in Toxicology (Front Toxicol, 2025 Dec 18, doi: 10.3389/ftox.2025.1720651, PMID: 41488760) by Junwoo Park and Sujee Lee from Sungkyunkwan University, Republic of Korea. The paper introduces MoltiTox, a novel multimodal fusion model for molecular toxicity prediction in drug discovery.

**Key Contributions and Methods:**
- MoltiTox integrates four complementary molecular data types: molecular graphs, SMILES strings, 2D images, and 13C NMR spectra
- Uses four modality-specific encoders: a GNN (GINEConv-based on Graph Isomorphism Network) for graphs, a Transformer (MolFormer-XL, pretrained on ~1.1 billion SMILES strings) for SMILES, a 2D CNN (ResNet-18 backbone from ImageMol, pretrained on ~10 million molecular images) for images, and a 1D CNN (pretrained NMR encoder from CReSS) for spectra
- Embeddings are fused through a multi-head self-attention mechanism to capture complementary structural and chemical information
- Uses 13C NMR data, a modality rarely used in toxicity prediction, which provides unique electronic environment information about carbon atoms

**Dataset and Experimental Design:**
- Evaluated on the Tox21 benchmark dataset (7,831 unique compounds, 12 binary toxicity endpoints: 7 nuclear receptor tasks and 5 stress response tasks)
- 7,823 valid molecules used for graph/SMILES/image encoders; 13C NMR spectra obtained for 2,851 compounds by matching InChIKeys against NMRShiftDB, NP-MRD, and HMDB databases
- Scaffold-based data splitting (Bemis-Murcko scaffolds, 8:1:1 train:validation:test ratio) repeated with five random seeds to prevent information leakage
- A learnable missing token introduced for compounds without NMR spectra (the majority of the dataset)
- Hyperparameters optimized using Optuna with TPE algorithm; early stopping based on validation ROC-AUC

**Results:**
- MoltiTox achieves a ROC-AUC of 0.831 across 12 endpoints on the Tox21 benchmark, outperforming all single-modality baselines
- Inclusion of 13C NMR spectra significantly improved performance on certain tasks, particularly where electronic and metabolic characteristics are critical
- Multimodal fusion enhances robustness and generalizability across diverse toxicity endpoints

**Key Conclusions:**
- Integrating diverse molecular representations enhances both robustness and generalizability of toxicity prediction models
- NMR data offers complementary chemical insights not fully captured by structure or language-based representations
- MoltiTox provides an extensible framework for more reliable computational toxicology models
- The study contributes: (1) a unified multimodal framework integrating four complementary representations, (2) introduction of 13C NMR as a novel informative modality, and (3) demonstration that multimodal fusion enhances robustness across Tox21 endpoints
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"We introduce MoltiTox, a novel multimodal fusion model for molecular toxicity prediction, designed to overcome the limitations of single-modality approaches in drug discovery." "MoltiTox integrates four complementary data types: molecular graphs, SMILES strings, 2D images, and 13C NMR spectra." "Evaluated on the Tox21 benchmark across 12 endpoints, MoltiTox achieves a ROC-AUC of 0.831, outperforming all single-modality baselines." "These findings highlight that integrating diverse molecular representations enhances both the robustness and generalizability of toxicity prediction models." "By demonstrating how multimodal integration enriches molecular representations and enhances the interpretability of toxicity mechanisms, MoltiTox provides an extensible framework for developing more reliable models in computational toxicology."
</key_excerpts>

URL: https://github.com/deepmodeling/Uni-Mol

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is the official GitHub repository README for the Uni-Mol series methods developed by deepmodeling, a universal 3D molecular representation learning framework family for drug design and molecular modeling.

KEY MODELS AND COMPONENTS:
- **Uni-Mol**: A universal 3D molecular pretraining framework with two models — a molecular pretraining model trained on 209M molecular 3D conformations, and a pocket pretraining model trained on 3M candidate protein pocket data. It outperforms state-of-the-art in 14 of 15 molecular property prediction tasks and excels at protein-ligand binding pose prediction and molecular conformation generation. Published at ICLR 2023 (Zhou et al.).
- **Uni-Mol+**: Designed for quantum chemical property prediction, generating initial 3D conformations from methods like RDKit, then iteratively optimizing to equilibrium conformations to predict QC properties. Ranks 1st in OGB-LSC (PCQM4MV2) and OC20 benchmarks. Published in Nature Communications (Aug 2024) and arXiv report (Mar 2023).
- **Uni-Mol Tools**: Easy-use wrappers for molecular property prediction, representation, and downstreams, installable via `pip install unimol-tools`. Documentation at unimol.readthedocs.io.
- **Uni-Mol Docking V2**: Industry-leading complex structure prediction comparable to AlphaFold3. Accurately predicts binding poses of 77+% of ligands in PoseBusters benchmark with RMSD < 2.0 Å, and 75+% passing all quality checks — up from 62% for the previous version. Generates chemically accurate predictions that avoid chirality inversions and steric clashes. Released May 2024.
- **Uni-Mol2**: A scalable molecular pretraining model using a two-track transformer integrating atomic-level, graph-level, and geometry-level features. Scales from 84M to 1.1 billion parameters, and is the largest molecular pretraining model to date, pretrained on 800M conformations. Published at NeurIPS 2024 (Ji et al.).

--- SOURCE 20: Uni-Mol3: A Multi-Molecular Foundation Model for Advancing Organic Reaction Modeling ---
URL: https://arxiv.org/html/2508.00920v1

SUMMARY:
<summary>
**Uni-Mol3: A Multi-Molecular Foundation Model for Organic Reaction Modeling** (arXiv paper, August 2025)

**Overview:** The paper introduces Uni-Mol3, a deep learning framework designed to extend single-molecular representation learning (previously advanced by Uni-Mol and Uni-Mol2) to multi-molecular systems, specifically for modeling organic chemical reactions. It addresses the limitations of existing approaches (descriptor-based, graph-based, and sequence-based/SMILES methods) which struggle to capture 3D spatial information, model inter-molecular dependencies, and unify diverse reaction tasks.

**Key Innovations:**
1. **Mol-Tokenizer (Stage 1):** A multi-scale molecular tokenizer that quantizes 1D atom features, 2D graph structures, and 3D coordinates into discrete tokens, creating a 3D-aware molecular language. It uses Finite Scalar Quantization (FSQ) and is trained with atom type reconstruction and atom coordinate denoising tasks.
2. **Molecular Pre-training (Stage 2):** Trains the encoder-decoder architecture on single molecules (using atom-level masked modeling and next token prediction) to learn molecular grammatical rules on ~19M molecules from the Uni-Mol dataset.
3. **Reaction Pre-training (Stage 3):** Extends pre-training to multi-molecular level using molecular-level masked modeling on ~11.97M reactions from a preprocessed Pistachio database (originally 16,678,201 reactions, filtered for validity, atom mapping, and ≤80 atoms), capturing thermodynamic/kinetic reaction principles.
4. **Fine-tuning (Stages 4&5):** Prompt-aware fine-tuning with task-specific prefix tokens enables adaptation to diverse tasks with minimal output-layer modifications. Tasks covered: product prediction (<forward-sep>, <forward-mixed>), retrosynthetic prediction (<reverse>), condition generation (<condition>), and yield prediction (<yield>).

**Architecture:** Uses a T5 backbone with 8 encoder and 8 decoder layers, hidden dimension 768, and 8 attention heads. Trained on 8 NVIDIA H100 GPUs using RDKit (2024.9.6), with 3D structures generated via ETKGD and optimized with MMFF.

**Results:** Uni-Mol3 outperforms baselines (Molformer, Chemformer, T5Chem, PRESTO) across 10 datasets for 4 downstream tasks.

- **Product Prediction:** On USPTO-MIT, achieves 90.8% Top-1 (separated) and 89.6% (mixed) vs. 90.2%/88.9% for T5Chem. On Pistachio-FP: 93.0% (separated), 91.7% (mixed) Top-1. On SMol-Reactions-FP: 38.7% Top-1, significantly lower invalidity (0.64% vs 4.54% for Molformer).
- **Retrosynthesis:** On Pistachio-RS: 76.9% Top-1; USPTO-50k: 49.0%; SMol-Reactions-RS: 29.1% Top-1 with lowest invalidity (0.20%).
- **Condition Generation:** Outperforms all baselines on all four metrics across Pistachio-CG, USPTO-500-MT, and USPTO-Condition.
- **Yield Prediction (Buchwald-Hartwig dataset):** Top performance on 11 of 12 metrics across 4 out-of-sample test sets. On Test1, beats T5Chem by 28.0% (MAE), 18.2% (RMSE), and 7.2% (R²).

**Ablation Insights:**
- Molecular pre-training is the most important stage (captures molecular grammatical rules ensuring valid molecule generation).
- The Uni-Tokenizer provides significant 3D structure-awareness gains, especially for condition generation.
- Reaction pre-training helps all tasks, with slightly less pronounced gains due to overlap with downstream fine-tuning.

**Multi-task Evaluation:** Mixed-task fine-tuning improves molecular validity for both T5Chem and Uni-Mol3 but introduces performance trade-offs for simpler tasks (less pronounced degradation for Uni-Mol3).
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
This paper introduces Uni-Mol3, a novel deep learning framework that employs a hierarchical pipeline for multi-molecular reaction modeling., Building on Uni-Mol2's superior single-molecular representation capabilities, this work introduces Uni-Mol3, a novel deep learning framework that enables unified multi-molecular reaction modeling via a hierarchical pipeline., Experimental results across 10 datasets spanning 4 downstream tasks show that Uni-Mol3 outperforms existing methods, validating its effectiveness in modeling complex organic reactions.
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 1: Leveraging In Silico and Artificial Intelligence Models to Advance Drug Disposition and Response Predictions Across the Lifespan ---
URL: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12180087

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This review article from Clinical and Translational Science (2025) discusses the application of in silico and artificial intelligence (AI) models to advance drug disposition and response predictions across the lifespan. Authored by Kyunghee Yang, Daniel Gonzalez, Jeffrey L. Woodhead, Pallavi Bhargava, and Murali Ramanathan (corresponding author), the paper addresses the underrepresentation of children, older individuals, pregnant/breastfeeding women, postmenopausal women, and people with disease states in clinical trials.

Key content:
1. **Clinical Pharmacology Considerations**: Optimal drug dosing requires consideration of genetics, age, and sex. Genetic polymorphisms (e.g., CYP2D6), age-dependent decreases in hepatic/renal function, and sex-related differences in body composition can alter pharmacokinetics. Real-world data (RWD) from electronic health records and patient registries serve as complementary resources for assessing inter-individual variability.

2. **PBPK Modeling**: Physiologically based pharmacokinetic models use differential equation systems to predict drug absorption, distribution, metabolism, and excretion. Virtual populations are detailed for:
   - **Pediatrics**: Models covering birth to 18 years (Johnson et al. 2006; Edginton et al. 2006), accounting for age-specific organ size, tissue composition, blood flow, and enzymatic activity. Knowledge gaps remain in pediatric drug absorption, drug transporter maturation, and blood-brain barrier development.
   - **Geriatrics**: Adult models for ages 65-100 years accounting for decreased renal/hepatic function and altered body composition.
   - **Pregnancy**: Virtual populations simulating increased cardiac output, blood volume, and enhanced renal/hepatic clearance with trimester-specific changes.
   - **Organ Impairment**: Renal impairment classified by GFR (mild 60-90, moderate 30-60, severe 15-30 mL/min per 1.73 m²), and hepatic impairment by Child-Pugh scores. Most populations represent adults only.
   - **Disease States**: Obesity (BMI ≥ 30 kg/m² in adults; >95th percentile in pediatrics), NAFLD/NASH, and cancer (including pregnant cancer patients).

3. **QSP/QST Modeling**: Quantitative systems pharmacology/toxicology models predict drug efficacy and safety. Only a handful of QSP models include age and sex demographics. 

4. **Case Study - DILI in Postmenopausal Women**: Postmenopausal women comprise ~1/8 of the world population but are underrepresented in trials. A simulated population (SimPops) was developed in DILIsym incorporating:
   - Reduced antioxidant enzyme activity (10% lower ROS/RNS clearance)
   - Reduced bile acid synthesis (40% lower CA and CDCA synthesis)
   - Reduced mitochondrial ETC flux (12-20% lower)
   - BMI/body weight distributions matched to literature values (124 healthy and 120 NAFLD individuals)
   - Results showed 15.7% of postmenopausal women on tamoxifen (20 mg BID for 5 weeks) predicted to have ALT ≥ 3× ULN (~2x the placebo rate of 7.4%), consistent with clinical observations. Acetaminophen (1g QID for 2 weeks) showed ~1% transient ALT elevations in both populations.

5. **Machine Learning and AI**: 
   - As of May 2024, FDA had approved over 850 devices with AI.
   - The IL-1 inhibitor anakinra was approved by the FDA in 2022 for COVID-19 based on AI/ML methods to identify appropriate patient populations — the first time AI/ML methods were used for regulatory decision-making. The model identified patients with suPAR levels ≥ 6 ng/mL as high-risk, using elastic net regression for feature identification and an artificial neural network for cutoff determination.
   - Generative AI approaches (GANs and variational autoencoders/AAEs) can generate synthetic data for clinical trial simulations where data is limited, such as in underrepresented populations.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"Incorporating inter-individual differences in drug disposition and responses is essential for ensuring the safe and effective use of drugs in real-world patients. Despite ongoing efforts, lower participation of children, older individuals, pregnant and breastfeeding women, postmenopausal women, and people with disease states and disabilities in drug clinical trials is frequent."
</key_excerpts>
