--- SOURCE 2: Frontiers | Combining mechanistic quantitative systems pharmacology modeling and patient-derived organoid testing in MET-aberrant non-small cell lung cancer for high-throughput combination efficacy analysis and personalized treatment design ---
URL: https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/pharmacology/articles/10.3389/fphar.2025.1685468/full

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is an original research article published in Frontiers in Pharmacology (24 November 2025, Volume 16, DOI: 10.3389/fphar.2025.1685468) describing the development of a quantitative systems pharmacology (QSP) model for MET-aberrant non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC). The study was conducted by researchers from Nanjing University, Nanjing Medical University, Nanjing Drum Tower Hospital, Jiangsu Avatarget Biotechnology Co., and Southeast University in Nanjing, China.

**Key Findings:**

**Background/Problem:** NSCLC with MET exon 14 skipping mutations or MET overexpression/amplification exhibits highly proliferative phenotypes. Approximately 3-4% of NSCLC patients have MET exon 14 skipping mutations, about 5% have primary MET amplifications, and 15% have secondary MET amplification. MET TKIs (capmatinib, tepotinib, crizotinib, savolitinib) have been approved, but treatment faces low response rates, limited response duration (e.g., tepotinib ORR of 45%, mDoR 12.6 months in VISION trial; capmatinib ORR 41%, mDoR 9.7 months in GEOMETRY mono-1 trial), drug resistance, and need for combination therapies.

**Methods:** The QSP model was built using ordinary differential equations (~130 molecular species, 69 equations) based on mass action kinetics and Hill-type reaction laws. It incorporates signaling pathways (MET, EGFR, ALK, ROS1), pharmacokinetic modules for 16 drugs (7 TKIs, 4 downstream kinase inhibitors, 5 chemotherapeutics). The model was calibrated using ~70 sets of in vitro data (over 450 datapoints), in vivo mouse tumor growth data (16 drugs, 34 doses), and validated against clinical trial data. Virtual patient populations (5000 patients each for METex14 and MET-amplified) were generated for virtual clinical trials. Patient-derived organoids (PDOs) from 5 NSCLC patients with MET amplification were integrated into the QSP framework for personalized treatment design.

**Results:** The model accurately reproduced in vitro signaling and cell viability data, in vivo tumor growth inhibition, and clinical trial responses for MET TKIs in both METex14 and MET-amplified NSCLC patients. Dose optimization simulations suggested capmatinib 600mg BID superior to 400mg BID, tepotinib optimal at 500mg QD (no benefit at 600mg), and savolitinib efficacy plateauing at ~500mg QD. Combination analysis found significantly enhanced patient response achievable using MET TKI combined with PI3K/AKT inhibitors. The hybrid QSP-PDO paradigm was used to design optimal personalized treatment regimens for 5 NSCLC patients with MET amplification.

**Conclusion:** This is the first multiscale QSP investigation of MET dysregulation for translational cancer drug research, opening a new route for personalized cancer medicine by integrating QSP modeling with PDO data.
</summary>

"To our knowledge, our work is the first multiscale QSP investigation of MET dysregulation for translational cancer drug research, and by integrating QSP model analyses with PDO data it has opened up a new route to facilitate future cancer personalized medicine."

--- SOURCE 3: Artificial Intelligence-driven Strategies and Modern Innovations to Surpass Biopharmaceutic Limitations in Traditional Drug Development ---
URL: https://www.xiahepublishing.com/2572-5505/JERP-2025-00025

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a scientific review article from the Journal of Exploratory Research in Pharmacology (DOI: 10.14218/JERP.2025.00025) titled "Artificial Intelligence-driven Strategies and Modern Innovations to Surpass Biopharmaceutic Limitations in Traditional Drug Development." The article examines how AI, machine learning, and modern formulation technologies can overcome biopharmaceutic barriers that cause drug development failures.

KEY STATISTICS AND FINDINGS:
- Drug discovery takes over 10 years and costs 1-2 billion dollars, yet more than 90% of drug candidates fail during clinical development
- Failure causes: lack of efficacy (40-50%), safety/toxicity (~30%), and poor drug-like properties (10-15%)
- Clinical success rate remains low at ~10-15%
- Approximately 40% of approved drugs and nearly 90% of drug candidates in development are poorly water-soluble
- CYP3A4, CYP2D6, and CYP2C9 together metabolize ~80% of commonly used drugs
- Propranolol has only ~25% bioavailability due to hepatic metabolism; midazolam is almost entirely metabolized by CYP3A4

MAIN BIOPHARMACEUTIC BARRIERS:
1. Solubility and permeability issues - The Biopharmaceutics Classification System (BCS) classifies drugs into four classes; Class II (e.g., carbamazepine) has good permeability but poor solubility, Class III (e.g., alendronate, acyclovir) dissolves readily but has poor permeability, and Class IV compounds lack both
2. Efflux transporters (P-gp and BCRP) - "cellular bouncers" that export drugs back into the intestinal lumen; drugs affected include digoxin, paclitaxel, and topotecan; overexpression of P-gp in tumor cells causes multidrug resistance
3. Metabolism by CYP450 enzymes - first-pass metabolism reduces therapeutic efficacy; genetic polymorphisms create "poor metabolizers" and "ultra-rapid metabolizers"; grapefruit juice inhibits CYP3A4 leading to elevated simvastatin levels

AI AND COMPUTATIONAL TOOLS:
- Traditional HT-ADME screening relies on expensive physical experiments
- SwissADME: free web tool using BOILED-Egg model, bioavailability radar, and Lipinski's Rule of Five
- Deep-Pk: predicts ADMET across 73 endpoints (external validation MCC of 0.58, ROC-AUC >0.80 for most tasks)
- kMoL: open-source ML library with ROC-AUC above 0.75
- SMARTCyp, DeepCYP, and MetaSite: predict vulnerable sites of metabolism
- AlphaFold: predicts 3D protein structures, with over 200 million structures available
- ZINC22 library contains 4.1 billion molecules
- RosettaVS: docked billion-molecule libraries in days, achieving 44% hit rate for Nav1.7 in seven days
- Caco-2 cell line for efflux studies takes 21-24 days to differentiate, making it unsuitable for high-throughput screening

FORMULATION INNOVATIONS:
- 3D printing (fused deposition modeling, stereolithography, selective laser sintering, binder jetting, SSE, hot-melt extrusion) enables personalized dosage forms; drug-loaded mesoporous magnesium carbonate achieved 15.3% w/w loading
- Biodegradable nanocarriers using natural polymers (chitosan, alginates, albumin) and synthetic polymers (polylactic acid); PLGA-PEG nanoparticles co-encapsulating gemcitabine and botulinic acid showed improved anti-tumor efficacy in pancreatic cancer

REGULATORY CHALLENGES:
- FDA's Emerging Technology Program provides real-time guidance on novel manufacturing
- Quality by Design principles (ICH Q8-Q11 guidelines) recommended to streamline approvals
- Concerns include AI bias from uncertain pharmaceutical datasets, nanocarrier biocompatibility, 3DP scalability and material safety

CONCLUSION: AI tools like SwissADME and DeepCYP, generative models, in silico transporter simulations, 3DP, and biodegradable nanoparticles are already making meaningful impacts on drug development, but must be aligned with regulatory frameworks and data transparency standards.

--- SOURCE 6: Digital Twins & Synthetic Control Arms — CASRAI ---
URL: https://casrai.org/guides/digital-twins-clinical-trials

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This page from CASRAI provides a comprehensive guide to digital twins in clinical trials, focusing on synthetic control arms and FDA's evolving regulatory posture. A digital twin is defined as an AI-generated, patient-specific prediction of how a trial participant would have progressed under a reference condition (placebo/standard of care), built from baseline characteristics combined with historical trial data and real-world data. The goal is not to replace control groups with pure simulation but to use these forecasts as statistical covariates to make a real, smaller control arm carry more statistical weight.

The key regulatory precedent is Unlearn.AI's PROCOVA (Prognostic Covariate Adjustment) methodology, which publicly reported receiving a qualification opinion from the European Medicines Agency (EMA) in September 2022—the first time a European regulator formally qualified a machine-learning-based covariate adjustment method for reducing sample size in pivotal trials. Unlearn.AI also reported positive FDA feedback, though this is described as REPORTED-tier information not independently verified from primary documents.

FDA's posture is described as "engaged, but explicitly cautious and not yet settled." The clearest primary-source evidence is a draft guidance issued January 6, 2025 ("Considerations for the Use of Artificial Intelligence to Support Regulatory Decision-Making for Drug and Biological Products," comment period closed April 7, 2025, still draft as of writing). This proposes a risk-based, seven-step credibility assessment framework for AI models used in regulatory submissions. FDA's Complex Innovative Trial Design (CID) pilot meeting program provides a channel for sponsors to discuss novel approaches. The page emphasizes that there is NO general FDA approval or qualification of "digital twins" as a category—each use case is evaluated on its own merits.

The page addresses common misconceptions: digital twins differ from synthetic control arms (which use existing datasets as comparators); using digital twins means FEWER patients receive placebo/standard of care (not fewer receiving investigational treatment); and training data comes from historical clinical trials and real-world data sources. Open questions remain around validation, including unresolved concerns about methodology credibility. Sponsors pursue this approach to reduce enrollment timelines, lower ethical burdens of withholding treatment (especially in rare/serious diseases), and reduce trial costs. The guide links to related CASRAI resources including AI in Clinical Trials, FDA AI Guidance, Risk-Based Monitoring, and Clinical Trial Monitoring guides. Last reviewed: 18 July 2026.
</summary>

--- SOURCE 7: Unleashing AI-Generated Digital Twins to Deliver More Efficient Randomized Clinical Trials ---
URL: https://asabiopreport.substack.com/p/unleashing-ai-generated-digital-twins

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This ASA Biopharmaceutical Report article by Arman Sabbaghi (Santen Inc.) discusses how AI-generated "digital twins" can be used to deliver more efficient randomized controlled trials (RCTs), addressing the challenge of Eroom's Law—the phenomenon where the cost and time to bring new drugs and interventions to market continue to rise despite technological progress.

**Key Concepts:**
- **Digital twins**: Predictive models that simulate the entire trajectory of control potential outcomes for trial participants. Summaries of these digital twins constitute "super covariates" that enable precise and powerful causal inferences in a regulatory-acceptable manner.
- **Super covariates**: Prognostic scores (per Hansen, 2008) obtained via AI-generated digital twins that summarize multidimensional covariate vectors (baseline data, demographics, etc.) into scalars highly correlated with control outcomes. AI algorithms should be pretrained on historical control data external to the target RCT.

**PROCOVA™ Methodology (Unlearn.AI's approach):**
The 5 essential steps are:
1. Pretrain an AI model on historical control data.
2. Apply the pretrained AI model to baseline covariates for treated and control participants to calculate prognostic scores.
3. Fit a linear regression model with the outcome as response and treatment indicator plus prognostic score as predictors.
4. Estimate the treatment effect via the linear regression model.
5. Obtain the standard error using the sandwich estimator approach.

**Regulatory Acceptance:**
- The EMA qualified PROCOVA as "an acceptable statistical approach for primary analysis" of Phase 2 and 3 trials with continuous endpoints (2022).
- The FDA stated they concur with the EMA and that PROCOVA does not deviate from their current guidance (2024).

**Methodological Extensions:**
- **Weighted PROCOVA** (Vanderbeek et al., 2023): Incorporates variances of digital twin distributions to enhance power, precision, and efficiency.
- **Bayesian PROCOVA** (Vanderbeek et al., 2024): Dynamically borrows information from historical controls, increasing precision without adding significant bias when historical controls and trial participants are exchangeable, and can discount discrepant historical controls.
- Methods have also been specified for time-to-event (Li et al., 2023), binary (Li et al., 2024), and repeated measures endpoints (PROCOVA-MMRM by Ross et al., 2024).

**Broader Implications:** The integration of AI with statistics can help address Eroom's Law and usher in a new generation of regulatory-acceptable, adaptive, efficient, and informative clinical trials, accelerating clinical development and improving patient outcomes. Key stakeholders across pharmaceutical companies, biotech, regulatory agencies, and technology companies must collaborate to realize this potential.
</summary>

--- SOURCE 11: The FDA Adverse Event Reporting System (FAERS) Explained | IntuitionLabs ---
URL: https://intuitionlabs.ai/articles/fda-adverse-event-reporting-system

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a comprehensive IntuitionLabs report (65 min read, updated August 1, 2026) explaining the FDA Adverse Event Reporting System (FAERS) and its historical evolution, architecture, stakeholders, and uses. 

**Historical Development:**
- Modern US pharmacovigilance traces to the 1962 Kefauver-Harris Amendments following the thalidomide tragedy. FDA began formal post-market ADR reporting around 1961-62.
- In **1969**, the FDA established the Spontaneous Reporting System (SRS), the precursor to AERS.
- In **1993**, FDA launched **MedWatch** under Commissioner Dr. David Kessler, standardizing voluntary reporting (Form FDA 3500) while manufacturers remained legally required to report via a mandatory system (Form 3500A). Dr. Kessler stated: "MedWatch is not just a new form; it's a new approach to making adverse event reporting part of routine medical practice."
- In **September 1997**, FDA launched **AERS (Adverse Event Reporting System)**, replacing SRS, enabling electronic submission of Individual Case Safety Reports (ICSRs) in ICH E2B format with MedDRA coding (replacing COSTART). By 1998 it was fully operational.
- By **2002**, AERS held ~2.3 million reports across 6,000+ drugs. In **2004**, FDA began quarterly public release of anonymized data. The **FDAAA of 2007** expanded post-market authorities, mandated REMS, and created the Sentinel active surveillance system.
- In **September 2012**, AERS was upgraded and rebranded as **FAERS**. In **2014/2015**, electronic submission of all postmarket reports became mandatory. In **2017**, the FAERS Public Dashboard launched.
- **2024-2025**: FDA began transitioning to ICH E2B(R3) standard (full compliance by April 2026), and in **August 2025** began real-time daily updates to FAERS data, replacing quarterly updates. Database now exceeds **31 million report entries** (with over 2 million new reports added annually), up from ~10 million in 2012 and 14 million in 2017. On **March 11, 2026**, data was moved into the new **AEMS (Adverse Event Monitoring System)** platform.

**FAERS Architecture & Reporting:**
- Collects ICSRs from healthcare professionals, consumers/patients, and manufacturers. ~75% of reports come via manufacturers who forward reports; the rest come directly to FDA via MedWatch.
- All events are coded using **MedDRA** terminology; drug names standardized (often to WHODrug or RxNorm). Duplicate detection and follow-up report linking are key functions.
- Signal detection uses disproportionality methods: Proportional Reporting Ratio (PRR), Reporting Odds Ratio (ROR), and Empirical Bayes Geometric Mean (EBGM/MGPS), often via Oracle Empirica Signal tools.
- Data tables include DEMO (demographics), DRUG, REAC (reactions), linked by case IDs.

**Stakeholders & Reporting Requirements:**
- HCP reporting is **voluntary** in the US; consumers use simplified **Form 3500B** (introduced 2013). Manufacturers are legally required to report serious/unexpected events within **15 days** (21 CFR 314.80 for drugs, 21 CFR 600.80 for biologics), plus periodic reports (quarterly then annually, now PBRER format). Manufacturers must search literature and report foreign adverse events.

**Data Access & Regulatory Use:**
- Public access via quarterly data extracts (since 2004), the **FAERS Public Dashboard** (2017, now updated daily), and the **OpenFDA API** (data from 2014, JSON format).
- FDA uses FAERS for: labeling changes (e.g., boxed warnings on fluoroquinolones for tendon rupture), safety communications, REMS decisions, product withdrawals, and compliance monitoring.
- Example decisions: 2013 zolpidem (Ambien) next-morning impairment warnings; 2004 rofecoxib (Vioxx) withdrawal (supported by AERS cardiovascular reports).
- Key limitations: reports do not prove causation, under-reporting is estimated at less than 1-10% of serious events, and reports cannot be treated as incidence data. Individual case narratives and personal identifiers are not publicly released (available via FOIA). Vaccine events go to VAERS, device events to MAUDE.
</summary>

--- SOURCE 13: Early Detection of Absurdity Signals in Pharmacovigilance: A Machine Learning Ensemble Approach to Identify Rare Adverse Drug Reactions | medRxiv ---
URL: https://www.medrxiv.org/content/10.64898/2026.02.06.26345783v1.full-text

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a medRxiv preprint by Rathi Dasgupta (XData Lab, USA) introducing "absurdity signal detection" - a novel pharmacovigilance framework that treats statistical outliers as potential harbingers of rare, serious adverse drug reactions (ADRs) rather than filtering them as noise. The study addresses the limitation that traditional biostatistical methods (disproportionality analyses like PRR, Bayesian approaches) systematically exclude rare events, potentially missing critical safety signals.

**Methods:** The author developed an ensemble machine learning framework combining five algorithms (Random Forest, Gradient Boosting, XGBoost, Neural Networks, Support Vector Machines) to analyze FDA Adverse Event Reporting System (FAERS) data. The system employs outlier-inclusive modeling, multi-dimensional cluster detection, and a novel "absurdity propensity score" calculated as: PS = 0.4 × Statistical Anomaly (Local Outlier Factor) + 0.4 × Clinical Severity Weight + 0.2 × Biological Plausibility, normalized to a 0-2 scale (scores >1.0 indicate high-priority signals). The framework was validated on Losartan using 500 adverse event reports (2010-2024), with additional validation against EudraVigilance and VigiBase databases. Dataset was split 60/20/20 for training/validation/testing.

**Results:** The ensemble achieved 75% accuracy in identifying high-risk adverse events, outperforming individual models (XGBoost 73%, Random Forest 71%, Gradient Boosting 70%, Neural Networks 68%, SVM 66%). The framework detected 15 distinct absurdity signals with the top five being: cough (propensity 1.525), angioedema (1.298), insomnia (1.290), nausea (1.180), hyperkalemia (1.114). Notably, angioedema (2.4% of reports) - a life-threatening reaction in Losartan's boxed warning - failed to reach significance with traditional methods (PRR=1.8, non-significant), while the new framework correctly prioritized it. Insomnia emerged as a novel signal not on the FDA label. Three ADR micro-clusters were identified: cardiovascular, renal/electrolyte, and immunologic/dermatologic.

**Key implications:** The approach preserves and analyzes rare events rather than excluding them, incorporates clinical severity weighting, detects ADR clusters, and demonstrates superior calibration (Brier score 0.18 vs. 0.22-0.28 for individual models). ADRs account for 5-10% of hospital admissions, over 100,000 annual US deaths, and $138 billion in global economic burden. Limitations include modest sample size (n=500) and spontaneous reporting biases. Future work includes full FAERS scaling, drug-drug interaction detection, conformal prediction methods, and regulatory validation.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"We introduce the concept of 'absurdity signal detection' - a novel framework that inverts the traditional paradigm by treating statistical outliers not as noise to be filtered, but as potential harbingers of rare, life-threatening adverse reactions. This approach recognizes that the most dangerous drug-related events may be precisely those that appear 'absurd' or anomalous from a population-level statistical perspective, yet represent genuine safety concerns for vulnerable patient subgroups."

- A product appearing on a quarterly report does NOT mean FDA has concluded the product has the listed risk or has identified a causal relationship; it means FDA has identified a potential safety signal and is evaluating it.

Quarterly reports include names of drug/biological products and potential safety signals, with "as of" dates indicating when additional information was updated. URL: https://mayoclinic.elsevierpure.com/en/publications/drpllm-a-large-language-model-based-framework-for-predicting-drug

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage is a Mayo Clinic research publication describing DRPLLM (Drug Response Prediction using Large Language Model), a novel framework for predicting cancer drug responses using multi-omics data. DRPLLM integrates the Llama-8b large language model (LLM) with a deep neural network (DNN) regression head, using embeddings from cell line gene expression, mutations, and drug properties formatted into natural language prompts. It was trained on the Genomics of Drug Sensitivity in Cancer v2 and Cancer Cell Line Encyclopedia datasets. The framework achieved a Spearman rank correlation coefficient (SCC) of 0.71, improving to 0.74 after hyperparameter optimization. Validation on a patient-derived xenograft (PDX) cohort showed the embedding-based approach significantly outperformed traditional prompt-engineering (SCC = 0.45, p < 1e-16 versus SCC = 0.06, p > 0.05), demonstrating its potential for accurate, generalizable drug response predictions in precision oncology.

The work is a conference contribution presented at the 17th International Conference on Bioinformatics and Computational Biology (BICOB 2025), held March 17, 2025 in San Francisco, United States. It was published in 2025 in the proceedings "Bioinformatics and Computational Biology" (Communications in Computer and Information Science, Volume 2535 CCIS) by Springer Science and Business Media Deutschland GmbH, pages 189-203. Authors include Rohan Gnanaolivu, Priyanka Vasanthakumari, Brenna C. Novotny, Jamie C. Overbeek, Yuanhang Liu, Alexander Partin, Nicholas D. Chia, Yitan Zhu, and Chen Wang. The publication ISBN is 9783031940385 and the DOI is 10.1007/978-3-031-94039-2_16.

SUMMARY:

This is a research article published in the journal Neural Networks (Volume 193, Article 108001, January 2026) by Elsevier, titled "Prediction of cancer drug response based on heterogeneous graph neural networks and multi-omics data." Authors: Junming Zhang, Shuwen Xiong, Yugui Xu, and Yongqing Zhang (funded by National Natural Science Foundation of China, Grant No. 62272067). DOI: 10.1016/j.neunet.2025.108001.

The paper proposes GraphTCDR, a model based on heterogeneous graph neural networks and multi-omics data for predicting cancer drug responses. The methodology involves: (1) constructing a cell line-drug heterogeneous network using multi-omics data and drug features as node attributes, (2) conducting node feature learning on the heterogeneous network, and (3) feeding learned features into fully connected layers to predict IC50 values.

Key technical details: The model integrates cell line genomic, epigenomic, and transcriptomic profiles (gene expression, CNV, and miRNA data) along with drug molecular fingerprints. High-dimensional omics data undergo dimensionality reduction via an autoencoder, while molecular fingerprints are processed using one-dimensional convolutional networks as drug node features. A heterogeneous graph Transformer architecture encodes the constructed network. Cell line and drug similarity networks are built through correlation analysis of DNA methylation profiles and molecular fingerprint data.

Results: Extensive experiments on the PRISM database (distinct from GDSC or CCLE) demonstrate GraphTCDR outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods across all evaluation metrics. Compared to the current best-performing model, GraphTCDR achieves improvements of 3.60% in PCC, 4.30% in SCC, 6.50% in R², and a 1.60% reduction in RMSE. It was compared against traditional deep learning methods (MLP, CNN), an advanced deep learning method (DeepTTA), and graph neural network methods (DeepCDR, NerD, GraphDRP). GraphTCDR maintains stable performance even with reduced training data, demonstrating superior robustness.

The paper highlights three key contributions: constructing a heterogeneous cell-drug graph network with heterogeneous graph Transformer for cancer drug response prediction; integrating multi-omics data for more biologically relevant and robust cell line feature learning; and utilizing the PRISM database, which is distinct from GDSC/CCLE and holds promise for discovering new anticancer medications.

The source code is available at https://github.com/ZhangLab312/GraphTCDR. Data sources include PRISM (https://doi.org/10.6084/m9.figshare.9393293) and PubChem. The article has been cited 4 times. ## scDrugMap: Benchmarking Large Foundation Models for Drug Response Prediction

This is a scientific research article (arXiv preprint, May 8, 2025, PMCID: PMC12083700, PMID: 40386575) from the University of Florida, Houston Methodist Research Institute, and Weill Cornell Medicine, authored by Qing Wang, Yining Pan, Minghao Zhou (equal contribution), Zijia Tang, Yanfei Wang, Guangyu Wang, and Qianqian Song (corresponding author: qsong1@ufl.edu). The work is licensed under Creative Commons Attribution-NonCommercial-NoDerivatives 4.0.

### Purpose
The study addresses drug resistance as a major barrier to effective cancer therapy, noting that of 85 FDA-approved cancer drugs, the median response rate is 41%, with nearly half below 40% and two-thirds showing complete response rates below 10%. The authors developed **scDrugMap**, the first comprehensive benchmarking framework evaluating ten large foundation models (eight single-cell-specific and two general-purpose language models) for drug response prediction from single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) data.

### Data Resources
- **Primary collection**: 326,751 cells from 36 single-cell datasets across 23 studies
- **Validation collection**: 18,856 cells from 17 datasets across 6 studies
- Total: 345,607 single cells spanning 14 cancer types, 3 therapy types, 5 tissue types, and 21 treatment regimens
- Models evaluated: eight single-cell foundation models (tGPT, scBERT, Geneformer, cellLM, scFoundation, scGPT, cellPLM, UCE) and two LLMs (LLaMa3-8B and GPT4o-mini)

### Methods
Two evaluation scenarios were used:
1. **Pooled-data evaluation**: Models trained and tested on aggregated data from multiple studies
2. **Cross-data evaluation**: Models trained on certain studies and tested on independent, unseen datasets

Two training strategies were applied: **layer-freezing** (averaged token embeddings passed to MLP classifier) and **fine-tuning** using **Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA)** (rank 8, alpha 8, dropout 0.05). GPT4o-mini was assessed via zero-shot prompt engineering.

### Key Results
- **Pooled-data evaluation**: scFoundation outperformed all others, achieving highest mean F1 scores of 0.971 (layer-freezing) and 0.947 (fine-tuning), outperforming the lowest-performing model by 54% and 57% respectively. scBERT performed worst.
- **Fine-tuning generally outperformed layer-freezing** across models.
- **Cross-data evaluation**: UCE achieved the highest performance (mean F1: 0.774) after fine-tuning on tumor tissue; scGPT showed superior performance (mean F1: 0.858) in zero-shot learning on tumor tissue. scFoundation showed reduced generalizability in cross-data settings.
- **GPT4o-mini** showed limited performance (near or below baseline in most settings), with its best performance in liver cancer (mean F1: 0.690) and notably poor results in pancreatic cancer (0.190) and melanoma (0.320).
- **Validation data**: scFoundation demonstrated the best performance across all categories (cell line: 0.901, tumor tissue: 0.965, organoid: 0.951 F1).
- UMAP visualizations revealed scFoundation, UCE, and scGPT effectively distinguished drug-resistant and drug-sensitive cells.

### Computational Scalability
scFoundation (encoder-decoder, 121.2 million parameters, output dimension 3,072) demonstrated the most efficient training (23.26 it/s) and inference (69.98 it/s) speeds. scGPT had 52.5M parameters and was less efficient (1.43 it/s training, 1.44 it/s inference).

### Availability
scDrugMap is available as a Python command-line tool and an interactive web server at https://scdrugmap.com/.

### Study Contributions
1. Model selection guidance based on dataset characteristics and evaluation scenarios
2. An integrated, interactive tool for drug response prediction, biomarker discovery, and resistance mechanism analysis
3. A benchmark framework to inform future drug discovery research

### Future Directions
The authors identify needs for: incorporating domain-specific knowledge into model training, integrating multi-modal data (transcriptomic, proteomic, genomic), exploring hybrid models combining single-cell and natural language foundation models, and incorporating explainable AI techniques for better model interpretability.

--- SOURCE 2: Deep Learning-Based Genetic Perturbation Models Do Outperform Uninformative Baselines on Well-Calibrated Metrics ---
URL: https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2025.10.20.683304v1.full-text

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a bioRxiv preprint (DOI: 10.1101/2025.10.20.683304) titled "Deep Learning-Based Genetic Perturbation Models Do Outperform Uninformative Baselines on Well-Calibrated Metrics." The study addresses prior reports (e.g., Ahlmann-Eltze et al.) claiming deep learning perturbation models fail to beat uninformative baselines, arguing these conclusions stem from limitations of benchmarking metrics rather than the models themselves.

**Key contributions and methods:**
- Introduces a framework for evaluating benchmark metric calibration using positive and negative controls, including a new positive control baseline called the "interpolated duplicate" and a quantitative calibration measure called the "Dynamic Range Fraction" (DRF).
- The interpolated duplicate combines the technical duplicate and mean baseline, weighting each gene by DEG p-values. Strongly perturbed genes are weighted toward the technical duplicate, weak/null genes toward the mean baseline.
- Explains prior artifacts: "control bias" (systematic control/perturbed differences inflating correlation metrics) and "signal dilution" (error metrics diluting meaningful biological signals).
- Analyzed 14 Perturb-seq datasets (~2.5 million cells across 9 cell types) and 13 evaluation metrics.

**Key findings:**
- Conventional metrics (MSE, control-referenced Pearson(Δ ctrl)) are often poorly calibrated, whereas weighted and rank-based alternatives (weighted MSE/WMSE, weighted Δ, Normalized Inverse Rank/NIR) exhibit consistent calibration.
- Under well-calibrated metrics, deep learning models outperform mean, control, and linear baselines on the unseen gene prediction task (validated in Replogle22 K562 and Nadig25 HepG2 datasets).
- Eight models evaluated: scGPT, GEARS, PRESAGE, scLambda, and four foundation MLP models (Geneformer, ESM2, scGPT, GenePT embeddings), plus a linear baseline.
- In the unseen combos task, PRESAGE exceeded the additive baseline in 12 of 13 metrics on the Wessels23 dataset; the additive baseline captures ~88% of the ideal performance gap in Norman19, limiting its value for benchmarking non-additive interactions (training sets cover only 0.63% of combo space in Norman19 vs 10.3% in Wessels23).

**Conclusions:** The apparent weakness of perturbation models arises primarily from metric miscalibration rather than model performance. The study recommends using calibrated metrics and cautions against using Norman19 as the sole benchmark for combinatorial perturbation modeling. PRESAGE and scLambda are highlighted as newer architectures worth including in future benchmarks. Code is available on GitHub at shiftbioscience/Perturbation-Models-Outperform-Baselines. Authors: Henry E. Miller, Gabriel M. Mejia, Francis J. A. Leblanc, Bo Wang, Brendan Swain, Lucas Paulo de Lima Camillo (Shift Bioscience Ltd., Cambridge UK; University of Toronto; University of Cambridge).
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"Calibrated evaluation thus explains prior reports of model underperformance, revealing that deep learning models do outperform uninformative baselines." (Abstract)

"In this context, 'calibration' refers to the degree to which a metric improves in response to a meaningful biological signal and correctly ranks informative predictions above null ones." (Introduction)

"Across datasets, WMSE also shows substantially better calibration than MSE, even for datasets with few DEGs." (Results, Measuring calibration)

"the additive baseline captured roughly 88% of the ideal performance gap in the best-calibrated metrics, comparable to the interpolated duplicate baseline which accesses held-out combination data... This evidence of additive baseline saturation, together with limited combinatorial coverage, limits Norman19's value for benchmarking models that aim to learn non-additive genetic interactions." (Results, Unseen combos prediction)

"The main limitation is not model capability but the use of uncalibrated benchmarks that obscure true performance." (Discussion)
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 3: Deep-learning-based gene perturbation effect prediction does ... ---
URL: https://www.nature.com/articles/s41592-025-02772-6

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a Brief Communication published in Nature Methods (volume 22, pages 1657-1661, 2025) by Constantin Ahlmann-Eltze, Wolfgang Huber, and Simon Anders, with 111,000 accesses and 212 citations. The study benchmarks five foundation models (scGPT, scFoundation, scBERT, Geneformer, UCE) and two other deep learning models (GEARS, CPA) against deliberately simple baselines for predicting transcriptome changes after single or double genetic perturbations. The key finding is that NONE of the deep learning models outperformed the simple baselines.

Key benchmarks and results:
1. DOUBLE PERTURBATION prediction: Used Norman et al. data (100 single and 124 double gene perturbations in K562 cells via CRISPR activation; 19,264 genes; 1,000 read-out genes). Models were fine-tuned on all single perturbations and 62 double perturbations, then tested on the remaining 62 (repeated 5 times with different random partitions). Baselines: 'no change' model and 'additive' model. All models had substantially higher prediction error than the additive baseline (measured by L2 distance). For predicting genetic interactions (5,035 identified at 5% FDR out of 124,000 potential), none of the models was better than the 'no change' baseline.

2. SINGLE PERTURBATION prediction: Used CRISPR interference datasets from Replogle et al. (K562 and RPE1 cells) and Adamson et al. (K562 cells). Baselines: 'mean' model and a simple linear model (equation 1: Y = GWP^T + b). None of the deep learning models consistently outperformed the mean prediction or the linear model.

3. Representation utility: When gene embeddings from scFoundation/scGPT and perturbation embeddings from GEARS were plugged into the simple linear model, performance matched or exceeded the original models. The linear model with pretrained perturbation embeddings (pretrained on Replogle data) consistently outperformed all other models, suggesting pretraining on perturbation data provided benefit but pretraining on single-cell atlas data provided only small benefit over random embeddings.

Conclusions: The authors conclude that the foundation models' goal of providing generalizable representations for predicting outcomes of not-yet-performed experiments "is still elusive." The results align with other benchmarks (Kedzierska et al., Boiarsky et al., Liu et al., and several 2024 preprints) showing deep learning models struggle to outperform simple baselines. They note limitations: only four datasets used, all from cancer cell lines with high mutational burden. They suggest some original comparisons in GEARS/scGPT/scFoundation papers were particularly 'easy' (e.g., CPA was never designed for unseen perturbations; scGPT's linear model reverted to no-change predictions).

Methods details: Software versions used (GEARS 0.1.2, scGPT 0.2.1, scFoundation, CPA 0.8.8, Geneformer 0.1.0, scBERT, UCE). Authors contacted original model developers to review their code. Genetic interactions classified as buffering (2.3%), synergistic (0.6%), or opposite (0%) based on deviation from additive expectation. Code available at github.com/const-ae/linear_perturbation_prediction-Paper and archived on Zenodo.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"None outperformed the baselines, which highlights the importance of critical benchmarking in directing and evaluating method development." (Abstract)

--- SOURCE 5: Benchmarking foundation cell models for post-perturbation RNA-seq prediction ---
URL: https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12864-025-11600-2

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This paper (published 23 April 2025 in BMC Genomics, volume 26, article 393) benchmarks two foundation cell models—scGPT and scFoundation—for post-perturbation RNA-seq prediction against baseline models across four Perturb-seq datasets (Adamson, Norman, and two Replogle subsets in K562 and RPE1 cell lines).

Key findings:
- Even the simplest baseline model (Train Mean—averaging training examples) outperformed both scGPT and scFoundation in most cases in the differential expression space (Pearson Delta metrics). Train Mean achieved correlations of 0.711, 0.557, 0.373, and 0.628 for Adamson, Norman, Replogle K562, and Replogle RPE1 respectively, versus scGPT's 0.641, 0.554, 0.327, and 0.596 and scFoundation's 0.552, 0.459, 0.269, and 0.471.
- A Random Forest Regressor using Gene Ontology (GO) features outperformed foundation models by a large margin (0.739, 0.586, 0.480, 0.648 across the four datasets).
- Raw gene expression space Pearson correlations were deemed unmeaningful because they are strongly influenced by baseline expression magnitudes; the authors recommend using Pearson Delta (correlation of differential expression profiles).
- The current Perturb-seq benchmark datasets exhibit low perturbation-specific variance (e.g., Adamson median intra-dataset correlation of 0.662 vs. Replogle K562's 0.117), making them suboptimal for distinguishing model performance. An inverse relationship was found between intra-dataset median correlation and model performance differences.
- Benchmarks currently focus exclusively on the PEX (Perturbation Exclusive) problem and neglect the CEX (Cell Exclusive) problem; datasets like LINCS-L1000 and Mix-Seq could improve future benchmarks.
- Foundation model embeddings showed weaker associations with pathway information (KEGG, REACTOME) than GO features or scELMO (NLP-based) embeddings, though scGPT embeddings had stronger association with gene regulatory networks (CollecTRI).

Methods: scGPT and scFoundation were fine-tuned on the GEARS/Perturb-seq benchmark datasets; baseline models included Train Mean, Elastic-Net, kNN, and Random Forest regressors using GO, scGPT, scFoundation, or scELMO embeddings as features. Evaluation used Pearson, Pearson Delta, Pearson Delta DE (top 20 differentially expressed genes), and Pearson Delta without target genes. The results align with an independent preprint by Ahlmann-Eltze et al. (2024) showing deep learning perturbation predictions do not yet outperform simple linear methods.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"Surprisingly, we found that even the simplest baseline model—taking the mean of training examples—outperformed scGPT and scFoundation. Furthermore, basic machine learning models that incorporate biologically meaningful features outperformed scGPT by a large margin."

--- SOURCE 6: Morphological Profiling in Image-Based Drug Discovery ---
URL: https://ardigen.com/the-applications-of-morphological-profiling-for-drug-discovery-the-success-stories

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This article from Ardigen (an AI-powered CRO) discusses the applications and success stories of morphological profiling (image-based/cytological profiling) in drug discovery. Morphological profiling captures a holistic snapshot of cell state by analyzing changes in cell shape, size, and texture in response to drug or genetic perturbations. The leading method is the Cell Painting assay, developed in Anne Carpenter's lab at the Broad Institute, which uses fluorescent dyes to visualize eight cellular components (nucleus, ER, mitochondria, Golgi) and generates thousands of morphological measurements per cell. Since its 2016 publication, the Cell Painting paper has been cited over 2,300 times (as of 2025).

Key industry success stories include:

1. **Recursion Pharmaceuticals**: Co-founded in 2013, was first to stake its platform on morphological profiling. In 2024, received FDA clearance for AI-discovered cancer drug REC-1245 (targeting RBM39) in under 18 months, one of the first AI-discovered molecules to reach patients. Also advanced REC-4881 for familial adenomatous polyposis (FAP) - first MEK1/2 inhibitor studied clinically for FAP (75% of patients responded at 12 weeks; 82% maintained reductions 12 weeks after stopping). Initially used the approach for drug repurposing for rare diseases, including cerebral cavernous malformation (CCM).

2. **AstraZeneca**: Trained deep learning models on 8,300 compounds combining Cell Painting images with bioactivity data from 140 assays, achieving ROC-AUC of 0.744±0.108, outperforming feature-based and chemistry-only approaches. Achieved up to 14.76× enrichment of true actives. Also used Cell Painting to profile PROTACs, discovering a distinct mitochondrial toxicity signature not evident from individual components.

3. **Bayer**: Developed machine-learning models showing morphological profiles perform better in predicting mitochondrial toxicity than chemical structures alone, improving predictive MCC by ~0.08-0.09 (10-25% relative gains).

4. **Janssen (J&J)**: Combined morphological image features with molecular structures to expand QSAR model applicability domain, achieving ~16% expansion in chemical space coverage and ~10% improvement in prediction accuracy.

The article also describes two Ardigen phenAID platform case studies: (1) improving prediction from sparse Cell Painting data (2× improvement in biological activity prediction, 20% increase in ROC AUC, 50% gain in loading/storage efficiency), and (2) multimodal AI for MoA/bioactivity prediction (4× faster pipeline, 34× lower computational cost).

Future directions include deep learning for automatic image representation, JUMP-CP open datasets, integration with transcriptomics/proteomics, and potential use in regulatory toxicity packages for IND submissions. The article quotes Anne Carpenter: "Images as a readout are extremely flexible in the kinds of things we can detect...There aren't many aspects of biology that can't be captured using imagery."
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"Instead of examining a single data point from a target-based assay, profiling casts a wide net, generating a rich fingerprint that characterizes the total impact of a chemical, genetic, or other perturbation at single cell resolution."

--- SOURCE 7: A Guide to Cell Painting for Drug Discovery Biologists | pixlbio ---
URL: https://www.pixl.bio/blog/a-guide-to-cell-painting-for-drug-discovery-biologists

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage is a comprehensive guide to Cell Painting for drug discovery biologists, developed by the pixlbio team. Cell Painting is a high-content, multiplexed fluorescence imaging assay that captures the morphological state of cells across multiple biological compartments using six fluorescent dyes across five imaging channels: Hoechst 33342 (nucleus/DNA, DAPI), Concanavalin A (ER, Alexa 488), SYTO 14 (nucleoli/RNA, Alexa 488), WGA (Golgi/plasma membrane, Alexa 568), MitoTracker (mitochondria, Alexa 568), and Phalloidin (F-actin cytoskeleton, Alexa 568). It was introduced by Gustafsdottir et al. (2013, PLOS ONE) and standardized by Bray et al. (2016, Nature Protocols).

The guide outlines an 8-step workflow: (1) experimental design and cell treatment (small molecules, genetic perturbations, biological stimuli, combinations), (2) fixation and staining (typically 4% paraformaldehyde), (3) high-content fluorescence imaging (9-16 fields at 20x magnification; platforms include PerkinElmer Opera Phenix, Molecular Devices ImageXpress, Yokogawa CellVoyager), (4) image QC and pre-processing, (5) cell segmentation (CellProfiler, Cellpose, StarDist, CellSAM), (6) morphological feature extraction via CellProfiler (1,000-2,000 features per cell), (7) profile aggregation and normalization (DMSO normalization, Z-scoring, spherize; pycytominer library), and (8) profile analysis and interpretation.

Key applications include mechanism of action deconvolution, early toxicity prediction (including DILI), disease phenotype characterization and phenotypic reversion, target identification, and gene function annotation. The JUMP-CP dataset includes 116,750+ compounds and 20,000+ genetic perturbations.

The guide highlights the scientific credentials and research of co-founders Jordi Carreras-Puigvert (CSO, Associate Professor at Uppsala University) and Ola Spjuth (CAIO, Professor of Pharmaceutical Bioinformatics at Uppsala, creator of CPSign). Key publications include: the 2025 Nature Methods 10-year review of Cell Painting (reviewing 90 papers from 2013-2023, co-authored with Anne Carpenter and Shantanu Singh); the 2023 AI in Life Sciences paper showing that combining Cell Painting with molecular fingerprint data improves MoA prediction; the 2021 BMC Biology antiviral phenomics paper achieving AUROC of 0.98 for distinguishing infected vs non-infected cells; and CPSign conformal prediction work (2024, Journal of Cheminformatics).

Advanced topics covered include foundation models and self-supervised learning (DINOv2, CellViT, DINO-based JUMP embeddings), Cell Painting in 3D and organoids, integration with other omics, and iPSC disease models for precision medicine. Common challenges addressed include batch effects, cell type optimization, data storage (50-200 GB per 384-well experiment), and interpretability.

pixlbio offers the pixCellPaint service, works with iPSC-derived hepatocyte models (pixHep) and disease models (MASLD, A1ATD, PFIC2, UCD), and positions the combination of human iPSC biology with AI-powered phenomics as the future of preclinical drug discovery. A comparison table shows Cell Painting offers very high information content with high throughput and medium cost compared to other profiling approaches.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"Cell Painting is a high-content, multiplexed fluorescence imaging assay designed to capture the morphological state of cells across multiple biological compartments simultaneously." "Unlike targeted assays that measure one or two specific markers, Cell Painting captures thousands of morphological features per cell in a single experiment. This makes it uniquely powerful for unbiased phenotypic profiling — you don't need to know in advance what biology is important." "The combination of human-relevant cell models with Cell Painting phenomics and AI-driven analysis is, in our view, the most powerful available approach to preclinical drug discovery today." "Cell Painting occupies a unique position — high information content at high throughput and moderate cost."

<summary>

The key advantage is capturing unbiased high-dimensional morphological data rather than focusing on specific biomarkers, generating large-scale data suitable for machine learning and AI-driven analysis.

**Basic Concept:** Cell Painting involves staining multiple cellular compartments with fluorescent dyes (e.g., nuclei in blue, lysosomes in red, actin in green, mitochondria in yellow), imaging them using high-content microscopes, and analyzing resulting images with machine learning and AI. Cell Painting utilizes a high number of features extracted from image processing tasks, on which high-dimensional data analysis (feature weighting, nearest neighbor or cluster analysis) is performed. **Applications in Drug Discovery:**
1. **Phenotype characterization of cellular responses** - used in iPSC donor selection and disease progression characterization

4. **Early toxicity and safety assessments (Safety/Tox)** - uses standardized, scalable equipment for fast turnaround; assesses thousands of features based on intensity, texture, and granularity of each dye; compares phenotypic changes against a database of compounds with known toxic effects

**Advantages of Cell Painting:**
- Unbiased, high-dimensional data acquisition
- Scalable and cost-efficient for high-throughput screening
- Compatible with AI and machine learning techniques
- Provides comprehensive insights into cellular behavior

Genetic perturbation prediction is easier than chemical perturbation prediction (due to higher specificity and much smaller search space ~2×10^4 genes vs ~10^60 small molecules). --- SOURCE 1: An agentic AI system for automated pharmacogenomic recommendation generation | npj Digital Medicine ---
URL: https://www.nature.com/articles/s41746-026-02590-w

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This scientific article, published in npj Digital Medicine (volume 9, article 541, 2026), describes the development and evaluation of the PGxAI-Recommender, an agentic AI system for automated pharmacogenomic recommendation generation. The system addresses limitations in current pharmacogenomics (PGx) guideline curation workflows, which are manual, resource-intensive, slow, and limited in coverage—with CPIC currently covering only 316 gene–drug pairs and roughly 8,000 cited articles.

**System Architecture:** The modular pipeline operates in three stages: (1) acquisition of relevant texts (PubMed, PMC, FDA drug labels), (2) LLM-based extraction of evidence, and (3) recommendation generation. A lightweight agentic controller using a perceive–reason–act loop coordinates the multi-step processing, with each module (literature retrieval, document annotation, FDA label parsing, evidence aggregation, recommendation generation) exposed as an independent callable tool. The system uses GPT-4.1 (OpenAI API, temperature=1e-5) and gathered evidence is aggregated by allele into CPIC-style evidence tables with qualitative levels of evidence (High/Moderate/Weak).

**Key Results:**
- The extraction module achieved 91.9% field-level accuracy across 22 pharmacogenomic articles (2,310 binary judgments from 3 annotators), with 94.7% of extracted fields judged correct by majority expert consensus. Structured fields (Study design, Genotyping method, Sample size) performed near-perfectly, while interpretive fields showed lower accuracy (Genotype distribution at 56% minimum).
- In blinded expert review of 24 random recommendations rated 0–10, PGxAI-Recommender achieved the highest mean score (9.0) compared to baseline LLMs (mean 6.2–7.8, p<0.01 in pairwise comparisons). The system achieved a pairwise win rate of 0.83 against CPIC reference recommendations, versus 0.17–0.78 for baselines.
- GPT-5 notably failed to improve quality despite being more advanced, occasionally generating detailed dosing instructions contradicting CPIC guidance (over-generation errors).

**Representative cases highlighting system strengths:** For efavirenz–CYP2B6, the system correctly generated phenotype-specific dose guidance (200–400 mg for intermediate/poor metabolizers; up to 800 mg escalation for ultrarapid metabolizers). For fluorouracil–DPYD, it correctly recommended standard dosing for normal metabolizers without unnecessary detail and categorical avoidance for poor metabolizers. For atorvastatin–SLCO1B1 poor function, it appropriately recommended ≤20 mg/day or switching to safer statins.

**Coverage:** The automated framework can identify up to 573 gene–drug pairs and retrieve nearly 20,000 relevant pharmacogenomic publications indexed in PubMed (1966–2025), compared to CPIC's current 316 pairs and ~8,000 articles. The system performs automated weekly literature scans with incremental re-processing of affected gene–drug pairs for continuous updates.

**Design Philosophy & Limitations:** The system is designed to complement (not replace) expert consortia like CPIC and DPWG, operating in de novo mode (uncurated gene–drug pairs) and updater mode (revisions for outdated guidelines). It involves no model training or fine-tuning—performance gains come from structured, evidence-aware prompting. Limitations include a small validation set (22 articles, 24 recommendations), accessibility gaps for paywalled articles (bias toward open-access literature), and lack of modeling for broader clinical contexts (drug–drug interactions, phenoconversion, comorbidities). The architecture is adaptable to other pharmacogenomic standards (DPWG) and could extend to additional molecular modalities.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"An agentic AI system for automated, scalable generation of CPIC-style recommendations using large language models (LLMs) guided by structured evidence."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 2: Journal of Medical Internet Research - Extracting Clinical Guideline Information Using Two Large Language Models: Evaluation Study ---
URL: https://www.jmir.org/2025/1/e73486

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a peer-reviewed research article published in the Journal of Medical Internet Research (JMIR 2025;27:e73486, doi:10.2196/73486) evaluating the use of two large language models (LLMs), GPT-4o and Gemini-1.5-Pro, for extracting and classifying pharmacogenomics (PGx) clinical guideline information for integration into clinical decision support systems (CDSS). The study was conducted by researchers from National Taiwan University, China Medical University Hospital, and China Medical University (Taiwan), led by corresponding author Shih-Sheng Chang, PhD. The study ran from October 1 to November 30, 2024.

**Methodology:** The researchers used the two LLMs to classify 385 PGx drug-gene interaction recommendations from the PharmGKB database (as of October 5, 2024), with each recommendation tested 20 times per model (7,700 responses per model, 15,400 total). Zero-shot prompting was used with a classification scheme of: "No action needed," "Consider dosage modification," "Change medication," "Monitor adverse effects," or "Other." Two strategies were tested: (1) repeated cross-comparisons flagging discrepancies between models, and (2) an agreement-threshold strategy designating predictions appearing in less than 60% of the 40 combined outputs as unstable. Five pharmacists performed expert validation.

**Key Results:**
- Reproducibility: GPT-4o achieved 97.8% (7534/7700), Gemini-1.5-Pro 98.9% (7612/7700)
- Accuracy vs. expert labels: GPT-4o 93.5% (Cohen κ=0.90, P<.001), Gemini-1.5-Pro 92.7% (Cohen κ=0.89, P<.001)
- Weighted average F1-scores: GPT-4o 0.929, Gemini 0.935
- Cross-comparison reduced manual review to 11.4% (44/385); the agreement-threshold strategy further reduced it to 2.9% (11/385) but slightly increased the error rate from 0.3% (1/341) to 0.5% (2/374)
- The models agreed on 341 of 385 items (reducing manual review by 88.6%), with only 1 disagreement (0.3%) with expert labels among agreed cases
- Total combined cost of both LLMs was only US $0.76 (GPT-4o: $0.43; Gemini: $0.33)
- Majority of guidelines (69%) came from Clinical Pharmacogenetics Implementation Consortium (CPIC); most interactions involved CYP2D6, CYP2C9, CYP2C19
- Drug classes: nervous system (38.2%), cardiovascular (29.9%), antineoplastic/immunomodulating (9.6%)

**Conclusion:** Using two LLMs simultaneously can effectively streamline PGx guideline integration into CDSS while maintaining high performance at minimal cost. Although selective manual review remains necessary, repeated cross-comparisons and agreement-threshold strategies offer a practical, scalable solution for PGx guideline classification in clinical workflows.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"These findings suggest that using 2 LLMs can effectively streamline PGx guideline integration into clinical decision support systems while maintaining high performance and minimal cost. Although selective manual review remains necessary, this approach offers a practical and scalable solution for PGx guideline classification in clinical workflows."
</key_excerpts>

URL: https://guidelines.carelonmedicalbenefitsmanagement.com/pharmacogenetic-testing-2025-11-15-updated-2026-01-01

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage is an ARCHIVED clinical guideline from Carelon Medical Benefits Management titled "Pharmacogenetic Testing" (Doc ID: GEN09-1125.2-UC0126). It was archived on 06/14/2026 because it contains outdated information and should not be consulted for clinical use. The document was effective 11/15/2025 with codes updated 01/01/2026, and its last review date was 07/17/2025. It is not effective for Anthem BCBS OH Medicaid.

The guideline establishes clinical appropriateness criteria (medical necessity) for pharmacogenetic testing. According to the framework, genotyping is considered **medically necessary** when ALL of the following conditions are met: (1) the medication is the most appropriate treatment for the individual's underlying condition; (2) the test has demonstrated analytical and clinical validity and utility for the individual; (3) the biomarker testing is focused on specific genetic polymorphisms relevant to treatment; and (4) the testing is referenced in the corresponding FDA package insert or NCCN guidelines. Genetic tests not specifically mentioned in the guidelines are considered not medically necessary.

**Table 1 lists the therapies and biomarkers considered medically necessary for genotyping:** ApoE ε4 (lecanemab, donanemab-azbt – Neurology), CFTR (ivacaftor – Pediatrics), CYP2C19 (clopidogrel – Cardiology), CYP2C9 (siponimod – Neurology; deuruxolitinib – Dermatology), CYP2D6 (eliglustat – Hematology; tetrabenazine – Neurology), DPYD (capecitabine, fluorouracil – Oncology), G6PD (rasburicase – Hematology; tafenoquine, primaquine – Infectious Diseases), HLA-B*1502 (carbamazepine, oxcarbazepine – Neurology), HLA-B*5701 (abacavir – Infectious Diseases), HLA-B*58:01 (allopurinol – Rheumatology), NAGS (carglumic acid – Gastroenterology), POLG (divalproex sodium, valproic acid – Neurology), and TPMT/NUDT15 (mercaptopurine, thioguanine – Hematology).

**Key evidence discussed in the rationale:**
- About 15% of US prescriptions have potential pharmacogenetic influence, but evidence supports genotype-guided prescribing for only a limited number of drugs.
- The INGENIOUS trial (26 drug-gene pairs) was negative for reducing adverse drug events within 1 year.
- **Psychiatric pharmacogenetic testing:** The GUIDED trial (GeneSight, 1167 outpatients with depression) found no statistically significant difference in response/remission rates; the PRIME study (1944 subjects across 22 VA medical centers) found only clinically insignificant gains (less than 2% improvement in remission at 24 weeks). Meta-analyses show risks of bias and lack of clinical utility evidence.
- **DPYD testing for fluoropyrimidines:** Approximately 3%-5% of White populations have partial DPD deficiency and 0.2% have complete deficiency. Four main DPYD variants are associated with impaired DPD activity: c.1905+1G>A (DPYD *2A), c.1679T>G (DPYD *13), c.2846A>T, and c.1129-5923C>G (Haplotype B3). DPYD variant carriers receiving standard fluoropyrimidine doses have ~70% risk of severe toxicity and ~3% risk of fatal toxicity. The NCCN updated guidance in 2025, moving from "not recommended" to stating DPYD testing "should be considered prior to fluoropyrimidine therapy." The EMA has required pretherapeutic DPYD screening since April 2020. A PREPARE trial secondary analysis showed carriers of actionable genotypes receiving dose adjustments had a 90% lower risk of clinically relevant toxic effects.
- **APOE ε4 testing in Alzheimer's disease:** APOE ε4 has worldwide prevalence of 14% and is the strongest genetic susceptibility factor for sporadic Alzheimer's (OR 8-12 for ε4/ε4 vs ε3/ε3), but testing is not recommended in routine clinical evaluation of cognitive impairment. In the Clarity AD trial for lecanemab, 15.8% of patients were homozygous APOE ε4 carriers with higher risk of symptomatic amyloid-related imaging abnormalities (9.2% vs 1.4% for non-carriers), leading to the FDA label recommendation to consider APOE ε4 testing when deciding to initiate lecanemab.

The document also includes comprehensive CPT codes delegated as "May Be Medically Necessary When Criteria are Met" (including codes for CYP2C19, CYP2D6, CYP2C9, DPYD, G6PD, NUDT15, TPMT, HLA typing, and APOE testing) and codes listed as "Not Medically Necessary" (including CYP3A4, CYP3A5, F2, F5, MTHFR, SLCO1B1, TYMS, UGT1A1, VKORC1, psychiatric genomic panels, and warfarin metabolism panels).
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"The NCCN issued updated guidance in 2025 stating 'Testing for DPYD genetic variants should be considered prior to fluoropyrimidine therapy.' This represents a change from the prior NCCN guidance which stated that routine DPYD testing prior to fluoropyrimidine therapy was 'not recommended.'", "DPYD variant carriers who receive standard fluoropyrimidine doses have ~70% risk of severe toxicity and ~3% risk of fatal toxicity, and these risks are even higher in the ~1/250 patients who carry two DPYD variants.", "The GUIDED trial was a randomized, double-blind, clinical trial evaluating the GeneSight pharmacogenomic intervention which did not find a statistically significant difference in response rates or remission rates when those tested were compared to those without testing.", "APOE ɛ4 has a worldwide prevalence of 14% and is the strongest known genetic susceptibility factor for sporadic Alzheimer disease (OR, 8-12 for ɛ4/ɛ4 vs ɛ3/ɛ3).", "In the intervention arm, carriers of any actionable genotype exhibited a 90% lower risk of clinically relevant toxic effects compared with the control arm."

This is a review article published in Advances in Integrative Medicine (Volume 12, Issue 4, December 2025, Article 100529) by Hrishikesh Khude and Pravin Shende, titled "AI-driven clinical decision support systems: Revolutionizing medication selection and personalized drug therapy."

**Purpose:** The review explores how Artificial Intelligence (AI) is transforming medication selection, personalized drug therapy, and clinical decision-support systems. It evaluates AI methodologies (machine learning, deep learning, and natural language processing) across ten core domains of clinical pharmacology.

**Key AI Applications Discussed:**
1. **Personalized medicine and precision drug therapy** – AI integrates genomic, proteomic, and clinical data with EHRs to predict drug responses and customize treatment regimens. Examples include IBM Watson for Oncology, CardioDx's Corus® CAD (a 23-gene panel diagnostic for coronary artery disease), and Verily Life Sciences (reported 29% reduction in sepsis-related mortality and 14% decrease in hospital readmissions).
2. **Drug-drug interaction (DDI) detection** – Platforms like Lexicomp and Micromedex use AI to evaluate interactions, with AI-powered systems achieving up to 90% accuracy in identifying known DDIs. A study assessed AI chatbots (Bard, ChatGPT-3.5/4, Bing AI) against 255 clinical DDI cases.
3. **Toxicity prediction** – ML models analyze chemical/physical properties to predict adverse reactions; LD50 predictors (LDFP-ADMET, Interpretable-ADMET) achieved 84% accuracy using Naive Bayes and Nearest Neighbors on 8,992 compounds.
4. **Drug discovery acceleration** – Pfizer partnered with IBM Watson (processing over 25 million immuno-oncology data points), shortening drug development timelines by 20%.
5. **Cost-effective prescribing** – AI recommends generic alternatives and therapeutically equivalent lower-cost medications; a study of 160 practitioners found drug price information led to cheaper medication choices in 42% of situations.
6. **Adverse drug reaction (ADR) prediction** – A machine-learning model using drug chemical, biological, and physiological data (SIDER database, 832 drugs, 1,385 side effects) achieved an AUC of 0.9524 with SVM, improving precision from 43.37% to 66.17%.
7. **Clinical Decision Support Systems (CDSS)** – A cervical cancer screening CDSS improved recommendation accuracy from 84% to 93% post-enhancement. CURATE.AI was positively received by oncologists for personalized dosing.
8. **Continuous monitoring** – AccuHealth in Chile uses AI remote monitoring for ~5 million chronic disease patients.
9. **Medication adherence alerts** – Tools like AiCure, MediSafe, and Dosecast use computer vision to track adherence.
10. **Telemedicine integration** – Los Angeles County diabetic retinopathy telemedicine reduced specialist visits by over 14,000, saving ~$1.5 million annually for over 12,000 patients.
11. **Medical literature analysis** – At Lahey Hospital, AI-assisted radiology reviews identified 15% more incidental findings, improved report accuracy by 20%, and reduced turnaround time by 18%.

**Challenges Addressed:** Data privacy (citing the Royal Free London NHS-Google DeepMind case involving ~1.6 million patient records without consent), algorithmic bias (e.g., breast cancer risk algorithms assigning Black patients to "low risk" more often), black-box interpretability (addressed via explainable AI techniques like SHAP and LIME), and regulatory compliance (FDA and EMA requiring explainability; FDA SaMD classifications).

**Methodology:** A systematic literature review searched PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, IEEE Xplore, and Google Scholar (January 2017–March 2024), retrieving 189 records; after excluding 42 duplicates and screening, 45 articles met inclusion criteria.

**Conclusion:** AI-driven systems show significant potential in optimizing personalized medicine, assessing drug interactions, predicting adverse drug reactions, and facilitating cost-effective prescribing, though successful integration requires addressing data heterogeneity, model interpretability, and regulatory complexities. --- SOURCE 5: Large language model as clinical decision support system augments medication safety in 16 clinical specialties ---
URL: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12629785

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a scientific article published in Cell Reports Medicine (Cell Rep Med, 2025 Sep 24;6(10):102323, doi:10.1016/j.xcrm.2025.102323, PMCID: PMC12629785, PMID: 40997804) describing a study evaluating large language models (LLMs) as clinical decision support systems (CDSS) for medication safety.

**Study Design:** The study was a prospective, cross-over, open-label design involving 91 simulated prescribing error scenarios based on 40 complex clinical vignettes across 16 medical and surgical specialties. Six pharmacists (4 junior with 2-5 years experience; 2 senior with >10 years) from two tertiary acute care institutions participated. Participants were randomized into two arms with washout periods between rounds. Expert panel (board-certified pharmacists and physicians with >10 years experience) developed reference standards using PCNE classification V9.1 and HAMEC severity tools.

**Key Findings:**
- Five LLMs were evaluated (Gemini Flash, Gemini 1.5 Pro, GPT-4 Turbo, GPT-4 omni, Claude 3.5 Sonnet) with and without retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) frameworks
- Shown: 31.9% of errors capable of causing serious harm, 52.7% moderate harm, 15.4% minor/no harm
- Claude 3.5 Sonnet was the best native model (accuracy 51%, F1 0.42 vs Gemini Flash's 16%, F1 0.16)
- RAG framework did not improve Claude 3.5 Sonnet's performance (accuracy decreased 2% to 49%)
- Three implementation modes tested: LLM alone, pharmacist alone, and co-pilot (pharmacist + LLM)
- **Co-pilot mode performed best with 61% accuracy** (precision 0.57, recall 0.61, F1 0.59) – a 32.6% improvement over pharmacist alone (46% accuracy)
- Co-pilot mode increased detection of serious-harm errors by 1.5-fold over pharmacist alone (66% vs. 43-52%)
- Performance declined in co-pilot mode for inappropriate dosage regimen detection (52% vs. 43%)
- No significant correlation between case complexity (MCRI score) and accuracy
- Most common drug-related problems: inappropriate dosage regimens, adverse drug reactions, and drug-drug interactions

**Conclusions:** LLMs used in co-pilot mode (in tandem with pharmacists) can augment medication chart review performance and improve patient safety in acute care settings. However, limitations include addressing only 5 DRP categories, small sample of fictional scenarios, lack of bias/fairness evaluation, single prompt testing, rapidly evolving LLM landscape, and dependence on local drug references. The study proposes a clinical workflow where LLM-CDSS acts as a co-pilot to summarize patient information and flag DRPs for pharmacist preview.

**Data availability:** Sample dataset and codes are openly available at https://github.com/Liyuan1Y/CDSS-LLM-Cookbook/tree/main. Lead contact: Dr. Daniel Shu Wei Ting (daniel.ting.s.w@singhealth.com.sg). The study was supported by Singapore National Medical Research Council, Duke-NUS Medical School, and A*STAR grants. This is an open-access article under CC BY license.
</summary>

## Multimodal EHR Integration

This webpage (updated 21 November 2025) provides a comprehensive overview of multimodal Electronic Health Record (EHR) integration—the process of unifying heterogeneous clinical data types (structured measurements, longitudinal time-series, unstructured clinical narratives, lab results, medical images, biologic signals, and genomic features) into unified representations for predictive modeling, clinical decision support, and healthcare analytics.

**Core Premise:** Single-modality models systematically underutilize the informational richness of EHRs and fail to capture critical cross-modal dependencies, redundancies, and synergies necessary for precision medicine.

### 1. Modalities, Preprocessing, and Representation
- Canonical modalities: tabular data (demographics, vitals, labs, medications), unstructured text (clinical notes, radiology reports), time-series, imaging (CT, MRI, X-ray), wearables, and genomics
- Each modality requires tailored preprocessing: tabular (MICE imputation, normalization, one-hot encoding), text (tokenization via WordPiece or subword), imaging (resizing, intensity normalization, CNN backbones), wearables (clinical-grade aggregation into multi-day feature vectors), genomics (GWAS variant pruning, quantile normalization)
- Each modality is encoded via dedicated subnetworks: feedforward layers (static/tabular), recurrent/Transformer encoders (time-series), pre-trained LLMs (text), CNNs (images), MLPs/transformers (genomics/wearables)

### 2. Fusion Strategies Taxonomy
- **Early fusion (feature-level):** Concatenated feature vectors fed to MLP; easy to implement but fails on semantically asynchronous modalities
- **Intermediate fusion (joint-representation):** Modality-specific networks project representations, then fused via attention pooling, bilinear pooling, or cross-modal transformers; cross-attention favored for capturing residual dependencies
- **Late fusion (decision-level):** Separate models produce logits combined via voting, learnable gates, or ensemble meta-models; prevalent with modality-missingness
- State-of-the-art favors dynamic, modality-adaptive fusion: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) frameworks with learned gating, disentangled transformation modules separating shared/specific subspaces, and Neural Architecture Search (NAS) approaches like AutoFM

### 3. Major Model Classes
- MAG-style attention gating (modality-adaptive with learned displacement)
- Multimodal transformers and cross-attentional networks (dominant approach)
- Domain-informed modules with contrastive objectives and hierarchical regularization
- Knowledge-augmented and RAG frameworks (grounding in PubMed, UMLS, PrimeKG knowledge graphs)
- Uncertainty-aware fusion using belief functions (Dempster–Shafer theory for ICU risk stratification)
- Image-EHR integration with Gated Multimodal Units (GMU)

### 4. Empirical Outcomes
Multimodal fusion consistently outperforms unimodal baselines by **2–12 absolute points** in accuracy, recall@k, AUROC, or F1:
- **CURENet:** F1_macro = 0.855 on MIMIC-III (10-disease prediction); removing text drops F1 from 0.855→0.663
- **MoE-Health:** mortality AUROC 0.818 (trimodal) vs 0.770 (EHR only)
- **MINGLE:** 11.8% relative F1 gain over hypergraph approaches on MIMIC-III phenotyping
- **MEDFuse:** >0.90 macro-F1 on multi-label diagnosis
- Ablations uniformly show **text modalities contribute the largest marginal improvements**

### 5. Challenges
- Modality-missingness (real-world data incompleteness)
- Fusion complexity and overfitting risks
- Computational cost of cross-attending O(M²) modality pairs and large LLM/KG usage
- Explainability and clinical trust (no standardized actionable explanations)
- Modality selection and scalability (few systems adaptively select fusion per-patient)

### 6. Emerging Directions
- **Genomics integration:** +0.025 AUROC for T2D 10-year risk prediction
- **Wearable data:** up to +12.2% delta AUROC for diabetes with 180-day wearable summaries
- **Automated fusion discovery** via NAS (AutoFM)
- **Uncertainty-quantified predictions** using belief function theory
- Open questions: multi-center generalization, federated learning for privacy, real-time streaming fusion
</summary>

<summary>
This scientific article (published in Translational Psychiatry, 2021, corrected 2022) presents methodology for clinical genotyping of CYP2D6 and CYP2C19, enzymes that metabolize many antidepressants, atomoxetine, and antipsychotics. Since no consensus methodology for clinical genotyping existed, the authors cross-validated multiple technologies against each other using 95 DNA samples from the GENDEP study (all White European ancestry, selected from 853 samples to represent the broadest possible range of genotypes, enriched for complex structural variants). 

The technologies compared included: AmpliChip CYP450, TaqMan SNV and CNV assays, Luminex xTAGv3 CYP2D6/CYP2C19, PharmacoScan, Ion AmpliSeq Pharmacogenomics Panel, long-range PCR (L-PCR) with Sanger sequencing and Luminex, and Agena MassARRAY (for CYP2C19). 

Key findings include: consensus genotypes resulted in revision of enzyme activity scores for 28/95 (29%) of CYP2D6 samples and 2/93 (2.2%) of CYP2C19 samples, mostly due to AmpliChip's inability to detect hybrids and CYP2D6*5. For CYP2C19, Luminex and PharmacoScan showed 100% concordance with consensus genotypes, with all technologies (except AmpliChip) 100% concordant for CYP2C19*2 and *17. Nineteen samples had hybrid configurations (9 CYP2D7-2D6 hybrids and 10 CYP2D6-2D7 hybrids), with L-PCR amplicons aligned to known CYP2D6*13 sequences (GQ162807, EU093102) and CYP2D6*4.013/EU530605/606 sequences. One novel haplotype (CYP2D6*13 + *4/*5) was identified.

The paper's novel contributions include: inter-technology concordance data across platforms, CYP2D6 amplicon Sanger sequencing methodology with primers, adaptation of the Luminex CYP2D6 assay for hybrid amplicon genotyping, customizable automated haplotype translation files, broader TaqMan SNV assay coverage (including CYP2D6*29 and *40), haplotype phasing methodology adaptable to other technologies, and a clinical workflow algorithm that includes hybrid configurations. The workflow algorithm includes multiplex SNV/CNV assays, haplotype phasing, and L-PCR with multiplex genotyping or sequencing. Study limitations include lack of coverage of rare variants (estimated to account for ~6.3% of olanzapine variance and 4.4% of CYP2C19 genetic variability) and a European-only sample set lacking haplotypes like CYP2D6*29 common in other ethnic groups.
