## Computational models in toxicity prediction

Computational models in toxicology provide powerful alternatives to traditional laboratory-based toxicity testing by predicting harmful effects of chemicals using mathematical algorithms and digital data. Among these, QSTR models are widely used to relate a compound’s structural and physicochemical properties to toxicity. Read-across and category-based methods extend predictions to untested chemicals based on similarities with known substances. Pharmacokinetic models, such as Absorption, Distribution, Metabolism, Excretion, and Toxicity (ADMET) models, simulate how chemicals behave in the body, offering valuable insights into exposure and dose-response. These models allow for rapid screening and prioritisation of potentially toxic compounds, significantly reducing the need for animal testing and accelerating safety evaluations in both pharmaceutical and environmental contexts.

1.   a)
Ecotoxicity models

Ecotoxicity prediction tools are essential in environmental protection, as they provide valuable data for assessing the risks associated with chemical exposure. This information is crucial for monitoring environmental pollution and developing effective strategies aimed at environmental conservation and restoration. Moreover, ecotoxicity prediction tools enhance our understanding of chemical behaviour and its ecological impacts. Human-induced chemicals in the environment serve as key drivers of environmental hazards, significantly affecting human well-being and exerting adverse impacts on the ecological conditions of affected regions (Gunjyal et al. [2023](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11356-025-37354-8#ref-CR73 "Gunjyal N, Rani S, Asgari Lajayer B, Senapathi V, Astatkie T (2023) A review of the effects of environmental hazards on humans, their remediation for sustainable development, and risk assessment. Environ Monit Assess 195:11353. 
                https://doi.org/10.1007/s10661-023-11353-z
                
              ")).

Ecotoxicity: Ecotoxicity (HC50) refers to the potential of a chemical substance or physical agent to exert harmful effects on the environment and living organisms, including fish, insects, microorganisms, wildlife, and plants (Roy & Kar, [2016](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11356-025-37354-8#ref-CR163 "Roy K, Kar S (2016) In silico models for ecotoxicity of pharmaceuticals. In: Benfenati E (ed) In silico methods for predicting drug toxicity. Springer, New York, vol 1425, pp 237–304. doi: 10.1007/978-1-4939-3609-0_12.")). An autoencoder model has been developed by Gao et al., [2022](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11356-025-37354-8#ref-CR61 "Gao F, Zhang W, Baccarelli AA, Shen Y (2022) Predicting chemical ecotoxicity by learning latent space chemical representations. Environ Int 163:107224. 
                https://doi.org/10.1016/j.envint.2022.107224
                
              ")) for predicting HC50 values. This model performs nonlinear dimensionality reduction and extracts meaningful latent chemical representations from the input data, offering a distinct approach to handling redundant, high-dimensional information compared to techniques like PCA, MDS, and UMAP. These derived representations enable substantial dimensionality reduction, thereby enhancing the accuracy of chemical ecotoxicity predictions over methods that rely directly on raw input features. For more information on ecotoxicity, refer to the EPA Series 850, Ecological Effects Test Guidelines.

Aquatic Toxicity: The increasing global contamination of freshwater systems with numerous industrial chemical compounds poses a significant aquatic environmental challenge. Although many of these substances are present at low concentrations, their occurrence, particularly as components of complex mixtures, raises serious concerns regarding both toxicological risks and aquatic toxicity (Schwarzenbach et al., [2006](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11356-025-37354-8#ref-CR172 "Schwarzenbach RP, Escher BI, Fenner K, Hofstetter TB, Johnson CA, von Gunten U, Wehrli B (2006) The challenge of micropollutants in aquatic systems. Science 313:1072–1077. 
                https://doi.org/10.1126/science.1127291
                
              ")). According to REACH registration, the substances are classified under the aquatic environmental hazard category as harmful to aquatic life with long-term effects from chronic exposure (CLP-GHS H412) (Andreassen et al., [2025](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11356-025-37354-8#ref-CR14 "Andreassen M, Rudén C, Ågerstrand M (2025) Mapping chemicals across EU’s legal frameworks towards a ‘one substance, one assessment’ approach. Environ Int. 
                https://doi.org/10.1016/j.envint.2025.109460
                
              ")). A web-based platform, AquaticTox, predicts the toxicities and modes of action of compounds in five aquatic species, such as Oncorhynchus mykiss, Pimephales promelas, Daphnia magna, Pseudokirchneriella subcapitata, and Tetrahymena pyriformis, using ensemble models. It enables users to input chemical structures for rapid predictions and provides free access to curated toxicity data (Shi et al., [2024](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11356-025-37354-8#ref-CR182 "Shi XX, Wang ZZ, Wang YL, Wang F, Yang GF (2024) AquaticTox: a web-based tool for aquatic toxicity evaluation based on ensemble learning to facilitate the screening of green chemicals. Environ Health 2:202–211. 
                https://doi.org/10.1021/envhealth.4c00014
                
              ")).

Algal toxicity: Algal toxicity refers to the harmful impact of chemicals or pollutants on algae, which serve as primary producers in aquatic ecosystems. Algal toxicity refers to the detrimental effects of chemicals or pollutants on algae. Pesticides can have adverse effects on algae, and prolonged exposure may trigger tolerance mechanisms (Rydh Stenström et al., [2021](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11356-025-37354-8#ref-CR167 "Rydh Stenström J, Kreuger J, Goedkoop W (2021) Pesticide mixture toxicity to algae in agricultural streams—field observations and laboratory studies with in situ samples and reconstituted water. Ecotoxicol Environ Saf 215:112153. 
                https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ecoenv.2021.112153
                
              ")). To predict the toxicity of chemical derivatives on algal species, robust Quantitative Structure–Activity Relationship (QSAR) models were developed using partial least squares (PLS) regression. Incorporating 2-D descriptors such as Extended Topochemical Atom (ETA) and non-ETA, the models demonstrated strong validation metrics. It also indicates that structural features such as ortho-positioned nitro groups, para-chlorine substituents, oxygen and nitrogen atoms at specific topological distances, aliphatic side chains, and others, contribute to toxicity (Seth & Roy, [2020](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11356-025-37354-8#ref-CR175 "Seth A, Roy K (2020) QSAR modeling of algal low level toxicity values of different phenol and aniline derivatives using 2D descriptors. Aquat Toxicol 228:105627. 
                https://doi.org/10.1016/j.aquatox.2020.105627
                
              ")). For more information on algal toxicity, refer to the regulatory guidelines, OECD Test Guideline No. 201 AQ(OECD 2011).

2.   b)
Animal toxicity models

Experimental approaches are often costly and time-consuming, which can delay the research process and the timely availability of results. Toxicity prediction tools allow rapid access to essential data on the adverse effects of chemicals which are exposed to both the environment and human health. Although numerous experimental methods are currently available for toxicity assessment, they are not universally applicable across all species and may fail to accurately capture environmental and health-related risks (Cunningham et al. [2010](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11356-025-37354-8#ref-CR42 "Cunningham FM, Elliott J, Lees P (2010) Comparative and veterinary pharmacology. Springer, Heidelberg")). Due to these limitations, we are moving towards computational and AI-based approaches that are increasingly enhancing the efficiency and accuracy of toxicity prediction.

Fish toxicity: Like humans and other animal species, fish have been reported to accumulate a wide range of chemicals, including pesticides such as Propoxur, Deltamethrin, Atrazine, and Furadan, as well as food additives, and various other pollutants or contaminants. Exposure to these chemicals can result in toxicity leading to the mortality of aquatic organisms such as fathead minnow (Pimephales promelas), water flea (Daphnia magna), and Tetrahymena (Tetrahymena pyriformis) (Dong and Moon[2025](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11356-025-37354-8#ref-CR50 "Dong B, Moon HB (2025) Toxicological effects of chemical pesticides in fish: focusing on intestinal injury and gut microbial dysbiosis. Pestic Biochem Physiol 211:106405. 
                https://doi.org/10.1016/j.pestbp.2025.106405
                
              "); Ogeleka et al. [2016](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11356-025-37354-8#ref-CR136 "Ogeleka DF, Ogbomida ET, Tongo I, Enuneku AA, Ikpesu TO, Ezemonye LIN (2016) Impacts of acute exposure of industrial chemicals and pesticides on the survival of fish (Tilapia guineensis) and earthworms (Aporrectodea longa). J Xenobiotics 6:5660. 
                https://doi.org/10.4081/xeno.2016.5660
                
              ")). A machine learning model, MS2Tox, predicts fish toxicity (LC50) from high-resolution tandem mass spectra without requiring full chemical identification. Trained on a dataset of 647 LC50 values from the CompTox database and validated on 219 chemicals with 420 spectra from the Mass Bank, the model achieved a low prediction error and accurately estimated LC50 values for multiple chemicals in water samples. MS2Tox outperformed simpler mass-based models, providing a fast method to identify potentially toxic compounds in water samples (Peets et al., [2022](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11356-025-37354-8#ref-CR146 "Peets P, Wang W-C, MacLeod M, Breitholtz M, Martin JW, Kruve A (2022) MS2tox machine learning tool for predicting the ecotoxicity of unidentified chemicals in water by nontarget LC-HRMS. Environ Sci Technol 56:15508–15517. 
                https://doi.org/10.1021/acs.est.2c02536
                
              ")). According to OECD TG 203, the acute toxicity of a substance can be evaluated by observing its lethal effects on juvenile fish over a 96-h exposure period, as updated in the 2019 version of the guideline.

Rat toxicity: The toxicity of chemicals varies based on the structure, mechanism of action, dosage and mortality. For instance, chemical agents like yellow phosphorus have high mortality for rodents (Jayakaran and Abhilash [2019](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11356-025-37354-8#ref-CR92 "Jayakaran JJ, Abhilash KP (2019) Rodenticide poisoning: literature review and management. Curr Med Issues 17:129. 
                https://doi.org/10.4103/cmi.cmi_54_19
                
              ")). A web-based computational framework, PredAOT, is designed to predict the acute oral toxicity (AOT) of compounds in mice and rats. The tool initially classifies compounds as ‘toxic’ or ‘less/non-toxic’ and subsequently estimates their LD₅₀ values using a regression model. This tool was developed using acute oral toxicity (AOT) data from 6,226 compounds in mice and 6238 compounds in rats. A key strength of PredAOT lies in its ability to predict AOT for both species concurrently, with predictive performance comparable to or exceeding that of current state-of-the-art tools (Ryu et al. [2023](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11356-025-37354-8#ref-CR168 "Ryu JY, Jang WD, Jang J, Oh KS (2023) PredAOT: a computational framework for prediction of acute oral toxicity based on multiple random forest models. BMC Bioinformatics 24:51. 
                https://doi.org/10.1186/s12859-023-05176-5
                
              ")). According to OECD TG 452 specifies that chronic toxicity testing can be performed via oral, dermal, or inhalation routes.

3.   c)
Organ toxicity models

The potential toxicological effects on organs such as neurotoxicity, pulmonotoxicity, hepatotoxicity, dermal toxicity, enterotoxicity, immunotoxicity, cytotoxicity, genotoxicity, ocular toxicity, endocrine toxicity, cardiotoxicity, renal toxicity, reproductive toxicity, myotoxicity, and osteotoxicity (Fig.[3](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11356-025-37354-8#Fig3)). These can be predicted using computational toxicity prediction models that emphasise on evaluating toxicity in multiple biological systems for comprehensive risk assessment.

### Neurotoxicity

Chemicals capable of disrupting the mammalian nervous system may be synthetically produced and referred to as neurotoxicants. Neurotoxicity typically refers only when concentrations in neural tissue exceed a specific threshold. In addition to biological sources, numerous environmental pollutants, such as industrial chemicals, e.g. toluene, are proven contributors to neurodevelopmental disorders like autism, ADHD, intellectual disability, and cerebral palsy (Grandjean and Landrigan [2006](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11356-025-37354-8#ref-CR68 "Grandjean P, Landrigan P (2006) Developmental neurotoxicity of industrial chemicals. Lancet 368:2167–2178. 
                https://doi.org/10.1016/s0140-6736(06)69665-7
                
              "); Soleimani et al. [2016](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11356-025-37354-8#ref-CR188 "Soleimani SMA, Ekhtiari H, Cadet JL (2016) Drug-induced neurotoxicity in addiction medicine. Prog Brain Res 223:19–41. 
                https://doi.org/10.1016/bs.pbr.2015.07.004
                
              "); Spencer and Lein [2014](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11356-025-37354-8#ref-CR190 "Spencer PS, Lein PJ (2014) Neurotoxicity. In: Encyclopedia of Toxicology, 3rd edn. Elsevier, pp 489–500. 
                https://doi.org/10.1016/B978-0-12-386454-3.00169-X
                
              ")). NeuTox 2.0 is a multimodal feature fusion model that integrates data on blood–brain barrier permeability, neuronal cytotoxicity, neural activity, and mammalian neurotoxicity to predict neurotoxic compounds. By combining molecular features with fine-tuned, self-supervised learning, it outperforms baseline models, particularly on small datasets. This transfer learning-based framework enhances high-throughput virtual screening and offers a more comprehensive approach to neurotoxicity prediction, addressing data limitations in environmental toxicity assessment (Pang et al. [2025](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11356-025-37354-8#ref-CR142 "Pang X, He X, Yang Y, Wang L, Sun Y, Cao H, Liang Y (2025) Neutox 2.0: a hybrid deep learning architecture for screening potential neurotoxicity of chemicals based on multimodal feature fusion. Environ Int 195:109244. 
                https://doi.org/10.1016/j.envint.2024.1092444
                
              ")). For more information on neurotoxicity, refer to the EPA, which first introduced its developmental neurotoxicity (DNT) testing guideline (83-6) in 1991 to assess the potential neurotoxic effects of certain chemicals and pesticides. Following the establishment of the Food Quality Protection Act in 1996, which aimed to enhance the protection of children’s health, the demand for DNT studies increased significantly, particularly for pesticide evaluation. In response, the EPA updated and revised its DNT guideline in 1998 (OPTS 870.6300). Later, in 2007, OECD adopted its own DNT testing guideline (TG 426), incorporating further methodological improvements (Tsuji and Crofton [2012](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11356-025-37354-8#ref-CR200 "Tsuji R, Crofton KM (2012) Developmental neurotoxicity guideline study: issues with methodology, evaluation and regulation. Birth Defects Res B Dev Reprod Toxicol 95:1–9. 
                https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1741-4520.2012.00374.x
                
              ")).

### Dermal toxicity

The skin plays a vital protective role against harmful toxic chemicals, including reactive oxidants and free radicals (carbon monoxide, reactive nitrogen species, and electrophilic aldehydes), which cause oxidative stress, weaken antioxidant defences, and trigger skin tissue damage. These chemicals also increase skin water loss, degrade connective tissue, and activate enzymes that break down collagen and elastic fibres (Kathuria et al. [2017](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11356-025-37354-8#ref-CR102 "Kathuria S, Puri P, Nandar S, Ramesh V (2017) Effects of air pollution on the skin: a review. Indian J Dermatol Venereol Leprol 83:415. 
                https://doi.org/10.4103/0378-6323.199579
                
              "); Li Pomi et al. [2025](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11356-025-37354-8#ref-CR111 "Li Pomi F, Gammeri L, Borgia F, Di Gioacchino M, Gangemi S (2025) Oxidative stress and skin diseases: the role of lipid peroxidation. Antioxidants 14(5):555. 
                https://doi.org/10.3390/antiox14050555
                
              ")). A novel web-based prediction model, Pred-Skin (3.0 version), for rapidly and accurately predicting skin sensitisation potential using rigorously validated QSAR models built on human, murine, and non-animal data. It provides binary predictions for skin sensitisation, Bayesian consensus results for human effects, and probability maps showing the contribution of chemical fragments. Notably, it is the first tool to incorporate human data and multiclass predictions for LLNA assays, achieving up to 89% accuracy in predicting human responses (Borba et al. [2021](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11356-025-37354-8#ref-CR29 "Borba JVB, Braga RC, Alves VM, Muratov EN, Kleinstreuer N, Tropsha A, Andrade CH (2021) Pred-Skin: a web portal for accurate prediction of human skin sensitizers. Chem Res Toxicol 34:258–267. 
                https://doi.org/10.1021/acs.chemrestox.0c00186
                
              ")). The user-friendly platform requires no programming skills and is freely accessible at [https://github.com/rcbraga/pred-skin](https://github.com/rcbraga/pred-skin). According to the OECD Guidelines, dermal toxicity assessment is primarily conducted through Test No. 402 for acute dermal toxicity and Test No. 404 for acute dermal irritation.

### Ocular toxicity

The ocular surface, comprising the cornea, limbus, conjunctiva, and tear film, is highly vulnerable to environmental hazards such as pesticides, chemicals, and pollutants. Exposure can cause irritation and damage, including edema, inflammation, and epithelial degradation, while severe or prolonged exposure may lead to chronic conditions like dry eye disease, corneal ulcers, cataracts, glaucoma, or permanent vision loss (Rauchman et al. [2023](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11356-025-37354-8#ref-CR157 "Rauchman SH, Locke B, Albert J, De Leon J, Peltier MR, Reiss AB (2023) Toxic external exposure leading to ocular surface injury. Vision 7:32. 
                https://doi.org/10.3390/vision7020032
                
              "))**.** StopTox is a freely accessible web portal that offers computational models as an alternative to in vivo 6-pack tests for predicting chemical toxicity hazards. It has been developed using OECD-compliant QSAR modelling practices and the largest publicly curated datasets for all 6‑pack assays, enabling accurate and transparent predictions across all endpoints, including eye and skin. While limited in predicting potency classes, the models are reliable for early-stage applications, such as drug discovery. STopTox ([https://stoptox.mml.unc.edu/](https://stoptox.mml.unc.edu/)) stands out for its extensive data curation, validated statistical accuracy, and public availability, making it a valuable tool for regulators and industries to screen chemicals inexpensively and efficiently (Borba et al. [2022](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11356-025-37354-8#ref-CR30 "Borba JVB, Alves VM, Braga RC, Korn DR, Overdahl K, Silva AC, Hall SUS, Overdahl E, Kleinstreuer N, Strickland J, Allen D, Andrade CH, Muratov EN, Tropsha A (2022) STopTox: an in silico alternative to animal testing for acute systemic and topical toxicity. Environ Health Perspect 130:027012. 
                https://doi.org/10.1289/EHP9341
                
              ")). For more information on ocular toxicity, refer to OECD, Test No. 405: Acute Eye Irritation/Corrosion.

### Renal toxicity

Renal toxicity is rapid decline in kidney function caused by the toxic effects of drugs or chemicals. It can occur through various mechanisms, including tubular toxicity, inflammation, glomerular damage, crystal nephropathy, and thrombotic microangiopathy (Al-Kuraishy et al. [2019](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11356-025-37354-8#ref-CR9 "Al-Kuraishy H, Al-Naimi M, Rasheed H, Hussien N, Al-Gareeb A (2019) Nephrotoxicity: role and significance of renal biomarkers in the early detection of acute renal injury. J Adv Pharm Technol Res 10:95.

              ")). CORAL software ([http://www.insilico.eu/coral](http://www.insilico.eu/coral)) offers an alternative approach to computational modelling for toxicity prediction. args.summary:
This is an open-access review article titled "AI/ML-based computational models for toxicity prediction," published on January 12, 2026, in the journal Environmental Science and Pollution Research. The authors are Sushmita Barua, Badhrinarayanan Balaji, and Seetharaman Balaji. The article has 11 citations and 8029 accesses.

**Purpose:** The review addresses toxicity prediction and chemical safety evaluation, focusing on computational models, data coverage, molecular descriptors, QSAR models, AI/ML-based approaches, explainable AI, predictive methodologies, regulatory relevance, and accessibility. The goal is to enable identification, prediction, and analysis of chemical toxicity across various biological endpoints while minimizing or eliminating animal testing.

**Key Statistics and Facts:**
- Approximately 25% of global mortality is linked to harmful chemicals
- In 2022, global agricultural pesticide consumption totaled 3.70 million tons; Asia exported 3.5 million tons valued at approximately USD 21.7 billion
- An estimated 385 million cases of unintentional acute pesticide poisoning occur globally each year, leading to approximately 11,000 deaths
- Nearly 44% of the 860 million global agricultural workforce farmers are affected by pesticide poisoning annually
- In developing nations, contaminated food causes almost 20,000 deaths per year
- According to WHO, approximately one million individuals are affected annually by acute pesticide poisoning, with mortality rates between 0.4% and 1.9%, and occupational exposure accounting for nearly 70% of deaths

**Chemical Examples Discussed:** Azodicarbonamide (ADA), bisphenol A (BPA), phthalates (dibutyl phthalate, diethyl phthalate), and pesticides such as malathion, chlorpyrifos, and bromoxynil are highlighted as substances with concerning toxicological profiles and regulatory inconsistencies across jurisdictions.

**Databases and Datasets:** Key toxicological databases include Tox21, ToxCast, PubChem, DSSTox, and REACH. The U.S. EPA lists several CompTox online resources including the ECOTOX Knowledgebase, ChemExpo Knowledgebase, CompTox Chemicals Dashboard (over one million chemicals), GenRA tool, and SeqAPASS tool. The article emphasizes FAIR (Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, Reusable) principles and highlights ethical concerns including transparency, data privacy, algorithmic bias, and accessibility.

**Computational Models Covered:**
1. **Ecotoxicity models** - including an autoencoder model for predicting HC50 values; AquaticTox web platform predicting toxicity across five aquatic species; QSAR models for algal toxicity using PLS regression with 2-D descriptors (ETA and non-ETA)
2. **Animal toxicity models** - MS2Tox machine learning model predicts fish toxicity (LC50) from mass spectra (trained on 647 LC50 values, validated on 219 chemicals with 420 spectra); PredAOT web tool predicts acute oral toxicity in mice (6,226 compounds) and rats (6,238 compounds)
3. **Organ toxicity models** - covering neurotoxicity (NeuTox 2.0 multimodal model), dermal toxicity (Pred-Skin 3.0 tool achieving up to 89% accuracy), ocular toxicity (STopTox web portal), and renal toxicity (CORAL software using SMILES representation)

**Regulatory Context:** Regulatory agencies including FDA, EMA, and OECD have established guidelines for chemical safety evaluation. Regulatory limitations vary significantly among countries, showing a marked absence of convergence. Regulatory adaptability is deemed key as AI evolves rapidly. The promotion of AI/ML tool integration and interoperable frameworks could substantially enhance the future of predictive toxicology. The WHO classification system categorizes chemicals as extremely hazardous (class I-a), highly hazardous (class I-b), moderately hazardous (class II), and slightly hazardous (class III).

**Regulatory Guidelines Referenced:** EPA's DNT testing guideline (83-6, 1991; revised to OPTS 870.6300 in 1998), OECD TG 426 (DNT, 2007), OECD Test Guideline 201 for algae, OECD TG 203 for fish acute toxicity (96-hour exposure), OECD TG 452 for chronic toxicity, Test No. 402 (acute dermal), Test No. 404 (acute dermal irritation), and Test No. 405 (acute eye irritation/corrosion).

The market is rapidly expanding due to the increasing demand for cost-effective and ethically conducted methods over traditional animal testing, along with the advancement in machine learning.

## Marke Overview

[Artificial Intelligence](../artificial-intelligence-market) (AI) in predictive toxicology refers to the application of [machine learning](../machine-learning-market), [deep learning](../deep-learning-market), and computational modeling techniques to predict the toxicological effects of chemicals, drugs, and biological compounds before clinical testing. These AI-driven systems analyze large biological datasets, molecular structures, and historical toxicity data to identify potential safety risks early in the drug discovery process. This technology reduces reliance on animal testing, accelerates [pharmaceutical](https://www.towardshealthcare.com/insights/pharmaceutical-market-sizing) R&D, improves regulatory compliance, and helps pharmaceutical, [biotechnology](../biotechnology-market), and chemical companies minimize costly late-stage drug development failures.

## AI in Predictive Toxicology Market Trends

* There is a growing focus on reducing reliance on traditional animal testing, which is driving the shift toward AI-driven predictive toxicology, enabling faster, more ethical drug development.
* Deep learning models are increasingly applied to analyze heterogeneous data such as omics datasets and chemical structures, achieving high accuracy (around 90%) in toxicity prediction, including mutagenicity detection.
* The integration of big data and multi-omics ([genomics](../genomics-market), [proteomics](../proteomics-market), [metabolomics](../metabolomics-market)) is enabling AI systems to identify potential adverse drug reactions at earlier stages of drug development.
* Regulatory support, including initiatives like the FDA Modernization Act 2.0, is encouraging AI-based non-animal toxicology methods, further accelerating market growth.
* AI is increasingly combined with [3D cell cultures](../3d-cell-culture-market), organoids, and other human-relevant biological models to improve the accuracy and validation of toxicity predictions.

### **Technology Insights**

**Why Did the Classical Machine Learning Segment Dominate the AI in Predictive Toxicology Market?**

The classical machine learning segment dominated the market with a major share of 38% in 2025 due to its offerings like high efficiency with structured chemical data, excellent interpretability, and less data requirement than deep learning. Also, classical ML is highly beneficial for analyzing chemical structures and numerical datasets found in toxicology. Additionally, widely used quantitative structure-activity relationship (QSAR) models in the chemical and pharmaceutical industries rely heavily on machine learning, further supporting the segment's market dominance.

Deep learning enables in-silico toxicity simulations, reducing reliance on costly and time-consuming animal studies. Additionally, these algorithms can automatically learn toxicological patterns from raw data, improving predictive performance and accelerating drug safety assessment.

### **Toxicity Endpoint Insights**

**What Made Systemic Toxicity the Dominant Segment in the AI in Predictive Toxicology Market?**

The systemic toxicity segment dominated the market with 34% share in 2025, driven by the growing need to evaluate the effects of compounds across multiple organ systems early in drug development, which helps reduce late-stage clinical failures and associated costs. AI-driven and in-silico toxicity models are increasingly being adopted to support systemic toxicity assessments while aligning with the 3R principles, namely Replacement, Reduction, and Refinement, to minimize animal testing. Additionally, regulatory agencies such as the U.S. Food and Drug Administration and the European Medicines Agency require comprehensive systemic toxicity data, further supporting the adoption of AI-based predictive tools.

![AI in Predictive Toxicology Market Share, By Toxicity Endpoint, 2025 (%)](https://www.precedenceresearch.com/insightimg/ai-in-predictive-toxicology-market-share-by-toxicity-endpoint.webp "AI in Predictive Toxicology Market Share, By Toxicity Endpoint, 2025 (%)")

Increasing pressure from regulatory and public bodies to reduce animal testing is accelerating the use of AI-based predictive approaches. Moreover, while traditional in vitro genotoxicity tests often generate false-positive results, AI-driven models can reduce these errors by up to 70%, improving the reliability of toxicity predictions at the early stages of testing.

**Why Did the On-Premise Platforms Segment Lead the AI in Predictive Toxicology Market?**

The on-premise platforms segment led the market with the largest share of 56% in 2025, driven by the need for full control over intellectual property and protection of sensitive compound data under strict regulatory requirements. Many companies prefer keeping AI models and training data within internal firewalls rather than using cloud services to minimize the risk of data leakage. Additionally, pharmaceutical R&D often relies on legacy IT infrastructure, making on-premise AI platforms easier to integrate with existing in-house databases and systems.

The cloud-based platforms segment is expected to grow at the fastest CAGR during the foreseeable period, as they offer excellent scalability and collaborative infrastructure required to manage and analyze huge datasets like large-scale screening libraries. Training advanced deep learning models requires significant computational power, which cloud platforms can provide efficiently. In addition, cloud environments enable the centralized integration of diverse data types, including omics data, chemical structures, and electronic health records, improving the accuracy and efficiency of predictive toxicology analysis.

--- SOURCE 1: Computational toxicology in drug discovery: applications of artificial intelligence in ADMET and toxicity prediction ---
URL: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12499773

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a scientific review article published in Briefings in Bioinformatics (2025 Oct 06;26(5):bbaf533, doi: 10.1093/bib/bbaf533, PMCID: PMC12499773, PMID: 41052279) titled "Computational toxicology in drug discovery: applications of artificial intelligence in ADMET and toxicity prediction." Authors: Jiangyan Zhang, Haolin Li, Yuncong Zhang (contributed equally), Junyang Huang, Liping Ren, Chuantao Zhang, Quan Zou, and Yang Zhang. Corresponding authors are from the Hospital of Chengdu University of Traditional Chinese Medicine and the University of Electronic Science and Technology of China. The article is Open Access under a Creative Commons Attribution Non-Commercial License.

Key content and findings:
- Toxicity risk assessment is crucial for clinical success and market potential of drug candidates; ~30% of preclinical candidate compounds (PCCs) fail due to toxicity, and ~40% of preclinical candidate drugs fail due to insufficient ADMET profiles, while nearly 30% of marketed drugs are withdrawn due to unforeseen toxic reactions.
- Traditional animal testing is costly, time-consuming (6–24 months per test), expensive (often exceeding millions of dollars per compound), and ethically controversial (3Rs principle: replacement, reduction, refinement), driving the shift to computational toxicology.
- The review surveys over 20 ADMET prediction platforms, categorized into three types: rule/statistical-based methods, machine learning (ML) methods, and graph-based methods.
- Broad-spectrum platforms mentioned: admetSAR 3.0, ADMETlab 3.0, vNN-ADMET, ADMETboost, Deep-PK; pharmacokinetic-focused platforms: Swiss ADME, FAF-Drugs4.0, ADMET-AI; toxicity-focused platforms: ProTox 3.0, VenomPred 2.0; CYP450-related tools: CypRules, BioTransformer 3.0, XenoSite, SOMP, SMARTCyp 3.0.
- The ADMET prediction platform framework consists of: input component (chemical structural data, experimental data, literature-derived data), tools/methods component (physicochemical property calculation via RDKit/Scopy, and ML/AI prediction module using SVMs, RFs, neural networks, gradient boosting trees), and output component (endpoints; comprehensive platforms can evaluate over 100 endpoints).
- ML methods (e.g., vNN-ADMET, ADMETboost with XGBoost, ProTox 3.0 with RF/DNN) handle complex patterns but depend on high-quality training data. Graph-based methods (GNNs: ADMET-AI, Interpretable-ADMET, HelixADMET, ADMETlab 3.0 with DMPNN, admetSAR 3.0, pkCSM) analyze molecular graph structures but require substantial computational resources and large training datasets.
- Toxicological databases are classified into four categories: chemical toxicity databases, environmental toxicology databases, alternative toxicology databases, and biological toxin databases.
- Chemical toxicity databases include PubChem (>119 million compounds, NIH-maintained), ChEMBL (>2.1 million, EMBL-EBI), HSDB (~5600 chemicals), CCRIS (>9000, carcinogenicity/mutagenicity), CompTox Chemicals Dashboard (EPA), TOXRIC (113,372 compounds, ML-ready), SuperToxic (~60,000), DrugBank, and specialized databases DILIrank, DILIst, LTKB (hepatotoxicity), hERGCentral (cardiotoxicity), and LCDB (carcinogenicity data from 1726 chemicals and 7745 experimental records).
- The field is transitioning from single-endpoint predictions to multi-endpoint joint modeling with multimodal features, incorporating generative modeling and interpretability frameworks.
- Network toxicology is applied to evaluate safety of traditional Chinese medicines (TCMs), and large language models (LLMs) show potential in literature mining, knowledge integration, and molecular toxicity prediction.
- Current challenges include data quality, model interpretability, and causal inference; future directions include multi-omics integration, interpretable AI models, and domain-specific LLMs for more efficient and precise preclinical toxicity assessments.
</summary>

--- SOURCE 2: LLM Benchmarks in Life Sciences: Comprehensive Overview | IntuitionLabs ---
URL: https://intuitionlabs.ai/articles/large-language-model-benchmarks-life-sciences-overview

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This IntuitionLabs report (updated July 21, 2026) provides a comprehensive survey of large language model (LLM) benchmarks in life sciences, covering biomedical NLP, question-answering, drug discovery, and genomics, with industry use cases and state-of-the-art model performance from 2020-2026.

**Biomedical Language Understanding:** Two foundational benchmark suites are covered. The BLUE Benchmark (2019, NCBI) is a domain-specific GLUE analogue with five task types across ten datasets (sentence similarity, NER, relation extraction, document classification, NLI), where BlueBERT achieved leading scores. The BLURB Benchmark (2020, Microsoft Research) aggregates 13 datasets across 6 task categories and uses macro-average scores; BioALBERT (large, PubMed-trained) set new SOTA on 5 of 6 task types by 2022, improving NER by +11.1% and QA by +2.8%, with NER F1 scores often exceeding 85% for top models.

**Biomedical Question-Answering:** 
- BioASQ (2013-present): Annual NLM-sponsored challenge; top systems exceed 80% accuracy on yes/no questions; BioASQ 2025 (13th edition) had 83 teams with new tasks (MultiClinSum, BioNNE-L, ELCardioCC, GutBrainIE); 14th edition scheduled for CLEF 2026 in Jena, Germany.
- PubMedQA (2019): ~1,000 question-answer pairs; fine-tuned PMC-LLaMA 13B achieved 77.9% accuracy; GPT-4 zero-shot reaches ~75%.
- MedQA (USMLE): GPT-4 zero-shot scored ~71.6%; Med-Gemini achieved 91.1% using uncertainty-guided search; GPT-5 reached 95.84% (95.22% average across all USMLE steps). Re-annotation revealed 7.4% of questions deemed unfit due to missing info or ambiguous answers.

**Drug Discovery and Molecular Benchmarks:**
- MoleculeNet (2018): Molecular property prediction suite; message-passing neural networks reached ~0.85-0.90 AUC on toxicity tasks.
- Therapeutics Data Commons (TDC, 2021): Standardizes 50+ datasets with leaderboards.
- GuacaMol (2018) and MOSES (2019): De novo molecule generation; top models achieve >95% validity.
- TOMG-Bench (2024): First text-based open molecule generation benchmark across three tasks (editing, optimization, generation); fine-tuned Llama3.1-8B surpassed GPT-3.5 by 46.5% on OpenMolIns.
- Bioinformatics benchmarks: Bioinfo-Bench (GPT-4 >80% on MCQs but struggled on coding), BioCoder (1,000+ coding problems), BioinformaticsBench (602 questions across 9 sub-domains), and DNA Long Bench/Genomics LRB (long DNA sequences up to 1 million base pairs).

**Key Trends and 2025-2026 Developments:**
- Split between tasks: domain-specific fine-tuned models still lead on information extraction, while large general models (GPT-4/5, Med-Gemini) excel at reasoning-heavy QA.
- PubMedBERT reached 82.91 BLURB score and 2.5M monthly downloads by 2025.

Key findings for RQ1 (ADR detection and classification): The best models achieved only 75.38 F1 in detection and 76.69 F1 in multiclass classification. All models exhibited "risk-averse" behavior with false-positive rates over 70%, struggling to distinguish nuanced ADR types (GPT-4 Turbo misclassified 51% of non-dose-related and 50% of time-related ADRs). Claude 3 Opus achieved the highest zero-shot detection accuracy at 77.41%, while Llama 3.1-405B performed best in few-shot classification (F1 76.69).

For RQ2 (expert-LLM response alignment): LLM responses were significantly harder to read than expert responses (higher SMOG scores vs. 12.44 for experts). There was no significant difference in emotional/tone alignment, though experts showed higher anticipation, affection, and helping tones while LLMs used more optimistic, polite, and trust-based tones. The best model (OpenBioLLM-70B) achieved only 70.86% alignment with expert harm-reduction strategies, and LLMs provided 12.32% less actionable advice on average. Notably, expert responses scored higher on practicality (0.83) and contextual relevance (0.73) but lower on specificity (0.17) and clarity (0.13), while LLMs showed the opposite pattern.

The authors emphasize the importance of "lived experience"—first-hand knowledge possessed by clinicians—which LLMs lack, and caution against increasing human-like features (anthropomorphism) in LLMs due to risks of over-trust in high-risk healthcare domains. Instead, they advocate for fine-tuning on specialized data. The study was funded by NSF grant #2230692 and grants from AFSP, JPMorgan AI Research, and Microsoft's AFMR program. The benchmark and code are available at https://github.com/mohit3011/Lived-Experience-Not-Found.
</summary>

"LLMs struggle with understanding the nuances of ADRs and differentiating between types of ADRs. While LLMs align with experts in terms of expressed emotions and tone of the text, their responses are more complex, harder to read, and only 70.86% aligned with expert strategies. Furthermore, they provide less actionable advice by a margin of 12.32% on average."

SUMMARY:

This is a scientific research paper published in Results in Engineering (Volume 28, December 2025, article 107362) titled "Benchmarking large language models for adverse drug reaction extraction in social media and clinical texts" by Oumayma Elbiach, Hanane Grissette, and El Habib Nfaoui. The paper is open access under a Creative Commons license.

**Purpose:** The study systematically evaluates state-of-the-art open- and closed-source Large Language Models (LLMs) for Adverse Drug Reaction (ADR) extraction, addressing challenges of ambiguity, under-reporting, and noisy biomedical or social media texts in pharmacovigilance.

**Methodology:** The researchers benchmarked GPT-3.5-turbo, GPT-4o-mini, Microsoft Phi-3-mini, LLaMA-3.2-1B, DeepSeek, and BioMistral-7B using two complementary approaches: fine-tuning and in-context learning (zero-shot, one-shot, and few-shot). - Results demonstrate progress but highlight challenges in handling noisy real-world texts.

**Conclusions:** While LLMs hold significant promise for enhancing ADR extraction, they still face challenges in capturing the complexity and variability of real-world ADR expressions. Further model adaptations and domain-specific refinements are required to improve effectiveness in pharmacovigilance applications. SUMMARY:
<summary>
This article from BioPharm International (published March 4, 2026) by Partha Anbil and Niraj B. Patel examines how artificial intelligence (AI), particularly large language models (LLMs) and natural language processing (NLP), is transforming drug safety surveillance. The FDA manages a database of over 140,000 drug labeling documents, and with 82% of American adults taking at least one medication, the scale of data necessitates automated solutions.

Key domain-specific AI models highlighted include:
- PharmBERT: A BERT-based model pre-trained on drug labeling documents achieving 89% accuracy in identifying adverse events.
- RxBERT: Developed by FDA's National Center for Toxicological Research, trained on 44,990 human prescription drug labeling documents, achieving 86.5 F1-score in adverse event classification.
- AskFDALabel: Combines retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) with locally hosted LLMs, achieving F1-scores of 0.978 for drug-induced liver injury and 0.931 for drug-induced cardiotoxicity classification.

Reported performance demonstrates 91.1% accuracy in adverse event extraction, 99.4% accuracy in DILI risk identification, and 99.5% accuracy for cardiotoxicity classification. Tasks that once took two to three weeks can now be completed in hours across all 140,000+ labels.

Security concerns drive locally hosted solutions; AskFDALabel runs on in-house GPU servers using open-source models like Llama 3.1-70B, keeping data within FDA systems. One FDA implementation reviewed 211 drugs for DILI risk in approximately 15 minutes versus 40-60 hours manually.

Limitations include context dependency, class imbalance making rare events hard to detect, explainability challenges with "black box" models, cost/computational requirements (230+ computing hours for pre-training), and the need for rigorous validation. Best practices include starting with pilot projects, establishing baselines, maintaining human oversight, and using domain-specific training data since generic LLMs significantly underperform.

Future directions include integrating multiple data sources (electronic health records, clinical trial data, literature, real-time pharmacovigilance data), addressing causality determination (Columbia University researchers are developing such methods), and proactive signal detection.

--- SOURCE 14: JMIR Medical Informatics - Predicting Drug–Side Effect Relationships From Parametric Knowledge Embedded in Biomedical BERT Models: Methodological Study With a Natural Language Processing Approach ---
URL: https://medinform.jmir.org/2025/1/e67513

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This paper, published in JMIR Medical Informatics (Vol 13, 2025; doi:10.2196/67513), presents a methodological study on predicting drug–side effect relationships using parametric knowledge embedded in biomedical BERT language models. 

**Background/Objectiive:** Adverse drug reactions (ADRs) pose serious public health risks, with approximately 2 million serious ADRs and 100,000 deaths reported annually in the US. Traditional context-independent word embedding models like Word2Vec have limitations in capturing biomedical domain specificity. The study proposes using BERT-based models pretrained on biomedical corpora to extract parametric knowledge and predict unknown drug–side effect relationships.

**Methods:** The study used 158,096 known drug–side effect pairs from the SIDER database (version 4.1) to build an adjacency matrix with 1,345 drugs and 6,123 side effects. Cosine similarity was calculated between word embedding vectors of drugs and side effects. Relation scores (combining drug-similarity and side-effect-similarity components using equations) were calculated for 8,235,435 total drug–side effect pairs. For Word2Vec training, 14,289,160 sentences mentioning drugs and 32,107,327 sentences mentioning side effects were extracted from PubMed (42,515,246 total abstracts, updated December 8, 2022).

**Results:** The clagator/biobert_v1.1 model achieved the highest AUC of 0.915 at an optimal threshold of 0.289 (sensitivity 0.870, specificity 0.830), outperforming Word2Vec (AUC 0.848) and vanilla BERT (bert-base-uncased, AUC 0.857). Other models tested included BiomedBERT (0.907), dmis-lab/biobert_v1.1 (0.901), and PharmBERT-uncased (0.882). All BERT models pretrained on biomedical corpora outperformed vanilla BERT. The cosine similarity-based extraction method outperformed Euclidean distance, Manhattan distance, Jaccard similarity, and dot product methods. The dual-similarity approach (relation score, AUC 0.915) significantly outperformed single-similarity methods (drug-only: 0.799, side-effect-only: 0.881).

**Validation:** External validation with FAERS data (October 2012–June 2023; 901,361 known relationships) confirmed high statistical significance (P<.001) with an odds ratio of 4.822 (Fisher exact test repeated 2,000 times). Case studies of top-ranked predictions not in SIDER (lenalidomide-arthropathy, rosuvastatin-sleep disturbance, gadolinium-acute pulmonary edema, cefazolin-hepatic failure) were confirmed as reported in literature published after 2016.

**Conclusions:** BERT-based models pretrained on biomedical corpora significantly outperform Word2Vec in predicting drug–side effect relationships due to contextual information capture. The methodology demonstrates practical applicability for pharmacovigilance and ADR prediction. Limitations include the SIDER database being last updated in 2015, challenges with non-dose-dependent reactions, case report generalizability issues, prediction limitations for novel drug candidates, and lack of patient-specific idiosyncratic reaction modeling. The research was supported by the Korea Health Technology R&D Project (grant RS-2022-KH125153).
</summary>

SUMMARY:

**Background & Technology:** Drug discovery traditionally takes over a decade and costs billions, with only ~10% chance of approval for candidates entering trials. The AlphaFold revolution began with AlphaFold 2 (2020) solving the protein folding problem (earning the 2024 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for John Jumper and Demis Hassabis). AlphaFold 3 (released May 2024, a joint DeepMind/Isomorphic effort) extended predictions to molecular interactions with proteins, DNA, RNA, and ligands, achieving "at least a 50% improvement" and in some cases doubling prediction accuracy. Isomorphic Labs was founded in 2021 in London by DeepMind veterans including CEO Sir Demis Hassabis and President Colin Murdoch, with the mission to "solve all disease" using AI.

**Funding & Partnerships:** In March 2025, Isomorphic raised a $600M funding round led by Thrive Capital (with GV and Alphabet). **Technology - IsoDDE:** Isomorphic built a proprietary AI drug design engine ("IsoDDE") integrating AlphaFold models with generative chemistry models. A February 2026 technical report showcased extremely precise predictions of protein-drug interactions and antibody structures. Columbia computational biologist Mohammed AlQuraishi called it "a major advance, on the scale of an AlphaFold 4."

**Pipeline:** Isomorphic's internal candidates focus on oncology (cancer) and immunology. Public reports hint at TIM-3 (an immune checkpoint) as a target. The company plans to license its drugs out after early-stage trials.

**Clinical Trials Timeline:** In July 2025, President Colin Murdoch said human trials of AI-designed drugs were "finally in sight" with the company "staffing up" to begin dosing patients. The Indian Express (July 9, 2025) reported the oncology drug created using AlphaFold 3 was set to enter human trials. SUMMARY:
<summary>
On February 10, 2026, Isomorphic Labs announced a significant advancement in AI-powered drug design with the introduction of the Isomorphic Labs Drug Design Engine (IsoDDE), a unified computational drug-design system that moves beyond AlphaFold 3 (AF3), which was released in 2024 in partnership with Google DeepMind. Key capabilities and results highlighted include:

The company demonstrated this by recapitulating the discovery of a novel cryptic allosteric site on cereblon (recently found experimentally by Dippon et al. 2026, published in Nature), predicting both the known thalidomide-binding pocket and the novel cryptic site from sequence alone.

--- SOURCE 6: Multimodal Clinical Trial Outcome Prediction with Large Language Models ---
URL: https://arxiv.org/html/2402.06512v3

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This paper presents LIFTED (muLti-modal mIx-of-experts For ouTcome prEDiction), a novel deep learning approach for clinical trial outcome prediction that addresses limitations of prior methods that rely on manually designed modal-specific encoders. LIFTED unifies multimodal data (disease, drug name, drug description, SMILES string, and eligibility criteria) by transforming them into natural language descriptions using Large Language Models (LLMs), then processes them through unified transformer-based encoders. Key innovations include: (1) a Sparse Mixture-of-Experts (SMoE) framework that dynamically routes representations from different modalities to shared experts, identifying similar information patterns across modalities; (2) representation augmentation with a consistency loss to make encoders noise-resilient; and (3) a Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) integration module that dynamically weighs modality importance for each trial, using only disease information to generate weights. An auxiliary unimodal prediction loss is also introduced to improve representation quality.

The method was evaluated on the HINT benchmark dataset (17,538 clinical trial records across Phases I, II, and III). LIFTED outperformed all baselines including HINT and SPOT across all three trial phases. Key results for PR-AUC were 70.7 (Phase I), 69.8 (Phase II), and 88.3 (Phase III); F1 scores were 71.6, 66.2, and 83.8; and ROC-AUC were 64.9, 65.1, and 73.5 respectively. Ablation studies confirmed the effectiveness of each component (representation augmentation, auxiliary loss, and LLM transformation). Modality analysis showed criteria (patient eligibility) was the most important modality while drug description was least important. The SMoE analysis demonstrated that certain experts (e.g., experts 6 and 7) were consistently selected across modalities, confirming their role in extracting similar patterns. Code is released at https://github.com/shenmishajing/lifted.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"These approaches rely on manually designed modal-specific encoders, which limits both the extensibility to adapt new modalities and the ability to discern similar information patterns across different modalities."

METHODS: The researchers evaluated three LLMs—GPT-4o-mini, MedGemma-27B, and LLaMA3-70B—using a clinician-annotated benchmark dataset of 750 unique DDI scenarios spanning three levels of diagnostic complexity. Interactions were labeled using LexiDrug categories (A=no known interaction, B=no action needed, C=monitor therapy, D=consider therapy modification, X=avoid combination). Three task formats were used: (1) pointwise two-drug classification, (2) pairwise three-drug discrimination, and (3) listwise 4–6 drug selection. All cases were independently reviewed by three board-certified clinical pharmacists. Standardized zero-shot prompting with nine repeated runs (temperature=0.7) and label shuffling was used. Metrics included precision, recall, F1, accuracy, and self-consistency. Datasets are available at github.com/sikora07/AIChemist.

RESULTS: Performance varied by task structure. In the pointwise two-drug task, LLaMA3-70B had the highest recall (61.7) and F1 (59.7), while GPT-4o-mini had the highest precision (65.7). In the pairwise three-drug task, GPT-4o-mini achieved the highest accuracy (86.6), followed by MedGemma-27B (84.9) and LLaMA3-70B (81.5). In the listwise 4-6 drug task, MedGemma-27B performed best (80.0), followed by GPT-4o-mini (71.3) and LLaMA3-70B (68.6). All models performed worst on Category C (moderate-risk) interactions. Self-consistency decreased as task complexity increased, and no model showed uniformly high reliability. Notably, models failed to identify Category X (avoid combination) DDIs in 24-30% of cases. Undetected high-risk interactions included enoxaparin/alteplase (bleeding risk), sulfamethoxazole-trimethoprim/spironolactone (hyperkalemia), and dronedarone/azithromycin (QTc prolongation).

LLMs showed moderate but uneven performance, degrading with increased complexity (more medications and requiring severity specification). The authors note rules-based software (e.g., LexiDrug) performs perfectly, and emphasize that LLMs are not yet safe for routine DDI identification without clinician backup. Limitations include small dataset size by LLM standards and lack of prompt engineering or knowledge-graph augmentation. The authors call for further model improvement and multi-format, reliability-aware evaluation frameworks before clinical deployment.

--- SOURCE 12: Benchmarking Computational Methods for Emerging Drug-Drug Interaction Prediction ---
URL: https://arxiv.org/html/2410.18583v4

SUMMARY:
<summary>
## DDI-Ben: A Benchmarking Framework for Emerging Drug-Drug Interaction Prediction Under Distribution Changes

### Overview
This paper by Zhenqian Shen et al. (Tsinghua University) introduces **DDI-Ben**, a benchmarking framework for emerging drug-drug interaction (DDI) prediction that explicitly addresses distribution changes between known and new drugs—a factor neglected by current evaluation methods. The code and data are available at https://github.com/LARS-research/DDI-Bench.

### Motivation
- Emerging DDI prediction is critical for new drugs with unknown pharmacological risks, as clinical experiments are time-consuming and expensive.
- Existing DDI datasets (DrugBank, TWOSIDES) lack drug approval timeline information, making it hard to simulate realistic drug distribution changes over time.
- Current evaluation methods assume known and new drugs follow the same distribution, using unrealistic i.i.d. drug splits, which makes evaluation results questionable.

### Distribution Change Simulation Framework
The framework uses **distribution changes between drug sets as a surrogate** for real-world DDI distribution changes:
1. **Drug distribution change modeling**: Introduces a cluster-based difference measurement γ(Dk,Dn) = max{S(u,v)} based on drug similarity (Tanimoto coefficient between fingerprints). Smaller γ indicates larger distribution changes.
2. **Drug data split**: Splits drugs into known and new drug sets.

The framework defines two emerging DDI tasks:
- **S1**: Determine DDI type between a known drug and a new drug.
- **S2**: Determine DDI type between two new drugs.

### Data Split Strategies Comparison
Eight split strategies were compared (random, drug frequency, drug usage, scaffold, LoHi, SPECTRA, DataSAIL, and the proposed cluster-based split). Key findings:
- LoHi and SPECTRA discard data points (undesirable given data collection costs).
- Only SPECTRA and the **cluster-based split** enable controllable distribution changes.
- The proposed cluster-based split achieved the **highest consistency index** with realistic drug approval-time-based splits.
- Real-world drug clusters emerge from new drug safety issues (1980s NSAIDs), technological breakthroughs (1990s ACE inhibitors), and new epidemics (2010s HCV NS5A inhibitors).

### Datasets
- **DrugBank**: Multiclass dataset, 1,710 drugs, 86 interaction types, 188,509 DDI triplets.
- **TWOSIDES**: Multilabel dataset, 645 drugs, 209 DDI types (frequency 3000–6000), 116,650 DDI triplets.

### Methods Benchmarked (10 representative methods)
- **Feature-based**: MLP
- **Embedding-based**: MSTE
- **GNN-based**: Decagon, SSI-DDI, MRCGNN, EmerGNN, SAGAN
- **Graph-transformer**: TIGER
- **LLM-based**: TextDDI, DDI-GPT

### Key Results
1. **Most existing methods suffer substantial performance degradation** when distribution changes are introduced, with a more severe decline on DrugBank (harder multiclass prediction) than TWOSIDES.
2. **LLM-based methods (TextDDI, DDI-GPT) are the most robust** against distribution changes. EmerGNN performed best without distribution changes but TextDDI and DDI-GPT outperformed others under distribution changes.
3. **Textual information and LLM processing are key**: TextDDI's LLM extracts key pharmacological knowledge from raw textual data, filters irrelevant information, and enables more accurate predictions. Transferable pharmacological knowledge (e.g., Aclidinium's bronchodilatory activities, Butylscopolamine's muscarinic receptor binding) is not available in fingerprints or biomedical networks.
4. **DDI-type analysis**: MLP and MSTE rely on sufficient labeled data (good on major DDI types, poor on long-tail types). DDI-GPT significantly outperformed others on medium and long-tail DDI types under distribution changes.
5. **Controlling γ**: As distribution change increases (γ decreases), most methods' performance drops significantly; DDI-GPT remains relatively best, suggesting LLM prior knowledge and textual side information help mitigate the negative impact.

### Evaluation Metrics
- **DrugBank**: Macro F1 (primary), accuracy, Cohen's Kappa.
- **TWOSIDES**: Average ROC-AUC (primary), PR-AUC, and accuracy across DDI types.

### Conclusions & Future Work
DDI-Ben highlights the importance of explicitly addressing distribution changes in emerging DDI prediction. Future directions include designing LLM-based methods to alleviate distribution change impact and domain adaptation methods for real-world robustness.
</summary>

This is a systematic review article published in the MDPI journal *Pharmaceuticals* (2026, 19(8), 1225, DOI: 10.3390/ph19081225), titled "Graph-Based Machine Learning for Predicting Drug–Drug Interactions: A Systematic Review." It was authored by Md. Tuhin Reza, Md. Abdul Kader, Wissem Inoubli, Md. Biddut Hossain, and Md. Kamrul Islam (corresponding author), from institutions in Bangladesh (Jashore University of Science & Technology, Daffodil International University, BANBEIS) and France (University of Artois). The article was submitted June 21, 2026, revised and accepted July 31, 2026, and published August 4, 2026, and belongs to the Special Issue "Drug Safety and Real-World Evidence: From Databases to Artificial Intelligence."

**Purpose & Background:** The review evaluates graph-based machine-learning methods for predicting drug–drug interactions (DDIs), which are major medication-safety concerns. Since experimental testing cannot cover the rapidly expanding number of drug pairs, computational DDI prediction is a critical complementary strategy for prioritizing risky combinations and supporting medication-safety workflows. The review focuses on graph neural networks (GNNs) and their architectures, data integration, interpretability, reproducibility, and clinical relevance.

**Methodology:** Conducted following the PRISMA 2020 framework. Searches covered IEEE Xplore (n=74), ScienceDirect (n=96), PubMed (n=67), and Google Scholar (n=53), totaling 290 records for studies published January 2021 through March 2026. After removing duplicates and ineligible records, 60 primary studies were included. Because studies used heterogeneous datasets and methods, findings were synthesized narratively rather than statistically (no meta-analysis). Risk of bias was assessed across seven domains: data leakage, negative sampling, generalization design, baseline/ablation adequacy, reproducibility, interpretability, and clinical applicability.

**Key Results:** Sixty studies met eligibility criteria. Methods progressed from graph convolutional networks and graph attention networks to graph transformers, contrastive learning, multimodal fusion, and LLM-enhanced representations. Representative reported results include 94.47% transductive accuracy for SSI-DDI, 99.74% warm-start accuracy for DrugDAGT, and 95.43% AUROC for KnowDDI on TWOSIDES — but these are study-specific and not directly comparable. Only three studies explicitly addressed data leakage; leakage-aware drug-disjoint, temporal, and external evaluations were uncommon. Uncertainty calibration, computational-resource reporting, complete reproducibility materials, and independently validated explanations were also limited.

The review identified five principal threats to validity: (1) leakage-prone random pairwise splits; (2) incomplete or noisy labels (unobserved interactions treated as confirmed negatives); (3) limited cold-start evaluation on unseen drugs; (4) scarce temporal evaluation; and (5) limited interpretability validation. The review covers three analytical questions: (RQ1) how graph construction, data modality, and validation design influence reported performance; (RQ2) when attention and multimodal fusion add demonstrable value; (RQ3) what evidence supports translation beyond benchmark performance.

Three core modeling concepts were defined: GNN architectures, multimodal fusion (combining molecular structure, SMILES, DDI networks, knowledge graphs, side effects, targets, pathways, or text), and attention mechanisms. Attention categories identified include graph attention, cross-/co-attention, hierarchical attention, knowledge-graph attention, transformer self-attention, feature/modality weighting, and contrastive attention.

**Conclusions:** Graph-based machine learning is promising for DDI prioritization and hypothesis generation but remains insufficient for independent clinical decision-making. The review recommends future studies use standardized benchmarks, leakage-aware validation, calibrated uncertainty, reproducible pipelines, validated explanations, and external or prospective evaluation. Keywords: drug–drug interaction; graph neural network; computational pharmacology; multimodal learning; attention mechanism.
</summary>

Search results: 



--- SOURCE 1: Comparing AI Biology Foundation Models: AlphaFold 3 & ESM3 ---
URL: https://intuitionlabs.ai/articles/biology-foundation-models-comparison

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This IntuitionLabs report (published April 19, 2026) provides an in-depth comparison of AI biology foundation models for molecular biology, focusing on AlphaFold 3 (AF3), ESM-3, Boltz-2, Chai-1, and RoseTTAFold. It analyzes their architectures, training data, capabilities, quantitative benchmarks, and real-world use cases in drug discovery.

**Key Models:**
- **AlphaFold 3 (AF3)**: Released May 2024 by DeepMind/Isomorphic. Uses a generative diffusion architecture predicting full atomic structures of complexes (proteins, nucleic acids, small molecules, modified residues) in one unified model. Achieves ~76% success on PoseBusters ligand benchmark (RMSD <2Å), far surpassing physics-based docking (~30-38%). Dramatically improved protein-ligand, protein-DNA/RNA, and antibody-antigen prediction. Closed-source (free academic use only) and can "hallucinate" structure in disordered regions (mitigated via cross-distillation training).
- **ESM-3**: From EvolutionaryScale (ex-Meta researchers), mid-2024. A 98-billion-parameter multimodal protein language model, generative and autoregressive like GPT. Trained on 2.78 billion sequences (771 billion tokens) using >10^24 FLOPS. Can generate protein sequences from partial cues; demonstrated design of a novel fluorescent protein (58% identity to known GFP, representing ~500M years of natural evolution). Smallest 1.4B version open-source; larger models commercial via AWS/Nvidia.
- **Boltz-2**: Announced June 2025 by MIT Jameel Clinic. Successor to Boltz-1 with equivariant diffusion backbone plus a unique "affinity module" predicting binding strength (IC50-like). Achieves FEP-level accuracy in relative binding energies (Pearson ~0.62) while running >1000× faster than physics-based simulations. Fully open-source (MIT license). Outperformed all submissions on CASP16-style binding challenge; used to identify TYK2 inhibitors in virtual assays.
- **Chai-1**: Released September 2024 by Chai Discovery. Open-source multimodal structure predictor using protein language model embeddings and supporting experimental restraints (crosslinks, epitope maps). ~77% success on PoseBusters ligand benchmark (vs AF3's ~76%). User "steering" with contact constraints doubles antibody-antigen accuracy. Pitched as "AlphaFold 3 power without limitations" - free for non-commercial use.
- **RoseTTAFold**: Released 2021 by Baker Lab using a three-track network (1D sequences, 2D distance maps, 3D coordinates). Achieved CASP14-competitive accuracy comparable to AlphaFold 2. Openly available; "All-Atom" 2024 update weaker on ligand docking (~42% top hits vs ~76-77% for newer models) but remains a standard comparator.

**Headline Benchmark Comparison (PoseBusters protein-ligand):** Physics-based methods 38%, AlphaFold 3 76%, Chai-1 77%, RoseTTAFold All-Atom ~42%.

**Implications:** These foundation models are transforming biology, enabling routine atomistic complex prediction (proteins with drugs, DNA, membranes) in hours rather than years. Drug discovery pipelines are exploiting end-to-end AI for generative compound design and antibody maturation. Concerns include hallucination issues (AF3), dual-use risks, licensing restrictions, and computational demands. The field is evolving rapidly with iterative improvements expected.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"The new AlphaFold model demonstrates substantially improved accuracy over many previous specialized tools: far greater accuracy for protein–ligand interactions compared with state-of-the-art docking tools, much higher accuracy for protein–nucleic acid interactions… and substantially higher antibody–antigen prediction accuracy compared with AlphaFold-Multimer v2.3." (AF3 Nature paper)
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 2: A survey of downstream applications of evolutionary scale modeling protein language models ---
URL: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12806033

SUMMARY:
<summary>
A survey paper published in Quantitative Biology (2025, Vol. 14, e70013) titled "A survey of downstream applications of evolutionary scale modeling protein language models," authored by Qingyu Yang, Jiale Yu, and Jie Zheng from ShanghaiTech University and the Shanghai Engineering Research Center of Intelligent Vision and Imaging. The paper (PMCID: PMC12806033, PMID: 41676321) reviews the ESM (evolutionary scale modeling) series of protein language models (PLMs) and their downstream applications in protein science and engineering.

**ESM Model Series Overview:**
- ESM-1b: First foundational BERT-style Transformer PLM, trained via masked language modeling (MLM) on 250 million protein sequences from UniParc (43M–670M parameters)
- ESM-MSA-1b (MSA Transformer): Uses tied row/united column attention on multiple sequence alignments for structure inference (100M parameters)
- ESM-1v: Specialized for variant effect prediction (650M parameters)
- ESM-IF1 (GVP-Transformer): Combines Transformer with GVP-GNN for inverse folding/fixed-backbone design (124M parameters)
- ESM-2: SOTA general-purpose PLM, one of the most widely used foundation models in protein science (8M–15B parameters)
- ESMFold: End-to-end single-sequence 3D structure predictor, comparable to AlphaFold2 in some key scenarios, significantly faster (3.69B parameters)
- ESM3: Protein design model reasoning across sequence, structure, and function (1.4B–98B parameters)

**Advantages of ESM over other PLMs:** best or near-best performance in most scenarios; well-developed complete series covering various protein research fields; widely used as base models in other works.

**Techniques of Using ESM (5 categories):**
1. **Direct use**: ESM-IF1 for fixed-backbone design, ESMFold for structure prediction (much faster than AlphaFold2 with minor accuracy loss, excels at de novo/orphan proteins)
2. **Integration with task-specific models**: ESM embeddings combined with MLP, ML classifiers, regression models, LSTM, CNN, attention, GRU; e.g., NERE, DSMBind (binding affinity), ESMFlow (flow matching for conformational sampling)
3. **Fine-tuning**: Both full fine-tuning and parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) including adapter tuning, prompt tuning, and LoRA (most widely used; PEFT-SP showed LoRA best for signal peptide classification); also FusOn-pLM and AntiFold
4. **Multimodality**: Fusing sequence and structure information via three main approaches (ESM embeddings as GNN node features; concatenation of representations; cross-attention); contrastive learning (e.g., ConPLex, CLIP-based methods like PepPrCLIP, Cut&CLIP, CSSP); structure-aware retraining (e.g., SaProt using Foldseek's 3Di tokens); continual training (ESM-S)
5. **Attention maps and evaluation**: Attention maps used for contact map prediction; ESM used for directed evolution assistance, mutation validation, structure evaluation (e.g., self-consistency perplexity with ESM-IF1, ESMFold pLDDT/pAE scores in UCSF ChimeraX)

**Key Comparative Findings:** Among well-known PLMs, ESM and ProtT5 show best performance in different scenarios (ProtT5 slightly better overall); ESM-1b highest for "extracellular" and "golgi apparatus" localization tasks; ProteinBERT performs slightly poorer.

**Downstream Biological Applications:** ESM models capture implicit structural/evolutionary information and apply to structure prediction (fold, secondary structure via NetSurfP-3.0, contact maps, 3D structure via OmegaFold, protein complexes via Seq2Symm) and function prediction (EC/GO via SaProt and ESM-GearNet, text-defined function via ProtST, functional annotation via NetGO 3.0, localization via ProtGPS, solubility via NetSolP, homology detection via PLMSearch).

The survey analyzed approximately 100 representative papers (each cited at least five times) from papers citing at least one of the six original ESM publications.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"The evolutionary scale modeling (ESM) series is promising to revolutionize protein science and engineering through large language models (LLMs), providing a robust framework for understanding the relationships among sequences, structures, and functions of proteins."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 3: Simulating 500 million years of evolution with a language model ---
URL: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=qeqbm8a1-ZA

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a seminar presentation by Roshan Rao, PhD, of the company EvoScale, given as part of the "ML for protein engineering seminar series" (posted 17 Sep 2024, ~7308 views). The talk presents ESM3, a frontier multimodal generative language model for proteins that can reason over sequence, structure, and function. The key claims: ESM3 can act as an evolutionary simulator, generating functional proteins far from known proteins. The team prompted ESM3 to design fluorescent proteins and found a bright fluorescent protein at 58% sequence identity from known fluorescent proteins—a distance comparable to over 500 million years of natural evolution.

Key technical details:
- Architecture: A simple Transformer with tokenized input/output tracks for sequence, structure, and function, plus a geometric attention mechanism that encodes 3D coordinates in an SE(3)-invariant and efficient way. Structure is tokenized with a new VQ-VAE (each residue token represents its 16 nearest 3D neighbors) with sub-angstrom RMSD reconstruction.
- Training: Three models trained at 1.4B, 7.7B, and 98.5B parameters. Deeper (rather than wider) architectures were found to be better for proteins. Training used large amounts of metagenomic and synthetic data (found to improve performance once model scale crossed a threshold), FP8 precision, sharding over 1000+ GPUs, and various stability techniques (layer norm on queries/keys, warmup, FP32 for key ops). Optimal masking rate increased with scale (15% at 650M params, 30% at 7B).
- Alignment (DPO fine-tuning): Models are aligned by scoring generated sequences computationally (constraint site RMSD, predicted TM score) and fine-tuning with DPO; larger models respond more strongly to alignment, improving prompt-following fidelity, pTM, and generation diversity.
- Wet lab validation with GFP: ESM3 was prompted with the structure/key chromophore, generating sequences that were synthesized. After one plate experiment and diversification/refinement, a fluorescent protein with high activity and ~58% identity to wild-type GFP was obtained, including mutations in core/alpha-helix positions.

Other points covered: data valuation (PDB is highest value; sequence data scales linearly), use of temporal holdouts and MMS-seq purging to avoid leakage, removal of viruses from the open model for biosafety (internal models retain them for academic partnerships), and future directions (genomic context, protein-ligand interactions, text annotations).
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"Here we show that language models trained on tokens generated by evolution can act as evolutionary simulators to generate functional proteins that are far away from known proteins."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 4: ESM3: Simulating 500 million years of evolution with a ... ---
URL: https://www.evolutionaryscale.ai/blog/esm3-release

SUMMARY:
<summary>
EvolutionaryScale, a public benefit company, announced ESM3, a frontier language model for biology that simultaneously reasons over protein sequence, structure, and function. In a preprint (June 25, 2024) updated with publication in Science Magazine in January 2025, the company described generating a new green fluorescent protein (GFP) called esmGFP. The paper was published in Science (DOI: 10.1126/science.ads0018), and the API is now in public beta through Forge. 

KEY MODEL DETAILS:
- ESM3 is trained on billions of proteins from diverse environments (Amazon rainforest, ocean depths, hydrothermal vents, soil microbes)
- Trained with over 1x10^24 FLOPS and 98B parameters—described as the most compute ever applied to training a biological model
- An order of magnitude larger than the previous model, ESM2 (which itself scaled from ESM-1b/1v and ESM-IF1)
- Uses a masked language modeling objective, tokenizing sequence, structure, and function into discrete alphabets within a single multi-track transformer
- Augmented with hundreds of millions of synthetic data points (predicted structures and functions)
- Uses alignment methods similar to RLHF, but ESM3 can self-improve with feedback on its own generations
- Capabilities emerge with scale (e.g., atomic coordination tasks) and improve with alignment

THE esmGFP RESULT:
- Prompted only with the structure of a few residues in the core of natural GFP, ESM3 reasoned in chain-of-thought to generate candidates
- First experiment: tested 96 generations; found proteins that fluoresce, including B8 (50x less bright, chromophore matured over a week)
- Second experiment from B8: tested 96 more proteins; found esmGFP (well C10), with brightness similar to natural GFPs
- esmGFP differs by 96 mutations out of 229 amino acids (58% sequence similarity to closest known fluorescent protein)
- This corresponds to an estimated equivalent of over 500 million years of natural evolution

RESPONSIBLE DEVELOPMENT:
- Public benefit company focused on AI for human health and society
- Cites the 1975 Asilomar Conference principles as inspiration, plus new responsible biodesign principles
- Four core tenets: communicate benefits and risks, rigorously evaluate risk before public deployment, adopt risk mitigation strategies and guardrails, and work with government/policy/civil society stakeholders

OPEN MODEL:
- Committed to open science; releasing weights and code for an ESM3 1.4B open model on GitHub (github.com/evolutionaryscale/esm)
- Examples of ESM ecosystem applications cited: evolving antibodies (Hie et al. with ESM-1v/1b), COVID variant detection (BioNTech/InstaDeep), clinical mutation effect prediction (Brandes et al.), anti-CRISPR engineering (Marsiglia et al.), protein evolution guidance (Shanker et al.), enzyme function prediction (Yu et al.), single-cell foundation models (Rosen et al.), and antibody design (Høie et al.)

FUTURE DIRECTION:
- API and open model available for scientists to explore protein design and synthetic biology
- Prioritizing beta API access based on potential to expand scientific knowledge
- Developing specialized ESM3 versions for drug design
- Roadmap envisions increasingly multimodal models integrating from molecules to cells
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"ESM3 takes a step towards the future where AI is a tool to engineer biology from first principles in the same way we engineer structures, machines and microchips, and write computer programs."
</key_excerpts>
